16191-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Number fifty-six of The Great Round World, dated December 2, 1897, reports a gallant deed on India's frontier. Soldiers of the Northamptonshire regiment marched to the summit of Saran Sar. They sought to learn whether Afridi forces camped nearby. They found a hastily vacated camp and sensed the enemy on the mountain with them. Fearing an ambush, their commander ordered a retreat, and the tribesmen appeared almost at once.

The children's paper tells the skirmish in short, admiring sentences, turning frontier war into a tale of courage and quick judgment. Young readers could follow Britain's Indian campaigns without adult jargon. The number keeps a young reader's record of empire, soldiering, and danger on the North-West Frontier.
16811-gurre-kamilaroi-or-kamilaroi-sayin:
William Ridley, a missionary, put out this 1856 Sydney book of Kamilaroi sayings, with cuts by W. Mason. It prints the sounds of the tongue, lists of words for kin, beasts, and things, and short sayings in Kamilaroi with a Bible verse as its motto. The Empire steam press printed it at George Street.

Ridley aimed to set down a living Aboriginal tongue before it faded, in a form mission folk and learners could use. Word lists and sayings give a glimpse of how Kamilaroi speakers named kin, land, and sky. The book now stands as an early record of an Australian language, valued by linguists and by descendants seeking old words.
25852-the-letters-of-charles-dickens-vol:
Charles Dickens speaks here in his own letters from 1833 to 1856, chosen by his sister-in-law Georgina Hogarth and his eldest daughter Mamie Dickens. The editors meant the set to fill a gap in John Forster's life of Dickens, which had room for few letters beyond those sent to Forster himself. Friends, kin, and fellow writers all lent letters for the book.

Read in order, the letters show a young writer growing into a famous man, with jokes, gripes, travel plans, and stage work mixed in. Early notes often carry only the day of the week, a loose habit Dickens dropped in later life, when his dates grew full and exact. The volume ends in 1856, still in the thick of his working years.
4642-the-vigilance-committee-of-1856:
James O'Meara, a pioneer California journalist, wrote The Vigilance Committee of 1856 from outside both camps. He says many accounts have been published, but all he has seen came from members of that organisation, or from persons who favoured it. As a result their accounts were partial to a greater or lesser degree, or imperfect otherwise, with much omitted, misstated, and misrepresented.

O'Meara was neither a member of the Vigilance Committee nor of the opposing Law and Order body, headed by General Sherman with Volney E. Howard next in rank. He never favoured mob or lynch law in any form, and so had neither sympathy nor disposition to join the committee. Yet he earnestly supported Law and Order, though he felt joining its organisation would not best serve that cause. Readers get a critical, independent history of San Francisco's vigilante year.
a-woman-of-thirty-pg4556: Marjorie Allen Seiffert's 1919 verse collection opens with The Old Woman, a morality play in which a doctor, a deacon and a landlady debate a woman who ought to die. Love poems, studies and designs follow, from Singalese love songs and a Taj Mahal evening to portraits, a police-station sketch and autumn elegies. Ageing, love, loss and the everyday sit at the centre of the book.
ady-candle-in-the-dark-english-1656:
Thomas Ady published A Candle in the Dark in 1656, in the middle of England's witch-hunting years. His treatise argues that most witchcraft charges rest on delusion, fraud, and wretched evidence. Ady writes as a Christian who believes Scripture, rightly read, condemns the accusers rather than the accused.

He takes apart the tests and tales used to hang supposed witches. Old women, melancholy, and spite make poor proof of a pact with the devil, he shows. His candle metaphor promises light in a dark business. The book is a brave plea for reason and mercy. It stands among the key English voices against the persecution.
arxiv-2509-00256:
Yutong Wang and Cindy Rubio-González present LLM4FP in 2025, a framework that uses language models to generate programs that expose floating-point inconsistencies across compilers. Floating-point arithmetic rounds real numbers, and distinct compilers can round differently, which undermines numerical software. Finding programs that trigger such gaps is key to testing.

Grammar-based generation and feedback-based mutation jointly produce diverse, valid programs. Across compilers and optimization levels, LLM4FP detects nearly two and a half times more inconsistencies than the prior best tool, Varity. Most gaps involve ordinary real values, not extreme cases like NaN or infinities. The widest mismatch appears between host and device compilers. Language-model guidance widens compiler testing coverage.
arxiv-2509-00456:
Weitang Li, Jiajun Ren, and Jun Yan compare two tensor network methods for nonadiabatic dynamics of exciton dissociation in 2025. Tensor networks compress quantum states efficiently; matrix product states form a chain, while tree tensor network states branch like a tree. Both are exact in the limit of large bond dimension, a size parameter, yet a prior study found a notable discrepancy between them.

Using the Renormalizer software, the team revisits a benchmark polymer-fullerene junction model. The discrepancy traces mainly to insufficient bond dimensions in the earlier work. Raising them cuts the relative difference in occupancy for weakly populated states from up to sixty percent to under ten percent. The study restores trust in both methods for exciton dynamics.
arxiv-2509-00556:
Kariane Calta leads a team of five authors on affine equivalence. Two sets are affinely equivalent if an affine map sends one to the other. An affine map shifts and stretches by linear rules. The team works with sets of binary strings of fixed length. They ask for a simple test for this equivalence.

Calta and her team build a Venn diagram for each set. The diagram comes from a basis of the set's affine span. Any basis gives the same diagram, up to region order. Two sets are equivalent just when a size-preserving reorder links their diagrams. They use this test to classify certain Sidon sets. Sidon sets are sets with distinct pairwise sums.
arxiv-2509-00656:
Shu-Hua Yang and one co-author, Fridolin Weber, argue that the compact star XTE J1814-338 can be explained as a strange star mixed with bosonic dark matter. A strange star is a dense star made of strange quark matter, and bosonic dark matter is unseen matter whose particles carry whole-number spin.

Yang and Weber show the explanation works provided the dark matter fraction exceeds about seventy percent. That condition yields a robust bound on the dark matter particle mass, tied to a dimensionless coupling constant that measures interaction strength. The bound does not depend on how the star formed or on microphysical details, and future observations by NICER and by LIGO and Virgo can test the claim.
arxiv-2509-00756:
Xixiang Zhang leads a team of six authors on oxidation of a thin oxide layer. The layer is a two-dimensional germanium dioxide monolayer. Oxides of this kind resist oxidation far better than most thin materials. The atomic reasons for that resistance were not clear. The team set out to find them.

First-principles calculations show the pristine layer repels oxygen molecules. Surface oxygen ions push them away by electric force. That blocks chemisorption, the bonding of oxygen to the surface. A layer with oxygen vacancies is weaker. Oxygen fills a vacancy at low energy cost. Yet splitting that molecule faces a higher barrier. Oxidation thus limits itself. The team also reports pressure and temperature effects. Their findings guide design of stable nanoelectronic devices.
arxiv-2509-00856:
A I Komech and E A Kopylova consider dissipation operators in quantum optics. These operators describe quantum spontaneous emission. Emission is the process by which an excited system sheds energy as light. Their setting is the damped driven Jaynes-Cummings equations. Those equations describe a one-mode light field coupled to a two-level molecule.

The main result concerns the basic dissipation operator of the field. Komech and Kopylova establish its symmetry. They also establish its nonpositivity. Nonpositivity means it does not increase a key quadratic quantity. Such properties matter for long-time behavior of quantum states. They shape how states decay and are driven over time. They also bear on the validity of equations used across quantum optics.
arxiv-2509-00956:
Riccardo Cescon, with two co-authors, studies robust linear quadratic control under unknown noise. The linear quadratic Gaussian regulator is a cornerstone of control theory. Its performance can degrade when noise deviates from the assumed model. The team proposes a robust generalization for finite horizons.

Noise laws are unknown within sets built around a nominal Gaussian. Those sets use an entropy-regularized Wasserstein distance as their radius. The team derives novel bounds on this Sinkhorn discrepancy. They prove structural traits of the sets that result. From those results, global optimality of linear policies follows. Numerical tests showcase improved robustness of the policy. Control stays sound when the true noise shifts away from nominal.
arxiv-2509-01056:
Xiao-Wu Chen and Zhengfang Wang study a branch of algebra that deals with modules, which are broad versions of vector spaces over a ring. They look at what happens when a module class is stabilized, meaning some maps are formally flipped so they can run both ways. The ring in their work is artinian, a type with a strong finiteness trait.

Chen and Wang show the stabilized class forms a Frobenius category, a setting with good duality traits. It matches the class of finitely presented modules over part of a Leavitt ring. From this they prove that a related object, the singularity category of the first ring, matches the stable module class of the second. The result ties two areas of algebra together.
arxiv-2509-01156:
Shocks in one market often spill into others, but noisy price data can hide those links. Abdullah Karasan and Ozge Sezgin Alp use a neural network to clean return and volatility data before measuring spillovers across markets. Their study covers developed and developing economies and key asset classes from late 2014 to mid 2025.

After cleaning the covariance matrices, the pair tracked spillovers in both fixed and time-varying frames. Developed markets mostly sent volatility shocks outward in calm times, yet became receivers during stress such as the Covid-19 pandemic. Developing markets switched roles more often and less steadily. Karasan and Alp argue that denoising first gives a clearer, sharper picture of how risk travels between markets.
arxiv-2509-01656:
Visual reasoning needs both sharp perception and sound logic, and giving language models access to vision tools is one route to it. Zetong Zhou, with eight co-authors, proposes ReVPT, a method that teaches multimodal models to reason with a suite of four visual tools through reinforcement learning. Earlier attempts used supervised fine-tuning, which needed costly data generation, careful filtering, and generalized poorly.

A new reinforcement learning algorithm, based on a group-relative method, trains the model to choose and use the tools. Experiments show state-of-the-art results on several perception-heavy benchmarks, beating supervised and text-only reinforcement baselines. Their three and seven billion parameter versions improved over their instruct counterparts by about nine points each on one benchmark. The work shows tool use itself can be learned by reward, not only by example.
arxiv-2509-02156:
Asif Mohammed Saad and Umme Niraj Mahi fine-tune a SegFormer model with dropout to remove hair artifacts from skin lesion images. Hair strands in dermoscopic photos can hide diagnostic features and mislead analysis. Their segmentation model isolates hair masks precisely so lesions can be cleaned. Dropout regularization, randomly muting units in training, guards against overfitting on a modest dataset.

Training uses hundreds of annotated dermoscopic images with repeated cross validation across folds. Optimization and early stopping follow a careful schedule per fold. Scores for overlap, similarity, and perceptual quality all come out strong in validation. High Dice and overlap values show accurate hair masks. Cleaner inputs should improve downstream skin cancer detection pipelines.
arxiv-2509-02456:
Galina Weinstein wrote a 2025 history of physics paper. It rebuilds the hidden working behind Einstein's 1905 paper on special relativity. The printed text shows a clean chain of equations. Most of the algebra that supports them stays out of sight.

Weinstein argues the spareness was a choice, not a limit. Einstein used modest tools. He leaned on algebra, Taylor expansions, and symmetry claims. Two postulates and clear definitions did the heavy lifting, not the dense machinery of electron theory. A closing contrast with Poincaré sharpens the point. Poincaré was a French thinker working on linked ideas at the same time. The paper restores the scaffolding behind a famously lean presentation.
arxiv-2509-02556:
Gaurab Kumar Dash, Subhendu Kumar Patra, Diptiman Sen, and Manisha Thakurathi present a 2025 condensed matter paper on periodically driven open quantum systems inside optical microcavities. Driving can create Floquet exceptional points, special parameter spots where states merge.

Using a quench protocol that jumps parameters in a cycle, the authors derive an effective Floquet Hamiltonian and locate several exceptional points inside its bands. Pairs of these points can be created or destroyed by tuning. Integer winding numbers label the zero and pi varieties robustly. A new fidelity measure, adapted to non-Hermitian systems, spikes exactly at those points and diverges when their count changes. The driven model also hosts edge states and a skin effect of higher order, where modes pile up at edges and corners.
arxiv-2509-02856:
Syomantak Chaudhuri and Thomas A. Courtade wrote a 2025 paper on privacy when people get to choose how strongly their data is protected. Standard methods often assume that what a person's data says has nothing to do with how much privacy that person wants. The authors show that this tidy assumption can break down.

They propose a new framework whose name shortens to AHDP. It tracks data and privacy wishes together, so links between the two cannot quietly weaken protection. They explain its promises through a testing lens, asking how well an outsider could tell two cases apart. They also build simple tools for averages, counts, and straight-line fits. Tests on computer-made data show the trade-offs involved.
arxiv-2509-02956:
Hai N. Ngo and 11 co-authors revisited a 2025 measurement of the giant black hole in the galaxy NGC 7052. They used ALMA, a large radio telescope array in Chile, to watch cold molecular gas swirling near the galaxy's center. Gas speeds reveal how much gravity, and so how much mass, sits in the middle.

Their model puts the black hole at roughly two and a half billion times the Sun's mass. That agrees with an earlier estimate, even though the new images are less sharp and still resolve the zone where the black hole's gravity dominates. The starlight part of the model changed more: including spread-out stars and the gas itself lowered the inferred mass-to-light ratio by about a tenth.
arxiv-2509-03056:
Sahil Rajesh Dhayalkar built a 2025 graph-based picture of how deep ReLU networks behave. A ReLU is a simple switch-like function used in most neural networks. It splits the input space into regions where the network acts as one plain linear rule.

In his transition graph, each region becomes a node, and regions differing by one flipped switch are linked by an edge. He proves that graphs from random starting networks spread connections widely, with predictable degree patterns and spectral traits. Small real networks matched those predictions when he built their graphs. Measures like region entropy and spectral gap tied to how well networks generalize, meaning perform on new data. The framework offers new ways to diagnose and improve such models.
arxiv-2509-03156:
Yan Lyu reviewed recent progress in 2025 on how charmed hadrons interact, as computed with lattice QCD. Hadrons are particles built from quarks, and charmed ones contain a heavy charm quark. Exotic states discovered in experiments, with names like Tcc and Pc, have made these interactions urgent to understand.

Lattice QCD simulates the strong force on a space-time grid, giving a reliable handle on low-energy behavior that formulas alone cannot reach. The review focuses on three representative pairings: two well-known charm mesons, a nucleon beside a hidden-charm system, and two triple-charm baryons. Each case shows what the lattice method can now say about attraction, binding, and scattering. The talk format makes it a guided tour of a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2509-03456:
Imad Aouali and one co-author contributed a 2025 research paper on off-policy learning, where a decision rule is learned from logged data instead of fresh trials. Their setting is offline contextual bandits with many possible actions. The paper questions a common focus on building ever better value estimators.

Theory and experiments together show that current methods often fail mainly during optimisation, especially as action counts grow. Shaping the policy form around the estimator helps, but does not remove the difficulty. Simpler weighted log-likelihood goals, which score past actions by their rewards, optimise far more smoothly. Those simpler goals still produce competitive policies, and often better ones, so optimisation deserves equal attention.
arxiv-2509-03756: Mehmet Sengonul's 2025 mathematics paper takes up Riesz means for sequences whose values are uncertain. Riesz means are weighted averages used to judge whether a series settles down. Their Tauberian properties state when one kind of convergence forces another. They come from uncertainty theory, a framework for quantities not known exactly. The paper studies how those ideas interact for such sequences. It reports several notable properties of the means in this setting.
arxiv-2509-03856:
X. Y. Sun and one co-author focus on shielding geometric quantum computation from decoherence without encoding logical qubits in a 2025 research paper. A geometric phase records the path a quantum system traces, not the timing details, which already gives geometric gates some robustness against control errors. Dynamical decoupling, pulses that average away environmental noise, can add more resilience.

Older protected schemes encoded each logical qubit into several physical ones, inflating hardware and complicating control of the logical operations. The new scheme protects physical qubits directly, skipping that overhead. It also handles a qubit's interaction with its surroundings fully, so it counters ordinary decoherence broadly rather than only dephasing, the narrow noise type most schemes address. Cheaper protection with wider coverage is the claim. The authors present the proposal as a more realistic route to geometric control that survives a noisy environment.
arxiv-2509-03956:
In a 2025 research paper, Minjong Yoo and three co-authors examine WorMI, a framework that implants world models into embodied artificial intelligence agents at test time. Embodied agents, like household robots, struggle to adapt to new domains without fresh data collection or retraining. A world model predicts how an environment responds to actions, and different domains need different ones.

WorMI composes a large language model's reasoning with world models learned independently for specific domains, attached only when needed and removable afterwards. Relevant models are retrieved by matching abstract trajectory representations, using prototypes for efficiency. A compound attention method, applied world by world, fuses the retrieved knowledge into the agent's policy and aligns internal representations. Policies thus gain domain knowledge without permanent retraining. On two household-task benchmarks, VirtualHome and ALFWorld, WorMI beats several language-model approaches in zero-shot and few-shot tests across unseen domains.
arxiv-2509-04156:
Serhii Svystun and four co-authors combine two detection models to find damage on wind turbines from drone images in a 2025 research paper. Drones carrying both ordinary and heat-sensing cameras can inspect blades and towers cheaply. Single models miss some flaws, though, since cracks show in visible light while other faults glow in thermal views. Their ensemble, meaning a team of models, pairs a general YOLOv8 detector with a specialist thermal one.

A fusion step merges the two models' marked boxes into one verdict. Scores on standard accuracy measures beat the single general model in tests. Gains were modest but consistent across visible and thermal defects. Maintenance crews could catch more damage per flight with such paired scanning.
arxiv-2509-04356:
Atikkhan Faridkhan Nilgar and two co-authors present an open-source toolkit for prototyping social robot characters in a 2025 research paper. The Wizard of Oz method lets a hidden human, or here a language model, drive a character while researchers test interactions. Their web toolkit, SRWToolkit, runs language models locally on the device instead of in the cloud. Visitors can talk by typing, pressing a speech button, or using a wake word, while a control panel adjusts appearance, behavior, language, and voice in real time.

Eleven participants built roles such as driving assistant, mathematics teacher, and hospital receptionist. Ratings for usability, trust, and experience came out positive. Human-robot interaction studies can spin up custom avatars quickly.
arxiv-2509-04556:
Jacopo Gliozzi and two co-authors derive how slowly patterned domains grow when higher quantities are conserved in a 2025 physics paper. After a sudden cooling into an ordered phase, patches of the Ising model normally grow with a square-root time law. Conserving the order parameter itself slows growth to a cube-root law. Fractonic systems, where particles move only under strict rules, conserve higher multipole moments tied to the order parameter, and that changes everything.

Analysis and simulation agree: conserving the m-th multipole moment yields growth following a one-over-two-m-plus-three exponent. Each conservation law thus brings its own dynamical critical exponent, forming a cascade. Each case forms its own universality family under non-equilibrium rules, giving fracton physics a tidy growth chart.
arxiv-2509-04956:
Hadron mass patterns can be worked backwards to reveal the field that confines quarks. Miguel Angel Martin Contreras and one co-author develop that inverse approach in a 2025 holographic quantum chromodynamics paper. Starting from a general form for nonlinear radial Regge trajectories, they apply a classic inversion formula to derive the large-distance behaviour of the confining potential.

The potential implies a non-quadratic dilaton profile whose parameters are fixed by the spectral parameters. Fitting heavy quarkonium spectra gives good agreement with experimental data. They extend the framework to tetraquark states by adding a diquark-based potential term, covering exotic hadrons as well.
arxiv-2509-05056:
Language models can be trained by gradually unmasking text rather than writing it left to right. Despoina Kosmopoulou, lead author with four co-authors, present a masked diffusion framework for data-efficient training in a 2025 paper. Their entry targets a challenge that limits how much training text models may use.

Frequency-informed masking prioritises learning from rare tokens while keeping the training objective theoretically valid. The team also explore noise schedules and weighting schemes inside the objective. On a benchmark suite measuring linguistic competence, world knowledge, and human-likeness, their results compete with hybrid baselines. They present diffusion training as a viable alternative under strict data limits.
arxiv-2509-05156:
Placing matter inside an optical cavity can shift its ground-state energy even without any light shining. Oleg V. Kotov, lead author with three co-authors, build a theory for that cavity effect in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Their model rests on Lifshitz's theory of vacuum energy and a Lorentz description of the material response.

The nonperturbative model includes infinitely many cavity modes with a continuum of wavevectors. It differs from the commonly used single-mode Hamiltonian picture. The authors show nonresonant polaritons matter for the shift, which is mainly caused by static screening at very low frequencies. Losses and temperature can be added straightforwardly.
arxiv-2509-05256:
Editing one sound inside a busy recording is the task taken up by Daniel P. W. Ellis and nine co-authors in a 2025 audio paper presenting Recomposer. Real sound scenes overlap in time, so deleting or fixing a single event without harming the rest is hard.

Recomposer takes a written edit request, such as enhancing a door sound, plus a graphic timeline showing when each event occurs. A transformer model works on compressed audio codes and was trained on synthetic pairs made by adding isolated sounds to dense real backgrounds. Tests show each part of the request, the action, the sound type, and the timing, matters for good edits.
arxiv-2509-05356:
Spiking neural networks, whose units fire in brief pulses like real neurons, are trained to steer robot arms by Justus Huebotter and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. Such networks have mostly served classification, leaving continuous motor control largely untested.

Their predictive framework trains a forward model of the arm's dynamics together with a policy network, using smooth stand-ins for the spiking gradients. Tasks include a flat reaching test and a simulated six-joint industrial arm under torque control. The spiking system matched ordinary recurrent baselines while using far fewer parameters. Studies of starting values, time constants, thresholds, and compression showed which choices keep training stable.
arxiv-2509-05756:
A detector falling through empty space heats up as if in a warm bath, and Zihao Wang with six co-authors trace that heating in a 2025 quantum thermodynamics paper. The Unruh effect says an accelerating detector sees the vacuum as thermal, and its path to equilibrium depends on what fields it couples to and the dimension of space-time.

Using coherence and heat as process measures, the authors follow distinct paths across the detector's state sphere. They propose heating and cooling protocols and find a Mpemba-like effect, where heating outruns cooling in a fidelity-based distance. A maximum fidelity difference cleanly separates Unruh heating from ordinary bath heating, a possible hallmark for future experiments.
arxiv-2509-05956:
A shopping problem where you pay to learn an item's size inspires Pandora's Knapsack, introduced in a 2025 paper led by Zohar Barak with five co-authors. The problem merges stochastic knapsack, where item sizes are random but known in distribution, with Pandora's box, where opening a box costs money and only then reveals what is inside. Here, size appears only after paying to open.

The authors ask how well simple decision policies can do. Adding opening costs, they show, changes the landscape completely: near-optimal policies must be sophisticated both in what they know and in how they adapt. With full distributional knowledge and a little extra adaptivity, a constant-factor approximation returns. One quantity, return on investment, smoothly governs how simple policies perform, and it also exactly captures the adaptivity gap in the classic Pandora's box problem.
arxiv-2509-06156:
Large well-behaved subspaces hiding inside wild sets are the quarry of spaceability research, and Manuel Saavedra and Manuel Stadlbauer give it a structural treatment in a 2025 paper on linear dynamics. For an operator T they define a set of operators h that T's iterates approximate along some of its steps on a dense set of points. Hypercyclic and recurrent subspaces, two classic effects, both emerge from this one construction.

To analyze the set, the authors introduce collections approximated at once by T and show every maximal such collection forms a closed affine manifold. For quasi-rigid operators a unique maximal collection contains the identity. Their tools refine earlier recurrent-subspace techniques and yield new spaceability results for several related sets. The search is for order inside sets that seem to have none.
arxiv-2509-06556:
Faster time stepping for heat-like equations is offered by Subhankar Nandi and one co-author in a 2025 numerical analysis paper. The equations are linear parabolic partial differential equations, which describe spreading processes such as heat flow. The classic Crank-Nicolson method is simple and stable but only modestly accurate in time.

The new schemes add radial basis function interpolation, a way of fitting smooth curves through points, and tune a shape parameter to raise accuracy. Analysis shows the methods are always at least as accurate as the classic scheme, and a simple parameter choice gains two extra orders of accuracy. Stability stays much the same. One-dimensional tests under varied boundary conditions confirm the theory, and with a good starting step the schemes rival far costlier implicit methods at a fraction of the computing cost.
arxiv-2509-06756:
Decoding quantum error correction codes while learning from the errors themselves is the advance claimed by Yi Tian and three co-authors in a 2025 quantum computing paper. Surface codes are a leading route to fault-tolerant quantum machines. Their decoders must model real hardware noise, where bit flips and phase flips often arrive correlated.

The new decoder iteratively reweights a minimum-weight matching: patterns of detected faults reveal correlated events, and their conditional probabilities update the weights on two matching lattices. The authors prove the procedure ends in finite time and keeps the code's distance guarantee. Under circuit-level noise, logical error rates fell by more than twentyfold in favorable settings, and the accuracy threshold rose noticeably. Extrapolations suggest far fewer physical qubits would be needed for a target reliability than with the standard decoder.
arxiv-2509-07456:
Sai Siddhartha Chary Aylapuram and 2 co-authors test whether machine unlearning can make vision models fairer in a 2025 paper. Neural networks often lean on spurious correlations, shortcuts in the training data, which produce biased predictions in sensitive fields like medicine and driving. Unlearning, which removes the influence of chosen data after training, offers a fix without retraining from scratch.

The authors selectively forget biased samples or feature representations and try several strategies, including gradient ascent, LoRA, and teacher-student distillation. Three benchmarks cover pose bias in bird photos, a synthetic patch bias, and gender bias in smile detection. Unlearning cut subgroup gaps sharply, with demographic parity gains up to about 95 to 97 percent on two datasets, at minimal accuracy cost. The work frames controlled forgetting as a practical fairness tool.
arxiv-2509-07556:
Cheuk Fung Lau, writing alone in 2025, proves an asymptotic formula for a smoothed shifted convolution of divisor functions. Divisor functions count how many ways a number can be built from divisors, generalized here to a family indexed by k. A shifted convolution adds products of such counts at arguments offset by a shift, and smoothing weights the sum to make it tractable. Sums like these encode deep information about the distribution of integers.

The formula comes with a power-saving error term, meaning the error shrinks by a definite power, and crucially the saving does not depend on k. For sufficiently large k, the result improves on a 2018 theorem of Topacogullari. Uniform control as the family grows is the kind of technical gain that analytic number theorists build on for later counting problems.
arxiv-2509-07656:
Bidyut Hazarika and 1 co-author treat black holes as bifurcation points in a 2025 paper on black hole thermodynamics. Bifurcation theory, borrowed from nonlinear dynamics, studies how a system's stable states appear, vanish, or swap stability as a parameter changes. Black holes have a thermodynamics of their own, with temperature and entropy, and they transition between phases much like ordinary matter.

By constructing a suitable bifurcating function, the authors track how the number and stability of fixed points change. Stable fixed points correspond to thermodynamically stable black hole states; unstable ones signal instability and decay. The system's dynamical evolution backs the reading: stable configurations settle toward equilibrium while unstable ones diverge from it. The dynamical lens offers a fresh way to classify black hole phases without solving the full gravitational problem.
arxiv-2509-08156:
Fairness in automated decisions is not one rule but many, and the rules often conflict. Swati Swati and 3 co-authors present MMM-fair in a 2025 research paper. MMM-fair is an open-source toolkit for exploring trade-offs among multiple fairness definitions at once. Intersectional bias, harm affecting people at the overlap of several traits, makes the problem harder still.

The toolkit uses boosting-based ensembles that adjust model weights to cut errors and fairness violations together. Users can define custom fairness constraints and explore the trade-off frontier interactively. A no-code, chat-based interface and language-model explanations keep it usable by non-specialists. The system also ships deployment-ready models. The authors argue that regulators and builders need this kind of hands-on tool, because fairness choices are context decisions, not purely technical ones.
arxiv-2509-08256:
Huge optimisation problems are shrunk into well-chosen subspaces by Yitong He and Pengcheng Xie in a 2025 optimisation paper. Local approximation subspace methods attack problems too large for direct solvers, a bottleneck across machine learning and scientific computing. The craft lies in picking subspaces that capture where progress actually happens.

New model-driven subspaces are introduced, and an algorithm built on them, called MD-LAMBO, is analysed in full: subspace properties, guaranteed function decrease, and global convergence. Model construction works even without derivatives. Responsible claims about a new optimiser require exactly this package of theory plus tests, because large-scale users cannot afford methods that stall silently on their most expensive problems.
arxiv-2509-08456:
A black hole's response to a magnetic field is captured by one number, its gyromagnetic factor, and that number changes with dimension. Claudio Gambino, Fabio Riccioni, and Victor Sanz Sanchis compute it from scattering amplitudes in a 2025 research paper. Their method rebuilds classic black hole spacetimes from the classic limit of quantum scattering sums. A non-minimal coupling term lets the factor vary freely.

Working at first post-Minkowskian order, the team derives the metric and electromagnetic potential for charged, rotating holes. They recover the known Kerr-Newman solution in four dimensions. They also recover a five-dimensional supergravity solution with a Chern-Simons term. For rotating charged holes in more dimensions, the factor takes a simple value set by the dimension count. Only in ordinary spacetime of four dimensions does minimal coupling suffice, a neat fact about gravity's structure.
arxiv-2509-08556:
Giuseppe Del Vecchio Del Vecchio and 1 co-author study first detection of quantum states in a 2025 paper. A fully connected quantum system evolves while random projective measurements check for a target subspace. The question is how long detection takes on average.

Exact formulas are derived for the mean first detection time and for the full probability distribution. Both depend on the starting state and on how often measurements occur. Exact counting of possible paths agrees fully with the formulas. The results give a precise picture of monitored quantum dynamics. They matter for search and control tasks where timing of a first hit is central.
arxiv-2509-08656:
Jiaqin He and 2 co-authors analyze underwater noise from marine energy converters in a 2025 paper. Licensing for sound emissions is a major barrier for tidal power projects. Too much noise can harm marine mammals, yet cutting output can hurt a project.

A computer model of a tidal converter tests two levels of response. Changing generator design to direct drive removes mechanical tonal noise and lowers sound levels. Lowering switching frequency, by contrast, raises electrical losses sharply with little acoustic gain. For geared systems, a small tuning change cuts risk to mammals with a modest energy loss. The authors propose matching the fix to site sensitivity.
arxiv-2509-08956:
Luke Snow and 1 co-author study multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning for detecting coordinated behavior in a 2025 paper. Inverse learning tries to recover utility functions, the goals agents act on, from observed decisions. Pareto-efficient means no agent can gain without another losing.

Necessary and sufficient conditions tell when noisy data fit Pareto-efficient coordination. An optimal detector minimizes false alarm error for that question. A second algorithm estimates utilities with the smallest worst case error over a set of plausible distributions. That robust form matters in adversarial settings. A radar example with several drones illustrates detection and utility recovery.
arxiv-2509-09156:
M. Ablikim and colleagues report observing a rare decay of the psi(3686) particle in a 2025 paper. The study uses a huge sample of psi(3686) events collected with the BESIII detector in China. The decay chain passes through eta(1405) and f0(980) states.

The eta(1405) decay to f0(980) plus a neutral pion is observed for the first time in psi(3686) decays via a photon. A product branching fraction, the share of decays following this exact chain, is measured. A related isospin violating decay is also seen with modest significance. No eta_c signal appears, so upper limits are set for those channels at ninety percent confidence.
arxiv-2509-09356:
A robot exploring an unknown building should head for the interesting rooms, not wander at random. Its small onboard policy cannot reason like a person, though. Abdel Hakim Drid and 3 co-authors give such agents a layered way to ask for help, in a 2025 research paper. Their deep reinforcement learning architecture targets resource-efficient semantic exploration.

A vision-language model supplies common-sense guidance, but querying it costs resources. The design makes the query a deliberate action the agent learns to use sparingly. A layered reward function carries the model's advice into learning. A curriculum strategy raises task complexity gradually for stable training. In experiments, the agent discovered objects at much higher rates. It learned to navigate toward semantically rich areas and to ask for guidance mainly when it paid. The method offers a practical route to self-guided exploration robots.
arxiv-2509-09756:
Caner Tanış proposes another new probability distribution in this solo 2025 paper, this time a record-based transmuted version of the Chen distribution. The construction uses the distributions of the first two upper record values, giving a three-parameter model for lifetime and failure data. The paper derives its quantile function, hazard function, median, moments, and ordering properties.

Nine well-known estimators are set against each other in a broad simulation study to see which recovers the parameters best. Two real data examples, one on failure times and one on iron sheet data, are used to compare the new model with competing distributions. The study is offered as a practical alternative for analysts whose data the standard Chen form fits poorly.
arxiv-2509-10256:
Young stars in the Ophiuchus cloud are blowing outflows into ultraviolet light, and I. M. Skretas and nine co-authors map that scene in this 2025 astronomy paper. Using mid-infrared spectral maps from the James Webb Space Telescope, they study five low-mass protostars still in their main growth phase. Their goal is to trace glowing hydrogen and charged atoms inside the jets and learn how outside radiation shapes the shocks there.

Four of the five stars show strong emission tied to their outflows. The hydrogen lines reveal two gas components, one moderately warm and one much hotter. Models suggest a mix of shock types can explain the data, but only when ultraviolet irradiation is included. Since excitation looks similar across the cloud, the radiation probably comes from inside each system.
arxiv-2509-10356:
Constrained guessing is the problem Yinzhuang Yi, Jorge Cortés, and Nikolay Atanasov solve in this 2025 paper on variational inference, a method that approximates a probability distribution with a simpler one. Sometimes the approximation must obey equality or inequality constraints, and enforcing them cleanly has been awkward.

Their idea borrows from control theory: a barrier functional on the space of densities encodes the constraints, and the Liouville equation connects changes in the density to how its sample particles drift. Turning that link into control barrier functions yields a safe particle flow, a moving swarm of particles whose limiting density respects the constraints by construction. The method comes with guarantees that constraints hold, and simulations show the flow behaving as promised.
arxiv-2509-10556:
Nina Wiedemann and twelve co-authors report a prospective clinical study of AI for lung ultrasound in this 2025 medical paper, called COVID-BLUeS. Lung ultrasound is light and non-invasive, but reading it takes time and expertise, and earlier AI results rested on poor training data. The team collected recordings from sixty-three COVID-19 suspects at Maastricht University Medical Centre, scanning six body locations and labeling severity by hand.

Human severity labels barely separated positive from negative patients. Image-based AI still identified infections with sixty-five percent accuracy when applied cold, and up to seventy-nine percent after targeted training, while models combining images with blood counts did significantly better. The authors blame dataset differences, frame-by-frame processing that ignores video, and weak multimodal design for the gap against earlier hype, and they publish their dataset for others.
arxiv-2509-10756:
Amanuel Anteneh estimates quantum parameters with neural network ensembles in this solo 2025 paper. Measuring a quantum system's properties from a continuous data stream is vital in the lab. Bayesian methods report uncertainty naturally, but they are slow. Plain machine learning is fast, yet silent about how confident it is.

Deep ensembles recover both speed and candor. Several networks are trained to disagree honestly. Anteneh shows that tuning for accuracy and for well-calibrated uncertainty together does not cost accuracy. The ensembles also flag when data drift away from training conditions. Inference runs far faster than Bayesian methods, whether likelihood-based or likelihood-free. The pitch is practical: real-time quantum measurements, with error bars an experimenter can trust.
arxiv-2509-10856:
G. S. Karapetian and 4 co-authors report a pattern in Milky Way star motions in this 2025 paper, offered as a possible clue to a puzzle from the James Webb Space Telescope. Webb has found massive, mature galaxies very soon after the Big Bang, sooner than standard models expect. The authors test whether our own galaxy's center shows signs of outward activity that could speed galaxy growth.

Using Gaia data, they averaged the radial motions of stars along the galaxy's south-north axis at fifty points on each side of the center. Northern stars drift one way, southern stars the other, in a near mirror pattern the authors read as expansion of the central region. They stress the interpretation is preliminary and needs further study.
arxiv-2509-11356:
Saad Eddine Baddis and four co-authors study an exotic black hole in this 2025 gravitation paper. The object is a charged anti-de Sitter black hole of Reissner-Nordström type. It sits in a noncommutative spacetime. A cloud of strings dresses it. So does quintessence, a dark-energy-like field.

The authors check the black hole's stability first. Global and local stability both get examined. They then study its critical behavior. Joule-Thomson expansion responses are computed too. Critical universal numbers shift with the quintessence parameter. The shift follows a tidy pattern. Van der Waals-like behavior returns under a charge constraint. The paper closes with light bending. It computes how light deflects in this modified geometry.
arxiv-2509-11656:
Jonas Becker and five co-authors release a workbench for studying AI debates. This 2025 artificial intelligence paper treats multi-agent debate. Several language model agents argue toward an answer. Joint debate can beat a single model. Past frameworks aim at tool use, skip scoring, or hard-code agent behavior.

Their open-source framework is MALLM. It mixes more than a hundred forty setups. Agent personas vary, from expert to personality types. Response styles, discussion forms, and decision rules vary too. Simple configuration files set each debate. Any text dataset from Hugging Face can be loaded. A scoring pipeline compares setups head to head. The parts of debate, and how they interact, become open to systematic study.
arxiv-2509-11956:
Guillermo Gamboa Quintero and 2 co-authors work on pure mathematics in a 2025 paper about ternary relations, statements involving three items at once. They revisit axiom systems from the early 1900s that aimed to capture betweenness, the idea behind linear order, and cycle order. Earlier work showed that several different axiom sets can define each order.

The authors add a new axiom, called F, to the common axioms. At first glance the added rule seems to allow many new systems. They prove that, with one axiom set, the systems still fall into the linear or cycle types. With a modified set, a larger family appears, and they characterize it completely using directed graphs, networks of points joined by arrows.
arxiv-2509-12056:
Splitting a hard integral into regions where different approximations rule is a workhorse trick in particle theory, and Leonid V. Bork with two co-authors refine it in 2025 for dual conformal integrals with slightly off-shell legs. The usual way of separating regions breaks the very symmetry that makes these integrals special.

Their fix mixes dimensional and analytic regularization in a combination that keeps dual conformal invariance intact, so each region's contribution stays invariant on its own. Calculations simplify dramatically as a result. The showcase is the slightly off-shell pentabox integral, evaluated through power corrections. All thirty-two regions reduce to products and ratios of gamma functions times powers of cross-ratios. Only logarithms remain in the final answer. A numerical check agrees with a recent, far messier published result.
arxiv-2509-12156:
Amirnezam Amiri and 3 co-authors map metals in the gas of nine nearby galaxies in a 2025 astronomy paper. Each galaxy hosts an active galactic nucleus, a bright center powered by a black hole. The gas-phase metallicity pattern, how elements heavier than helium vary with distance from the center, records how a galaxy grew.

Using data from the MAGNUM survey and emission-line diagnostics, the team measured metallicity separately in the disc, in outflows, and in the narrow-line region near the center. Most galaxies showed negative gradients, meaning metal levels fall outward. That pattern suggests active centers do not simply push metals to the outskirts. Instead, the results fit an inside-out growth story, where inner regions form stars earlier and enrich sooner.
arxiv-2509-12256:
Temitayo Adefemi applies entropy, a measure of disorder, to parallel computers in a 2025 paper. Since Claude Shannon's work on communication, entropy has spread into many fields. Here it is used to describe incompatibility between components in a parallel cluster, a source of noise and disorder that can waste computing power.

Adefemi builds a mathematical model based on graph theory and logarithms, adding up contributions from each system in a cluster. He then computes entropy for the ten fastest supercomputers in the Top500 list. Lower entropy correlated strongly with better performance on the LINPACK benchmark, a standard speed test, and the link was statistically significant. The framework suggests that reducing mismatch inside a machine may be a measurable path to efficiency.
arxiv-2509-12356:
The jackknife, which recomputes a statistic while leaving out one observation at a time, is the workhorse for estimating variance, yet its justification thins out for exotic estimators. In a solo 2025 paper, Jakob R. Juergens proves the jackknife stays ratio-consistent for a broad family of generalized U-statistics.

The key structure is dominance: the statistic's variance must be governed by its Hájek projection, the best additive approximation, plus a mild law-of-large-numbers condition on the squared projection terms. Delete-d variants of the jackknife are covered too. One application gives variance estimates for a two-scale nearest-neighbor regression method under much weaker conditions than before.
arxiv-2509-12456:
Rafael Zimmer and Oswaldo Luiz do Valle Costa apply reinforcement learning to market making in a 2025 paper. A market maker quotes buy and sell prices and profits from the spread, while facing risk from changing prices. Reinforcement learning lets an agent learn a policy by interacting with a limit order book, the record of outstanding orders.

Their market model is built to capture stylized facts of real markets, including clustered order arrivals, shifting spreads and return drifts, and random order sizes and volatility. The agent uses the Proximal Policy Optimization algorithm. The authors implement the system and compare its financial return and risk metrics across varying market conditions in simulation. Domain knowledge in the simulator is meant to stabilize learning.
arxiv-2509-12756:
El-Mehdi Mehiri and Mohammed Nadji settle a grid puzzle in 2025 about how a spread that starts at a few cells can take over a board under power rules. The puzzle grows from power control on networks and had an open guess from earlier work on grid boards.

They prove that guess false and give the exact count for grids. They also find repeat rules for the count and count how many best starting sets exist. For some grid shapes those counts match known lists, such as words that avoid set patterns and the large Schroder numbers. The work ties a network game to classic counting.
arxiv-2509-12956:
Diogo Boito and Marcelle Caram check in 2025 the theory value for a key collider ratio below the charm mass. The ratio gauges strong force effects in electron hits. New data from BES-III raised strain with older sets.

They weigh theory doubt from known growth ghosts with a ghost-free mass scheme. Dual breach terms prove large up to a set energy, then fade. Adding those terms lifts fit with data. All data sets prove fit with each other when joined. Theory fits the joined data, though strain with BES-III alone tops three standard steps.
arxiv-2509-13656:
Yingao Yao and three co-authors tackle testing for machine learning notebooks in a 2025 software engineering paper. Jupyter notebooks mix code, data, and charts in one interactive document. But they barely support testing. Silent regressions that change results without crashing often slip through during development.

Their tool NBTestGen automatically writes regression assertions for the notebook. The checks cover data processing, model building, and evaluation steps. A companion plugin, NBTest, runs cell-scoped checks without blocking the session. It also plugs into standard test pipelines. On several hundred Kaggle notebooks, the generated assertions caught most artificial faults. They also caught about seventy percent of real historical regressions. A user study with developers found the framework intuitive and useful.
arxiv-2509-14156:
Leonardi and a large international team confirm a hidden planet through transit timing in a 2025 astronomy paper. HIP 41378 hosts five transiting planets with periods from about two weeks to well over a year. Planets tug on each other gravitationally, shifting transit times. Those shifts can betray worlds that never cross the star's face.

The team combined fifteen new CHEOPS observations with TESS, K2, Spitzer, Hubble, and HARPS data. They modeled the two inner sub-Neptunes dynamically. Their transits arrive early or late by up to hours, near a two-to-one period resonance. The timing pattern confirms a sixth, non-transiting planet. Its orbit runs about sixty-four days and its mass is roughly seven Earth masses. The pattern hints at a resonance chain. It also pins down the inner pair's masses and possible volatile-rich compositions.
arxiv-2509-14256:
Arka Dutta and four co-authors report a shared task entry in 2025 on hidden ads inside chatbot answers, for the Touché Lab at CLEF. Hidden promotion is a risk when a helpful reply quietly favours a product. The team had to both create such ads and learn to spot them.

For creation, their system used user context and query intent to write ads that fit the reply. Prompting tricks and paired training data made the ads less obvious. For spotting, they tried two text only methods: a classifier built on a cross encoder model, and a prompt based check built on a second language model. Both methods worked from the reply alone, which keeps them practical for live systems.
arxiv-2509-14456:
Amber Shore and three co-authors uncover a trade off in 2025 between solving coreference and noticing when it is ambiguous. Coreference is linking a pronoun to the person it refers to. Humans use wide embodied context to spot genuine ambiguity in such links.

With minimal prompting, language models do well at choosing a referent and also do well at flagging ambiguity. They cannot do both well at the same time, the authors show. Success on one task tends to deploy the skill in a way that hurts the other. The authors name that tension the Correct-Detect trade off. Because coreference sits inside nearly every language task, the trade off warns against single score claims of human like understanding.
arxiv-2509-14556:
Charmi Bhatt and thirty-five co-authors report in 2025 the first find of the methyl cation in a planetary nebula, the glowing shell shed by a dying star. The nebula NGC 6302 is rich in oxygen, yet hosts much carbon chemistry. That mix is a puzzle for chemists.

Infrared views from the James Webb Space Telescope found the methyl cation, a key driver of organic chemistry under ultraviolet light. Its glow sits with carbon monoxide, hydrogen, ionised hydrogen and ring shaped hydrocarbons in the resolved maps. Heat and density fits to the glow pin down local states. Finding this reactive ion in an oxygen rich nebula sharpens the hunt for routes that build complex molecules in shed star stuff.
arxiv-2509-14856:
Hanyang Guo leads a team of seven authors introducing a benchmark for automated code review in a 2025 software engineering paper. Language models are increasingly asked to review code, but older benchmarks test isolated sub-tasks on simplified data. Real review work is holistic and context-rich, so those tests leave a reality gap.

CodeFuse-CR-Bench contains several hundred curated cases from seventy Python projects, spanning nine kinds of pull-request problems. Each case bundles the issue, the pull request details, and the repository state, enabling true end-to-end evaluation. Scoring combines rule-based checks on location and syntax with model-based judgments of review quality. The team's large assessment of leading language models finds no single model best at every aspect of review, setting baselines for future work.
arxiv-2509-14956:
Diego Gosmar and Deborah A. Dahl propose Sentinel Agents as a security layer for multi-agent AI systems in a 2025 paper. When many AI agents talk and act together, one compromised or misbehaving agent can endanger the whole system. Their framework stations watchdog agents throughout the network.

Sentinel Agents monitor inter-agent messages with semantic analysis, behavioral analytics, retrieval-based verification, and cross-agent anomaly detection. They can flag threats, enforce privacy and access rules, and keep full audit records. A Coordinator Agent sits above them, ingesting alerts and adapting policy: it can isolate or quarantine a bad agent to contain damage. Together the two layers aim to keep multi-agent ecosystems reliable enough for sensitive deployments, where unchecked agent failures would carry real risk.
arxiv-2509-15356:
When can a language model guess facts about a person from a table of data? Kevin Ren and his co-authors test this question at large scale. People have used such models to fill gaps in surveys and to score risk. Yet the models do well on some tasks and poorly on others, with no clear rule for when to trust them.

The team runs many table based tasks and studies where the models fail. They find that when a model does well on a basic task, its stated chances track real accuracy more closely. They also build simple checks, needing no labeled data, that can warn when a task is a poor fit. These checks help users decide before they rely on a model.
arxiv-2509-15556:
Ping Guo leads a large team that decides how much training text each language gets. Big language models now serve users worldwide, so skill across languages matters. The right mix is hard to set: languages affect each other, and the best mix shifts with data size. The team build a frame, Climb, to set the mix on firm grounds.

Climb first gauges how languages interact, then folds that into each language's true share. A two step plan then evens out the gain per language and scales the mix up. Tests confirm Climb measures cross language links well in many settings. Models trained with its mixes do better across languages.
arxiv-2509-15656:
C. S. Preenu, R. S. Indu, and Sijo George study graphs built from the ideals of a semigroup. In their graph, each non zero item is a point, and two points join if the ideals they generate share a non zero item. They focus on inverse semigroups, a class with a rich internal order. They also coin a new graph notion called a skeletal.

A skeletal keeps one point for each class of items that share the same ideal links. They show the ideal graph of an inverse semigroup always has such a skeletal. For the symmetric case, the skeletal matches a known graph on all subsets of a set. The paper maps the structure of these graphs.
arxiv-2509-15956:
Alexandre Pacheco leads a team that lets a swarm of robots feed trusted facts to blockchains. Blockchains verify well but cannot see the real world. Oracles supply outside data, yet past designs cut autonomy or reintroduce trust. A robot swarm offers a fresh oracle: mobile, spread out, and fault tolerant by design.

Their Swarm Oracle sends robots from many owners to sense the world and report jointly. Mixed ownership blocks single party bias but invites bad actors. A Byzantine fault tolerant protocol lets the swarm agree anyway. Their joint verdicts beat single robot estimates in quality. Robots can travel to remote spots on demand. The work joins swarm robotics with trustless contracts.
arxiv-2509-16056:
Patching is a method that builds global math objects from local pieces spread over many fields. Nguyen Manh Linh extends a classic patching result to crossed modules over a limit field, building a six-term exact sequence for them. When the module is a two-term complex built from tori, the sequence grows to nine terms, with no extra cover condition on the fields.

As a payoff, patching is shown to hold for a nonabelian form of second Galois cohomology for a class of groups. A weak local-global rule follows for the simply connected case. The work also recovers a known rule about indices of central simple algebras.
arxiv-2509-16156: Matias G. Delgadino and Luca Melzi prove that a classic family of traveling waves for fluid flow on a sphere holds its shape under small disturbances. The waves, of degree two in the Rossby-Haurwitz family, solve the Euler equation for flow on a ball. Their proof is described as short and quantitative, giving explicit bounds rather than just existence. It is also meant to be easy to follow in concept. The result adds firm ground to the study of large-scale flow patterns like those in planetary atmospheres.
arxiv-2509-16356:
A central question in the Langlands program asks when a special value of an L-function forces a period integral to be nonzero. Weixiao Lu, Danielle Wang, and Zhiyu Zhang attack a twisted form of that question for Asai L-functions. They build new relative trace formulas for period integrals tied to Weil representations, with careful handling of the geometric side.

By matching global terms, local distributions, and orbital integrals, they prove the twisted conjecture in any dimension, under some local conditions that allow number fields to ramify. The result extends a major line of work on periods and L-values.
arxiv-2509-16456:
Reasoning models waste much of their training on easy steps, while the hard turning points of a solution get little focus. Jiahao Yu and three co-authors present a fine-tuning strategy that hunts for the critical step in each reasoning chain, the point where the model must proceed with care to succeed. An advantage estimate locates that step.

Training then restarts the model from the critical step, samples fresh continuations, and weights learning toward them. The strategy plugs into several existing optimization methods and lifted all of them on hard reasoning benchmarks. Theory and broad tests support the gain.
arxiv-2509-16756:
Yuchen Liang, Yingbin Liang, Lifeng Lai, and Ness Shroff give new guarantees for discrete diffusion models in a 2025 paper. Such models build text or graph data by refining noise in steps. How fast and how well the sampler works drives their value. The team offer a fresh analysis of that sampler.

Their proof rests on a new trick with differential inequalities. The trick bends more easily than the classic change-of-measure method. It may help analyze other random processes too. Stronger guarantees tell builders how many steps a sampler truly needs. That knowledge can cut wasted compute in language and graph tools.
arxiv-2509-17056:
Ruijie He, Xiangcun Meng, and Zhenxin Lei count reflection-effect systems among hot subdwarf stars in a 2025 astronomy paper. A hot subdwarf with a close dim companion shows a reflection effect, as one side heats the other. Light curves reveal these systems, and some also eclipse. The team estimate how often the effect appears in each subclass.

Rates above the main band match rates on the band itself, across set temperature ranges. Stars near the galactic plane show a higher rate than those at high latitudes. These fractions constrain how such tight pairs form. Binary evolution models must reproduce the pattern the counts reveal.
arxiv-2509-17156:
Samar Hadou and Alejandro Ribeiro present a 2025 arXiv paper on solving constrained optimization problems with graph neural networks. Their idea is to unroll a classic method, dual ascent, into two linked networks. One network plays the primal role and the other tracks the dual values, and the pair meet at each layer.

The primal network seeks a steady point for a fixed dual value, while the dual network refines its guess step by step. Training forces both networks to mimic the rises and falls of the classic method, and the two take turns updating. In tests, the approach found answers that were near best and near feasible. It also held up well on new problems unlike those it was trained on.
arxiv-2509-17556:
Richard J. Murchie, Dolf Huybrechts, Aaron Strangfeld, and Mateusz P. Mrozowski model a lidar trick for reading clouds from space. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns cloud thermodynamic phase, whether cloud tops are ice or liquid, a key climate variable. Space lidars that look straight down can be fooled by specular reflection, the mirror-like glint off flat ice crystals.

A second lidar biased toward that glint, flown alongside a standard one, could calibrate the phase reading. The candidate is quantum parametric mode sorting lidar, which uses a nonlinear process and time-frequency mode selection to reject noise beyond what linear filters can do. With noise suppressed, the signal can run weak, which boosts the specular share of the return. The authors give a theoretical model of that scenario. It is meant to judge whether the approach could work before hardware flies.
arxiv-2509-17656:
Adrian Chitan, writing alone, reviews and refines a quantization scheme for three-manifold invariants. His 2025 arXiv paper revisits how Jeffrey and Weitsman formalized Witten's invariants, which assign numbers to three-dimensional spaces. The scheme integrates over a Lagrangian leaf tied to flat connections on a bounding surface that extend into a handlebody.

Chitan formalizes how that leaf stratifies, layer by layer, and lets the smooth structure guide a stratified quantization. Volumes and half-densities live on the stratified tangent bundle, and the pairing is set so the torsion still appears in the invariant's integrand. The stratification yields a natural constant half-density and trims the structure group at reducible connections. With the integral's conditions refined, the change reproduces the invariant exactly for many three-manifolds and extends it to some new ones.
arxiv-2509-17856:
T Banks argues that a finite heat-like count in quantum gravity means a finite count of states. His 2025 paper builds on work by Jacobson, Fischler, Susskind, and Bousso. Black hole facts hint that a patch of space-time holds just so much information.

Banks says string models of de Sitter space, with endless states, miss the key point. The hard part is to define how such a space decays and what far-off measures show. For times short next to its life, he argues, a finite-state model can describe the space well. The claim is a stance in a live debate.
arxiv-2509-17956:
Lin Luo and 4 co-authors ask non-expert folk how fair an AI system feels, in their own terms. Their 2025 study notes that fairness checks are most often run by AI experts. Those experts pick the traits, scales, and cut-offs used to judge outcomes.

The team gave lay folk a credit-score scene and let them make those picks. Their picks were far more complex than expert norms. They used traits past the legally guarded set, set stricter cut-offs, and shaped scales to the case. Many even wanted a fully custom scale. The results argue for a real voice for folk affected by AI.
arxiv-2509-18156:
Haoyu Wang and 4 co-authors use a twin trick to tell if one event truly caused a second in text. Their 2025 paper deals with event causality, a task that must split cause from mere linked timing. Word clues and graph hops can fake a cause link where none exists.

Their frame casts the first event as a treatment and the second as its outcome. A true twin would share the lead figure's past but face a changed treatment. Since text holds no such twin, they build one with a synthetic control method. Text code blends and un-blends make that twin from past data.
arxiv-2509-18756:
Bell state measurements sort pairs of qubits into the four maximally entangled Bell states. Luca Bianchi, Carlo Marconi, and Davide Bacco review the state of that art for light-based quantum systems in this 2025 paper. Such measurements power teleportation, entanglement swapping, and fusion-based computing. In photonics they are notoriously hard to do well with plain linear optics.

The review walks through the known proposals for carrying out these measurements. It stresses their fundamental limits and the strategies built to beat them. Recent work on high-dimensional systems gets its own survey, since bigger alphabets promise fatter quantum networks and higher-capacity links. The authors also flag open challenges that block routine use. The paper serves as a map for researchers entering photonic quantum information. It gathers scattered results into one reference.
arxiv-2509-18956:
Mirrors break the tools that rebuild a 3D scene from photos. Zijing Guo and two co-authors note that reflections bend light in ways that depend on viewpoint, so standard methods produce warped scenes. Past fixes treat mirrors mostly as symmetry tricks and throw away what reflections show. Yet a reflection is a real extra view of the room, and it can supply detail that direct views miss.

The team first built MirrorScene3D, a dataset of indoor scenes with mirrors, more than a thousand photos, and marked mirror masks. On top of it they built ReflectiveGS, a method that uses reflections as extra viewpoints to fix scene shape and recover missing detail. In tests it beat past methods on image quality scores and trained faster as well.
arxiv-2509-19056:
Signals that live on networks, like sensor readings on a road grid, often arrive with gaps and noise. Razieh Torkamani and three co-authors tackle graph signal recovery: rebuild the full signal from the few values that were actually seen. The hard part is the prior, the assumed pattern of what such signals look like. For real data that pattern is rarely known in advance.

Their method learns the prior from training samples with a Bayesian convolutional neural network built for graphs. Its filters rest on Chebyshev polynomials, and its inner layers act like a flexible family of distributions. The learned prior feeds a variational Bayesian routine that also estimates how noisy the data are. Tests on synthetic and real graph data show accurate, robust recovery, even when signals follow complex non-Gaussian patterns.
arxiv-2509-19156:
Spiking neural networks promise cheap, brain-like computing at the edge, but running them fully on small devices is slow and power-hungry. Maurf Hassan and four co-authors split the work between device and cloud in a system called NeuCODEX. Two ideas drive it. A learned compressor squeezes the network's spike signals before sending them, and an early-exit rule stops work once the answer looks confident enough.

The design was tested on still images and on event-camera streams, and prototyped on two standard network backbones in a real edge-to-cloud setup. Data transfer fell by up to about two thousand times, and edge energy use dropped by more than ninety percent. End-to-end delay fell to about a third of edge-only running. The cost was an accuracy drop under two percent, a trade the authors judge well worth making.
arxiv-2509-19256:
Young stars blast jets into space, and Noah Otten and five co-authors watch how one jet, from the star DG Tau, has changed over eighteen years. Their tracer is forbidden emission lines, light from rare atomic transitions that only glow in thin gas. These lines split into speed components, and the slow one may come from a disk wind, but which kind of wind is unsettled. Spectra from three epochs let the team track both jet and slow component.

The jet's speed fell by about a hundred kilometers per second between 2003 and 2021, matching its known slowing. The slow component splits into three sub-parts that the authors link to entrained jet material, a disk wind, and the dense upper disk. While jet parts vary, the slow component stays stable, shifting in relative brightness. The data cannot yet settle the wind's origin, though one height limit favors a magnetic wind.
arxiv-2509-19356:
Manish Yadav and three co-authors test an alternative theory of gravity against the expansion history of the universe. In Hoyle-Narlikar gravity, a creation field continually generates matter, and this study gives that field a new mathematical form. The model also includes a bulk viscous fluid, which adds friction-like effects to cosmic expansion. The authors fit the model jointly to observed Hubble expansion data and the Pantheon supernova catalog.

The fit finds the creation-field coupling always positive, a present expansion rate near seventy-one kilometers per second per megaparsec, and a universe age around thirteen and a half billion years. Acceleration is predicted to have begun at a specific transition redshift. That expansion rate sits above the local SH0ES measurement, which the authors say could ease the Hubble tension. Checks of energy conditions and stability support the model's account of late-time acceleration.
arxiv-2509-19556:
Selling farm output for cash can lift rural incomes, but women farmers may share unevenly in that shift. Wei Li, Kashi Kafle, and Anna Josephson study the gender gap with panel surveys from Ethiopia, Nigeria, and Tanzania. The data follow the same households over time. Their method strips out fixed household traits so the gender link stands out more clearly.

In Ethiopia and Nigeria, households led by women, or with more land run by women, sold less into markets. That gap was sharpest where farms mainly fed themselves. Yet women-led households that did sell favored market buyers over single buyers. In Tanzania the gaps were weaker and less steady. The authors urge country-specific policy rather than one blanket fix, since local markets and rules shape the gap.
arxiv-2509-19656:
When plasma meets fields as strong as those near pulsars, radiation pushes back on the particles that emit it. Haidar Al-Naseri studies how that recoil reshapes the spread of particle momenta in a hot relativistic plasma. Three setups are treated in turn. A pure magnetic field carves a ring-shaped pattern in momentum space. A pure electric field carves a partial ring, changing only certain angular sectors.

Combined fields produce their own mixed pattern, worked out in the third case. Anisotropy matters because it steers how the plasma radiates, conducts, and possibly forms beams. The analysis tracks which sectors change and which stay near their start. Such plasmas appear in extreme astrophysics and in laser labs that mimic it. Knowing the momentum pattern is a step toward predicting their light.
arxiv-2509-19756:
A hypothetical heavy boson, the Z prime, might decay into particles that leave no trace in a detector. Jyotiranjan Beuria hunts that invisible decay at a future muon collider, where it would appear beside a single photon. Events are placed in a six-dimensional space of motion variables. Groups of events are then read with topological tools that count holes and loops in their shape.

Those shape summaries feed a multiple-instance learning classifier. It beat standard machine learning on plain event variables by a wide margin. The author also maps which mass ranges could be excluded at high confidence. Topology captures patterns that single numbers miss. If muon colliders are built, such tools could extend their reach into dark sectors.
arxiv-2509-19956:
Disease histories unfold in stages, and registries now track those stages for whole populations. Simon Wiegrebe and six co-authors extend piecewise exponential additive models to multi-state disease histories. Real data bring dependent left-truncation, several time scales, index event bias, and interval censoring all at once. Simulations test whether the extended models survive that pile-up.

The models handled dependent truncation and multiple time scales. A multiple-scale version proved less robust to the data-generating process than a stratified single-scale one. Index event bias was measured across settings and tied to covariate completeness. Biobanks and registries keep growing, so methods must match their messiness. Honest bias accounting matters before such models inform prognosis or policy.
arxiv-2509-20056:
Tomas Halada and five co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv review of meshfree collocation methods. These are numerical methods for solving differential equations without a grid or mesh. Instead, they work with scattered points, sometimes called particles, spread over the region of interest. The review pulls together decades of work in this area.

The authors explain how several known methods estimate smooth functions and their derivatives at scattered points. They trace how key ideas developed over time. They also sort the methods by the principle used to derive them. Some methods look alike but differ in subtle and important ways, and the review makes those gaps clear. A single unifying formulation shows how each method follows from one frame. The paper closes with a proposed general recipe for building such methods in the future.
arxiv-2509-20356:
Decentralized markets for digital resources promise open trading without a central manager, but their workloads strain blockchains. Mohamed Najd and Ghada Almashaqbeh present chainScale, a scaling design for such markets, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Earlier blockchain scaling tools ignore how these markets actually split their work. Their design starts from the market's own modules.

Each module gets its own dependent sidechain, so traffic processes in parallel without costly cross-chain transactions. Overloaded modules subdivide further through hierarchical sharing. Miners with a stake in the system are weighted toward guarding critical modules. Sidechains sync back to the main chain as the single source of truth, and stale records are pruned. A prototype storage market beat a single-sidechain design fourfold in throughput and cut confirmation delay fivefold.
arxiv-2509-20856:
Identifying a plant from a photo is easy for common species and hard for the thousands with few pictures. Herve Goeau, Pierre Bonnet, and Alexis Joly report on the LifeCLEF 2017 plant identification challenge in a conference paper from the CLEF 2017 forum in Dublin. The challenge covered ten thousand species.

The dataset held about one point one million images of plants from Europe and North America, drawn from sources such as the Encyclopedia of Life. Deep learning had just made such continental-scale identification plausible. Still, most species remained poorly illustrated, making the training data noisy and uneven. The paper describes how systems coped with that noise and how well they scored, marking a milestone toward automated plant identification.
arxiv-2509-20956:
Radioactive isotopes that decay within a few million years were present when the solar system formed, and they time-stamp its birth. Thomas Truemam and three co-authors model two of them in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The isotopes are iron-60 and manganese-53.

Iron-60 comes only from core-collapse supernovae, while manganese-53 also comes from Type Ia supernovae.
