Standard fairness toolkits, built for parity across groups, fit poorly where choices are relational, existential, and culturally varied.

Ahmad maps the major fairness notions onto realistic end-of-life scenarios and then reads them across moral traditions. Fairness in this setting, the argument runs, goes beyond equal outcomes. It also covers moral representation and fidelity to the patient's own values, relationships, and worldview. The paper offers an ethical framework for judging surrogate systems on those richer terms, where a technically even-handed answer can still betray the person it claims to represent.
arxiv-2510-16256:
Cesar Mello Fernando Medina da Cunha lays a math base for a new kind of ultrasound imaging. Standard ultrasound maps echoes, but his method, called functional spectral imaging by ultrasound, reads how tissue shifts a set of tones. Each spot's density and stiffness nudge the tones of a vibrating region in their own way.

The paper builds the full chain: a model operator and formulas linking local traits to tone shifts. It also gives math for running that link backward. Computer tests under ideal low noise place features within about a tenth to three tenths of a millimeter. They also flag masses near a milligram. Keeping just ten to fifteen tones preserves about eighty-five percent of a feature's contrast while cutting noise. The work is theory and simulation only, setting up trials in fake tissue and living bodies next.
arxiv-2510-16656:
Noah El Rimawi-Fine and six co-authors present StructureFlow, a way to learn both the hidden network structure and the random motion of a physical system at the same time. Their main test case is single-cell biology. There, measurements destroy the cells, so scientists get separate snapshots of cell groups rather than tracks of the same cells over time.

StructureFlow trains without running costly simulations, which sets it apart from older methods that usually handled structure or motion, but not both together. The team shows the method working on population data that is partial and noisy. Readers get a clear plan for recovering causal links and change over time from snapshot data alone.
arxiv-2510-16856:
Liang Chen and Thomas W. Kephart examine dense clumps of axions in a 2025 physics paper. Axions are hypothetical particles proposed to solve puzzles about matter. They may also make up part of the dark matter. A cluster is a tight swarm of many axions held by gravity.

Under strong gravitational squeezing, most axions in a clump can change fast. They convert into photons, which are particles of light. Some setups give off light with clear, patterned signals. The authors estimate what solid remnant each event leaves behind. Some remnants could be black holes. Other flashes might match fast radio bursts, the brief radio blasts seen from deep space.
arxiv-2510-16956:
Mark Towers, Yali Du, Christopher Freeman, and Timothy J. Norman test explanations of game-playing agents in a 2025 paper. Explainable reinforcement learning tries to say why an agent acted. Debugging is a leading use for such explanations. Yet few studies compare explanation methods head to head.

Their test asks users to name an agent's goal from its explanation. The setting is the classic game Ms. Pac-Man. Four explanation algorithms produced the material users judged. Only one method let users beat random guessing. Users also felt confident even when they were wrong. Their reported ease of understanding did not track accuracy at all. The findings warn that pleasant explanations can still mislead their readers.
arxiv-2510-17056:
Luis F. G. Campos, Leonardo C. Marques, and Walter T. Nakamura ask whether AI can inspect software usability in a 2025 paper. Usability inspection means experts hunting interface flaws before users suffer. It works well but costs time and specialist knowledge. Generative AI models can now read interfaces and comment on them.

A prototype was judged by four specialists and two AI models. The models were GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Scores compared precision, recall, and a combined measure. Human inspectors kept the best precision and coverage overall. The AI models found many genuinely new defects alone. They also produced more false alarms and repeated findings. Combining humans and AI gave the best overall results. The authors conclude AI augments inspectors rather than replacing them.
arxiv-2510-17156:
Takaaki Nomura, Hiroshi Okada, and Yoshihiro Shigekami build a model where lepton masses grow from loops in this 2025 paper. Leptons are light matter bits like the electron and muon. In their model, charged lepton masses arise at one loop via a broken merge rule. Neutrino masses arise at one loop with the rule kept.

Loop-made masses let the model speak to rare flavor shifts as well. It also speaks to muon spin quirks and tiny charge splits. Number tests scan phase picks that fit known masses and mix angles. Trends link those phases to a rare double decay with no neutrinos. The work ties mass birth to tests labs can check soon.
arxiv-2510-17256:
Shahin Atakishiyev and ten co-authors review how to explain large language models in this 2025 paper. Users cannot see why a model picks its next word. Models also make false claims that look sure and smooth. Both flaws make trust hard in high-stakes fields.

The review sorts local tricks that explain one output at a time. It also sorts work that maps inner parts to clear roles. Case work in health care and self-driving shows how trust shifts. Lay readers weigh such notes quite unlike trained experts. The authors close with open gaps and paths to more honest notes.
arxiv-2510-17556:
Inflation, the burst of expansion in the very early universe, comes in many model flavours, and the simplest axion version predicts more gravitational ripples than observations allow. Federico Greco, writing alone, studies a variant called aligned natural inflation, where two axion fields guide the expansion along a path near a saddle point of their shared energy landscape. That route fits current limits and will be probed by future microwave background experiments.

Greco shows that this model generically splits inflation into two stages, joined by a brief phase of rapid field oscillation. When a further field couples to the axions, that transition can pump out gravitational waves with a strongly scale dependent spectrum. Where the spectrum peaks depends on how long the second stage lasts, which decides which future detectors could see it.
arxiv-2510-17756:
Younghyun Koo and Maryam Rahnemoonfar predict how Arctic sea ice moves and thins. Satellite data now floods in, and machine learning models use it heavily. Purely data-driven models can break physical rules and fail on new conditions. Arctic ice is also thinning fast, which shifts the patterns models learned.

Their model adds physics rules into a neural network design. A physics-based loss guides outputs toward plausible ice motion and coverage. The model beat a fully data-driven version on daily forecasts. Gains were largest during melting and early freezing seasons. It also did better near fast-moving ice, even with little training data.
arxiv-2510-17856:
Abhinav Jangir and Anees Ahmed study how electron and positron pairs form from a strong electric field in empty space. They solve a quantum equation that tracks how the pairs move and build up. The setup varies the field shape, the pulse shape, and a phase term that shifts the wave.

Pair counts and motion patterns proved very sensitive to each of these choices. For some settings, the pair count rose by two to three orders of magnitude over plainer cases. A wave-based reading helps explain why flat-topped pulses and short falling edges help. The results guide laser work that aims to create matter from light.
arxiv-2510-17956:
Kassidy E Kollmann and four co-authors ask how the inner shape of a dark matter clump changes whether strong lensing can spot it. Small halos bend light from distant galaxies, but the signal depends on how steeply density rises toward the center. Models of dark matter predict both hollow cores and steep inner rises.

Fake observations styled on three major space telescopes show the effect clearly. Steep clumps can be found at masses far below those needed for the standard profile. Added complexity in the main lens model barely hurt detection of steep cases. The findings sharpen plans to hunt tiny dark structures.
arxiv-2510-18056:
Daniel Lenz and Nicolae Strungaru connect the settling of certain time averages to the hidden frequencies of a dynamical system. Wiener-Wintner averages are a classic tool in this area, and the link to eigenvalues drives the whole paper. In the topological setting they define a special kind of point where the averages behave well.

Such points fill almost all of the space in the ergodic case. They also tie to a form of near-periodicity. For systems built from translation-bounded measures, the key models of aperiodic order, these are exactly the points where a clean diffraction theory works.
arxiv-2510-18156:
Xiaoyan Xie, with seven co-authors, separates heat from chemistry in a solar flare using three space instruments. Images in extreme ultraviolet and X-ray light come from two observatories, plus full-Sun spectra from a small satellite. The analysis finds a thin, hot plasma cloud floating above the flare loops.

Cloud and loops follow independent temperature paths over time, which points to different heating at work. The authors read the cloud as an erupting filament heated directly in the corona during magnetic reconnection. Earlier chemistry readings at the flare peak are also checked against the sharper images, refining what the full-Sun data can claim.
arxiv-2510-18356:
Enrique Macías-Virgós, with Ángel Méndez-Vázquez and David Mosquera-Lois, works on a problem in topology, the branch of mathematics that studies shapes and maps between them. The authors want better tools for measuring how far apart two continuous maps can be, a quantity called homotopic distance. Direct measures are hard to compute, so lower bounds that are easier to find carry real value.

The paper introduces two new algebraic measures, called cohomological and homological distances, and shows they give computable lower bounds for homotopic distance. These new measures also improve on older estimates based on cup-length. A version for maps between simple building-block shapes is then defined, and a theorem shows it matches the continuous version after enough repeated subdivision. Worked examples close the argument.
arxiv-2510-18456:
Cristina Martinez Montes and her five co-authors test whether large language models can help with thematic analysis, a common method where qualitative researchers code interview text and group codes into themes. No shared, repeatable method existed for using these models in that process. The team wrote and refined prompts for the middle phases of a well-known reflexive version of the method, then compared model output with themes from experienced researchers.

Their material was fifteen interviews about the well-being of software engineers. Four expert judges, who did not know which output came from whom, preferred the model-generated codes sixty-one percent of the time and found them useful for the research question. Judges also flagged real limits: needless splitting of data, missed deeper meanings, and themes with fuzzy edges. The paper closes with guidelines on where models can assist and where human judgment must lead.
arxiv-2510-18556:
Svetlana Maslenkova and her nine co-authors examine trust in language models trained for medicine. Such models could reshape care, yet their behavior, including hidden bias, depends heavily on the data they were trained on, and current curation practices are rarely transparent. The study focuses on one concrete risk: whether a clinical model suggests opioid prescriptions differently depending on a patient's ethnicity, gender, or age.

Alongside the bias analysis, the team introduces HC4, a carefully curated health pretraining collection of more than eighty-nine billion tokens. Their evaluation mixes standard general benchmarks with a new health-specific method designed to surface downstream bias. The authors present the work as a step toward evaluation frameworks that make clinical models fairer and safer, arguing that trust must be earned through open data practices and direct bias testing.
arxiv-2510-18656:
John Ellis works with Marcos Garcia, Keith Olive, and Sarunas Verner. They test models of cosmic inflation against new sky data. Inflation says the early universe expanded extremely fast. Attractor models are a favored family of such theories. The team merged cosmic microwave background data from four sources. They include the Planck satellite. They include ground telescopes in Chile and at the South Pole.

Two classic families were checked in depth. The E-model family fits the merged data well. That family holds the canonical Starobinsky model. One data mix puts that model at the edge of the allowed zone. Hotter reheating after inflation improves its fit. T-models predict slightly lower values. They face some tension with the data. Steeper generalized versions match the newest ground data better. Deformed variants can reach higher values still.
arxiv-2510-18756:
Marcin Chrapek and his six co-authors secure a data center storage design. Storage sits apart from the computers and is reached over a fast fabric. The design performs well, but confidential computing is hard to layer on top. It isolates sensitive workloads, and speed or guarantees tend to suffer. Their system, Hazel, extends the standard storage protocol while honoring the confidential computing threat model.

Hazel promises confidentiality, integrity, and freshness for stored data. Its control path uses a leasing scheme for counters. Its data path speeds checks with a new form of Merkle tree that fits the disaggregated setting. All of this stays compatible with the existing protocol, and work can be offloaded to capable network cards. A prototype on current hardware showed speed losses of only about one to two percent. That held across synthetic tests, AI training, and standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-18856:
Omer Angel and his four co-authors study growing random trees with limited memory. In the classic recursive tree, each newcomer picks an earlier vertex uniformly. Here, a new vertex sees only recent arrivals. It picks uniformly among that window. Decisions rest on a partial snapshot of the network. Social networks and distributed computing motivate the setup.

Two regimes are analyzed, set by how the window scales. When the window is a fixed fraction of the past, a branching process describes local structure. It runs in continuous time and depends on that fraction. The tree's height grows logarithmically in this regime. A link to a known scaled-attachment model proves it. When the window excludes only a thin slice of the oldest past, the local limit is a Poisson branching process. That holds for every window exponent. The height then grows polynomially, by a distinct argument.
arxiv-2510-18956:
Paolo Arnaudo, Javier Carballo, and Benjamin Withers show that signals from a disturbed black hole can be written as a complete sum of modes everywhere in spacetime. At late times the familiar quasinormal modes converge, but at early times a different set, tied to the thermal circle of Euclidean time, does the job.

The two regions meet at a light cone scattered by the black hole. The authors test the idea on several spacetimes, including Schwarzschild, where the branch cut part becomes a sum of de Sitter modes. Their proofs rest on careful study of how the terms behave at large values.
arxiv-2510-19056:
Kuai Yu and eight co-authors propose POLAR, a reinforcement learning method for stealthy backdoor attacks on federated learning. Federated systems train across many clients without sharing raw data, but an attacker who poisons a few key layers can hide a backdoor while keeping normal accuracy high.

Older attacks pick those critical layers by fixed rules and ignore how layers interact, making them weaker and easier to catch. POLAR instead learns a policy for choosing layers, treating selection as a decision problem. The work matters mainly for defenders, since it exposes a smarter attack that security tests must learn to detect.
arxiv-2510-19156:
Lei Ni and Nolan Wallach give new proofs of classic results about compact complex manifolds that carry a transitive group of holomorphic symmetries. Such homogeneous spaces were classified through work by Wang, Tits, and others, and the original arguments can be heavy for newcomers to use.

Their Lie algebra approach uses only standard results from Lie theory, making the theory more accessible. A key step associates a canonical abelian Lie algebra with each integrable complex structure on a compact Lie algebra, extending older work by Samelson and Pittie. Cleaner proofs help geometers build on the classification with confidence.
arxiv-2510-19556:
A. Deur explains how the Bjorken sum rule gives access to the strong coupling of quantum chromodynamics across an unusually wide range of scales. The coupling, usually written alpha-s, runs with the energy scale at which it is probed, even deep into the infrared. Data from Jefferson Lab combined with the world data set trace that running over five orders of magnitude in momentum.

Deur then outlines two proposed measurements that would extend the map further. One would run at the future Electron-Ion Collider, the other at Jefferson Lab with a twenty-two giga-electron-volt beam. Together they would fill gaps in the mid-range of scales where the coupling's behavior is less firmly pinned down.
arxiv-2510-19856:
Eranga Bandara and eleven co-authors propose Model Context Contracts, a framework letting large language models interact directly with blockchain smart contracts. The Model Context Protocol standardized how AI systems reach external data, but no equivalent existed for blockchains. Under their design, users phrase requests in natural language and AI agents invoke the matching contract functions.

A language model was fine-tuned on pairs of user inputs and the correct protocol functions, which substantially improved how accurately requests map to actions. Smart contracts in the architecture effectively act as agents that understand natural language and execute transactions. The team validated the idea with an end-to-end prototype on the Rahasak blockchain using a fine-tuned Llama-4 model, claiming the first use of the protocol concept for blockchain integration.
arxiv-2510-20456:
Bernhard Haeupler, Yonggang Jiang, Yaowei Long, Thatchaphol Saranurak. Shengzhe Wang give a fast parallel method for sending several goods through a network at lowest cost, with limits and prices on both links and nodes. Parallel speed matters because huge flow problems stall when each step must wait for the last.

Earlier near optimal work methods still needed depth that grew with network size, even in simpler flow cases. The new method reaches near optimal work and near constant depth for fine accuracy levels. Its core advance is a shortcut structure for length limited flows that keeps slack small on length, crowding, and steps, extending a classic hopset idea with added control over crowding.
arxiv-2510-20656:
Tobias Hartnick and Filippo Sarti prove a transfer result in bounded cohomology for measured groupoids that arise from cross sections of a group action. Bounded cohomology tracks algebraic invariants with a size limit, and classic results move those invariants between a lattice and its host group.

In their wider setting, pattern groupoids from strong approximate lattices serve as leading examples, and a hitting time condition keeps the setup workable. For unimodular host groups, the groupoid invariants match those of the group with function based coefficients. Consequences include vanishing results for amenable hosts and an injection for the comparison map, plus new values in higher degrees for certain Lie groups.
arxiv-2510-21456:
K. G. Strassmeier and three co-authors measure surface activity on twenty-one dwarf stars in the Hyades cluster, a nearby family of stars born together. The cluster is a favored yardstick for how solar-like stars spin down, stir their interiors, and change chemically as they age over time.

Working along a sequence of the cluster's cool dwarfs, the team gathers quantitative tracers of surface activity, including lithium abundance, an infrared activity index, and magnetic measures. They then ask what drives the patterns: the stars' spin, or the churning of their outer layers, timed by a turnover scale. Their conclusion assigns the main role to those convective motions, expressed through the turnover time, while spin and its extra mixing contribute less, and sometimes push the other way.
arxiv-2510-21756:
Alexandr Fonari, Farshad Fallah, and Michael Rauch describe how open-source packages power the Schrödinger Materials Suite. The suite is used to search for new materials. A typical workflow moves through several stages, from building candidate structures to screening them. Open packages are built in at every stage.

The paper walks through that workflow and shows how the packages are used to handle materials data through a strong programming interface. It also discusses recent machine learning work for materials discovery in the suite. Open tools helped that work reach results faster and with less effort. The account shows how a commercial platform can lean on open scientific software at each step of a real discovery pipeline.
arxiv-2510-21956:
Armin Gerami and Ramani Duraiswami speed up a leaner form of the attention mechanism at the heart of Transformers. Standard attention compares every token with every other, so its cost grows with the square of the sequence length. Linear attention promises cost that grows gently instead, but real implementations have lagged behind the theory.

The pair redesigned how the forward and backward passes of linear attention are computed and built a heavily optimized graphics-processor kernel to match. Their version ran more than three times faster than the best prior approach while using far less memory. To prove the gain is real in practice, they trained a language model with over a billion parameters end to end and found reasoning skill on major benchmarks comparable to ordinary attention.
arxiv-2510-22056:
Mohammad Ali Etemadi Naeen, Hoda Mohammadzade, and Saeed Bagheri Shouraki aim surveillance anomaly detection squarely at people. Odd events in public footage are diverse and rare, and busy backgrounds clutter the view. The team's pipeline first strips the scene down to its human subjects before judging behavior.

An open-vocabulary detector finds people in each clip, a tracker keeps their identities steady across frames, and everything outside the person boxes is blurred away. The cleaned frames pass through a pretrained image network for spatial features, then through a two-direction memory network that reads motion forward and backward to classify the event. Tested on a five-class anomaly dataset, the human-first design is offered as a robust way to spot trouble while ignoring scene-specific distractions.
arxiv-2510-22456:
Oleh Savchuk examines whether tiny proton lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider show collective, fluid like behaviour. One predicted sign is a ring shaped vortex formed as the proton passes through the lead nucleus. Savchuk proposes reading that motion through correlations between pairs of unlike particles, namely protons and pions, a method called femtoscopy.

Because protons and pions differ in mass, they respond differently to the swirling flow, leaving an uneven emission pattern. That unevenness links directly to the starting vorticity of the created matter. The proposal gives experimenters a fresh, sensitive way to measure rotation in small collision systems.
arxiv-2510-22756:
Smoothness of special surfaces can fail at a sharp threshold. Arunima Bhattacharya and W Jacob Ogden prove that point in 2025. Their objects are Hamiltonian stationary Lagrangian graphs. Such graphs must stay merely Holder continuous at first. Holder continuity is a weak form of smoothness.

If the Holder exponent beats one third, the graph is smooth. This needs a supercritical phase condition. That condition gives a helpful convexity in the potential. The bound is best possible. At exactly one third, they build explicit singular solutions. Those solutions stay singular even under the strongest phase condition. This departs sharply from special Lagrangian theory.
arxiv-2510-22856:
Ion pairing shapes how electrolytes turn from liquid to vapor. Patrick B Warren and Andrew J Masters use Wertheim theory in 2025. Their model is the restricted primitive model. It treats ions as charged hard spheres. Pairing dominates the low temperature vapor phase.

They build a reference fluid with pairing suppressed. A tuned interaction makes its free energy stationary. That fluid admits real solutions over wide ranges. The new step allows neutral clusters. Ion pairs can assemble into such clusters isodesmically. Isodesmic means each addition step is alike. This improves match with Monte Carlo results. It may also explain anomalous underscreening data.
arxiv-2510-23056:
Panneer Selvam Santhalingam and four co-authors built VC4ASL, a system that lets American Sign Language users join video calls when bandwidth is too low for video. Without video, Deaf users lose hand shapes, body movement, and facial cues that carry meaning. Audio-only fallback thus shuts them out of meetings others take for granted.

VC4ASL sends sign communication through the audio channel of existing conferencing apps, so no new platform is needed. It works even when reliable video is absent. The design aims to keep ASL conversation possible on weak connections, a practical step toward equal access in remote work and school.
arxiv-2510-23556:
Yury Solyaev finds a cleaner path through the math of light inside materials whose response shifts slightly from place to place. In such media, the classic Maxwell theory needs extra terms for electric quadrupole and magnetic dipole effects. He writes the material rules in operator form and picks a gauge rule that lets the field potentials be handled one at a time.

From that setup he gets separate wave equations for the potentials, and for steady tones the answers split into parts of Helmholtz type, set by the medium's traits. A closed-form answer for a plane wave striking a flat surface shows the energy flow must include the quadrupole part, which some earlier work missed. He also derives the full set of boundary rules from the least action principle, including faint extra wave parts that reflected and transmitted light must carry.
arxiv-2510-23756:
Nicki Barari and two co-authors ask why a concept-forming model resists catastrophic forgetting, the tendency of learning systems to erase old skills when taught new ones. Their earlier model, Cobweb/4V, builds a hierarchy of concepts and had shown unusual stability on visual tasks. Three candidate explanations are on the table: adaptive restructuring, sparse selective updates, and learning driven by information-theoretic statistics rather than gradients.

To test them, the authors compare Cobweb/4V with neural baselines, including a new neural version of the same framework, on image sets from MNIST up to CIFAR-10. Each hypothesis held up: restructuring boosted plasticity, sparse updates cut interference with old knowledge, and the statistic-based learning kept prior knowledge without replaying old data. The results point to concrete design ingredients for continual learning systems that stay stable while remaining adaptable.
arxiv-2510-23956:
Alejandro Escontrela and seven co-authors introduce Neural USD, a framework for editing generated scenes one object at a time. Generative models can conjure rich images, but touching one object — recoloring a chair, swapping a background — usually warps the whole scene. The authors borrow the Universal Scene Description standard from computer graphics, which stores scenes as structured hierarchies of objects.

In Neural USD, scenes and objects are represented in that same structured, layered way. The format accepts many kinds of control signals, avoids model-specific constraints, and gives per-object control over appearance, shape, and pose. A fine-tuning step keeps those control signals disentangled, so moving an object does not drag its color or the lighting along. The team evaluates several design choices and shows the representation supports step-by-step, incremental editing workflows. They present it as first steps toward generative tools that behave like real scene editors.
arxiv-2510-24056:
Agnideep Aich and Ashit Baran Aich introduce a new test for whether a model fits data that have linked variables. Standard tests can miss subtle links, such as how extremes move together. Their test works directly on the copula, the part of a model that holds the dependence between variables alone.

For a common family called Archimedean copulas, the test has a closed form built from a single generator function. The authors prove it can detect weak changes in the dependence pattern and can be estimated at a good rate. They also extend it to other families. Tests can run fast, with cost growing in a simple way as dimension rises.
arxiv-2510-24156:
Sarai Dery Folkestad and thirty six co-authors announce version 2.0 of eT, an open source program for molecular electronic structure. The program focuses on speed and modular design, with strong coupled cluster methods that rival or beat commercial tools in some cases. It also supports other wave function models and density functional theory.

The new release adds special tools for strong coupling between light and matter. It brings many speed ups and algorithmic improvements, plus new features for mapping energy surfaces and modeling other properties. The paper surveys what eT can do and how the code is organized, giving chemists a free, fast option for demanding quantum chemistry work.
arxiv-2510-24256:
Jack Merullo and three co-authors show how memorization in transformer models can be separated from general learning by looking at loss curvature. Prior work found that memorized training points sit in much sharper parts of the loss landscape than other points. Sorting weight components by curvature can thus reveal memorized content without explicit labels.

Based on this, the team builds a weight editing method that suppresses recitation of untargeted memorized data more effectively than a recent unlearning method, while keeping perplexity lower. The decomposition works in both language models and vision transformers. The paper frames a spectrum from memorization to reasoning in terms of curvature.
arxiv-2510-24656:
Alexander Lidiak leads a team with fourteen co-authors who built a code twin for a quantum dot device. Spin based bits in such dots are a strong path to quantum machines, but tuning them is slow and hard. Their twin uses a graph based code with deep nets to speed the slow parts.

With the twin, they gauge how gates cross talk, then build fake gates that undo that cross talk. They checked the plan on a real twin dot made in a germanium and silicon mix. The work points to faster design, tests, and control of such chips as they grow in size.
arxiv-2510-25356:
Abhishek Purushothama, Junghyun Min, Brandon Waldon, and Nathan Schneider examine legal meaning. Their 2025 paper questions language models in court work. United States judges often ask about ordinary meaning. That means how ordinary speakers understand legal text. Scholars recently proposed using large language models there. Models might reveal how people normally use words.

The authors argue models need rigorous evaluation first. Pretraining on huge data may not be enough. Their controlled experiments found troubling robustness failures. Slight changes in question format altered conclusions wildly. Interested parties could exploit that vulnerability in litigation. They compared model answers with human judgment data. Models correlated only moderately with human responses there. That level falls short given legal stakes. Criminal law and civil rights cases raise concerns. Models should not be treated as authoritative, they conclude.
arxiv-2510-25456:
Kiyoon Eum studies the Quillen metric in Kahler geometry. His 2025 paper generalizes a famous moment map picture. The Donaldson-Fujiki picture treats scalar curvature as a moment map. That space contains compatible almost complex forms. A fixed symplectic manifold underlies that space. Eum uses equivariant determinant line bundles as approach.

He starts from a prequantization of a compact manifold. For each natural number k, he constructs a bundle. The bundle is equivariant under the automorphism group. It carries an invariant Quillen metric in his construction. Its curvature admits an asymptotic expansion over settings. Coefficients yield a sequence of invariant closed forms. Corresponding moment maps take values in smooth functions. Each map arises from varying the metric logarithm. Kahler potentials vary while complex form stays fixed. He shows these maps match Z-critical formulas. Those formulas were presented by Dervan and Hallam. A generalized fiber integral formula is also stated.
arxiv-2510-25656:
Cynthia A Huang, Mitchell O'Hara-Wild, Rob J Hyndman, and Matthew Kay propose ggtime. Their 2025 paper creates a grammar of time graphics. Visualizing change over time is basic to learning. Anticipating the future also relies on time graphics. Time semantics can be complicated for current tools.

Bespoke plot helpers are commonly used instead. Their grammar encodes time semantics declaratively for visualization. New composable elements support many time forms. Standardization of irregular durations is built in. Matching of time points across granularities is possible. Varied time zones can also be aligned properly. Interoperability with other semantic variables is designed in. Navigation across visualization space preserves time semantics throughout. Data analysts gain principled tools for time graphics. Grammar-based plotting extends the ggplot tradition to time. Complex calendars become representable.
arxiv-2510-25756:
Grayson R Frazier and Yi Li study triplet pairing in superconductors. Their 2025 physics paper studies frustrated spin textures. Couplings between d-vectors stabilize spatially varying pairing orders. Spin triplet superconductors host those d-vector orders.

Couplings are analogous to Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya effects in magnetism. Such couplings cannot originate from spin-orbit coupling. They arise when itinerant electrons couple to exchange fields. Frustrated spin moments compose that local exchange field. A T-matrix expansion shows the coupling mechanism. The barrier between superconducting grains hosts those configurations. Nonvanishing spin chirality can originate the diode effect.
arxiv-2510-26056:
Chijul B. Tripathy, working alone, revisits the strong birthday problem, a harder cousin of the classic birthday paradox. The classic problem asks how large a group must be before two people likely share a birthday. The strong version asks for the smallest group where, with chance at least one half, every person shares a birthday with at least one other person, so no one is left alone.

Tripathy builds counting and probability based recurrence frameworks for groups spread over a set number of days. Each day must end up empty or hold at least two birthdays. He finds a new link to associated Stirling numbers, a family of counting numbers, and uses it for faster recurrences. Dynamic programming implementations show the methods scale well in practice.
arxiv-2510-26556:
Claus Kadelka counts special rules in Boolean networks, the on-off models widely used for gene regulation. A variable is canalizing when one of its values alone can fix the output, which gives the network order and robustness. Degeneracy is the opposite pull: some variables are fully dominated by others and add nothing.

Kadelka derives recursive formulas, step-by-step counting rules, for Boolean functions with a set number of essential variables and stated canalizing traits. In particular, he counts the non-degenerate canalizing functions, where every variable matters and at least one can dominate. The formulas extend earlier counts of canalizing and nested canalizing functions. They give a firm base for asking how often canalization shows up in random functions, and why it appears so often in real biological networks.
arxiv-2510-26656:
Georgios Kamaras, Craig Innes, and Subramanian Ramamoorthy improve a step in teaching robots from simulation. Likelihood-free inference identifies a system's traits from black-box models, without a tractable formula for the odds. It samples from a support, a chosen range of traits, and sharpens a prior into posteriors. If that range is set wrong, the results can be suboptimal yet overconfident.

Kamaras and his two co-authors let each round's posterior guide the next range, using three simple heuristics named EDGE, MODE, and CENTRE. They first test the idea on standard stochastic benchmarks with a wrongly set range. Then they apply it to a robot handling a deformable linear object, such as a cable. Inference sorted the objects by length and stiffness more finely, and policies trained with those posteriors performed more robustly.
arxiv-2510-27056:
Arman Bolatov leads five co-authors in analyzing a classifier that uses more mixture parts than the data truly contain. Mixture discriminant analysis sorts items by fitting each class with blended bell-shaped components. Using extra components, called overspecification, is common in practice for images and text, but its error behavior lacked firm theory.

The study fits two components per class to data drawn from a single component and tracks both algorithm behavior and classification error. With suitable starting values, the standard fitting algorithm converges very fast at the population level, and finite-sample error approaches the best possible rate steadily. Remote sensing experiments support the theory. The results explain why a common practical shortcut often works well.
arxiv-2510-27256:
Xin Tang leads nine co-authors in ECVL-ROUTER, a scenario-aware router that sends each vision-language query to the right-sized model. User needs vary between fast response, high quality, and low energy use. Cloud giants answer everything at high latency and energy cost, while small edge models handle simple tasks cheaply, so choosing per query saves resources.

The framework introduces a routing strategy and evaluation metrics that pick a model per query to maximize overall utility under the stated requirement. A multimodal response-quality dataset tailored for router training supports the design. Extensive experiments route over eighty percent of queries to the small model while dropping problem-solving success by under ten percent. The authors call it the first scenario-aware routing framework for vision-language models.
arxiv-2510-27356:
Núria Fagella and Leticia Pardo-Simón look back at a paper that reshaped a field, in this 2025 survey. The paper, by Eremenko and Lyubich, came out in 1987 in the Journal of the LMS. Its subject was entire functions, formulas defined for every complex input, and how points move when the formula is applied again and again.

The 1987 paper built examples with wild behavior no one had seen in this setting. The trick was a clever stretch of classic approximation theorems, tools for mimicking one function with another. Those examples set methods the field still uses. They also raised questions that guided much later work on such dynamics. Fagella and Pardo-Simón trace that influence across the decades since.
arxiv-2511-00256:
Zongyang Du and six colleagues release NaturalVoices, a speech dataset built for voice conversion, the task of making one voice sound like another. Most speech collections are acted in studios, so they miss real feeling and natural style. NaturalVoices instead draws on spontaneous podcasts, with more than five thousand hours of recordings from thousands of speakers.

Each recording carries automatic labels for emotion, sound quality, transcript, speaker, and sound events. An open pipeline lets researchers filter custom subsets for their own tasks. Tests show the data helps build conversion models that sound natural and expressive. The scale also exposes weak spots in current models, making the set a tough new benchmark.
arxiv-2511-00356:
Yuma Furuta, Yuya Kusuki, and Toshiki Onagi study conformal interfaces, boundaries where two quantum field theories meet, and a number that describes how much energy crosses: the transmission coefficient. That number usually depends on messy details of the specific setup. The authors introduce a new viewpoint based on a phantom current, a hidden current that appears when the interface is folded into a simpler picture.

A spin-2 phantom current, they show, completely determines the transmission coefficient. With a single such current, the coefficient is fixed by one quantity alone, the current's conformal dimension. The framework explains known results for minimal models and the free boson in one stroke. It also makes concrete predictions for interfaces that no one had computed before.
arxiv-2511-00456:
Kiran Shahi and Anup Bagale aim to locate pneumonia on chest X-rays without paying for pixel-level annotations, which are costly and slow to produce. Their weakly supervised framework learns from image-level labels alone: each X-ray is simply marked sick or healthy. Gradient-weighted class activation mapping then paints heatmaps that show which lung regions drove the decision.

The team trains seven pretrained models, including a vision transformer, under identical conditions, with focal loss and patient-wise splits to stop data leakage. All models classified with high accuracy, in the mid-to-high ninety percent range. ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0 led overall, while MobileNet-V3 offered a light alternative. Heatmaps focused on clinically relevant lung regions, supporting explainable AI as a screening aid that clinicians can inspect rather than trust blindly.
arxiv-2511-00556:
Peng Ding and seven co-authors expose a jailbreak that works by shifting intent rather than hiding it. Most attacks bury a harmful request under extra context or adversarial tokens, leaving the intent intact. Their intent shift attack instead transforms the request so the model misreads it as a benign ask for information. Only minimal edits are needed, and the prompts stay natural and human-readable.

Across open and commercial models, the attack beat direct harmful prompts by a wide margin in success rate. Fine-tuning on benign data rewritten in the same templates pushed success close to total, a stark warning. Existing defenses proved inadequate, though the authors explore both training-free and training-based mitigations. The findings point to a fundamental weakness in how models infer intent, and a pressing need for stronger safety reasoning.
arxiv-2511-00656:
Digvijay Singh, Pankaj Sharma, and Narayan Mohanta design a superconducting diode that lets current flow one way more easily than the other, tuned by a magnetic texture. Their device is a planar Josephson junction with d-wave superconducting regions, the kind found in high-temperature cuprates, laid over a skyrmion crystal, a lattice of tiny magnetic swirls. The skyrmion field pattern breaks both inversion and time-reversal symmetry.

That double breaking produces an asymmetric current-phase relation with an anomalous phase shift, the heart of the diode effect. Calculations with a shunted junction model and the Bogoliubov-de Gennes method show efficiency tuned widely by gate voltage and skyrmion size. Because the superconductor is a high-temperature one, the diode could run warmer than conventional designs, a practical, field-free route to tunable superconducting electronics.
arxiv-2511-01256:
Yasamin Foroutani and colleagues improve how a surgical robot inserts a needle into the eye. Precise tool paths are undermined by poor alignment, hidden dynamics, and actuator errors. In their setup, a four degree of freedom robot arm must rotate the needle during insertion, and misalignment of the fourth joint makes plain rotation unsteady.

Their plan is iterative learning control: the robot repeats the insertion, measures the position error each time from optical coherence tomography volume scans, and adjusts the joint commands for the next attempt. A careful motion calibration comes first. Tested on subretinal injection in ex vivo pig eyes, the learned turning path reached higher success in tissue piercing and injection than straight insertion. The authors say the result may transfer to other precision tasks of this kind.
arxiv-2511-01356:
Rana Alaa and colleagues make split learning verifiable. In split learning, a neural network is cut in two: the client runs the first part on its raw data and sends intermediate activations to a server that finishes the computation. The split suits partners who cannot share data or compute, but neither side could check the other's honesty.

Their framework attaches zero knowledge proofs, specifically zk-SNARKs, to both the forward and backward passes on the server side, so correctness can be verified without revealing the underlying values. They compare it with a blockchain based variant that records updates but proves nothing. The comparison concludes the proof based system achieves verifiability and correctness, while the blockchain version is lighter but unverifiable.
arxiv-2511-01656:
Nick Sheridan constructs the big relative Fukaya category of a smooth complex projective variety taken relative to a normal crossings divisor. Fukaya categories, built from a space's Lagrangian submanifolds and Floer theory, are central to mirror symmetry; the relative version keeps track of a chosen divisor inside the variety.

Earlier work with Perutz built the small version under a semipositivity assumption. Sheridan now generalizes the construction, adds the closed-open and open-closed maps that relate the category to the variety's ordinary cohomology, and proves Abouzaid's split-generation criterion in this setting. He also sets out a general framework for chain-level Floer operations here, handling signs and bounding cochains efficiently, groundwork for follow-up work with Ganatra on the cyclic open-closed map.
arxiv-2511-01956:
Marcos Florencio and Francielle Prieto ask what schools should teach now that AI tools can do much mental work. The fear that thinking machines might replace human thought is as old as the term artificial intelligence itself, coined in the mid twentieth century. For decades that fear stayed mostly abstract. Chatbots built on large language models, such as ChatGPT, have now made it real and urgent.

The pair map the limits of current AI systems, above all those rooted in language models. They argue the root causes of those limits cannot be fixed by the methods in use today. Their answer lies in constructivist teaching, where students learn by building knowledge through inquiry and reflection. Schools, they urge, should shape the human skills that stay valuable beside AI. That path would guard the long term edge of human intelligence over AI tools.
arxiv-2511-02056:
Marco Torri, Fulvio Ricci, Marco Giammarchi, Lino Miramonti, Valerio Toso, and Chiara Sigala survey how gravitational waves could test quantum gravity, an area where direct experiments are out of reach. When two black holes merge, the final black hole rings down like a struck bell, and that signal probes spacetime near the event horizon in the strongest gravity available. Quantum gravity models suggest black hole surfaces, and hence entropy, come in discrete steps.

The authors focus on what ringdown observations could reveal about that presumed quantised structure. Data from the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA network will later be joined by the Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer. The paper maps out why these future observations make black hole ringdowns a promising frontier for fundamental physics.
arxiv-2511-02156:
Xunmo Yang, Taylor Pospisil, Omkar Muralidharan, and Dennis Sun argue that data analysis needs its own grammar, separate from the grammars used to manipulate data. In their design the building blocks are metrics and dimensions: the quantities being measured and the axes along which they are broken down. Composing those primitives expresses an analysis the way a sentence composes words, rather than as a pile of ad hoc operations.

A Python implementation called Meterstick puts the grammar to work. It does not care where the data live, operating the same way over an in-memory table or a SQL database. The paper is short and programmatic: it lays out the primitives, the composition rules, and the implementation, proposing a cleaner shared language for everyday analysis work.
arxiv-2511-02456:
Bing-Yi Jing, Weiming Li, Jiahui Xie, Yangchun Zhang, and Wang Zhou study how accurately the standout eigenvalues of a data matrix can be estimated. Sample covariance matrices are the workhorse of multivariate statistics, and their spiked eigenvalues, the few that rise above the bulk, carry the signals practitioners care about. The theory the authors use rests on laws describing the eigenvalue distribution at two scales: global laws for the whole spectrum and local laws for fine detail.

Their analysis allows the sample size and the dimension to grow at general relative rates. The dimension can be far smaller than, comparable to, or far larger than the number of samples. With those global and local laws established in that generality, they determine the convergence rates of spiked eigenvalue estimates. That is the basic precision statement behind methods that count and locate signals in high-dimensional data.
arxiv-2511-02756:
Matthew Koc and six colleagues built tiny waveguide filter banks that could power spectrometers on a chip. Such chips would let telescopes map gases across the sky at millimeter and far-infrared wavelengths, a goal called line intensity mapping. Earlier devices wasted too much light, so efficiency was the hurdle for the 2025 work.

The team etched the devices from silicon and plated them with gold for use in millimeter spectroscopy. The design packs pixels tightly, keeps light losses low, and pairs easily with sensitive detector arrays. A test filter matched simulations well, reaching a resolving power of 263 and a high loss quality factor at room temperature. Bigger multi-color versions now look within reach for future instruments.
arxiv-2511-03056:
Victoria Ebert, Rishabh Singh, Tuochao Chen, Noah Smith, and Shyamnath Gollakota formalize a privacy-driven problem. Often only one side of a conversation can be recorded, as in telemedicine, call centers, and smart glasses. Their 2025 paper names this the one-sided conversation problem and studies two tasks: rebuilding the missing speaker's turns as the chat unfolds, and summarizing from a half transcript.

Tests on three dialogue data sets used human comparisons and model judges. Knowing one future turn and the length of missing speech helped reconstruction a lot. Placeholder prompts cut invented content. Big models did well from prompts alone, while small ones needed fine-tuning. Good summaries, notably, did not require rebuilding the missing turns first, a relief for privacy-aware design.
arxiv-2511-03556:
Zhongqi Zhao and colleagues improve a regression trick that cancels noise in today's imperfect quantum computers. Clifford data regression learns the noise pattern from easy circuits, then corrects hard ones. Their test bed is a four-hydrogen molecule solved with a variational method under a realistic noise model from a real device.

Two upgrades sharpen the correction. Energy sampling keeps only the lowest-energy training circuits, biasing the fit toward the target state. A non-Clifford extrapolation step stretches the correction further along a tuned path. Careful tuning studies show which settings drive the gains. Cleaner energies from noisy hardware matter for quantum chemistry, where small errors can flip a predicted reaction.
arxiv-2511-03756:
Aniket Jivani, Cosmin Safta, Beckett Y Zhou, and Xun Huan build a cheaper stand-in model for field outputs that depend on uncertain inputs. Their method pairs many low-cost simulations, which capture the main trends, with a few costly high-fidelity runs that correct bias. A Karhunen-Loeve expansion joined to polynomial chaos keeps the link between inputs and output fields explicit.

Active learning chooses each new costly run where error looks largest, guided by cross-validation and a Gaussian process model. Tests cover an analytic case, a convection-diffusion system, and a turbulent jet flow. Gains depend on low-fidelity quality, and in some settings a high-fidelity-only model still wins, which the authors report openly.
arxiv-2511-03856:
Yanahan Paramalingam and Adam Noel model how signalling molecules spread through a growing biofilm, the bacterial community that coordinates behaviour by quorum sensing. Earlier work showed that water channels in some biofilms make spread direction-dependent. As the film matures those channels develop, so spreading itself changes over time.

Their 2D model shifts from uniform spread to directional spread, matching that growth. Particle simulations show the time-varying case blends features of both regimes. Mutual information between sender and receiver rose with more signal molecules, shorter distance, stronger direction dependence, and shorter symbol overlap. A scaling analysis suggests the results carry to other sizes, relevant to fighting resistance and to bioprocessing uses.
arxiv-2511-04656:
Jocelyn Finbar Russell, writing alone, builds a geometric model for renormalizing indifferent fixed points. The maps are holomorphic with two critical points and an irrationally indifferent fixed point. Arithmetic traits of the rotation number shape the local dynamics.

The model also encodes the angle between the two critical points. From it, Russell creates a topological picture of the dynamics near the point. The topology of the largest invariant set is explained in the same frame. Such models help mathematicians see how number theory steers complex dynamics in bi-critical cases, where two critical points interact at once.
arxiv-2511-04856:
Thore Gerlach and two colleagues build quantum Boltzmann machines for sample-efficient reinforcement learning. Their continuous semi-quantum design supports actions that vary smoothly, not just discrete picks. Exponential-family priors govern the visible units of the model.

Quantum Boltzmann distributions handle the hidden units, cutting qubit needs while staying expressive. Gradients for the continuous variables come out analytically, a rare convenience. That lets the model plug straight into actor-critic learning loops. Their continuous Q-learning swaps global maximization for sampling from the machine, sidestepping an instability that plagues continuous control with classical value functions.
arxiv-2511-05456:
Naveen Raj Manoharan and co-authors add a light conditioning trick so graph-based physics simulators can shift across materials, not just one. Graph simulators learn fluids, soft solids, and grain flows well and adapt to new shapes, but a model trained on one material fails on others.

Using grain flows as the test case, they condition the model on material values with few added parameters. One simulator can then mimic many grain types. That flex could bring learned simulators to real design work, where the material mix changes from job to job.
arxiv-2511-05656:
Damien Easson examines what happens at the inner horizon of a charged black hole in a simplified quantum model. Theory predicts that light falling toward that horizon gets amplified, which may destroy the horizon itself. The reduced Polyakov model makes one part of this effect exactly calculable.

Easson finds that the amplified flux diverges at a set rate unless a precise balance holds. That balance at the inner horizon differs from the matching condition at the outer horizon. Common choices for the quantum state do not meet it. Other effects, like classical tails falling in late, change the strength of the divergence in ways he works out case by case.
arxiv-2511-05756:
Husam Farraj leads a team squeezing lead titanate, a well-known ferroelectric, to pressures found deep in planets. They used synchrotron X-rays and diamond anvil cells, plus computer theory, to watch how the crystal responds up to a hundred gigapascals. Heat, they found, changes everything.

Compressed cold, the material held its known phase all the way up. Laser-heated, it broke apart into lead oxide and titanium oxide, just as theory said it should above a set pressure. The lead oxide took new forms, including one never reported before. One form is predicted to turn metallic under pressure while the others stay semiconducting. The work shows the path taken, hot or cold, decides which phases appear.
arxiv-2511-05856:
Rui Huang leads a team cataloging X-ray sources across the Andromeda galaxy, our large neighbor. As part of a legacy survey with the XMM-Newton telescope, they chart how many sources shine at each brightness level, a tool called a luminosity function. More than four thousand sources fall in their field.

They built the functions for the disk and halo separately, using the halo as a background estimate for the disk. Low-mass X-ray binaries, where a compact object feeds from a normal star, dominate the disk. Andromeda's output per unit of stellar mass runs lower than in other galaxies, likely due to its long quiet spell in star formation. The inner arm region suggests those binaries fade fast after about a billion years.
arxiv-2511-05956:
Daomin Cao and Jie Wan prove that tight clusters of swirling tubes can exist in an ideal fluid, shaped as helices that turn together. They start from an elliptic equation tied to vortex motion. For tiny core size, they build solutions whose spin clusters near one point at a stated scale.

The build uses the Green function of the operator and a finite-size reduction, which shrinks the problem to a functional set by the medium and a charge-like term. As a use case, they prove that traveling, rotating helical vortex tubes exist for the 3D Euler equations in an endless cylinder. The tubes are thin and carry any chosen strength. The result confirms a picture proposed in the nineteen-nineties and covers lopsided layouts of the helices too.
arxiv-2511-06156:
Maximilian Schaller and Stephen Boyd consider how a seller should price a set of products to earn the most profit. Prices must respect set limits, and each product's sales respond both to its own price and to the prices of the others. The authors show the task can be written as maximizing a sum of a convex and a concave function.

Three solution methods are compared head to head. One applies the convex-concave procedure, one uses a custom minorization-maximization scheme built on quadratic programs, and one uses a general nonlinear programming solver. In numerical tests all three reliably reach the same best prices, suggesting those prices are likely the global optimum.
arxiv-2511-06856:
Andrea Testa, Søren Hauberg, Tamim Asfour, and Leonel Rozo generalize the Schrödinger bridge, a system for steering a random process between two probability distributions. Current bridge methods assume energy is conserved along the way, which limits the shapes they can model. Real processes, from robot motion to molecular dynamics, often gain or lose energy.

Their non-conservative bridge is built on contact Hamiltonian mechanics, which allows energy to vary with time. By parameterizing the space of distributions, the bridge problem becomes a geodesic computation in a finite-dimensional space, solved non-iteratively with near-linear cost and implemented as a residual network. The method also supports guided creation through task-certain distance measures, and the authors validate it on manifold navigation, molecular dynamics, and image creation.
arxiv-2511-06956:
Xian Jing-Tian and eleven co-authors model the stray light that will contaminate images from the China Space Station Telescope. Stray light from bright sources outside the field of view degrades detection sensitivity, and its level depends on the telescope's orbit and pointing, not just its baffles. The team built an analytical model tailored to this telescope for fast, realistic estimates.

The model accounts for backgrounds from moonlight, starlight, and earthshine arriving off-axis, adds zodiacal light, and includes scattering and ghost images from bright stars inside the field. Because it evaluates conditions quickly and accurately, it can feed both image simulations and observation scheduling, helping planners avoid the worst stray-light geometry. The work supports realistic scientific simulations for the survey mission.
arxiv-2511-07056:
Frédéric Jaron and Valentí Bosch-Ramon disentangle the clockwork of LS I +61 303, a gamma-ray binary pulsing from radio to very high energies. Its light curves show periods near twenty-six point five days and twenty-six point nine days, plus a long cycle of four point six years. A signal near twenty-six point seven days appears occasionally, and all are interrelated by beating, so astronomers debate which are physical and which are interference artifacts. A fifth period near twenty-six point three days was recently claimed.

Staying purely phenomenological, the authors ran generalized Lomb-Scargle analyses on archival radio data and compared them with synthetic curves containing selected signals. Only synthetic data including all three periods together reproduced the observations, down to the noise level. All three, they conclude, could correspond to real physical processes.
arxiv-2511-07256:
Charles Livingston makes a classic knot invariant computable for large knots. In 1928 Alexander defined a sequence of knot polynomials; the first is the famous Alexander polynomial, and the rest refine it. They are defined through the homology of the knot's infinite cyclic cover and computed, in principle, by putting an associated matrix into Smith normal form. In practice, standard Smith form algorithms slow to impracticality even on some sixteen-crossing knots.

Livingston develops methods that effectively compute these higher Alexander polynomials for knots with up to one hundred crossings. The advance turns a theoretically defined but practically inaccessible family of invariants into a usable tool for distinguishing knots and probing their structure. The paper details the algorithmic ideas that tame the normal form computation.
arxiv-2511-07456: Ilijas Farah poses a playful but deep question about matrices: as square complex matrices grow without bound, do their algebras start to look alike? The short abstract admits nobody knows the answer yet. Farah frames the problem as a game, inviting readers to play along and see how far the play leads. As a brief, openly exploratory piece on a hard open question in operator algebras, it offers an entry point and a challenge rather than a settled theorem.
arxiv-2511-07956:
Qiuyue Liang, Kimihiro Nomura, and Hidetoshi Omiya explore whether pulsar polarization can reveal parity violation in gravity waves. Pulsar timing arrays already probe nanohertz gravity wave backgrounds, but timing alone cannot sense their handed part. Light signal arrays track how pulsar light is angled, offering a varied channel.

From geometric optics, the authors derive how a gravity wave background rotates electromagnetic polarization during travel. Cross-correlating timing and polarimetry signals isolates circular polarization while keeping the Hellings Downs pattern. With future facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array, this route could rival current astrometric sensitivity to that handed signal.
arxiv-2511-08056:
Nived Johny and colleagues report a tabletop all optical oscillator that mimics negative mass for quantum noise cancellation. Precision optical sensors suffer radiation pressure noise from their own measurement light. Pairing a sensor with an effective negative mass system can cancel that back action noise across a broad band of frequencies.

Their device copies an optomechanical interaction using down conversion and beam splitting, with flexible wavelength and compact size. Because many parts interact, the team built an in place characterization scheme to measure the coupled parameters. The values meet earlier targets, projecting a clear reduction in quantum back action noise at the best frequency.
arxiv-2511-08656:
Roman Cherniha writes a comment on a recent Physica D study of fluid flow through a porous medium in a channel whose walls dilate. That study modeled an unsteady, two-dimensional, viscous incompressible flow and then simplified the model to a fourth-order partial differential equation.

Its main claims were the Lie and nonclassical symmetries found for that equation, results that later work might build on. Cherniha argues those symmetry results are incomplete and misleading as published. Comment papers like this one serve as formal corrections inside the journal record. Readers of the original study are pointed to the gaps so they do not rely on symmetry claims that do not hold as stated.
arxiv-2511-08756:
Al Nahian Mugdho and four co-authors design a two-hop wireless link meant for sixth-generation networks that mix ground and aerial platforms. The first hop blends free-space optics with terahertz radio, switching between them as conditions change, and the second hop bounces signals off a reconfigurable intelligent surface carried in the air.

Closed-form formulas are derived for outage probability and bit error rate under both hard and soft switching strategies. The hybrid design improves performance by roughly half compared with a traditional radio-optical framework, and the aerial surface alone adds about forty percent. Placing the surface lower and midway between endpoints works best. High signal-to-noise analysis pins down the diversity order, and Monte Carlo simulations confirm the formulas.
arxiv-2511-08956:
Jens Malmquist asks when a jump process obeys the elliptic Harnack inequality. A jump process is a random motion that moves by sudden leaps. The inequality is a regularity principle saying that well-behaved functions for the process cannot oscillate too wildly. His processes are isotropic unimodal Lévy processes, a symmetric family whose behavior is encoded in a jump kernel.

Probabilistic methods developed here often settle the question from the kernel and its truncated second moments alone, without heavy analysis. Subordinated Brownian motions, an important subclass, get special attention. Malmquist produces the first known example of such a motion that fails the inequality. He also shows that many processes already known to satisfy it keep satisfying it under bounded perturbations. The group includes geometric stable and relativistic variants. And he settles cases earlier methods could not decide.
arxiv-2511-09256:
Mohammed Srati presents a new family of function spaces for nonlocal problems whose behavior changes with direction and place. The spaces blend fractional smoothness, directional bias, and Musielak-style variable growth in one approach. They extend two older families: fractional Orlicz-Sobolev spaces with directional bias, and variable-exponent fractional Sobolev spaces.

Srati works out the spaces' basic traits and embedding results, setting up a solid variational approach. He then studies long-range eigenvalue problems with variable growth and direction-dependent fractional operators. Using critical point theory and modular analysis, he proves eigenvalues exist. The results extend and unify several earlier models for long-range partial differential equations, the author argues.
arxiv-2511-09656:
Ethan Payne, Lee McCuller, and Katerina Chatziioannou propose counting individual photons to hear the faint ring of merged neutron stars. The postmerger signal carries dense-matter physics, but it stays rare and weak even for next-generation detectors. Above a kilohertz the data are dominated by quantum noise, which makes a photon-counting readout natural.

In that scheme, signals and noise arrive as discrete photon counts in a chosen mode basis. Simulations show roughly one in a hundred signals with very low signal-to-noise can still yield a single detecting photon. Accumulating tens of thousands of signals could double the precision on a neutron star's radius, they estimate. Reducing classical noise would tighten the constraints further.
arxiv-2511-10056:
Zijing Liu, Bin Feng, He Cao, and Yu Li study protein structure tokenization, which converts three-dimensional protein shapes into discrete tokens that language-style models can process alongside sequences. They first show that using these tokens well depends on rich pre-trained sequence embeddings to bridge the gap between the sequence and structure vocabularies. Looking inside the structure vocabulary itself, they find heavy redundancy.

Many distinct tokens encode nearly identical local geometries, acting as structure synonyms. Rather than a flaw, that redundancy becomes a tool: swapping synonyms perturbs a predicted structure into alternative shapes, generating conformational ensembles almost instantly. The lightweight method reproduced protein flexibility competitively with state-of-the-art models, offering a cheap route to protein dynamics that normally needs heavy simulation.
arxiv-2511-10156:
S Rahul and A Harshitha explore competing ways that waves can become trapped on a disordered, non-Hermitian random graph lattice. Their tight-binding model has three controls: asymmetric hopping, on-site disorder, and a random long-range coupling that defines the graph itself. Two localization mechanisms are in play, one driven by the non-Hermitian skin effect and one by ordinary Anderson disorder.

Sweeping the parameters, the authors find strong competition between the two mechanisms across regimes. Even under strong disorder, skin-effect localization coexists with Anderson localization rather than being destroyed by it. They close by discussing what this competition could mean for machine learning architectures and for information propagation in complex networks, where similar graph structures and asymmetries appear naturally.
arxiv-2511-10356:
Chenyi Li, Wanli Ma, Zichen Wang, and Zaiwen Wen present SITA, an approach for autoformalizing theorems that instantiate abstract mathematical structures in concrete settings. Language models reason informally with growing skill but stumble when a research result must be written as a machine-checked Lean proof about a specific example of an abstract theory. SITA treats formalized abstract structures as modular templates carrying definitions, assumptions, operations, and theorems.

For a given instance, the system generates the Lean definitions and declarations, wires them through the typeclass mechanism, and builds verified theorems by checking the structural assumptions. Language model generation is refined with feedback to keep output formally correct. Tests on optimization problems show the approach formalizing diverse instances grounded in abstract structures.
arxiv-2511-10456:
Ivan Biočić, Bruno Toaldo, and Lena Zuspann build a new kind of branching process to model how cancer spreads through the body. In their model, particles stand for tumor cells or clusters that can be absorbed, keep moving, or settle in place, and the process records where each particle sits.

The team constructs the process rigorously and proves its Markov property by embedding it in a larger process that tracks labels, positions, and phases of living particles. They then study the Feller property of the related semigroup, proving it for a simplified version that counts particles in each class. For that version they also derive an explicit generator, which opens the door to Feynman-Kac formulas for computing quantities of interest.
arxiv-2511-10756:
Jonathan Teo, Lee Xin Wei, and Hoong Chuin Lau investigate why equivariant quantum circuits work so well on the travelling salesman problem, and how far that success can be pushed. These circuits reach near-optimal solutions on small problems of up to twenty cities using just two parameters at depth one, but simulating larger cases explodes in time and memory.

The authors propose Size-Invariant Grid Search, a training optimization for quantum reinforcement learning. They use it to simulate a trained depth-one circuit on problems up to 350 cities. At one hundred cities, simulation time fell by more than 96 percent compared with reinforcement learning simulations, while the optimality gap stayed within a whisker of the trained model. They also give a theoretical account of the size-invariance behind the speedup.
arxiv-2511-11156:
Anand Dessai shows that in every odd dimension from five upward, large families of closed shapes carry infinitely many genuinely unlike geometries with positive Ricci curvature. Ricci curvature measures how volume grows around a point compared with flat space, and positive values mark a kind of rounded, closed-up geometry. A geometry here means a full distance rule on the shape, not just its outline.

The count is made precise through the moduli space, the space whose points are the geometries themselves. For these shapes, that space splits into infinitely many separate pieces, so no continuous path can turn one such geometry into another. The result gives a sharp picture of how rich positive-curvature geometry can be.
arxiv-2511-11656:
Luca Marzari and three co-authors take a probabilistic route to a hard verification problem: finding all inputs for which a neural network's output satisfies a given property. Exact methods exist, but the problem is fundamentally hard in the worst case, so exact tools scale poorly.

Their method, RF-ProVe, trains an ensemble of randomized decision trees, a random forest, to propose candidate input regions where the property holds, aiming for high-confidence guarantees with bounded error. Randomized and bootstrap ideas let the method capture complex, high-dimensional regions. For safety checking of learned systems, probably-right answers delivered quickly may serve better than exact answers that never arrive.
arxiv-2511-11756:
J. W. Moffat and E. J. Thompson clarify a regulator used in nonlocal quantum field theory. In such theories, interactions are smeared out to tame ultraviolet divergences. The regulator is an entire function of a covariant operator. It is chosen to respect gauge invariance. Its legitimacy needed a careful check.

The work uses the background-field formalism around flat backgrounds. Plane waves then diagonalize the wave operator. So the regulator becomes a simple factor in momentum space. After rotation to Euclidean momenta, loop integrals gain strong damping at high energy. No new poles or branch cuts appear. The result gives the nonlocal program a gauge-safe basis for a core tool.
arxiv-2511-11856:
The SNO+ Collaboration reports a new measurement of reactor antineutrino oscillations from one point four six kilotonne-years of data gathered between May 2022 and July 2025. Antineutrinos arriving mainly from reactors at two hundred forty, three hundred fifty, and three hundred fifty-five kilometers carry an oscillation pattern in their energy spectrum.

Spectral analysis yields a mass-squared difference close to, and now rivaling, the precision of KamLAND, the only other long-baseline reactor measurement of its kind. Combined with solar neutrino results, the global mixing parameters tighten further. The same data improve the geoneutrino signal, neutrinos from Earth's interior, sharpening a rare probe of our planet's radioactive heat.
arxiv-2511-11956:
Andreas Habring fills a rigor gap in the theory of Langevin annealing. It is a sampling scheme where a diffusion chases a moving target distribution. Recent proofs measure progress with the Kullback-Leibler divergence. That is the gap between the sampler's density and the target. They differentiate it in time without checking that the derivative exists.

The short paper derives that time derivative with care. The scheme is a generalized one, driven by the score of the time-dependent target. The formula is justified, with its conditions made explicit. Every convergence argument built on it gains protection. Annealing samplers support Bayesian computation and generative modeling. Their foundations deserve this kind of load-bearing check.
arxiv-2511-12156:
M. Barbillon and three co-authors make three-dimensional maps of dust extinction in the disc of the Milky Way. Dust dims and reddens starlight, so knowing where it sits is vital for correcting observations and for reading the galaxy's structure. Their maps use data from the Gaia mission.

The method starts from a Gaia catalogue of about five point six million stars whose physical traits were measured from spectra in a way that does not depend on dust. By comparing each star's observed color with its expected color, they estimate extinction, then build high-resolution maps around the Sun. The maps let them compare dust patterns with tracers of the galaxy's spiral arms.
arxiv-2511-12456:
Sukanya Kudva, Edward Dowling and Anil Aswani design auctions that stay truthful even when bidders collude. Collusion can cut revenue and harm honest bidders, and standard mechanisms are vulnerable to it. Their approach uses a machine learning classifier that predicts, even imperfectly, which bidders are likely colluding.

A first result shows collusion seriously harms standard multi-unit auctions mainly when the colluding group is large, so the design focuses there. Building on the classic Vickrey-Clarke-Groves mechanism, they propose two variants that charge posted prices to suspected colluders while running the standard rule for others. Keeping truthfulness while splitting items dynamically between the groups is the technical core.
arxiv-2511-12656:
Dana Fisman and Noa Izsak ask what languages cellular automata can generate. Cellular automata are grids of cells that update in lockstep from simple local rules, and they are famous for producing rich behavior from plain beginnings. Earlier work mostly simulated their dynamics; this paper treats them formally as language generators. The languages collect finite words read from the active parts of configurations that a one-dimensional automaton can reach from regular starting patterns.

To capture structured motion, the authors define gliders as one-cell carriers that move at a fixed velocity and interact under set rules. They then prove a surprise: even with regular starting patterns and local rules, the generated languages can be non-regular and even non-context-free. That makes these automata a richer computing model than their simple rules suggest, with possible uses in checking systems of many ordered agents.
arxiv-2511-12856:
Anuradha Madugalla and four co-authors argue that safety-critical software must be engineered around vulnerable users, not just around technical faults. Systems for healthcare, defense, transport, and disaster management demand strict requirements work, but that rigor usually targets the technology.
