Valeria Díaz Moreno and co-authors check whether quiet neighbor qubits spoil a key quantum gate in fluxonium circuits. Fluxonium qubits are prized for clean control, and clean two qubit gates exist for pairs. Bigger chips, though, park idle spectator qubits next to the working pair.

The team models four linked fluxonium qubits and runs the CNOT gate on two of them. Errors from spectators shrink fast when their tones sit far from the working pair tones. With the right tone layout, gate errors fell below one in ten thousand, with gates under 100 nanoseconds. Since links are local, the same layout rules should scale to long chains, a hopeful sign for bigger machines.
arxiv-2512-12856:
Saad Alqithami looks at how AI agents that talk with people over long periods should handle memory. Storing everything is costly and raises privacy risks. Forgetting too much, by contrast, makes an agent lose track of goals and people.

He presents MaRS, a memory plan inspired by human cognition, with typed records for events, facts, social ties, and tasks. Six forgetting rules balance recall, privacy, and cost. A test suite called FiFA checks agents on story sense, goals, social recall, privacy, and cost. Across 300 test runs, a hybrid forgetting rule scored 0.911 overall, the best result reported.
arxiv-2512-13156:
Viktoria Freingruber and co-authors present a new model of microbial aggregates, clumps where several bacterial species live and grow together. Inside a clump, species compete for shared food, and some benefit from the waste products of others. Space matters as much as chemistry here.

Their model uses partial differential equations with cross-diffusion and reaction terms. Bacteria spread passively, pushed by population pressure, and grow as food allows. Numerical tests show the model reproduces the key spatial patterns seen in earlier individual based simulations across three check scenarios. They also derive a competition system from a biased random walk on a lattice.
arxiv-2512-13256:
Bilal Kousar and co-authors report steady, reproducible quantized transport in a graphene quantum Hall system, a platform whose quirks have limited its use in topological superconductivity. Screening long-range interactions with a metallic bismuth selenide back gate stabilized the effect at low magnetic fields.

Beyond resistance plateaus, they built gate-defined junctions between chiral and helical channels that can pass or block a single helical channel on demand. That control is not possible in standard time-reversal symmetric systems. They traced quantization breakdown to contact induced doping and fixed it with large area contacts. The system suits future topological devices that need superconducting proximity.
arxiv-2512-13956:
Zishan Bai and co-authors present AOI, a multi-agent framework for autonomous IT operations in cloud-native systems. Incidents unfold across microservices while logs and metrics flood in faster than operators can read them. Recovery actions must be coordinated without losing the causal context that makes them safe.

AOI splits duties across an Observer, a read-only Probe, and a guarded Executor, linked by dynamic scheduling. A hierarchical memory system with LLM-based compression preserves context across long incidents. In AIOpsLab simulations and Loghub-derived scenarios, AOI raised task success to 94.2% and cut mean time to resolution by 34.4% versus the strongest baseline. It compressed context by 72.4% while keeping 92.8% of diagnostic information.
arxiv-2512-14356:
Dominik Pacholski, Sandro Mereghetti, and Martin Topinka present a catalog of magnetar bursts from the INTEGRAL satellite in a 2025 paper. Magnetars are young neutron stars powered mainly by magnetic energy, and they emit short bursts of hard X rays lasting under a second.

The team searched more than twenty years of archival data from the IBIS instrument, covering 15 keV to 1 MeV. They found 1349 bursts from 21 of the 34 magnetars and candidates examined. Burst durations follow a lognormal distribution centered near 0.1 seconds. Most bursts came from three very active sources. Their spectra fit an exponentially cut off power law, with peak energies mostly between about 20 and 100 keV, depending on the source.
arxiv-2512-15256:
Hoang-Anh Le and two coauthors argue that entanglement between fractional charges can draw a curved space into being. Some topologically ordered materials host anyons, particles with fractional charge and exotic statistics. The authors study pairs of half charged semions that arise on opposite zigzag edges of a disordered graphene nanoribbon.

Though far apart, the pair shows long range quantum entanglement. The team analyzes how that entanglement scales, using mutual information, and embeds the ribbon into a bulk geometry like anti de Sitter space. In that picture, the entanglement defines minimal surfaces in the bulk, giving a geometric view of the edge correlations. The result is a holographic portrait of fractionalized degrees of freedom in a nearly one dimensional system. It shows emergent geometry from entanglement even without conformal symmetry.
arxiv-2512-15656:
Pavel Sekatski and Jef Pauwels show that all entangled states are nonlocal in the broadcast scenario in a 2025 paper. Entanglement and Bell nonlocality are not the same: some entangled states admit a local hidden variable model for all local measurements. That gap has stood as a basic fact of quantum theory.

In a minimal broadcast extension of the Bell setup, the gap disappears. For every entangled state, the authors find local broadcasting maps and measurements whose four party correlations no separable source across the main cut can reproduce. They also show all multipartite states, mixed ones included, can be broadcast self tested under a natural operational definition.
arxiv-2512-15756:
Yoon Pyo Lee and co authors show that scientific feedback can push generative models beyond the conventions in their training data in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Human design habits narrow the options present in training sets, and models learn those narrowed preferences. Feedback tied to real performance might reopen the search.

Tests cover reactor lattice design with simulated feedback and chemical reaction choices with measured yields. In both, adaptation improved performance while raising the share of choices that training data had excluded. In the reaction case, use of excluded ligands rose from 0.29 to about 0.70 as yield error fell. Controls link the shift to the scientific objective itself.
arxiv-2512-16156:
L Levin leads a large SKA working group team in surveying neutron stars in a paper made public on arXiv in 2025. More than 3,500 non-accreting neutron stars are known, from ordinary pulsars to magnetars with extreme magnetic fields. The SKA telescopes should swell that census, adding radio pulsars to every branch of the family and likely revealing new kinds of sources.

The authors review the types of neutron stars and the questions a bigger sample can answer. Open puzzles include how isolated pulsars evolve, how magnetars connect to high-field and long-period pulsars, and what dense matter inside these stars is made of. More pulsars in binaries and triples would sharpen tests of gravity and general relativity. The paper maps how SKA sensitivity, wide views, and many beams enable that research.
arxiv-2512-16256:
Rahul Thakur and three co-authors test modified gravity in their 2025 arXiv paper. They study f(R, phi) theories in the Palatini formalism, where curvature and a scalar field jointly drive cosmic expansion. The goal is one model that covers both the early inflation era and today's accelerating universe.

Assuming the curvature part behaves like Starobinsky gravity, they check stability after inflation and find two fixed points that give a stable, accelerating late universe. Data from the DESI survey, cosmic chronometers, and supernovae tighten the picture further. One surviving fixed point has expansion driven by a phantom scalar field, which acts more strongly than a cosmological constant. Timescale arguments suggest that point may be temporary, with the universe later settling into potential-driven expansion.
arxiv-2512-16456:
Masashi Hatano and five co-authors synthesize human movement in an arXiv paper published in 2025. Before picking something up, people spot the target from afar, a behavior called gaze priming, then approach and reach. Generating realistic motion with that two-stage pattern is the paper's focus.

The team curated 23,700 gaze-primed reaching sequences from five public data sets, the first collection of its kind. They pretrained a text-conditioned diffusion model for motion, then fine-tuned it on goal poses and target locations from those sequences. A new metric, Prime Success, joins Reach Success in judging whether generated motion truly imitates the natural pattern. Across all five data sets, the model produced varied full-body motion showing both priming and reaching, beating baselines and recent methods. Such synthesis supports animation, robotics, and virtual character control.
arxiv-2512-16856:
Nenad Tomašev and coauthors argue that AI safety must cover groups of agents, not just single systems. Most safety work assumes one monolithic general AI, yet capability may first arrive as patchwork teams of lesser agents with split skills that coordinate.

With tool-using agents now deployed and able to talk and team up, the authors call this an urgent gap. Their frame for distributional AGI safety centers on virtual agent sandbox economies, markets whose rules are sealed or semi-sealed. Agent trades there would run under robust market rules with audits, reputation tracking, and oversight, aiming to curb joint risks that single-agent checks cannot see.
arxiv-2512-16956:
Shravan Chaudhari and coauthors present SpIDER. It is a retrieval method that helps coding agents find the right functions in a large codebase. The query may be a bug report or a request. Sparse word matching ignores the graph shape of code. Dense embedding search ignores it too. That shape holds the calls and containment links.

SpIDER grows its candidate set along that graph. It tags each added function with the seed and link type that brought it in. The set thus stays auditable at a fixed budget. The graph is built from syntax trees on demand. On SpIDER-Bench, recall at 20 rose by at least 13 percent relative on containment links. It rose by at least 27 percent once call links were added. The bench draws on three SWE benchmarks across four languages.
arxiv-2512-17256:
Shakir Ali and three co-authors build special matrices used to scramble data inside ciphers. An MDS matrix spreads each input across many outputs, which makes coded messages harder to untangle. Recursive kinds are prized because they can be built step by step on cheap hardware. The team works over Galois rings, number systems richer than plain fields.

Their recipes grow out of skew polynomials, where the order of terms matters. They prove rules that tell which polynomials yield good matrices, plus one rule based on the roots of a linked polynomial. The methods widen the known family a great deal, even in the non-commutative setting. The binary case used in real ciphers gets special attention as a target for fast diffusion layers.
arxiv-2512-17556:
L. Lafforgue and coauthors based in Innsbruck probe how bosonic erbium atoms in mixed spin states scatter off one another. Tuning the atoms near resonances reveals how their collisions can be turned up, down, or nearly off.

The team reports scattering resonances between and within spin states that have an asymmetric shape and a clear dip in atom loss. A simplified model with several coupled channels traces the shape to destructive interference between pathways, the classic Fano effect. A whole series of these Fano Feshbach resonances across the spin channels ties back to one molecular state. Such control over collisions is a basic tool for building quantum matter from ultracold atoms with many internal states.
arxiv-2512-17856:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a hunt for heavy new particles that decay into a top quark and its antimatter twin. The search uses 140 inverse femtobarns of proton collisions at 13 TeV from the Large Hadron Collider. Chosen events hold one or two light particles called leptons, missing energy, and at least two jets.

Targets span masses from 0.4 to 5.0 TeV and cover three guessed particle types, from new force carriers to gravity related states. The counts matched what the Standard Model predicts, so no new particle showed up. Instead the team sets firm caps on how often such particles could be made, which narrows the space for future hunts.
arxiv-2512-17956:
Victor Stasiu presents a small toolkit for checking how chatbots state their confidence and handle ranking tasks. Safety tuning can make leading models hedge or refuse too often, which hurts teamwork. His Victor Calibration method asks a model to recheck its own evidence in several passes and report a rising or falling confidence score.

Two companion checks audit model behavior without claims about inner feelings, and stress test whether rankings stay stable and fair. Trials on several Claude models showed smooth confidence paths and no broken safety rules. Stasiu is clear that one person ran the work, with one session per model, so the results are early hints that others should test.
arxiv-2512-18056:
Daniel David builds probabilistic digital twins of people, not machines. Apps often sum up a user with one fixed vector of numbers, which hides doubt and meaning. His twin treats each user as a hidden random state that gives rise to the answers and clicks we see.

A variational autoencoder learns those states from a survey style data set, keeping the math fully about chance rather than fixed traits. A checking pipeline then ties each hidden axis to real behavior with plain statistical tests. Axes lined up with traits like opinion strength and decisiveness. Most user differences formed smooth ranges, not tight clusters, which favors soft, doubt aware profiles.
arxiv-2512-18456:
Qilong Wu and three co-authors survey the security of AI-for-code systems, the tools like GitHub Copilot that now write, translate, and check software. Their systematization paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, covers three core uses and finds the same gaps recurring. Benchmarks lean on Python and toy problems, standard security datasets are missing, test data leaks into training, and defenses against attacks stay fragile.

A comparison of six leading models shows the problems in practice. Insecure patterns persist in generated code, and flaw detection breaks under attacks that preserve meaning. Fine-tuning can pull security goals off course, and translation gives uneven gains. The authors chart three fixes: secure defaults in generation, stronger detection benchmarks, and translation into safer languages.
arxiv-2512-20056:
Hao Li leads a nine-author team locating disaster photos on the map when seconds count. Cross-view geolocalization matches a ground photo against satellite views. It estimates where the shot was taken. ProbGLC reworks that task for disaster response. The events span hurricanes, wildfires, floods, and tornadoes. The frame joins probabilistic and fixed-output models in one. It does not make the user pick between them.

The probabilistic side gives uncertainty. It yields full distributions over places, plus a localizability score for each scene. That score says how findable the scene is. It backs clear choices on where to send resources. Tests ran on two cross-view disaster data sets. Accuracy sat near the top at both one-kilometer and twenty-five-kilometer tolerances. Data and code are public.
arxiv-2512-20856:
NVIDIA introduces the Nemotron 3 family, three open language models named Nano, Super, and Ultra. All share a hybrid Mamba-Transformer design with mixture-of-experts layers, built for agent tasks, reasoning, and conversation. Context windows reach one million tokens across the family.

Super and Ultra add two refinements: training in a compact four-bit format and a LatentMoE method said to raise quality, plus prediction layers that speed up text generation. Post-training used reinforcement learning in many environments, teaching tool use and adjustable reasoning budgets. Nano ships first with open weights; the larger two were announced to follow. NVIDIA pledges weights, software, recipes, and releasable data.
arxiv-2512-20956:
Xianjin Yang, Houman Owhadi, and four co-authors teach a machine-learning method to solve equations whose unknowns are entire functions. Functional renormalization group equations track how a physical theory changes across scales and are notoriously hard beyond perturbation theory. Their framework uses Gaussian process operator learning, building the representation directly on function space so it depends on no particular equation or grid.

Physical knowledge can enter through the prior mean or the kernel design, keeping the solver honest where data is thin. On the Wetterich and Wilson-Polchinski equations the method matches or beats the standard local-potential approximation while remaining far more flexible. Because it handles non-constant fields, it opens a route to configurations such as instantons that cruder approximations cannot reach.
arxiv-2512-21156:
Kiyoshi Sogo exhibits a three-way mirror in classical analysis. Many quantities can be written simultaneously as an infinite product, an infinite series, and a continued fraction. Three languages say one thing. He calls such an identity a triplicity. The point is computational. When the three forms agree, whichever is easiest to evaluate hands you the value of the others. That includes series that resist direct summation.

Triplicity reaches even divergent series, assigning them definite sums. Among the examples stands a ferociously divergent alternating series recorded in Entry 7 of Gauss's diary. Its terms explode through powers of two. The method obtains a finite value for it, about 0.4275 and then further digits beyond. Analysts fond of Ramanujan-style identities gain a unifying frame: products, sums, and fractions are not three toolboxes but one, and even divergence can be negotiated with rather than merely feared.
arxiv-2512-21256:
Alaa Alburai, Lluis Galbany, and twenty co-authors profile the dim cousins of cosmology's standard candles. From the Zwicky Transient Facility's second data release, 3,628 Type Ia supernovae, they extract 124 subluminous events, the largest single-instrument sample of its kind. The split runs 87 of the 91bg-like subtype, a dozen 86G-like, 18 04gs-like, and 7 02es-like explosions. Template fits, velocity and line-strength measurements, and averaged spectra per subtype anchor the picture.

Nearly all subluminous events prove intrinsically red, not merely dust-dimmed. Standard light-curve fitters, never trained on such objects, compensate by distorting their color parameters. The explosions favor massive, red host galaxies and the reddest local environments, with two subtypes erupting unusually far from their galactic centers. Two spectral diagnostics, a blended absorption strength near 4300 angstroms and a color-stretch measure, suffice to subclassify them, giving surveys a cheap sorting key for these faint but informative deaths.
arxiv-2512-21456:
Sukanya Krishna, Marie-Laure Charpignon, and Maimuna Majumder compare ways of estimating excess deaths from substance overdose in the United States during the COVID-19 pandemic. Excess mortality means deaths beyond what pre-pandemic patterns would predict. Getting this count right matters for judging the pandemic's toll.

The authors train models on national CDC data from 2015 to 2019 and project forward through 2023. They test the traditional SARIMA method against three deep learning designs: LSTM, Seq2Seq, and Transformer networks. The LSTM gives the best point estimates and the best-calibrated uncertainty ranges. Attention-based models do worse, apparently because they overfit historical averages instead of following new trends. The team also releases an open pipeline with prediction intervals, ready for state health departments. Their conclusion is that carefully validated neural models can beat classical statistics for public health forecasting under sudden change.
arxiv-2512-21656:
Yingying Yu, Chungang Zhu, and their co-authors tackle a reliability problem in 3D modeling: Coons volume mappings can fold over themselves. A Coons volume fills a solid by interpolating between its boundary surfaces, and it is widely used to generate meshes. If its Jacobian determinant touches zero or goes negative, the mapping is no longer regular and later work turns unstable.

The authors build a check with three parts. First, a general sufficient condition works for any boundary parameterization. For Bézier-form volumes, a second test reduces the check to the positivity of control coefficients of the Jacobian. A third, necessary condition, built from subdivision and Bézier blossoming, guarantees regularity in every subdomain. Together these yield an algorithm the team validates numerically. Regularity tracks how alike the two boundary surfaces are. Tests are fast, and the method extends to multi-patch B-spline volumes.
arxiv-2512-22056:
MaxCut, an NP-hard graph problem, tempts quantum methods, but such algorithms hit barren plateaus and hardware limits at scale. Yuefeng Lin and colleagues extend their distributed variational quantum eigensolver with a hybrid perturbation strategy, solving weighted MaxCut problems of up to one thousand vertices with only ten qubits.

Results show the method beats the classical Goemans-Williamson algorithm, and warm-starting from that algorithm's solutions improves them further. As a test, the team applied the solver to phasing on sequencing data for the human ABCA1 gene, producing haplotypes rivaling a projected classical run. It is NISQ-compatible and scalable for near-term quantum-enhanced optimization.
arxiv-2512-22156:
Jin Sob Kim, Hyun Joon Park, Wooseok Shin, and Sung Won Han describe their entry to a sound event localization and detection challenge run under DCASE 2022. The task asks systems to spot sounds in recordings, name their class, and estimate where each sound came from. The team built a ResNet-based model inside a system designed to survive messy real-world audio.

Their recipe leans on heavy data augmentation and a training mix that blends real sound scenes with simulated ones while keeping enough real samples in every batch. External sound sources add further variety. At test time they apply augmentation again and ensemble models by clustering confident predictions. The system beat the challenge baselines and stayed competitive on real recordings.
arxiv-2512-22356:
Ella M. Mansfield, Delaney A. Dunne, and Dongwoo T. Chung sharpen a technique for finding faint cosmic signals by stacking. Line-intensity mapping charts the universe at low resolution through spectral line glow, and stacking co-adds small map cutouts at known emitter positions to lift signal out of noise. Their upgrade fits an assumed signal shape rather than simply averaging, in two spatial dimensions or in three including the spectral axis.

They also stack at source coordinates more precise than the map's resolution. Tested on simulations mimicking the COMAP Pathfinder, the fitting methods gained up to twenty-five percent in detection significance over the plain stack. The best profile was wider than the telescope beam and Lorentzian in frequency. Clustering effects, including fingers-of-God smearing, shape what works best.
arxiv-2512-22656:
Argha Kamal Samanta, Deepak Mewada, Monalisa Sarma, and Debasis Samanta benchmark machine learning for reading brain-wave recordings across many disorders at once. Clinical EEG reading is manual, slow, and variable, and most automated work targets single problems like seizure spotting. This study instead classifies eleven brain disorders, from time-critical acute conditions to chronic childhood disorders and conditions with only faint EEG signs.

Recordings were processed in a standard bipolar montage and summed up by features spanning time statistics, spectra, complexity, and channel links. With severe class imbalance, the team tuned decision thresholds explicitly for sensitivity. Recall exceeded eighty percent for most kinds, and calibration lifted recall for rare conditions by fifteen to thirty points. Important features matched known clinical EEG markers.
arxiv-2512-22756:
K. S. Babu, Rahool Kumar Barman, and Dorival Gonçalves study whether the Large Hadron Collider could see lepton number violated by two units, a striking signal tied to how neutrinos get their mass. Their setting is the leptoquark version of the Zee model, where Majorana neutrino masses are generated in a loop of particles that includes leptoquarks, hypothetical particles linking quarks and leptons.

Those leptoquark interactions can produce two same-sign leptons plus jets in proton collisions, a signature with few ordinary backgrounds. After applying current experimental limits, the authors identify the main production channels and run a detailed collider analysis. They find the high-luminosity LHC could probe leptoquark masses up to about one and a half trillion electron volts in mass units. Seeing such a signal would directly confirm lepton number violation and prove neutrinos are Majorana particles.
arxiv-2512-22856:
Matthaus Zering, Jolyon Joyce, Tal Gurfinkel, and Jingbo Wang compare two remedies for a known weakness of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. That quantum algorithm is a favorite candidate for beating classical optimization, but random starting parameters usually make its gradients vanish, so training stalls. One remedy pretrains parameters with a Lie-algebraic classical simulation; the other, called NV-QWOA, restricts the search to a small subspace steered by only three hyperparameters.

The test bed is the unweighted MaxCut problem at deep circuit depth, run across hundreds of random and regular graphs with sixteen vertices each. Both strategies beat randomly initialized runs by a wide margin. NV-QWOA reached a mean approximation ratio close to ninety-nine percent within sixty iterations, while the pretrained approach improved more slowly over five hundred iterations. The authors read this as evidence that a well-structured small parameter space trains more robustly than pretraining.
arxiv-2512-23156:
Ivan Gonoskov, Christian Hünecke, and Stefanie Gräfe explain how laser-driven matter can emit light with quantum, nonclassical properties. Their focus is high-order harmonic generation, where an intense laser makes atoms radiate at many times the driving frequency. Starting from a Pauli-Fierz model of coupled light and matter, they split the joint wavefunction into a field-driven electronic state and a quantized light mode obeying coupled equations.

Inside that framework, nonclassicality has a simple dial: the bend in the electronic dipole's response to the light mode's coordinate. A nearly constant dipole yields coherent radiation. A linear response produces squeezed light. Stronger bends generate Wigner-function negativity, a stronger signature of quantumness. The mechanism is shown on atomic and molecular models, and its scaling with many emitters is checked. The authors present the picture as a design basis for engineering quantum light in intense laser-matter settings.
arxiv-2512-23356:
Xin Zhang and co-authors propose SGR, a framework that steadies large language model reasoning by grounding each step in a knowledge graph. Models answering complex questions often absorb noisy or irrelevant material during generation and drift into confident errors. SGR's response is to build a small external subgraph tailored to the query, pulling relevant entities and relations from a knowledge base before the model starts reasoning.

The model then works through the problem step by step over that structured subgraph, rather than free-associating over raw text. Several reasoning paths are generated and finally integrated into one answer. Across multiple benchmark datasets, the framework consistently beat strong baselines, which the authors attribute to the subgraph filtering out noise and giving each inference step explicit factual footing. The work is aimed at question answering and other tasks where deep, verifiable logical inference matters more than fluency.
arxiv-2512-23456:
Sukanya Mitra studies relativistic hydrodynamics, the theory that describes hot, fast-moving fluids such as the matter formed in heavy-ion collisions. Working from the relativistic kinetic equation, she uses a proposed collision kernel built to conserve both energy-momentum and particle current exactly. The paper appeared in a version accepted by Physics Letters B.

Mitra analyzes the poles of the kinetic equation and the dispersion relations that follow from them. In the long-wavelength limit these relations show the gradient structure expected of hydrodynamics, with spatial and time gradients appearing together in a single relaxation operator. She argues that keeping this structure, including time derivatives, is what protects the theory from breaking causality at any truncation order. The paper runs to just seven pages.
arxiv-2512-23556:
Xiaolin Zhang and five co-authors assess how well proposed Moon-based gravitational-wave detectors could locate sources on the sky. A lunar interferometer would fill the frequency gap between space missions such as LISA and TianQin and detectors on Earth. The team studies CIGO, a planned observatory on the rim of a lunar crater near the north pole, using the Fisher-matrix method for steady sources in the decihertz band.

Above a tenth of a hertz, CIGO localized sources better than LISA or TianQin and dominated a combined network. That holds provided lunar noise can be controlled at low frequencies. An upgraded design adding a fourth station at the crater floor, forming a tetrahedron, improved angular resolution about fivefold and widened sky coverage across the target band.
arxiv-2512-23756:
Pierre Mackenzie surveys and tests sparse random projections, a dimensionality reduction tool with a famous guarantee behind it. The Johnson-Lindenstrauss theorem says a cloud of points in a high-dimensional space can be mapped into far fewer dimensions while nearly preserving all pairwise distances. The classical construction multiplies by a dense Gaussian random matrix, which is slow when data are huge.

Sparse random matrices, with most entries zero, multiply much faster and are preferred in applications. Mackenzie outlines the constructions and proofs of Achlioptas and of Kane and Nelson, the contemporary standard, and then implements the sparse constructions to compare them empirically against the standard Gaussian version. The paper reads as a guided tour from theorem to practice, showing what sparsity costs and what it buys.
arxiv-2512-24056:
Wenye Li, Hongxu Chen, Jiacai Liu, and Ke Wei analyze policy mirror descent. The method is a general framework in reinforcement learning. Many policy gradient methods are special cases of it. The open question is sample complexity. How much data does the method need? Here samples arrive as one Markovian stream. Values are learned on the fly by temporal difference updates.

Earlier analyses assumed a simulator with free restarts. Others assumed values precomputed to a set accuracy. This paper studies two variants that learn values alongside the policy. One is off-policy. The other is mixed. With a small fixed step size, near-optimal performance is proven. The sample count scales like one over the squared error target. Adaptive step sizes remove a leftover logarithmic factor. The results tighten expectations for online data.
arxiv-2512-24156:
Evgenii Rudakov, Jonathan Shock, and Benjamin Ultan Cowley take on ARC-AGI-3. The benchmark holds game-like tasks. An agent must infer the rules by playing. Feedback is sparse, and levels grow harder. Leading language models fail these tasks badly. The authors try the opposite of learning. They use careful, systematic exploration tracked in a graph.

The agent breaks each frame into visual parts. Possible actions are ranked by visual salience. Explored states and transitions form a directed graph. The agent remembers what has been tried. It steers toward untested state-action pairs by the shortest path. On the preview challenge, it solved a median of thirty levels. That was out of fifty-two levels across six games. It placed third on the private leaderboard. The code is open source.
arxiv-2512-24256:
Dominic Batzler and five colleagues measure tritium sticking to fusion materials. Tritium adsorbs on surfaces and causes problems. Fusion plants and tritium laboratories both face them. How much accumulates depends on the material. Contaminated surfaces then need cleaning, preferably in place. Ozone under ultraviolet light is one candidate method.

A single setup at Tritium Laboratory Karlsruhe addresses both questions. Samples meet gaseous tritium while activity is tracked over time. The chamber can then fill with dry air, plain or ozonated. Beryllium and tungsten were the test materials. Both matter for fusion. Beryllium accumulated tritium over four times faster than tungsten. The cleaning tests brought a surprise. Ozone alone did no better than dry air. Ultraviolet light proved to be the required ingredient for real decontamination.
arxiv-2512-24456:
Gentian Zavalani speeds up solving PDEs on surfaces meshed with triangles. A fast direct solver framework exists for meshes built from four-sided cells. Each cell there uses tensor-product basis functions. Triangular meshes were locked out of that framework. Many real surfaces come in triangles, though. Zavalani removes the restriction.

Two high-order strategies handle the triangles. A reduced step converts them into four-sided cells for the existing machinery. A second method builds basis functions on triangles directly, using Dubiner's basis. Tests confirm the changes keep the framework's accuracy. Speed and the fast direct-solver structure survive as well. Time-dependent and moving surfaces are also covered. Reaction-diffusion systems demonstrate the method. Surface flow driven by geometry provides a second demonstration.
arxiv-2512-24556:
Muhammad Abdullahi Said and Muhammad Sammani Sani audit language model safety across languages and time frames. Safety tuning is usually tested in English. Whether it transfers to other languages is often assumed, not checked. The authors build HausaSafety, an adversarial dataset grounded in West African threat scenarios. Three leading models face it in English and Hausa.

A factorial design crosses language with temporal framing across many evaluations. The expected simple story did not appear. One model was safer in Hausa than in English, thanks to uncertainty-driven refusals. A deeper pattern dominated instead. Past-tense framing slipped past defenses badly. Future-tense framing triggered heavy over-refusal. Safety swung widely between the safest and weakest configurations. The authors conclude that models lean on surface heuristics. They propose invariant alignment for safety that survives language and tense shifts.
arxiv-2512-24856:
Sergio Alvarez-Telena and Marta Diez-Fernandez seek conceptual clarity for agentic AI through the lens of algorithmization, their field concerned with turning tasks into algorithms. Discourse on agents has fragmented, so precise definitions are offered from intelligence up to agentic AI itself. Their prior decade of work is reviewed to show how methods accumulated.

Distinctions between related notions structure the analysis that follows. Readers get an analytical framework meant to restore shared meaning to fast-moving terms. The historical framing, signaled by the back-to-the-future subtitle, argues current agent systems continue an older methodological trajectory rather than appearing from nowhere.
arxiv-2512-24956:
Domingos Salazar derives a matrix thermodynamic uncertainty relation for transport of non-Abelian charges, amounts whose parts do not commute and cannot be watched in one standard frame. Standard uncertainty relations bound current precision by entropy production, but quantum charge transport breaks their givens. Starting from an working entropy production defined by a distance between states, he singles out the experimentally accessible bath contribution.

A fully nonlinear, saturable lower bound follows for any current vectors. Quantum thermodynamics readers get a precision limit that respects noncommuting charges. Such bounds govern how exactly tiny-scale devices can move charge, spin, or energy at a given loss cost.
arxiv-2512-25056:
Liliang Wang and Alex Gorodetsky present a variational approach for stepwise Bayesian estimation of both settings and states in dynamic systems from noisy, incomplete observations. Digital twins need exactly this: continual updating of what a system is doing and what its model settings are, with honest uncertainty and fast computation. The joint distribution of states and settings given data is the target.

Their online method aims at reliability and speed together, rather than trading one for the other. Estimation readers get machinery for real-time digital twins. Decisions based on twins are only as trustworthy as the uncertainty attached to their estimates.
arxiv-2601-00056:
Nikolay V Gnezdilov and co-author Andrei I Pavlov offer a fresh route to thermalization, the puzzle of how an isolated quantum system comes to look statistical. Their 2026 paper sets aside the usual explanations based on quantum chaos, eigenstate thermalization, and typicality. Instead they consider a many-body system under strong random perturbation, where chaotic eigenvectors plus one global energy constraint do the work.

In their mechanism, the canonical ensemble appears directly as the first moment of the distribution describing those chaotic eigenstates, and the energy constraint sets the temperature. That yields thermal expectation values for both local and global quantities without splitting the system into a part and a bath. Numerical tests on a one-dimensional Ising chain show the predicted thermal behavior in eigenstate projectors and spin correlations. The authors note the scheme could prepare thermal states on a quantum computer.
arxiv-2601-00256:
Lixin Xu, writing alone, unifies two languages for symmetry in geometry and gauge theory. Equivariant cohomology tracks spaces with a group action. It comes in two main models, named for Cartan and Weil. A known transform links the two models explicitly. Xu lays out that bridge in full detail.

He then ties the frame to BRST quantization of gauge theories. The BRST complex turns out to match the Cartan model. Two deformations can both be read as gauge fixing steps. Joining them yields an equivariant Witten deformation. That joined view gives a clear analytic proof of a classic localization formula. Integrals of closed forms collapse to fixed point data. Worked examples on complex projective spaces ground the theory. Coordinate level calculations fill out the picture.
arxiv-2601-00356:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim study two classic counting procedures, called the A-algorithm and the B-algorithm, in a deformed setting. Adding a parameter called lambda bends the rules of each procedure. Their 2026 paper follows what the bending does to the sequences the procedures produce, using deformed Stirling numbers, which count ways to split sets into groups.

The pair derive plain formulas for the final sequences in terms of the starting ones. They also link the ordinary generating functions of the starting sequences to the exponential generating functions of the final ones. Under special starting choices, the deformed procedures output deformed versions of the Bernoulli and Euler numbers, two famous families in number theory.
arxiv-2601-00656:
Biraja Ghoshal is the sole author of a 2026 paper on quantum runs of bits of proteins. The aim is to learn how electrons act in the active sites of proteins. Ghoshal builds a hybrid frame: a quantum method does the hard core sums.

The test case is a small four-orbital bit of a serine protease, a protein that cuts other proteins. The method hit the mark set for chemical accuracy, a very tight error bar. It also won back about ninety-five in each hundred of the energy that plain methods miss. The author then tried the frame on wider cases. One case was a target tied to the virus that causes Covid-19. One was a liver protein that breaks down drugs, where it called most sites right. The work maps a path for quantum help in drug science.
arxiv-2601-00756:
Thomas Katraouras and Dimitrios Rafailidis address how large language models can keep learning after deployment without forgetting what they know or drowning in stored data. Memory-augmented approaches give a model an external memory bank to consult, but in real data streams that bank grows without limit. Full fine-tuning, the alternative, is expensive and prone to wiping old knowledge.

Their model, MBC, compresses the memory bank through a codebook optimization strategy applied during online adaptation. Instead of keeping every stored item verbatim, the bank is distilled into a compact codebook that preserves what matters for future queries. The goal is continual adaptation that stays affordable as streams grow, updating a model with new information while retaining prior knowledge.
arxiv-2601-01056:
Ifeanyi Ezuma and Ugochukwu Ugwu test automated ways to sort medical images of tissue samples into five classes, using a public set called LC25000. Such sorting helps doctors in digital pathology, where slides are scanned and read on screens. The team fine-tunes a deep network, InceptionResNet-v2, both as a direct classifier and as a source of image features for other models.

Used directly, the tuned network scores about ninety-six percent accuracy. Models fed its deep features do far better, with one neural network reaching near-perfect scores. Adding edge-shape features, known as HOG, helps in clean images but less when noise is added. Models built on deep features also hold up best as noise grows. The study gives labs a practical guide to which feature mixes stay reliable when image quality drops.
arxiv-2601-01656: David Montenegro and Giorgio Torrieri extend an earlier framework for diffusion that respects relativity in full. Their journal paper adds random Gaussian swings around the diffusion flow. It also deals with conserved charges, quantities that cannot be created or destroyed in the system. They comment on a seeming gap between two terms in the math. One term is tied to chemical potential, and the other to diffusion itself.
arxiv-2601-02056:
Holography builds a gravitational theory in one extra dimension. It starts from a quantum field theory on the boundary. Polchinski's exact renormalization group equation is one route to that construction. Semanti Dutta and B. Sathiapalan examine the symmetry hiding in that equation.

For a special choice of cutoff function, the bulk action obtained lives in anti-de Sitter space with its expected symmetry group. The authors prove a stronger claim. The evolution operator carries that same SO(1,d+1) symmetry for any cutoff function. The special conformal generators then depend on the cutoff. The result extends to the full Wilson action as well. A field redefinition does the work. The symmetry is thus a property of renormalization itself, not of one convenient cutoff.
arxiv-2601-02156:
Gaps in the debris belts around other stars, like the Kuiper belt gaps carved by our giant planets, betray unseen worlds. R. Bendahan-West and nineteen co-authors used the James Webb Space Telescope's MIRI coronagraph to hunt for planets in three gapped exoKuiper belt systems, HD 92945, HD 107146, and HD 206893.

No planet candidates appeared; everything detected matched background stars or galaxies. Combining the Webb non-detections with archival limits and measured stellar accelerations still rules out a large share of the possible planet parameter space. Testing scenarios from in-situ clearing to resonance shaping by inner planets, the authors conclude any planet causing the observed proper motion anomaly must sit within the inner twenty astronomical units.
arxiv-2601-02256:
Visual Autoregressive models, called VARs, build images step by step at growing scales, and Shikun Sun and co authors study how to train them with reinforcement learning. Unlike text models or diffusion models, a VAR sees a different kind of input at each step. That mismatch creates conflicts in the training signal, leading to unstable learning and poor fit to the training goal.

Their fix adds three parts to a group based policy method. An intermediate reward guides early steps, a step weighting scheme assigns credit more carefully over time, and a mask method borrowed from reward feedback learning limits effects in space and time. Together the parts raise sample quality and goal fit well above the plain baseline method.
arxiv-2601-02456:
Junhao Cai and a large InternVLA team present InternVLA-A1, a robot model that joins scene understanding, prediction of what will happen next, and action in one system. Models built only on multimodal language models understand instructions well but cannot deduce physical dynamics. World models that predict video capture dynamics but lack semantic grounding and break when their predictions err.

A unified mixture of transformers design runs three experts, for understanding, visual foresight, and action, linked by shared attention. Built on InternVL3 and Qwen3-VL, the model comes at two and three billion parameter scales. Pre training mixes real robot data with synthetic data and other sources. The aim is a manipulation policy that both knows what a command means and can picture its physical consequences before acting.
arxiv-2601-03156:
Sofie Goethals, Foster Provost, and João Sedoc ask a pointed question about generative AI. What is it about a prompt that makes the system produce output with a specific trait, such as toxicity, negative sentiment, or political bias? Groups deploying these systems need causal answers of exactly that kind, more and more. The authors adapt counterfactual explanations, a standard explainable-AI technique, to this setting.

Off-the-shelf counterfactuals fail here, because generative systems are non-deterministic and open-ended. The proposed framework works where downstream classifiers can reveal key traits of the outputs. An algorithm built on it produces prompt-counterfactual explanations: minimal prompt changes that would flip the trait. The authors demonstrate the approach on generative tasks. It gives decision-makers a concrete way to trace system behavior back to input choices.
arxiv-2601-03356:
Antoine Rignon-Bret and Matthieu Vilatte continue their null-infinity treatment of black hole thermodynamics by drawing a close parallel with open quantum systems. In semiclassical gravity, proofs of the generalized second law use information-theoretic tools on null surfaces. Those proofs structurally resemble the thermodynamics of open quantum systems. Such systems sit weakly coupled to heat reservoirs and follow Markovian dynamics. The authors build an explicit dictionary between the two settings.

Late-time boundary conditions play the role of the reservoir choice, vacuum states act as fixed points of the dynamics, and modular Hamiltonians become thermodynamic potentials. Building on the companion paper's dual second law, they show extra terms in the potentials admit a natural interpretation in this language. The second part applies the dictionary to work extraction from non-rotating black holes.
arxiv-2601-03556:
Sabrina Haque, Sarvesh Ingale, and Christoph Csallner study whether coding agents actually write tests in the pull requests they submit. Tests guard software correctness over time, so agent habits here matter as these tools join real projects. Using the AIDev dataset, the team measured how often tests appear, when they are added, and how test-bearing requests differ from others.

Requests containing tests grew more common over time. They also tended to be larger and slower to finish, while merge rates stayed about the same as for requests without tests. Agents differed from each other in test habits and in the balance between test code and production code. The study gives project maintainers a factual baseline for setting expectations of automated contributors.
arxiv-2601-03656:
Philipp Stärk and six co-authors compare ways to teach machine learning models two kinds of atomic charge at once. Static charges drive the electric forces between atoms, while dynamic charges describe how atoms answer an external field. Learning both well matters for accurate simulations of materials and liquids, yet the two are usually handled separately.

Using bulk water and water clusters as test cases, the team compared learning the charges independently with two coupled schemes. Coupling uses the physical link between the charges and must correct for dielectric screening. A single global screening constant worked poorly in uneven systems like clusters, where a local, environment-dependent factor did better. The findings guide builders of atomistic models toward charge schemes that respect real chemistry.
arxiv-2601-04056:
Yuanfeng Xu, Yuhao Chen, Liang Lin, and Guangrun Wang propose a unified way to generate both text and images. Text is discrete and images are continuous, so the two are usually modelled apart. Masked models read both directions well but have lagged in generation quality, and mixing modes adds alignment trouble.

Their framework, CoM-DAD, splits generation into two linked stages. A continuous latent diffusion process first plans high-level meaning on a smooth manifold. A discrete absorbing diffusion process then makes the tokens, guided by a changing noise schedule and the evolving plan. A mixed-modal transport step aligns the two modes without heavy paired encoders. The authors report better stability than standard masked modelling.
arxiv-2601-04156:
David A. Coulter leads ninety co-authors in reporting the most distant supernova ever confirmed by spectrum, a Type II event magnified by strong lensing. The explosion, nicknamed SN Eos, sits in a galaxy that emits Lyman-alpha light. It went off when the universe was only about a billion years old, soon after it turned transparent to ultraviolet light.

Archival Hubble images taken a year earlier catch far-ultraviolet light from the first days after the blast, a sign of shock breakout or impact with nearby material. Webb spectroscopy shows the parent star formed where metals were scarce, at most a tenth of the solar level. That makes SN Eos the first direct proof of massive star birth in such a poor setting, possible only because lensing brightened it so much.
arxiv-2601-04256:
Riccardo Camerlo and Francesco Dagnino measure how complex the family of monitorable sets can be. They study a countable space from a topological point of view. Monitorable sets arise when one asks what can be checked while a system runs. The authors use descriptive set theory to place the family in the Borel and projective hierarchies.

When the space is second countable, the family sits at a stated Borel level. The pair determine exactly which levels it can take there. If the space is not second countable, the family can be much more complex. They give an example where it is complete for the first projective level. That is the highest rung they consider. The contrast shows how one mild countability rule tames the family.
arxiv-2601-04356:
Zhengtong Xu and Yuki Shirai teach robots to feel where a held object touches the world, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such extrinsic contacts — between the grasped object and its surroundings, not the gripper — carry the context a robot needs to plan and learn. earlier estimators assumed fixed grasps, known contact types, or calibrated cameras, and broke in messy settings.

Their framework, UNIC, needs no prior knowledge and no camera calibration. It reads the scene directly in camera coordinates, represents possible contacts as affordance maps. fuses vision with the robot's own body sensing and touch, using random masking during training so missing senses do not break it. In experiments it locates unseen contacts with average error under a centimetre, handles new objects and moving viewpoints, and stays robust when a modality drops out.
arxiv-2601-04856:
Zeyu Liu and Pengfei Zhang ask how two kinds of quantum error can be told apart in a 2026 paper. Coherent errors come from imperfect control of the system's Hamiltonian, while incoherent errors come from coupling to the environment. In chaotic quantum systems both grow exponentially as information scrambles, and both drive the dynamics toward irreversibility, making them hard to separate.

The authors study multi-round time-reversed dynamics, running evolution forward and backward repeatedly, using objects called scramblons to track the damage. They look for distinct signatures each error class leaves on the failure to reverse. Distinguishing error sources guides whether engineers should improve control electronics or better isolate a device from its surroundings.
arxiv-2601-04956:
Crop maps from satellite image time series help farms and governments track what is planted where. Juyuan Kang and 8 co-authors present TEA, a segmentation method for such series, in a 2026 paper. Existing approaches assume a fixed sequence length of images, and the authors find their accuracy drops sharply when the number of observations varies, as happens with clouds, orbit schedules, or different regions.

TEA is built for temporal adaptivity, staying resilient when sequence length changes. Parcel segmentation, drawing field boundaries, is the essential step it performs. Robust crop mapping across variable image counts matters for yield forecasting and subsidy checks, where a model that only works on one fixed calendar of images is of limited real use.
arxiv-2601-05856:
Hugo Nielsen proves in 2026 that the number of solutions to the n-queens problem is divisible by four whenever the board size is at least six. The classical problem asks how many ways n queens can sit on an n-by-n chessboard so that none attacks another. Counting those arrangements exactly is notoriously hard as boards grow.

Nielsen's result concerns the count's arithmetic structure rather than its exact value. Divisibility by four is a strong constraint that every correct count for board sizes from six upward must satisfy. It can therefore serve as a check on large enumerations produced by search programs: a computed total that is not divisible by four must contain an error. Structural results of this kind also guide later work on the solution-count sequence.
arxiv-2601-05956:
Juaren Steiger and Bin Li argue in 2026 that the age of the oldest queued packet is a more robust signal than queue length for learning-based wireless scheduling. Scheduling under unknown channel conditions is often modeled as a constrained bandit problem. Standard algorithms pair bandit learning with virtual queues that track constraint violations, and they aim to shrink those queues.

When channel conditions change abruptly, constraints can become infeasible and virtual queues grow without bound, destabilizing the design. Head-of-line age dynamics behave better under such shocks. Their age-based policy matches state-of-the-art performance under stable random conditions. Crucially, it also remains stable after abrupt channel changes and recovers quickly from periods when constraints cannot be met.
arxiv-2601-06156:
Channel knowledge maps help wireless networks adapt to their environment, but building them from sparse measurements is hard. Ziyu Huang and 4 co-authors propose a faster construction method in a 2026 paper. A channel knowledge map records how signal quality varies by location.

Diffusion models can fill such maps, but their repeated random sampling is too slow for real-time use. The new framework uses guided flow matching, following straight optimal-transport paths as a deterministic equation, which cuts inference steps sharply. It handles both channel gain maps and harder spatial correlation maps. Building outlines guide edge recovery, and a symmetry rule keeps correlation maps physically valid. Simulations showed better fidelity at about twenty-five times the speed.
arxiv-2601-06256:
Yi-Neng Zhou analyzes how fast open quantum systems settle to equilibrium in a 2026 paper. Such systems obey the Lindblad master equation, which includes both internal dynamics and dissipation from the environment. The time to mix, meaning to lose memory of the starting state, matters for preparing states in experiments.

Zhou shows mixing time depends not only on the Liouvillian gap, the usual speed measure, but also on a trace-norm factor for each decaying mode. Together these serve as universal predictors. From them, general conditions for fast and rapid mixing follow. In strong and weak dissipation regimes, the conditions become sparsity requirements on the Hamiltonian and local dissipation operators. The framework guides designing dissipation to reach a desired mixing speed.
arxiv-2601-06456:
AI agents do not stay as they were shipped. They learn from use, from notes back, and from the world they act in. Shaunak Biswas and 2 co-authors say that trait breaks the old ops playbook in a 2026 paper. That book was built for code that acts the same each run.

Marks, saves, and rollbacks all rest on that same-run faith. Agents break it as their paths drift apart with time. The team calls for a shift: from tight loops of control to a shared growth of agents, gear, and human watch. Their frame, CHANGE, names six skills: set the scene, tune the parts to one key, look ahead, deal and trade, make new paths, and grow. A help desk tale shows the frame at work. It lays a base for tools that run agents whose change is a fact of life.
arxiv-2601-06856:
Aswathy Menon Kavumpadikkal Radhakrishnan and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers probing the microscopic origin of prompt and non-prompt d 0 D^{0} production through. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Heavy-flavour hadrons are produced in the early stages of ultra-relativistic collisions at the LHC via hard partonic interactions and experience the whole system evolution.

The study of prompt and non-prompt D 0 D0 mesons provides. An independent avenue to test the theories of quantum chromodynamics and to investigate beauty hadron production. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07756:
Johannes Erdmann, Nitish Kumar Kasaraguppe, and Florian Mausolf automate a tedious choice in particle physics analysis: where to draw bin boundaries. Analysts sort events using discriminant scores, often from machine learning classifiers. Boundaries are still commonly chosen by hand. Simple habits include argmax projections of multi-class scores and evenly spaced bins for one-dimensional scores. Their 2026 preprint proposes direct optimization instead.

Their method optimizes binning for signal significance in multi-dimensional discriminants. Better bins can raise sensitivity without collecting more data. Hand choices may waste the information a good classifier provides. Automating the choice also makes analyses easier to reproduce. The paper speaks to high-energy physicists who build searches and measurements around binned data. It treats binning as part of the measurement, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-07956:
Harrison M. Bonner and Matthew R. Kirchner estimate the parameters of a general model of human pilot response. A human model is essential for analyzing the dynamics of piloted vehicles. Controllers and aircraft must be designed around how people actually respond. Their 2026 preprint presents a method for finding the single model that best fits response data. Data come from a simulator, with many trials combined.

Fitting one model across many trials separates steady pilot behavior from trial noise. Simulator data are safe and repeatable, unlike flight tests. The resulting model can predict pilot-vehicle behavior for new tasks. That prediction supports control design and handling studies. The paper serves aerospace engineers and human factors scholars. It treats the pilot as part of the dynamic system, not an afterthought.
arxiv-2601-08056:
Sibo Wang-Chen and Pavan Ramdya wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on neuromechanical digital twins. These are computer models that link a brain, a body, and the moves that body makes. The work spans models of humans, roundworms, rodents, zebrafish, and fruit flies.

Digital twins let researchers test how neural control and body mechanics shape behavior together. The models named include systems for walking and flying fruit flies, plus worm and fish models. For readers, the paper maps a fast-growing way to study movement without running every test on a live animal. It also shows how one approach can span very different species.
arxiv-2601-08256: Yilan Jiang, Cindy Xiong Bearfield, Steven Franconeri, and Eugene Wu study how data values themselves create visual groupings. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that reading a chart means weighing design and data together. Past work focused on affordances from design elements like color or chart type. How design interacts with data values to shape interpretation has stayed under-explored. The authors ask how readers find groupings that the data induce. Their results matter for chart designers who must predict what patterns viewers will actually see, not just what was encoded.
arxiv-2601-08456: Kiyoshi Sogo wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on two series in Entry 7 of Gauss's diary. Both series diverge, which means their sums run off with no bound in the plain sense. Sogo extends both series by adding new parameters to each. He then calls on three known tools: Rogers-Fine identities, Ramanujan's continued fractions, and Heine's relations for basic hypergeometric series. With those tools, he finds new series that match the old ones. The new forms let him compute the sums of the divergent series in question.
arxiv-2601-08956:
Satyaki Roy Chowdhury and Golrokh Mirzaei work on clean marks of brain growths in scans. True marks guide care and cuts. Deep nets can draw the marks, yet they oft leave rough, noisy edges where a growth seeps into sound tissue. Those rough edges are just where a doctor needs most trust in the mark.

The team adds a cost term that fines shaky marks. The term acts as a learned smooth rule, tied to a drop out trick used at train time. Marks that jump round from run to run get fined more. A reader in brain scans gets a way to calm edge noise. It may make auto marks more fit for real care plans.
arxiv-2601-09056:
Robert Dilworth writes on how to hide who wrote a text from style checks. Style checks can name an author from word picks and pace. They aid law work and fraud hunts. They can also harm a source who must stay hid, or a writer in a strict land. Dilworth seeks a way to mask style while it keeps sense.

His method is called StegoStylo. It stitches text in a way that keeps the facts, but shifts the style marks. The aim is not to lie. It is to stop a style print from name the hand that wrote the words. A reader in text safety gets a mask plan, and a warn on how strong style prints now are.
arxiv-2601-09356:
Emily Klass and six co-authors tackle a measurement problem in biophysics: finding the forces inside living, self-organizing matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats actomyosin systems, networks of actin and myosin that turn chemical energy into motion. They frame the task as an inverse source problem for the Stokes equation.

Knowing the forces is the key to grasping how these active systems work. Cells and tissues build order by spending energy and doing mechanical work. If the hidden forces can be read back from what is seen, experiments gain a direct window on that process. The paper sets up the math needed for such a recovery.
arxiv-2601-09456:
Stephan Ferenz, Oliver Werth, and Astrid Nieße design a metadata schema for energy research software. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets the findability and reuse of code in energy research. Good metadata lets other teams discover software and judge whether it fits their own work.

Many fields still lack a settled schema, and energy research is one of them. The authors built theirs from a requirement analysis, following the FAIR principles for research software. They then evaluated the schema through user testing. A shared schema would let catalogs index energy software the way libraries index books.
arxiv-2601-09656:
A. Arnold, S. Egger, V. Mehrmann, and E. A. Nigsch link two theories of how systems settle down. Their 2026 arXiv paper connects hypocoercivity with hypocontractivity through the Cayley transform. Both theories describe decay toward equilibrium for evolution equations in Hilbert spaces.

One theory works in continuous time, the other in discrete steps. The Cayley transform is the bridge that turns one setting into the other. The authors give new proofs that pin down the short-time decay, including the constants in the leading terms. Sharp decay rates matter for kinetic models, from gas dynamics to plasma physics.
arxiv-2601-09756:
David Brundage weighs synthetic data as a tool for cleaning veterinary health records. His 2026 arXiv paper studies de-identification of veterinary electronic health records under a fixed compute budget. Such records are rich for surveillance and research, but free-text notes often carry private identifiers.

The PetEVAL resource provides expert-labeled animal clinical narratives with identifier spans marked. That allows a fair test of de-identification methods in a low-resource field. Synthetic data may help train scrubbers without exposing real notes. The paper weighs the benefits, the limits, and the safety trade-offs of that route in full.
arxiv-2601-10056:
Jinyuan Shang and Haiping Hu study how quanta move in a near repeat lattice. Such a lattice is named quasiperiodic. Its sites follow a rule that near repeats but never quite does. The test case is the Aubry André Harper lattice.

The pair set the lattice in a two lead rig. The leads sit at zero heat. They work out the flow with a Green based method for out of balance rigs. Odd marks show up at band edges. Sharp points can form there. The flow can also wave in a log based beat as terms change. The work maps these odd acts.
arxiv-2601-10156:
Yutao Mou and co authors guard the tool calls of AI agents. An agent that can call tools can do real work. It can also do real harm if a call is wrong. A bad call may leak data or break a file. The risk grows with each step the agent takes.

The team built ToolSafe, a guard that acts step by step. It checks each call before the call runs. If a call looks unsafe, it can block or flag it. It also gives feed back to the agent. The aim is safe tool use with no need to wait for harm to show.
arxiv-2601-10356:
Mesut Ceylan, Alexis Tabin, Patrick Langer, Elgar Fleisch, and Filipe Barata explain pulse based health calls in plain terms. Wristbands track the pulse wave all day. Models read that wave to call heart rate, breath rate, and blood oxygen. A call with no grounds is hard to trust in care.

The team give counterfactual notes. Such a note says what change in the wave would flip the call. It is built for time data that map to a score. The notes help a pro see why a model made its call. They also flag when a call rests on a weak trait.
arxiv-2601-11056:
E. Garcia-Sanchez, D. Leung, M. Taylor, and P. Tradacete study Banach lattices. Banach lattices are spaces that mix order with a norm. Their 2026 preprint deals with upper p-estimates in such spaces. Two traits, p-convexity and p-concavity, sort these spaces into a scale.

Spaces on that scale act like the classic Lp spaces. Upper and lower p-estimates refine the scale with more care. They are modeled on Lorentz spaces, named Lp-infinity and Lp-one. The team studies new norms that fit the upper case. They also study how such spaces split into simpler factors. The work sits deep in functional analysis, a core of pure math.
arxiv-2601-11556:
Boyang Wang and five coauthors benchmark symbolic music reasoning in LLMs. Their 2026 preprint is named CSyMR, with MIR tool integration. Large language models now reason about music in symbolic form. Scores and chord symbols are text-like inputs for them.

Existing benchmarks stress isolated facts or atomic analyses. Real music thought connects structures across a whole piece. That integrative, compositional reasoning is the gap named here. The bench tests it with music information retrieval tools in hand. Models must combine tool outputs into joined judgments. The dataset is shared on Hugging Face for reuse. Such a bench can steer music AI toward deeper skill.
arxiv-2601-11956:
Yuyin Lu, Ziran Liang, Yanghui Rao, and their co-authors seek more trust in large language models. Such models can state false claims with full faith. Adding knowledge graphs can lift fact skill, but past tools do not gauge doubt in the proof they fetch or in the model's own steps.

Their frame, named DoublyCal in the work, rests on a double-calibration rule. It gauges doubt in both the fetched proof and the chain of thought. A model that knows its doubt can flag weak replies. That flag helps users judge when to trust an output.
arxiv-2601-12356:
Joel M Thomas and Abhijit Chakraborty study how Indian states differ in what they can make and do. They build a network that links each state to its industries. The links come from firm level data on firms on record and the paid up capital behind them.

The pair work out an index of economic complexity for each state. They also use a fitness and complexity method to score each place. These tools show how wide and how skilled the base of work is in each state. The study also covers two union territories. It gives a clear map of local skills that can guide plans for growth in each region.
arxiv-2601-12756:
Hiroyasu Ando analyzes how non adiabatic effects change convective modes in stars and fluids. A convective mode describes how buoyant blobs of fluid move and grow. In adiabatic analysis, no heat is exchanged, and a propagation diagram serves as a useful tool. That diagram shows how the mode behaves across a system.

Ando conducts a systematic analysis using a wave energy relation. For a strongly non adiabatic case, he finds a qualitative change. A monotonically growing convective mode becomes oscillatory instead. Heat exchange thus does not just tweak growth rates; it can change the character of motion. The result matters for stellar interiors, where convection carries energy.
arxiv-2601-13256:
Wenzhong Zhang, Zheyuan Hu, Wei Cai, and George Karniadakis survey deep nets as solvers for hard partial differential equations. Such laws rule heat, flow, and price moves. In high dims, grid based solvers collapse. The count of grid points blows up with each added dim, a flaw called the curse of dimensionality.

Deep nets give a mesh free swap. They can guess law answers in tens to thousands of dims. The team sets out how such nets are built and taught. They also weigh where the nets shine and where they fail. For maths and physics staff, the survey marks a path past a wall that blocked old tools for decades.
arxiv-2601-13756:
Adam Kaminer and co-authors prove a pattern in a tuned cell process in 2026. Their problem is an eigenvalue optimization tied to mRNA translation. In translation, ribosomes build proteins from mRNA code in the cell. The team studies the ordered list of optimal parameters for this model.

They prove a turnpike property for that list. The list has three parts: a short first part, a short third part, and a long middle. All values in the middle part are about equal. Such flat middles make control of the system far simpler to design.
arxiv-2601-14056:
Andrea Rigo and co-authors give image generation consistent 3D layout control in 2026. Text-to-image diffusion models can place objects in odd spots or warp their shape. Prior methods use 2D cues or copy-warp-paste steps to fix placement. Those often distort object geometry and fail to preserve consistency across edits.

Their POCI-Diff uses 3D-layout guided diffusion for placement. Objects can be positioned consistently and interactively, then edited in place. A scene that stays stable across edits suits design and story work. Users gain control that plain text prompts cannot give. The user can move an object and see the scene stay in shape. That kind of live control is what most text prompts lack.
arxiv-2601-14156:
A. W. Shaw and a large team report a rare dimming of the binary star system BG CMi in 2026. BG CMi is an intermediate polar, a white dwarf pulling gas from a companion star. They present multi-wavelength observations of its first recorded low state. Optical monitoring came from members of the American Association of Variable Star Observers.

The source faded by about half a magnitude for about fifty days in early 2025. X-ray and other data from XMM, Suzaku, Swift, and ground telescopes join the record. Low states reveal how accretion can stall in such systems. Amateur and pro data combined to catch this rare event.
arxiv-2601-14356:
Carlos Hernandez-Olivan, Hendrik Vincent Koops, Hao Hao Tan, and Elio Quinton work on music repair in this 2026 paper, set for ICASSP 2026. Audio restoration means undoing damage to a digital signal. The goal is to recover the pristine sound from before the damage. The task matters most for archives of old recordings.

Some archived music has high historical value. For those works, a clean version may be lost or may never have existed. The team's task is bandwidth extension, filling in sound detail that old recordings lack. They do it in a single step with flow matching, a generative method. Their method is also controllable, so users can steer the result.
arxiv-2601-14456:
Valerio Belcamino and three co-authors test what planning models really learn in this 2026 paper. Fine-tuned large language models can reach high valid plan rates on PDDL planning tasks. PDDL is the standard language for stating planning problems. It is unclear if the scores show transferable planning competence or mere memorization of one domain.

The team fine-tuned a 1.7 billion parameter model on 40,000 domain-problem-plan tuples from ten IPC 2023 domains. They then evaluated both in-domain and cross-domain generalization. Their title names the gap they study. The paper also tests verifier-reward reinforcement learning as a way to close that gap.
arxiv-2601-14556:
Andrew Crossman, Jonah Dodd, Viralam Ramamurthy Chaithanya, and their co-authors classify cyber-attack text in this 2026 paper. MITRE ATT&CK is a cybersecurity knowledge base. It organizes threat actor and cyber-attack information into tactics. Tactics describe the reasons and goals threat actors have for attacks. Each tactic has a set of techniques that describe the potential methods used.

Reports on attacks arrive as free text, and analysts must tag them by tactic and technique. The team constructs multi-label hierarchical classification models for MITRE ATT&CK text. Multi-label means one report can carry many tags. Hierarchical means the model respects the tactic-to-technique tree. Readers get an automated tagger for threat reports.
arxiv-2601-15056:
Maria T. Tagliaferri and Inseung Kang test a hip exoskeleton that helps people keep their footing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with falls, the top cause of injury-related hospital stays and deaths in older adults. A device that steadies the gait could cut that risk.

Lower-limb exoskeletons may help users stay stable while they walk. The team varies the help settings of a hip device in a planned way. They then test gait stability when the ground slips under the user. The goal is to find which settings guard best against a fall.
arxiv-2601-15256:
Ruichuan Zhang carries logarithmic geometry into the derived and spectral worlds. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with log geometry, which tracks spaces together with a record of their boundary-like parts. The derived version uses animated rings in place of plain ones.

Zhang develops deformation theory for animated log rings and for their spectral kin. He studies the stacks of derived and spectral log structures that arise. He then defines moduli stacks for these structures. The paper establishes that those stacks are representable, so they behave like genuine geometric objects in their own right.
arxiv-2601-15356:
Xiang Li, Xueheng Li, and co-authors teach a model to look closer before judging a photo's quality. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with image quality assessment. Reinforcement learning has helped multimodal models match human taste in scoring images.

But most such models judge from a coarse global view. Fine local flaws in a high-resolution image escape them. The authors present Q-Probe, which probes the image in context-aware steps. An agentic process picks where to zoom. Quality scoring then scales to high resolution without missing the small local image defects it finds.
arxiv-2601-15956:
Brant E. Robertson and a large team publish the photometric backbone of a major survey in a 2026 arXiv paper. The catalog is part of JADES Data Release 5. JADES provides deep imaging and spectroscopy of the GOODS-North and GOODS-South fields. Its wavelengths span the optical to the infrared, using JWST and Hubble instruments. The science reaches from nearby galaxies to the first few hundred million years. Photometry measures each source's brightness across filters.

A photometric catalog is the survey's phone book. Every later study starts by looking sources up in it. Brightness in many bands yields colors, distances, and rough masses. The care in such catalogs decides the quality of hundreds of papers. This release documents the measurements so others can build on them with confidence.
arxiv-2601-16256:
Mathias Driesse and coauthors sum how black holes bend paths when they pass. Their 2026 preprint works at fifth order in a key scale. The scale counts powers of the gravity pull in the pass. They also add the first self force terms at next order. The maths frame is world line quantum field theory, a line based tool.

The team finds the bend angle and push for a clean pass. Clean means no waves are shed in the sum, just the pass. Sharp sums test wave forms used for real black hole pairs. They also push maths tools to new depth. The work serves groups who model loud space wave events.
arxiv-2601-16356:
Simret Gebreegziabher and coauthors study how user values shape web agent acts. Their 2026 preprint deals with agents that run web tasks for users. Such agents now do more day to day tasks on their own. It is not known how user likes and values bend agent thought. Both clear likes and hid likes may shift each act.

The team tests agent acts as values in prompts shift. Shifts show which values move acts and which do not. Clear links help teams set guard rules for agents. They also help users know what cues to give. The work maps the act cloth of GUI agents.
arxiv-2601-16456:
Ferida Mohammad and coauthors build a test set for AI code help tools. Their 2026 preprint, named RubberDuckBench, deals with aid tools that reply to code asks.
