Coders now turn to such tools for help with their own code. Past tests oft use toy asks cut off from real work. Real asks rest on the full code base and its past.

The team draws asks from real GitHub pull threads. Each ask comes with the code and talk that frame it. True frame lets tests weigh if aids grasp real needs. Scores on real asks guide which aids earn trust. The work gives a sound test base for code aids.
arxiv-2601-16656:
More and more people turn to chatbots for comfort and company. Tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot now hear private fears and hopes. Trust sits at the heart of these talks. Yet we know little of how that trust grows. A 2026 preprint studies this new bond in depth.

Users chat with these tools with no guide at hand. The talks can feel close, like talks with a friend. The study asks how users come to trust the bot. It also asks what that trust feels like from inside. Such work can help set safe rules for care bots. It can also warn users of risks in deep trust.
arxiv-2601-16756:
Mauro Guerra and a large team refine the math for a rare atomic decay. Beryllium-7 atoms can grab one of their own inner electrons. That grab leaves the atom in a stirred state. Some stirred atoms shake off an electron as they calm. The shake-off forms a tail in the energy spread. Their 2026 preprint builds a sharp model of those tails.

Past models lacked key traits, like linked electron moves. They also skipped the skew that fast moves bring. New gauges with cold sensors now set the best bounds on ghost bits called sterile neutrinos. Bad tails blur those bounds. Sharp tail math thus guards a real hunt.
arxiv-2601-16956:
Avinash Maurya, M. Mustafa Rafique, Franck Cappello, and Bogdan Nicolae speed saves for vast AI models. Big models now train on thousands of chips at once. Their state must be saved oft to guard the run. A crash with no save can waste weeks of work. Saves of such sprawl are slow and hard to steer.

Their 2026 preprint builds DataStates-LLM for those saves. State parts come from plug-in providers that stack. The stack serves data, tensor, and pipeline splits at once. Fast saves guard runs and let teams pause and probe. They also help trace why a run went wrong.
arxiv-2601-17056:
Zahra Vaseqi and James Clark rethink tests for head-cam video tools. Head-cam shots show the world from the wearer's view. Tools must name acts in those shots in new homes. New homes shift light, gear, and scene in big ways. Past tests mixed two kinds of shift at once. Their 2026 preprint splits those shifts with a score rule.

Their rule, Ego4OOD, scores how far a test set has shifted. Input shifts split clean from sense shifts. Clean splits let teams grade true spread skill. Such grades matter for aid tools for the blind. They also matter for work and sport head cams.
arxiv-2601-17156:
E. Eduardo Sanchez-Karhunen, Jose Quesada-Moreno, and Miguel Gutiérrez-Naranjo open the black box of intent tools. Intent tools tag what a user wants from a query. Firms lean on them for sales and support work. Deep nets rule the field, but their guts stay opaque. Their 2026 preprint finds a new way to read those guts. It tracks how loop nets build their tags step by step.

Loop nets read a query in a chain of steps. The team traces which words steer each step. Clear traces let firms trust and fix their tools. They also show where a net leans on stray cues.
arxiv-2601-17456:
Bo Hou builds Lie bialgebras from dendriform D-bialgebras. Dendriform algebras split one operation into two linked parts. That split gives rich structure to work with. Hou studies how tensor products with perm algebras yield Lie algebras from them. He gives two such methods. One route runs through associative algebras.

The work also maps links to the classical Yang-Baxter equation. Solutions of that equation drive integrable systems and quantum groups. New sources of solutions widen both fields. Affinization is the thread that lifts small algebras to big ones. Hou's methods give algebraists fresh stock. Each new Lie bialgebra can seed whole families of models.
arxiv-2601-17956:
Kumar Gautam, Akshit Dutta, and Kumar Shubham describe a radar design based on quantum light. Their 2026 preprint uses the Born-Feynman path integral view to frame the system. The radar rests on five parts. A source based on quantum dots makes pairs of entangled photons. A transmission module sends one photon of each pair toward the target, while a delay line holds its twin.

A detection module then compares what comes back with the held twin. A signal unit works out what the match says about the target. Entangled pairs can help a radar pick weak returns out of noise. The paper lays out the full chain of parts and the theory that ties them. It is a design study for a young field.
arxiv-2601-18156: Anirban Mukherjee and Hannah Hanwen Chang propose a distributional test of distinctiveness for machine-generated works, aimed at intellectual property law. Their 2026 preprint moves beyond pairwise comparisons between single works. A test based on whole distributions can say whether a body of machine output stands apart as a class. The question matters as courts weigh the status of AI-made works.
arxiv-2601-18456:
Kohei Asai and three colleagues join two speech tasks that are most often done one by one. Real tapes mix many voices with noise, hiss, and room echo. That mix cuts both how much speech a lab can use and how clean it sounds. Teams can clean the tape first and then split the voices. In that chain, flaws from the first step pass to the next.

Their tool, Geneses, does both jobs in one pass with a model that builds speech anew. A build-anew model can fix harms that a plain chain cannot, such as echo on top of noise. The aim is one clean track per voice, fit for training new speech tools. More clean speech means speech tools that work for more people in more real rooms.
arxiv-2601-18656:
Sarika Aggarwal and three colleagues study how the length of a flood shapes the harm it does to health. Past work links floods to more ill health in the days and weeks that come next. But floods are not one thing. A flash flood hits in hours, while a slow flood can sit for weeks. That span may change who gets sick and how.

The team build a model that lets the health link shift with the length of the flood. Their model can show a short, sharp harm for fast floods and a long, slow harm for ones that sit. Such maps could help health teams plan for each kind of flood in its own way. They could also guide aid to the zones where harm lasts most.
arxiv-2601-18756:
Marko Maležič and Johann Ostmeyer hone a way to run the long tale of a quantum crowd with less drift. A crowd of bits that pull on each other changes in a smooth flow of time. Tools chop that flow into small steps. Each chop adds a small flaw, and the flaws stack as the tale runs long. Plain chops are easy to code but their stack grows fast.

The pair build chops of a higher grade that stack their flaws far more slow. Such chops can reach far times with the same count of steps. That reach is key for crowds whose tale must run long to show its marks. The work serves both plain and quantum tools that chase such tales. Less drift means claims about long runs can be made with more trust.
arxiv-2601-19456:
Simon N. Chandler-Wilde and Siavash Sadeghi study how sound and waves scatter off objects. The governing model is the Helmholtz equation, which describes waves of a fixed frequency. A common way to solve it is to rewrite the problem as an integral equation on the object's surface. These boundary integral methods are powerful, but their cost can grow as the frequency rises.

The authors derive estimates that show exactly how the method's operators depend on the wavenumber. The wavenumber measures how many wavelengths fit in a unit of space. Their bounds hold for general compact obstacles, not just simple shapes. Knowing the frequency dependence helps design solvers that stay fast at high frequency. Radar, sonar, and medical imaging all lean on such computations.
arxiv-2601-20156:
Velásquez-Toribio A.M studies a string-inspired model of the universe in which a field called the dilaton couples to all matter. In such models the equivalence principle, which says all objects fall alike, can be slightly violated. The author uses dynamical systems methods to track how the universe evolves in the Damour-Polyakov regime.

The work is set in a flat expanding universe filled with pressureless matter. Its aim is to make clear how cosmic relaxation drives any violations down over time. That link matters because tests of the equivalence principle are very precise, so the model must show why no violation is seen today.
arxiv-2601-20256:
Xuanyu Su, Diana Inkpen, and Nathalie Japkowicz present SoftHateBench, a benchmark for testing content moderation models against soft hate speech. Hard hate uses slurs and threats. Soft hate sounds reasonable on the surface but uses framing and value claims to steer readers toward blaming or excluding a group.

The authors test whether moderation models catch this policy-compliant hostility, which is driven by reasoning rather than insults. Many filters key on bad words, so they may pass text that is harmful in effect. A benchmark of this kind shows platforms where their tools are blind.
arxiv-2601-20356:
Debashree Priyadarsini Das and Sasmita Mishra study how a sterile neutrino, motivated by dark matter, would show up in neutrinoless double beta decay. This rare decay, if seen, would prove that neutrinos are their own antiparticles. In a type-I seesaw framework, an exact relation ties the active and sterile neutrino sectors through their masses and mixing angles.

The authors use a model-independent approach inside that setup. They trace the sterile contribution to the half-life of the decay. Experiments now push half-life limits ever higher, so theory must say what a sterile partner would do to the expected rate.
arxiv-2601-20656:
Diogo J. Paulo, Hugo Proença, and João C. Neves present FD-MAD, a frequency-domain method for detecting face morphing attacks. A morph blends two faces into one image that can match both people, threatening face recognition at identity enrolment and border control. The hardest case is single-image detection, where no trusted reference photo exists.

Despite much research, morph detectors struggle when tested on new datasets. The authors analyze residuals in the frequency domain, where blending leaves traces. Stronger morph detection protects passport and ID systems that now rely on a submitted photo.
arxiv-2601-20756:
Elizabeth Baker, Alexander Denker, and Jes Frellsen extend diffusion models to functions, not just finite data. Their 2026 paper works with score-based diffusion models on infinite-dimensional function spaces. Such models can help solve inverse problems that come from partial differential equations. An inverse problem asks what hidden cause produced a set of noisy observations.

In the Bayesian view, the goal is to sample from a posterior distribution over functions. That distribution blends prior knowledge with the observed data. The paper adds supervised guidance to steer that sampling. Guidance uses extra information to push samples toward answers that fit. The work matters wherever the unknown is a whole function, not a single number. It shows how modern generative models can serve classic inference tasks.
arxiv-2601-20856:
Seljon Akhmedli constructs examples that separate two views of order in dynamical systems. The 2026 paper concerns nilfactors, a key structure in ergodic theory. A system can be described through its measurable nilfactor or its topological nilfactor. The two need not match. Akhmedli asks which combinations of behavior can occur. The answer is all of them, and the paper builds systems to prove it.

The examples are minimal and uniquely ergodic. Minimal means every orbit fills the space. Unique ergodicity means time averages settle to one outcome. The construction adapts an idea from Furstenberg. He built a system on the two-torus that was minimal but not uniquely ergodic. The new work extends that trick to control both nilfactors at once. It completes a picture that theorists use to classify complex motion.
arxiv-2601-21256:
Tia Pandit and Bipin Singh Koranga review how the density of Earth affects long-baseline neutrino experiments. As neutrinos pass through Earth, its matter changes how they switch between types. The effect is strongest for the change from muon type to electron type, which sits under tests of a deep symmetry of nature.

The review shows that real changes in density along the path add structure that simple average-density models miss. It pulls together theory, past observations, and open questions for future work. Getting the density right matters because small errors can shift what experiments conclude about how neutrinos behave.
arxiv-2601-21656:
Tianqi Zhao, Guanyang Wang, Yan Shuo Tan, and Qiong Zhang cluster tabular data with a network fitted on synthetic tasks. Clustering tables is hard because columns mix types, the hidden generating process varies, and tricks rarely transfer between datasets. Prior-fitted networks have done well at supervised table tasks by mimicking Bayesian inference.

The authors extend that idea to clustering, where no labels exist at all. A network trained on a broad synthetic prior can cluster a new table in one pass. Transferable clustering would help analysts facing fresh tables daily, from hospital records to sales data, with no time to tune per dataset.
arxiv-2601-21756:
Alexey Orlov classifies supersingular elliptic curves in characteristic three. Elliptic curves over finite fields power much of modern cryptography and number theory. Supersingular curves are the special family whose point counts sit at the extremes.

The author lists the isomorphism classes of these curves explicitly in this characteristic. Formulae for the number of points on each curve are given as well. Explicit lists turn abstract theory into data that can be checked and used. Characteristic three is small enough to compute with directly, which makes a complete catalogue a useful test bed for broader conjectures.
arxiv-2601-21856:
Shujaat Khan and co-authors work on cleaning up ultrasound images without needing perfect examples to learn from. Ultrasound reading is hampered by speckle, a grainy noise built into the method, by blur from the imaging process. And by artifacts that vary with the scanner and the operator.

Supervised enhancement methods assume access to clean target images, which medical practice rarely provides. The team's 2026 preprint instead models the degradation itself, guided by the physics of ultrasound, and learns in a self-supervised way. Better images from ordinary scans could help clinicians in small clinics and low-resource settings most, where the machines are older and expert readers are scarce.
arxiv-2601-22156:
Yingfa Chen and co-authors make hybrid attention architectures practical for extremely long texts. Hybrid Transformers mix softmax attention blocks with recurrent networks, a pairing with an attractive balance of quality and speed for long-context work. Studies and adoption have lagged, though, partly for lack of efficient training recipes.

Their 2026 preprint tackles the problem with efficient distillation and effective architecture choices. Distillation transfers the skill of a full attention model into the faster hybrid, so quality survives the speedup. Long-context models serve law, research, and code, where documents run to hundreds of thousands of tokens. A hybrid that trains cheaply could move long-context ability from flagship systems to everyday tools.
arxiv-2601-22256:
Yinuo Yang, Ashley Ge Zhang, Steve Oney, and April Yi Wang built a tool to help teachers watch class coding work as it happens. Their 2026 preprint presents Spark, a live monitor for tasks with many linked steps. Such tasks have no fixed order and are hard to sum up at a glance.

Spark aims to show who is stuck and where the class shares the same snag. The work grows out of a real pain point for staff who teach coding. A clear live view can let a teacher step in early. It can also shape help for the whole room.
arxiv-2601-22356:
Kiwan Wong, Wei Xiao, and Daniela Rus teach robots to stay safe when rules clash. Their 2026 preprint, PoSafeNet, notes that safety rules are not all equal. Some can bend before others, but the order is only partial, not a full list from top to base.

Fixed orders or flat rules can freeze a robot or make it act in brittle ways. Their nets build the partial order into the learner itself. The robot can then trade rules off in a sane way when it must. The work targets robots that work near people. It aims for safe moves that still get the job done.
arxiv-2601-22556:
Weizhi Liu, Yue Li, and Zhaoxia Yin hide a proof of origin inside generated speech without spoiling its sound. Synthetic speech now sounds fully human, which raises the risk of misuse. Their 2026 preprint, VocBulwark, notes that past marks trade sound quality against strength, by noise overlay or deep model edits.

Their method injects a small set of added parameters instead. The mark aims to survive edits while the voice stays clean. Sound, lasting marks help platforms trace fake audio. The work seeks both goals at once. It is a guard for the voice era.
arxiv-2601-22856:
Yilong Zuo and five co-authors work on graphs whose nodes carry both text and images. Such multimodal graphs model many real systems, from products to papers. A problem arises when the meaning implied by node features clashes with the graph's own links.

Their method, OptiMAG, aligns the two views using a form of optimal transport that allows uneven matching. When features and links agree, tasks like labeling nodes work far better. The approach fits social, shopping, and science graphs where text and images meet. When structure and meaning line up, downstream tasks gain from both the graph links and the rich node content.
arxiv-2601-22956:
Boyin Tan and five co-authors add a planning step before AI writes code for a software issue. In practice, teams often draft several candidate fix proposals, then debate and pick one golden plan. Most AI research skips that step and jumps straight to code generation or repair.

Their system, SWE-Manager, selects and synthesizes the best proposal first, then codes from it. Choosing the plan before coding mirrors how careful human teams avoid wasted work. It could cut the common failure of fluent code that solves the wrong problem.
arxiv-2601-23156:
Damion Harvey and four co-authors discover reusable skills in behavior data without any labels. Skill discovery splits long trajectories into segments that can be reused as options. Most current methods need action labels, rewards, or hand-made notes, which limits where they apply.

Their unsupervised method finds both the segments and the hierarchy among them. Skills learned from raw footage could let agents reuse past competence on new tasks. That ability matters for robots trained on large, unlabeled logs of experience. No action labels, rewards, or handcrafted annotations are assumed, which is what makes the discovery method unsupervised.
arxiv-2602-00056: Sophia N. Wilson and coauthors trace the sustainability costs of the shift from gathering data to making data for frontier AI, a turn they call hyper datafication. They study about 550000 data sets on the Hugging Face Hub for growth, storage energy, carbon, and language coverage. They add views from data workers in Kenya on pay, jobs, and graphic content. The pattern they find is stark: environmental costs climb while labor risks and representation harms fall on workers and groups far from the firms that gain.
arxiv-2602-00156: Jaya Vasavi Pamidimukkala and colleagues speed de novo genome assembly with a hybrid quantum and classical method. Building a genome from scratch without a reference is costly in time and accuracy. Their approach solves Hamiltonian and Eulerian paths in the assembly graph with gate based quantum computing. It uses a higher order binary form with a variational quantum eigensolver. Classical prep work readies the problem, and a new bitstring recovery step helps the search move well through the space of possible answers.
arxiv-2602-00256: Tania Robens reviews interference effects in new physics searches within and beyond the Standard Model. Such effects follow from a correct description of physics theories, yet many theoretical accounts and experimental searches neglect them. Neglect can yield wrong kinematic distributions, at least in UV complete models. The review surveys the current status, the most common descriptions, and existing studies of interference. Its focus is models with extended scalar searches, where interference shapes what experiments should expect to see.
arxiv-2602-00356: Atilio Barreda and team examine community driven data science practices through two partnerships for social justice. The first example, VECINA, is a place based partnership focused on environmental justice, introducing a framework for fruitful local collaborations. The second, SToPA, began with citizens requesting analysis of their town policing data, then asks how to scale such work beyond one place. Both cases show how community members and mathematical researchers can collaborate actively, even when projects grow beyond a single community.
arxiv-2602-00456: Amanda Dsouza and team present UNDERWRITE, an expert-first insurance underwriting benchmark built with experts for real enterprise challenges. As AI agents enter enterprise apps, evaluation demands benchmarks matching real operational needs. UNDERWRITE adds realism factors absent in current benchmarks: private business knowledge, noisy tools, and imperfect simulated users needing care. Across 13 frontier models, the authors uncover gaps between lab performance and enterprise use. Top accuracy models are not the most efficient, models invent domain knowledge despite tools, and repeat passes show a 20% performance drop.
arxiv-2602-00556: David Cohen and colleagues discretise a stochastic wave equation on the sphere in semilinear form, driven by Gaussian noise. Time stepping uses a trigonometric integrator, while space uses a spectral Galerkin scheme. They show the explicit fully discrete scheme converges strongly and almost surely, in both senses. Numerical experiments also confirm those rates for the scheme in practice.
arxiv-2602-00656: Yingxu Wang and colleagues tackle graph domain adaptation. Here classifiers must move across domains that differ in both meaning and topology. Euclidean adversarial methods, they argue, tangle and suppress label-relevant structure. Their DisRFM method places graph points on a constant-curvature manifold in geodesic polar coordinates. It sets radial scales and keeps class semantics through chosen angular alignment. A topology-conditioned polar flow then couples matching samples. It learns a metric-corrected field along geodesic paths. Tests under varied shifts beat leading methods.
arxiv-2602-00856: Luca Apadula and colleagues describe the most general forms of input-output vagueness for bidirectional quantum devices. Such devices swap input and output ports and are described by bistochastic quantum channels, maps that preserve both trace and identity. They build a hierarchy of higher-order maps from transformations of such channels. Some levels combine channels in a definite causal order while using every channel in an indefinite input-output sense. Other levels mix unclear local way with unclear global causal order among processes.
arxiv-2602-00956: Faisal Ahmed pairs shape math with a DenseNet121 net to sort MRI scans into four Alzheimer stages. Topological data analysis picks up shape traits of brain tissue that nets tend to miss, while DenseNet121 learns spatial traits from scan slices. Fusing the two kinds of traits sharpens the split between stages. On the OASIS Kaggle MRI set, the fused model tops prior methods, with an accuracy of 99.93% that beats recent convolutional, transfer, ensemble, and multi-scale designs. The authors present it as a strong aid for automated Alzheimer diagnosis.
arxiv-2602-01156: Shunpeng Yang and co-authors build PolicyFlow, a PPO-style plan for flow-based control laws, dodging full-flow odds math. Plain PPO leans on odds that are easy for bell-curve laws but pricey and wobbly along a full flow path. PolicyFlow gauges odds ratios from speed-field shifts on a plain blend path, cutting cost with no steadiness loss. A Brownian rule then curbs mode collapse and spurs varied acts. Tests on MultiGoal, mazes, and robot sims match or beat bell-curve PPO, with richer multi-mode acts.
arxiv-2602-01356: Noor Islam S. Mohammad builds bucket calculus, a fresh math frame for parallel machine scheduling. The strongly NP-hard two-machine task with release dates and makespan goal gets an adaptive time-slicing plan that slashes complexity from time-power to bucket-power while keeping near-best quality. A bucket-indexed mixed-integer plan exploits uneven precision needs, cutting choice variables sharply and promising a huge theoretical speedup on 20-job cases. Tests on 20 to 400 jobs show high machine use, near-perfect balance, and optimality gaps below 5.1%.
arxiv-2602-01556: Hong Su proposes a simulation framework letting AI systems form questions and set tasks autonomously. Most systems use set tasks and fixed prompts, limiting what problems they spot as conditions change. The framework treats question formation as a primary step before task selection, combining internal, environmental, and inter-agent prompting to widen coverage. It learns question formation from experience, improving adaptability and decision quality. In multi-agent simulation, environment-aware prompting cut no-eat events, with inter-agent-aware prompting cutting them further over a 20-day run.
arxiv-2602-01656: Sahat Nainggolan and colleagues revisit recovering diffusion coefficients that vary in space for stationary elliptic equations, using boundary Cauchy data. They add a gradient weighted term to the coupled complex boundary method and pose the task as regularized optimization over coefficients. They prove the map is continuous and differentiable, the cost is Lipschitz, minimizers exist, and it stays stable under noise and converges as noise vanishes. Sobolev gradient descent across noise levels, inputs and shapes gives steadier results with fewer high frequency flaws for large but not too big weights.
arxiv-2602-01756: Jun He and colleagues turn text to image generation from pixel decoding into a knowledge driven workflow. Static decoders miss intentions, unified models improve intent but struggle with knowledge reasoning, and fixed priors cannot track change. Their Mind-Brush simulates a think research create loop retrieving evidence that grounds unseen concepts and using tools to resolve constraints. They propose Mind-Bench with 500 samples spanning news, concepts, math and Geo-Reasoning. Mind-Brush improves models, leaping from zero to one for Qwen-Image on Mind-Bench and beating WISE and RISE.
arxiv-2602-01856: Przemysław Andrzej Wałęga and colleagues study which modal logics survive embeddings, injective maps and maps. They focus on Kripke models that stay the same when unwound a bounded amount. Embeddings match existential graded modal logic, injective homomorphisms existential positive graded modal logic, and homomorphisms existential positive modal logic. A well quasi ordering shows tree shaped models of bounded height form a well quasi order under embedding. Monotonic GNNs capture exactly the second logic, while monotonic GNNs with MAX capture the third.
arxiv-2602-02056: Duc Hoang and colleagues show Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks align with rapid online learning demands, where learning must occur fast. These needs demand low-latency fixed math, where MLPs are slow and unstable. They spot two key traits: KAN updates using B-spline nearness stay sparse, giving better scaling, and KANs resist rounding. Training online with fixed points on FPGAs, they show KAN-based learners beat MLPs. To their knowledge, this is the first model-free online learning at sub-microsecond latency.
arxiv-2602-02456:
Albert Gassol Puigjaner and 2 co-authors give robots a relationship-aware map of their surroundings, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard mapping methods rebuild geometry, and semantic versions label objects, but neither captures how objects relate or what tasks they afford. Scene graphs add that hierarchy, organizing places, objects, and connections.

Their enhanced graph integrates open-vocabulary features at several levels of abstraction. A vision-language model infers semantic relationships between objects, such as support or containment. A task reasoning module then combines a large language model with the vision model to interpret the graph and plan actions. The team deployed the system on a quadruped robot across multiple environments and tasks. The robot reasoned about its surroundings more intelligently than with metric maps alone. Structured relationships, not just labels, carry the understanding.
arxiv-2602-02556:
Xuancheng Li and 4 co-authors store an agent's experience inside a small trainable plug-in instead of a database, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Language models are largely static: they redo their work and repeat mistakes. Retrieval-based reuse is similarity-driven, can inject noise, and adds latency at run time.

Their module, SEAM, writes a structured experience entry tailored to each case in a single forward pass to guide a frozen executor model. Training tunes the module for utility, scored by the executor's own rollouts under group-based reinforcement learning, while the executor never changes. After deployment, logged successful runs can fine-tune the module further. Math reasoning benchmarks showed steady accuracy gains across different executors with low overhead. Ablations explain why the stored experience helps and confirm its robustness. The design turns memory into a learned, generative skill.
arxiv-2602-02656:
In a 2026 study, Taj Jankovič and 3 co-authors simulate a star repeatedly smashing through an accretion disc around a supermassive black hole, a leading explanation for quasi-periodic eruptions. Those eruptions are bright X-ray bursts recurring every hours to days near galactic centers. Each disc crossing should shock gas into outflows that radiate.

The three-dimensional radiation-hydrodynamics simulation treats the star as an unperturbed solid sphere crossing a local disc section. A nearly paraboloidal bow shock forms ahead of the star. Heating spreads sideways as the shock expands, not just in the column directly ahead. The star injects momentum along its motion, so the two outflows emerging on opposite disc faces differ sharply. The forward outflow is faster, more massive, more energetic, and about twice as luminous. That built-in asymmetry may explain alternating strong and weak flares seen in several eruption sources.
arxiv-2602-02756:
Alaa M. Ali and 6 co-authors print working gear trains smaller than a hair's width and spin them with light, in a 2026 paper. Miniaturizing gears and micromotors has stalled on powering: wires and batteries do not scale down gracefully. Optical tweezers, which trap and move microscopic objects with a focused laser, offer contact-free actuation.

Two-photon polymerization printing fabricates the micromachines directly. Designs include single gears, trains of two or three gears, and bevel gears producing out-of-plane rotation, a motion traditional micromachining cannot easily make. Components print without unwanted adhesion, so assemblies actually turn. Under optical tweezer actuation the gears rotated continuously, transmitted motion through trains, and amplified either velocity or torque depending on the gear ratio. The authors target biomedical and lab-on-a-chip systems, where precise, minimally invasive control at the microscale is essential and light can reach where wires cannot.
arxiv-2602-03056:
Predicting what a person will like from their long history is benchmarked by Lu Ren and 25 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Language models could personalize recommendations by thinking over past actions. Item-focused benchmarks, however, cannot judge preferences for items that are entirely new, and short-term requests do not reflect enduring interests that persist across years of activity.

Their benchmark, ALPBench, predicts combinations of attributes a user will find interesting instead of given items. Ground truth then exists even for newly introduced items. Histories are written as natural-language sequences, supporting interpretable thinking. The task remains highly challenging for current models. It requires capturing complex interactions among many attributes and thinking over long actions sequences at once.
arxiv-2602-03256:
Physics-informed features can shrink the neural networks that predict aircraft battery voltage, according to Eymen Ipek, working alongside 1 co-author. Electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft need battery systems that predict voltage under aggressive power demands. Pure data models reach high accuracy but need complex architectures and extensive training data, raising the cost of on-board deployment in weight and power constrained vehicles.

Circuit models offer physical interpretability but struggle with nonlinear behavior at high discharge rates. Using an open eVTOL battery dataset, the authors compare pure data-driven models against models fed physics-based features. The physics-informed versions matched complex models' accuracy while using up to three quarters fewer trainable parameters. Computational overhead fell significantly, supporting potential deployment on board the aircraft.
arxiv-2602-03356:
Metrics compatible with a contact-symplectic form are studied by Amine Hadjar in solo work on characteristic foliations. A contact-symplectic pair combines two forms on a manifold. Each has its own characteristic foliation, a splitting into curves or sheets following the form. Hadjar studies metrics that are compatible with, or associated to, such a pair, and asks what those metrics must share across the whole family.

Integral curves of the Reeb vector field are geodesics for any compatible metric. All associated metrics share a common volume element, given in full. When the two characteristic foliations are orthogonal under an associated metric, their leaves, and those of a third foliation, are minimal. Clear examples on nilpotent Lie groups and nilmanifolds show the foliations need not both be totally geodesic.
arxiv-2602-03456:
Entanglement between a levitated nanoparticle and light sounds fragile, yet Q. Deplano and 3 co-authors report exactly that in a 2026 paper. A nanosphere floats in an optical tweezer set inside a cavity, and its center-of-mass motion becomes quantum-linked to the electromagnetic field. The experiment runs at room temperature, not in a deep cryostat.

Using heterodyne detection, the team reconstructs the full set of correlations between the motion and the light's quadratures. The measurements violate separability bounds, the mathematical test that rules out any purely classical explanation. The entanglement survives across a broad range of parameters. The result supports levitated optomechanics as a route to quantum communication and to tests of macroscopic quantum physics.
arxiv-2602-03556:
A flaky test passes one run and fails the next on identical code, poisoning trust in automated checks. Alexander Berndt and 2 co-authors study flakiness inside SAP HANA, a large industrial database system, in a 2026 paper. Hand-labeling hundreds of fixed flakiness reports would be slow, so they use language models as annotators instead.

Consistency checks within and across models make the automatic labels trustworthy enough to map the root causes. Concurrency problems dominate, appearing in about 23 percent of the 559 analyzed reports. Different test types show different flakiness profiles, the authors find. They urge future mitigation research to test whether fixes generalize across test types rather than assuming one cause fits all.
arxiv-2602-03956:
When does a flowing system admit a single surface that every path crosses? Slobodan N. Simić gives a new test in a 2026 mathematics paper on volume-preserving flows, which keep the volume of any region constant as they evolve. The flow lives on a closed smooth manifold and never stops.

Simić's criterion involves choosing a metric matched to the preserved volume. If a certain derived quantity stays below one in size, a global cross section exists. Better, another metric then makes a canonical form harmonic. Cross sections reduce flow problems to maps, so a checkable criterion widens the cases analysts can handle.
arxiv-2602-04056:
Robots driven by foundation models need safety in layers, argue Joonkyung Kim and colleagues. Their 2026 paper divides robot safety into action safety, decision safety, and human-centered safety. A physically safe motion can still be semantically wrong or violate what a person actually wanted.

Static verification, single controllers, and end-to-end learned policies each miss parts of that stack, especially as tasks stay open-ended. The authors propose modular guardrails: monitoring layers that evaluate behavior and intervention layers that can step in. Modularity lets each layer adapt as tasks, environments, and human expectations shift over time.
arxiv-2602-04456:
Advice online often forces a choice between growth and care, security and respect, or other competing values. Zhiyi Chen and 6 co-authors study those trade-offs in a 2026 paper on what large language models prefer when people ask for everyday advice.

First the team built a value framework from posts in four advice communities on Reddit. Networks of co-occurring values showed that career advice differed sharply from advice about relationships. The authors then tested language models on the same dilemmas. Across models and settings, the models favored exploration and growth over kindness and connection. That steady tilt raises concern that AI advice could narrow human choices.
arxiv-2602-04656:
Yun Jiang and Ji Wang design a safe controller for a coupled heat-and-motion system in a 2026 paper on parabolic PDE-ODE cascades. Part of the plant follows a partial differential equation, part an ordinary one, and both carry unknown parameters.

Their strategy combines an adaptive control barrier function, a tool that keeps states inside safe limits, with batch least-squares identification. The identifier pins down the unknown parameters exactly in finite time. The controller guarantees that the output state farthest from the input stays positive, which encodes safety here. It also drives the whole plant state exponentially toward zero. Simulations demonstrate the method's effectiveness, illustrating a route to safe control under uncertainty.
arxiv-2602-05156:
Robotic hands fail at tasks fingertips find easy, like peeling an orange or lifting a single sheet of paper. Dong Ho Kang and 5 co-authors present the PLATO Hand in this 2026 robotics paper. It is built around a hybrid fingertip: a rigid nail, an embedded fingertip bone, and a soft pulp, shaped for how contact begins, bears load, and transmits force.

A strain-energy model of bending and indentation guided the design, explaining how stiffness and contact geometry divide deformation inside the fingertip. In tests, the hand showed steadier pinch grasps, better force transmission through nail-side contact, and clearer proprioceptive signals than a soft design. It completed jobs that defeat grippers, including separating one paper sheet from a stack, picking up a card, and peeling an orange. The authors argue that mechanically structured contact, paired with a transparent force-motion finger mechanism, is a principled route to precise manipulation.
arxiv-2602-05356:
Byzantine agreement lets processors reach consensus despite some of them lying, and a classic lower bound says deterministic protocols need quadratically many messages. Andrew Lewis-Pye, writing alone, asks what that quadratic cost truly buys in this 2026 distributed computing paper. Even the trivial need for each honest processor to receive something already forces much of the cost. So the bound may be about spreading the answer, not about deciding it.

Lewis-Pye proves the distinction is real. A relaxed task allowing a small fraction of honest processors to err can be solved deterministically with near-linear communication. It reaches the point where the outcome is fixed, called univalency, without the quadratic bill. One all-to-all exchange and a majority vote then finishes the full protocol, confirming the old bound prices dissemination. An authenticated variant, extractable agreement, is also solved with communication depending only on the count of faults.
arxiv-2602-05756:
Group actions on Stone spaces, the totally disconnected spaces of topology, have a rich minimal dynamics theory that María Isabel Cortez and Till Hauser extend. They study minimal equicontinuous actions, which they call subodometers, with no assumption that the space is metrizable and none on the acting group. The central question is what data classify such actions up to equivalence.

They show the set of eigenvalues is a complete invariant for subodometers. Minimal rotations, called odometers, are characterized by a stability property of their eigenvalue sets. Any family of odometers has a unique minimal common extension and maximal common factor, while the authors give counterexamples showing the same fails for subodometers. Both classes are built as inverse limits of finite actions. A universal odometer exists that has all subodometers as factors. The paper is a pure mathematics contribution to topological dynamics, aimed at specialists in minimal systems.
arxiv-2602-06056:
Search engines and chat tools lean on embeddings, compact number lists that capture meaning from text and pictures. Zihang Wang and 6 co-authors ask whether a newer kind of model, the multimodal diffusion model, can make good embeddings. They compare it directly with standard autoregressive vision and language models.

Diffusion models build outputs in parallel and look both ways across a sequence, which sounds promising. In practice, their embeddings trailed the standard models on grouping, question answering, and search tasks. One strong diffusion model stayed close, while another fell far behind. The team traces the gap to weak matching between picture and text signals inside diffusion models.
arxiv-2602-06156:
Signal peaks that spike too high are a known headache in OFDM, the transmission scheme behind Wi-Fi and mobile data. Bianca S de C da Silva and 2 co-authors revisit their earlier neural network built to tame those peaks. The first study never tested the network on truly unseen data.

This case study adds those missing generalization checks. The network still pushed the peak-to-average power ratio down to the target level on fresh data. It also did so with less computing effort than rival approaches. The authors say the new results refine, rather than overturn, their first conclusions. The method looks practical across a wider range of conditions than first shown.
arxiv-2602-06256:
Adjusting a language model's inner activations at run time, called steering, can change its behavior without retraining. Navita Goyal and Hal Daumé ask a sharper question: does steering change only what it should? They name that quality specificity, and split it into three parts.

General specificity means fluency and unrelated skills survive. Control specificity means related behaviors stay put. Robustness specificity means those behaviors survive when inputs shift. In two safety cases, cutting over-refusal and cutting faithfulness hallucinations, steering worked and passed the first two checks. It failed the third: steered models grew far more open to jailbreak attacks. The authors say robustness checks must join standard steering evaluations.
arxiv-2602-06456:
Data streams change over time, and a whole field of detectors exists to spot those changes, called concept drift. Brandon Gower-Winter and 2 co-authors challenge the foundations of that field. Most detectors compare two windows of the stream and declare drift when the windows differ enough, but the windows themselves shape what gets seen.

They call this the Window Dilemma: perceived drift can be a product of windowing rather than of the process generating the data. Worse, claimed drift events can rarely be verified in practice, making detection ill-posed. An illustrative example and empirical comparisons back the claim. Plain batch learning often beat drift-aware methods, which raises hard questions about what detectors are for.
arxiv-2602-06656:
V. V. Enaldiev and Z. Z. Alisultanov study a layered material built from graphene resting on a twisted ferroelectric bilayer. The twisted layer forms a pattern of polar domains, which prints an electric superlattice pattern onto the graphene without any chemical change. The paper asks how this patterned stack absorbs light and turns it into electric current.

Adding charge carriers to the graphene reshapes its energy bands, because the carriers screen the pattern. Where the density of states spikes, the stack shows resonant absorption of light and a photovoltaic effect that produces current without any applied voltage. The authors show the current comes only from one mechanism, a shift current, since symmetry forbids the other usual contribution.
arxiv-2602-06756:
Long Tran, Antti Koskela, Ossi Räisä, and Antti Honkela examine how to keep a privacy budget when a data analyst adapts on the fly. In differential privacy, a privacy filter is a stopping rule that halts the analysis before a total budget is overspent. The paper asks whether the natural filter built from f-differential privacy, a refined accounting framework, can be trusted in this fully adaptive setting.

The answer is no. Tracking the accumulating trade-off curve and stopping when it crosses the budget line turns out to be fundamentally invalid. That blocks the use of fast standard accounting tools. The authors pin down exactly when that natural filter could work. They also prove a central limit theorem for privacy loss under full adaptivity. Finally, they build a closed-form approximate filter for a common mechanism family that beats a popular alternative in the extremes.
arxiv-2602-06856:
James Ratcliffe, Ronnie Rodgers, and Sangsoo Ryu study probe branes set inside the curved space made by other branes. Their shapes are fixed by any smooth complex function on the probe's own world sheet, a free choice that yields whole families at once. Most of these shapes keep a quarter of the background's supersymmetry, and half when the two brane kinds match.

Two cases in the near view of a D3-brane background show what the shapes mean in dual terms. D5 probes match defect matter with a complex mass, which at low energy shrinks to lines sitting where the mass hits zero. D3 probes match states with Gukov-Witten surface defects in a four-dimensional gauge theory. The families give a bendable kit for studying defects by holography.
arxiv-2602-07656:
Tag-based trackers help find lost items but also enable stalking, and advanced rogue trackers defeat label-based defenses by rotating labels fast. Abhishek Kumar Mishra and three co-authors present AirCatch, a passive detector that uses a physical-layer constraint instead.

While logical labels change freely, a transmitter's analog imprint stays stable and occupies a compact, persistent region in carrier frequency offset feature space. A modulation-aware fingerprint plus a tracking detection method based on high core density turns that stability into a catch. Privacy and security teams get a defense that survives label rotation because it fingerprints hardware, not labels.
arxiv-2602-08356:
Physicists hunt for a critical point in the phase diagram of nuclear matter, a spot where matter changes character in a special way. Yu Zhang and three co-authors review the search through net-proton fluctuations measured by the STAR experiment at RHIC. Their arXiv paper gathers results from the second beam-energy scan, in both collider and fixed-target modes.

The review presents fluctuation ratios up to fourth order and compares them with lattice, hadron-gas, fluid, and transport models. It also weighs the distorting effect of volume fluctuations, which matter most at fixed-target energies. The paper closes with an outlook on future experiments. Readers get a clear status report on one of nuclear physics' most watched quests.
arxiv-2602-08456:
Dense Wi-Fi networks waste spectrum when access points all shout at full power and refuse to share the air. Francesc Wilhelmi and four co-authors propose a decentralized way to tune power and sensing thresholds so neighboring networks can transmit at once. Their arXiv paper targets spatial reuse, a cheap path to higher efficiency in crowded deployments.

The algorithm uses regret matching grounded in internal regret minimization, steering selfish agents toward correlated equilibria that mimic coordination without any messages between them. Simulations show near-optimal global performance, beating the usual inefficient equilibria of greedy tuning. Readers get evidence that scalable, message-free coordination may beat heavy centralized schemes for next-generation Wi-Fi.
arxiv-2602-08756:
Two puzzling hydrogen structures near a faint white dwarf star sit inside a vast cavity in interstellar gas around the Upper Scorpius-Centaurus OB association. Gerrit L. Verschuur examines high-resolution 21-centimeter survey data and proposes an origin story. His arXiv paper hypothesizes that the pair of features, at velocities of plus 12 and minus 6 kilometers per second, are remnants of an old planetary nebula.

The cavity itself may have been carved by an ancient supernova, and the nebula, some three hundred thousand years old, cooled until its gas turned neutral and glows in the 21-centimeter line. Expanding into gas-poor space preserved its shape, since little surrounding gas could erase it. Readers get a testable hypothesis linking a white dwarf, a cavity, and two ghostly gas structures.
arxiv-2602-08856:
Reinier Sorgdrager proves a size bound for a class of p-adic representations, the number-theoretic objects that encode symmetries of p-adic groups. For an admissible Banach representation of GL_2 over a p-adic field, whose locally analytic vectors carry an infinitesimal character, the Gelfand-Kirillov dimension is at most the field's degree over the p-adic rationals.

The same bound holds for the units of the quaternions over the same field. The proof, which assumes p is larger than 2, also yields side observations about p-adic Banach representations that may help other work. It is a technical advance in the representation theory of p-adic groups.
arxiv-2602-08956:
Two fireballs in NASA's CNEOS database may have come from beyond the Sun's family, Richard Cloete and one co-author report. Using a calibrated error model for post-2018 velocity measurements, they convert fireball paths to Sun-centered orbits and test interstellar origin with million-draw Monte Carlo simulations. Two events clear solar escape speed by wide margins.

CNEOS-22, over the eastern tropical Pacific in July 2022, exceeds escape by 5.18 kilometers per second, an 8.7-sigma margin. CNEOS-25, over the Barents Sea in February 2025, exceeds it by 3.22 kilometers per second, a 5.5-sigma margin. In neither case does any simulation yield a bound orbit, though the authors note error underestimates of five to nine times would be needed to change the verdict.
arxiv-2602-09056:
Enso O. Torres Alegre proves a rigidity result for chance rules in infinite-dimensional operational theories. Under three rules, no faster-than-light signals, normal steering through purification, and sigma-affinity under countable mixes, any chance rule built from transition chances between pure states must collapse to the identity rule. Nonlinear detours, the proof shows, would enable signal distinctions in steering setups.

The Born rule thus emerges as the unique assignment compatible with no-signaling in theories admitting normal steering. The result is linked to standard quantum mechanics through von Neumann algebras and the GNS picture, recovering the usual Born rule for projective and generalized tests. It also constrains proposed post-quantum changes in continuous-variable and field-theoretic regimes.
arxiv-2602-09256:
As growing numbers of young women in China live solo, they face knotted privacy, security, and safety risks across smart homes, web platforms, and public base. Shijing He and five co-authors run six hands-on threat-model workshops with 33 joiners. They build a human-first model of how online-aided physical violence, harassment and scams, and wide watch by people, companies, and the state reinforce each other.

Joiners describe four fix plans: device settings, boundary handling, social habits, and social-media tactics, each bringing new weak spots and emotional burdens. The authors respond with a digital safety guidebook for young women living alone, plus design effects for devices and platforms and policy, legal, and school tips. Their title quotes a participant's demand: build environments that protect women rather than selling anxiety.
arxiv-2602-09556:
Twist shapes effects from lab reactions to carrier shape math, yet no direct large-scale probe for crystal twist existed, above all in reversal-even systems with faint circular light uptake. Nikolai Peshcherenko and three co-authors propose the Chiralometer in their 2026 paper, a motion-based meter that drives spin carriers out of balance. First-principles math and semi-classic transport theory back the design.

A heat gradient in non-metals, or a voltage field in metals, induces leftover spin in phonons or charges. That tilt yields a large-scale motion torque within reach of modern magnet meters and lever sensors. Robust marks appear in chiral crystals including Te, SiO2, and the exotic half-metal CoSi. The paper sets motion torque as a basic marker for twist, with promise for orbit tech.
arxiv-2602-09756:
Peter A. Clarkson and two co-authors derive discrete rules from Bäcklund shifts of the fifth Painlevé rule in their 2026 paper, including a new discrete rule with ternary balance. Two classes of ratio answers of the fifth Painlevé rule are treated: one shown through general Laguerre polys, the other through general Umemura polys. Both classes can be shown as Wronskians of Laguerre polys.

Ladders of ratio answers of the discrete rules are derived in terms of the general Laguerre and Umemura polys. Known non-single ratio answers of the fifth Painlevé rule are then used: pairs of twin ratio answers yield distinct ladders of ratio answers fitting the same discrete rule. One discrete rule can thus carry several distinct ratio answer ladders.
arxiv-2602-10056:
Attention powers modern neural networks, but its cost grows with the square of sequence length. A 2026 paper by Tobias Schröder and Lester Mackey introduces WildCat, a high-accuracy, low-cost compression of attention. Instead of attending to everything, WildCat attends over a small weighted core set picked by a fast, spectrally accurate sampling method called randomly pivoted Cholesky.

Weights are tuned to cut rebuild error, and the error falls very fast while runtime stays near-linear for bounded inputs. Earlier practical approximations either lacked error guarantees or needed square-law time for such fidelity. A GPU-optimized code release and tests on image generation, classification, and language-model cache compression show the benefits.
arxiv-2602-10156:
Genetic perturbations aimed at the same gene can produce different cellular responses depending on their exact genomic locus. A 2026 paper led by Boyang Fu, with seven co-authors, introduces STRAND, a generative model that forecasts single-cell transcriptional responses from regulatory DNA sequence. Instead of collapsing distinct interventions into one gene representation, STRAND encodes the sequence at each perturbation's locus.

That sequence representation parameterizes a conditional transport process from control cells to perturbed cells. Because perturbations are represented by sequence rather than fixed gene identifiers, STRAND infers zero-shot at unseen loci and expands genomic coverage from about one and a half percent to about ninety-five percent. Tests on CRISPR data in three cell lines show gains up to a third in low-sample regimes and best average rank on unseen-gene benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-10256:
The Bernstein-von Mises theorem describes how posteriors concentrate around truth, but classical versions demand technical smoothness assumptions. A 2026 paper by Victor-Emmanuel Brunel, sole author, proves new, general versions of the theorem for well-specified models and for misspecified ones. The setting requires only a log-likelihood concave in the parameter and a log-concave prior distribution.

Unlike classical versions, these versions need no smoothness assumptions at all, relying solely on convex analysis. The result broadens the theorem's reach to models where smoothness cannot be assumed, giving Bayesian asymptotics a cleaner foundation built on convexity rather than differentiability conditions.
arxiv-2602-10356:
Computer-use agents face varied, shifting digital settings where unseen cases and distribution shifts demand ongoing learning, yet high-quality setting-grounded training data without human annotation is scarce. A 2026 paper led by Tianci Xue, with seven co-authors, introduces ACuRL, an Autonomous Curriculum Reinforcement Learning setup continually adapting agents to chosen environments with no human data. The agent first surveys an environment to gather initial experiences.

During repeated training, a curriculum task maker uses those experiences plus last-round feedback to build new tasks fitted to current capabilities. A sturdy automatic judge, CUAJudge, matches human judgments ninety-three percent of the time, supplying steady reward signals. The method enables intra- and cross-environment ongoing learning with three to twenty-nine points of absolute gains on target settings without catastrophic forgetting. It also softens decline under version updates, platform moves, and resolution shifts.
arxiv-2602-10456:
Devansh Jalota and Matthew Tsao analyze the minibuses and shared auto-rickshaws that carry millions in large cities in a 2026 paper. These informal services fill gaps where formal transit is thin and alternatives are unaffordable. Drivers choose routes for profit, however, and those choices need not serve the whole system well.

The authors build a game-theoretic system with a fixed menu of routes, measuring how much speed decentralized driver choices lose. They then design incentive plans that nudge drivers toward better system-wide outcomes. The work speaks to cities that depend on informal transit. It shows how to keep the bend of driver-led service while reducing the waste of uncoordinated competition.
arxiv-2602-10556:
Lihan Zha and seven co-authors pursue a generalist robot policy that needs no retraining for new bodies in a 2026 paper. Vision-language-action models pretrained across embodiments still cling to their training robots and demand costly fine-tuning for each new one. The field's long-standing goal is zero-shot transfer to unseen embodiments.

Their recipe, Language-Action Pre-training, represents low-level robot actions directly in natural language. That aligns action supervision with the pretrained vision-language model's own input-output spread, requiring no learned tokenizer, no costly annotation, and no embodiment-exact system. Their model, LAP-3B, is presented as the first vision-language-action model with large zero-shot transfer to unseen embodiments, tested across multiple robot platforms.
arxiv-2602-10656:
Jingru Lin and three co-authors benchmark audio thinking that needs outside information in a 2026 paper. Audio-language models perform well on sound, speech, and music tasks, but current benchmarks test only internal knowledge. Real questions often demand retrieval: naming a sound may require looking something up.

Their benchmark, AudioRAG, mixes generated and manually curated question-answer pairs in realistic web settings, testing thinking augmented by retrieval. Tests show even leading audio-language models struggle with these questions. The authors also propose an agentic pipeline combining audio thinking with retrieval-augmented making as a stronger baseline. The benchmark sets a harder, more realistic bar for audio intelligence.
arxiv-2602-11256:
Charged black holes at extremality can grow hair through curved evolution. Zachary Gelles and Frans Pretorius construct asymptotically extreme black holes by evolving a charged scalar field, spread tuned wave packets in an initially super-extreme spacetime. The resulting horizon carries diverging energy density and near-constant charge density.

Viewed through key collapse, dynamical extreme black holes act as universal threshold solutions, modulo family-dependent hair. Outside the horizon the scalar decays, as in straight theory, but just inside, scalar curvature appears to grow without bound. That suggests near-threshold solutions without a black hole could still show large curvatures visible from afar, a striking endpoint for charged horizon instability.
arxiv-2602-11356:
A dusty filament in Ophiuchus glows brighter in microwaves than standard sources explain. Simon Casassus and five co-authors image the rho Ophiuchi W region with ALMA Band 1, mapping excess microwave emission at high fidelity. The filament tracks infrared bands from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and its signal drops sharply above about thirty gigahertz.

A deep mosaic yields a spectrum by cross-link, with flux-loss and bias values from simulations and ancillary data. The spectrum follows a power law with no fine structure, and Band 1 power rises at high spatial rates relative to infrared. A compact radio-only source with no infrared counterpart stands out. Multi-rate intensities are provided for spectral building of spinning dust.
arxiv-2602-11556:
Physicists who smash particles together often estimate a group of particles by a shortcut that assumes each particle energy and sideways momentum dwarf its mass. M. P. Fewell asks how good that shortcut really is, working out correction terms step by step up to the fourth power of the mass-to-energy ratio. The news is reassuring: the first correction is quadratic rather than linear, and cancellations shrink both it and the next term.

The same treatment is extended to groups of three and four particles, with a path sketched for larger groups. Strikingly, the simplest zero-order formulas for these multi-particle cases turn out to be very plain, plainer than their reputation suggests. The note argues those simple forms deserve wider use in collider analysis.
arxiv-2602-11756:
Knowledge graphs promise unified data, but integrated data rarely arrive as graphs. They come as spreadsheets, XML files, or relational tables. Luigi Asprino and one co-author work with Façade-X, a method that gives direct access to many formats through a meta-model that specializes RDF to fit general data structures. That model lets SPARQL queries target sources with those structures.

Façade-X uses only a fraction of RDF, so not every SPARQL query has a solution over a Façade-X graph. The paper consolidates the method and studies when basic graph patterns are satisfiable. It pairs the theory with an algorithm for deciding satisfiability, plus experiments with a proof-of-concept tool, including real-world queries. The results pave the way for smarter query execution and more efficient data integration systems.
arxiv-2602-11956:
The visual cortex interprets scenes through learned regularities, formalized as inference under a prior, but whether task priors can be learned flexibly on demand remains open. Balázs Meszéna and six co-authors build a model of primary visual cortex, optimized for a simple sorting task, and analyze it alongside large-scale mouse recordings. Treating V1 activity as latent beliefs lets them probe task-related priors in neural responses.

To make task learning efficient, they extend the VAE formalism so a task can be acquired by reusing prior learning. The resulting Task-Amortized VAE learns task priors that, when stimuli break trained patterns, produce uncertainty marks in the model matching bimodal response profiles in V1 traces. The model also captures within-day updates to group signals, confirming that flexible context priors can be learned on demand and deployed at the entry level of visual cortex.
arxiv-2602-12156:
Preparing exact photon-number states, known as Fock states, gets harder as the photon count rises, because control grows messy with size. Shan Jin led this work with 12 co-authors, proposing resonant subspace engineering, a method that traps the maths in a small, safe space. That space links a starting coherent state to the target state.

Once trapped there, moving to the target becomes a simple rotation on a synthetic sphere, guided by resonance rules the team writes in closed form. For single Fock states, time and gate depth grow only like the fourth root of photon number. The frame also handles mixed superpositions, needing only a few rounds for photon numbers from 70 to 100.
arxiv-2602-12256:
Writing unit tests by hand is slow, and tests from old search-based tools often read poorly and prove hard to use. Alex Chudic led this work with one co-author, Gül Çalıklı, testing whether few-shot prompting can lift language-model test writing. In few-shot mode, the model sees examples in the prompt, and the source of those examples may matter as much as the model itself.

Tests on HumanEval and ClassEval with GPT-4o compare human, search-based, and model-made examples, judging correctness, coverage, readability, mental load, and upkeep in mixed human-AI code. Few-shot models can produce high-quality tests, and human examples give the best coverage and correctness. Picking examples by combined problem and code similarity works best of all.
arxiv-2602-12356:
Benchmarks and leaderboards rank AI systems, but they rarely ask whose priorities those rankings serve. Philip Waggoner works alone here, proposing a theoretical frame that recasts benchmarking as a multilayer, adaptive network linking metrics, model parts, and stakeholder groups through weighted ties. As AI enters varied, high-stakes settings, a purely technical scorecard misses the social context of deployment.

Conjoint-derived utilities and a human-in-the-loop update rule let human trade-offs enter benchmark structure directly, while benchmarks evolve over time yet keep stability and interpretability. Classical leaderboards emerge as a special case of the wider formulation. The result is a foundation for evaluation protocols that are more context-aware, accountable, and aligned with human values, plus new tools for analysing benchmark structure itself.
arxiv-2602-12556:
Mixture-of-experts models scale language models by letting experts specialise, yet in practice that specialisation often fails. Ruijun Huang led this work with 18 co-authors, analysing expert failure from a spectral view of parameter and gradient spaces. Some experts become functionally similar, while others act as de facto shared experts, limiting effective capacity and performance.

Three findings explain the failure. First, experts share highly overlapping dominant spectral parts in parameters. Second, dominant gradient subspaces align strongly across experts, driven by ubiquitous low-rank structure in human text. Third, gating preferentially routes inputs along those dominant directions, further limiting specialisation. The fix, Spectral-Decoupled MoE, decomposes both parameter and gradient in spectral space. It improves downstream performance, enables real expert specialisation, adds minimal compute, and integrates into existing mixture-of-experts architectures including Qwen and DeepSeek.
arxiv-2602-12756:
Large language models can forecast time series, but the usual step-by-step approach feeds each prediction back in as input, so small early errors snowball into large drift. Xingyu Zhang and four co-authors recast the problem through control theory. Their closed-loop system, called F-LLM, adds a learnable observer that watches the forecast and corrects it, rather than letting errors pass along untouched.

The authors prove that, under stated contraction assumptions, this feedback keeps step-by-step errors bounded within the local model. Tests on time series benchmarks show the method cuts error growth and performs well overall. For long-horizon forecasting, where drift is the main enemy, a feedback loop that steadies the trajectory is a natural fix, and this paper gives it both theory and experiments.
arxiv-2602-13156:
Cyber incident response must adapt as attacks evolve, but reinforcement-learning approaches need handcrafted simulators and discard useful meaning in raw logs and alerts. Yiran Gao and two co-authors propose an end-to-end language-model agent that uses pretrained security knowledge and in-context learning instead. One lightweight 14-billion-setting model integrates perception, thinking, planning, and action: reading logs to infer network state, updating attack conjectures, simulating response consequences, and acting.

By comparing simulated outcomes with real observations, the agent refines its attack model and response repeatedly, demonstrating in-context adaptation without a hand-built simulator. The approach runs on commodity hardware. On incident logs from the literature, the agent recovers up to 23% faster than frontier language models, suggesting agentic language models can carry incident response without heavy mock run infrastructure.
arxiv-2602-13456:
Resistive shunts are workhorses of superconducting electronics, damping oscillations, stabilizing switching, aiding current sensing, and protecting circuits during quenches. In nanowire single-photon detectors, the shunt also sets how fast the sensor resets between events. This paper steps outside the superconducting state to study how the shunt resistor shapes the resistive state of a superconducting wire at elevated currents still below the critical current for full transition.

Shunt resistance is shown to control system dynamics and the onset of distinct resistive phases, including hot-spot and phase-slippage events. Dynamic current redistribution in the circuit further affects local heating and helps govern the resistive state, a factor that grows more important at higher operating temperatures. Khalil Harrabi leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13556:
Meaning-first messaging sends meaning rather than raw bits, and Discernment applies that idea to physical signals such as baseband radio and audio, using generative AI models that work in discrete spaces. The system adapts to channel damage, modeled as erasure channels, by switching between an autoregressive generator and a diffusion-based generator depending on the erasure pattern.

Even as channel capacity degrades severely, Discernment keeps meaning intact, with only small and graceful declines in labeling accuracy and faithfulness of the rebuilt meaning. That resilience, plus spectrum thrift and low model complexity, suits Internet-of-things devices and motivates further work on meaning-first channels. Silvija Kokalj-Filipovic leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13656:
Learning fast, acrobatic motion from video could spare humanoid robots costly motion capture, but video lacks height stability, force data, and robustness. KungfuAthleteBot tackles those gaps as one unified framework, starting from a high-dynamic motion data set built with professional martial artists. A physics-guided parabolic trajectory correction removes height drift and global jitter in aerial and landing phases, enforcing physical plausibility.

A three-stage curriculum bridges human and robot actuation differences, progressively enabling stable learning of dynamic moves, while a teacher-free paradigm jointly learns disturbance rejection and fall recovery in a single policy. That policy recovered in about 0.7 seconds, the fastest reported for a unified policy, and real-robot tests showed strong robustness under severe disturbances. Zhongxiang Lei leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14056:
Musashi Kato and one co-author propose a 2026 arXiv paper on a new kind of exceptional point in non-Hermitian physics. These are points where states merge, and the new type, called interaction-enabled, is protected by topology yet barred at the non-interacting level. Both bosonic and fermionic systems host them, the authors show.

The twofold points rest on zero-dimensional topology and shift the loss rate, a quantity cold-atom experiments can measure. Threefold points rest on one-dimensional topology that lies beyond point-gap classifications. Together they hint at a wider family of interaction-enabled degeneracies, protected by charge, pseudo-spin-parity, and PT symmetries.
arxiv-2602-14356:
Areez Muhammed Shabu and two co-authors tackle a 2026 arXiv fairness problem in skin cancer AI. Early detection saves lives, yet diagnostic tools trained mostly on light skin perform worse on darker skin. The ISIC benchmark holds over 70% light-skin images and under 8% dark-skin images, a gap that threatens equitable care.

The paper presents a generative augmentation pipeline that fine-tunes Stable Diffusion with low-rank adaptation on the dark-skin subset of ISIC. It then makes synthetic dermoscopic images keyed to lesion kind and skin tone. Tests on two downstream tasks probe whether those synthetic images lift accuracy and fairness for darker skin, a practical step toward diagnostic tools that serve all patients.
arxiv-2602-14756:
Christian Ventura-Meinersen and others give a shape-based plan for tuning pulses in multi-level quantum gear, aiming for fast, true state hops past the slow limit. Their plan slides smoothly between slow and fast drive, cutting stray jumps while boosting the jumps sought, even with many levels in play.

For one-knob pulse control, tuning shrinks to solving a plain first-order rate law, a striking cut in work. Spin-based demos, setting a state and moving a qubit state, show the slow-fast plans at work. Quantum control gains a short, geometric road to fast, true hops.
arxiv-2602-14956:
Mikheeva and colleagues map the star-forming region S255IR at about 1 millimetre with the Submillimeter Array in Hawaii, covering 210 to 250 gigahertz. They detect 53 molecules, including complex organics. Rotational temperatures of 100 to 200 kelvin are found in the hot core SMA1. Methanol line depths suggest that rarer oxygen-bearing organics are optically thin there.

Most molecules fall into two groups. One group is seen only toward SMA1. The other is also seen in a ring-like structure west of it, likely the walls of a cavity carved by fast outflows from young stars in SMA1, SMA2, and possibly SMA3. Methanol lines put the cavity walls near 50 to 60 kelvin. The team plans deeper stacked spectra to measure other organics in the ring.
arxiv-2602-15056:
Harder and Flemming use machine learning to rebuild carbon monoxide reanalysis when satellite observations vanish. The Copernicus Atmospheric Monitoring Service blends model runs with satellite data to produce composition reanalyses, and quality swings with data availability. Instruments come and go, as with MOPITT carbon monoxide observations ending in early 2025, leaving gaps in the record.

Machine learning offers a fix by learning systematic gaps between model setups. The study tests learning methods that predict monthly-mean total column carbon monoxide reanalysis from a control model run alone. The aim is a steadier long-term record that survives the loss of any single satellite data stream.
arxiv-2602-15156:
Rajesh and colleagues propose Panini, a continual learning approach in token space with structured memory. Language models increasingly reason over untrained content: new documents, changing knowledge, and user data. Retrieval-augmented generation stores exact texts outside the model, fetching subsets at query time. That wastes test-time compute and risks off-topic context that breeds unsupported answers.

Panini instead keeps the base model fixed, folding each new experience into an outside semantic memory that builds over time. Texts become Generative Semantic Workspaces, entity- and event-aware networks of QA pairs. From them, a model can rebuild situations and mine latent knowledge through logic chains. At query time, Panini walks only the workspace, fetching likely chains. Across six QA benchmarks, it leads on average by 5 to 7 percent over rival baselines. It uses 2 to 30 times fewer answer-context tokens, supports open-source pipelines, and cuts wrong answers on no-answer queries.
arxiv-2602-15256:
Abril-Bermúdez and colleagues show that higher-order group structure can emerge from shared random environments, even without direct links. Group conduct is commonly blamed on direct links among system parts. Using a tiny random model, the team shows random swings induce both overlap and synergy-based links, with the latter filling larger regions of link space. Quantified via O-information, they prove a no-go rule: fixed coupling between system parts and a shared random environment rules out synergy-based higher-order conduct.

Key point: that constraint can be overcome in time. Shifts between overlap and synergy arise from time-changing random coupling or from the mix between shared environments and direct links. Together, the results name random go-between as its own route to higher-order group order beyond the usual link-based view.
arxiv-2602-15356:
Bridges and colleagues detail the plan, build, and tests of an MPI-based GPU message API allowing easy-to-use, high-speed, CPU-free message flow. Cutting the CPU from the message fast path is key to lean GPU-based ML speed. Current GPU message APIs either keep leaning on the CPU for message flow or put heavy syncing loads on coders.

This API rests on earlier offered MPI extras and uses HPE Slingshot 11 net powers. The team shows use and speed by showing how the API plainly allows CPU-free gather/scatter halo exchange bits in the Cabana/Kokkos setup. A matchup with Cray MPICH on the Frontier and Tuolumne giants backs the wins. Findings show up to a 50 percent cut in mid note lag in plain GPU ping-pong swaps. They also show a 28 percent boost growing a halo-exchange test to 8,192 GPUs of the Frontier giant.
arxiv-2602-15456:
Khan and colleagues guess that when data is credited to outlets such as press, papers, or sites, today's LLMs show hidden tastes, picking outlets over others. LLM agents are deployed as doors to online data, sifting, picking, and blending data from stores. In these cases, LLM agents steer what users get, pulling focus to certain fetched data.

While prior work has aimed on slants in data LLMs make, less focus has been paid to what shapes picks for users. Through tests on twelve LLMs from six makers, across fake and real-world jobs, they find some models show firm tastes.
