Tests on LunarLander and CartPole show faster convergence and lower training variance than standard normalization.
arxiv-2604-23256: Gupta and LaGrow show that in differentiable symbolic regression, the recovered formula depends on the fixed architecture routing variables, not the grammar. Three depth-3 architectures across twenty-four operator-shape-leaf combinations show recovery swinging from zero to full success on the same target. Trees holding two equal-depth subtrees fail in all tested setups. A proof-of-concept fix trains a small architecture set and picks the expression with the lowest held-out error. On the jointly run subset, this lifts recovery from about one-third to 50.1 percent.
arxiv-2604-23356: Xiang and nine colleagues present VeriLLMed, a visual system for debugging medical models with biomedical knowledge graphs. Developers often lack medical expertise to read errors clinically and face diverse failures across inputs and tasks. They struggle to spot recurring patterns with instance-centric manual review. VeriLLMed turns outputs into matched reasoning paths, builds knowledge-graph references, and names three error classes: relation, branch, and missing errors. Case studies and expert review show it helps developers spot implausible reasoning and generate useful insights.
arxiv-2604-24256: Yao and colleagues present in-orbit checks of the SVOM Visible Telescope, using Gaia Data Release 3. Star positions beat a small fraction of an arcsecond for bright stars, degrading for faint targets. Shortly after launch, buildup cut light by about 40 percent, but an initial bake-out restored it, and gradual new buildup cost about 20 percent of light over 100 days before leveling off. Routine star checks still hold precise zero-point values with steady photometry. Model stellar spectra yield links to Gaia, SDSS, and Johnson-Cousins systems with small errors.
arxiv-2604-24356: Bournez shows primitive recursion can be expressed equally in three moving systems. They are bounded loops of a fixed looping ReLU network and robust work by a fixed polynomial ODE. They include loops of a fixed poly map with an outside step-size knob. In each, the time bound is itself primitive recursive, and chaining grows out of motion. The match exposes a gap: no fixed poly map rounds evenly to the nearest integer or realizes exact phase selection. Poly ODEs do both robustly through steady flow.
arxiv-2604-24956: Boas traces the history of three math ideas: equivalence relations, Cauchy sequences and metric spaces. He argues for reviving disused definitions of these notions, which could prove profitable. The paper shows how each concept took shape and where older wordings fell out of use. Reviving them, he claims, would serve math well today.
arxiv-2604-25056: Moharana and nine colleagues analyse V446 Cephei, a beta Cephei pulsator in an eclipsing binary. Using TESS photometry and HERMES spectra, they derive stellar parameters. The primary star has a mass of about 10.7 solar masses. They find 21 pulsation frequencies, with the main mode near a harmonic of the orbital frequency. Timing shifts reveal a tertiary companion of about 4 solar masses on about a 2,300-day orbit. They conclude V446 Cephei is a triple with a compact third body or a hierarchical quadruple.
arxiv-2604-25156: Wang, Xu and Yu put forth online learning for autoregressive multilayer block models, stationary and not. Dynamic multilayer networks link one node set through many relation types over time, but past ways assume independence or drift. Their AR(1)-MSBM sets edge change odds from latent community ties shared across layers. When steady, they give online estimation with recursive updates and spectral refinement, with rates, minimax optimality, and recovery pledges. For non-stationarity, an adaptive windowed way adjusts to unknown shifts, with matching segmentwise pledges. Number tests back the findings.
arxiv-2604-25456: Venkateswaran and three colleagues probe linguistic bias in LLM recommendations. They vary prompts across Southern American English, Indian English, and Code-Switched Hindi-English, using Yelp and Walmart data. They add name lists balanced by cuisine and category, and zero-shot prompt LLMs to pick top-20 recommendations per dialect prompt. Dialect shapes restaurant picks, with mistral-small-3.1 and llama-3.1 models more sensitive to Indian and Code-Switched prompts. For products, llama-3.1-70B is most sensitive to Code-Switched prompts, in four of seven categories. No broad size trends emerge.
arxiv-2604-25556: Stamoulis studies rainbow matching: finding a largest matching with at most one edge of each colour. Rainbow matchings equal stable sets in an augmented graph formed from the line graph by completing each colour class into a clique. He defines a deletion parameter: the fewest colours whose removal lands the residual graph in a hereditary class. Deletion into a rank-r exact class yields Lasserre exactness at level k plus r. Articulation colours induce clique-sum decompositions, so membership tests run block by block.
arxiv-2604-25856: Azenhas defines slack for recording tableaux in the quantum Littlewood-Richardson map, showing it carries the data needed to define the map's inverse. The enriched slack packs the reverse Schensted column insertion routes for computing the inverse. The authors then use the slack data on highest-weight symplectic tableaux. The paper gives a concrete combinatorial route to inverting the quantum Littlewood-Richardson map.
arxiv-2604-25956: Aebi and Cairns characterize integer lattice triangles whose centers are lattice points. For an integer perimeter l, an acute integer lattice triangle can have a lattice-point orthocenter only in special cases. It exists exactly when l equals 6 or l is at least 8. Matching results hold for the circumcenter and the centroid. The authors contrast these findings with obtuse and right triangles.
arxiv-2604-26056: Sanetullaev offers a pedagogical MKS unit system for electromagnetism, setting vacuum constants epsilon_0 and mu_0 to 1/c. The system keeps Maxwell's laws while making the speed of light clear. Electric units reduce to motion units, cutting base units. Resistance becomes unit-free, capacitance and inductance take time units, and radiation pressure becomes the size of E cross B. Student surveys of 46 and 39 students show significant gain in perceived clarity of the wave equation, with most liking unit-free resistance.
arxiv-2604-26156: Mavoa and four colleagues explore inflation in modified gravity where a scalar field couples nonminimally to the nonmetricity scalar. They track the coupling's effect on the scalar spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. For de Sitter inflation, Planck-matching predictions survive only in a narrow coupling window. The index rises and the ratio falls as coupling grows, with theory imposing a matching upper bound. A cosh-type model is more robust, with a spectral index near 0.97 at sixty e-folds matching current observations.
arxiv-2604-26456: Akhil Rajeev P and Annarao Kulkarni built Naamah, a large synthetic Sanskrit name-finding dataset of 102,942 sentences. Turning Sanskrit books into digital text is slowed by a lack of labeled examples, and generic language-model add-ons often err and miss classical grammar depth. The team took seed entities from DBpedia and made text with a 24-billion-parameter hybrid reasoning model, giving grammatical, varied training data. They tested two transformer designs on it: huge multilingual XLM RoBERTa and lean IndicBERTv2.
arxiv-2604-26556: Kitagawa studied rational-curve moduli on cubic hypersurfaces in characteristic other than 2 or 3. He proved a claim for every degree d of at least 1. The Kontsevich stable-map space on a smooth cubic hypersurface is irreducible once that dimension reaches 4 or more. The result maps curve-family geometry in positive characteristic. The work covers every degree from 1 upward.
arxiv-2604-26656: Arnold studies how differentially private rewriting reshapes the style of texts. Privacy tools have moved from word swaps to full sentence rewrites with language models, but their effect on a text's register was largely unexplored. Close study of rewritten texts shows the privacy cost reaches far beyond word choice: interactive markers, context references, and complex subordination all thin out. Both autoregressive rewording and bidirectional substitution push texts toward a flat, non-involved, non-persuasive register. Meaning survives, but the style marks of human writing get smoothed away.
arxiv-2604-26756: Cavicchioni, Guerrini, and Lavauzelle study codes over whole numbers under local-repair constraints, where each symbol can be rebuilt from a small set of other symbols. They introduce a weighted notion of local repair over products of cyclic groups , proving a Singleton-like bound for locally fixable codes. The paper also proposes code builds with local repair, including whole-number versions of Tamo-Barg codes.
arxiv-2604-27056: Rogers and twelve colleagues give the first calibration of Ne23, an abundance diagnostic using mid-infrared neon lines insensitive to electron temperature. Optical strong-line methods suffer temperature-driven errors, limiting their use as metallicity tracers, especially in dusty metal-rich gas. From JWST/MIRI views of ten H II regions plus eight metal-poor galaxies with oxygen measures, Ne23 tracks oxygen abundance over a range. The relation scatters just six hundredths of a dex in oxygen at fixed Ne23, enabling oxygen estimates out to redshift 0.8 from JWST/MIRI spectra.
arxiv-2604-27156: Booth and Varzinczak explore belief revision, the rules by which a rational agent updates beliefs on new information, beyond total preorders of possible worlds. Standard accounts rank worlds in one total order and keep sentences true in the most preferred models of the new input. The authors study interval orders, which give each world a range of plausibility, and biorders, which generalize them by allowing intervals to have negative parts in a structured way.
arxiv-2604-27456: Filienko, De Cock, and Pentyala enable data holders to train a synthetic RNA-seq maker without showing raw data, easing strict gene work access. Their approach pairs secure multiparty computation, which keeps inputs private, with differential privacy, which limits leakage from shared data. That mix matters for rare-disease studies, where sites hold data for only a few patients and scale needs pooling across sites. On real RNA-seq cohorts in federated settings, they make useful data, showing safe synthesis works even when data are spread across places.
arxiv-2604-27556: Rossi addresses the large-time behavior of reaction-diffusion equations in periodic media. He outlines a proof of the Freidlin-Gärtner formula, which describes the asymptotic shape of the invasion set and holds for general reaction terms. He then presents recent results, obtained with Guo and Hamel, for weakly bistable equations. These include a regular version of the formula and convergence in profile toward pulsating fronts, for cases with bounded or unbounded support.
arxiv-2604-27756: Dean and nine colleagues present a metasurface design that splits a scene into color and polarization measurements in a single shot. Operating at 532 nm and 700 nm, the design proves robust in simulation, matching color and angular bandwidth needs. They build the design by nanopatterning a titanium dioxide film and show polarization reconstruction for both wavelengths with one structure. The compact design suits lightweight drone imaging, from cells to farm surveying.
arxiv-2604-27856: Taye tests a heartbeat claim: a pygmy shrew pulses near 1,000 times a minute and dies within two years. An elephant pulses 28 times a minute and lives seven decades, yet each racks up near a billion heartbeats before death. That near-constancy was first noted by Rubner in 1908 and sized up by Lindstedt and Calder in 1981, but never tested this way on a fresh set. Taye builds that set from 230 species spanning primates, bats, whales, birds, and cold-blooded kinds, and runs a log-scale heartbeat count through four tests.
arxiv-2604-28056: Wu and colleagues study when language-model-generated rewards can be trusted during reinforcement learning training. Their RHyVE protocol compares small reward sets from shared checkpoints with short-horizon fork tests, since rankings prove unreliable while the policy is weak but informative later. Deploying rewards in a phase-aware way improved peak and retained performance on a sparse manipulation task, though no fixed warm-up schedule works everywhere.
arxiv-2604-28156: Huang and Li present FlexiTac, a low-cost, open-source tactile sensing kit for robot grippers built from thin flexible pads plus a compact readout board. A sealed three-layer laminate with electrodes printed into flexible circuits improves fabrication throughput and repeatability while fitting rigid and soft grippers. Streaming at 100 Hz, it supports contact-aware learning pipelines including visuo-tactile fusion, cross-embodiment transfer and real-to-sim-to-real tuning.
arxiv-2605-00056:
T Ansah-Narh and eight co-authors build a framework for predicting heavy metal pollution in groundwater in Ghana's Densu Basin. The target is the Heavy Metal Pollution Index, a skewed measure built from correlated contaminants, which biased models read poorly without transformation. Conventional methods also miss the basin's spatial patchiness, so the team pairs response transformations with ensemble machine learning.

Three transformations of the index, raw, logarithmic, and Gaussian copula, are tested across six learners under nested cross-validation. Raw-scale fits look deceptively perfect, while the copula version proves most reliable, with the stacked ensemble on top. Clustering points to iron and manganese as the main contributors, matching the regional hydrogeochemistry. The authors note the limits: random rather than spatial validation, and a single basin, with spatial checks left for future work.
arxiv-2605-00156:
Nitin Choudhury and 7 co-authors tackle robocall detection, a field held back by a lack of public data due to privacy concerns. They first build Robo-SAr, a synthetic dataset with about two hundred unwanted calls and about twelve hundred legitimate ones. The fake calls attack along three lines: manipulative wording, emotion-driven speech, and cloned voices.

Their system, RoboKA, combines sound and language cues in one model. It aligns the two kinds of signal, then classifies calls with a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network head, a design meant to capture tangled links between cues. In tests both inside and outside its home data, RoboKA beat strong single-mode and mixed baselines on recall and F1 score, the measures that matter most for catching scam calls.
arxiv-2605-00256:
Osmar Luiz Ferreira de Carvalho and 3 co-authors adapt a strong image segmentation model, SAM2, to the huge scenes captured by satellites and aircraft. Two problems arise: strict settings give precise masks but leave most of a scene unmarked, while loose settings cover more at lower quality. Tiling the scene also splits objects across tile edges.

Their open-source pipeline, Remote SAMsing, runs the model over each tile again and again, painting accepted masks black so later passes see a simpler scene. Thresholds loosen only when coverage stalls, so the sharpest masks come first. Padding and a matching step rebuild objects split by tiles. On seven scenes, coverage rose from well under two-thirds to above nine-tenths in most cases.
arxiv-2605-00356:
Tianyu Hu and 4 co-authors speed up the memory decisions of long-term conversational agents. Such an agent must decide, at every turn, what is worth storing for later recall. Recent systems make that call by generating text with a large model at every turn, which is slow and costly. MemRouter replaces the call with a learned embedding-based router.

The router encodes each turn with its recent context, passes the result through a frozen language model backbone, and classifies it with light heads, training only a small set of parameters. On a standard long-conversation benchmark, with retrieval and answering held identical, MemRouter beat a language-model memory manager on every question type. It also cut the delay of each memory decision from about a second to a small fraction of one.
arxiv-2605-00456:
Zhijun Zeng and 3 co-authors solve fractional diffusion equations, which model spread with memory and long jumps, in high dimensions and over time. Direct discretization of the memory term and the nonlocal spatial operator is painful, especially as dimension grows. Their Deep-Picard framework rests on a nonlinear Feynman-Kac fixed-point form of the equation, which trades those operators for simulation of the underlying random motion.

Each Picard update is done by generating labeled samples from that simulation and fitting a neural network to them by supervised regression, avoiding any residual loss built from fractional derivatives. The random paths couple a beta-stable clock with walk-on-spheres sampling of a stable Lévy process. On tests up to one hundred dimensions, the iteration converged stably and matched reference solutions accurately, offering a route where grid methods cannot go.
arxiv-2605-00556:
Ashwin George and 7 co-authors test whether drivers of partly automated cars stay meaningfully in control. Under partial automation the driver is legally responsible yet mostly inactive, a tension the framework of meaningful human control tries to resolve. It asks that systems track human reasons and that humans remain genuinely in charge. Methods to evaluate that state empirically, however, are underdeveloped.

In a simulator, twenty-four drivers overtook on a two-lane road with automated speed control and partly automated steering, while silent automation failures made their intervention necessary to avoid crashes. Two modes were compared: haptic shared control and traded control. Measured behavior, post-trial ratings, and interviews were linked together. Drivers who felt the car understood them showed less steering conflict. Mismatched intentions and resistance to driver inputs eroded the sense of control, while gentle guidance aligned with intent helped it.
arxiv-2605-01056:
Ismail Belgacem argues that logistic functions give far more reliable modeling of gene regulatory networks than the widely used Hill function. Networks translated from Boolean rules become large continuous equation systems. Their numerical integration underpins attractor, sensitivity, and control studies. Two failure modes for the Hill kernel are shown in this study.

Because the Hill function vanishes at zero input, a bistable circuit can become trapped in an absorbing off state. A logistic model with strictly positive basal production escapes on a timescale matching an analytical estimate. With a non-integer Hill exponent, solver overshoot into negative concentrations can silently produce complex values and spurious trajectories on a large benchmark, while that form finishes cleanly. A global error bound is also proved.
arxiv-2605-01356:
Ruiqi Xue and four co-authors teach safe control policies from logged data when the logs hold almost no unsafe cases. In high-stakes settings no one can gather violations by trial and error, yet standard methods need many unsafe samples to learn where the danger line sits.

The gap hides a trap: states that look safe now but lead to a breach within a few steps. Their framework, PROCO, first learns a model of how the world moves from the logs. It then grounds plain-language facts about unsafe states, drawn from a large language model, into a cautious cost function that can flag risk with no observed breach. Rollouts in the learned model create fresh fake unsafe cases, which support checks of reachability and guide policy learning. Across Safety-Gymnasium tasks, PROCO plugs into many offline safe learning methods and cuts violations.
arxiv-2605-01656:
Tingting Dan and Guorong Wu build a learning machine out of rhythm, copying how the cortex thinks in synchrony. In the brain, parcels of neurons encode facts in both firing rates and exact spike timing set by shared rhythms, so the authors let timing itself run the computation.

Each parcel of the target system, a brain region or a single image pixel, becomes a spiking neuron on a fixed wiring scaffold. Neurons group themselves and fire over time; past spikes gather over a memory window into an oscillatory pattern, the bottom-up route. Since real brain synchrony is partial and brief, a time-delayed coordination rule lets that pattern steer the spiking from the top down. The resulting network, S2-Net, is reported to do well across neural decoding, low-energy signal work, temporal binding, and semantic reasoning.
arxiv-2605-02456:
Mathijs Barkel and Renata Sotirov study the largest part of a graph that can be colored with a set number of colors, a hard optimization problem. They work with a semidefinite programming relaxation, a tractable stand-in whose value bounds the true answer. That bound itself becomes an object of study, treated as a graph parameter with its own properties.

From those properties, the pair show the problem can be solved in efficient time for a class called k-perfect graphs. They add two new families of valid inequalities to tighten the relaxation, and solve the stronger form with a cutting-plane method. In extensive tests, their upper bounds beat the best known from prior work. A second method, built on an exact binary form, produces high-quality feasible colorings to match.
arxiv-2605-02656:
Danyal Maheshwari and four co-authors compare two quantum machine learning designs for forecasting financial time series. One is a quantum version of long short-term memory networks; the other is quantum reservoir computing, where a fixed quantum system provides rich dynamics and only a readout is trained. Both are hybrids that pair quantum circuits with classical training.

Data enter the quantum states by amplitude encoding, with lagged values forming the input. The team varies lag structure for single-series and multi-series cases on real financial data, and benchmarks against classical versions of the same designs. With good lag choice, the quantum models matched classical baselines on single series and modestly beat them on multi-series cases with correlated inputs. The study maps where quantum encoding seems to help.
arxiv-2605-02756:
Paolo Pin and Roberto Rozzi study how peer pressure can evolve when people's beliefs about their own returns are wrong. Agents choose effort under varied, possibly mistaken returns, and social contact does not change payoffs directly. Some agents trade off doing well against matching what they expect peers to do, which is where conformity enters.

For any set of beliefs, the authors characterize the best response and show a single optimal level of peer pressure exists. Within groups sharing the same mistaken belief, that level is evolutionarily stable. It is zero for agents with correct beliefs and can be positive for mistaken ones. In a key case, mistaken agents end up choosing the truly best effort, so their error confirms itself and persists. Pressure need not distort outcomes, but it gives social information a perceived value.
arxiv-2605-02956:
J. Medina Diaz, F. Peña-Garcia, and Irbin Llanqui study how chains of molecules could keep stable mixes before true copying began. They follow steady growth where each chain comes from one precursor and is lost by decay or by growing longer.

For fixed starting material, they prove a single positive steady state exists and that the system moves toward it fast. When two types compete for a shared food source, positive states appear only above a sharp threshold, with one stable and one unstable branch. Adding template copying keeps the old state only under neutral fitness.
arxiv-2605-03256:
Yosuke Mori, Kiwamu Yoshii, and Satoshi Takada give a complete analytic solution for stress inside an elastic sphere pressed by a concentrated load on its surface. Knowing the full interior stress field matters for contact problems, yet closed forms for this classic setup have been elusive.

Starting from the dynamic elasticity equations, they expand displacement and stress in potentials and spherical harmonics, fixing every coefficient from the surface traction conditions. The static solution follows as the long-time limit. Formulas cover all stress components anywhere inside, and rotation extends the result to any load position, with multiple loads handled by superposition.
arxiv-2605-03556:
Petteri Kaski, Heikki Mannila, and Chandra Kanta Mohapatra revisit a probability problem that goes back to Boole's Laws of Thought from 1854. Given the probabilities of some intersections of events, what can be said about the probability of their union? Hailperin recast the question with linear programming in 1965, linking it to probabilistic logic.

The authors describe the geometry of the problem through coordinate projections of a simple polytope built from the atoms of a Venn diagram. They then prove that computing the optimal interval for the union probability is NP-hard. That result closes an apparent gap in the literature noted by Pitowsky, and it ties the old problem to cut polytopes and graphical models.
arxiv-2605-03656:
Mohammed Mahyoub, Wael Jaafar, Sami Muhaidat, and Halim Yanikomeroglu tackle a security risk in multi-slice low Earth orbit satellite networks. When virtual network functions from different network slices share the same satellite, a cross-slice exposure channel opens. They cast risk-aware placement of service function chains as a mixed-integer linear program over a changing constellation.

The model jointly optimizes co-location risk, CPU use, and migration stability under capacity, link, and delay limits, with a risk model grounded in ISO and NIST principles. Their three-stage optimizer, combining preprocessing, annealing warm-start, and branch-and-bound, cut co-location risk by forty percent and avoidable migrations by eighty percent against a greedy baseline.
arxiv-2605-03856:
Dongqi Chen and four co-authors design a new sensor array to estimate the direction of arrival of non-circular signals. More degrees of freedom in the receiver array mean more sources can be resolved, so array geometry matters. Their design builds on an extended coprime framework and uses a sliding translation technique to place sensors well.

Crucially, the rearranged structure keeps the difference co-array continuous, while the sum co-array shifts to merge with it, removing redundancy. That expands both the virtual aperture and the degrees of freedom a lot. Simulations and comparisons against nested arrays and other benchmarks show better degrees of freedom, larger virtual aperture, and improved estimation accuracy for non-circular signals in practice.
arxiv-2605-03956:
Shravya Kanchi and four co-authors built PoVSmith, a tool that generates proof-of-vulnerability tests on its own for applications built on third-party libraries. When a library vulnerability is reachable from application code, developers often demand concrete, runnable evidence before acting, because many reported flaws pose no practical risk to their specific application. Crafting such tests by hand is hard, and prior automation fell short.

PoVSmith combines call path analysis, exemplar tests, code context, and feedback into prompts that guide a coding agent and a large language model through generation, execution, and assessment. Evaluated on thirty-three application-library Java pairs, it revealed 158 unique application entry points calling vulnerable library APIs and correctly identified nearly all of them with their call paths.
arxiv-2605-04156:
Kalyanbrata Pal and four co-authors study gas falling into a black hole that spins, using a model where the flow is symmetric around the spin axis. They allow the gas to change its heat behaviour from place to place, and they treat the flow as a mix of species.

Their steady solutions can cross the speed of sound more than once and can hold a standing shock. The authors check that these solutions stay stable, then describe sound horizons in the flow, including a white hole at the shock, and work out the pull felt at each horizon.
arxiv-2605-04456:
Haruhi Enomoto, Shoji Mori, and Satoshi Okuzumi study how magnetic winds drive gas in protoplanetary disks to fall onto a young star, a key step in disk evolution and planet formation. The standard alpha prescription is only phenomenological, and how the accretion rate depends on basic disk properties remains unclear.

Local simulation boxes are efficient but suffer an artefact: shear keeps winding up the magnetic field inside the box until the geometry no longer resembles a global disk. Their diffusion scheme damps the averaged field and holds a realistic geometry for hundreds of orbits. Comparisons with self-similar solutions support the method and its measured accretion rates.
arxiv-2605-04556:
Cyril Allauzen and four co-authors benchmark leading large language models on a broad standard test of audio understanding, as audio-native models begin to challenge pipelines built from specialised sound encoders. The benchmark covers eight core capabilities, from classification to retrieval.

Their evaluation compares members of two major model families against the benchmark's tasks and weighs how close audio-native systems come to matching text-side performance. A significant gap in performance and robustness remains, and the evidence does not settle which architecture is best. The authors conclude the choice depends on a use case's needs for speed, cost, and depth of reasoning.
arxiv-2605-04656:
Bishal Dey and three co-authors design an adaptive predictive controller. It tracks a desired trajectory with a linear system whose parameters are uncertain. Hard limits apply to states, inputs, and how fast inputs may change. Earlier methods usually handled only some of these ingredients at once, or only the simpler task of holding a fixed setpoint.

Input-rate limits couple the control choices across time, which breaks the standard argument that a feasible plan today stays feasible tomorrow. The authors combine online parameter estimates with a learning process. Both sit inside a reformulated predictive control framework. They prove the scheme stays recursively feasible. It pursues zero tracking error despite full parametric uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-04856:
Sapna Sachan and Amulya Kumar Mahto build CT-like images from three-dimensional ultrasound scans of the kidney, aiming to guide operators in real time. CT gives clear reference views but uses ionising radiation. Ultrasound is safer and common, yet depends heavily on operator skill and lacks firm tissue measures.

Their system first aligns paired ultrasound and CT scans from the TRUSTED dataset using landmarks. A network mixing residual blocks with a transformer bottleneck then creates pseudo-CT volumes, checked by a discriminator for local realism. Scores for structural fidelity beat established baselines. The authors note the paired dataset is small, which may limit how widely the method generalises.
arxiv-2605-04956:
Han Wang and five co-authors build KernelBenchX, a benchmark for judging GPU kernels written by language models, asking where that skill breaks down and why. Their suite holds one hundred seventy-six tasks across fifteen categories, scored for both correctness and hardware efficiency. Five representative generation methods are compared systematically.

Task structure mattered more than method design, they find, with fusion tasks failing across all methods and maths tasks solved reliably. Stepwise refinement raised correctness but lowered average speed, and nearly half of correct kernels still ran slower than a plain baseline. Quantisation tasks went entirely unsolved, exposing a systematic weakness in numerical code generation.
arxiv-2605-05156:
Ondřej Wojewoda and thirteen co-authors shape how spin waves act in a magnetic film without cutting the material away. Spin-wave band structure is usually built by removing material to make a magnonic crystal, which shortens how far the waves survive. Instead, the team grow a thin Permalloy film over an array of three-dimensional nanopyramids, letting surface curvature sculpt the magnetic field landscape.

Light-scattering readings confirm a complete in-plane band gap with flat-band modes whose waves localise strongly in the pyramid valleys. The gap can be opened and closed by varying an external magnetic field, matching model predictions. The platform suits two-dimensional signals and magnonic computing parts.
arxiv-2605-05556:
Vision models trained on fine distinctions come to resemble the primate brain, or so a decade of work suggests. Yash Mehta and Michael F. Bonner test the opposite direction: how coarse can the training task be? They trained hundreds of networks to sort images into as few as eight broad categories.

Those coarsely trained networks matched or beat thousand-class models at aligning with human brain responses. They also matched human similarity judgments better than every model tested, including big self-supervised ones. The results hint that human-like visual representations need far simpler learning signals than assumed.
arxiv-2605-05656:
Statistical models sometimes break in quiet ways: parameters become unidentifiable, or the Fisher matrix turns singular. Rodrigo Labouriau's notes explain those flaws with geometry, using transversality theory. The setting is distributional models, where a kernel turns data into a feature map, and the flaws become kinks in that map.

Written as a teaching text, the notes start from the statistical facts themselves. Transversality then says just when such kinks are freak events rather than built-in traits. The payoff is a language for judging when a model is well-behaved enough to support robust estimation.
arxiv-2605-05956:
Karolina Połczyńska and six co-authors report a route to quantum light emitters that work at telecom wavelengths. Quantum communication needs sources that emit single photons, and pairs of entangled photons, on demand at set wavelengths. Making such emitters in a repeatable, symmetric form has been a standing hurdle.

The team use local droplet etching to form indium gallium arsenide quantum dots inside symmetric etched holes. Checks under a microscope confirmed the dots' structure and makeup in detail. Light tests showed narrow emission lines and clear single photon emission under both steady and pulsed excitation. Numerical modeling backed the measurements and traced how the emission survives up to liquid nitrogen temperatures.
arxiv-2605-06056:
Martin Jonáš and four co-authors introduce the multi-agent stochastic shortest path problem. Several agents move through a shared uncertain system, each striving to reach a target state. The shared goal is to minimize the expected time until any one of the agents arrives, which links their choices in ways single agent versions never face.

The authors analyze the problem in two settings, one where agents act on their own and one where they coordinate. For each they study how hard the problem is to compute and how complex good strategies must be. They design efficient algorithms that synthesize such strategies. Experiments on instances of growing size compare the algorithms against natural baselines and test how the approach scales.
arxiv-2605-06156:
Abdelghani Ghanem and Mounir Ghogho improve offline reinforcement learning with expressive generative policies. Flow matching policies can capture complex, multi modal behavior from fixed data sets. A prior method stabilizes their training through the continuous adjoint method, but stays bound to the behavior distribution in the data. That tie creates two flaws the authors name popularity bias and support binding.

Their framework, Maximum Entropy Adjoint Matching, attacks both flaws inside the flow formulation. An entropy maximization objective, set by mirror descent, counters the bias toward common actions. A mixture behavior prior widens the support so high reward actions outside the data manifold can be reached. Across sparse reward control tasks, the method matched or beat leading approaches while keeping the generative field well behaved.
arxiv-2605-06356:
Liu and five colleagues make high-resolution image-to-video generation practical. At 2K resolution, end-to-end models demand prohibitive memory and time. Cascading low-resolution generation with generic super-resolution hallucinates details and drifts from the input image. SwiftI2V follows a two-stage design. It first generates a low-resolution motion reference to cut token costs, then performs strongly image-conditioned 2K synthesis guided by that motion to recover faithful detail with controlled overhead.

Conditional segment-wise generation synthesizes video piece by piece with a bounded per-step token budget. Bidirectional context within each segment improves coherence and fidelity across segments. On VBench-I2V at 2K, SwiftI2V matches end-to-end baselines while cutting total GPU time about two hundred fold. It runs practical 2K generation on a single datacenter or consumer GPU in about two minutes.
arxiv-2605-06556:
Tyler C. Wunder and Joseph Cutrone study how often apportionment methods break the quota rule when every group must receive at least one item. Apportionment divides seats that cannot be split among groups, and a classic theorem says no method can keep both monotonicity and quota always. Guaranteed minimum shares, like one House seat per state, create extra violations worth measuring exactly.

For the three-state case they use a statistic that indexes population distributions and prove quota behavior stabilizes as populations grow. Exact violation probability formulas follow for the five classical divisor methods, and as seats increase the probabilities settle to method-specific constants. The results quantify fairness trade-offs precisely.
arxiv-2605-06856:
Ishani Mondal and Shweta Bhardwaj argue that generative AI should be judged by real-world utility, not benchmark scores. Across twenty-eight deployment cases in education, healthcare, software engineering, and law, they find systems that shine on benchmarks yet fail users. They name three recurring evaluation failures: proxies replacing real goals, snapshots replacing change over time, and averages hiding uneven effects across groups.

Their proposed SCU-GenEval framework runs in four stages, from mapping stakeholder goals to measuring utility longitudinally as capability changes through sustained use. Supporting tools include structured deployment protocols, context-conditioned user simulators, and persona-aware proxy metrics. The paper closes with domain-specific calls to action for outcome-based evaluation.
arxiv-2605-07256:
Jeon and two colleagues improve how vision transformer designs are found automatically, a search task known as transformer architecture search. Existing search methods train many candidate networks inside one shared supernet, but shared weights make the candidates collapse toward the same features. That feature collapse limits how well each individual candidate can perform.

The authors add low rank adaptation, called LoRA, a parameter efficient way of tuning, so each candidate can learn its own features without heavy cost. Their TAS-LoRA method uses a mixture of LoRA experts, with a lightweight router that assigns experts based on each candidate design. A group wise router starting setup pushes experts toward varied features early in training. Tests on ImageNet and transfer benchmarks including CIFAR sets, Flowers, CARS and INAT-19 show the method eases feature collapse well. It improves performance over the leading transformer architecture search methods by a clear margin.
arxiv-2605-07356:
Shuai Zhang and six co-authors unify two- and three-dimensional semantic segmentation for scenes such as roads and city models. Camera images and LiDAR point clouds describe the same world but distort it differently, making fusion unstable. Their insight is that features from both views share some semantics while keeping modality-specific parts.

UniD-Shift splits features from an image encoder and a geometric encoder into shared and private subspaces, then fuses only the shared part with attention. Training keeps the subspaces aligned yet independent. On two driving benchmarks the method improved accuracy at competitive cost, and a cross-country test showed stable performance when conditions shifted.
arxiv-2605-07756:
Ivan Karpukhin and Andrey Savchenko make pretraining with several loss terms cheaper to tune. Modern models are often pretrained on data with missing labels using composite objectives, and the weights balancing those terms are hyperparameters. Searching them with random or Bayesian methods means many full training runs, which is expensive.

Their gradient-based bilevel method learns the weights online during a single run, aligning the composite pretraining gradient with a downstream objective. Tricks based on the loss structure avoid the repeated backward passes that truncated backpropagation usually needs, holding the overhead to roughly thirty percent over one training run. On event-sequence modeling and self-supervised vision, the method matched or beat carefully tuned baselines.
arxiv-2605-08056:
Francisco Riberi solves a quantum walk problem from first principles. A walker moves along a line while a sink at the boundary can absorb it, with the sink strength left free. Projecting onto the part that survives turns the setup into a non-Hermitian tight-binding model with one imaginary defect.

Riberi obtains closed forms for the exact propagator, from which first-passage statistics follow. Weak coupling absorbs little because transfer into the sink is poor. Strong coupling also absorbs little, since a Zeno-like reflection keeps the walker away from the edge and a localized mode forms there. The two suppression routes turn out to share an asymptotic duality in their absorption probabilities.
arxiv-2605-08156:
Hu and three colleagues improve zero shot recognition, where a model classifies an image by picking the most compatible label with no task specific training. In fine grained settings the telling evidence sits in local parts or textures, not the whole image, so whole image matching fails. Recent local methods compare descriptions against many regions, but they rely on random or redundant crops that raise cost and add weak candidates.

The team proposes LAGO for efficient and robust zero shot local visual text alignment. It first finds object centred candidates without class labels, giving a stable starting point. It then refines those regions with language guidance scaled by confidence, avoiding an error amplifying loop. Object level, contextual and full image evidence combine through a dual channel aggregation strategy. Across standard zero shot benchmarks and distribution shift settings, LAGO tops performance while needing far fewer regions at inference time.
arxiv-2605-08256:
Alexander Povolotsky studies a number sequence built from primes. Take one more than a prime, split off its largest prime factor, and keep the remaining cofactor for the cases where that factor exceeds the index. Collecting those cofactors and sorting the distinct values by how often they occur gives a new sequence starting two, six, four, eight, and so on.

The article explains how the construction grows out of the OEIS sequence A223881 and why family patterns appear in plots of the values. A heuristic model based on classical results about primes in arithmetic progressions explains the observed frequency ordering, and numerical evidence supports the model.
arxiv-2605-08556:
Khurram Yamin, Jingjing Tang, Eric Horvitz, and Bryan Wilder ask what goals a language model's choices reveal. Rather than trust what a model says, they record its probability judgments and decisions, then fit a choice model that finds the cost pattern best matching that behavior. The test runs across four medical diagnosis settings with leading and open models.

Many models show real inner consistency, yet they often fail to state their own goals faithfully or adopt a user's stated goals when prompted. For high stakes choices under uncertainty, stated aims and acted aims can part ways. Alignment research gains a rigorous check that compares what models do with what they claim.
arxiv-2605-08656:
Yuming Zhang and four coauthors fix bias in a broad class of regression models. In these models, part of the fit is a set of terms that can grow in size. Part is a smooth curve. Past work cared most about sharp fits for the terms. It set the curve and the spread aside as side terms. Yet bias can be large when terms are many or spread is high. That bias can spoil the fit.

Their SABRE plan checks a first fit against what a simple stand in model would give. For a wide model class, SABRE cuts bias in both the terms and the spread. It needs no sparse fit. It keeps the first fit's sharp edge. Tests and a gene study in Alzheimer's disease back the gain.
arxiv-2605-08856:
Adeel Pervez and Francesco Locatello show why learned sims of real world flows drift on long runs. Each step can look right, yet the path veers off. They draw the path in lines and study the slope maps on it. When those maps are skewed, small slips grow for a while. The path drifts, though the true flow is stable in the long run. Growth of error is built in, not bad luck.

Their fix fines both flaws in training. The fines cost near nil at run time. A bound on the path step counts the gain. On made and real space time data, and on climate casts, fixed models hold the path for thousands of steps. Base models veer off.
arxiv-2605-08956:
Harshit Bisht and four coauthors say AI science agents are not built for full lone search. They work well as aides at the bench. Four set flaws ground the case. Task choice bends to what can be counted with ease. Training stock lacks the tacit craft and fail lore of lab life. Taste tuning in late training squeezes takes toward the pack's view. Most tests grade one shot calls, with no word back from real trials.

Fixes call for new build picks, not just more scale. Sims can serve as checks in training. A live store of views and aims can cross a whole hunt. A shared log can hold all machine claims in advance. Tasks should come from need, not from tools at hand.
arxiv-2605-09156:
Ahan Chatterjee heads four co-authors in tracing how grammatical gender changed as Latin turned into Occitan, one of the Romance languages. Their 2026 study uses an interpretable deep learning framework to work at two levels. Latin had three genders, masculine, feminine, and neuter, while most Romance languages kept only two, so the team asks where gender information lives as that system shrank.

First they show standard token splitting is not robust enough for this low-resource historical setting, and their proposed tokenizer beats those baselines. Next they measure how word-form traits help predict gender for single words, and which word classes in a sentence carry gender clues in context. Together the tests map how gender knowledge is split between a word itself and its surroundings. Code, datasets, and results are public, giving historical linguists a reusable tool for studying language change with modern methods.
arxiv-2605-09856:
Tang and three colleagues improved human mesh recovery under occlusion, where hidden body parts yield wrong poses and jittery motion. Their insight is that pose sequences carry a more reliable motion prior for occluded parts than occluded image features do. MoPO, short for Motion Prior for Occluded mesh recovery, has two main components.

A motion de-occlusion module detects joint visibility in space and time, then a lightweight motion predictor fills occluded joints from pose history. A motion-aware fusion and refinement module merges the completed joint sequence with image features to estimate shape and initial pose, then refines the final pose through inverse kinematics. MoPO reached state-of-the-art results on both occlusion-specific and standard benchmarks, with better accuracy and temporal consistency.
arxiv-2605-10056:
Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong prove new hardness-amplification results for LPN (Learning Parity with Noise), a problem at the heart of code-based cryptography. In LPN, the goal is to recover a secret vector from noisy linear samples. Each sample pairing a random vector with a bit equal to its inner product with the secret plus a random error. Building on Hirahara and Shimizu's direct-product framework, they show an instance-fraction amplification theorem.

Any algorithm solving LPN with small success probability can be converted into one succeeding almost always on a related LPN distribution with rescaled parameters. There, noise and dimension shrink by a factor tied to the target probabilities. In plain terms, solving a few instances implies solving almost all of them, a self-amplification result. The same approach extends to LPN over larger finite fields and to sparse LPN, where each query vector has few nonzero entries.
arxiv-2605-10156:
Stewart and eight co-authors simulate radio galaxy remnants after their jets switch off, using 3D hydrodynamic models of fifteen galaxies. Remnant radio-loud active galactic nuclei are hard to identify because their shapes and spectra vary. The simulations cover group settings of low density and cluster settings of high density, re-gridded from cosmic particle runs. The remnants range from amorphous blobs to double-lobed forms.

Jet power correlates with spectral slope, and surface brightness hinges strongly on environment. Group remnants are dimmer and more amorphous than cluster remnants, suggesting observations undercount dim sources. Models estimate a nearby, fifty-million-year-old remnant from a weak progenitor in a ten-trillion-solar-mass group should be detectable at three sigma with LOFAR. Twenty to thirty percent of its emission would stay hidden in reasonable time. Young remnants show low-frequency spectral indices like active sources.
arxiv-2605-10356:
Alexandra Voce, Emmanouil Giannakakis, and Claudia Clopath borrow a brain design to make artificial learning more efficient. The cerebellum and cerebral cortex form tight circuits thought to support flexible time processing, yet how that link shapes cortical learning is unclear. Their 2026 paper adds a cerebellar-style feedforward module to a recurrent neural network, which processes sequences over time.

The resulting cortico-cerebellar net learned faster and hit higher peak scores than size-matched fully recurrent baselines across varied regimes. Key test: freezing the recurrent core after brief training and handing later learning to the cerebellar module kept the efficiency edge. That suggests the cerebellar module drives much of the gain, with the cortical net largely acting as a fixed reservoir. Mixed modular design, the authors conclude, can serve as a strong structural bias for neural systems.
arxiv-2605-10556:
Vittorio Palladino and three colleagues model the energy cost of serving language models. As models span dense, mixture-of-experts, and state-space designs on mixed chips, tuning inference energy now rivals tuning speed and throughput. Existing approaches treat speed as an energy proxy or rely on data-hungry black-box stand-ins. Their 2026 paper presents EnergyLens.

EnergyLens uses symbol fitting over profiling data to derive a 12-factor energy model from traits such as parallel work, batch size, and sequence length. Unlike black-box stand-ins, it separates tensor and pipeline parallel work and prefill from decode energy, for clear, useful predictions. Fitted from just 50 profiling measurements, EnergyLens achieves 88.2 percent Top-1 setup accuracy across scenarios, compared with 60.9 percent for the prior math baseline. It matches ensemble ML methods with 10 times fewer samples and extends well to unseen batch sizes and platforms.
arxiv-2605-10756: Yang and five colleagues propose TINS, a test-time method for spotting out-of-distribution images with vision-language models. Instead of fixed negative labels, TINS learns sample-specific negative text embeddings by image-to-text inversion, kept apart from in-distribution semantics by prototype-separated regularization. Group-wise aggregation scores plus a buffer update stabilize the expansion. On the Four-OOD benchmark with ImageNet-1K as in-distribution data, it cuts the average false-positive rate at 95 percent recall from 14 point 04 to 6 point 72 percent.
arxiv-2605-10956:
Manho Park, Christopher V. Rackauckas, and Christopher W. Tessum speed up air-flow simulations with a learned solver that keeps full spatial detail. Earlier learned solvers either gained little speed or gave up detail, while this solver takes larger time steps than the standard stability rule allows.

A convolutional network takes pollutant levels and stability numbers as inputs and outputs mass flux, mimicking ten-day ground-level wind transport with strong fidelity at four to thirty-two times the baseline step. Speed trades against accuracy in a measured slope, reaching ninety-two times faster while staying fairly true to the baseline. The January-trained solver also works across seasons and seventy-two heights. Air modelers get detail-preserving speed.
arxiv-2605-11256:
Chong Qi gives a rigorous proof of the Strutinsky energy theorem and foundations for nuclear density functional theory. The proof gives a proper reading of the shell-correction breakdown, ending decades of muddle, and lays a base for building nuclear density functionals.

Shell structure has shaped nuclear physics for nearly six decades, encoded in the single-particle energy spectrum from model fields such as Woods-Saxon or Nilsson-type models. It can also be derived from a base two-body interaction. A key catch is that nucleons build their own mean field from mutual forces, so filled single-particle levels cannot simply be summed to total binding energy without double counting shares. His shell-correction method was the key breakthrough in sizing nuclear shell effects. Nuclear theorists get a firm footing for the shell picture and for density functionals built on it.
arxiv-2605-11356: Hassan Tavakoli, Thinh Nguyen and Bella Bose introduce RankGuard-Polar, a framework for safely publishing some polar codeword bits on shared public resources. Against a strong spy who sees the published bits, they show leakage has an exact closed form. They build an explicit linear extractor that names the leaked combinations. From this identity they give efficient procedures for working out and proving leakage, plus a proven algorithm. The goal is to share codeword parts in public while keeping the rest safe, and to prove just how much leaks.
arxiv-2605-11756: Yuxin Du and nine colleagues let users steer depth estimation toward a chosen region of a single image. Their FocusDepth framework takes box or text prompts. It fuses multi-scale features from Segment Anything Model 3 into a Depth Anything-style model through gated, scale-specific fusion. This sharpens target edges while keeping global scene geometry intact. On their new FDE-Bench benchmark it beat globally fine-tuned baselines, most clearly at target edges and foregrounds.
arxiv-2605-11856: Houcheng Jiang and six colleagues unify reasoning in multimodal language models into a single visual workspace. Their 2026 framework, UniVLR, renders reasoning traces and auxiliary images into one shared view, then compresses that view into compact visual latent tokens. At inference the model reasons through visual latents alone and decodes the answer directly, with no external tools and no verbose text reasoning. It beat prior visual latent methods while using far fewer reasoning tokens.
arxiv-2605-12356: Akashi and Soker simulate a collapsing star exploding through three pairs of jittering jets, then compare the wreckage with remnant G11.2-0.3. The first wide jets trigger the blast and squeeze gas into a shell and a flat plane. The second pair clears that plane except for a dense bar, while narrow third jets punch through to form two opposite rings. The match supports the jittering-jets picture, since rival models struggle to explain such point-symmetric remnants.
arxiv-2605-12456: Sander and twelve colleagues introduce TextSeal, a mark for language model output. It builds on Gumbel-max sampling. Dual keys restore output diversity. Entropy-weighted scoring and multi-region localisation sharpen detection. The scheme supports speculative decoding and multi-token prediction at no added cost. It beats the SynthID-text baseline on detection strength. It stays robust when diluted in mixed human and AI text. It preserves downstream performance, and human tests find no quality gap. The mark also transfers through distillation, exposing reuse of a marked model.
arxiv-2605-12556: Aboelwafa, Elmongui and Torki brighten dark images by adding depth and meaning to the Retinex recipe. Low-light shots suffer amplified noise, artefacts and colour distortion, and single-modality RGB methods miss cues that survive darkness. Their M2Retinexformer fuses RGB with depth cues, luminance priors and semantic features across scales, using cross-attention with adaptive gating. Depth gives geometry that does not change with light, while luminance and semantics guide brightness and scene sense. Tests on four low-light benchmarks beat Retinexformer and recent rivals.
arxiv-2605-12756: Du, He and Su study whether next-token training induces weight structure. They analyze a program with output projection and embeddings as variables. Their analysis shows target symmetries transfer to minimizers precisely. When tokens exhibit cyclic-shift symmetry, like days of the week or months of the year, the logit matrix is circulant, and Gram matrices are circulant. For distributions under the symmetric group, the projection forms a simplex equiangular tight frame, while logit matrix and embeddings inherit it.
arxiv-2605-12856: Al-Lawati and five colleagues tackle moderation in multi-agent systems, where harmful agents can post content that looks benign while behaving badly across many turns. Their framework, BOT-MOD, judges intent rather than single posts, probing a suspect agent through a multi-turn exchange that narrows down its likely goals. Tested on a dataset built from the Moltbook community, it reliably flags malicious intent while rarely mislabelling benign behaviour.
arxiv-2605-13056: Dzhalilov studies a resonant instability of supersonic shear flow in collisionless plasmas, asking how uneven heating and parallel heat flux shape it. Using 16-moment transport equations from the Vlasov-Maxwell system, he analyses oblique waves in a magnetised plasma with shear flow lined up with the ambient field. The wave equation at hand yields an endless discrete spectrum of complex eigenfrequencies. It peaks when wave phase speed matches mean flow speed, and dies out in the vortex sheet limit, unlike the classic Kelvin-Helmholtz case.
arxiv-2605-13156: Liu and eight co-authors analyse object hallucination in vision-language models, where models describe content absent from the image. Using activation patching across five diverse architectures, they identify a visual grounding pathway supporting correct predictions and a hallucination pathway driving wrong outputs. Conditional Pathway Analysis shows grounding parts stay strongly redundant in both cases but flip polarity, backing truth on correct samples and the hallucinated answer on wrong ones. Suppressing hallucination-pathway parts cuts object hallucination by up to 76% with minimal accuracy cost.
arxiv-2605-13356: Serban and colleagues study anomalous large angle alpha scattering from equal proton neutron nuclei. They fold an alpha nucleon interaction with densities from relativistic and nonrelativistic mean field models. A single unified parameter set, with only two parameters varying by mass, matches the anomaly in sd shell nuclei fairly well. The result supports microscopic densities plus a Gaussian interaction as a sound account of large angle scattering.
arxiv-2605-13656: Xiao Xiao and Arun Bansil uncover a symmetry-constrained route for nodal topological superconductivity in altermagnets. In fourfold collinear altermagnets, the native crystal antiunitary symmetry TC4z usually forbids pure spin-singlet pairing. It selects pairings with Bogoliubov-de Gennes models carrying new chiral symmetries. Those rules yield robust nodal topological phases across broad regimes. They include a nodal-point phase with flat bands and two nodal-loop phases with chiral Majorana edge states.
arxiv-2605-14256: Huang, Wang and Xu study inner product estimation across sites for n-qubit states with local random measurements. Minimax kernel optimization reduces to one unbiased Hamming kernel. Under Clifford sampling, a sharp fourth-moment bound yields worst-case complexity near the square root of 4.5 to the n, attained by stabilizer states. Under Haar sampling, a twirling identity sets its fourth moment against the Clifford fourth, giving the same bound, though lossy. This motivates a conjectured sharper Haar scaling near the square root of 3.6 to the n, attained by products.
arxiv-2605-14356: Ming Xu, Yihao Chen and Ji Guan bring model checking, systematic checks against stated requirements, to matrix product states. These tensor-network forms describe one-dimensional quantum ground states. They propose Linear Chain Logic, a spatial logic for properties of periodic state families as system size grows, such as nontriviality on rings. Each periodic state induces a completely positive map on its virtual space, so inner products can be computed without brute-force expansion. Approximate checking then verifies nontrivial cases and detects large-size patterns on test families.
arxiv-2605-14456: Athulya and Verma work out the dual space of a Hardy space linked to a Dunkl-Schrodinger operator. That operator pairs the Dunkl Laplacian with a potential from a reverse Holder class. They show the dual sits inside the Dunkl version of classical bounded-mean-oscillation space. Atomic decomposition gives the result, with a cancellation rule set by a critical radius, and the uncentred maximal function is shown to be bounded there.
arxiv-2605-15156: Ryan Wei Heng Quek and eight others offer MeMo, a framework that stores new knowledge in a separate memory model while leaving the language model itself frozen. It captures cross-document links, resists retrieval noise, avoids catastrophic forgetting, and needs neither model weights nor output logits, so it plugs into open and proprietary models alike. Retrieval cost stays independent of corpus size at inference time. Across BrowseComp-Plus, NarrativeQA, and MuSiQue, MeMo performs strongly against existing methods.
arxiv-2605-15256: Zeqing Wang and six colleagues present ReactiveGWM, a game world model with flexible control roles for players and non-player characters. Existing models bind roles to fixed characters, failing multi-character games where different characters take external control while NPCs react. ReactiveGWM assigns control modes at initialization and simulates controlled players alongside reactive NPCs. Spatial role binding grounds character handles to regions in the first frame, and unified agency conditioning merges player actions and NPC rules into per-character control tokens.
arxiv-2605-15756: Esther Bosch splits acute psychological stress from exertion in signals. Five signals were tracked in 19 people under cognitive stress and physical activity, alone and mixed. Stress came from an n-back task with pressure and cash reward. Tasks were sitting, walking, and cycling. Tonic electrodermal activity rose with both stress and exertion, with no interaction, making it the top pick for stress spotting. Heart rate and neck muscle signals tracked exertion almost alone, with no stress sign. RMSSD and breathing rate tracked activity, with little sign of load or stress.
arxiv-2605-15956: Anastasia Golovin and seven colleagues present TeraGram, a long-run dataset of Telegram content with over 5.9 billion messages from 2015 to 2025, from 712 thousand channels and groups, with metadata on forwards, reactions and polls. It spans Russian, Farsi and Western languages, covering mainstream countries and sub-communities. By language, it offers an algo-free platform example, unlike social media shaped by opaque curation code. It enables side-by-side studies across tongues, communities and user bases under platform rules, backing research on engagement, network growth and group building without algorithmic sorting.
arxiv-2605-16756: Qureshi, Barklow and Schwartzman study single Higgs making in 125 GeV photon-photon collisions at the XFEL Compton Collider concept. Their analysis targets major hadron, semi-lepton, and full-lepton final states, including Higgs decay to strange pairs. A set-based deep-learning framework acting on particle-flow point clouds, paired with a genetic search, sifts signal from background far better than older methods. The authors conclude such a machine could probe the Higgs sector very well, adding to planned electron-positron machines.
arxiv-2605-16956: Hinz and Mehiri build a unified algebraic theory of the weighted Tower of Hanoi, with move costs by disc and peg. From an optimality recurrence with one- and two-move strategies, they derive matrix forms and explicit formulas for minimal transfer cost. One-move dynamics follows a linear operator tied to Jacobsthal and Lichtenberg series, while two-move dynamics grows purely exponentially. Classical sequences as disc weights yield new derived sequences, and forbidden-move models show a phase transition where the best strategy switches regimes beyond a finite threshold.
arxiv-2605-17256: Abukhousa, Zonouz and Meliopoulos benchmark eight deep learning designs for spotting faults and cyber-attacks in inverter-dominated power grids. They use signals from an industry-grade transient simulator. All models classified two multi-event sequences in real time, deciding within one cycle. Yet end-to-end latency ran 50 to 90 milliseconds, past three cycles. That gap exposes the distance between algorithmic speed and protection-grade deployment needs.
arxiv-2605-17356: Zhao and colleagues present UniPPTBench, a shared benchmark for slide-deck generation across four input types: vague prompts, long texts, mixed-media texts and multi-source material. A companion test plan mixes shared scores with type-specific ones for grounded condensing, visual-text alignment and cross-source synthesis. Tests reveal wide gaps across types and repeat failures in grounding and synthesis. Glossy generic scores, they warn, often mask weak task fulfillment.
arxiv-2605-17456: Li and Su argue that attention weights are poor evidence in whole-slide multiple-instance learning. Attention is tuned for classification, not for finding patches that truly support a diagnosis. Attention-picked patches prove insufficient, unnecessary and unrecoverable against explicit sufficiency, necessity and recoverability criteria. Their GCE-MIL wrapper adds grounding, noisy-OR coverage and threshold-plus-repair. Across 81 backbone-dataset mixes it lifts accuracy and shrinks the continuous-discrete gap. Inference runs up to five times faster after tile pre-filter.
arxiv-2605-17656: Parvez and colleagues introduce MUIAnno, an expert-annotated dataset for mobile UI understanding drawn from diverse applications across categories on the iTunes platform. Each app was explored by hand to capture typical screens reflecting varied layouts and design patterns. A custom web-based tool lets UI/UX experts label screen items by drag-and-drop and generate structured JSON annotations. MUIAnno covers buttons, input fields, navigation items and other key items, plus benchmark experiments for UI element detection with baseline results, offering a start for future research.
arxiv-2605-17756: Makoto Kawashima gives the first criteria for linear independence of multiple polylogarithm values over algebraic number fields. In particular, he derives new results on products of polylogarithms at distinct points over such fields. His method builds explicit Padé-type approximants tailored to multiple polylogarithms. The work supplies a fresh test for when these special values stand in no linear relation over algebraic numbers, opening a path for further results on polylogarithm values.
arxiv-2605-17856: Ziwei Li and seven colleagues build KISS, a knowledge scaffold that turns Earth-science know-how into agent-usable tools. Process-based models hold decades of science, yet climate-vulnerable communities often cannot run them. KISS turns know-how into checked modeling operators, staged domain protocols, and diagnostic recovery steps. On a 3,000-trial coupled-hydrology benchmark, scaffolded agents finished physically plausible, verifiable simulations in up to 84% of trials, versus under 40% without it. A Knowledge Dissection Toolkit then built scaffolding for 117 more models across fourteen domains.
arxiv-2605-17956: Bob Osano proves extensivity from microscopic conditions, rather than taking it as given. He starts with one- and two-particle densities of the Gibbs state and builds a coarse-graining operator on phase space. That operator yields probabilities over cells in space and momentum. Under stability, temperedness, and exponential cluster decomposition, the Ursell expansion shows coarse-grained entropy equals cell entropy totals plus a tiny correction. That correction fades per cell for short-range systems, recovering the Ruelle-Fisher result. For long-range forces, the correction stays.
arxiv-2605-18556: Jingjing Fan and three co-authors present Key-Gram, a 2026 conditional-memory system that separates language-derived world knowledge from visual-state reasoning in embodied control. An instruction splits into task-specific key-grams, static linguistic priors arrive via hashed lookup, and retrieved entries enter hidden layers through gated fusion. The backbone then focuses on visual reasoning and action inference, while knowledge stays in extensible external memory. Across RoboTwin2.0, LIBERO, and real dual-arm tasks, Key-Gram lifts both tested backbones substantially.
arxiv-2605-18756: Robert Farr models, in a 2026 report, market dynamics from scratch. Actors trade many goods for money, which has no use value itself but serves as a medium of exchange. Simulated through market rules forming a double auction per good, the actors show steady rational behavior, trading off purchases of different goods. Stable prices require time-preference in the model. Price swings have fat tails, and adding inflation expectations produces complex damped or undamped swings. Input-output dynamics prove hard to keep stable.
arxiv-2605-18956: Bizhu Wu and seven colleagues close the granularity gap in motion-language models, which handle motion coarsely and lack fine control over body parts. Their MotionMERGE framework models motion at part and time levels inside a language model, giving precise control for understanding and local editing. A training strategy supervises matching across granularities, temporal grounding, localized matching, coherence and motion-grounded reasoning. The team also releases MotionFineEdit, a dataset of 837 thousand atomic and 144 thousand complex triplets with fine-grained instructions, and shows strong zero-shot transfer to other motion tasks.
arxiv-2605-19056: Shreyaa Raghavan, Cameron Hickert, Monica Chan and Cathy Wu swap one shot traffic tune for a rolling view. Plain one shot fits on bumpy cost land oft yield wobbly fake traffic, denting trust and what if tests. Cast as a live control task, fits hold shape and truth amid noise. On real I-24 MOTION data, the live view lifts forecast truth by forty eight percent and stands up better to knocks.
arxiv-2605-19156: Zhengxin Zhang and three colleagues ask how good agent papers are, noting feasibility is not quality. They build ResearchArena, a scaffold letting agents run the research loop. Across thirteen seeds, the scaffold yields 117 agent papers, judged by manuscript-only review, artifact-aware peer review, and human meta-review. Manuscript-only scores look optimistic, with one agent matching the human ICLR 2025 submission, but artifact-aware scores drop. Audits find rigour the main bottleneck: fabricated results, weak experiments, and plan-execution mismatch. None reaches a top-tier acceptance bar.
arxiv-2605-19756: Bielawski, Chotibut, Falniowski, Misiurewicz and Piliouras examine maps in one dimension whose bifurcation diagrams depart from familiar shapes. A diagram of this kind shows how a system's long-run behaviour shifts as one setting changes, and here the pictures look unlike the usual ones. The team sets out and shows with examples several odd effects that turn up in this family of maps.
arxiv-2605-19956: Jia-Wei Hai, Yijun Wang and Xiu-Shen Wei defend vision-language models against adversarial attacks without losing fine detail. Their attention-guided prompt tuning at test time finds meaning-bearing image regions that survive attack and varies augmentation strength across space accordingly. Experiments show the method, called A-TPT, beats existing test-time adaptation on both attacked and clean data, including fine-grained tasks.
arxiv-2605-20156: Ashkan Bayat and Barry Sanders benchmark sliding-mode clock steering against linear-quadratic-Gaussian and bang-bang control. All three run in one framework on a two-state clock model with white and random-walk-frequency noise. Accuracy repeats over 100 seeds for four periods, a week, a month, a year and ten years. SMC stays competitive with LQG across timescales and noise, and both outperform BB. SMC stability nearly matches LQG stability over the range, while BB shows early instability.
arxiv-2605-20456: Koch argues agentic AI coding has not removed engineering discipline from software and hardware work. Agent systems inspect repos, plan work, edit files, call tools, run tests and file pull requests, yet trials show mixed gains and persistent setup failures. He proposes Agentic Agile-V, pairing an Agile-V lifecycle with a task-level SCOPE-V loop that turns talk into structured artifacts and acceptance evidence. The framework adds input-artifact rules, a dialogue-to-contract gate, risk-adaptive workflows and an evidence-bundle acceptance model.
arxiv-2605-20756: Nikhil Nayak and nine colleagues correct random update bias in preconditioned language-model optimizers. Such optimizers are central to training, but their random rules are usually read as direct approximations to population descent with scaling. The authors show two finite-sample biases: gradient-scaler coupling from shared minibatches, and bias from inverting or rooting a noisy scaler estimate. Their single-batch framework uses cross-fitted scaling and variance-corrected inversion to address both.
arxiv-2605-20856: Hanxiang Ren and three colleagues present DISC, a method that splits instruction from state-conditioned control via policy generation. Language-conditioned policies usually share network parameters for instructions and observations. That lets networks find scene-to-action shortcuts that skip language grounding. DISC instead uses a hypernetwork to generate a full task-specific visuomotor policy from the instruction alone, so observation leakage has no pathway to emerge.
arxiv-2605-21056: Yang Lu and colleagues present a unified family of conditional mutual information bounds for generalization error, built on leave-m-out cross-validation error. The unified bound envelops and reproduces many known conditional mutual information bounds and bridges mutual information and conditional mutual information bounds as m grows large. It also yields new, sharper bounds. When loss is bounded, trimming conditional terms tightens the bounds further, and examples show gains over prior results.
arxiv-2605-21156: Elena Mason and colleagues argue for high-resolution spectroscopic monitoring of stellar transients. They test the case of the outburst NGC 300 OT2008-1, for which low- and high-resolution spectra were taken a day apart. The low-resolution data name few lines and leave ejecta energy guesswork. The high-resolution data show many lines whose shapes imply complex geometry and motion, which low-resolution work cannot reveal and may even misread.
arxiv-2605-21356: Zhaoze Wang and co-authors present a unified recurrent network model in which grid and place cells co-emerge. Grid cells and place cells together support spatial navigation, and reciprocal links pose a chicken-and-egg problem for development. Their model instantiates Dale's Law, with every neuron excitatory or inhibitory, and trains to predict the next sensory observation from masked prior observations and egocentric motion. It is the first single-objective model where both cell types co-emerge without supervision.
arxiv-2605-21456: Cihad Kıbrıs and co-authors ask whether negative neutrino mass or negative dark energy explains a cosmological tension. DESI and CMB analyses show tension between the inferred sum of neutrino masses and the minimum allowed by oscillation tests. This assumes standard Lambda-CDM cosmology. They explore alternative dark energy models, including negative-density models reproducing effects of negative effective neutrino masses. Such models can ease tension by changing expansion over a redshift range relevant for CMB lensing.
arxiv-2605-21556: Zhaoqi Zhang and co-authors propose joint optimization for multi-slot guaranteed display ads, beyond the single-slot assumption. Guaranteed display ads are crucial for platform income. Yet existing tools often assume a single slot, limiting gains across multi-slot page views. Their approach frames allocation as an offline bipartite matching problem with a contract roulette rule for slot exclusivity and Page View limits for impression control. A scalable allocation algorithm supports efficient large-scale use. Wide online tests on the Meituan advertising platform show significant gains over existing methods.
arxiv-2605-21656: Madjid Eshaghi Gordji and co-authors ask why groups stay in inferior institutions when superior options are known. Their model lets agents choose actions and changes: ones through taxes or subsidies, hard ones through deletion or replacement. With status-quo bias and partly reasoned play, finite taxes shift conduct but cannot eliminate use of the old action, whereas removal bypasses inertia by removing the action. Antagonistic social preferences can block reforms beneficial to every player. Hard restrictions dominate soft incentives under inertia, with applications to climate transition and platform rules.
arxiv-2605-21756: Hailu proposes a framework for quantum decision trees built on a laser-driven four-level atomic system. A diamond-shaped energy layout is analyzed with Lie-algebraic methods, while a Stokes pulse and a pump laser couple pairs of atomic states. Pulse profiles sharing the same time shape but differing in amplitude redistribute population from the ground state to other levels, mimicking a decision tree. The method scales to systems with any number of levels, offering uses in quantum computing and decision-making.
