arxiv-2605-21856: Yifan Lan and coauthors expose evasive data contamination in language models, where publishers paraphrase benchmark data to dodge detection and inflate leaderboard scores. They uncover that reasoning traces hide memorization. Their Zero-CoT Probe cuts the chain-of-thought process to expose latent shortcut mappings, comparing zero-CoT scores on the original benchmark with a perturbed reference set. A Contamination Confidence metric gives chance and severity beyond binary verdicts. Tests on known contaminated models and fine-tuned contaminated models show the probe detects direct and evasive contamination.
arxiv-2605-22156: Yang and co-authors present OWPO, one-way policy optimization for evolving language models trained with checked rewards. Sparse binary verifier rewards cause low efficiency and wobble, and existing token constraints relative to a reference policy penalize deviations blindly. OWPO applies one-sided treatment, with gain locking where the policy beats the reference. Iterative reference updates create a ratchet effect locking in gains. Tests show OWPO beats strong baselines including DAPO, OPD, and MOPD, breaking the fixed-prior bottleneck for evolution without external reference models.
arxiv-2605-22256: Hamon and colleagues simulate a society of reinforcement learning agents in a changing ecological world and watch farming appear on its own, with no direct instruction. Four ingredients drive the shift: planning for delayed rewards, vulnerability to cheaters, social learning that blocks cheater spread, and a lock-in that makes farming hard to abandon once established. The work offers a test bed for how cultural innovations take hold.
arxiv-2605-22356: Milano and Marocco test whether language models can be tuned to mimic pathology-like behaviour patterns. They fine-tune models on decision tasks built from synthetic data inspired by depression and paranoia. The tuned models then show stable shifts in next-token probabilities across contexts. Negative and threat-related readings gain probability in open-ended text. Different tunings yield distinct response styles, not just generic skew. The findings frame language models as policy systems where behavioural constraints shape how text is generated.
arxiv-2605-22456: Qiu and Schotten present SteinsGateDrive, a latency-decoupled planner for cloud-hosted LLM driver agents. Their architecture lets the LLM pick counterfactual driving futures, reusing the forecast only while safety contracts hold. Three roles are built: alpha nominal futures, beta interaction counterfactuals, and gamma hazard-stress futures such as braking and cut-ins. The chosen branch becomes a StrategicForecast with horizon, validity, fallback and authority. In highway tests, GPT-5.4 mini cuts effective lag from plus 3.07 seconds to minus 0.01 seconds as horizon grows, with no collisions.
arxiv-2605-22756: Lebeda and others build Lumberjack, a differentially private random forest that keeps utility where prior private forests degrade into impracticality. The method grows large random trees, then prunes them with a privacy preserving heavy hitter detector that keeps only well populated nodes. That detector's error scales with the square root of log tree height, allowing far deeper trees than earlier work. Benchmark tests show Lumberjack beats prior private random forest methods across practical privacy budgets, closing much of the gap to non private forests.
arxiv-2605-22956: Saberi and twelve coauthors argue that ultraviolet spectra from HST/STIS remain unmatched for stellar physics. Evolved stars enrich galaxies through winds, yet the heat and motion of their wide chromospheres stay poorly known. HST/STIS spectra at resolving powers of 30,000 to 100,000 fill a niche no current tool matches. The authors urge keeping and prioritizing such programs. They would anchor atmosphere models and guide the Habitable Worlds Observatory.
arxiv-2605-23256: Jaguzovic and Vujadinovic study Toeplitz operators with one positive symbol on pluriharmonic Fock spaces over complex n-space. They describe the conditions under which the Toeplitz operator is bounded, compact, or falls in the Schatten class S1. They also give a necessary rule for a Toeplitz operator to belong to Sp for p at least 1, and under an added assumption, they prove the sufficiency of the condition.
arxiv-2605-23456: Wroe and colleagues build RadMaps, an open mapping framework that models radiotherapy access through both machine capacity and travel distance at once, where earlier studies handled each factor alone. Running on Uber's H3 hexagonal grid, it merges people counts, cancer rates, and clinic lists. Demand then goes greedily nearest-first under both limits. Applied worldwide with a 200-kilometer threshold, capacity alone allows 70 percent access and geography alone 91 percent, but together only 60 percent, exposing combined gaps planners can target.
arxiv-2605-23556: Bangachev and colleagues ask why low-dimensional embeddings still let retrieval models scale to billions of points. They study maximal-margin embeddings. Query and document vectors score above a margin for relevant pairs, below its negative otherwise. Their theorem shows the unrestricted margin is nearly reachable in dimension on the order of margin to the minus two times log n, improving an earlier result. With a matching lower bound, dimension on the order of k log n over k works for k-sparse rows. Sigmoid loss beats InfoNCE empirically.
arxiv-2605-23956: Nilayam and Nayak measure how changes ripple through compound AI systems chaining language-model calls into directed graphs. Their tool, QUIVER, defines a sensitivity matrix sorting edges into amplifiers, absorbers, or threshold-sensitive links, plus divergence split into value drift, path drift, and step-count drift. It sets bifurcation thresholds, the smallest change that alters the path, and a check of test data against production data. Tested on over 8,200 logged traces, it shows distinct profiles, predicts split-prone nodes from data alone, and pinpoints stale test artefacts.
arxiv-2605-24056: Jacobs builds the first database of player impact measured possession by possession for NBA seasons before play-by-play records began, covering regular seasons from 1984-85 through 1995-96. Every game was rebuilt by hand from broadcast video: lineup changes logged at each dead-ball substitution, possessions tallied from footage, and points per lineup recorded. As of writing, 2,179 regular-season games span 435,760 logged possessions and 1,012 player-seasons. Regularized Adjusted Plus-Minus is estimated by weighted ridge regression on the rebuilt stint data, with uncertainty from posterior credible intervals and validation across several criteria.
arxiv-2605-24556: Yosef Worku Alemneh, Kidist Amde Mekonnen, and Maarten de Rijke test whether multilingual retrieval scores transfer to Amharic, a morphologically rich language with little representation. Under one shared passage-retrieval protocol, the best zero-shot multilingual retriever trailed the best monolingual Amharic retriever. The gap was 23 percent relative MRR at rank 10. Fine-tuning multilingual models on Amharic data gained 32 to 60 percent, yet still fell short of the monolingual leader. The authors conclude that retrieval for underrepresented languages must be judged and adapted in-language, not from aggregate benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-24656: Md Sharif Hossen, Vijay K. Shah, and Ismail Guvenc analyze how drone height affects radio spotting. That is the ability to detect and track drones sharing airspace through cellular networks. At greater heights, clearer line-of-sight views expose drones to many base stations at once, making strong inter-cell interference. Links turn noise-led, with broken linkup regions and more uneven link quality. Helikite-based spectrum measurements and matching models show the same height-linked trends, guiding height-aware and noise-aware cellular design.
arxiv-2605-24756: Suresh Raghu and co-authors argue that agentic uncertainty scores mix ranking skill with true odds. Common metrics test ranking, calibration, or short summaries, but none elicit the full success trace. They introduce the Trajectory Proper Score, a family of rules for any per-step uncertainty signal, built on prequential scoring. They prove it elicits the success process in full view. An extension handles cut-off runs by mapping them onto the stopped part. Tests on four benchmarks show recalibration shifts the score while rank metrics stay nearly unchanged.
arxiv-2605-25156: Kasra Jalaldoust and Elias Bareinboum study prediction failure when the target distribution differs from the source. Valid inference about unseen data needs invariant causal mechanisms, yet those cannot be identified from source data alone. The authors show the optimal target prediction is partly identifiable. It factors into abduction and deduction maps: one infers hidden variables, the other predicts the label. A representation transplant linearly alters abduction content while keeping deduction intact. It lets them search plausible targets for a minimax-optimal prediction.
arxiv-2605-25256: Niklas Weller and Emilio Barkett ask whether a language model follows an organization's own decision rules, not just its final verdicts. Their process-alignment yardstick shows wide variation across models, tracking neither price nor general test scores. In European human-rights rulings, closer process match predicts more accurate outcomes, and spelling out past policy lifts weak models. In credit decisions, alignment stays low and models resist the firm's weighting of protected traits, so tighter matching is not always desirable.
arxiv-2605-25556: Austin Shen and Yunong Shi remove a bottleneck in parallel tactic search for Lean 4 proofs. Each branch now rebuilds its proof state by reloading imports and rechecking the theorem context, a cost that eats over 99 percent of branch time. Their snapshot method captures the elaborated state once and reuses it across branches through a small language-server extension. Across 48 miniF2F-v2 problems it runs about six to fifty times faster than the fallback, averaging fourteenfold, with gains growing as branches multiply.
arxiv-2605-25956: Abioye and six colleagues extend RAPTOR, a system that reads urgent suspected colorectal cancer referrals. The old version relied on a separate text-reading step. The new version, RAPTOR+, uses vision-language models that link each extracted fact to visible evidence on the form. On 223 curated forms, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B reaches 96.1 percent reading accuracy and 60.6 percent strict safety. Zero-shot models read well but rarely ground answers. The authors argue task-specific tuning is essential for auditable triage.
arxiv-2605-26256: Jeongeun Lee, Chanyoung Park, and Dongha Lee propose POLAR (2026), a memory-augmented framework that personalizes embodied agents over long user contact. Past interactions enter a multimodal knowledge graph holding semantic memory for personal context and visual ideas, plus episodic memory for past trajectories. At run time, POLAR pulls relevant memories to read the current request and steer execution. Tests across several model backbones and settings show steady gains, largest when tasks demand reasoning across interactions or tracking shifting user context.
arxiv-2605-26356: Mingchen Li and four colleagues treat retrieval-augmented generation as in-context optimization. They show one linear self-attention layer takes a gradient-descent step on a unified linearized retrieval goal. The match holds under controlled linear cases but turns data-dependent under nonlinear designs. Their method for frozen retrieval models predicts a context-tuned update to the interface, beating a baseline across seven benchmarks, in a 2026 paper.
arxiv-2605-26656: Jianfei Zhao and five others give vision tokens direct labels during fine-tuning of multimodal language models. Today only text tokens carry supervision, so picture tokens learn just as background and fine detail suffers. DV-SFT labels each picture token with the word in its patch, using text-image links in OCR scenes. It trains through plain next-token prediction with no new parts. It beats standard tuning on seven test sets, three close to training and four farther afield, sharpening fine-grained sight.
arxiv-2605-26856: Nagarjuna and Karnam propose the Sensation Modulating Network, a model of the mind as the whole body, not the brain alone. In this model, body parts that both sense and act link into zones, and gravity, stretch, and body shape build a self-model, a world-model, and a sense of objects. Their key claim is haltability: holding a rival balance steady is what lets felt resistance grow into a true object.
arxiv-2605-27256: Alkalaev and co-authors link conformal partial waves across flat, thermal, and defect settings using the shadow formalism. They show that scalar one-point thermal blocks follow systematically from flat-space four-point and defect two-point counterparts under specific operator setups. The frame yields the thermal Casimir equation as a diagonal cut of the flat-space Casimir system, with no chemical potentials introduced. They further show that defect blocks with a spin-l exchange match one-point thermal blocks for an external spin-l case.
arxiv-2605-27356: Simon Wili and colleagues find a resistance paradox in superfluid channels between one and two dimensions. Widening the channel raises resistance at the crossover minimum, where phase slips and vortices are both suppressed. Narrower channels follow phase-slip theory across more than ten orders of magnitude, while wider ones match a finite-size vortex model.
arxiv-2605-27756: Tomoki Koike, Prakash Mohan, Marc Henry de Frahan, Elizabeth Qian, and Julie Bessac present SparseModesNet, a neural method for sparse mode choice in flow data. A linear encoder pairs with a nonlinear decoder through LassoNet, forcing ranked sparse structure through a skip link that keeps a linear path. In channel-flow turbulence at friction Reynolds number 5200, rebuild error falls 51 to 78 percent against polynomial manifold methods.
arxiv-2605-27856: Yang and colleagues put a fine-tuned open language model to work inside a large live advertising system, not as a ranker but as a side predictor. Given a user's profile and history, it forecasts which advertisers fit, giving later ranking stages a head start. The setup delivered strong offline gains and measurable real-world business impact.
arxiv-2605-27956: Cho and colleagues recast higher-spin gravity, a theory of massless fields with arbitrarily high spin, as particles tracing worldlines. Their double-line picture gives a geometric rule for joining worldlines at interaction points, much like strings joining in string theory. From it they build vertex operators for every massless higher-spin field and recover known boundary correlators.
arxiv-2605-28056: Feng and colleagues give portrait animation finer control over the eyes, a region coarse emotion labels describe poorly. CogPortrait first turns high-level labels into facial keypoints through three planning agents, then renders video from those keypoints, portrait, audio, and text. In the available results it beats rivals on eye-region precision while holding visual quality and identity steady.
arxiv-2605-28256: Indranil Biswas and Anoop Singh study links on bundles over rationally connected shapes. Under set rules in this setting, they show a bundle takes a holomorphic Lie algebroid link exactly when the bundle itself is plain. They also show every such link is flat, so both having a link and being flat come down to plainness.
arxiv-2605-28356: Rybka and colleagues plan power-system expansion with storage by shrinking time series exactly, not by rule of thumb. Cost guesses learned by machine guide grouping to keep the full model's live limits, so the gap to the full model can be sized. Cost-led grouping beat input-only grouping by a wide margin on plan quality.
arxiv-2605-28556: Tomer Keren and five colleagues reverse agent-benchmark construction to beat saturation: instead of writing scenarios then mapping them to tools, they start from tool sequences. Their TASTE method samples valid tool sequences with an adaptive contrastive n-gram model fit on language-model validity judgments, clusters representatives, and evolves difficulty iteratively. The resulting tau-c-Bench extends three domains of tau-2-Bench with far broader tool coverage. Models near saturation on the old benchmark drop sharply on the new tasks, suggesting high scores reflected saturation more than robust skill.
arxiv-2605-28656: Sichang Qiu and eight colleagues report the first lab-made orbital altermagnetic photonic crystal. It gives momentum-dependent spin splitting without net magnet pull, but its light version stayed hard because light bits differ deeply from electrons. Their crystal uses an antiunitary link between a local p-orbital doublet and crystal motion, giving angle-dependent splitting with flipping pseudospin tilt and a d-xy-wave form. It also supports spin-selective transport, including spin splitting and sifting of light waves, opening a path to spin-photonic devices.
arxiv-2605-28756: Philip D. Mannheim faults Breit-Wigner scattering, where the phase shift takes a simple form at resonance. In the square well he finds the Breit-Wigner form often misses the real curve, the width can turn below zero, and the complex pole is not a value. Dying states have wave functions growing fast, he calls bad. This clears through the anti-linear PT balance of the square well. Its solutions come in complex pairs with a steady chance that neither grows nor decays, and one peak, not two.
arxiv-2605-29556: Haoyang Liu and ten colleagues present Opt-Verifier, a system that checks language-model-built optimization models from two sides. Building such models matters in operations research but demands human skill, and auto methods often skip checks on constraint rationality and answer validity, hurting fixes and scores. Structure-side checks align the model's structure with the first problem text, holding constraints and needs. Answer-side checks read and grade answers, proving the models sound in logic and math. Tests on popular benchmarks show score gains above twenty percent.
arxiv-2605-29656: Yundong Kim and Heyoung Yang present TRACE, a metric for judging chain-of-thought in open-ended outputs. Current metrics lean on final-answer scores or surface stats, leaving the thought process itself ignored. TRACE inspects how claims are built, mixing Toulmin's theory with Flavell's thinking system to assess thought shape. Tests on 26,300 question-answer samples across seven models show strong link with benchmark scores. TRACE also works as a learning reward, beating score-only rivals, which suggests sound thought leads to better answers.
arxiv-2605-29756: Jung Hyun Lee and three colleagues fix a spot in low-bit quantization for long-form generation. Block-wise methods match precision on basic tasks yet fade on long answers and thought chains. The team traces the fade to two gaps: the output layer escapes tuning, and mean-squared-error training misaligns token odds. Their fix, LFQ, quantizes the final block by matching token odds through cross-entropy against the full-precision model. Across model families it lifts complex generation over block-wise rivals while holding parity on basics.
arxiv-2605-30156: Oto Mraz and four colleagues argue that current tests of databases spread across regions miss what matters most. Benchmarks assume stable networks, ignore where data and users sit, and overlook transfer costs, while covering few spread patterns. Their Gaia framework tests existing transaction systems spread across cloud regions under varied patterns and shaky networks. Most systems prove sensitive to network wobbles, network costs dominate bills, and fault tolerance adds critical-path overhead. Future designs, they argue, must rethink speed, fault tolerance and cost together.
arxiv-2605-30256: Amrita Mazumdar and eight co-authors present VideoFDB, the first benchmark for full-duplex audio-visual agents that speak, listen and read nonverbal cues at once. Current benchmarks cover speech only. VideoFDB contributes 237 dyadic clips spanning 11 dynamics from video calls, a taxonomy separating perception from generation, and a rubric-based judge evaluation with clear quality axes. Across vision-speech agents, failures appear: captioning collapse and visual-stream ignorance, with vision used for visual question answering but not streaming audiovisual grounding. Cascaded speech-to-avatar systems fundamentally cannot produce nonverbal cues.
arxiv-2605-30456: Shraman Pal and Can Li propose DisjunctiveNet, a unified end-to-end framework for forcing hard, input-tied mixed integer linear constraints in neural networks. Their approach writes rules as disjunctive constraints and applies layered convex steps to obtain convex hull forms. These steps give usable linear constraints fitted as smooth tuning layers while meeting rules exactly. They show the framework on real-world data, with perfect rule keeping and strong results.
arxiv-2605-30556: Leutenegger tracks how training changes neural networks' likeness to early visual cortex, measured against human brain scans. A single epoch of training cut alignment with primary visual area V1 sharply, and the first draft said predictive coding and a spike-timing rule preserved more alignment than backpropagation. A later fix withdrew that contrast: a batch-normalization defect had skewed the comparison, and repaired analysis shows predictive coding degrading V1 alignment more than backpropagation. The broad finding that training degrades V1 alignment for every rule tested still stands.
arxiv-2605-30956: Marty builds on a series that mapped partial cross-sections for broad flow types, following Fried's approach to global cross-sections, and draws out what it means for Anosov flows. A homology test settles, for each cohomology class, whether a partial cross-section can be found there. Only finitely many such cross-sections can share one class. Applied to three-dimensional hyperbolic manifolds, these findings make every Anosov flow homologically full.
arxiv-2605-31056: Li, Chen, and He test how well large language models handle Chinese zero pronouns, common in pro-drop languages and a long-standing challenge for language systems. They test models on five tasks: identification, referentiality classification, referential type classification, resolution, and translation. Results show Chinese zero pronouns stay hard, mainly for early tasks like identification and referentiality classification. Translation is also low: even the best reasoning models translate fewer than half of Chinese zero pronouns into English.
arxiv-2605-31156: Zi-Rong Li and colleagues pretrain a model that reads a dataset and draws its causal graph in one pass. Such models often trail strong classical methods, and the authors trace the gap to how pretraining tasks are made. Their TabCausal model trains across many made-up causal worlds, varying graph shapes, mechanisms, noise, sizes and intervention types. Tasks built on the fly teach structure that transfers. It beats a wide set of baselines on large synthetic tests and recovers structure well, most of all when interventions are present.
arxiv-2605-31256: Benfenati and colleagues prune embodied language-model controllers during reinforcement learning, not after training. Timing matters because controllers pass through several training phases, and pruning after the fact ignores the closed-loop feedback shaping the final controller. Their Before Parc Fermé strategy removes parts of the model at set intervals during RL, or after supervised fine-tuning and then during RL. It gives the best trade-off among strategies tested, and compact models decode up to 27 percent faster on a Jetson AGX Orin board.
arxiv-2605-31356: Campbell and Jalowy link the Pólya-Schur study of root-preserving operators on polynomials with free probability theory. They show that any free infinitely divisible distribution can appear as the weak limit of root patterns from Appell polynomials as n grows. Their method also covers limits with unbounded support, gives a fine-grained picture of the roots, and extends to multiplicative cases and rectangular free convolution.
arxiv-2605-31556: Marin-Llobet, Henniger, and Banaji find that vision-language models suppress female representations under ambiguous input. Ambiguous images, like a worker in full gear, are far less studied. Minimal prompting exposes occupation-gender defaults: models default to male even for strongly female-stereotyped jobs. A new metric, the Latent Association Leaning Score, shows inner encodings and outputs often decouple. Models may encode a female link yet output male, as male signal grows while female signal peaks mid-network, then fades.
arxiv-2606-00356:
Karne tests how far auto-made tags for model traits hold across tongues and scripts. Sparse coder tools split a model's acts into named traits. Auto tags are the main lens on what each trait means. Karne asks if a tag tracks its sense when the tongue shifts.

Serbian, writ in two scripts with a fixed swap rule, forms the test bed. Trait sets lit by the same sense in twin forms share much ground. That share beats chance by a wide mark. Auto tags lag that ground, though. Tags miss the sense in Serbian far more than in English. They miss the Cyrillic form more than the Latin one. The gap grows with depth, and tags give no warn of it.
arxiv-2606-00456:
Lasso and Veloz build a shape-led route to photon spheres and black hole shades. Zones near a black hole strain most math tools in use. Photon spheres ring such holes, where light can loop in place. Big-bit skins and shade size flow from that ring's traits.

Their route grows from a small-shift base in past work. It rests on in-built bends, like path bend and Gauss bend of the space. At first rank, it finds the shift span for time-like paths. That case had not been worked in print till now. In the light case, it gives back past small-shift marks. Mass shifts are tracked through sphere and skin spans as well.
arxiv-2606-00556:
Shah, Sethi, and Gandhe chain two sight tools to pin things in far sky shots by words. Word-led hunt for a named thing in a shot is called grounding. Far shots hold packed scenes, small things, and wide scale swings. One tool in lone use most oft falls short there.

Their chains start with RemoteSAM, a tool tuned for far shots. SAM3 then hones that first mark to a clean shape. Two chain forms are built, one plain and one bunch-aware. A vote plan blends six such chains for yet more trust. Each chain brings a split strength to the vote. Tests show chains and the vote beat each lone tool. Marks land more true and more firm across scenes.
arxiv-2606-00656:
Zhang and co-authors tackle fair machine learning in this 2026 paper. Their focus is multi-class tasks, where a model picks one label from many, not just two. Bias in such models can treat groups in unequal ways. Most past fixes were built for the two-class case and do not carry over well.

The team first writes down, in exact form, the best fair classifier for this setting. That form maps the best trade-off that accuracy and fairness can reach. They then build two ways to hit that trade-off in practice. One acts while the model trains, and one tunes its output scores after training. Both skip the group label of each case. Tests on several datasets show a strong balance of accuracy and fairness, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-00856:
Dulaunoy proposes a decentralized system for naming security flaws in this 2026 paper. Today's CVE system is central: it gives strict control and widely known IDs. But many makers post advisories on their own, with no shared fabric to find, link, or enrich them. Good data ends up scattered.

His model, GCVE, spreads the work out. Autonomous numbering authorities assign IDs under light shared rules. Publication stays distributed, guided by open best-practice texts that can evolve. Global uniqueness of IDs is kept, while each party posts on its own terms. A flaw record grows wider than an assignment. It can hold disclosures, sightings, rejected IDs, and notes on exploits or enrichment. A reference tool, vulnerability-lookup, pulls records from many sources into one view. Extension points, some aimed at AI, let the standard grow without central control.
arxiv-2606-00956:
Takeno puts regret bounds under a look-ahead optimizer in this 2026 paper. Bayesian optimization picks costly test points with care, guided by a probabilistic model. One-step lookahead methods, like entropy search, work well in practice. But they lean on intractable approximations, and their regret guarantees lag behind their fame.

His subject is a leaner method he calls optimal-point variance reduction, or OVR. It needs only posterior samples and Monte Carlo estimates. He bounds the Monte Carlo error of its acquisition score, evenly across the whole input domain. A slight tweak, regularized OVR, adds a push for exploration. For that form he proves the expected simple regret shrinks to zero over time, in the Bayesian sense. Numerical tests check both forms in action. The paper gives practitioners a look-ahead method with both receipts: strong runs and a proof that misses decay.
arxiv-2606-01056:
Xu and co-authors trap a falling magnet with feedback control in this 2026 physics paper. A free ferromagnet should show pure Larmor precession in near zero field. That motion could serve fine magnetometry and gyroscopy, and probe deep physics. No one has yet seen it in a macroscopic particle. True free fall is needed, since clamps leak energy and skew the read.

The trap must be weak enough to fake free fall yet tough enough to survive launch. Their design pairs a PID controlled coil set with a master control coil. It flew in the Einstein-Elevator drop tower. In the microgravity phase, the trap held a ferromagnetic particle steady against shocks up to 1.5 g and tracked its motion in both trials. One trial ran a low field setup, and one ran pure free fall. The work is a step toward free fall ferromagnetic sensors in space.
arxiv-2606-01156:
Cezaro, Hafemann, and Leitão sharpen blurred barcodes with a level set method in this 2026 maths paper. A blurred linear barcode is a semi blind deconvolution problem: the code and the blur must both be recovered. Their base is the Piecewise Constant Level Set frame from a 2013 paper by Cezaro's team. It suits signals that jump between flat levels, as barcode bars do.

Their method wraps that frame in an augmented Lagrangian scheme. It seeks stable approximate answers that hold up under noisy readings. They prove that generalized multipliers exist for their functional. They also prove no duality gap stands in the way. Those results ground the regularization claims of the method. An ADMM type iteration computes the approximate barcodes in practice. Tests sweep blur strengths and noise levels to check the design. The authors report the method works well across those settings.
arxiv-2606-01256:
Saha and Ramdas ask where a change fell after a test flags it. Sequential tests can spot a shift in a data stream. They say little about when that shift took place. Past fixes need known pre- and post-change laws. Saha and Ramdas need no such laws at all. Their method builds confidence sets for the change time. It sits after a detection step that uses conformal test martingales.

They prove finite-sample coverage if detection was right. They also bound the expected size of the sets. In large samples, that size stays uniformly bounded. Tests on fake and real data show strong results. The work is a first general distribution-free frame for this task.
arxiv-2606-01556:
Wang and co-authors learn friendlier subspaces for 4-bit model quantization. Four-bit quantization shrinks memory and latency for LLM inference. Its aggressive precision cut can hurt accuracy badly. Prior methods split each weight matrix into two parts. A low-rank part handles outliers at high precision. A residual part holds the bulk at low precision. Those splits minimize real-valued residual energy, not post-quantization error. TwinQuant learns decomposed subspaces that quantize well instead.

It reshapes both parts with learned transformations. Joint optimization runs over Stiefel and general linear manifolds. Distributions flatten and dynamic-range imbalance falls. A fused kernel pipelines the two-stage computation on chip. Across LLaMA3 and Qwen3 models, accuracy nears FP16. Speed rises up to 1 point 8 times over the FP16 baseline.
arxiv-2606-01956:
Sanchez Almeida measures inner star density slopes in dwarf galaxies from photos alone. The inner slope probes how dark matter behaves. Cored star profiles clash with cuspy cold dark matter forecasts. Photometry offers a cheap way to constrain that slope. Faint galaxies matter most for dark matter studies.

Turning surface density into volume density is ambiguous. Noise makes deprojection of the profiles unreliable. Sanchez Almeida derives a direct formula to avoid it. The slope comes from radial derivatives of surface density. Spherical symmetry and smooth profiles are assumed. All projected profiles share one central functional form. That form yields the inner slope cleanly. The method suits large samples of faint galaxies.
arxiv-2606-02056:
Kennerberg introduces a new class of processes called Special Dirichlet processes. Each such process splits into two parts. One part is a local martingale. The other part has jumps that can be predicted from past information. The class comes from changing special semimartingales with functions.

Kennerberg shows that these changed processes have more structure than was known. Their split has a clear form, with the jump part kept apart from the rest. He proves that this split is unique. He also proves the class stays stable under many rough changes. These include primitives of locally bounded functions with at most countably many breaks. He gives an explicit formula for the split in terms of jump data. He also shows the split stays stable under two forms of convergence.
arxiv-2606-02456:
Reyes-Calderón and co-authors study the local spin motion of long spin-1 condensates. The density profile is uneven along the length. Nonlinear and quantum effects mix through that profile. After a global quench, distinct dynamical regimes appear. The motion is far from simple.

One finding is a sharp split of domains. Regions with unlike dynamics coexist, split by a robust interface. That interface acts as a spatial excited-state quantum phase transition. Elsewhere, the local motion turns chaotic. Its course is irregular and ultra-sensitive to starting conditions. The team maps the full phase diagram of regular versus chaotic regimes. The map separates the two kinds of motion. Ongoing experiments can probe these regimes directly. The work links local spin physics to chaos theory.
arxiv-2606-02556:
Zheng and co-authors test whether language models can infer hidden rules and act on them. Their benchmark, HERO'S JOURNEY, uses text games. Agents must learn rules from demonstrations. They must then execute multi-step plans under those rules. Eight tasks span two induction families. Attribute and procedural induction are both covered.

Each task has four structural rule forms. Lexical grounding can be controlled. Identifiability conditions are set per task. Top models show real signs of rule induction. The skill is limited and uneven across tasks. Process execution adds a bottleneck of its own. Surface semantics barely matters by contrast. Steering methods aimed at induction help on attribute tasks. They give no reliable gain on procedural tasks. Procedural induction, the authors conclude, stays an open challenge.
arxiv-2606-02656:
Ughradar and co-authors read information measures of a Bose-Einstein condensate from phase-space pictures. Wigner and Husimi distributions give those pictures. The condensate obeys the Gross-Pitaevskii equation in a harmonic trap. From the mean field ground state, both distributions are built. Their position and momentum marginals follow. A wide set of measures is then computed.

Entropies of Shannon, Wehrl, and Rényi types lead the set. Fisher information, residual entropies, and mutual information join it. Several divergences are also tracked. All vary with the s-wave scattering length for a rubidium-85 condensate. Stronger repulsion spreads the phase-space picture. Shannon and Wehrl entropies grow in step. Fisher information rises in position space and falls in momentum space. Wigner and Husimi mutual information converge at strong coupling. The authors note the mutual information here is statistical dependence, not true particle entanglement.
arxiv-2606-02756:
Gonzalez and co-authors propose a photonic route to simulating lattice gauge theories with matter. The target is a one-plus-one-dimensional U(1) theory. Their scheme rests on the Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard model. An array of interacting cavities runs in the strong-coupling regime of cavity QED. The array maps onto the alternating matter and gauge sites of a spin-1/2 quantum link model.

Gauge-invariant dynamics arise through hopping of polaritonic excitations. Precise tuning of polariton resonances in each cavity sets the map. Exact diagonalization checks the scheme. The Jaynes-Cummings-Hubbard evolution matches the quantum link model closely. Routes to beyond-classical capability are discussed. Photonic and superconducting platforms both offer scalable paths. The work opens a new way to study real-time dynamics of gauge theories with dynamical matter.
arxiv-2606-03056:
Bai and co-authors present SkillDAG, a way for language-model agents to choose skills from large libraries. Which skills reach the prompt decides what an agent can do. Standard retrieval treats skills as independent documents. But skills depend on, conflict with, and duplicate one another. The closest match to a task may name it yet omit a prerequisite.

SkillDAG exposes a typed skill graph to the model as a callable interface. Search returns vector matches, typed-edge neighbors, and conflict signals. A propose-then-commit protocol lets the agent register execution-backed edges as it works. Across two benchmarks and three model families, SkillDAG beat full-library prompting, vector retrieval, and a graph pipeline rival. It gained 14.3 points of success on ALFWorld. Its ranking held across a tenfold pool expansion. The authors argue inter-skill structure is worth more when the agent can query and revise it.
arxiv-2606-03156:
Wang describes a dataset of tropical species built to cross domain lines. The snapshot holds 410,499 active species in three groups: tropical plants, tropical aquatic life, and tropical pets. These groups share a trade and rules life cycle, but records sit in kingdom-based databases that do not join up.

It merges taxon IDs from six sources. An ontology re-sorts taxa by trade and care contexts. A Chinese names layer gives each name a clear source trail, and drops names that lack checks. A third layer links each taxon to its CITES entry in Species+. About 99.5 percent of taxa carry a Chinese name that differs from the Latin one. Wang is clear that this rate shows coverage, not translation quality. The dataset is on Zenodo under a CC-BY license, and a blind outside audit is named as the main open task.
arxiv-2606-03256:
Kaminaga studies black hole echoes in a controlled toy model, with care about what the model can show. Echo models posit a reflecting wall near where a horizon would be, in place of a purely ingoing boundary rule. The aim here is not a new mechanism or a claim about real data. It is to analyze the standard cavity denominator with clean normalizations.

The model pairs a compact one-dimensional barrier with a Robin wall at a set cavity length. Kaminaga proves a local result: one resonance zero per cell, with a localization error that falls as the inverse square of the length. A factorization splits the poles, set by the cavity, from the residues, set by the source. Direct numeric work on the true Regge-Wheeler potential gives the same near-even comb of resonances. Smooth source shapes change peak weights but not pole places.
arxiv-2606-03356:
Hainzl, Saxler, and Seiringer bound the ground state energy of a two-dimensional Fermi gas. The gas is dilute, with repulsive short-range interactions. Their bound is the two-dimensional analogue of a formula by Huang and Yang for the three-dimensional case. Such formulas matter because they pin how energy grows as the gas gets denser.

The bound captures the first three terms of an asymptotic expansion. The small parameter blends the density with the square of the scattering length. Three terms is a sharp haul in two dimensions, where the expansion is more delicate than in three. The result gives a firm ceiling that the true ground state energy cannot cross. The work should interest mathematical physicists who study cold gases. Upper bounds of this kind pair with lower bounds to trap the true energy in a narrowing band.
arxiv-2606-03456:
Csizmadia and co-authors present an updated tool for modeling the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect. That effect distorts a star's spectrum while a planet crosses its face. It reveals how tilted the planet's orbit is against the star's spin. The tool lives in the exoplanet analysis code TLCM. The model is described in full detail.

Nine known systems check the code against TESS light curves and archive velocity data. New data then target HD 2685, also known as TOI-135. This hot, evolved star hosts a hot Jupiter of just over one Jupiter mass. Its orbit takes about four days. Fresh HARPS velocity data, in and out of transit, join six new TESS sectors. The team refines the system values and detects the effect in this system. The sky-projected tilt comes out near 56 degrees. Wider prior tests keep that value stable, though with larger error bars.
arxiv-2606-03756:
Shaffer and co-authors learn navigation functions that transfer to new environments with no retraining. Reactive navigation needs a value function that guides motion to a goal. Learned planners that predict that function directly often fail on new geometry. Neural-NF puts learning inside a structured elliptic planner instead. The planner's form is fixed by construction, while its local coefficients are learned.

Laplacian-based features of the space map to PDE coefficients. Solving the boundary value problem yields a global value function on each new domain. Every learned model gives a collision-free policy by construction. Descent is monotonic, and the global minimum sits at the goal. The setup also admits a linearly solvable optimal-control reading. Tests show strong zero-shot transfer across diverse shapes. Accuracy beats direct value prediction by up to five times. Robotics teams get planners that carry guarantees into unseen spaces.
arxiv-2606-03856:
Rivasseau extends the loop vertex expansion to cumulants of a matrix model. Constructive field theory has advanced through such expansions. Cumulants capture connected correlations of a model. One of the simplest matrix models is treated here, in the bounded rank regime. Both plain and scalar cumulants are analyzed.

Scalar cumulants come from the Weingarten calculus. They are key to the topological expansion in field theory. The results hold for any large positive coupling. That reach is new for this technique. The variational approach, proven on simpler targets, now covers cumulants head-on. Field theorists get firmer ground for expansions that were formal before. Matrix model work gains rigorous backing at strong coupling.
arxiv-2606-03956:
Tan and Brouwer study how operators spread in random quantum circuits. Their gates come from ensembles with orthogonal or symplectic symmetry. That choice sets the work apart from the well-studied unitary case. Spread shapes how fast local facts turn into scrambled, spread-out form. The pair track Pauli-string weights as they relax over time.

They find the mean weights settle into a three-value pattern, not two. The wall between plain and scrambled zones keeps finite width here. In the unitary case with Haar gates, that wall stays sharp. Gate choice within the orthogonal group also splits results in two. One sector bounds the butterfly speed away from zero for any gate law. At local dimension two, that speed can top the Haar value.
arxiv-2606-04056:
Sajjad Khan documents in 2026 how software agents driven by large language models can run up huge bills when a retry loop spends tokens unchecked. His central evidence is a catalog of sixty-three confirmed production incidents drawn from twenty-one agent frameworks between 2023 and 2026.

Each incident is backed by a public issue report and, where known, a dollar loss, and the set is organized into eight failure clusters. As one remedy, Khan built a small Rust library that treats a budget as something that cannot be copied or spent twice, enforced by the compiler itself. In tests, a runaway delegation pattern that always overshot under a common Python setup was rejected before running, and live tests across providers showed no cap violations.
arxiv-2606-04256:
Silvia Paparini, Giulio Giusteri, and Angela Mihai model in 2026 how topological defects steer the growth of living tissue. Defects are spots where the local order of cells twists or breaks. In many tissues, they mark where new structures will form.

The team built a continuum model of a cell sheet laced with a cytoskeletal network. Defects in the network concentrate stress. The tissue then remodels around those spots. In simulations of Hydra, the freshwater polyp, placing defects where the mature animal has them reproduced regrowth. Defects of one charge drove bumps such as tentacles. Defects of the other steadied flat regions. The work links a physics idea to a classic puzzle in development.
arxiv-2606-04356:
Takeshi Fukasawa studies step-by-step methods in 2026 for estimating structural economic models that must obey equilibrium rules. The usual nested approach recomputes an equilibrium for every candidate parameter set. That is costly.

For maximum likelihood and method-of-moments estimation, he studies methods with a zero-Jacobian property. They converge nearly quadratically in large samples. One iteration from a consistent starting estimate already gives an efficient estimator. He then proposes a method covering a broader class of models. It never needs the rules' Jacobian computed outright. It runs several times faster than the nested fixed point standard. Two tests, a dynamic game and a dynamic demand model, show the gains.
arxiv-2606-04456:
Alemán Espinosa and Schlomberg sharpen the bounds for routing many shipments through one network without splitting any of them, in a 2026 arXiv paper on graph algorithms. In the multicommodity flow problem, each source-sink pair has a demand, and an unsplittable flow sends each demand along a single path. A constant, alpha, measures the worst-case capacity overflow of such a flow, relative to the largest demand, when a split flow exists.

For outerplanar graphs, networks that can be drawn with all vertices on a circle and no crossings inside, the best known upper bound was 3.6. The authors prove alpha lies between four thirds and two, a large improvement. Their technique, pinning on tight cuts, uses global parameters of the whole instance rather than local structure alone, and may help wherever cut conditions nearly guarantee a feasible flow.
arxiv-2606-04656:
Zhang and colleagues quantify how uncertain an object detector's bounding boxes are, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They work one detected instance at a time and without retraining. Post hoc methods fit deployment. The authors use the Laplace approximation. Existing linearized methods need multiple backpropagations per instance, which is slow. Sampling methods are not fully post hoc.

Their method, Monte Carlo generalized linearized model, provides instance-level, approximately post hoc uncertainty. The number of Monte Carlo samples is constant. It does not grow with the number of detected instances. So the computation parallelizes well. The resulting uncertainties show good quality. They are large where the detector is actually unreliable. The work targets the practical setting where a deployed detector must flag its own doubtful boxes cheaply, in real time.
arxiv-2606-04856:
Abiad, Yang, and Zhou derive sharp spectral bounds for graph parameters governing coloring and packing problems, in a 2026 arXiv combinatorics paper. Distance colorings assign colors so that vertices within a certain distance differ, and packing parameters count how many distant vertices a graph can hold. Using spectral graph theory, the authors obtain bounds for the injective chromatic number, the open packing number, the injective chromatic index, and the strong chromatic index.

The new spectral bounds improve several bounds. Applying the bounds for the first two parameters to hypercubes, they estimate the code covering number and open packing number, obtaining new exact values and strengthened bounds relative to the literature. The work illustrates the power of combining spectral and semidefinite methods on coloring and packing problems.
arxiv-2606-04956:
Berezhnoy and colleagues synthesize a niobium-scandium superconducting film and measure whether it suits cryogenic electronics, in a 2026 arXiv superconductivity paper. They develop magnetron co-sputtering from separate niobium and scandium targets to deposit alloy films. Superconducting properties are then measured on microbridges fifty micrometers long, two wide, and thirty nanometers thick, using transport, magnetoresistive, and magnetic measurements.

The critical temperature peaks at 6.35 kelvin for about fifteen percent scandium content. The critical current density reaches as high as 2.5 mega-amperes per square centimeter. With the field perpendicular, they extract an upper critical field of 3.2 tesla at zero temperature. The authors conclude the synthesized intermetallic compound shows promise for functional cryogenic electronics devices.
arxiv-2606-05156:
Júlia Baligács proves that temporal cliques admit linear-size spanners in this 2026 arXiv paper, settling a question that had resisted years of effort. In a temporal graph every edge carries time labels, and a path counts only if its labels never decrease along the way. A spanner is a small subset of edges that preserves temporal connectivity between all pairs of vertices. Sparse spanners are not guaranteed to exist for temporal graphs in general.

For temporal cliques, where every pair of vertices is joined by an edge, the best known bound on spanner size had remained on the order of n log n. Baligács proves every temporal clique on n vertices admits a spanner of size 7n, linear in the number of vertices. Moreover, such a spanner can be computed in polynomial time, giving both the tight structural guarantee and an efficient construction.
arxiv-2606-05356:
Sandesh Kalantre and colleagues map the Fermi surface of rhombohedral tetralayer graphene, the normal state beneath a chiral superconductor, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Work found superconductivity in this material emerging from a time-reversal-broken normal state, hinting at chirality. Whether chirality is possible depends on the normal Fermi surface's symmetry and shape, which had not been measured.

Using oscillation measurements across the phase diagram, including inside the superconducting region, the team reproduced the high-density state: a spin- and valley-polarized quarter metal with a connected Fermi pocket. As carrier density drops toward superconductivity, the oscillations change into a multitone pattern that persists through the superconducting region and cannot come from a simply connected quarter metal. Their modeling's next-simplest candidates, polarized annular, nematic, and three-pocket states, are inconsistent with the data. The normal state is richer than envisaged, reshaping the search for the pairing mechanism.
arxiv-2606-05456:
Christopher Eagle and Timothy McNicholl prove that the continuous functional calculus is computable, in this 2026 arXiv paper at the meeting point of operator algebras and computability theory. It is a core tool of C*-algebra theory. Given a normal element and a continuous function on its spectrum, it produces an element of the algebra. It extends plugging a matrix into a polynomial.

The paper gives the full treatment. Take a computably presented C*-algebra whose unit is computable, and a computable normal element. Its spectrum is compact in the computable sense. Applying such a function yields a computable element, uniformly. Two consequences follow. Such algebras possess effective approximate units, sequences that act like an identity element in a way an algorithm can produce. And the Spectral Theorem for compact operators on separable Hilbert spaces also gets computable content.
arxiv-2606-05656:
Jia, Wang, and Zhang build the quantum machinery for a higher form of symmetry in a 2026 arXiv paper. One-form symmetries act on lines rather than points and pervade field theory. Gauging them means quantizing a two-form gauge field, an object pictured as a gerbe. The BV-BRST method, the standard ghost bookkeeping, needs a geometric home here. The authors construct one from the gerbe's local patching data.

They package the symmetry structure as a Lie 2-algebroid, a layered version of the usual algebra. With its partner Courant structure, it frames the ghost tower of the theory. A higher Russian formula organizing field strengths falls out of the gerbe relations. The paired complex of forms then gives a clean setting for anomaly descent, the ladder linking anomalies across dimensions. Worked examples in Maxwell theory show the machine in motion. This is part one of a planned series.
arxiv-2606-05856:
Ebisu, Han, and Cao reframe deconfined quantum critical points inside an enlarged Landau picture in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such points join two phases that break mismatched symmetries, which the classic Landau rules forbid. The authors gauge part of the symmetry, trading an anomaly for a symmetry type. The new symmetry is categorical and noninvertible: its fusion closes only loosely. In that mirror world, the critical point becomes an ordinary pattern-breaking transition.

Two spin chain examples carry the argument. A magnetic to valence-bond transition lands in one dihedral-flavored category. A second transition lands in a quaternion-flavored category. The two categories share fusion rules yet differ in their F-symbols, so they stay distinct. The universal content of such critical points lives in the full category, not the fusion ring alone. The paper gives crystalline phases a Landau-style grammar that once seemed impossible.
arxiv-2606-06156:
Rebecca Potts and co-authors build a trust-aware system for predicting gas turbine emissions in this 2026 arXiv paper. Predictive emissions monitoring systems estimate pollutants such as nitrogen oxides from sensor data instead of measuring exhaust directly. The catch is that true emissions labels exist for only a small subset of a fleet, sometimes a single turbine. A prediction is of little use if operators cannot tell when to trust it.

Their framework combines a recurrent prediction model with learned confidence scores, ensemble uncertainty, and checks on feature distance and operating range. Keeping only the most confident tenth of predictions cut the mean absolute error from just over two tenths to seven hundredths, showing the scores track real error. Unlabelled and out-of-distribution turbines drew higher uncertainty and lower confidence, as they should. The result is a per-sample trust score that flags which fleet predictions deserve caution.
arxiv-2606-06456:
Zane M Rossi and Rahul Sarkar improve basic matrix operations for quantum computers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum algorithms usually transform a matrix's spectrum, its list of eigenvalues, through tools like quantum singular value transformation. But some useful operations act entry by entry instead, applying a function to each element of the matrix separately. Whether quantum machines could do that efficiently, or at all, was unclear, and earlier attempts contained mistakes.

The authors construct new algorithms for element wise polynomial transforms and fix errors they found in previous constructions. Their headline gain is in space: the extra memory needed shrinks exponentially in the degree of the applied polynomial compared with prior work. They also treat the Hadamard product, the entrywise product of two matrices, within the same framework. Applications sketched along the way touch machine learning, physical simulation, and signal processing, anywhere entrywise operations like rectification or pointwise products appear.
arxiv-2606-06556:
Elis Karcini and co-authors argue that robot learning is starving in the wrong way in this 2026 arXiv position paper. The standard recipe for generalist robots is scale: more demonstrations, bigger vision language action models. The authors say the bottleneck lies elsewhere. The world overflows with behavioral data. Human motion, internet video, and simulations abound. But almost none of it arrives labeled with the robot specific actions, contacts, and rewards a policy needs.

They identify four missing interfaces. Data interfaces would auto label unstructured behavior. Embodiment interfaces would retarget human motion onto robot bodies. World model interfaces would add physics grounded 3D reasoning. Reward interfaces would infer task progress from video and language. Their agenda: build the machinery that turns messy physical experience into grounded supervision. Today's policies are just one layer of a larger stack.
arxiv-2606-06756:
The double integrator is the simplest system in control theory: push a mass, and it accelerates. Burachik, Kaya, and Liu use it as a proving ground in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study optimal control, the search for the cheapest push that meets set end conditions. Their tool is a primal-dual penalty algorithm.

Penalty methods trade constraint breaking against cost. This paper works out every possible case of the problem. The authors split the boundary conditions into thirteen disjoint classes. For each class they derive closed form formulas. Those formulas give the dual functions and the optimal controls. They also pin down the least exact penalty parameter, the smallest penalty that still enforces the rules. Finally, they compare step size rules for the algorithm. Trajectories of the constraint functions show exactly when the dual behavior switches.
arxiv-2606-07056:
Modern symmetry in physics acts on lines and surfaces, not just points, and it can clash with itself. Jia, Wang, and Zhang catalog those clashes for one form symmetries in this 2026 arXiv paper. A one form symmetry has line like charged objects and couples to a two form background field. Its anomalies, quantum inconsistencies, decide which theories can exist.

The tool is bordism, a way of classifying shapes up to smooth deformation. The authors compute bordism groups for a key classifying space through degree eight. Spectral sequences and geometric arguments resolve the hard extension problems. Two discoveries stand out. Five dimensional theories carry a new mixed anomaly linking the symmetry to spacetime diffeomorphisms. Seven dimensional theories carry a new discrete anomaly valued in two elements. Both have boundary realizations the paper constructs explicitly. The work is the second part of a series on quantum aspects of higher symmetries.
arxiv-2606-07256:
Capuzzo Dolcetta honors Guido Barbiellini Amidei, an Italian physicist who died in 2024, in this 2026 arXiv review. The paper traces how modern high-energy astrophysics grew up with particle detector technology. Barbiellini's career ran from early electron-positron colliders to space missions watching gamma rays and cosmic rays. The author uses that career as a thread linking lab physics with astronomy.

The review covers his work on silicon tracking detectors, which record particle paths with precision, and on calorimetry, the measurement of particle energies. It discusses his roles in the AGILE and Fermi gamma-ray telescopes and the PAMELA cosmic-ray experiment, which hunted antimatter in space. His leadership in large global collaborations is another theme. The paper closes by assessing how the detector methods he championed now underpin routine study of the high-energy universe.
arxiv-2606-07656:
Ramani and colleagues introduce SC-cubed, a benchmark for predicting solubility across many solvents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Solubility, the most of a substance that will dissolve in a liquid, shapes drug design and chemical manufacturing, yet published prediction scores rest on inconsistently cleaned data. The team rebuilds the data from BigSolDB with a reproducible curation pipeline and tiered agreement levels.

Their collection holds more than one hundred thousand measurements covering over thirteen hundred solutes and two hundred six solvents, split into gold, silver, and bronze tiers by agreement between sources. Recalibrating measurement noise gives an error floor near one tenth of a log unit, roughly six times tighter than the figure usually quoted. Even so, the best of thirty-one tested models still errs about five times above that floor, a gap no deep model in the study closes.
arxiv-2606-07756:
Peterson, Mayers, and Han study how to judge the distance of a drone from one camera image, in this 2026 arXiv paper. At long range a drone may cover only a few pixels, so range estimation fights background clutter, changes in target size, and noisy detector boxes. Their setting is practical: a detector first proposes a candidate region, and the model predicts distance from that crop plus the box geometry.

Against a DroneRanger-style baseline, the team introduces DroneDAR, which pairs a convolutional image backbone with bounding-box features joined through a gating mechanism. The gate lets the model lean on box size when the picture is uninformative and on appearance when texture survives. Experiments vary backbone size, crop resolution, and loss functions across distance ranges. Distant targets fail through sensitivity to box noise and lost texture, and the paper turns those findings into design guidance for long-range estimators.
arxiv-2606-07856:
Strozzi asks a question about models that train on their own output, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Does self-training create new capability, or express what the base model already had? His test rig is teacher-free: a generator, a critic, and a verifier work on a puzzle domain where answers are cheap to make, hard to guess, and free to check. All of it runs on one quantised model on one graphics card.

Three findings follow. A critic's selection beat verifier-filtered best-of sampling by about nine points, all of it on tasks where candidates disagreed. Self-training raised the ceiling but never sped learning up. The decisive test varies the budget. The trained model wins with eight attempts allowed. At sixty-four attempts the base model overtakes it, on each run. Self-training, he concludes, concentrates probability on known solutions, not wider reach: amplification, not compounding.
arxiv-2606-07956:
Khai-Hoan Nguyen-Dang computes the shape of a family of number fields and shows how much of the field that shape remembers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pure number fields come from adjoining an n-th root of a whole number a to the rationals. Their Minkowski shape is a geometric fingerprint, roughly the lattice formed by embedding the field's integers into Euclidean space.

Under an explicit local hypothesis at the primes dividing n, the shape factorises neatly: a rational change of basis times a diagonal part from normalised monomials. The consequences split by parity. For odd degree, the shape is a complete invariant, determining the field entirely. For even degrees it determines a smaller core field. On squarefree families it is complete up to sign, though infinitely many non-isomorphic pairs share the same shape. Discriminant formulas and a description of where shapes live complete the picture.
arxiv-2606-08056:
Oline Ranum, Simon Hadfield, and Richard Bowden show that sign language recognition systems systematically miss the pointing, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Signers use spatial indexing constantly: a point assigns a person or object to a location in the signing space, and later points back to that spot refer to it. These gestures make up roughly ten to fifteen percent of signing content, yet models trained to output gloss sequences barely recover them.

The authors build a targeted evaluation of indexing and split the problem in two: detecting the index points, and linking each one to the discourse entity it refers to. The resulting mention representations support automatic annotation of non-lexical structure, the grammar word lists miss. They also package the machinery as an auxiliary indexing expert that augments a frozen recognition model, improving index awareness without retraining it. The work establishes a baseline for index-aware sign language modelling.
arxiv-2606-08456:
Pérez-Román, Good, Ong, and Rosu extend a classical geometric description of relativistic motion in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Frenet-Serret equations describe a curve through its curvature and torsion, how it bends and twists. For timelike worldlines in Minkowski spacetime, the authors allow curvature and torsion to depend on proper time, corresponding to non-uniform proper acceleration. They build the moving frame from the four-velocity and its derivatives.

This construction relates the Frenet-Serret parameters to kinematic quantities such as proper acceleration, four-jerk, and four-snap. The authors then treat simple analytic cases for the jerk invariant and torsion, obtaining explicit curvature profiles and reduced forms. These examples clarify how non-constant acceleration and torsion modify the geometry of such motion. The work matters for the physics of fast, turning flight paths and the frames that ride along with them.
arxiv-2606-08556:
Claros, Carlos Pérez, and Zheng strengthen a family of inequalities central to modern analysis in this 2026 arXiv paper. Poincaré inequalities bound how much a function can vary by how large its gradient is, and Poincaré-Sobolev versions strengthen the conclusion by measuring variation in a better norm. A powerful self-improving method shows that generalized Poincaré inequalities automatically upgrade themselves under mild conditions. The authors establish several improvements to recent main results in this line.

The paper works in the setting of spaces of homogeneous type and related general frameworks, where the underlying geometry may be far rougher than Euclidean space. Self-improvement matters because it converts a weak, scale-by-scale estimate into a stronger integrated one without new hypotheses. Sharper versions widen the class of functions and geometries covered. The authors also develop related applications that follow from the strengthened inequalities.
arxiv-2606-08856:
Briat unifies optimal control, energy analysis, and games for systems whose state is a matrix, not a vector, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such systems arise where the state is a covariance, moment, or Gram matrix, central in stochastic control, transport, and signal processing. The systems are impulsive, flowing continuously and jumping at events, and the class covers linear systems, switched systems, and stochastic hybrid moment dynamics.

Three tools do everything: an identity linking cost, trajectory, and a dual variable, an extended Schur complement lemma, and a Schur inner-product decomposition, applied alike to flows and jumps. From them flow necessary and sufficient conditions and explicit policies for control, steering, dissipativity, and games, extended to the infinite horizon. Steering reduces, by duality, to an unconstrained problem solved by a forward-backward algorithm. Dwell-time versions marry a Riccati equation over a timer interval to a discrete one at its end.
arxiv-2606-09056:
Ishaan Preetam Chandratreya and colleagues generate long videos that remember their beginnings by summarizing each frame at several detail levels, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Video generators build footage chunk by chunk. Once early chunks leave context, their content is forgotten, so layouts drift. MilliVid first trains an autoencoder compressing every frame into a hierarchy of tokens. The coarsest levels hold a few tokens capturing layout and semantics; finer levels add texture.

A video diffusion model then generates these tokens coarse-to-fine. At each step it controls how much detail past frames contribute. Coarse summaries preserve geometry and object permanence over long ranges. Fine detail is spent only where it matters visually. That keeps compute in check where longer context would explode quadratically. Tests used long Minecraft videos, where drift is easy to spot. MilliVid produced more consistent long rollouts than baselines, where rivals lost track of their content.
arxiv-2606-09156:
Wang and colleagues unify image generation from almost any instruction into one autoregressive model, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Autoregressive models predict one token at a time, as language models do, and are strong for images too. Existing visual models accept one condition type, usually text, while real tasks mix conditions: depth maps, masks, images to edit, frames to continue. OmniGen-AR tokenizes them all, visuals through a shared visual tokenizer, text through a text tokenizer, training one transformer on the stream.

To stop content tokens peeking at condition tokens, Disentangled Causal Attention splits the mask into condition and content pathways in training, leaving inference untouched. One model handles text-to-image, segmentation- and depth-to-image, editing, frame prediction, and text-to-video. It scored 0.63 on GenEval and 80.02 on VBench, state-of-the-art or competitive across benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-09456:
Yifan Niu and his colleagues remove a hidden restriction on on-policy distillation, a leading technique for transferring skills from big language models to smaller ones, in this 2026 arXiv paper. On-policy distillation trains the student on its own generated text, scored token by token by the teacher. Until now it required teacher and student to share the same tokenizer, the component that chops text into units, which confined it to single model families.

Different tokenizers split the same text into comparable fragments because all rest on a shared byte-level foundation. Exploiting that, the authors built a precise token-mapping algorithm that carries the teacher's probability signals across mismatched vocabularies, with chunk-level credit assignment to keep the alignment faithful. Cross-tokenizer distillation proved significantly more compute-efficient than the usual fallback of fine-tuning on teacher-written answers.
arxiv-2606-09556:
Yinan Wang tests whether an AI analyst's skill or its evidence matters more, using drug-asset valuation as the arena, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Valuing a drug asset means judging whether a target, treatment type, and disease combination deserves a go or no-go call. Wang ran a controlled three-arm ablation on a production valuation agent.

The plain agent had only web search. The second added public tools and a fourteen-dimension playbook. The third added a proprietary database of curated pipeline, trial, and deal intelligence. Tools improved how evidence was used, lifting tier accuracy from eighty to eighty-nine percent, but they could not break a factual ceiling. The first two arms recovered only a quarter and thirty-eight percent of the gold competitive record, against ninety-six percent with proprietary data. Wang therefore crowns the evidence substrate, not the reasoning scaffold, as the binding constraint.
arxiv-2606-09656:
Antonio Bjelčić, Ibrahim Abdurrahman, and Kyle Godbey simulate the neutrons flung out at the instant a nucleus splits in this 2026 arXiv paper. When a heavy nucleus fissions, its neck snaps and the two halves rush apart. Most prompt neutrons boil off the hot halves later. A few, called scission neutrons, are shed at the snap itself, and their mark is hard to isolate.

The team used time-dependent density functional theory on a much larger grid than past runs. They studied three systems: uranium and plutonium fission, plus californium splitting on its own. At the angles they tracked, scission neutrons were absent below about one and a half to two mega-electronvolts. Adding this piece to a standard boil-off model matched the measured high-energy yield. Boil-off alone fell short, which marks a real scission share in known data.
arxiv-2606-09856:
Liyi Zhang and her co-authors teach language models to reason from scant clues by training them on machine-made worlds in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most tuning targets deduction, where answers can be checked. Real judgment is often inductive: beliefs must be formed from sparse, murky signs. Labels for that are dear, and the right answers are spreads, not points.

Their method, Program-based Posterior Training, builds the data from scratch. A model writes open-world scenes as probabilistic programs. True inference on each program then yields soft, spread-out labels for its questions. Fine-tuning on ten thousand such scenes taught the skill. Scores rose sharply on held-out puzzles of the same kind. The tuned models also matched human calls more closely, and gains spread to outside tests of estimation and calibration. A plain heat tweak on outputs could not match the gain.
arxiv-2606-09956:
Rozanov presents a lightweight way to pinpoint buggy lines in code, in a 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering. AI code generation has sped up development, but checking code remains slow and costly. Agent tools can spend minutes and thousands of tokens per file, while cheaper methods locate bugs only at whole-function level. Debugging needs precise line-level answers.

His approach pairs a token alignment algorithm, fixing mismatches between text splitting and line boundaries, with a multi-task language model carrying extra decoding heads for bug classification. The model needs only a single generated token per file, cutting latency by orders of magnitude compared with agentic tools. It reached state-of-the-art results among similar setups for line-level localization with full-file context. Performance on the Defects4J and PypiBugs benchmarks rivaled agentic approaches, and a small out-of-domain Python test showed strong generalization.
arxiv-2606-10056:
Amato and Scozzari test whether theoretically optimal analysis operators are worth their cost in practice, in a 2026 arXiv paper on program analysis. Static analysis of logic programs uses abstract interpretation, which reasons about program behavior using simplified abstract domains. Optimal operators extract the maximum precision those domains allow, but implementing them is complex and may slow analysis badly.

Building on earlier proposals of optimal operators for unification and matching, the authors implemented them and their domains inside the PLAI analyzer, part of the CiaoPP preprocessor. Their experiments measure how increasing operator precision affects both the accuracy of the overall analysis and its running time and resource use. The study gives implementers empirical guidance on when optimal operators pay off. It also illuminates the structure of the abstract domains themselves, showing where extra precision changes analysis outcomes rather than merely costing more.
arxiv-2606-10156:
Narasimhan and Narasimhan build a benchmark that grades conversational recommender agents with verifiable answers instead of subjective judges, in a 2026 arXiv paper on artificial intelligence evaluation. Recommender systems are becoming multi-turn conversational agents, but benchmarks often rely on language models as judges, adding subjectivity, cost, and inconsistency. Their benchmark, tau-Rec, replaces that with verifiable rewards checked against structured catalog predicates.

A pass-to-the-k reliability metric tests whether an agent succeeds consistently across repeated attempts, not just once. Evaluating nine configurations across five model families, including GPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Qwen systems, reveals a steep reliability cliff. Even the best model achieved only about fifty-seven percent on single attempts and about thirty-five percent when four consecutive successes were required. The authors release all code and data publicly, arguing the gap shows current conversational agents are not ready for dependable deployment.
arxiv-2606-10256:
Evans and Zheng present a Bayesian approach to uncertainty intervals and test it on a classic particle physics problem, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. Probability theory defines evidence for or against an event through the principle of evidence, and proper Bayesian analysis must respect the likelihood ordering that principle imposes. Relative belief inferences satisfy that requirement and, when their errors are controlled, also meet frequentist goals such as achieving stated confidence levels. The authors construct relative belief intervals for a Poisson signal observed with background noise.

That signal-plus-background problem is famous in physics because naive intervals behave badly at low counts, prompting the Feldman-Cousins construction now standard in particle physics. The paper argues that intervals built from relative belief give a principled uncertainty quantification. They satisfy both Bayesian evidence requirements and frequentist confidence targets, bridging two traditions often presented as rivals.
arxiv-2606-10356:
Massimino and colleagues compute how the masses of light and strange baryons would shift inside dense matter, in a 2026 arXiv paper on nuclear theory. Baryons are three-quark particles such as the proton, and their masses in a medium like a neutron star or heavy-ion fireball affect what particles get produced. The team solves the Goldstone-boson-exchange relativistic constituent quark model using the Faddeev approach, a rigorous three-body method. The model reproduces the vacuum mass spectrum of light and strange baryons below two gigaelectronvolts reasonably well.

The baryon spectrum proves most sensitive to the quark-meson coupling, and masses generally decrease as constituent quark mass drops. They estimate the impact on ideal-gas baryon yields. Absolute yields can change significantly with mass shifts of only tens of megaelectronvolts. Yield ratios shift strongly only when the compared baryons depend differently on quark mass.
arxiv-2606-10456:
Zhang and Gao probe a weakness in how AI systems are monitored for misbehaviour, in this 2026 arXiv paper on AI control. Safety monitors usually score each action alone and alarm when one looks suspicious. The authors build an attack that spreads a fixed harm budget across many innocent-looking steps. The signal hides in how scores correlate over time, while the distribution of single-step scores stays identical to harmless behaviour.

Three checks organise the experiments. The attack's score distribution sits only 0.013 from the benign one at high harm levels, so it is truly stealthy.
