Van Goethem and co-authors hunt antibiotic resistance genes in pristine Antarctic soils. Soil bacteria make antibiotics and carry matching defenses. Remote soils may hold the ancestral pool of those genes. Human-touched sites dominate most surveys so far.

Shotgun sequencing of 17 remote soils found 177 resistance genes. Most built pumps that eject several drugs at once. Others broke down common antibiotic families. Few mobile elements sat near the genes. That pattern marks them as ancient, passed down in place. Richer soils held fewer resistance genes per sample. Readers get a baseline of resistance before human influence.
europmc-pmc5840256:
de Boer and co-authors report the final results of PORTEC-3, a phase 3 trial in high-risk endometrial cancer. Their paper appeared in The Lancet Oncology. The trial enrolled women at 103 centers. It asked whether adding chemotherapy to pelvic radiation helps after surgery.

660 women entered the final analysis, split evenly between the two arms. Five-year survival was about 82 percent with combined treatment and 77 percent with radiation alone. That gap was not statistically firm. Freedom from failure did improve with the combination. Severe side effects hit 60 percent of the combined group, against 12 percent on radiation alone. Nerve damage also lingered more often.
europmc-pmc5860356:
Rogers and co-authors present FATHMM-XF, a method for judging point mutations. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. The method predicts which single-letter DNA changes may cause disease. It draws on a wide set of features from genome databases. Training data came from a human mutation database and the 1000 Genomes Project. The method covers both coding and non-coding parts of the genome.

The authors report that it beats rival tools on benchmark tests. Gains were largest in non-coding regions, where most harmful changes may sit. Each prediction carries a confidence score for the user. Careful use of top scores pushed accuracy above 94 percent. A web server and genome browser tracks are provided. Predictions use the GRCh37 human genome build.
europmc-pmc5868856:
Ratzke and Gore study how pH change drives interactions between bacteria. Their article appeared in PLoS Biology. Microbes alter their surroundings as they feed and excrete waste. One common change is a shift in acidity. That shift feeds back on the microbes themselves. It can help growth, hinder it, or wipe a population out.

The team ran experiments with single species first. Knowing how each kind changed pH let them predict pair outcomes. Set patterns emerged, such as bistability and successive growth. One stark pattern saw a species drive itself to extinction. The authors argue these motifs may recur across many systems. Any shared environmental factor could play the pH role.
europmc-pmc5870856:
Hebditch and co-authors present Protein-Sol, a web tool for protein solubility. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. Solubility matters for making proteins in industry and medicine. Predicting it from sequence alone is hard. The tool was trained on E. coli protein data. Those data came from a cell-free expression system. It computes 35 properties from the amino acid sequence.

The server returns a predicted solubility score for each entry. It also flags which features stray most from average. Two more profiles run along the sequence in windows. They track fold tendency and segment charge. An example with thioredoxin shows how these views help. The tool is free online with no account needed.
europmc-pmc5877356:
Seth and co-authors report overdose deaths in the United States for 2015 to 2016. Their article appeared in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. The team used national death records to class deaths by drug. In 2016, 63,632 people died of drug overdoses. Opioids played a part in 66 percent of those deaths. Rates rose across every drug category examined that year.

Deaths involving synthetic opioids doubled in rate, they report. Cocaine deaths rose by over half at the same time. Illicitly made fentanyl likely drove much of the surge. Gains in deaths spanned ages, places, and urban levels. The authors call for faster, fuller surveillance of the epidemic. They also urge wider naloxone access and safer prescribing.
europmc-pmc5955356:
Harrington records a rare case of embolism of the spinal cord. His case report appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Embolism of splenic, renal, or cerebral arteries is familiar in infective endocarditis. Embolism of the spinal cord vessels seems very rare, he notes. The patient was Agnes B., a telegraphist aged 42. She entered Glasgow Royal Infirmary in August 1922.

She had lost power and sensation below the waist over five days. The illness began with sudden dragging pain in the lumbar region. Her left knee gave way, then she collapsed at home. On admission, reflexes in her legs were absent. Harrington sets out her history and signs in full.
europmc-pmc5964356:
Abisado and co-authors review bacterial quorum sensing and microbial community interactions. Their minireview appeared in mBio. Many bacteria use quorum sensing to coordinate behaviour by population density. They release signals and respond to them as numbers grow. In many species this system controls virulence. Half a century of work has mapped its molecules and gene sets.

Recent work treats quorum sensing as social behaviour. It coordinates cooperation and competition within and between species. Synthetic ecology models with mixed populations drove these insights. The review discusses several such models and their findings. The lessons may guide studies of natural communities. They may also shape new medicines against infection.
europmc-pmc5990556:
Hedge, Powell, and Sumner explain the reliability paradox for classic cognitive tasks. Their paper appeared in Behavior Research Methods. Tasks such as Stroop and Flanker give robust group effects. Yet they often fail as tools for individual differences. The authors blame the very trait that makes them popular. Low spread between people yields strong group results. That same low spread crushes test-retest reliability for ranking people.

They measured reliability across seven classic tasks in three studies. Values ran from 0 to .82, mostly surprisingly low. Weak correlations with brain measures may follow from this flaw. Taking reliability into account can flip study conclusions, they warn.
europmc-pmc6017056:
Karrouchi and co-authors review how pyrazole drugs are made and what they do in the body. Their review was published in Molecules. The pyrazole ring is a prized base in drug design. Drugs built on it span many fields of care. One fights swelling and pain, and one curbs hunger. More act on mood, thought, and pain in the nerves. Such range drew chemists to study the ring with care.

The review sums up ways to build the ring from groups round the globe. Acts of the drugs in body tests are set out too. Uses reach past drugs into farms and tech. Germ killing, cancer, and virus effects all show up. The ring stays a rich base for new drugs.
europmc-pmc6057056:
Wang and co-authors review unmet care needs in advanced cancer. Their systematic review appeared in BMC Palliative Care. It covers patients and the family members who care for them. Ten databases were searched through December 2016. Fifty studies passed the quality checks.

Twelve need domains emerged for patients. Psychological, physical, and information needs led the list. Emotional support and fatigue were the top single items. Caregivers most lacked illness and care information. Patient needs tied to symptoms, anxiety, and quality of life. The review also catalogs the survey tools in use. Readers get a full map of gaps in late-stage cancer care.
europmc-pmc6180056:
HogenEsch and co-authors wrote a review in NPJ Vaccines on getting the best from aluminum vaccine additives. These additives, called adjuvants, have boosted vaccine response for over 90 years. New work has clarified how they act in the body. The authors call them the gold standard for the field.

They argue that new vaccine candidates should be tested with these proven additives first. Known materials ease both trials in people and the path to approval. Yet the additives are complex in how they hold antigens and how processing changes them. Small shifts can change the results in ways makers may not expect. The title holds the warning: you might just get what you want.
europmc-pmc6180456:
Moody and co-authors offer a systematic review in BMC Public Health on how common self-reported child maltreatment is worldwide. Measuring maltreatment is hard, with no clear gold standard for what counts. Self-report studies offer one window. The team gathered them to compare rates by type and by gender.

They searched major databases and grey literature from 2000 to 2017. Sexual abuse was the most studied form across the world. Reported lifetime prevalence varied widely between studies and continents. Rates also differed for boys and girls. Method choices, such as who was asked and at what age, explained much of the spread. The review is a caution and a guide for comparing such numbers.
europmc-pmc6198856:
Stepniewska-Dziubinska and co-authors present a methods article in Bioinformatics on a deep learning model that predicts drug binding strength. Structure-based discovery tests how tightly small molecules bind target proteins. Machine learning is reshaping that work. Judging binding affinity well can save much lab time.

Their neural network represents each protein-ligand complex as a three-dimensional grid. A 3D convolution then extracts features, treating protein and ligand atoms in the same way. The model was tested on the CASF-2013 scoring benchmark and the Astex Diverse Set. It outperformed classical scoring functions on those tests. The study shows deep networks can learn binding features directly from structure rather than from hand-built rules.
europmc-pmc6223056:
Pound and Ritskes-Hoitinga examine why animal models often fail patients. Few human diseases have approved treatments. Many drugs that work in animals fail in people. Past debate blamed poor study design and bias. The article appeared in the Journal of Translational Medicine.

The authors focus on external validity instead. That means how well findings transfer across settings and species. Animal samples often fail to represent patients. Models cannot mimic full human disease complexity. Lab settings differ greatly from clinics. Species differences add a further gap. The authors argue translation needs both kinds of validity. They suggest some fixes, but warn limits are deep. Most animal models, they argue, are bound to fail.
europmc-pmc6268056:
Seo and co-authors review antimicrobial peptides as future medicines. Their review appeared in Molecules. Such peptides occur in many living things as part of innate defence. They kill a broad range of bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Their attack style differs from standard antibiotics. That makes them of interest against drug resistant germs.

Barriers still block clinic and market use. Some peptides can harm human cells. Gut and blood enzymes can chew them up fast. Making them costs a lot per dose. The review focuses on very short peptides, under twelve building blocks. Shorter forms cost less and may dodge some flaws. Links between their shapes and killing power are mapped in detail. Design tricks, such as swapped building blocks, are also covered. The goal is strong action kept in a small, stable form.
europmc-pmc6291456:
The GBD 2016 Traumatic Brain Injury and Spinal Cord Injury Collaborators measure the global burden of these two injuries. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet Neurology. It tracks new cases, people living with injury, and years lived with disability. Data came from hospital records, surveys, and past studies. Coverage spans all countries from 1990 to 2016.

The team reports 27.08 million new brain injury cases in 2016. New spinal cord cases numbered 0.93 million that year. Falls and road crashes caused most new cases in most regions. Brain injury prevalence rose over the study years. Spinal cord prevalence stayed broadly flat. The authors warn that ageing and more traffic may push numbers up. They note that care for these injuries is complex and costly.
europmc-pmc6324056:
The wwPDB consortium outlines the Protein Data Bank as a single global archive. Their report appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The archive holds three-dimensional structures of large biological molecules. These come from experiments, not predictions. A worldwide partnership has run it since 2003. The partners handle deposits, checks, curation, and open access.

The core archive held over 144,000 structural models at the time. They cover proteins, DNA, RNA, and their complexes. Metals and small molecules bound to them are included. Data use a shared format that can grow with new methods. A joint deposit and validation system, OneDep, raised data quality. Specialist task forces check structures method by method. The paper closes with current challenges and future plans.
europmc-pmc6326956:
Haubner and co-authors map pairs of surface markers on leukemia stem cells. Their study appeared in Leukemia. Acute myeloid leukemia, or AML, is hard to target cleanly. Its cells share markers with healthy blood cells. Minor clones can also survive and cause relapse. The team sought marker pairs found on leukemia but not normal tissue.

They profiled six markers in 356 patient samples. Normal bone marrow samples served as comparison. All six markers appeared widely on AML cells. Each also showed up somewhere in healthy blood making. Pairing markers changed the picture a lot. Two pairs, CD33 with TIM3 and CLL1 with TIM3, stood out. They were far stronger in AML than in healthy tissue. Such pairs could guide safer combination therapies.
europmc-pmc6372756:
The GBD 2016 Multiple Sclerosis Collaborators present a systematic analysis in The Lancet Neurology. The study estimates the global burden of multiple sclerosis from 1990 to 2016. It models prevalence, deaths, and disability for every region, and relates burden to a country's development level.

In 2016 the team counted about 2.22 million people living with multiple sclerosis worldwide. Age-standardised prevalence had risen 10.4 percent since 1990. Rates were highest in high-income North America and western Europe, and lowest in sub-Saharan Africa and Oceania. The disease caused 18,932 deaths and about 1.15 million disability-adjusted life-years. The authors note large data gaps in many regions.
europmc-pmc6414456:
Mollica Poeta and co-authors review chemokines as immunotherapy targets in Frontiers in Immunology. Chemokines guide immune cells around the body. Cancers twist this system to recruit help and block attack.

Altered chemokine signals decide which immune cells enter a tumor. They also feed blood vessel growth, cell growth, and spread. Early trials try to block the harmful signals or add helpful ones. The review covers those first attempts and their limits. It argues the chemokine system deserves a place beside checkpoints in cancer immune care. Trials in patients are still few.
europmc-pmc6414756:
Bertolino and co-authors review leaf pores and water use in Frontiers in Plant Science. Almost all water a plant takes up escapes through stomata, the tiny pores on leaves. Climate change will cut water for major crops like wheat, rice, and maize.

Plants tune pore opening minute by minute to balance carbon gain and water loss. Over longer spans they also change pore size and number. The review asks how those traits could be bred or engineered. Crops that yield well on less water are the goal. Stomatal traits are a direct lever on that goal.
europmc-pmc6435756:
Traag and co-authors expose a flaw in the Louvain algorithm, a favorite tool for finding communities in large networks, and offer the Leiden algorithm as its replacement. Testing showed Louvain can return communities that are badly connected internally, or even split into disconnected pieces. Up to 25 percent of its communities were badly connected and up to 16 percent disconnected.

Leiden guarantees connected communities and, when iterated, settles into a partition where every subset of every community is locally well assigned. A fast local-move design also makes it run quicker than Louvain. On benchmark and real networks it found better partitions, so network analysts gain both speed and a proof-backed result.
europmc-pmc6447556:
Kraus and co-authors review what predicts outcome in major depression and which plans might finally improve it. No tool in routine care yet sorts patients by likely course or predicts who will respond. How long depression goes untreated tracks with worse results, so spotting it early leads the advice. Early gains themselves predict response and full recovery, while other illnesses stretch the episode out.

Candidate biomarkers span memory-center volume, cingulate activity, BDNF, and inflammatory markers such as interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein, none ready for daily care. Gene tests for drug-processing enzymes may help set doses. A stepwise plan orders first- to third-line treatments, with shock therapy, newer stimulation methods, and ketamine held for cases that resist the rest.
europmc-pmc6460256:
Chen and co-authors survey single-cell RNA sequencing and the computing methods its noisy data demand. Protocols differ in how cells are pulled apart and their transcripts caught, each trading speed against depth. Since single-cell data are sparser and jumpier than bulk data, standard pipelines mislead.

The review walks the analysis steps in order: quality control, mapping, counting, batch fixes, scaling, gap filling, dimension shrinking, grouping, and tracing cell paths. Gene activity contrasts, splice variants, gene copy use from each parent, and gene network rebuilding each get their own treatment. It closes with where the field heads, from embryo maps to tumor variety studies.
europmc-pmc6510456:
Haldane and co-authors review evidence on community participation in health services. Their systematic review appeared in PLoS ONE. It covers high and upper-middle income countries. The question is whether involving local people improves services and health.

The team searched five databases for studies from 2000 to 2016. Screening began with 27,232 records. After duplicates and screening, 49 studies met the entry rules. Outcomes fell into process, community, health and empowerment groups. The authors report broad evidence of positive impact on health. Gains were strongest where organisational and community processes were strong. They stress that progress is not linear. Social and cultural factors shape each result.
europmc-pmc6611156:
Papadopoli and co-authors review mTOR, a growth switch tied to aging. Their article appears in F1000Research. mTOR senses nutrients and steers cell growth and division. Blocking it with rapamycin extends life in yeast, worms, flies, and mice. How it shapes aging, though, is still not fully clear.

The kinase works inside two complexes, mTORC1 and mTORC2. They differ in parts, duties, and drug response. The review links mTOR to protein balance and cleanup by autophagy. It also covers mitochondria, cell senescence, and stem cell decline. Nutrient sensing ties these threads together. The authors stress mammals while sketching wider evidence. The survey points to aging diseases from diabetes to neurodegeneration.
europmc-pmc6616856:
Kraemer and co-authors review antibiotic pollution in the environment. Their review appears in Microorganisms. Heavy antibiotic use in medicine and farming has a cost. The drugs leak into sewage, soil, and waterways. Resistance genes evolve in these hotspots. They then travel widely through many vectors. The first half of the review traces that spread. It maps where resistance builds and how it moves.

The second half covers harm beyond resistance itself. Antibiotics reshape natural microbial communities directly. They also affect invertebrates and vertebrates in the wild. The closing section surveys regional policies on the problem. It flags where rules remain underdeveloped. The authors call for coordinated mitigation worldwide.
europmc-pmc6656856:
Cui and co-authors review circulating microRNAs as cancer biomarkers and therapy tools. Their review appears in Frontiers in Genetics. MicroRNAs are tiny non-coding RNAs that tune genes. Cells release some into the blood. There they survive in remarkably stable forms. Carriers include exosomes, lipoproteins, and protein complexes. Levels shift as cancers start and progress. Basic lab techniques can detect those shifts. That makes the molecules attractive noninvasive biomarkers.

The review covers their biology and transport routes. It explains how cells exchange them in signalling. Roles in targeted therapy get their own treatment. The authors then list hurdles to clinical use. Standardisation and validation remain unfinished work. Promise is high, but practice lags behind.
europmc-pmc6688256:
Orth and co-authors review pancreatic cancer and joint treatment approaches. Their review appears in Radiation Oncology. The disease is devastating and rising in incidence. Five-year survival sits below eight percent. It is usually found late. Only 10 to 20 percent can have surgery. Surgery plus follow-up drug treatment is the sole curative path. FOLFIRINOX nearly doubles life span in spread disease. Gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel also improves outcomes. Side effects limit both drug plans in frailer patients.

Radiochemotherapy plays a growing supporting role. It can convert borderline tumours toward removal. Pinpoint radiation widens the local options. The review integrates biology and immune hallmarks. Combined protocols are the future path offered.
europmc-pmc6704256:
Spangenberg and co-authors wipe out microglia with a CSF1R blocker in an Alzheimer's mouse model. Their study appears in Nature Communications. These brain immune cells depend on CSF1R signalling to live. The team designed a brain-penetrant selective blocker. PLX5622 wipes the cells out fully and for weeks. Treatment spanned the plaque-forming period in 5xFAD mice. Without microglia, plaques in the tissue failed to form. Spots where some cells survived were the exception. Amyloid instead deposited in cortical blood vessels. That pattern resembled cerebral amyloid angiopathy.

Hippocampal gene expression changes were reversed. Leftover plaque-forming cells showed disease-linked profiles. Microglia therefore start plaque formation. Their lysosomes accumulate clumped amyloid early. The blocker is offered as a research tool.
europmc-pmc6723656:
Dimidi and co-authors review fermented foods and gut health. Fermented foods are made through controlled microbe growth that changes the food's components. Their popularity has surged on claims of health benefits. The review defines and describes eight common ones, from kefir and kombucha to kimchi and sourdough bread.

Live microbes in these foods may act as probiotics. Fermentation also creates active peptides and strips out anti-nutrients. Human trials exist for kefir, sauerkraut, natto, and sourdough, with kefir the most studied. No trials yet test kombucha, miso, kimchi, or tempeh for gut effects. The evidence, the authors show, is thinner than the hype.
europmc-pmc6737756:
Greenhalgh and co-authors reviewed frameworks for involving patients and the public in research. Many such frameworks exist, but the literature is scattered and built on mixed theories. The team searched six databases, eight journals, and expert contacts. They graded the frameworks with a Canadian evaluation tool and tested findings in five co-design workshops.

The final set held 65 frameworks, most scoring highly. They differed in origin, purpose, strengths, and limits. The authors grouped them into five families. Few frameworks had clear records of real use. The review aims to help researchers pick and apply the right framework. It also offers design principles to make future frameworks easier to use.
europmc-pmc6769656:
Krüger-Genge and co-authors update the biology of vascular endothelial cells. The endothelium is the single-cell lining of arteries, veins, and capillaries. It touches the blood directly. Far from a passive wall, it acts like an endocrine organ. It sets vessel tightness and controls what leaks from blood into tissue.

These cells steer blood flow region by region. They guide inflammatory cells to injury or infection. They balance clotting and clot breakdown, platelet behavior, and immune responses. Endothelial cells differ along the vessel tree and between organs, each tuned to local jobs. Flow patterns matter too: straight, fast flow protects artery walls, while swirling flow invites disease.
europmc-pmc6790056:
Baran and co-authors present MetaCell, a method for analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing data. Each cell profile is a partial sample of that cell's RNA, and the cell can never be sampled again. Analysis must separate sampling noise from real biology. MetaCell partitions profiles into metacells: small, uniform groups that could plausibly come from the same cell.

Unlike clustering, the algorithm seeks fine-grained groups rather than the largest possible ones. Metacells then serve as building blocks for detailed maps of gene activity, without smoothing the data away. Screening also exposes outlier cells and overactive gene modules, such as stress-response genes. The method ships as an R and C++ software package for other researchers.
europmc-pmc6822756:
Chen and Song set out a method for mapping a research field, in PLOS ONE. Reviews that chart a whole field depend on first gathering the right set of papers. Miss key works and the map misleads. Search terms alone often leave gaps. The authors propose building the set by following citations instead.

Their method expands outward from seed papers through generations of citing works. Tests grew one seed set to 748 papers in three steps and about 60 times larger in five. The authors show how to judge whether a set fits the field in both focus and coverage. The aim is reviews that others can repeat and check.
europmc-pmc6857056:
Walker and co-authors review vesicle-based drug delivery in Theranostics. Cells naturally shed tiny bubbles called extracellular vesicles. These carry proteins, RNAs, and fats between cells as messages. Their surfaces bear molecules that steer them toward certain tissues. Drug makers hope to borrow that courier system to treat cancer.

The review covers how vesicles are collected and loaded with drugs. It also covers changes made to help them circulate longer and hit tumours more precisely. In mouse studies, drug-loaded vesicles shrank tumours more than the same drugs given free. Some even worked better on drug-resistant cells. The authors weigh remaining hurdles in dosing, manufacture, and safety.
europmc-pmc6902756:
Li and co-authors report a cohort study in JAMA Network Open on mood and the heart. Depression has been tied to cardiovascular disease in many settings. Whether single symptoms carry the risk, in Chinese adults specifically, was less clear. The team enrolled 12,417 middle-aged and older Chinese adults free of heart disease at the start.

Participants with depressive symptoms at baseline went on to develop cardiovascular disease at higher rates than those without. The link held after adjusting for other risk factors. Two symptoms stood out on their own: restless sleep and loneliness. Each predicted new disease independently. The authors suggest symptom-level screening might sharpen prevention in this population.
europmc-pmc6942256:
Alam and co-authors map how gut bacteria fall out of balance in inflammatory bowel disease. Their study appeared in Gut Pathogens. The disease group includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which inflame the gut and affect millions worldwide. Patient gut communities differ from healthy ones, but the pattern across bacterial ranks was unclear.

Stool samples showed lower microbial diversity in patients than in healthy people. Four major phyla, which make up over 98 percent of gut bacteria, shifted in abundance. The team then built a co-abundance network from public data covering more than 22,000 samples. Bacterial families that grew in disease sat poorly connected to the rest. Families that shrank were hub members, well linked to many others.
europmc-pmc6959356:
Schafflick and co-authors compare immune cells in blood and spinal fluid in multiple sclerosis. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Spinal fluid bathes and protects the brain and spinal cord, and sampling it helps diagnose disease. Its immune cells, though, remain poorly mapped.

Single-cell sequencing showed spinal fluid cells follow a distinct, location-tied pattern. In multiple sclerosis, blood cells grew more varied in gene activity. In spinal fluid, the cell mix itself diversified, with more killer-style helper T cells. A new analysis method flagged extra follicular helper T cells, which may drive the known rise of B-lineage cells there. In mice, those helper cells did push B cells into the central nervous system and worsened disease. Immunity in this disease, the authors argue, runs in separate compartments.
europmc-pmc6981156:
Ghorbani and co-authors teach deep learning to read heart ultrasound scans. Their study appeared in NPJ Digital Medicine. Echocardiography is the most common heart imaging method, capturing fine detail in space and time. Human reading is slow, and some patterns escape the eye.

Their model, EchoNet, learned from a large new set of scans. It spotted pacemaker leads and an enlarged left atrium with strong accuracy. It measured heart chamber volumes and pumping strength, the ejection fraction. It also guessed body traits that humans cannot read from a scan: age, sex, weight, and height, each with moderate accuracy. Checks confirmed the model attends to the right structures for explainable tasks. The authors see help for busy clinics and for places short of cardiologists.
europmc-pmc6982256:
Pajak and co-authors review a fake sugar that starves cancer cells, and its improved cousins. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The compound, 2-deoxy-d-glucose or 2-DG, mimics glucose, the cell's main fuel. Cancer cells lean hard on sugar burning, even when oxygen is present.

Inside the cell, 2-DG gets trapped and jams two key enzymes of glycolysis. Energy production stalls and cells die. Other cell processes shift as well. The review covers attempts to make 2-DG more drug-like, and its use alongside standard chemotherapy. New analogs designed to hit harder are surveyed as candidate anticancer agents. The strategy, the authors argue, exploits a true weak point of malignant cells while sparing normal ones.
europmc-pmc6985156:
Sun and co-authors review hydrogen sulfide, a gas signal that guards blood vessel linings. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Endothelial cells line blood vessels and keep the circulation balanced. When they falter, diseases follow: artery hardening, high blood pressure, obesity-linked damage, and diabetes among them.

Failing linings show skewed vessel widening and narrowing, excess reactive oxygen, inflammatory factors, and too little nitric oxide. Hydrogen sulfide, made in vessel walls and heart muscle, acts on many pathways to counter that decline. Faulty sulfide supply may itself flag endothelial inflammation. The authors summarise recent work on the gas in vessel health and disease. They also judge its promise as a therapy for inflammation-linked cardiovascular disorders.
europmc-pmc7015856:
Darrah and a large team of co-authors report a vaccine study in Nature. They test the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis in rhesus macaques. BCG is normally given into the skin, and its protection against lung tuberculosis varies. The team asked whether the delivery route changes the result.

Macaques received BCG by skin, by aerosol, or into a vein. Six months later they were exposed to virulent tuberculosis bacteria. Nine of the ten vein-vaccinated animals were highly protected, the authors report. Six showed no detectable infection at all. The vein route also raised far stronger T cell responses in blood and lung tissue. The authors say this route deserves study for future vaccine design.
europmc-pmc7027356:
Dalgleish and co-authors open a special section on transdiagnostic approaches in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. Standard diagnosis sorts mental illness into set boxes. More and more experts think those boxes no longer serve research or care well. Transdiagnostic work cuts across the lines between boxes, or sets them aside.

Dropping those lines opens new ways to group problems and to think about the processes behind them. It also changes how experts view the start of a problem, what keeps it going, and how treatment and recovery work. The authors first trace the history of the diagnosis-led approach and the troubles it now faces. They then survey newer transdiagnostic schemes and set the scene for the studies gathered in the special section.
europmc-pmc7039956:
Xu and co-authors report a data study in the International Journal of Oral Science. ACE2 is the main doorway the new coronavirus, 2019-nCoV, uses to enter cells. The team asked whether that doorway is present in the mouth. A positive answer would mark the mouth as a likely infection route.

The team mined RNA data from two public databases, TCGA and FANTOM5 CAGE. They also used single-cell data made in their own lab. ACE2 was present in the lining of the mouth, they found. It was richest in the surface cells of the tongue. Levels were lower in cheek and gum tissue. The authors say the findings matter for dental practice and daily prevention.
europmc-pmc7053956:
Parker, Fonseca, and Carding review gut microbes and the blood-brain barrier in the journal Gut Microbes. The gut holds diverse communities of bacteria, archaea, viruses, fungi, and protozoa living in balance with their host. When that balance breaks, organs far from the gut suffer, the brain included. Gut microbes have been proposed as contributors to blood-brain barrier breakdown and to neurodegenerative disease.

The blood-brain barrier is the seal that protects the brain from blood-borne threats. The reviewers summarise evidence that microbes and their chemical products can loosen or tighten that seal, and how the resulting signals affect brain function. They map the communication networks of the gut-brain axis that microbes may tune. The closing discussion weighs strategies that adjust the microbiota as tools for protecting and restoring brain health, an idea moving from speculation toward early trials.
europmc-pmc7074356:
Agriopoulou and co-authors review mycotoxin control in foods in the journal Foods. Mycotoxins are poisons made by moulds that contaminate many foods. They can cause cancer and damage genes, development, kidneys, and the liver, and they sicken people and livestock worldwide. The classes of greatest farm and trade importance include aflatoxins, ochratoxins, fumonisins, trichothecenes, and ergot alkaloids.

Fighting contamination works at two stages. Before harvest, prevention keeps moulds from producing toxins in the field. After harvest, detoxification and decontamination methods inactivate or remove toxins already present. The review gathers recent advances on where the main mycotoxins turn up in important farm products, and on the methods used against them, from biological controls to chemical and physical treatments. Some natural additives also help: capsaicin from peppers cut ochratoxin production by moulds on grapes substantially in studies reviewed. The goal is food reaching the table with toxins reduced or eliminated.
europmc-pmc7096556:
Shi and co-authors review how to choose the right wound dressing for different wounds, in Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology. Wound healing is a changing process, and modern dressings are proven to help. Yet reports on matching a dressing to a specific wound type are few, leaving clinicians with little guidance.

The authors trace the history of dressings and classify the modern types. They weigh the strengths and weaknesses of mainstream dressings for diabetic foot ulcers, pressure ulcers, burns and scalds, and chronic leg ulcers. The healing mechanisms behind each wound type are explained as well. The result reads as a practical guide for selecting dressings by wound, rather than by habit.
europmc-pmc7152756:
Gordon and co-authors show exactly how the antiviral remdesivir blocks the copying enzyme of the MERS coronavirus, in the Journal of Biological Chemistry. No antiviral was approved for human coronaviruses when they wrote. Remdesivir mimics a building block of RNA and jams the viral polymerase that assembles new genomes.

Working with the MERS enzyme complex grown in insect cells, they found the drug's active form competes with the natural building block ATP and is taken up even more efficiently. Once built into the growing RNA chain, it halts copying three letters later, a delay that may hide it from the virus's proofreading enzyme. The mechanism helps explain the drug's strong effects in cell tests.
europmc-pmc7299956:
Yan and co-authors build a cell atlas of the human retina, comparing its center with its edges. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Most irreversible blindness comes from retinal disease, yet the retina's cell types were incompletely catalogued. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, they profiled about 85,000 cells from the fovea and peripheral retina of seven adult donors.

They identified 58 cell types in 6 broad classes, from photoreceptors to ganglion cells. Nearly all types appear in both regions, but their proportions and gene activity differ. The atlas let them map where 636 genes linked to blinding diseases are switched on, often in strikingly specific cell types. Over 90% of human types matched macaque monkey types, supporting that animal as a model for eye disease.
europmc-pmc7371956:
Rodrigues and Plotkin survey the full value of vaccines in Frontiers in Microbiology, across health, money, and society. Systematic vaccination drives in the twentieth century began closing global gaps in protection against deadly infections. Access remains unequal, which the authors, a clinician and a leading vaccine scientist, treat as the core problem.

Beyond preventing illness and death, vaccines save treatment costs, keep parents at work, and support schooling and social stability. Benefits reach all regions and age groups, the evidence they gather shows. The piece was written as COVID-19 vaccine work raced ahead at record speed. The authors urge that the wider benefits be measured and communicated to the public and policymakers.
europmc-pmc7399356:
Zhang and co-authors report in Cell Research that SARS-CoV-2 can infect human brain cells grown in the lab. Neurological symptoms, from lost smell to seizures and confusion, were common in patients, and viral RNA had been found in some brain biopsies. Direct experimental proof in human neural tissue was missing.

The team grew neural progenitor cells, neurospheres, and brain organoids from human stem cells. The progenitor cells carried the virus's entry machinery, and SARS-CoV-2, unlike its older cousin SARS-CoV, replicated in them. Infection was harsh, cutting cell viability to a few percent of normal within days. Organoids were also infected. The brain, the results suggest, is a real target of the virus, not only a bystander of lung disease.
europmc-pmc7427556:
Sekine and co-authors map T cell responses to SARS-CoV-2 in people who had COVID-19. They studied unexposed people, exposed family members, and patients in acute or healing phases. Memory T cells are likely key to long-term protection.

During acute illness, virus-specific T cells looked highly active and toxic to infected cells. Their traits tracked with markers of disease severity. In healing patients, the cells were more varied in role and showed a stem-like memory form. T cells also appeared in exposed family members with no antibodies and in people whose illness was mild or silent. The results suggest that infection can leave broad, lasting T cell protection and may guard against severe repeat illness.
europmc-pmc7435056:
Lin, Zhang, and Luo study how microsatellite status shapes the tumor setting in colorectal cancer. Tumors with high microsatellite instability respond far better to immune checkpoint drugs. The team compared these tumors with stable ones across immune traits.

They used immune treatment cohort data plus mutation and gene data from The Cancer Genome Atlas. High-instability tumors had more immune cell entry, more immune gene activity, and stronger immunogenicity. Patients with such tumors gained more from checkpoint drugs. A score that predicts instability status tracked with the same immune traits. Colon and rectal cancers may differ in their immune settings, though. The results help explain why instability status guides immune therapy choices.
europmc-pmc7460856:
Chen and Liu review indices used to judge the nutritional value of fatty acids. Fats in food are mixes of saturated and unsaturated fatty acids. Their health worth must be summed up in clear scores.

Classic scores, such as total saturated fat or the n-6 to n-3 ratio, get a pass here. The authors cover newer ones, such as the index of atherogenicity and the index of thrombogenicity. They also define the health-promoting index, the unsaturation index, and the flesh lipid quality score. Two indices, atherogenicity and thrombogenicity, see the most use. Each index has strengths and flaws, so choice must fit the food and question. The mini-review aids sound picks in food science work.
europmc-pmc7470456:
Moreland and co-authors study how stay-at-home orders changed movement in the United States. CDC and the Georgia Tech Research Institute used anonymized mobile device data. The study window ran from March 1 to May 31, 2020.

Orders came from all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and five territories in the data set used for this work. During the period, 42 states and territories issued mandatory stay-at-home orders. Counties under mandatory orders saw movement drop sharply from pre-order levels. The drop held across rural and urban county groups alike. The authors say such orders can cut acts tied to viral spread. Less movement means fewer close contacts outside the home. The report helps judge one core tool of community mitigation.
europmc-pmc7488756:
Blake and co-authors recalculate the cost of coccidiosis, a parasite disease of chickens. The last full estimate dated to 1999 work by Williams. Since then the world chicken flock has doubled and farming has changed.

Using industry data, the team updated the old cost model. They estimate the disease cost the UK £99.2 million in 2016 by their updated model of farm losses and control costs. Models for seven other countries fed a global figure. The worldwide cost came near £10.4 billion at 2016 prices when regional estimates are scaled up across producing regions. That equals a small charge on each bird produced. Firm cost baselines help judge vaccines, drugs, and farm systems, the authors say.
europmc-pmc7527156:
León-Castillo and co-authors classify tumors from the PORTEC-3 trial. The trial tested added chemotherapy for high-risk endometrial cancer. It compared chemoradiotherapy with radiotherapy alone.

The team tested tissue from 423 consenting patients. Molecular results succeeded for 410 tumors. Four groups emerged: p53 abnormal, POLE mutated, mismatch repair deficient, and no specific profile. Five-year recurrence-free survival was 48% for the p53 abnormal group. It was 98% for the POLE mutated group. Added chemotherapy helped the p53 abnormal group most. The authors argue that molecular class should guide risk grouping and future trials.
europmc-pmc7585656:
Papachristoforou, Lambadiari, Maratou and Makrilakis review glycemic indices, oxidative stress and diabetic complications. High blood sugar can drive free radical formation. It can also weaken antioxidant defenses in the body.

Several pathways link high glucose to vessel damage. They include glycation products and protein kinase C activation. Hexosamine and sorbitol pathways also play a role. These steps can drive insulin resistance and poor secretion. Vessel lining function can fail as a result. Glucose swings also link to oxidative stress. Low blood sugar episodes may add vascular harm too. Inflammation and clotting effects are part of that picture. The review ties all three glucose patterns to complications.
europmc-pmc7681156:
Morales and co-authors call for action on mental health gaps in rural America. Rural and city rates of mental illness are much the same. Yet rural patients get care less often, and from staff with less specialist training. About 6.5 million rural residents live with mental illness.

The authors urge use of a national research framework on minority health and disparities. It sorts influences by level, from the body to society, and across the life span. This lens can shape better study designs and fresh care models. The goal is to close a stubborn gap that standard care has not fixed.
europmc-pmc7753756:
Nardo and co-authors review how COVID-19 injures the liver. Lung injury is the main killer in this disease. Liver failure is rare without prior liver disease. Still, liver involvement tracks with worse illness and may flag risk of grave lung failure. The authors sort the paths by which the liver gets hurt.

The virus may infect liver cells direct. Body-wide inflammation and low oxygen can harm it from afar. Drugs and ventilators add strain of their own. Old liver disease can flare under the load. The review weighs proof for each route and notes what long-term liver harm might follow for survivors.
europmc-pmc7762756:
Xu and co-authors identify a circular RNA that helps liver cancer resist a key drug. The drug is sorafenib, the first-line therapy for advanced liver cancer. Resistance often grows within months and caps its value. The RNA, called circRNA-SORE, runs high in resistant cancer cells.

Removing this RNA made sorafenib kill cells far better. The RNA binds a master cancer protein, YBX1, and shields it from destruction. Cancer cells also ship the RNA in exosomes, which spreads resistance to neighbor cells. In mouse models, silencing the RNA with injected siRNA beat resistance. The authors propose this axis as a drug target.
europmc-pmc7852556:
Keller and co-authors review blood tests for tumor DNA in cancer care. Tumor DNA floats free in the blood of patients. Most studies so far hunt for mutations in it. Such tests can spot drug resistance without a tissue biopsy.

Test sensitivity now reaches very low levels. Panels can check many genes at once. The authors push past mutation hunting, though. Blood DNA also carries methylation patterns. Piece sizes, gene activity traces, and viral loads can be read too. Each opens new uses for liquid biopsy samples. Challenges in proof and routine use are weighed. The review maps where the field can go next.
europmc-pmc7907956:
Levine and co-authors report a cohort study of sex differences in cognitive decline among adults in the United States. Whether women and men lose thinking skills at the same pace has been unclear. The team pooled data from several long-running cohorts. They compared test scores and rates of change between the sexes.

Women started with higher scores than men. That held for global cognition, executive function, and memory. Over time, though, women declined faster in global cognition and executive function. Memory decline did not differ by sex. The authors suggest women may hold a larger reserve of thinking skill. But once decline starts, it may run faster in women. The pattern matters for how doctors judge early warning signs. It may also shape how trials count outcomes for each sex.
europmc-pmc8038056:
Meherali and co-authors review how pandemics affect the mental health of children and adolescents. Their rapid systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines. The search retrieved 5,828 articles, of which 18 met the inclusion rules. The studies spanned COVID-19 and earlier pandemics. The team sorted findings by theme.

The included studies report stress, worry, and helplessness among young people. Social and risky behavior problems rose too, from substance abuse to school absence. Depression and anxiety rates run high during and after pandemics. The authors then judge the interventions on offer. Art-based programs helped ease symptoms. Support services and clinician-led mental health services also worked. School closures and isolation, they note, hit young people even when infection spared them. Tailored, age-appropriate services are the pressing need.
europmc-pmc8139856:
Tarashansky and co-authors build SAMap, a method for matching cell types across distant animal species. Single-cell atlases now exist for creatures across the animal tree. Comparing them could reveal where cell types came from. Gene histories tangle that comparison badly over long distances. Their earlier manifold method, SAM, offered a starting geometry. SAMap extends it to align atlases between species.

The method finds shared expression programs in homologous cell types. It works even where matching tissues arise from different germ layers. A surprise ran through the gene-level results. Many genes resembled their own paralogs more than their orthologs. Stand-in genes may swap roles in evolution more often than thought. Reaching across phyla, from sponge to mouse, exposed deep families. Ancient contractile and stem cell families surfaced in the maps. Both may date to the dawn of animal life. Cell evolution gains a working compass here.
europmc-pmc8419056:
Hsu and co-authors review pyroptosis, an inflammation-linked form of programmed cell death, and its place in cancer care. Many past chemotherapies aimed at apoptosis, but tumors often evade that path. Newer death forms such as pyroptosis may open fresh attack routes.

The review explains how pyroptosis drives cancer growth or slows it. It also links this death form to immunity inside tumors. Pyroptosis bridges innate and adaptive immune defense. The authors report that it can boost checkpoint inhibitor drugs and CAR T-cell therapy. They discuss the switch between apoptosis and pyroptosis as well. The piece frames pyroptosis as a partner for immune therapy.
europmc-pmc8430856:
Neophytou and co-authors explain how broken cell-death control helps cancers resist many drugs at once. Multi-drug resistance means a tumor shrugs off agents that work in unlike ways. Faulty apoptosis, or programmed cell death, is a chief driver of that state.

The review maps the major apoptotic pathways first. It shows how cancer cells tune pro-death and pro-life proteins to gain an edge. Signals for survival and death cross-talk inside the cell. The tumor surroundings also help block death signals. Chemical marks on DNA form one more lever. The authors end with current and future ways to beat this resistance.
europmc-pmc8442456:
Wick and co-authors present Trycycler, a tool that builds consensus genome assemblies for bacteria. Long-read sequencing can assemble whole bacterial genomes. But single assemblies carry a range of errors. Trycycler merges several input assemblies of the same genome into one.

In benchmark tests, Trycycler output held fewer errors than any single-tool assembly. A polishing step cut errors further still. Those polished consensus genomes were the most accurate in the study. The tool needs some hands-on steps, so results are not fixed in advance. Yet many users land on near-identical assemblies. All of them beat automated single tools. The work targets users of Nanopore and PacBio reads.
europmc-pmc8450356:
Malekmohammad and co-authors review how lipid build-up and inflammation drive atherosclerosis. This chronic disease grows in artery walls where fat handling goes wrong. Inflammatory signaling fails to settle, and plaque forms over years.

Low-density lipoprotein is the main source of cholesterol in the wall. Changed forms of it spark vessel damage, draw in white blood cells, and build foam cells. The review works through these steps at molecular and cell level. It covers how the body takes in, stores, and clears lipids. A short section treats medicinal plants and RNA regulators. Their roles span disease cause, treatment, and prevention.
europmc-pmc8475356:
Zhu and co-authors review combination strategies that widen the gains of cancer immunotherapy. Checkpoint blockade and adoptive cell therapy changed care for once hopeless cases. Yet most patients still fail to gain lasting benefit. Resistance, early or late, is the main block.

The review first links immune response to resistance mechanisms. It then covers pairings with chemotherapy, radiation, and targeted drugs. Approved combinations are listed and weighed. Cytokine drugs, cell therapies, viruses, vaccines, and innate immune boosters all feature. Insights from a 2020 China immuno-oncology workshop close the piece. The authors argue smart pairing is the road to broader success.
europmc-pmc8524356:
Benedet and co-authors compare blood and spinal fluid levels of GFAP across the Alzheimer disease span. Glial fibrillary acidic protein, or GFAP, marks astrocyte activity. Blood markers that spot Alzheimer pathology early could screen large groups with ease. Which fluid reads GFAP better was not settled.

In this cross-sectional study, blood GFAP rose in both early and symptomatic stages. Its levels ran higher than those in spinal fluid. Blood GFAP also beat spinal GFAP at telling amyloid-positive from amyloid-negative people. That edge held even before symptoms began. The authors call blood GFAP a sensitive marker for early care and trials.
europmc-pmc8704656:
Wicherska-Pawłowska, Wróbel, and Rybka review three receptor families that guard the innate immune system. These receptors spot patterns from germs and from damaged tissue. Toll-like receptors sit in cell membranes. NOD-like and RIG-I-like receptors work inside cells. Each family wakes signal chains that switch on defense genes.

The same system also helps watch for cancer. Natural and lab-made triggers for these receptors can kill malignant cells. They can draw killer immune cells into tumors. Such triggers are now tested as aids in cancer immune therapy. The review covers structure, signals, and control of each family. Blood diseases get focus as a treatment target.
europmc-pmc8750456:
Enaru and co-authors review what makes anthocyanins break down and lose their color and health value. These plant pigments color foods from red to blue and purple. They also show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in studies. Industry uses them as natural pigments in many products.

Their big weakness is low stability. Heat, light, pH, and oxygen can all degrade them. Sulfites, vitamin C, and enzymes also play a part. Pairing with other pigments can help or harm. The review sums up the effect of each factor. Knowing these effects can cut losses and keep the health gains of these pigments.
europmc-pmc8853656:
Belsky and co-authors introduce DunedinPACE, a blood test for the pace of aging. Trials of aging-slowing treatments need a fast yardstick. Waiting decades for outcomes is not workable. The team built the test from the Dunedin birth cohort study. That study tracked decline in 19 measures of organ health. The tracking spanned two decades of adult life.

The authors distilled the two-decade pace into one blood reading. They used DNA methylation patterns with strict reliability checks. The test then faced five outside datasets. It proved stable on repeat testing. It tracked illness, disability, and death. Young adults with childhood hardship aged faster by this measure. It added prediction beyond a leading aging clock. The authors offer it as a tool for geroscience trials.
europmc-pmc8878656:
Panieri and co-authors sound an alarm over PFAS, a vast family of industrial chemicals. The group holds over 4,700 compounds. They resist heat and chemical breakdown almost completely. Industry has used them for nearly 60 years. They appear in countless products and processes. That toughness now cuts the other way. The chemicals persist in nature and build up in bodies.

The review starts with PFAS chemistry and uses. It traces their path through air, water, and soil. Human exposure routes get detailed treatment. So do documented effects on health and wildlife. The authors then survey European Union regulation. They cover rules on making, importing, and using PFAS. Cleanup technologies for polluted sites close the piece. Substitution plans are weighed as well. The authors urge prompt, coordinated action.
europmc-pmc8942856:
Meng and co-authors explain Omicron's changed route into cells and what it does to infectivity. Omicron's spike binds the ACE2 receptor more tightly than Delta's. Yet its behavior in lung and gut cells shifted. Replication there ran lower than Delta's. The spike was also cut less efficiently. Entry tests with pseudotyped virus located the defect. The key lay in a cell surface protease, TMPRSS2. Omicron uses that protease poorly.

Delta leans on TMPRSS2 for fast membrane entry. Omicron depends more on the endocytic route. Cell-cell fusion by its spike was badly impaired. Tissue preference shifted away from TMPRSS2-rich cells. That shift may help explain altered disease patterns. Antibody findings fill out the picture. Two-dose vaccine sera lost much force. A third mRNA dose rescued and broadened neutralization. The antiviral drugs tested kept their efficacy.
europmc-pmc8993156:
Menni and co-authors track how COVID-19 vaccine protection fades and how boosters perform, in a UK community study. Data came from the ZOE app, where users report tests and symptoms. The main group held 620,793 people with two doses. Three vaccines were in use. Positive tests over eight months measured waning. A booster group of older adults was followed as well. Side effects after boosters were counted from self-reports.

Protection fell as months passed after dose two. The slide was steeper past age 55. People with other health conditions also lost ground faster. Boosters restored strong protection in the older group. Side effects stayed mostly mild and brief. Mixing vaccine types for the booster looked safe. The authors give timing evidence for booster policy. Community data, they show, can track national programs in near real time.
europmc-pmc9061756:
Xiao and co-authors built a metabolic atlas of triple-negative breast cancer, a form lacking the usual hormone targets. They profiled 330 tumor samples and 149 paired normal tissues, covering both small molecules and lipids. The tumors fell into three metabolic subgroups, from fat-rich profiles to quiet ones with little disturbance. Layering this map over gene data refined the known subtypes.

Model tumors pointed to drug targets inside the pathways. Blocking one lipid signal slowed the androgen-driven subtype, and another metabolite drove high-risk tumors. The team released the dataset as a public resource for precision treatment.
europmc-pmc9122856:
Mann and co-authors give screening advice for women with extremely dense breasts, on behalf of a European breast imaging society. Dense tissue both raises breast cancer risk and hides cancers on mammograms. Women with extremely dense breasts are thus poorly served by mammogram screening alone. New trial proof supports added MRI screening.

The society urges screening providers to tell women their breast density. For women aged 50 to 70 with extremely dense breasts, it advises MRI screening every 2 to 4 years. The authors accept MRI cannot be offered at once everywhere. They still urge swift action and sound quality checks. Shared choice with each woman should guide the final plan.
europmc-pmc9174056:
Lee and co-authors reveal faulty autolysosome acidification as an early driver of Alzheimer's disease in mouse models. Autophagy, the cell's recycling system, is badly impaired in this disease. The team used a neuron-specific probe and advanced imaging in five mouse models. They tracked acid levels inside autolysosomes in living brain.

Acidification fell well before amyloid plaques appeared outside cells. A weakened proton pump drove the drop, and amyloid pieces built up inside the swollen compartments. Badly hit neurons formed flower-like rosettes packed with amyloid, a pattern also seen in human brains. The team shows such neurons are the main source of senile plaques. The work reframes where plaques begin and why recycling fails.
europmc-pmc9710656:
Badia-I-Mompel and co-authors introduce decoupleR, a package that infers biological activity from omics data. Omics profiles hold thousands of measures per sample. That bulk makes direct reading of the data hard. Prior knowledge can shrink the view to the acts that matter.

The package gathers many inference methods under one roof. It runs in both R and Python for wide lab use. Any method can pair with any knowledge resource in the frame. It draws on OmniPath, a meta-resource of over 100 databases. Methods can use weights and modes of control, not just lists. The team tested the set on gene and phospho data from drug trials. Plain linear models did well in those tests. A consensus score across top methods did even better. The authors say the shared frame eases fair method choice.
europmc-pmc9748256:
Pejaver and co-authors calibrate computing tools that judge whether missense variants cause disease. Clinical rules count such tool scores as supporting evidence only. Tool makers set their own score cutoffs without hard backing. The rules also asked for agreement among several tools.

The team built a math frame that turns scores into evidence strength. It rests on local predictive value at each score band. They scored thirteen tools on carefully built data sets. New cutoffs mark supporting, moderate, and strong evidence bands. Most tools reached the supporting band for both call types. Several reached strong bands at their best score ranges. One tool hit the very strong band for benign calls. The group gives advice for updating the clinical rules. Single tools can now carry graded weight on their own.
europmc-pmc9835956: McCallum and co-authors examine how the epsilon variant of SARS-CoV-2 slips past immune attack. Their study centers on a variant of concern that rose during the first variant waves. It asks how strongly the variant's altered spike resists the antibodies left by infection or vaccination. The hosted text holds the study's framing pages and its full reference list rather than the article body. This record therefore points to the evasion study and its stated subject, the spike driven escape of that lineage.
europmc-pmc9963556:
Stoumpos and co-authors analyze digital transformation in healthcare through technology acceptance. Wearables, virtual reality, and the Internet of Things are reshaping care delivery. Patients gain wider choices and a more patient-centered system. The study asks how these changes appear in the research record.

The team ran a systematic bibliographic review across Scopus, ScienceDirect, and PubMed. Their search covered work from 2008 to 2021 and ran in August 2022. It found 5,847 papers, and 287 articles entered the final set. Five themes emerged, from health information technology to telemedicine and security. Education effects and e-health acceptance formed two more themes. The authors sort a fast field into a usable map.
frus-1861-d156:
On 14 October 1861, William Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a calm mid autumn report. The dispatch is document 156 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's mid October report comes from the heart of the autumn file. France still held its neutral course, and he could say so. A calm report from Paris was good news in itself for a cabinet beset on other fronts. Good news by silence was a phrase the cabinet learned to value that year. Silence from Paris, in that season, was a form of good news in itself.
frus-1861-d256:
Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a dispatch to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands on 28 September 1861. The printed record keeps it as Document 256 in the President's message volume for 1861. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d56:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 June 1861. The dispatch is document 56 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The longest day of the year found Adams reporting the state of play in London. Summer brought no break in the watch on shipyards, agents, and notes. His letter adds one more dated layer to the fullest run of letters in the whole 1861 volume. The Adams file is the spine of the 1861 volume, and this letter sits near its heart. Near its heart sits the summer when the post was won and held by paper.
frus-1862-d156:
Two Adams reports reached Washington under the date 3 October 1862; this second one is Document 156 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Envoys often split their news across two letters sent the same day, one for talks held and one for papers enclosed. The habit makes the printed file dense but rich. For readers now, paired dispatches like these show how much paper a single week of wartime diplomacy could produce at the London legation. Cotton hunger in British mill towns kept the war a kitchen-table topic across the North of England.
frus-1862-d256:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, answered Paris on 27 February 1862 with a dispatch to William L. Dayton, printed as Document 256 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The same date carries a Dayton report, so the two letters likely crossed.

Crossed letters were a fact of life before the Atlantic cable: each side wrote against stale news. Skilled envoys wrote for the situation they expected, not the one they last saw. The paired papers of 27 February show that discipline at work in the Paris file. With policy stated plainly enough to survive a fortnight at sea. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d356:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, on 7 February 1862. In a letter printed as Document 356 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

February brought the Union victory at Fort Henry, the kind of news that steadied Seward's hand with foreign envoys. France was then deciding whether to press deeper into Mexico after its allies wavered. A letter to Mercier in this month belongs to the quiet fencing by which Washington sought French restraint on both the war and Mexico. Mercier had served in Washington since 1860 and knew the capital's politics at close range.
frus-1862-d456:
On 20 January 1862 John Lothrop Motley reported from Vienna to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 456 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Motley's January report covered the Austrian court's temper in the weeks after the Trent affair had nearly brought war with Britain. Vienna's rulers disliked rebellion on principle but distrusted republican success almost as much. His letters home weighed that balance for Seward. For the modern reader, the Vienna file shows the Union's diplomacy at its most patient. A famous historian, posted to a cool court, argues the case there. His client is a democratic government fighting to survive.
frus-1862-d556:
On 23 May 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Henry Shelton Sanford, the American minister to Belgium. The instruction is Document 556 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Late May 1862 was the high-water mark of Union confidence that spring, and Seward's letters abroad carried that confidence to every post. Sanford in Brussels was charged with keeping Belgium's court and press on the Union's side. He was also charged with watching the Confederate agents. Those agents used Belgium as a base. The instruction is one of several that spring that treat Brussels as a working front. It was a front in the war of opinion, not a backwater. Sanford fought on it with real relish.
frus-1862-d56:
Charles Francis Adams reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in a dispatch dated 2 May 1862. The printed record keeps it as Document 56 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It was written in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d656:
Late in his time as minister to Japan, Townsend Harris received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 19 November 1861. It is document 656 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. The two men had traded letters across the Pacific for years by then.

Much of Seward's outward mail that fall dealt with the war and the risk that other lands might back the South. His letters to Japan kept a smaller file in order at the same time. This one shows the reach of his desk. From a capital at war, he still wrote to a lone envoy on the far side of the world.
frus-1863p1-d156:
A stray comma rides in the title of this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 16 April 1863. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date; the title of this one even keeps a stray comma in the printing. Adams was the American minister in London; the letter is document 156 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Mid-April mail from the legation kept the watch on Britain's yards and courts after the raider's seizure. Adams's reports stayed cool and exact, the style that had served the Union well. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day. The stray comma in its head is a small print quirk in a file of great weight.
frus-1863p1-d256:
On 31 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 256 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Read in sequence, these reports show a diplomat testing how far he could push a stronger power without provoking a second war. That balance was the heart of Adams's whole mission. It was written in the month of Gettysburg and Vicksburg, twin Union wins that changed how Europe judged the war. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d356:
Washington's business with Britain on 9 January 1863 included this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The paper is document 356 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Britain had claimed neutral rights at sea, while the Union navy stopped British ships suspected of aiding the South. The friction from those seizures runs through this whole exchange. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d456:
Document 456 in the volume is a letter of 11 April 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d556:
Among the day's business on 8 June 1863 was a letter from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d56:
On 28 October 1862, Christopher G. Memminger wrote to Messrs. Fraser, Trenholm & Co. for the second time in four days. Memminger was the Confederate treasury chief; the Liverpool firm handled the South's money in Britain. The letter is document 56 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Two letters in four days to the same bankers point to fast-moving deals. Cotton, credit, and ships all ran through this firm's books, and Richmond's letters kept the flow in step with the war's needs. This one closes the treasury run in the printed group. It is a plain sheet with great weight behind it: the South's purse, held abroad.
frus-1863p1-d656:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State on 6 November 1863. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d156: Minister Kirk wrote on November 21, 1943 to Hassanayn, chief of the Egyptian royal cabinet, and the letter is Document 156 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Host-government letters in the final hours before a summit dealt with the crown's part in the proceedings, though this record names no subject. The parties and the date are what the catalog gives. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d256: The facts given about this Cairo meeting, and the names of those who took part, come from the President's Log, the editors state. No record of the subjects discussed at the meeting has been found. The editors point the reader to their note on the Roosevelt and Churchill dinner meeting earlier in the volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d356:
An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume reconstructs a warning delivered at Tehran on 27 November 1943, for which no official record was made at the time. The account rests on a letter Ambassador Harriman wrote to the department's Historical Office in 1954, more than ten years later.

Molotov, Harriman recalled, summoned him and the British ambassador, Sir Archibald Clark Kerr. He told them that German agents in Tehran knew of Roosevelt's presence. The agents were planning a demonstration, which might involve an attempt at assassination. Stalin therefore urged the President to move into the British Legation or the Soviet Embassy, where a house stood ready. Harriman, General Connolly, and security chief Reilly agreed to recommend the Soviet compound, Roosevelt consented, and the move took place the next afternoon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d456:
On the last day of the Second Cairo Conference, December 6, 1943, American and British officials agreed the minutes of a joint meeting, later printed in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. An agreed text had to satisfy both delegations, so it states the version of events neither side disputed. The conference communiqué went out the same day.

Inside is the shared record of business done as the summit ended, when the decisions taken with Stalin at Tehran and refined at Cairo became the allies' settled course. Readers who want the conference's outcome rather than its gossip start with records like this one. They show what the two governments committed to, in words both approved.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d556:
President Roosevelt wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on March 3, 1944, the same day two Churchill messages reached him. The exchange gives the day's correspondence a back-and-forth shape. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Roosevelt's style with Churchill mixed warmth, humor, and firm refusal when the two disagreed, as they often did over Mediterranean strategy that spring. His replies kept the partnership balanced between London's experience and Washington's growing power. For readers, this message shows the President holding his end of the alliance's central conversation in the last spring of preparation before the invasion of France.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d56: Secretary of State Cordell Hull set down a memorandum on October 25, 1943, during the Moscow Conference, and it stands as Document 56 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Memoranda of this kind fixed what was said and agreed while memories were fresh, and they anchor the official record. The catalog gives the author and the date and no topic. Hull's paper is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d156:
Joseph Grew, director of the Office of Far Eastern Affairs, sent Secretary Hull a warning memorandum on August 28, 1944. Behind the formal British request for a French mission in Southeast Asia, he reported, British secret operations in Indochina were already moving. His memo draws on a July cable from Colombo and an August report from Ambassador Murphy.

According to Grew, British SOE had already dropped a de Gaullist agent into Indochina using American facilities in China, keeping General Chennault in the dark. Two more drops were approved at a staff meeting the American coordinating officer was told had been cancelled.
