London meant to proceed without Washington's clearance, Grew wrote, though the operations were more political than military.
frus-1944-quebec-d256:
Future operations in the Mediterranean are the subject of C.C.S. 677, the United States Chiefs' paper of September 12, 1944. It answers General Wilson's progress reports with American preferences. Part or all of the Fifth Army, the chiefs held, should be transferred to France if it could be used effectively in the attack on Germany.

Timing and route, overland or by sea, would depend on the Italian offensive's outcome. If Eisenhower did not require the American forces in Italy, they should instead clear the Germans from Italy and assist British operations northeastward toward Vienna. The Twelfth Air Force's transfer would follow the same logic, while the Fifteenth Air Force could best perform its mission remaining at its Foggia bases.
frus-1944-quebec-d56:
Under Secretary of State Edward R. Stettinius recorded this memorandum on September 6, 1944. Stettinius was fresh from the Dumbarton Oaks conference, where the plan for a United Nations organization had been drafted. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Six days before Quebec, the department's positions needed final shaping, and Stettinius's memoranda did much of that work. His interests ran to the peace organization as much as to the war's endgame. For readers, the paper shows the State Department preparing to argue, at a soldiers' and financiers' conference, for the political structure of the postwar world.
frus-1945-50-intel-d156:
The Director of Central Intelligence (Vandenberg) addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Board on 20 June 1946. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 156 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Washington was still building a peace-time spy service, run for the moment by the National Intelligence Authority and the Central Intelligence Group.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d256: The title "Department of State Briefing Memorandum" heads a text dated 17 December 1947. The State Department prints it as document 256 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. A new order was taking shape: the National Security Council now met at the top, with the CIA as its intelligence arm. Findings come first in a reader's eye, but the body of a report is where the proof sits, fact by fact.
frus-1945-50-intel-d356:
On 17 December 1948 the Intelligence Advisory Committee sat, and the minutes of the session survive here. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 356 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d56:
McCormack wrote to both Secretary Patterson and Secretary Forrestal on 15 December 1945. The State Department's intelligence chief addressed the two military secretaries together, as his own secretary had done five days earlier. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

McCormack's office at State and the military departments had to divide the work of the new system between them. December was the month of dividing. A letter to both secretaries at once kept the terms even: neither service could claim a private deal. Readers see the negotiation entering its drafting stage here, where courtesies thin and clauses thicken. The McCormack papers of December are the State intelligence office's last stand before the January settlement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d156:
On 18 December 1944 the State Department told the public where the United States stood on Poland. The press release, printed in full in the Malta and Yalta volume, puts the policy in numbered points. It had already been passed to the governments concerned, Poland's included.

First, the United States stands for a strong, free, and independent Polish state. The Polish people keep the untrammeled right to order their own internal life. Second, boundary questions have always been left, in American policy, until the fighting ends. But if the nations directly concerned reach a friendly agreement first, Washington would not object. Such a deal could even help the war against the common enemy, the statement adds.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d256:
Stalin spoke with unusual frankness about the Pacific war on 17 October 1944, and Harriman cabled the President that night. Their long session with General Antonov covered detailed planning for Soviet entry. The report is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Stalin admitted his weakness in certain areas if Japan struck early. Against that, he set his plan for a strong land offensive to encircle and destroy the Japanese forces in Manchuria. One subject needs urgent American study, he said: help in building up supplies in the Far East through Pacific ports before the fighting starts. His list of needs, for ground and air forces, comes to about a million tons of goods.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d356:
Talking points, not treaty text, fill this American paper of February 6, 1945. It arms the Secretary of State with extra arguments for the United States plan on voting in the Security Council. The first point is blunt: the new world body might never be accepted if the American proposal failed.

American opinion, the paper warns, might reject a body that gave small nations an unfair place. The Latin American states and the British Dominions might do the same. It also cites the Tehran Declaration, where the three powers promised a peace commanding the good will of the world's peoples. The paper shows persuasion being prepared as carefully as policy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d456:
China's divided house prompts this memorandum from Stettinius to the President, dated February 10, 1945. As the day's meeting was likely the final plenary, Stettinius suggested Roosevelt find a moment to speak. He should urge Stalin and Churchill to see that their governments fully encouraged unity between the Kuomintang and the Communists in China.

The aim was China's war effort against Japan. United Chinese efforts, the memo says, must be important to all three governments. A penciled note by Hiss adds Bohlen's word: the President had already taken the matter up with Stalin, with satisfactory results. The memo shows Yalta reaching beyond Europe.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d56:
Weather, not politics, is the worry in Churchill's telegram to Roosevelt of 14 January 1945. He uses the code names of the day: Malta is “Cricket” and Yalta is “Magneto.” The message belongs to the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, which prints the leaders' private traffic.

Churchill reports that Anthony Eden is glad Edward Stettinius will reach Malta on 31 January if he can. Stalin, he says, expects him at Yalta on 2 February. But winter flying may force delays, and the two Western leaders might not meet Stalin until the 3rd. He closes by welcoming Harry Hopkins's trip to London.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d156:
Acting Secretary Grew briefed Truman on Palestine in a memorandum dated June 16, 1945. The memo is document 156 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Zionist representatives at the San Francisco conference had asked to meet the President before he sat down with Churchill, expecting Palestine to come up at the summit.

Grew says the Department is preparing material on Palestine for possible use at the meeting, since the British will soon have to decide that country's future. He does not think the question will need detailed discussion, or any decision by Truman, during the meeting with Churchill. Still, it would help to know the British government's intentions. The short memo is an early sign of the Palestine problem moving toward the center of American policy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d256:
A State Department memorandum set the American line on liberated Europe, in an extract dated June 30, 1945. The extract is document 256 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It states what the United States should propose under the agenda item on carrying out the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe.

For Romania, Bulgaria, and Hungary, the three Allied governments should agree in principle to reorganize the present governments to include all significant democratic elements. Recognition and peace treaties should wait until that is done, and three-power consultation should work out the procedures, looking toward early free elections. For Greece, the paper proposes that the three governments send observers to supervise the elections due later in the year. France might join them. This builds on an Anglo-American approach already being made to Athens.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d356:
Edwin Pauley, reporting from Moscow on June 19, 1945, warned against fixing reparations totals too soon. In talk after talk, the Soviet negotiator Maisky kept returning to the twenty billion dollar figure discussed at Yalta. Of that sum, half would go to the Soviet Union, forty percent to Britain and America, and ten percent to all others.

Pauley had not openly resisted that basis, since the three leaders had agreed at Yalta to use it for discussion. But he judged it too early to name an exact amount before a first survey of what Germany could pay. Other claimant countries, he added, also had to be counted first.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d456:
Soviet troops massing in Bulgaria are described in Ambassador Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of June 29, 1945. General Oxley, head of the British delegation on Bulgaria's Control Commission, had just toured from Sofia to Varna. He went north of the Balkan mountains and returned by a southern route. Russian officers worked hard to keep his party from talking to anyone unwatched.

Oxley saw Russian troops in Lovech, Trnovo, and Shumen, perhaps advance parties for larger arrivals. Two Russian divisions stood near Varna and Burgas, and traffic through those ports ran to food and former prisoners out, cotton and planes in. His summary impression: Russian forces were massing in depth north of the Greek and Turkish frontiers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d556:
Cloyce Huston, who headed the State Department's Southern European desk, wrote to his colleague Walworth Barbour on July 11, 1945. The extract is document 556 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Attached is a long memo on Yugoslavia since the Crimea Conference.

The memo argues that Poland and Yugoslavia face the same core problem. Both are farming lands now ruled by governments under Soviet sway. It lists the Crimea terms for Yugoslavia one by one. The Tito-Subasic deal was to take effect at once, and a wider assembly was to form a short-term parliament. It also cites the Declaration on Liberated Europe and its pledge that peoples may choose their own form of rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d56:
President Truman answered Churchill's housing proposal in a one-line top secret telegram on June 11, 1945. The reply is document 56 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Churchill had asked that each delegation at Berlin have its own quarters and guards, rather than live as Soviet guests as at Yalta.

Truman's whole answer is that he agrees, and that he will instruct General Eisenhower to make the needed arrangements. A note in the volume shows the order moving the next day, when General Marshall passed Churchill's words to Eisenhower with the President's backing. The tiny exchange set the physical terms on which the three delegations would live and meet at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d656:
Washington explained to Ambassador Winant why Moscow need not sit in the Tangier talks, June 25, 1945. The secret wire is document 656 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It was signed by Grew and Loy Henderson.

The Department argues that leaving the Soviets out can be justified. Moscow, it says, has never shown any interest in the Tangier zone. It has kept no representative there and never claimed a party's rights under the Algeciras treaty. Imperial Russia had been a party to that treaty, but the Soviet state never acted on it. The United States, by contrast, kept a post in Tangier the whole time. It also kept exercising its treaty rights there, though it never signed the 1923 statute.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1056:
Nikolai Novikov, secretary of the Soviet delegation, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn on July 25, 1945. Acting on Molotov's instructions, he encloses a Soviet aide-mémoire about German troops in Norway. Moscow has received reports that the terms of unconditional surrender are not being fully applied there.

The enclosure cites two bodies of troops: some 260,000 men between Mo and Trondheim, and 140,000 near Tromsö. These men, it claims, still hold their arms and light equipment. They have not been interned and move about freely. Since Allied command holds supreme control over surrendered troops in Norway, Moscow asks Washington and London to note the report.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1156:
Fetter, chief of the division for lend-lease and surplus war property, wrote to Clayton and to Collado on 28 July 1945. His division ran the books on the weapons and goods America had lent its allies. Collado directed the office for money policy and growth abroad.

As the war in Europe ended, the fate of all that gear became urgent business. Who kept it, who paid, and what was written off were choices with long shadows. This note shows the money-and-gear track running beside the summit. It is the ledger side of alliance war, kept while the leaders talked.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1256:
Sato cabled Togo on 27 July 1945, reporting again from Moscow. The day before, the Allies had issued the Potsdam Declaration, giving Japan terms for surrender. Tokyo's answer was not yet set, and its Moscow bid still hung in the air.

Sato's embassy remained Japan's last hope of a softer end through Soviet hands. His report reached Tokyo as its leaders weighed the Allied terms. What Moscow would or would not do bore straight on that choice. This cable is the Moscow thread at the declaration's moment. It shows the envoy still reporting, while the ground under his mission gave way.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1356:
The Soviet delegation laid a further proposal before the Potsdam Conference on 22 July 1945. Written proposals were the working tools of the summit, each one a draft the three sides could fight over line by line. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Every Soviet paper in the volume marks a point where Moscow stated its terms in fixed form. Comparing the run of Soviet proposals with the closing protocol shows readers the shape of the bargain that ended the talks. Some asks survived whole, some were cut down, and some vanished. This proposal is one tile in that mosaic, and its date places it in the summit's busy middle week.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-156: Standing after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume, this editorial note is a piece of the volume's frame. The series' historians wrote notes like this to cite sources and link related papers. They keep a reader from mistaking a gap for a fact. The note does its work quietly, in a few lines.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-56:
A United States delegation memorandum of July 21, 1945, takes stock of the conference at its midpoint. Titled Status of Problems Before the Conference, it is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Potsdam papers. Its first part lists the problems on which substantial agreement had been reached.

The Council of Foreign Ministers heads the list. The proposal stands substantially approved, with minor textual improvements to come. London is fixed as the meeting place, and September 1 as the latest date. On Germany, the revised paper on the Control Council's authority in political questions has approval. The German fleet and merchant marine will be divided in three parts, the memo records. A substantial share of the submarines will be destroyed, and all the merchant ships, Russia's share included, will serve the war against Japan. On Austria, Soviet consent for U.S. and British forces to enter Vienna is noted.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d756:
The British Chiefs of Staff set out their view in this memorandum of July 24, 1945. Document 756 brings the British military voice into the Potsdam record. London's chiefs advised their own leaders and worked with the American staff. Their agreed paper joined the second Potsdam volume.

Allied strategy was a shared product. A British chiefs' memo shows the other half of that partnership thinking. Readers can set it beside American staff papers of the same days. The pair reveals where the allies agreed and where they merely cooperated. The document keeps the volume honest about the alliance's joint mind.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d856:
The Subcommittee on German Political Questions reported on July 19, 1945, in document 856. The group handled the political shape of beaten Germany: its government, parties, and borders of authority. Its report went to the conference's senior levels in the first week. The text joined the second Potsdam volume.

Political questions about Germany cut deepest at Potsdam. Who would rule, and under whose watch, shaped the continent's future. Readers find the experts' account of that argument in this report. The document shows the conference's layered method at its most serious. Staff wrestled the hardest topic first, so leaders could settle it last.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d956:
Edwin Pauley wrote to the Secretary of State on July 30, 1945, after reading William Clayton's reparations memorandum. The two men differ on one figure: how much movable factory equipment sits in the Soviet zone. Clayton says 40 percent. Pauley's own estimate runs near 45 percent, some 200 million Reichsmarks more.

Pauley lists seven reasons the gap could arise, from coverage of transport and utilities to wartime damage in the west. He then waves the dispute aside as beside the point. For practical purposes the Soviet zone holds about half of all reparations material, he says. The sides stand close enough to strike a bargain.
frus-1947v03-d256: Secretary of State Marshall sent this short letter to President Truman on September 24, 1947. It transmits the first report of the Committee of European Economic Cooperation, chaired by British Foreign Minister Ernest Bevin. Sixteen states signed the report in Paris on September 22, 1947. Their work had run since July 12, 1947. The report set out Europe's recovery problems, national plans, and the aid sought from the United States. Sector studies covered food, energy, steel, transport, timber, and labor.
frus-1950v07-d756: Everett Drumright, the chargé in Korea, sent this secret cable from Seoul on November 6, 1950. Eighth Army reports said South Korean units had taken seven more Chinese prisoners near Pyongyang. About 18 hostile Yak aircraft had been seen over the northwest. They seemed to have risen from Manchurian fields. Current estimates put 25,000 to 27,000 Chinese troops in the northwest sector. A force of about one division faced the Tenth Corps in the northeast.
frus-1977-80v29-d156:
A transcript of a phone call between President Carter and General Torrijos forms document 156 in Volume XXIX of the 1977-1980 series. Carter calls on the eve of the Senate vote on the neutrality treaty. He warns that the vote is very close. He asks Torrijos to make no public statement before it. Senate reservations, he says, do not change the treaty's terms. Torrijos replies that Panama has reached the limit of what it can concede.

Torrijos promises total silence until the vote is taken. He urges Carter to let himself fall with the parachute of dignity, which lands, he says, in the field of peace. Carter promises to send Christopher and Jordan to Panama after the vote.
gao-gaoreports-b-295956:
Firma Hermann Leis challenged an Army award for roofing work in Germany in this GAO bid protest decision, B-295956, dated May 19, 2005. The Army sought the work for the 411th Base Support Battalion. The awardee was Dachbau Kurpfalz GmbH. Leis said the winner lacked the needed track record and that the scoring was flawed.

GAO denied the protest on both points. The rules required proof of 5 years of roofing work. GAO found the contracting officer had a sound basis to find that mark met. GAO also found the scoring and the pick fit the stated factors. Readers can use the ruling for how a hard entry rule is checked.
gao-gaoreports-b-299156:
Free&Ben Inc. protested a Defense Logistics Agency purchase order for 25,000 plastic tent stakes. The order went to Middle Tennessee Plastics, Inc. The Defense Supply Center Philadelphia ran the buy. GAO decided B-299156 on February 20, 2007.

The firm guessed that the winner got a late chance to cut its price. No proof backed that guess. It also said the agency should have weighed stake thickness. The terms asked for no facts on thickness. They set no test based on that trait. An agency need not weigh a trait its terms never raise. The review kept to the stated scheme. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299456:
Lockmasters Security Institute protested terms in a Coast Guard request for quotations. The buy covered technical support for the Office of Security Policy and Management. The agency sought bids under one schedule class. GAO decided B-299456 on May 21, 2007.

The firm held a deal under a distinct schedule class. That class had served the same needs in the past. It said the new path shut it out of the contest. GAO found a sound base for the agency's pick of class. An agency may shift a buy to a new schedule home. The shift must rest on a fair ground, and it did. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1056:
U.S.-China Trade, GAO-05-1056 of September 29, 2005, asks why a shield built for import surges from China has never been used. When China joined the World Trade Organization in December 2001, it let trade partners curb goods that flood a market. U.S. law holds two more shields of the same kind. One is section 406 for communist states. One is section 201 for world trade.

GAO sets out how the China shield works and how far it has been tried. It weighs the wide room the President has to use it or let it rest. The report is one of a set on fair trade with China.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-256:
Immigrant Investors, GAO-05-256 of April 1, 2005, asks why a visa built to draw wealth to U.S. firms drew so few takers. The EB-5 path, made in 1990, gives a green card path to those who fund a firm that aids the U.S. economy and makes at least 10 full-time jobs. A trial stay of 2 years comes first. Then a full stay may follow.

A 2003 law told GAO to count who came. GAO lists how many took part and from which lands. It lists the firms they built and where. It tells how many sought full U.S. citizenship. Rules still in draft share the blame.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-356:
Aviation Security, GAO-05-356 of March 28, 2005, takes the full grade of a flyer screen still in its test phase. Secure Flight would move the name match task from the airlines to the Transportation Security Administration. Congress set 10 points of keen care for the build, in Public Law 108-334. Each point gets a check here.

GAO asks how far the build and its tests have got. It asks what could blunt the screen's force. It asks how the work is watched and run. It asks what guards the rights and ease of flyers. Build and tests move, the title grants; risk must be held in hand as it grows.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-456:
Defense buying done through other agencies' franchise funds is the subject of GAO-05-456, a report dated July 29, 2005. The Defense Department is the largest user of such services. Franchise funds are fee-for-service shops run inside government that award and manage contracts for a fee. GAO checked whether two funds, GovWorks and FedSource, secured fair prices and whether the department weighed other options.

GAO reviewed $249 million of orders and work assignments. GovWorks often sought rival bids but did not get them. It also added work worth up to 20 times the value of one order without checking that prices were fair. FedSource rarely ensured competition or checked prices at all. For its part, the department chose the funds for ease of use, not proven value. Neither side set clear results or watched contractor work well. The report shows convenience winning out over value.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-556:
Funding the daily running of military bases is examined in GAO report GAO-05-556, issued on June 15, 2005. Base operations support pays for the services that keep installations working. A sister pot of money covers the upkeep and renewal of buildings. Congress has raised base funding in recent years. GAO traced where the money really went, how well needs are forecast, and what two services gained by centralizing base management.

Services often spent base money faster than Congress provided it. To cover the gap, they moved hundreds of millions of dollars meant for building upkeep and other work.  The Army felt the strain most. War costs added pressure in fiscal year 2004. Forecasts of base needs are weak. The services do not even define the work in the same words.  Central control in the Army and Navy shows promise, GAO said, but needs more time to judge.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-656:
Screening firms that sell medical gear to Medicare is faulted in GAO-05-656, dated September 22, 2005. Medicare wrongly paid an estimated $900 million for equipment and supplies in fiscal 2004, partly to fraud. A clearinghouse checks sellers against 21 standards before they may bill. GAO found its license checks rest on sellers' own claims, never matched to later bills. Twenty-two sellers were paid for oxygen work without the state license required. In Florida, over half of $107 million for custom limb and brace work went to unchecked sellers.

Required site visits were skipped for an estimated 605 sellers. GAO urges stronger standards and oversight; the Medicare agency largely agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-856:
Health care prices in the federal staff plan are studied in GAO-05-856, a report from August 15, 2005. The plan is the nation's largest private health cover. Prices vary a lot by place, and the causes are not well mapped. GAO used claims data from big national plans in the program. It measured how far hospital and doctor prices vary by city area. Then it tested what market traits track the gaps.

GAO found hospital prices varied by 259 percent across city areas. Doctor prices varied by about 100 percent. Areas with the least competition had hospital prices 18 percent higher than the most competitive areas. Doctor prices ran 11 percent higher there. Bargaining leverage from managed care plans also tracked lower prices. GAO found no evidence that the gaps come from cost shifting between payers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-956:
Electronic voting systems and their flaws fill GAO-05-956, a report from September 21, 2005. A 2002 law set up a commission to aid election running. It funded wider use of electronic systems by states and towns. Reports of faults since then have raised security and reliability fears. GAO gathered the main concerns raised. It matched them with recommended practices. It then described federal steps taken or planned.

Concerns include weak security controls, design flaws, and poor version control. Testing gaps, bad setup, and vague standards were also named. Many claims rest on one make of machine or one place's election, GAO noted. No consensus exists on how widespread the faults are. Still, some have caused real election problems. Practices urged include building audit trails in from the start. Federal efforts to manage the systems' full life cycle are under way, but key work remains.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1056:
The next generation nuclear plant gets a status report in GAO-06-1056, dated September 20, 2006. The Energy Department began the advanced reactor in 2003. It aims to make both electricity and heat for hydrogen production. A 2005 law requires design and building to finish by 2021. GAO checked progress against the schedule. It also judged the approach to making the plant sellable.

Headings show early movement. The department has made initial progress toward near-term milestones. An overall schedule is in place. Fuel and materials work has begun, and a licensing path is being built with the regulator. The department chose a more advanced design than rival options to win commercial interest, GAO found. It has applied some advice to cut research risk. It has not applied advice meant to speed the design work, the headings add.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-156:
Large truck safety enforcement is reviewed in GAO-06-156, a report issued on December 15, 2005. Crashes with large trucks kill about 5,000 people a year and injure over 120,000. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration runs federal enforcement and funds state programs through grants. In 1999 Congress doubted that the agency's approach worked. The agency then pledged stronger action. GAO tracked how its methods changed and how it judges their worth.

Enforcement grew stronger after 2000, GAO found. The agency still lacks proof of which tools save the most lives. It does not measure how well its civil penalties work against carriers. Grant oversight also needs work, despite deep cuts to the grant program's headquarters staff. GAO urged the agency to test the effect of its penalties. It also urged tighter use of planning and oversight steps for state grants. The aim is grants that clearly buy safer roads.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-356:
Buying a fighter jet before flight tests prove it works is the risk here. Fronted as GAO-06-356, dated March 15, 2006, the report covers the Joint Strike Fighter. The jet is the Defense Department's costliest aircraft program. It makes up 90 percent of the planned funds left to renew the aging tactical aircraft fleet.

Law requires GAO to review the program each year for five years. This second report checks the buying approach. It asks whether key choices rest on solid knowledge. GAO also sets out a different path to improve results. Its finding is in the title. The department planned to enter production before testing showed good performance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-656:
Sorting workers into employees or independent contractors is the subject of GAO report GAO-06-656, issued on July 11, 2006. Millions of United States workers hold contingent jobs, such as temporary or part-time work. The Department of Labor enforces laws that set minimum wage, overtime pay, and child labor rules. Whether a worker counts as an employee decides if those protections apply.

GAO found that contingent workers made up a fairly steady share of the workforce and came from many backgrounds. A smaller share of them had job benefits or coverage under key labor laws than other workers. The labor department found and acted on misclassification through investigations. But its local offices varied in how often they sent cases to other federal and state agencies. GAO urged better outreach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1156:
Retiree benefits at state and local governments are mapped in GAO report GAO-07-1156, dated September 24, 2007. Such benefits sit mostly outside the federal rules that guard private retiree plans. In 2004 new accounting rules called for reporting the future cost of retiree health care. As those sums come to light, doubt grows on benefit levels.

GAO set out the types of benefits given, and how they are built. It told how benefits are guarded and run. It gave the fiscal outlook for paying them, and what governments do to meet future costs. Site visits to three states show varied paths, from sound to strained.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-156:
Taxpayers stuck in disputes with the tax agency can turn to an advocate office for help. GAO reviewed that office in GAO-07-156, a report dated February 22, 2007. The Taxpayer Advocate Service handles cases and pushes fixes for wider problems. Its caseload has grown since 2004. GAO asked why the load grew and how well the office serves people. It also checked how the office measures its broader reform work.

Taxpayers reported strong satisfaction with their case help, GAO found. Quality scores were solid as well. But the office lacked a true measure of how efficiently it works cases. It also lacked a broad measure of whether its reform pushes succeed. The caseload rise alone did not prove failure, GAO said. Shifts in tax enforcement and the economy also drive case volume. GAO urged the Advocate to add cost and outcome measures. It also asked for clearer reporting to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-256:
Hackers prize the market regulator's files, and its defenses were still catching up. GAO audited the systems in GAO-07-256, issued March 27, 2007. The audit supports GAO's review of the commission's financial statements. GAO checked fixes for flaws found in 2005. It also tested controls guarding private and financial data. Staff examined policies and ran technical tests.

The commission had fixed or eased 58 of 71 old flaws, GAO found. Security training and incident response had improved. Senior managers were engaged in the work. But 13 old flaws remained open. GAO found 15 new ones in access controls and system settings. User rights for a major system were not documented. Patches were not always installed on time. Fixes listed as closed in action plans were sometimes not done. The agency had closed 11 of the 15 new flaws by the review's end. GAO urged steady follow-through.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-356:
A 1982 law bars most federal aid in fragile coastal zones to discourage building there. GAO checked whether building slowed in GAO-07-356, issued March 19, 2007. The system covers 585 coastal units. GAO mapped structures in 91 sampled units. It gathered aid and permit data from eight agencies. The update follows a 1992 study that found growth despite the ban.

Most units stayed empty of new building, GAO found. An estimated 84 percent saw no new structures. About 13 percent saw light growth of under 20 structures. About 3 percent grew heavily, with 100 or more new structures. Officials credited poor land and state laws, not the federal ban. Four agencies still gave banned aid. The flood program held 73 policies worth $20 million in the zones. One housing agency insured 5 loans worth $384,000. That agency lacks screening steps entirely.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-56:
Nurse anesthetist staffing at veterans hospitals is studied in GAO report GAO-08-56, dated December 13, 2007. Certified registered nurse anesthetists give most of the anesthesia care veterans receive. Many are near retirement age, and demand for their skills is expected to grow.

About three-fourths of chief anesthesiologists surveyed said hiring these nurses is hard. Some 54 percent reported closing operating rooms at times, and 72 percent reported delayed elective surgeries. GAO projects 26 percent of the nurses will retire or leave within 5 years. Pay below local market rates is the main cause named. Hospitals can use bonuses, education payments, and locality pay adjustments, but only some do. GAO urged faster training on the pay policy. The department generally agreed.
gobineau-moral-intellectual-diversity-ra:
Henry Hotze published his English translation of Arthur de Gobineau's work as The Moral and Intellectual Diversity of Races in 1856. Gobineau's Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races had appeared in French in 1853 and 1855. Hotze, a Swiss-born editor in Alabama, shaped the English version for American readers.

Gobineau argued that race explains the rise and fall of civilizations, and that mixing of races brings decay. Hotze cut and framed the text to fit debates over slavery in the United States. The book became a foundational text of racialist ideology in the nineteenth century. Histories of racism cite it widely, and it is preserved here as a primary source for that record.
golden-bull-1356:
Emperor Charles IV issued the Golden Bull in 1356 to fix how Holy Roman Emperors would be chosen. Named for its gold seal, the decree ended years of disputed elections and rival claimants. It named seven prince-electors as the only men allowed to choose the emperor.

The text spells out where electors meet, how they vote, and what rights each elector holds at home. It also regulates successions inside the electors' own lands, keeping those lands undivided. These rules gave the empire a stable frame for centuries. The bull stayed in force until the empire itself ended in 1806.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_openness:
Hungary's 1956 revolt against communist rule began with grief at a graveside. On October 6, Hungarians ceremonially reburied Laslo Rajk, a former minister who had been wrongly accused and executed. This briefing book, written sixty years later, traces the revolt's echoes in neighboring Romania.

The reburial drew out long-suppressed anger at a repressive, economically failing regime. On October 23 the discontent exploded in Budapest, in a mass demonstration demanding political and economic reform. Soviet tanks crushed the rising, but its example crossed borders. The Romanian angle matters because unrest there was watched and punished quietly, leaving a thinner record that postings like this help rebuild.
gurre-kamilaroi-or-kamilaroi-sayings-185:
William Ridley, a missionary in New South Wales, printed Gurre Kamilaroi at Sydney in 1856. The title means Kamilaroi sayings: gurre is the word for speech or a saying. Kamilaroi was the language of a large Aboriginal people of the northern rivers. Ridley's motto is Paul's word to the Romans: to whom he was not spoken of, they shall see. The book opens with the alphabet he devised for the tongue.

Picture pages tie letters to words: a kangaroo for b, a man for g, a woman for i. Then come sayings, dialogues, and Scripture turned into Kamilaroi, so that the people might read in their own speech. Ridley worked from talk with Kamilaroi men and set down what he heard with care. The small book is now a treasure for the revival of a language that policy later drove near silence.
hesiod-callimachus-theognis-bohn-1856:
The Reverend J. Banks translated Hesiod, Callimachus, and Theognis into prose for Bohn's library in 1856. The volume joins three Greek poets of very different ages and tempers. Hesiod, the farmer poet of Boeotia, is the oldest voice in the book, from the eighth century BCE.

His Works and Days teaches farming, justice, and the myth of the five ages of man, while the Theogony orders the gods. Callimachus, the scholar poet of Alexandria, adds his polished hymns. Theognis gives short elegies of counsel, pride, and exile from old Megara. Banks's version was the road by which many English readers first met the Elegies of Theognis.
jami-salaman-absal-fitzgerald-1856:
Jami sang the soul's journey in Salaman and Absal, and Edward FitzGerald Englished it in Miltonic verse in 1856. The Persian poem tells of Prince Salaman's earthly love for Absal and the slow turning of his heart toward divine love. FitzGerald, later famed for the Rubaiyat, found in Jami a kindred spirit, and the rendering here comes complete from the 1909 centenary edition.

The allegory works on two levels at once, a love story that is also a map of the spirit. FitzGerald's stately English gives the Sufi tale a grave music of its own. The piece stands as the companion to his Rubaiyat, the other pillar of his Persian work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-josep: Aaron ben Joseph of Beaugency, a French Bible commentator and rabbinical scholar, is named in this very brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He flourished in the twelfth century at Beaugency, near Orleans. He was a contemporary of Rabbenu Tam, whose dates are given as about 1110 to 1175. The two kept up a scholarly correspondence, the entry states. No works of Aaron are named here. The entry rests on two cited sources, Zunz and Gross's Gallia Judaica, given by page.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-bar-pappai: Abba bar Pappai was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century, who died in 375. He is named as the second link in the chain that passed on the haggadic sayings of Levi. Joshua of Siknin was the first link, and the two are most often named together. Abba also took part in legal debate. He put halakic questions to Jose and to Mani, son of Jonah. Those two, in turn, brought their own legal problems to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abetment-256:
Abetment is the legal term for urging, aiding, or prompting an unlawful act. An abettor may take no part in the act itself, the entry notes. In capital cases, Talmudic law takes no account of thoughts or words alone. To face a death penalty, a man must be the chief actor in the crime. A ruling maxim backs this: no one can be an agent in an unlawful act.

One stark case turns on a shield snatched away as an arrow flies. Neither the shooter nor the man who took the shield can be put to death, the entry says. A lone gap in the rule is the man who lures others to idolatry. In the God-ruled state that act was treason, and he was stoned even if no one followed him. In money cases, false witnesses pay, not the man who hired them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-isa:
Spanish Talmudist Abraham ben Isaac ha-Levi was born at Barcelona early in the fourteenth century. He died at Narbonne in October 1393. He led the Jewish community of Gerona in Catalonia and also wrote religious verse.

Praise for him stresses his honest, selfless service more than his deep Talmud learning, though both are noted. He likely left Gerona during the fierce persecution of 1391 and settled at Narbonne. A Passover poem and four poetical lamentations from his pen survive in manuscript. In 1394 Profiat Duran wrote a memorial notice of him, later printed in Ma'aseh Efod at Vienna in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adaiah-the-lord: Adaiah is a name borne by seven men in the Bible. The first was a man of Boscath. He was the father of Jedidah, mother of King Josiah. Two men of the Bani family who had wed foreign wives bear the name in Ezra. A son of Joiarib of Judah lived in Jerusalem. A Levite of the house of Gershon bears it too. In one list he is called Iddo. Last come a priest's son and a father who helped crown Joash.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adrammelech-856:
Adrammelech is named in II Kings xvii. 31 as a god of Sepharvaim. Folk from that town were moved to Samaria by Sargon of Assyria. There they kept their old gods, Adrammelech and Anammelech. Their rites are said to have burnt children in fire. Yet no god of that name stands in Assyrian or Babylonian lore. Clay texts show no rite of human burnt gifts at all.

That gap casts doubt on the town's place. If Sepharvaim were Babylon's Sippar, the god should be a by-name of the sun god Shamash. No such by-name is on record. Many scholars place the town in Syria instead, near Hamath and Arpad. Then no Assyrian root for the god names should be sought. The entry weighs a root in Adar, a god tied to the year's last month. It finds that root far from sure as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahab-son-of-kol:
Ahab, son of Kolaiah, was one of the first captives deported by Nebuchadnezzar to Babylonia. There he acted as a false prophet. Jeremiah wrote to the exiles and denounced him. The prophet said he would be roasted in the fire by Nebuchadnezzar. The cause may have been urging the people to revolt.

Rabbinic tradition pairs him with Zedekiah, son of Maaseyah. It says the two tried to lure the king's wife, or daughter, to sin. Their false claim was that she would bear great kings and prophets hostile to Israel. The king then cast both men into the furnace, and they were roasted alive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alabaster-1056:
The alabaster of the ancients was a stone unlike the modern kind. Theirs was the stalagmitic form of carbonate of lime. The stone now called alabaster is a sulphate of lime. From the ancient stone, vases were cut to hold unguents. In time the vases themselves were called alabasters. That shift explains a word in the Septuagint.

The stone came from mines in Oran, in Algeria. It was also found at Thebes and west of the Tigris. In Assyria it served for bas-relief work under the name pilu. Its use runs back past the ninth century B.C. Babylonia must have traded in it early, since the mineral is not found in the south of that land. It was usually grayish and striped in look.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-usski: Alexander Üsskind ben Moses of Grodno was a great cabalist of the eighteenth century. He died at Grodno, in Lithuania, in 1794. His book is "Yesod we-Shoresh ha-'Abodah," The Essence and Root of Worship. It came out at Novydvor in 1782 and was often reprinted. It gives directions for the ritual and explains the daily, Sabbath, and holy day prayers. It also holds essays on Rashi, the Holy Land, and the Temple. He left an ethical will for his sons. It was printed at Grodno in 1794.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allegorical-int:
Allegorical interpretation reads a verse as meaning more than it says. The reader holds that the writer meant something other than the plain sense. The entry splits the method into two kinds. One kind is symbolic and grew in Palestine. The other is drawn from thought and grew in Egypt.

Both kinds spring from one root cause. A people's old book stays dear as views change. New thought must then be found inside the old words. The entry traces the method from Hosea onward. It runs through Daniel and the Greek Bible. Long later pages weigh Philo and the schools that came after him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-am-ha-arez-1356:
Am ha-Arez is a Hebrew term for a man who lacks learning. In plain speech it means an ignoramus. The stress falls on lack in Jewish matters. Sages of the second century defined it in many ways. One test was food eaten in priestly purity. One test was the due payment of tithes. One test was the reading of the Shema.

The words mean the people of the land at root. In Ezra's day the term marked those set apart. Pharisees kept a sharp line against such men. No marriage ties were made with them. Harsh words flew on both sides. The entry traces that feud at length. It closes with a kind word for teaching their sons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anammelech-more: Anammelech was a god of the Sepharvites in Samaria. He was paired with the god Adrammelech. The pair is named in the second book of Kings. The name means Anu is prince, more or less. Anu headed the old trinity of Babylon. If Sepharvaim is Sippara in north Babylonia, the link is clear. One hard point fills the last part of the entry. Kings says babes were burned to this god. No proof shows such gifts were made in Babylonia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aria-lewis-1756:
Lewis Aria was a merchant and philanthropist who died at Portsea in 1874. Born to a Sephardic family, he was trained for business. The fortune he made over a long career he gave to one cause: a theological college to train Jewish youth for the ministry.

The college was set up at Portsea and has turned out several Jewish ministers. By a curious term of his will, men who have lived in Hampshire, the county of Portsea, are to be preferred for admission. The entry names the Rev. I. S. Meisels as the college's principal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-baerm:
Baermann Ashkenazi, also called Baer, was a Polish writer on Bible and Midrash of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The entry calls him the foremost of all Midrash commentators, yet says the only fact known about him is that he lived at Szczebrzescin. He died there after 1608, not at Hebron as scholars from Conforte to Zunz had claimed.

Two books carry his name. Mareh Kohen, printed at Cracow in 1589, treats seventeen topics of Jewish theology and indexes the Scripture passages outside the Pentateuch that the Zohar cites. Mattanot Kehunnah, Priests' Gifts, printed at Cracow in 1586 and revised in 1608, comments on the Midrash Rabbah. His great merit, the entry argues, was joining wide knowledge of Midrash to sound critical judgment, above all in fixing a correct text.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-astruc-elie-ari:
Elie Aristide Astruc was a French rabbi and author. He was born at Bordeaux on Nov. 12, 1831. He studied at the rabbinical college of Metz on a scholarship from Bayonne. In 1857 he became assistant to the chief rabbi of Paris and chaplain to Paris schools. In 1860 he was one of the six founders of the Alliance Israélite Universelle.

In 1866 Astruc became chief rabbi of Belgium, though he stayed a French citizen. He served through the Franco-Prussian war, helping care for the wounded. In 1879 he gave up the Belgian post and later served as chief rabbi of Bayonne, from 1887 to 1891. His books include a short history of the Jews and their beliefs, sermons, and a study of the roots of anti-Semitism from 1884. The king of the Belgians made him a knight of the Order of Leopold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auxerre-2156:
Auxerre is the chief city of the department of Yonne, France. A strong Jewish community stood there from the eleventh century. Its rabbis, called the sages of Auxerre, wrote back and forth with Rashi. Several of them sat in the synod called by Rabbenu Tam and Rashbam at Troyes in the middle of the twelfth century.

The Jews of Auxerre were treated kindly, as a rule. They could own farms, fields, and vineyards, paying tithes to the clergy. In 1208 they refused to keep paying those tithes. The bishop carried the case to Pope Innocent III. The pope could only order Christians to shun the Jews until the clergy were paid. A paper of 1379 set the terms on which Jews could lend money in the town. By the royal edict of Sept. 17, 1394, all Jews were driven from France. From that date, the entry says, Auxerre had no Jewish community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baptism-2456:
Baptism is a religious washing that stands for purification or consecration. Washing the body in water was always the custom in Israel, and washing clothes was required before the Revelation on Mount Sinai. The rabbis tie to that the duty of full immersion, "ṭebilah." Sprinkling with blood went with immersion, and tradition makes both part of the rites that bring converts under the wings of the Shekinah.

The entry insists baptism is not only for wiping out one sin. It belongs to holy living and draws a person nearer to God. Josephus is quoted on John the Baptist: the washing served to purify the body, the soul having first been purified by righteousness. Later parts trace the rite among Essenes, Ebionites, and Hemerobaptists, and find penance by standing in water as far back as the tale of Adam and Eve.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barth-jacob-255:
Jacob Barth, a German professor of exegesis, religious philosophy, and Semitic languages, was born at Flehingen, Baden, in 1851. He studied at Leipsic under Fleischer and at Strasburg under Nöldeke. In 1874 he became professor of Hebrew, exegesis, and religious philosophy at the Berlin Rabbiner Seminar. In 1880 Berlin University made him professor of Semitic languages. For ten years he has also lectured at the Veitel Heine Ephraim Institute.

His greatest work is "Die Nominalbildung in den Semitischen Sprachen" (1889–91; second edition 1894). It traces for the first time the genetic development of Semitic noun-forms and is called epoch-making. Followers of Lagarde protested, but most of Barth's results are now becoming standard. His earlier works include studies on Job (1876) and Isaiah (1885) and etymological studies on the Hebrew lexicon (1893). He also edited Tha'lab's "Kitab al-Fasiḥ" and parts of Tabari's "Annalen."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bath-2656:
Bath is a city and county capital in Somersetshire, England, known since Roman times for its hot springs. The entry says Jews seem to have lived there only in recent times. No record places them there in the twelfth century, and there was no archa in the thirteenth.

Without an archa, the entry explains, Jews could not settle in the town. The present congregation was founded about 150 years before the entry and stayed small. The larger congregation at nearby Bristol overshadowed it. Its synagogue stood in Corn Street. A French writer of the twelfth century warned a boy against the town in harsh terms, the entry recalls.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beerah-2756: Beerah was a descendant of Reuben and head of that tribe when Tiglath-pileser carried it into captivity, as First Chronicles states. A second part turns to rabbinic lore. There Beerah is matched with Beeri, father of the prophet Hosea, and is himself called a prophet. His name is read as well, since he was a wellspring of knowledge. God let him die in exile, the tale says, so his piety could serve his fellow exiles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-sir-be: Benjamin Benjamin, later Sir Benjamin, was mayor of Melbourne and was born at London in 1836. At age nine he went with his parents to Victoria. He worked first with a merchant firm, then in partnership with Edward Cohen. City office came in 1870, and he rose to alderman in 1881. He gave much time to the Melbourne Hebrew Congregation and its schools and charities. Elected mayor in October 1887, he was reelected without dissent, and knighthood followed in May 1889 for his civic service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bereshit-rabbah:
Bereshit Rabbah is a Midrash on Genesis, the first book of the Pentateuch. Tradition assigns it to the amora Hoshaiah, who worked in Palestine in the third century. It comments on nearly the whole book, verse by verse and often word by word. Only bare lists of names and repeated tales are passed over.

Its pages mix plain word glosses fit for the young with rich legendary matter from synagogue lectures. The chapters on Creation draw the fullest treatment. The entry notes its sublime thoughts, its jabs at heretics, and its habit of reading biblical figures in the light of its own day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berr-emile-3156:
Emile Berr was a French journalist. He was born at Lunéville on June 6, 1855. He first worked in commerce and exchange. In 1886 he turned fully to journalism. After the "Petit Parisien," he joined the "Figaro" in 1888. He stayed with that paper for years. At times he signed his work "Fabien."

The entry follows his reporting trips across Europe and beyond. In 1891 he interviewed Stambuloff at Sofia. His Norway notes became a book in 1900. Its title was "Au Pays des Nuits Blanches." He also edited the "Figaro" literary supplement. In 1900 he received the Legion of Honor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bibago-abraham-:
Abraham ben Shem-Ṭob Bibago was a Spanish philosopher and preacher. He was born at Saragossa. He lived at Huesca in 1446. He was still alive in 1489. As a young man he debated a Christian sage. Their topic was the Trinity dogma. He knew Christian theology well. That let him defend Judaism in scholarly form.

His chief work is "Derek Emunah," the Path of Faith. It defends Judaism as the road to knowledge of God. Its three treatises cover God, intellect, and faith's fundamentals. He defends Maimonides' creed warmly there. Abravanel later reused his arguments. The entry lists six more works by him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blau-heinrich-3: Heinrich Blau was a German journalist and playwright. He was born in Neu-Stettin on September 21, 1858. His parents moved to Berlin in his childhood. At thirteen he translated the Psalms into meter. In 1878 he went to London. He worked on the "Londoner Journal" there. He rose to be its chief editor. He wrote in both English and German. He corresponded for German papers from London. He also studied Sanskrit and Oriental literature. His dramatic poem "Gautama" grew from that study. He wrote libretti for operas and oratorios.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-book-trade-3556:
Book trade among Jews ran long before printing, the entry begins. A twelfth-century bookseller's catalogue was found in the Fostat Genizah. About 1300 a seller named Aaron of Toledo brought 180 Hebrew manuscripts to Italy.

With printing, the trade centered first in Italy. Wandering sellers carried stock from Venice, Mantua, and Padua. Frankfort-on-the-Main later became the fair center for German and Polish books. Amsterdam then led the Hebrew book trade for a long span. The entry closes with firms in Germany, Turkey, and the United States. Prices tell the strain on buyers: one commentary on the Pentateuch sold for 9 reichsthalers in that unorganized trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bruck-lajos-375:
Lajos Bruck was a Hungarian painter born at Pápa in November 1846. His father wanted him in commerce, but he chose art instead. He studied at the Academy of Art in Vienna and earned money from portraits. A government stipend sent him to Italy in 1871. He spent two years in Venice, then worked in Rome and Naples.

His picture The Rialto at Venice brought him before the public in 1873. Later travel took him through many European cities, and in 1874 he settled in Paris. There his style shifted toward forceful scenes of real life. Paintings of Hungarian folk life, shown at the Salon from 1876, made him widely known. The entry says he later moved to London and ranked among its popular painters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-canaanites-the-:
Canaanites can mean all the non Israelite people west of the Jordan, or only one part of them. The entry tracks that double use through the Old Testament. At times the name sits in a list beside other tribes of Palestine. At other times it marks the coast dwellers alone, where it matches Phoenicians. In Zephaniah it is even laid on the Philistines of the southern coast.

Because the name covered the Phoenicians, it slowly took the sense of traders. Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Proverbs all use it that way. Source critics note that one Bible strand favors Canaanite while another uses Amorite for the same people. Egyptian and Amarna texts point the same way. The narrow coast sense, the entry argues, came first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chartres-4256: Chartres is the chief town of the department of Eure-et-Loire, in France. Jews lived there from old times, in a special quarter called Rue aux Juifs. In 1394 their synagogue, in the Rue Saint-Père, was turned into a hospital. The town had a mint whose coins were called Chartrain. Noted rabbis of Chartres include Mattithiah, a scholar of Rashi's time, Joseph, a Bible commentator, and Samuel ben Reuben, a liturgical poet. The brief entry gives those points and little more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chosroes-khosru:
Chosroes, also Khosru II Parwiz, ruled Persia from 591 to 628. Claiming to avenge his murdered father-in-law, the Byzantine emperor Maurice, he invaded Asia Minor and Syria. Jews joined his forces in large numbers under Benjamin of Tiberias, a man of great wealth who enlisted and armed them. Together with Persian troops they took Jerusalem by storm in July, 614.

The entry then follows a failed move on Tyre and about fourteen years of freedom from Christian rule in Palestine. Hopes for a Jewish commonwealth went unmet, and Chosroes turned harsh. Jews shifted to the emperor Heraclius, who promised amnesty in a treaty of 627. Chosroes, beaten in battle, was seized and executed on Feb. 28, 628.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-abner-445: Abner Cohen, born about 1860, is called the pioneer of Krugersdorp in the Transvaal Colony. He emigrated to South Africa in 1881 and worked his way north. He learned the Boers' language and traded with them. In 1887, bound for Johannesburg, he pitched his tent on a heap of stones seventeen miles west of that town. The spot became Krugersdorp, and he was its first English settler. As president of its congregation he won two freehold sites from President Kruger for the Jewish community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-colophon-4556:
Colophon names the inscription or device set at the end of a book. It gives the title, the writer or printer, the date, and the place of printing. It began as the illuminator's certificate on manuscripts. Early printers used it to vouch that the work was done by a reputable hand and in a reputable way.

In time colophons grew long enough to stand in for the title-page itself. Hebrew colophons carry a strong religious tone, thanking God for a happy finish or blessing the helpers. Some hold poems, lists of backers, or pages of corrections. The entry ranges from the first Hebrew prints of about 1490 to a Karaite Pentateuch of 1833 swollen with extras. Steinschneider and Cassel anchor the sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cordovero-aryeh: Aryeh Löb Cordovero, also called Tarcziner, was rabbi of Zamosz, Poland, at the end of the seventeenth century. He wrote a book called Pene Aryeh Zuṭa, printed at Wilhelmsdorf in 1720. The entry reports, on Wolf's authority, that the printed book shortens a larger work, Pene Aryeh Rabbah. That larger work, a commentary on the Pentateuch, stayed unpublished. Four standard bibliographies are cited at the close. The entry gives his town, office, and books, but no birth or death dates and no details of his life or teaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corfu-4656:
Corfu, the most northerly of the Ionian Islands, held native Jews of three distinct origins. Greek Jews came from Thebes in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Spanish and Apulian groups arrived in later waves. Benjamin of Tudela, visiting in 1147, found only one Jew there, the dyer Joseph. Numbers grew after the island passed to the Angevin kings of Naples.

The long article treats each division in turn, with its own customs and rites. It follows legal rights under Venice, taxes, lawyers admitted to the bar, and blood charges. Community records and Greek, Italian, and Hebrew sources support the account. Readers get a full island history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-courage-3656:
Courage is defined as the quality that lets a person meet danger with firmness and calm. The Hebrew phrases behind it urge a man to be strong and of good courage. Physical courage grew from the struggle to live, the entry says. The Hebrews prized it highly. Singers hailed David's kills in war, and Gideon was greeted as a mighty man of valor.

Yet the Bible sets moral courage above bodily daring, the article argues. Its heroes include the Maccabean martyrs. Eleazar chose death over breaking the law. Seven brothers died under torture rather than eat forbidden food, while their mother watched. Such stories, the entry holds, explain Jewish power to resist across the ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crescas-don-vid: Don Vidal Crescas, of Perpignan, was a French Talmudist. He flourished in the first half of the fourteenth century. Probably born in Spain, he reached Perpignan just before the Maimonides controversy broke out. His brother and Solomon ben Adret pressed him to join the attack on the philosophy party. He stayed neutral instead. His letters show sympathy for the other side. He held that the young should study Talmud, but with full liberty in philosophy and science too.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dalphon-4856: Dalphon was the second of the ten sons of Haman. The entry is only two lines long. It states that all ten sons were killed by the Jews and hanged upon gallows. The reference given is Esther, chapter nine, verses 10 to 14. A variant is added: the Septuagint reading of the name is Delphon. Nothing more is said about Dalphon himself. He has no act, speech, or trait of his own in the entry. Readers learn his father, his rank among the brothers, and his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-delaware-5056:
Delaware, a state on the Atlantic coast of the United States, had few Jews before 1860, this entry reports. The first known Jewish resident was Solomon Solis, born at Wilmington on March 13, 1819. Nathan Lieberman settled at Wilmington in 1860, and his brother Henry went to Dover. The Jewish population is given as 928, with over 800 in Wilmington.

Wilmington held the state's only Jewish organizations. Its congregation was organized in 1885. A free Hebrew Sunday school, started on January 1, 1896, had over 300 pupils by 1903. Charities included a benefit society from 1883 and a Hebrew Charity Organization from 1902 with an interest-free loan fund. Small groups of families lived in a dozen other towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dew-5156:
Dew is moisture gathered in drops from the air, and in Palestine it matters greatly. It falls on cloudless summer nights and refreshes plants that would otherwise suffer. Westerly winds off the sea bring it as fine mist onto the summer crops. The Bible links dew with rain as a source of fertility and new life.

Without dew, as without rain, the land is cursed. It soaks a fleece left out overnight, yet vanishes by morning. Scripture uses dew as a picture of God himself, of freshness, and of resurrection. Later writing gives dew a spirit dwelling at the ends of heaven, and rabbis told of treasuries of good and harmful dews in the sixth heaven.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-didache-or-the-:
Didache, or the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is an old manual of instruction. Bryennios found it among ancient Christian manuscripts at Constantinople in 1873 and published it in 1883. The book had been named by writers of the fourth century but was lost since the ninth. Scholars widely debated where it came from.

The entry presents the theory of Charles Taylor, from 1886, which Harnack accepted in 1895. On this view the first part of the Didache, the teaching of the Two Ways, began as a Jewish manual for bringing proselytes into the Synagogue. Christians later reshaped it and added rules on baptism, fasting, prayer, and church order. The article studies that Jewish core closely.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dohm-christian-:
Christian Wilhelm von Dohm was a German historian and political writer born at Lemgo on Dec. 11, 1751. He was a friend of Moses Mendelssohn and an advocate for the Jews. He died on his estate near Nordhausen on May 29, 1820.

At Mendelssohn's urging, Dohm wrote a two-volume work on Jewish emancipation in 1781. A Christian voice, Mendelssohn thought, would carry more weight. The book argued for political equality on grounds of humanity and justice. It ran through two editions at Berlin and drew wide notice. Some accused Dohm of being in Jewish pay, while Jewish communities voted him thanks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dumashevski-arn:
Arnold Borisovich Dumashevski was a Russian lawyer born at Mohilev-on-the-Dnieper in 1836. Born to poor Orthodox Jewish parents, he ran away from home at fourteen. He entered the Agricultural School at Gorigoretzk and graduated in 1855. He died at St. Petersburg in 1887.

Pirogov, the surgeon, helped Dumashevski into the Richelieu Lyceum to study law. He graduated from St. Petersburg University in 1862 and studied abroad on government funds. A new law then barred Jews from law professorships, closing a promised chair. He rose instead in the Senate's third department. For years he edited, then owned, a leading law journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ben-jose: Elijah ben Joseph was a Turkish Talmudist and commentator. He lived at Salonica in the sixteenth century. The entry names two works from his hand. One is a set of homilies on the Pentateuch. Salonica printed that book in 1562. The other bears the title Sefer ha-Tikkunim. It comments on Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and other Bible books. That second work was never published at all. No facts of his life are given beyond his town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enemy-treatment:
Treatment of an enemy is the theme of this long entry. It asks how Jewish teaching tells men to act toward a foe. Hate of a foe is a raw urge of early peoples. Grace to a foe marks a higher moral growth. The entry traces that growth through Bible and Talmud. Harsh verses in the Bible aim at the nation's foes. They can sit with a kind heart in private life.

The laws of the covenant open with a plain duty. A stray ox or ass of one's foe must be brought back. A foe's beast sunk under its load must be raised with him. Leviticus bans hate of a brother in the heart. Proverbs warns men not to gloat when a foe falls. The entry builds case on case from that base. Talmudic and later texts push the same softening line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eskeles-bernhar:
Bernhard Eskeles was an Austrian financier born at Vienna in 1753. He died at Hietzing, near Vienna, on August 7, 1839. He was the posthumous son of Rabbi Berush Eskeles. Sent to Amsterdam young, he ran a trading house at seventeen, then lost his father's fortune. In 1774 he returned to Vienna and married a daughter of Daniel Itzig.

With his brother-in-law Arnstein he built the banking house of Arnstein and Eskeles. It rose high during the Congress of Vienna, and statesmen filled his rooms. Joseph II and Francis I sought his money advice and sent him abroad. He founded the Austrian National Bank in 1816 and ran it for twenty-three years. Vienna raised him to baron in 1822.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezekiel-jacob-5: Jacob Ezekiel, a Beni-Israel Jew, was the third of his community to visit the Holy Land, the entry says. The first two named are Isaac Solomon and Joel Samuel. Ezekiel made the pilgrimage in 1894 with his wife. His book Travels to Jerusalem, printed at Bombay in 1895, records what he saw. It holds descriptions and photographs of the places visited, and some account of Jewish rites as performed in Jerusalem. No dates or home details beyond the journey are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-feis-jacob-6056: Jacob Feis was a German merchant and author who died on July 7, 1900, in London, his home for many years. He spent his literary skill mostly on turning English classics into German. His versions include Tennyson's In Memoriam and Oenone, plus pieces from Ruskin. In 1884 he published in English a book on Shakespeare and Montaigne. It set out to prove that changes in later editions of Hamlet aimed at the new thought in Montaigne's Essays. The entry cites two Jewish Chronicle notices as its sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fischmann-nahma:
Nahman Isaac Fischmann was an Austrian author whose home was in Lemberg. He died in 1873. His first listed work is a set of Hebrew poems printed there in 1827. Next came a critique of the works of Rapoport, Luzzatto, and Reggio on language and old remains. It was printed at Lemberg and Ofen in 1837-39.

In 1841 Fischmann published a two-act Biblical drama. It tells of the fall of Sisera and the freeing of Israel by Barak and Deborah. His later works include a full commentary on Job, printed in 1854. A poem followed in 1870. So did a five-act Biblical drama in that same year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fountain-hebr-6:
A fountain is a natural spring of water. Palestine as a whole has scant water, the entry says, yet it has a number of fountains. They often rise in the hollows of cliffs, though wells have also been dug. The Old Testament draws no sharp line between dug wells and springs. Among the best known fountains are the sources of the Jordan near Banias and Dan.

The Gihon spring near Jerusalem is another. So are the Harod fountains and those near Nazareth. Many towns took their names from the springs that gave them life. En-dor, En-gedi, and En-hazor are among them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-freund-wilhelm-:
Wilhelm Freund was a German word scholar born on January 27, 1806, at Kempen in Posen. He died on June 4, 1894, at Breslau. He studied at Berlin and Breslau from 1824 to 1828. He then opened a Jewish school at Breslau, but strict opposition forced him to close it. He later headed the schools at Hirschberg and at Gleiwitz, the second shaped by his own plans. From 1870 he gave himself wholly to writing.

Freund's great work is a dictionary of the Latin language in four volumes, printed from 1834 to 1845. It became the base of all Latin-English dictionaries of later times. Turned into English in 1850, it was used widely in England and America for a generation. Freund took an active part in the fight for Jewish rights in Prussia. He helped bring Abraham Geiger to Breslau. A Prussian Jewish law of 1847 grew out of his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gad-6456:
Gad was the seventh son of Jacob and the first-born of Zilpah. His name means good fortune. He fathered seven sons. The tribe that bore his name counted 40,000 men fit for arms in the desert. Rich in flocks, it settled east of the Jordan with Reuben and half of Manasseh.

Gad men had a name as fighters. They joined the taking of the lands east of the river and later backed David. Rabbinic tales say Gad lived 125 years and that Moses was buried in Gad land. A note on the Moabite Stone calls Gad folk old dwellers at Ataroth. Critics read that as a sign the tribe stock was not pure Israelite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ghirondi-6656:
Ghirondi is an Italian family of Padua whose founder settled there near the end of the sixteenth century. The name shows he came from Gerona in Spain. He was also called Zarfati, the Frenchman. Benzion Ghirondi, the founder, wrote a short guide to the laws of animal slaughter. That work was never printed.

Mordecai Samuel Ghirondi, born at Padua in October 1799, became its chief rabbi in 1831. Rabbis of many towns sought his rulings. His chief work is Toledot Gedole Yisrael, a life and book guide to Italian rabbis and scholars. He added 831 entries of his own to an older work by Nepi. His son printed the joint book at Triest in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldschmidt-her:
Hermann Goldschmidt, who wrote as Herman Taber, was a German novelist and playwright. He was born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on July 18, 1860. He read law at Heidelberg, Leipsic, and Marburg. In 1888 he became a court assessor in his home city.

Soon after, he chose a literary career instead. His social novel "Ein Weg zum Frieden" appeared in 1890. Seven plays followed, among them "Fortuna," "Goldene Lüge," and "Frau Lili." The entry says they played on German and foreign stages alike. The court theaters of Berlin, Vienna, and Munich all staged his work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gurland-jonah-h:
Jonah Hayyim Gurland was a Russian and Hebrew writer. He was born at Kleck in 1843 and died at Odessa on March 14, 1890. At ten he entered Wilna's rabbinical school and graduated as rabbi in 1860. At St. Petersburg he studied Semitic languages under Chwolson. His thesis on Arab philosophy's sway over Maimonides won a gold medal. He spent three years on the Firkovich Karaite manuscripts in the Imperial Library.

From 1873 he inspected the teachers' colleges at Jitomir for seven years. Illness sent him to Germany in 1880. Back in Russia, he founded a college at Odessa with Jewish history and Hebrew in its course. In 1888 he became government rabbi of Odessa. His works include studies of Karaite manuscripts and records of the 1648 persecutions in Poland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hariph-7256: Hariph appears in the Book of Nehemiah as a name tied to the return from exile. The children of Hariph, one hundred and twelve in number, came back with Zerubbabel. Hariph was also one of the chiefs who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah. The entry notes that the matching list in Ezra gives the name as Jorah instead. It also links the name to the form Hariphite and to the related name Hareph in Chronicles. No life details are given beyond these Bible lists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hays-7356:
Hays follows a family that came from Holland to the New York area in the early eighteenth century. Six brothers anchor the account. Their sons backed the colonial side in the Revolutionary war. Jacob Hays helped build the first home of Congregation Shearith Israel in 1730.

Later members fill many roles. One Jacob Hays served as New York's high constable from 1802 to 1849. Moses Michael Hays led the Masons of Massachusetts. His nephew Judah Touro won fame across America for giving to good causes. Other branches produced a mayor in Maryland, farmers in Westchester, and a lawyer who led city boards. The piece works like a family tree in prose.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenthal-nauma:
Naumann Löwenthal (1819–1855) was a German teacher and writer born at Schmiegel, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling gives his short life. He studied philosophy, mathematics, and the natural sciences at Berlin and Breslau. He took his degree at Halle in 1841 and passed his teaching examination at Berlin in 1844.

Löwenthal then became the first Jew in Prussia appointed a head teacher, serving at a municipal technical school in Posen, where he died. The article notes his many treatises in technical periodicals and his one named book, “Die Physiologie des Freien Willens,” printed at Leipsic in 1843. That book’s title means the physiology of free will. The entry is brief, but it preserves a notable first in Prussian education and the outline of a career cut short at thirty-six.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magdeburg-law-m:
Magdeburg Law, a system of town privileges, is examined in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia for its effect on Jews. The law secured the self-government of municipalities. It spread widely through Germany, Poland, and Bohemia. German merchants and artisans usually brought it to Slavic cities for their own benefit.

The article shows Jews on the losing side of that spread. Living under separate privileges, they were not counted as part of the town's people. They were shut out of the law's benefits, and their position often worsened where it arrived. Wilna's Jews were expressly excluded. Yet the Jews of Troki won Magdeburg rights for themselves in 1444, directly from the grand duke. One strange clause protected Jewish buyers. A Jew could not be forced to name the person who sold him goods later claimed as stolen. The entry exposes both the harm and the loopholes of a famous legal system.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandl-christof-:
Christof Mandl, a Hungarian author who converted to Christianity, gets a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He converted in 1534. His godfather was George, Margrave of Brandenburg. To that prince he dedicated his book of 1536. Its title declares that Jesus Christ is the eternal Word.

The article lists two more works in the same vein. A Reckoning of the Seventy Weeks of Daniel appeared in 1552. Another book of 1557 again described Jesus as the Messiah. The entry gives no details of Mandl's life before his conversion. Its source is a Hungarian history of the Jews in Budapest, printed in 1901. The short notice preserves a convert whose writings served his new faith's arguments, and whose baptismal sponsor was a German prince.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marzroth-pseudo:
Märzroth, the pen name of the Austrian author Moritz Barach, is the heading of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar. Barach was born in Vienna on March 21, 1818, left the university in 1844, and went into journalism, where his work helped open the way for a more liberal press. He died at Salzburg in 1888.
