No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no results.
plos-pone-0003356:
Chihiro Hiramatsu, Amanda D. Melin, Filippo Aureli and colleagues test primate fruit finding in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Trichromatic primates have a red-green chromatic channel in addition to luminance and blue-yellow channels. It has been argued that the red-green channel evolved in primates as an adaptation for detecting reddish or yellowish objects, such as ripe fruits, against a background of foliage.

The authors assess importance of achromatic contrast in short-range fruit foraging of primates. Readers learn brightness contrast may matter more than colour at close range. That nuance revises a classic story about why primates evolved colour vision.
plos-pone-0003456:
Rahul Regulapati and co-authors proposed an origin for split genes in this 2008 paper. Genes of complex cells come in pieces, coding parts split by long non-coding stretches. Why genes took that fractured form stayed unsolved for thirty years. The authors focused on genes of the spliceosome, the machine that joins the pieces.

They argue the split structure could arise from random genetic sequences. Their solution claims to explain the pattern without special design. A random start would make split genes a byproduct of chance. The paper offers a testable story for a basic puzzle of biology.
plos-pone-0003556:
Semir Zeki and John Paul Romaya scanned the brain during hate in this 2008 study. Hate is a strong emotion that science had barely explored with imaging. Seventeen volunteers lay in a scanner for the tests. Each viewed the face of a person they hated.

They also viewed faces of acquaintances who stirred no strong feeling. Comparing the two sets mapped the neural correlates of hate. The active pattern was distinct from neutral face viewing. Mapping base emotions helps explain behavior driven by them. Hate drives real-world violence, which makes its brain roots worth mapping.
plos-pone-0003656:
Yuh-Man Sun, Megan Cooper, Sophie Finch, and colleagues published this development study in PLOS ONE in 2008. As stem cells become neurons, whole sets of genes must switch off and on in order. REST is a protein that shuts down neuron genes in non-neural cells.

The team found REST also controls genes for the extracellular matrix, the mesh that surrounds and supports cells. That control proved crucial for neural development to proceed well. The study widens REST's role beyond switching genes off inside the cell. It also shapes the scaffold the growing brain builds around itself.
plos-pone-0003756:
Christian Krintel, Peter Osmark, Martin R. Larsen, and colleagues published this enzyme study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Hormone-sensitive lipase is a key enzyme that frees fatty acids from stored fat. Its activity is switched on by phosphorylation, the adding of phosphate tags. Protein kinase A does much of that switching.

Working on the human enzyme, the team found two serine sites, 649 and 650, matter most. Those spots are the major determinants of activation by protein kinase A against fat substrates. The precise mapping shows exactly where the body flips its fat-release switch.
plos-pone-0003856:
Eduardo R. Ropelle, Maria Fernanda A. Fernandes, Marcelo B. S. Flores, and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2008. AMPK and mTOR are key regulators of the cell's energy balance and of how leptin, the satiety hormone, curbs food intake. Acute exercise makes animals more sensitive to leptin.

The team asked whether exercise acts in the brain's control centers on those energy sensors. They found exercise increases the AMPK and mTOR response to leptin there. The result shows physical activity rewiring appetite control at the molecular level, not just burning calories.
plos-pone-0003956:
Dennis Eckmeier, Bart R. H. Geurten, Daniel Kress, and co-authors studied how zebra finches use vision in flight in 2008. Fast-flying animals read optic flow, the motion pattern across the eye. Flow from straight flight carries depth cues about the surroundings. Flow from turning carries no such depth information.

Their PLOS ONE article asks how free-flying finches solve that mix. The birds must separate turning from straight motion to judge space. Their gaze strategy likely steadies the image during key moments. The work explains how small birds navigate clutter at speed. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004056:
Christine Stabell Benn, Ane Bærent Fisker, Amabelia Rodrigues, and co-authors studied birth vaccines in Guinea-Bissau in 2008. Oral polio vaccine at birth was policy in many low-income countries. The policy aimed to raise coverage of the vaccine. Its effect on overall infant survival was never studied.

During a vitamin A trial there, some newborns missed the polio vaccine at birth. That accident created a natural experiment on the policy. Their PLOS ONE article reports effects that differed between boys and girls. Such non-target effects matter for vaccine schedules worldwide. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004156:
Karli Watson, Jason Ghodasra, and Michael Platt published this primate study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Serotonin signalling shapes social behaviour in humans and other primates. In humans, a variant near the serotonin transporter gene affects social anxiety and how strongly the amygdala reacts to social cues.

The team asked whether the same gene variant changes how rhesus macaques respond to social reward and punishment. Linking gene variants to social choices in monkeys helps separate biology from upbringing. The study gives a controlled animal window on how one gene can tilt social life.
plos-pone-0004256:
Rachel Lubong Sabado and colleagues published this HIV immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. What it takes to prime HIV-specific T cells, and why those responses look the way they do in infected people, remained undefined. In lymph nodes, T cells must touch dendritic cells to activate, and that same contact can pass HIV between cells.

The team recreated priming in the lab, in vitro, and compared it with responses in the body. Their system recapitulates in vivo responses, and it reveals a rapid loss of virus-reactive CD4 T cells in acute infection. That early loss is one reason the immune system never gains the upper hand.
plos-pone-0004356:
Ana Pérez-Berná and colleagues published this membrane study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The team had recently identified the membranotropic regions of hepatitis C virus proteins E1, E2, core, and p7. They did so by watching how peptide libraries disturbed model membranes. Those regions are the parts of the virus that interact with cell membranes.

Here they screened a peptide library by two physical methods, DSC and SAXD, and compared the results with the biological function of the parent proteins. Checking whether lab behaviour matches real function validates the shortcut of studying virus pieces instead of whole viruses.
plos-pone-0004456:
Two kinds of small players in human genes may have evolved together, argue Stefan Lehnert, Peter Van Loo, Pushpike Thilakarathne, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. One player is the microRNA, a short RNA that dials gene activity down after genes are read. The other is the Alu repeat, the most common repeated stretch in the human genome.

The team showed that the seed part of some human microRNAs matches Alu sequences well enough to pair with them. That pairing could let microRNAs control genes that carry Alu copies. It also suggests the two spread through the genome in step with each other. The claim adds a new chapter to how repeated DNA, long dismissed as junk, may shape gene control.
plos-pone-0004556:
Chemical marks that keep a herpesvirus asleep are loosened when it wakes, show Zhangsheng Yang, Haidong Tang, Hai Huang, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Gammaherpesviruses share a life pattern: latency, hiding quietly in cells, and lytic replication, bursting out to make new virus. In murine gammaherpesvirus 68, a mouse virus of this family, the balance is controlled by one gene, called RTA.

The team studied the promoter, the on-switch region, of the RTA gene during reactivation. They found its demethylation, the removal of silencing marks, and changes in histone acetylation, a loosening mark on DNA packaging. Those changes help explain how a sleeping virus throws its master switch. Related viruses cause human cancers, so the mechanism matters beyond mice.
plos-pone-0004656:
A Golgi protein folds into an unusual armadillo shape, show Harald Striegl, Yvette Roske, Daniel Kummel, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is p115, a general vesicular transport factor. The golgin family gives identity and structure to the Golgi apparatus, the cell's shipping and sorting station, and forms part of a complex protein network at its membrane.

P115 is targeted by the GTPase Rab1a and contains a large globular head and a long coiled-coil stalk. The team solved its head's structure and found an unusual armadillo fold, a curved stack of repeating units. That shape is a scaffold for binding partners. Knowing it helps explain how the Golgi grabs incoming cargo sacs and holds its own shape.
plos-pone-0004756:
Matthew Gegg and colleagues found that silencing the PINK1 gene harms mitochondrial DNA and energy output in dopamine cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Faults in mitochondria, the cell power plants, are tied to Parkinson disease. Damage to the energy chain and extra deletions in mitochondrial DNA have both been reported in the illness.

PINK1 is a gene whose loss can cause inherited Parkinson disease. The team silenced it in dopamine producing cells and watched the effects. Energy output fell and mitochondrial DNA suffered. The result ties one gene to the power failure seen in the disease. These findings offer a firm starting point for the next round of testing.
plos-pone-0004856:
Justin Remais, Lin Chen, and Edmund Seto studied leveraging rural energy investment for schistosome control in rural China, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cooking and heating are the most energy intensive activities among the world poor, and clean energy access is key to Millennium Growth Goals. Anaerobic digesters convert waste to biogas while also inactivating schistosome eggs in human and animal waste fed into household systems.

Energy and health benefits arrive together in one investment. Digesters cut indoor smoke and parasite transmission simultaneously. Co benefits strengthen the case for subsidies. Rural growth can bundle goals efficiently. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004956:
Linking a trait to a nearby DNA marker usually requires pedigrees. Family trees are often missing, though. Shuhei Mano, Takaho Endo and Akira Oka offered a workaround in PLOS ONE in 2009. They detect linkage in a randomly mating population. No pedigree record is needed at all.

Standard linkage methods lean on extended family trees. Those trees must be reconstructed from records. The new approach draws the needed information from population data itself. If it holds up, gene mapping widens greatly. Populations where pedigrees can never be built become fair game for trait studies.
plos-pone-0005056:
Some images can be seen two ways. The brain flips between the interpretations. That flipping is called bistability. Gijs Joost Brouwer and colleagues studied what controls it in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used a bistable stimulus with incongruent depth cues. Volunteers watched while the team measured brain activity.

Metric changes in the incongruence changed the flipping rate. Cortical responses changed along with it. Mismatched senses tune the brain's switching. The work maps how conflicting clues steer perception. It shows perception as an active negotiation. The brain weighs evidence, then commits, then reconsiders. Such studies help explain illusions and, more broadly, how stable vision emerges from unstable input.
plos-pone-0005156:
Malaria parasites live inside red blood cells. They devour the hemoglobin there for food. Shoba Subramanian and colleagues mapped that meal in PLOS ONE in 2009. Two parasite enzymes do much of the cutting. They are falcipain-2 and falcipain-3, both cysteine proteases. Hemoglobin digestion was thought to follow an ordered process.

The study pinpointed each enzyme's cleavage site specificity. The two falcipains cut at different, precise spots. The maps reveal the parasite's dining rules. They also flag the enzymes as drug targets. Blocking digestion starves the parasite inside its host cell. Other proteases start the process, but these finish key cuts. Precise cut maps help chemists design blockers.
plos-pone-0005256:
Recognizing an object means joining what the eyes see with what the ears hear, while ignoring rival objects. Suied and Viaud-Delmon timed that joining process in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their results suggest the brain handles animal sounds in a special way.

Knowing an object's category helps the brain bind its cues together. Reaction times pointed to specific processing for animal sounds compared with other sounds. Fast, dedicated handling of animal calls makes sense for survival, and it shows how meaning shapes basic perception. Fast tracks for the sounds of beasts make sense in a world where a growl or a cry can mean food, threat, or a mate close by.
plos-pone-0005356:
Variants in mitochondrial DNA are suspected of shaping risk for many diseases, including cancer. One common variant, written A10398G, had conflicting evidence behind it. Pezzotti and colleagues tested its link to breast cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009, including interaction with alcohol.

Alcohol use is itself tied to breast cancer risk, so a gene and lifestyle interaction is plausible. Testing the variant alone and together with drinking gives a fuller picture. Careful studies like this sort real risk factors from noise in a crowded field. Mito genes come from the mother alone, so a risk tied to them would pass down the female line. A point that changes how a family should be told of its risk.
plos-pone-0005456:
Melanie Rauch and colleagues studied what keeps mature B cells alive, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. B cells make the antibodies that fight germs. A signal called BAFF, working through its receptor, was known to help young B cells grow past an early stage.

The team showed that the same signal is also needed to keep full-grown B cells alive and in place. Without it, two major B cell groups fail to form or fade away. That finding helps explain some immune defects and informs drugs that block BAFF in diseases where B cells cause harm.
plos-pone-0005556:
Suomeng Dong and co-authors identified a disease gene of a soybean pathogen in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A water mould called Phytophthora sojae causes root and stem rot that can ruin soybean crops. Whether a strain can infect a soybean variety depends on matching genes in mould and plant.

The team found the mould gene Avr3c and read what it makes. The protein it codes for is sent into plant cells and varies between strains. Matching these genes to soybean varieties helps breeders keep ahead of the mould. Soybean is a major world crop for food and feed, so even small losses to this mould carry a high cost.
plos-pone-0005656:
Matti Uusitupa and co-authors reported ten-year outcomes of the Finnish Diabetes Prevention Study in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. That trial had shown that lifestyle change can prevent type 2 diabetes in people at high risk. Whether it also cut deaths and heart disease over a decade was the open question.

The authors followed the trial groups for ten years and counted deaths and cardiovascular events. The lifestyle group had already gained years with lower diabetes rates. Their long follow-up tells health systems what sustained prevention is worth. Diabetes prevention by lifestyle had already been proven; the open ground was death and heart outcomes over time.
plos-pone-0005756:
Jonathan Song and co-authors built a tiny vessel model in 2009 to study how breast cancer cells stick to vessel walls. Cancer spreads when stray cells leave the blood and seed new tumors. Modeling that sticking step well is key to blocking it.

Their microfluidic device lines a small channel with living endothelium, the vessel's inner skin, under flow. Cancer cells tumble through as they would in blood. Watching which cells grip, and why, names targets for anti-spread drugs. The device gives a controlled stand-in for a step that is nearly impossible to watch inside a body.
plos-pone-0005856:
Zhou Xing and co-authors showed in 2009 that a booster shot up the nose greatly strengthens TB protection in guinea pigs. A virus-vectored TB vaccine had already worked well in mice, alone or as a boost after BCG. Guinea pigs, though, model human lung TB more faithfully.

Animals first primed with BCG, then boosted through the nose, resisted lung infection far better. Delivering the boost at the airway surface, where TB enters, likely explains the gain. The result supports mucosal boosting as a strategy. It moves the vaccine platform one step closer to human relevance.
plos-pone-0005956:
Gene therapy often parks new DNA inside a patient's own genome, where it lands at random. Romain Desprat and Eric Bouhassira took up a known risk of that approach in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. A parked gene can switch on a nearby cancer gene, and a DNA stretch called the chicken HS4 insulator may act as a shield.

The question was whether the shield works for all genes or only some. Their answer points to gene-specific effects, so the same shield does not guard every case alike. That nuance matters for making gene therapy safer: a guard that works in one spot may fail in the next, and each use must be checked on its own.
plos-pone-0006056:
Eating a particle is a cell's way of clearing debris and germs, but the meal has stages. Craig Blanchette, Youn-Hi Woo, Cynthia Thomas and colleagues pulled those stages apart in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies epithelial cells eating beads coated with InlA, a bacterial protein, using dyes that sense acidity to follow the act step by step.

Taking the bead in, turning its compartment acidic, and merging it with the cell's digestion sacs can each run on its own clock. Older studies often blurred those stages into one. Parting them lets researchers assign each drug or gene to the exact stage it touches, a gain for cell biology and for infection studies alike.
plos-pone-0006156:
Fear learned in one moment binds a sound, a place and a shock into one memory. Sabiha Barot, Ain Chung, Jeansok Kim and colleagues imaged the neurons where those strands meet in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses functional imaging of stimulus convergence in amygdalar neurons during Pavlovian fear conditioning, the classic model for studying learning and for understanding phobias and anxiety.

Showing which amygdala cells receive both the harmless cue and the shock names the memory's meeting point. Fear conditioning is among the best-mapped forms of learning, and each mapped point sharpens it further. The work also serves anxiety research, where the same circuit fires without a real threat.
plos-pone-0006256:
The human body gives off light far too faint for eyes to see. Masaki Kobayashi, Daisuke Kikuchi, and Hitoshi Okamura imaged that glow in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. The light comes from energy changes in metabolism and is about a thousand times weaker than what eyes can detect.

Sensitive cameras captured the emission rising and falling across the day. A diurnal rhythm in body glow ties light output to the body clock. The pictures make an abstract fact vivid: metabolism literally shines. Tracking the glow could one day offer a non-invasive window on metabolic state.
plos-pone-0006356:
Gene shape bears marks of both random mutation and natural selection. Salvatore Camiolo, Domenico Rau, and Andrea Porceddu examined Arabidopsis genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Features of gene expression profiles had been associated with build features of genes across many taxa.

Selection acting through expression patterns appears to shape gene structure, alongside bias in gene change. Highly used genes evolve different architecture from rarely used ones. Arabidopsis, the lab workhorse plant, gives clean data for such tests. The findings add to a picture of genomes fine-tuned by their own activity. The plant is small and fast to grow, which makes it a clean test case for such claims.
plos-pone-0006456:
Michael McCoy, Andrew Allen, and James Gillooly asked how much of genome layout is chance, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Open reading frames are stretches of DNA that could code for proteins. Knowing their size and number across genomes may reveal what controls genome complexity. The team examined how these frames are spread out in full genomes.

They studied the pattern of start and stop signals that bound each frame. From that pattern they built predictions of how frames should be distributed. If chance explains much of the layout, genome design looks less finely planned. The work gives a baseline for spotting where natural selection truly shapes genomes.
plos-pone-0006556:
Niels Høgslund and co-authors read gene activity in a model legume plant in PLOS ONE in 2009. Work on plant mutants had found key genes in the talk between legumes and Rhizobium bacteria. Those bacteria live in root nodules and give the plant nitrogen. The genes also guide how the nodules form and work. The team read all active genes at once in Lotus japonicus mutants.

By comparing mutants, they could pull apart the steps of this partnership. Legumes gain nitrogen from their bacteria, so farms need less fertilizer for them. Knowing the partnership gene by gene could help spread this trait to more crops. The plant is a main model for this field.
plos-pone-0006656:
Ana Martins and co-authors studied drug efflux pumps in resistant E. coli in PLOS ONE in 2009. Resistance-nodulation-division efflux pumps of Escherichia coli extrude antibiotics and toxic substances before they reach their intended targets. Whereas these pumps protect bacteria in many settings, their activity varies with pH. The team examined pH modulation of efflux pump activity in multi-drug resistant E. coli.

Their title highlights protection during passage through acidic body compartments. A pump that works harder at low pH helps bacteria survive the stomach or urinary tract. Understanding that modulation suggests ways to jam the pumps. Pump jammers could restore antibiotic power.
plos-pone-0006756:
Matthew B. Hale and colleagues tracked signaling errors in a mouse model of lupus in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lupus is a complex autoimmune disease of unknown cause. Many cell types and cytokines interact in its development. The starting events remain poorly understood. The authors focused on cytokine signaling through STAT proteins.

They found regulation of that signaling goes wrong in stage-dependent ways. Early and late disease showed different signaling faults. A fault that changes with stage needs stage-matched treatment thinking. Mapping when each error appears helps explain disease progression. It may also reveal windows where intervention works best in lupus.
plos-pone-0006856:
William Y. Y. Lai, Trevor Lane, and Alison Jones audited medical news on American newspaper front pages in PLOS ONE in 2009. Front-page medical stories reach a wide audience. How they are prepared and distributed had not been systematically studied. The authors quantified the visibility front-page medical stories achieve. They also traced where the stories come from.

Source tracing shows how much front-page health news starts as press releases. Coverage patterns reveal which institutions and journals dominate. Readers often treat front-page placement as a mark of importance. Knowing the pipeline helps readers judge health claims critically. It also presses newsrooms to check the origins of medical stories.
plos-pone-0006956:
Jennifer Bromberg-White, Elissa Boguslawski, and Nicholas Duesbery studied anthrax toxin in mouse eyes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Anthrax lethal toxin includes an enzyme called lethal factor. That enzyme cuts and disables signaling proteins known as MEKs. In cell and animal studies, the toxin targets the cells lining blood vessels.

The team disturbed eye development with the toxin and watched the result. They tracked how retinal blood vessels formed under its influence. The eye offers a clear window on vessel growth. Their work helps explain the vascular damage seen in severe anthrax infection.
plos-pone-0007056:
Erika Mileti, Gianluca Matteoli, Iliyan Iliev, and colleagues compared probiotic bacteria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Probiotics have been proposed to treat inflammatory bowel disease. So far, their clinical benefits have been limited. The team tested three Lactobacillus strains in complex lab culture systems that mimic the gut.

They compared how strongly each strain calmed immune activity. The goal was to predict which strains would work in the body. Lab systems that forecast real effects save wasted trials. They may also explain why probiotic results vary so much between products and patients.
plos-pone-0007156:
Araceli Castillo-Romero, Gloria Leon-Avila, Armando Perez Rangel, and colleagues studied the cell skeleton of a parasite in PLOS ONE in 2009. Giardia lamblia is a gut parasite that causes diarrheal disease. Its microfilaments, built from actin, drive movement, division, and uptake. Yet these structures are poorly understood in this organism. The team stained actin and viewed it with confocal microscopy.

They found actin takes part in both growth and encystation. Encystation is how the parasite forms the hardy cysts that spread infection. Blocking that step could break transmission. Basic cell biology of a parasite often reveals its weakest points.
plos-pone-0007256:
Margaret Kweku, Jayne Webster, Martin Adjuik, and colleagues tested ways to deliver malaria prevention to children in 2009. Intermittent preventive treatment gives children antimalarial doses at set times. It is a promising intervention, but delivering it widely to families is a practical challenge in many regions.

The authors ran a community randomized trial in Ghana. They compare coverage achieved by two different delivery systems for the treatment. Their PLOS ONE paper measures what each system can actually reach. Health planners can use those coverage figures to choose delivery routes that reach more children.
plos-pone-0007356:
Salama A. Salama, Marwa W. Kamel, Shaleen Botting, and colleagues studied an estrogen byproduct in uterine tumor cells in 2009. Uterine leiomyomas are common benign tumors, and optimal medical treatments remain a significant challenge. A compound called 2-methoxyestradiol is an endogenous estrogen metabolite with anti-tumor activity in several models.

The metabolite is formed by enzymes including catechol-O-methyltransferase, called COMT. The authors examine COMT expression and the metabolite's effects in leiomyoma cells. They report effects on microtubule dynamics and on steroid receptor signaling. Their work supports developing this natural metabolite pathway for fibroid treatment.
plos-pone-0007456:
Yuqi Wang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on signaling control in baker's yeast. A transcription factor called Tec1 governs invasive growth in yeast. It works within MAP kinase pathways, the signaling chains cells use to respond to their surroundings. Part of the Tec1 protein carries a small tag called SUMO. The team studied what that tag does.

They mapped how sumoylation of Tec1 is regulated and what it changes. The tag alters how Tec1 interacts with the MAPK pathways it serves. In effect, the cell gains a subtle dial for adjusting growth behavior. Small chemical tags like SUMO are easy to overlook, yet they fine-tune major decisions. The study clarifies one such dial in a model organism used worldwide.
plos-pone-0007556:
Antonio Julià and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on predicting who benefits from the arthritis drug infliximab. The drug blocks TNF alpha and is a treatment of choice for rheumatoid arthritis patients who fail standard therapy. Yet a considerable share of patients show no real response. The team searched blood gene activity for a signature that separates responders in advance.

They found an eight-gene expression profile that predicts the response. Eight genes is few enough for a practical blood test. Such a test could spare non-responders months of costly, ineffective treatment. It could also move likely responders to the drug sooner. Personalizing treatment this way is a central goal of modern medicine. The study shows it can be done with a compact signature.
plos-pone-0007656:
Ingrid Müller and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how Staphylococcus aureus manages vitamin B1. In its active form, B1 is an essential helper for key enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism. Mammals cannot make it and must salvage it from food. The human pathogen, by contrast, runs its own B1 production. The team examined how the bacterium controls that production.

Control operates at two levels: the enzymes themselves and the transcription of their genes. Two-layer control keeps the vitamin supply steady under changing conditions. It also gives drug designers two kinds of targets in one pathway. Blocking a pathway the bacterium needs but humans lack is a classic antibiotic strategy. The study maps the control points that such a strategy would strike.
plos-pone-0007756:
Norbert Mucke and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares microscope images of thread-like molecules with computer models of the same threads. Filamentous biopolymers, such as protein fibers, have stiffness that shapes cell life. One measure of stiffness is persistence length.

Scientists often gauge stiffness from flat images of molecules stuck on a surface. How a filament lands can follow two main scenarios. The authors used atomic force microscopy images and Brownian dynamics simulations. Matching the two tests whether image-based stiffness values can be trusted. That matters for all work on biological fibers.
plos-pone-0007856:
Sophie Javerzat and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It links gene regulation to blood vessel growth in the chick embryo. Building vessels requires many genes to act in concert. Their activity must be tuned by place, timing and dose.

Finding which genes drive vessel maturation is crucial for medicine. Blocked or excess vessel growth drives many diseases, from cancer to blindness. The authors correlated global gene patterns with angiogenesis in the chick's extra-embryonic vessels. This accessible system lets them watch vessels form in real time. The gene lists point to new therapeutic targets.
plos-pone-0007956:
Xiaomei Niu and colleagues measured blood signs of heart and lung strain in young people with sickle cell disease, for PLOS ONE in 2009. The disease bends red blood cells into stiff shapes that harm vessels over time. High lung pressure and a stiff heart are two feared results.

Blood samples from children and teens were checked for signs tied to vessel growth and inflammation. Some signs rose in step with the heart and lung changes doctors could measure. Such marks could flag the young patients who need close watch and early care, before harm turns grave.
plos-pone-0008056:
Ravi Kavasery and colleagues ran routine HIV testing inside a men's jail for PLOS ONE in 2009. Millions of people pass through United States jails each year, and health officials urge testing for all unless a person opts out. Jails resisted, citing cost and disorder.

Their controlled trial worked out the steps in a real facility and counted what the testing found. Undiagnosed infections came to light, and the process ran without wrecking the jail's routine. The trial gives other jails a tested script for a policy that can catch illness early.
plos-pone-0008156:
Wen Zhang and colleagues looked for pig-to-human spread of hepatitis E in central China and found none in PLOS ONE in 2009. The virus infects people and several animals, with pigs named the main source for human cases worldwide. Close gene kinship between pig and human strains backed that view.

In this region, human and pig strains did not show the kinship that fresh crossover would leave. Local spread may run through other routes, or older shared strains. A negative result with clear bounds still guides action: control efforts there should not rest on pigs alone.
plos-pone-0008256:
Guifen Chen, L. Phillip Wang, and Joe Z. Tsien recorded memory activity in mouse brains in PLOS ONE in 2009. A core goal of neuroscience is to watch memory traces form and return in real time. The hippocampus is a brain region central to associative memory. Its CA1 area is a key site for these traces. The team recorded groups of neurons there as mice experienced events.

They described short-lived ensemble patterns that tracked specific memories. Population-level traces linked neural activity to later retrieval. Watching memories at the group level bridges single cells and behavior. The work advances real-time study of how the brain remembers.
plos-pone-0008356:
Matthias an der Heiden, Udo Buchholz, and Gérard Krause modeled influenza policy in PLOS ONE in 2009. On June 11, 2009, the World Health Organization declared a pandemic of novel influenza A/H1N1. By late September the virus had reached all continents. Impact in most northern countries had stayed limited so far. A larger wave was expected in the coming season.

Their model estimated how public health measures could defer the epidemic peak. Delaying the peak spreads cases over more time. That relieves hospitals and buys time for vaccination. The study, titled Breaking the Waves, guides pandemic planning.
plos-pone-0008456:
Rebecca Smith and co-authors use mice to study father's age in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Human studies link older fathers to higher risk of some mental disorders in children. Those links cover autism, schizophrenia, and early bipolar disorder. But human data alone cannot prove cause. A mouse model lets the team test age apart from other factors.

Pups of older mouse fathers show flaws in social acts. They also explore less than pups of young fathers. The pattern backs a causal role for father's age. It gives a model for tracing how age changes sperm and brain growth.
plos-pone-0008556:
Jose Abisambra and co-authors study a cholesterol receptor in Alzheimer models in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Alzheimer disease is the most common form of dementia. The major genetic risk for late-onset disease is the epsilon-4 allele of apoE. ApoE is the main cholesterol transporter in the brain. The low-density lipoprotein receptor, LDLR, helps cells take up cholesterol cargo. The team examine LDLR in mouse and human cell models of the disease.

They find LDLR expression and localization are altered in those models. The receptor is made in wrong amounts or sits in wrong places. Such changes could disturb brain cholesterol handling in Alzheimer disease. They add a trafficking flaw to the disease picture.
plos-pone-0008656:
Maximiliano Rapanelli and co-authors link gene expression to learning in rats in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Plasticity in the medial prefrontal cortex plays a key role in learning and memory circuits. Several genes, like BDNF, support that plasticity. The team train rats on an operant learning task, where actions earn rewards. They measure prefrontal gene expression as learning proceeds. Then they link those changes to a computational theory of learning.

Their model explains how gene-driven plasticity supports the learned behavior. Expression shifts track the stages predicted by theory. Bridging molecules, behavior, and computation strengthens both sides. The work offers a template for studying learning disorders.
plos-pone-0008756:
Shuzi Zhang, Hehua Dai, Ni Wan, and colleagues found a way to teach mice to accept foreign tissue. Their transplant study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Donor MHC antigens mark tissue as foreign and provoke attack. Showing those antigens early can sometimes train tolerance instead. A growth signal called IL-2 shapes which T cells respond. Its availability during training was the lever tested here.

Adjusting IL-2 while donor antigens were presented changed the outcome. Regulatory T cells grew, and attack responses faded. Calmer immunity means grafts might survive with fewer harsh drugs. The recipe offers a path toward transplant tolerance.
plos-pone-0008856:
Filip Simunovic, Ming Yi, Yulei Wang, and colleagues compared gene activity in dopamine neurons from men and women with Parkinson disease. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Men develop Parkinson disease more often than women. Symptoms and disease course also differ by sex. The substantia nigra, rich in dopamine neurons, is where the disease strikes hardest. Molecular reasons for the sex gap were largely unknown.

Transcription profiles split clearly along sex lines in their samples. Different genes dominated the male and female patterns. Separate profiles suggest treatments may need sex-specific tuning. Parkinson research gains a reason to analyze men and women apart.
plos-pone-0008956:
Maik Grohmann and colleagues catalogued the many edited forms of a brain enzyme's messages, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The enzyme, TPH2, is the rate-limiting step in making serotonin in the brain. Serotonin helps regulate mood, and its faults are tied to several mental illnesses. TPH2 was the second form of this enzyme to be discovered.

The team found that the gene's RNA messages are cut and rejoined in varied ways. On top of that splicing, the messages are also edited at many points. Each variant could tune how much enzyme the brain makes, or how well it works. That variety may help explain links between TPH2 and mood disorders.
plos-pone-0009056:
Hung-Chung Huang, Daniel Jupiter, and Vincent VanBuren sorted genes by the shape of their activity data, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some genes behave like switches, either fully on or fully off. Finding those switch-like genes reveals the logic of gene control networks. They also make promising biomarkers, since their state is easy to read.

The team's method uses distribution metrics on expression profiles. Instead of averages alone, it reads how values spread across samples. Switch-like genes stand out by their two-humped pattern. The classification should sharpen models that treat genes as on-off circuits.
plos-pone-0009156:
Arthur Talman, Andrew Blagborough, and Robert Sinden engineered a malaria parasite that glows through its whole life, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plasmodium falciparum causes most malaria deaths worldwide. Its life spans human blood, liver, and the mosquito gut. Tools to watch the parasite at every stage were badly needed.

The new strain expresses green fluorescent protein throughout the life cycle. Researchers can now follow it in mosquito and mammal alike. A glowing parasite exposes stages that drugs and vaccines might attack. The strain is a workbench tool for the whole malaria field.
plos-pone-0009256:
Ekaterina Kotelnikova and co-authors published this bioinformatics paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Microarrays measure the activity of thousands of genes at once. A single experiment can flag hundreds of genes that change in a disease. Turning that long list into biological meaning is the hard part.

The authors built an atlas of cell signaling pathways for that job. Researchers can map their gene lists onto the atlas to see which pathways are involved. Instead of staring at raw gene names, they get a picture of the cell's wiring at work. The tool aims to make expression data quicker and easier to interpret correctly.
plos-pone-0009356:
Ivo Francischetti and co-authors published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyr61 is a protein that works outside cells, in the matrix that holds tissues together. It belongs to the CCN family, whose members carry four working modules in a row. One partner of interest is vitronectin, a blood and tissue protein.

The team found that Cyr61 binds vitronectin with high affinity. The grip lands on one specific stretch of vitronectin, its somatomedin B domain. A tight, mapped grip suggests the pair works together in processes like wound repair and blood vessel growth. The study pins down one contact in a web of matrix signals.
plos-pone-0009456:
Tanya Cunningham and co-authors tested two natural mineral mixes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some mineral products sold for health use can kill bacteria. Why they do so was not clear. The team put the mixes in liquid with bacteria and measured the effect. They varied the acidity of the liquid as they worked.

Killing power rose and fell with acidity. The minerals release metal ions that can poison bacteria, and acidity controls that release. So the same mix can be strong in one setting and weak in another. The work turns an old folk remedy into a process that can be measured and tuned.
plos-pone-0009556:
Eva Kucerova and colleagues sequenced the genome of a food borne germ in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cronobacter sakazakii can contaminate powdered infant formula. Infections in newborns can be deadly. The team read the full genome of one strain, called BAA-894. They then compared it with other members of the Cronobacter group by a hybridization method.

The genome gives a full parts list for a germ of real concern to food safety. Comparisons show which genes the harmful species share and which they do not. Those details can improve tests that detect the germ in factories. They can also point to the genes that make it dangerous.
plos-pone-0009656:
Wuyang Zhu and co-authors studied how Sindbis virus enters cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sindbis is a mosquito borne virus used widely as a model. Its coat carries a protein called E2. That protein makes first contact with the cell it will infect. The team tested whether E2 binds heparan sulfate, a sugar chain found on cell surfaces.

The binding proved crucial for the virus to infect cells. Without that grip, infection faltered. Naming the handshake gives antiviral work a clear first target. A drug that blocks the grip could stop the virus before it gets inside, a strategy of interest for related viruses too.
plos-pone-0009756:
In times of hunger, people may eat wild plants they would normally avoid. Emily Gurley and colleagues investigated a fatal outbreak in northeastern Bangladesh tied to one such plant. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The plant was Xanthium strumarium, and people had eaten its seedlings during a time of food scarcity. The investigation traced the outbreak to that food source. Cases like this show how hunger can turn a toxic plant into a meal. The report helps health workers prevent repeat poisonings in lean seasons. Food scarcity was the backdrop to the whole event.
plos-pone-0009856:
During a flu pandemic, emergency medical workers must decide whether to report for duty. Daniel Barnett and colleagues gauged that willingness across the United States. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The workers surveyed staff ambulances and emergency calls nationwide.

The assessment framework weighed threat and efficacy, what workers fear and what they think helps. Willingness to respond decides whether ambulances keep running in a crisis. Knowing what sways the choice helps agencies plan staffing before disaster hits. The results speak to every service that must hold during pandemics.
plos-pone-0009956:
Zhongwang Yu leads a 2010 PLOS ONE rat and cell study on alpha-synuclein, a protein that clumps in Parkinson's disease. In patients, clumps in brain cells carry a chemical change called nitration, where nitrogen groups attach to the protein. Whether that change itself harms nerve cells was unknown.

The team sent the changed protein into cultured dopamine nerve cells, which died far more than with the normal protein. Given into the key brain area of rats, the changed form killed dopamine cells there and caused Parkinson-like movement problems. The normal protein did much less harm. Nitrated alpha-synuclein, the authors argue, may be a main driver of the disease.
plos-pone-0010056:
Erik J Thompson and colleagues test computer models of proteins in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Such models, called force fields, set the energy rules for simulating how proteins fold and move in water. Small rule flaws can bend results, so checks against real data matter.

Using a shared global computing network, the team ran long simulations of spiral-shaped peptides and a larger five-spiral protein. One common model broke spirals too easily, and another gave several wrong traits. A third model kept the protein stable and matched lab measures well. The study helps simulators pick rules that keep helical, or spiral, proteins true to life.
plos-pone-0010156:
The authors were Mark Bain, Emily Cornwell, Kristine Hope, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study mapped a fish virus across the Great Lakes. The virus causes viral hemorrhagic septicemia and kills cultured and wild fish. Native to northern oceans and European fresh waters, it had become established in the Great Lakes, with large wild die-offs.

The team related the virus distribution to shipping, a likely route for spread between waters. Knowing how an invasive pathogen travels helps managers target inspections and ballast rules. Early mapping can slow the next waterway invasion before it takes hold.
plos-pone-0010256:
The authors were Makoto Kuroda, Harutaka Katano, Noriko Nakajima, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study read the 2009 pandemic flu virus with new sequencing tools. The H1N1 virus had emerged worldwide the year before. The team used a next-generation sequencer to read all RNA in lung tissue. The sample came from a patient killed by viral pneumonia.

Reading everything present, without targeting one germ, can reveal unexpected pathogens. They characterized quasispecies, the swarm of near-identical viral variants inside one host. That swarm view matters, because drug resistance and severity can hide in minor variants.
plos-pone-0010356:
Lucia Talamini and colleagues studied memory in early schizophrenia for PLOS ONE in 2010. People with the illness often struggle to recall past events well. An earlier model from the same group blamed weak use of context. In that view, memories are stored without enough of the surrounding detail. Retrieval then fails because the cues are too thin.

The team tested people in a first episode of the illness. Results fit the model's prediction: context effects on recall were reduced. Testing early cases matters, since long illness and medication can muddy results. If context binding is a core problem, training could target it directly. The study links a computer model of the mind to a real patient test.
plos-pone-0010456:
Qin Wang and colleagues found a new job for a calcium-based Wnt signal in prostate cancer for PLOS ONE in 2010. Wnt signals guide development and, when faulty, fuel disease. Their workings in prostate cancer were little known, though the cancer kills many men. The team measured a Wnt protein across human tissue samples first. They then tested the calcium branch of Wnt signaling in prostate cancer cells.

That branch reshaped the cells' inner skeleton and changed how they move. Cell movement underlies metastasis, the spread that makes prostate cancer deadly. A signal that drives movement is a candidate drug target. The study also connects a developmental pathway to a common adult cancer. It widens the map of what to block in advanced disease.
plos-pone-0010556:
Heleen Slagter and co-workers used brain imaging to watch conscious targets compete over time in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mind can only handle so much at once. That limit shows in the attentional blink: a second target seen too soon after a first is often missed. Theories agree the blink reflects competition for conscious access. The team scanned brains while subjects faced rapid streams with two targets.

Imaging revealed how brain activity for the targets rose and fell against each other. Neural competition, not simple erasure, seems to cause the blink. That view helps explain why the second target sometimes survives. It also links a classic psychology effect to measurable brain dynamics. Consciousness research gains a timed map of a bottleneck.
plos-pone-0010656:
Rebecca Baron and colleagues tested a compound that calms severe inflammation in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. During endotoxemia, a body-wide reaction to bacterial toxins, inflammation itself can kill. A protein called HMGA1 helps switch on many inflammatory genes at once.

The compound distamycin A blocked HMGA1 from gripping its DNA targets. With that grip broken, inflammation in lung and liver eased. Survival-related measures improved as well. Targeting a master switch, rather than one inflammatory signal at a time, offers a different strategy for treating runaway inflammation in critical illness.
plos-pone-0010756:
Steven Teo and Barbara Block compared tuna catches in the Gulf of Mexico, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Gulf is the main western Atlantic spawning ground for bluefin tuna. Directed fishing for bluefin there has been banned since the 1980s, yet longlines set for other species still catch them.

The team related yellowfin and bluefin catches to water conditions. The two species answered the same ocean in different ways. Temperature and depth patterns that drew one did not draw the other. Those differences are practical: fleets can adjust where and how they fish to keep yellowfin while sparing spawning bluefin.
plos-pone-0010856:
Anatoliy Kravets, Hong Qin, Ausaf Ahmad and co-authors published this yeast study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Candida albicans, a fungus that can infect people, sometimes survives harsh conditions by gaining or losing a whole chromosome. That trick creates a gene imbalance, and the authors asked how the fungus copes while the imbalance lasts.

They compared gene activity in normal cells with two copies of chromosome 5 against cells left with only one copy. At least two-fifths of the genes on the single chromosome were fully boosted back to normal output levels. Only a smaller share stayed reduced. Kravets and colleagues call this dosage compensation, a genome-wide balancing act. Understanding it may expose weak points in a pathogen that already resists many drugs.
plos-pone-0010956:
François Normand-Lauzière, Frédérique Frisch, Sébastien Labbé and co-authors published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fat in the blood after meals is suspected of damaging tissues and seeding type 2 diabetes. People whose parents both have diabetes showed abnormal fat handling when fat was infused, and the team asked whether the same fault appears after real eating.

They traced labeled fat through healthy offspring of two diabetic parents, healthy people without diabetic relatives, and patients with diabetes, during fasting, insulin infusion, and steady oral intake of a standard meal. In the offspring, the abnormal pattern seen with infusions was not fully established after food. Normand-Lauzière and colleagues map how an inherited diabetes risk develops step by step, before disease itself arrives.
plos-pone-0011056:
Benny Chen, Divino Deoliveira, Ivan Spasojevic and co-authors published this radiation study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Few drugs can rescue victims after lethal radiation exposure, a gap for both accidents and attacks. The authors tested human growth hormone, given after irradiation, in mice and then in monkeys.

Irradiated mice treated daily with the hormone survived at several times the rate of controls. Even a five-day course helped. Blood counts came back faster across white cells, T and B cells, natural killer cells, and above all platelets. Chen and colleagues extend the result toward monkeys, the needed step before human stocking decisions. A familiar hormone that is easy to make, and that buys survival after exposure, would fill a clear hole in radiation care.
plos-pone-0011156:
Chiavolini, Rangel-Moreno, Berg and colleagues tested a tularemia vaccine in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Tularemia is a severe infection that can be inhaled. After nasal vaccination, the team looked at immune tissue that forms in the airways and whether its presence tracked with survival.

Mice that formed this airway immune tissue were more likely to survive infection. That makes the tissue a useful sign that a vaccine is working. Vaccine makers can use such a sign to judge designs without waiting for full challenge tests. The work guides vaccines given through the nose, the route this germ naturally takes.
plos-pone-0011256:
De Meijer, Sverdlov, Popov and colleagues tested liver enzyme blockers in mice for PLOS ONE in 2010. Enzymes that remodel tissue can drive both injury and healing in the liver. Blocking the whole family curbed inflammation and liver injury in their mouse experiments.

Yet the same broad blockade made liver scarring, called fibrosis, worse. That paradox warns against blunt drugs in a system where the same enzymes do harm and good. Finer drugs that block only the harmful members may be needed. Liver doctors gain a clear caution for designing safer therapies.
plos-pone-0011356:
Matt Bianchi and co-workers examined in 2010 how sleep apnea changes the way sleep itself unfolds. In obstructive sleep apnea, the airway keeps closing during the night, and sleep breaks into short, restless pieces. Standard sleep scores count how long each stage lasts, but they miss how often the brain jumps from one stage to another.

The team tracked those stage-to-stage jumps and found that apnea alters the pattern of transitions through the night. Sleep in apnea patients does not just get shorter; it flows along different paths, with more abrupt shifts. Measuring transitions gives sleep doctors a richer picture of broken sleep than stage totals alone. It may help explain why patients still feel unrefreshed and could sharpen how treatment success is judged.
plos-pone-0011456:
Jun Song and co-authors profiled in 2010 the most dangerous minority inside head and neck tumors. These cancers contain a side population of cells that behaves like cancer stem cells, able to renew the tumor and survive treatment. The team isolated those cells and measured how they differ from the bulk of the tumor.

The side population proved highly invasive, resistant to chemotherapy, and marked by abnormal activity in the Wnt signaling pathway. That triple profile explains much treatment failure: therapy kills the ordinary cells while the toughest ones persist and rebuild. Profiling them gives drug hunters precise targets. A treatment that cannot kill this subpopulation will likely watch the tumor return, so future trials should be judged by whether they clear these cells too.
plos-pone-0011556:
Andreas Sjödin and co-authors read whole genomes in 2010 to compare lab-raised and wild strains of a feared bacterium. Francisella tularensis causes tularemia and is watched as a possible bioweapon, so knowing whether an outbreak strain came from nature or a laboratory has forensic weight. The team sequenced closely related strains with different histories: laboratory propagation versus natural circulation.

The two histories left distinct mutational patterns in the genomes, like different handwriting from different lives. Lab passage, with its bottlenecks and rich food, mutates a genome differently from survival in animals and ticks. Those signatures could help investigators attribute an outbreak correctly, a task where a wrong answer has political and medical consequences. The study also warns lab scientists that their strains drift from wild reality faster than they may assume.
plos-pone-0011656:
Michael Stern explored why people differ in their appetite for risk, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Willingness to take risks has a genetic component, and specific genes contributing to it have been found. Since risky choices often look irrational or harmful, it is puzzling that natural selection would favour them at all.

Stern argues that inherited wealth, or patrimony, changes the pay-off of gambling across generations. What a family stands to lose, or has to fall back on, shifts which risks are worth taking. His account links economic inheritance to the evolution of risk-taking behaviour in a fresh way.
plos-pone-0011756:
Matthew Angel and Mehmet Yanik found a way to make stem cell reprogramming with RNA work better, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making patient-matched pluripotent stem cells without using DNA would be safer for therapy. Delivering lab-made RNA into cells can express reprogramming proteins directly, but cells sense foreign RNA and raise innate immune alarms.

By suppressing that innate immune response, the authors enabled frequent repeated transfection with the RNA. Repeated doses are what reprogramming requires. Calming the cell's alarms thus opens the door to efficient, DNA-free production of stem cells for future treatments.
plos-pone-0011856:
Federico Degrange and co-authors analyzed in 2010 how an extinct terror bird fed, using the skull of Andalgalornis steulleti. Terror birds were flightless South American predators with huge hooked beaks and no close living match. This species was mid-sized for the family, at roughly forty kilograms, and built for life on the ground.

The team applied engineering-style mechanical analysis to the fossil skull, testing how it handled stress while biting and striking. Those tests suggest how the bird killed and processed prey without risking its own beak. Rebuilding feeding mechanics from bone turns a silent fossil into evidence about how one of South America's top predators actually made its living.
plos-pone-0011956:
Guanghou Shui and co-workers examined in 2010 which raw materials two yeast enzymes prefer when building membrane fats. Phosphatidic acid is the starting point for all the glycerophospholipids that form cell membranes. It is made when enzymes of the LPAAT family attach a fatty chain to a simpler precursor.

Using lipidomic measurements, which catalog fats in bulk, plus a direct activity assay, the team characterized the substrate tastes of the yeast enzymes Slc1p and Cst26p. Knowing which chains each enzyme favors explains how yeast tailors its membrane mix. Membrane composition affects everything from drug sensitivity to stress tolerance, so enzyme preferences are levers for engineering yeast.
plos-pone-0012056:
Duncan Menge, Jeanne DeNoyer, and Jeremy Lichstein put in 2010 a neat tale about old woods to the test, and the tale failed. The puzzle is plain. Trees that make their own nitrogen with the help of root germs are rare in old woods of the mild zone. Yet those woods are often short of nitrogen. One tale blamed the family tree of the woods: no old-woods kind in these parts, it said, comes from stock that can fix nitrogen.

The team's checks show that the shape of the family tree does not in fact explain why the fixers are so scarce. With the stock tale cleared away, eyes turn back to the woods as they are: poor light and some nitrogen in the soil may make fixing not worth the cost. Tests that kill a neat tale are how field science keeps its tales true.
plos-pone-0012156:
Alexandra Le Bras, Chantal Samson, Matteo Trentini, and co-authors studied a gene switched on in blood vessel lining cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. New vessels sprout from old ones during growth, and the lining cells lead that sprouting. The gene they studied is mostly active in those lining cells, which made its control switches a natural target for study.

They found two control regions for the gene: a far-off enhancer and a nearby promoter, both directed by two vessel-cell regulators. Control maps like this show how a cell keeps the right genes on for its job. They also flag switches that vessel diseases, or vessel-growing tumors, might hijack.
plos-pone-0012256:
Frank Emmert-Streib proposed a new measure of complexity in PLOS ONE in 2010. Judging how complex an observed object or pattern is has resisted a single good answer for decades. The classic approach, based on the shortest possible description, is elegant but often impossible to compute for real data, and it treats random noise as maximally complex, which clashes with intuition.

His measure, statistic complexity, joins that classic idea with an ensemble approach that samples many descriptions. It is designed to rate structured patterns as complex and both total order and total randomness as simpler. A workable complexity measure is useful anywhere patterns must be compared, from genomes to markets to machine learning.
plos-pone-0012356:
Mykola Maydan, Paul McDonald, Jasbinder Sanghera and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2010 that a disputed cell protein truly works as a kinase. Integrin-linked kinase, or ILK, helps cells stick to their surroundings and organize their inner skeleton. Some scientists doubted that ILK could add phosphate tags to other proteins at all, which left its true job in doubt.

The team showed that ILK needs manganese to work and that it places a phosphate tag on a key target, GSK-3 beta, which controls many cell decisions. Proving ILK is a real, working kinase settles a long argument. It also makes ILK a clearer target for drugs aimed at cancer and other diseases of cell growth.
plos-pone-0012456:
Fei Wang, Shi Huang and Long Ma studied gene clusters in the worm Caenorhabditis elegans, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. In worms, some genes sit in operons, groups read together from one switch and then cut into separate messages. Splicing can also make several message versions from one gene, adding variety.

The team found operon genes carry more multi-version genes than average and use their splice sites in distinctive ways. The pattern shows operons are not plain read-through systems; they fine-tune output per gene. Worms are a basic model for gene control, so these rules inform genetics far beyond one small animal.
plos-pone-0012556:
Arno van Kuijk, Jeroen DeGroot, Rishma Koeman and colleagues measured blood markers in early psoriatic arthritis drug trials, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Drug developers want soluble biomarkers — blood signals — that show quickly whether a new treatment engages joint and bone damage, before large trials commit. The team compared the drug adalimumab with placebo in small proof-of-concept trials.

Markers of cartilage and bone metabolism shifted in informative ways under treatment. On the group level, such markers can screen candidate drugs cheaply and early. For psoriatic arthritis, where joint damage accumulates silently, fast readouts shorten the road to better therapies.
plos-pone-0012656:
Bol, Desjardins, Reusens and co-authors asked whether a mismatch between early and later diet sets male mice up for disease. Surveys and animal work link poor feeding before birth, followed by rich food later, to the metabolic syndrome. Their 2010 study tested that chain in mice, watching blood pressure and blood vessels.

The design follows pups whose early nutrition differed from their adult diet. Outcomes in such mice test whether the mismatch itself, not just rich food, drives high blood pressure and artery disease. Answers matter for advice given to mothers and infants worldwide.
plos-pone-0012756:
Hall, Espinoza, Benbow and co-authors charted HIV infection across America's large cities. The national epidemic stays centred in urban areas, yet each city has its own pattern of who is hit hardest. Their 2010 study gathered city-level data to compare those local profiles side by side.

The contrasts matter because a plan that works in one city may miss the mark in another. Prevention money and testing sites do the most good when aimed at the local pattern. Their survey gives city health departments a shared evidence base for tailoring the response.
plos-pone-0012856:
Vivithanaporn, Maingat, Lin and co-authors showed that a hepatitis C protein stirs brain immune cells and worsens HIV's brain harm. Hepatitis C genetic material and proteins are found in human brain tissue. What HIV and hepatitis C co-infection does to the brain, though, was unclear when they wrote in 2010.

Their study found the HCV core protein activates neuroimmune responses and adds to HIV-1's toxic effect on neurons. Co-infected patients face brain risks beyond either virus alone. The result supports brain screening in co-infection care.  Brain cells in culture let the team isolate the effect.
plos-pone-0326556:
Nelson Pang and Jessie Yeung traced how Canadians use four kinds of mental health providers over time: family doctors, psychiatrists, psychologists, and social workers. Seven cycles of a national health survey from 2007 to 2020 supplied the trends, and the most recent cycle supported a deeper analysis of who uses which door into care.

Family doctors were consistently the most accessed, and psychiatrists the least, while use of psychologists and social workers climbed late in the period. Women used family doctors and social workers more than men but psychiatrists less, and older adults showed their own pattern. Knowing which door each group actually uses helps planners fix the bottlenecks that matter instead of expanding the wrong service.
plos-pone-0331156:
Vanessa Mitschke, Francesco Grassi, Alperen Doğaner, and Anne Schacht wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. Their field is emotion research, and their subject is how people judge the social meaning of scenes that carry feeling. The work is built as a large-scale rating study with several dimensions rated at once.

Participants rated affective scenes, meaning pictures that stir emotions, on how socially relevant each scene feels. Gathering many ratings across many scenes lets the authors map which features make a scene feel socially important. Other researchers can use that map when choosing picture sets for experiments on emotion, attention, and social judgment.
plos-pone-0336456:
Ulla Lichtenhagen and co-authors ran two experiments in 2026 on eyewitness lineups when a crime had several culprits. Guidelines say to show suspects in separate lineups, yet seeing culprits together might jog memory through familiar faces.

Volunteers watched a staged crime video with four culprits, then faced lineups shown together or one by one. The first experiment found no clear difference in spotting that a culprit was present. Further testing probed the idea that one recognised face cues another. The question matters for police practice, where a small gain in detection must be weighed against fairness to suspects.
plos-pone-0339756:
Janerra Allen, Elliot Hong, and Fow-Sen Choa published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It works with task-based fMRI, brain scans recorded while people perform set tasks. The authors build models of the brain's energy landscape and its changing states, aiming to extract biomarkers for schizophrenia.

A biomarker is a measurable sign that can help identify a condition or track its course. Modeling brain activity as states that rise and fall may reveal patterns plain averages would hide. If such signs prove reliable, they could support earlier or more objective assessment in schizophrenia, which is still diagnosed mainly by interview and observation.
plos-pone-0340156:
Xia Guan and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about maize, the corn plant. Gibberellins are plant hormones that drive growth, and bioactive forms control height and flowering. The authors measure natural variation in these hormone levels across maize tissues in North America.

Knowing how hormone levels differ between tissues and plant lines is basic knowledge for breeding. Breeders selecting for stature or stress tolerance work with growth hormones whether they measure them or not. A map of natural variation gives them starting material and targets. Plant scientists across the maize belt are the readers for this kind of baseline survey.
plos-pone-0340256:
Leonardo Sorbelli and colleagues described a fossil bovid from an early Pliocene lake site in Catalonia, Spain, in 2026. Fourteen animals were found, several as near complete skeletons, an unusual wealth of material for sorting out tangled fossil cattle naming.

After close comparison with related fossil genera from Europe and Africa, the team placed the animal in Parabos and recognised five valid species across two genera. The skeletons point to life in wet, plant rich surroundings. Whether these animals were the first of the modern cattle line or the last of an older one remains open, and the rich material frames that question sharply.
plos-pone-0340756:
Valeria Rios Montoya and co-authors compared vaccine coverage and infant deaths across countries from twenty ten to twenty twenty-three, using World Health Organization and UNICEF records for six routine childhood vaccines. They grouped countries by income to test a blunt question: does wider vaccination lower child deaths even where poverty and weak services hold coverage back?

Richer countries had both higher coverage and far fewer infant deaths, while poorer countries lagged on both counts. Coverage dipped worldwide in the pandemic year and had only partly recovered three years later. Once income was accounted for, most links between coverage and survival faded. The team concludes that unfair starting conditions, not vaccine effort alone, drive the gap in child deaths.
plos-pone-0341756:
Ueamporn Summart and four colleagues published this 2026 study adapting a short social support questionnaire for Thai patients with blood cancers. The eight-question scale asks how much illness-specific support patients feel. The team translated it, adjusted it for Thai culture, and tested it on several hundred patients at three hospitals in the northeast.

Statistical checks on split halves of the sample confirmed the scale's structure and accuracy. Summart concludes the Thai version is a quick, valid way to gauge support, and urges cancer teams to weigh family and social backing as part of care.
plos-pone-0342856:
Shira Linsk, Anna Thonis, and Kristin M. Winchell count moths across New York City to see how city life treats them. Moths react quickly to harm in their surroundings, so they work well as warning species. Their 2026 study merges public sightings posted by residents with the team's own night sampling in twelve spots across six parks.

Moth variety fell as built-up land and night lighting rose. Places with more broad-leaf tree cover and open land held richer moth life. The public records missed some species the team caught by hand, so both data sources were needed. Keeping parks darker at night and holding on to tree cover emerge as simple ways to help city moths persist.
plos-pone-0343756:
Juan Xiang and co-authors built a cheap DNA fingerprinting kit for cowpea, an important legume grown worldwide. Breeders need fast ways to tell varieties apart, protect their rights, and check seed purity. Their 2026 study sequenced nineteen cowpea accessions and mined the results for stable genetic markers.

The scan found hundreds of thousands of variants, narrowed to a high-quality set for analysis. The accessions fell into three genetic groups. From the data, the team picked just six core markers, all inside genes, that together separated every accession. Each variety received a fingerprint profile and its own QR code. Xiang and colleagues offer the kit as a low-cost tool for breeding and seed testing.
plos-pone-0344656:
Qing He and colleagues charted the chemistry of ageing in base liquor for Sichuan's strong-aroma baijiu, sampled at one, five, ten, fifteen, and twenty years. Seventy-five flavour compounds were tracked with mass spectrometry, metabolomics, and three-dimensional fluorescence scans to see how the spirit's character is built and lost over time in storage.

Esters, the fruity backbone, fell steeply after year five. Acids peaked at five years, alcohols at ten, and polyphenols at fifteen, each then declining. Fluorescence shifted toward longer wavelengths, signalling growing molecular complexity and richer flavour. The authors say the timeline gives distillers a scientific grip on ageing and quality control.
plos-pone-0345056:
Collins Mukubesa and colleagues reviewed records of three hundred sixteen tuberculosis patients treated at a rural general hospital in Zambia, asking who dies during treatment and why. Nearly one patient in five died, a heavy toll for a curable disease. The team followed patients from the start of treatment to their recorded outcome over up to a year.

Death risk rose with age, with a diagnosis made on symptoms alone rather than lab proof, and in patients also living with HIV. Two things protected people: being watched over by family-based treatment supporters and starting treatment at a higher body weight. For rural programs, the message is plain: confirm cases in the lab, support patients at home, and treat weight loss as a warning sign, not a side note.
plos-pone-0345356:
Rayhanah Almutairi and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a cross-sectional study of nurses working in Saudi Arabia. The authors look at job satisfaction and burnout, and at how feeling supported and skilled at work connects with both.

The central idea is resilience, the ability to recover from strain, acting as an indirect pathway between workplace support and outcomes. Nurses who felt their skills were growing and their institution backed them are examined alongside their resilience levels. Hospital managers concerned with keeping nurses in the job are the readers most likely to use these links.
plos-pone-0345956:
Sawera Qureshi and colleagues built machine learning classifiers that read short summaries of aviation incidents and sort each as an incident or an accident, matching the official label. The dataset covers eighty years and more than fifty thousand events from Canada's transportation safety board. Manual sorting is slow and inconsistent, and wrong labels can hide safety problems.

Three classic text classifiers were compared on the same word-weighted features. Fast automatic triage can flag possibly mislabeled reports and speed severity checks when reports flood in. Aviation runs more than a hundred thousand safe flights a day, and its safety culture depends on learning from every occurrence. Studies like this test whether algorithms can shoulder the sorting work reliably.
plos-pone-0346056:
Sangrok Lee and Taehyun Jung asked if AI inventions act like the rare tools that change whole industries. Steam power and electric grids did this in the past. The pair tested the idea with patents from one firm, Samsung. They looked at filings from 1982 to 2018 and matched AI patents with like non-AI ones.

The AI patents won on all three counts. Later work built on them more. They reached into more fields. And they paired with other tech more often. The gaps held up under many checks. Lee and Jung say this helps explain why firms keep pouring cash into AI.
plos-pone-0346156:
Cristina Davino and colleagues set out to measure educational poverty, the lack of real chances to learn and grow, among teenagers in Naples, Italy. Rather than count only school results, they surveyed young people aged fifteen to nineteen about their family life, their schooling, and the world around their homes. Then they looked for the hidden patterns that tie those answers together.

Three broad forces stood out: family, school, and environment. Grouping the teenagers by these forces showed clear types, from well supported to badly deprived, and family background, language grades, gender, and school type all tracked with the groups. The authors offer their model as a first tool for spotting which young people are being left with the fewest chances.
plos-pone-0346656:
Mayuko Harada and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on the silkworm Bombyx mori, the moth whose larvae spin silk. The authors identify an atypical microRNA in it, a small gene-regulating molecule that breaks the usual pattern. The molecule also carries sequence variation between individuals or strains.

MicroRNAs fine-tune gene activity, and an unusual one can reveal new biology or serve as a marker. Silkworms are both an industrial animal and a model insect, so findings spread in two directions. Insect geneticists and sericulture researchers, who breed silkworms for silk, share the audience for this identification.
plos-pone-0346756:
Hussam Hamou and colleagues test machine learning for predicting brain bleed relapse in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Chronic subdural hematoma is a slow blood collection under the skull covering, and surgery is followed by relapse needing a second operation in a share of cases. Predicting relapse could focus follow-up scans on those at risk.

The team studied five hundred and sixty-four surgery patients at one center and trained three model types on thirty-one routine variables. The best model scored only modestly on held-out patients and was overconfident in its single-patient risks. At a cautious threshold it could spare scans for only about a third of non-relapse patients. Relapse likely depends on factors routine records miss.
plos-pone-0347556:
Angela Esohe Adeoti-Lawani and colleagues measured lasting protein leakage in urine samples from children in Nigeria who live with sickle cell anaemia. Such leakage is an early warning of kidney damage that single tests often miss. Nigeria carries the world's heaviest burden of the disease. One hundred forty-nine affected children and the same number of matched healthy children gave urine samples, repeated after at least three months for those testing positive.

Nearly a quarter of the sickle cell group had persistent proteinuria, against under three percent of controls. Children with the leakage had lower levels of fetal haemoglobin, the protective form that softens the disease. The authors urge routine repeated screening so kidney damage is caught while still reversible.
plos-pone-0347656:
Lori Reider and colleagues recorded parents and young children in the United States and Hong Kong reading a picture book about snakes, spiders, lizards, and turtles, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Thirty-one families in each place took part, and the team coded how much fear and negative language crept into the talk, alongside questionnaires on fear beliefs.

Across both cultures, snakes and spiders drew more fear and harsher words than lizards and turtles. Hong Kong parents expressed more snake fear than American parents, passing a stronger signal even where children's own beliefs were similar. The study shows one quiet route by which animal fears are handed down: the words parents choose at story time.
plos-pone-0347856:
Marielle Ribeiro Feitosa, Fernanda Rebelo, and co-authors followed new mothers in a Brazilian city to find what most threatens the early bond between mother and baby. The months after birth place heavy demands on women, and a weakened bond can affect both mother and child. Their 2026 study assessed mothers at three and six months after delivery, measuring bonding quality and depression symptoms with standard questionnaires, in a group considered low risk.

Postpartum depression stood out as the strongest predictor of impaired bonding at both time points, including specific problems like damaged attachment and anxiety about the baby. Social support pulled the other way, protecting the bond.
