Right-heart dysfunction made no microbial difference either. Across the wider heart failure spectrum, though, clear shifts showed up, including in Streptococcus, Alistipes, and Bacteroides. The authors read cachexia's gut signal as subtle at most and call for much larger cohorts. Heart failure does reshape the gut; the wasting stage may add no signature of its own.
pmc-13245756:
Panth, Devkota, and Waiba examined a sacred tree's chemistry for diabetes potential, in this 2026 PLOS One study. Elaeocarpus angustifolius, the rudraksha tree, is used traditionally across South Asia. The team screened its bark extracts for plant compounds, measured antioxidant strength. Tested whether the extracts block two starch-digesting enzymes that diabetes drugs target, then ran a twenty-eight-day feeding study in animals and computer docking analyses.

The extracts were rich in phenolics and flavonoids, scavenged free radicals more strongly than the reference compound quercetin in one fraction. Inhibited both enzymes far more potently than the standard drug acarbose in test tubes. Treated animals showed lower fasting glucose, modestly better blood fats, and fuller liver glycogen stores. The authors present the tree as a credible source of antidiabetic leads needing clinical study.
pmc-13247256:
Yuan, Zhang, and Xiang evaluated a Chinese farm policy's effect on the urban-rural income gap in this 2026 Scientific Reports study. Agricultural socialized services, organizations that sell farmers services like mechanized planting and pest control, were piloted in selected cities to raise rural earnings. The team used panel data from prefecture-level cities between 2012 and 2024 and a difference-in-differences design that tracks policy rollouts over time.

Pilot cities did see their income gaps narrow, a result surviving placebo and robustness checks. The narrowing worked through industrial upgrading and faster urbanization. Benefits were stronger in central and western provinces and major grain areas, but insignificant for the lowest-income groups. The authors offer the findings as a reference for other developing countries building farm service systems.
pmc-13247656:
Yennurajalingam and Bruera defend their pilot trial in this 2026 response letter in Palliative and Supportive Care. Their study had tested a stimulant, methylphenidate, combined with physical activity against cancer-related fatigue in patients receiving PD-1 immunotherapy, and another researcher's letter had questioned aspects of the work. The authors answer point by point in this published reply.

They explain that the many secondary outcome measures were deliberate: a pilot study should learn which fatigue instruments respond most sensitively, to arm the larger trial properly. Strict eligibility criteria, they argue, minimized the worst confounders, while questions of optimal dose, duration, cancer subgroups, and broader representation are reserved for an adequately powered phase III study now planned. Their bottom line: the combination looks very promising and justifies that bigger test.
pmc-13248356: Wang and colleagues published this correction in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2026. It concerns their paper on nanoparticles coated with platelet membrane, designed to carry drugs to tumors. Figure 7a in the original article was wrong, showing material from an incorrect injection time point. The authors identified the right data, prepared a revised figure, and display both versions in the notice for transparency. The original article has been updated, and its findings stand as reported.
pmc-13248956:
HyeSeong Jeon and JungYoon Kim reframe childhood bedwetting through family therapy in a 2026 review. Bedwetting care often stops at the child's body, yet family habits steer whether care sticks. The authors bring in medical family therapy as a joining framework.

Their search crossed international and Korean databases for studies on body, mind, and family factors. Combined approaches beat single-track care in the gathered proof. Parent understanding, coping style, and family communication all shaped outcomes. The therapy model adds shared goal setting and relapse prevention to standard steps. The authors say this wider lens lifts both symptom control and family wellbeing.
pmc-13249956:
Liu and colleagues model a software firm's leap from selling programs to running a platform, in a 2026 Scientific Reports study. Using evolutionary game theory, they set three players in motion: a government offering subsidies, a platform organizer, and users deciding whether to join. Simulations followed the ecosystem through early, mature, and ideal stages.

Subsidies and cost sharing proved decisive for whether the platform stabilized. Sharing twenty to forty percent of costs encouraged users to adopt without spoiling the organizer's incentives. Beyond forty percent, organizers grew reluctant to offer advanced services, risking the whole ecosystem. The authors advise stage-specific subsidy withdrawal and carefully tuned cost sharing for industrial software policy.
pmc-13250756:
The EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes issued this 2026 safety opinion on a food enzyme made by a common mould. The enzyme, a glucosidase that breaks down starch chains, is produced by the Aspergillus niger strain AE-GN and is planned for use in 13 food-making processes.

The panel estimated daily intake across European diets and compared it with rat safety tests. Genetic damage tests raised no concern, and the safe dose in rats sat hundreds of times above expected intake. Two matches with known breathing allergens were found, so an allergy risk cannot be fully ruled out, though it is judged low. The panel concluded the enzyme raises no safety concern as intended.
pmc-13251656:
Daniel Ahari and a large team map the published evidence on idiopathic granulomatous mastitis in a 2026 scoping review. The condition is a rare, chronic breast inflammation of unknown cause, with uneven diagnosis and treatment around the world. The team wanted to judge how strong and how global the research base really is.

Their search found 225 primary studies and five systematic reviews covering 13,062 patients in thirty-nine countries, with Turkey contributing the most. Most studies were small, retrospective, and run at single centers. About one patient in six appeared in possibly overlapping cohorts, since some author groups published repeatedly on the same populations. Judged by standard evidence levels, most treatment reports ranked as weak case series, and only three randomized trials existed. The authors conclude that current evidence cannot firmly guide practice and call for prospective, randomized work.
pmc-13253656:

pmc-13277356:

pmc-13279656:

pmc-13279956:

pmc-13280456:

pmc-13280656:

pmc-13280756:

pmc-13281856:

pmc-13282256:

pmc-13283456:

pmc-13283656:

pmc-13283956:

pmc-13284156:

pmc-13284756:

pmc-13284856:

pmc-13286356:

pmc-13286856:

pmc-13286956:

pmc-13287056:

pmc-13288056:

pmc-13289256:

pmc-13289356:

pmc-13289456:

pmc-13289656:

pmc-13290556:

pmc-13291356:

pmc-13291556:

pmc-13291656:

pmc-13291756:

Third-generation concentrated growth factor, spun at variable speeds, holds dense fibrin and CD34+ progenitor cells. A newer purified fraction keeps mainly tiny vesicles and exosomes, which may act through microRNA signals that shape hair follicle cycling. The letter closes by noting early signs of better injection comfort with that fraction.
pmc-13291956:
Yawen Hu, Klorenta Nitaj, and Cristina Nevado achieve remote alkene difunctionalization with strict handedness control in 2026. Adding two different groups across a double bond is a fast route to complex molecules. Doing it five atoms away from the starting point, while fixing mirror-image form, has resisted chemists because radical steps are fleeting and wild. Their cascade starts by cracking open a strained vinylcyclopropane ring with light-driven catalysis.

The opened radical then passes through a sulfinyl-Smiles rearrangement that transfers chirality in a controlled step. This route sidesteps a slow hydrogen transfer step that blocked earlier attempts. Both sulfur-centered and carbon-centered radicals fit the sequence. Products were enriched amides with a double bond left at the far end, formed in high mirror-image purity. Conditions stayed mild throughout the cascade. The authors present the method as a general platform for remote, asymmetric editing of alkenes.
pmc-13292256:
Min Hong, Chunrong Ma, and Gang Chen open a 2026 research topic editorial on making energy storage materials in greener ways. Demand for batteries and supercapacitors keeps rising, and their production footprint matters for carbon neutrality goals. The collected articles mix green synthesis, modern manufacturing, AI, and recycling.

One contribution uses neural networks and support vector machines to tune microalgae systems that clean waste while yielding carbon for electrodes. Another applies machine learning to speed catalyst discovery for hydrogen production and carbon dioxide reduction, cutting reliance on costly simulations. The editors frame the collection as a roadmap toward circular, lower-impact energy storage. They also flag open issues such as how well AI models transfer across materials and scales.
pmc-13292356:
Jana D Javakhishvili and co-authors issue a 2026 position paper for the Global Collaboration on Traumatic Stress on mental health support while war is still raging. Most existing frameworks assume the disaster is over, leaving helpers little guidance under continuous threat. The paper blends a literature search, a scoping review on support during ongoing conflicts, and the authors' clinical experience.

They argue that demand for scalable, culturally fitting care outstrips what current systems supply. Recommendations span policy, training, staff care, and research. The authors champion trauma-informed, rights-based systems that build local capacity and lean on measurement-guided, stepped care blending digital tools with transdiagnostic models. Their stated hope is to spark research, innovation, and worldwide cooperation for communities under enduring armed conflict.
pmc-13292656:
Christine Zürcher and colleagues run a 2026 pilot trial on oil pulling, the Ayurvedic mouth-swirling ritual now viral on social media, asking whether it lifts oral health-related quality of life. Eighty gingivitis patients at a university dental hospital were randomized to swish sesame oil or distilled water for fifteen minutes each morning over eight weeks, alongside normal hygiene. Impact scores were taken at baseline, four weeks, and eight weeks.

Both groups improved significantly on the OHIP-14 questionnaire by week four and held the gains at week eight. Yet the oil group never beat the water group at any time point; the between-group gaps were all statistically insignificant. The authors read the result plainly: the daily ritual itself, whatever the liquid, seems to carry the benefit. They suggest oil pulling may support mechanical hygiene as a feel-good add-on.
pmc-13292756:
A letter to the editor by Jiamin Wang and a co-author, published in 2026, questions how well a recent study links faster biological aging to diabetic retinopathy. The study under discussion used UK Biobank data and three aging measures.

Wang argues that the cohort does not match routine diabetes care, since most participants were of European ancestry and people with missing data were left out. The letter also notes that only a starting blood sugar value was used, not control over time. Eye disease was counted from hospital records, which miss early cases found by community screening. The authors urge caution before using aging scores in clinic.
pmc-13292856:
Eti Apriyanti and co-authors review, in 2026, the chemistry and drug promise of Piper crocatum, known as red betel. The plant is used in traditional care across Southeast Asia, yet its compounds and effects had not been pulled together.

Following standard review steps, the team screened records from 2000 to 2026 and kept 102 original studies. Forty compounds are reported from the plant, spanning several chemical families. Lab work links them to killing microbes, blocking biofilms, and easing inflammation, oxidation, and high blood sugar. Four compounds look most promising as starting points for new drugs, though body handling tests are still needed.
pmc-13293656:
Nicha Puangmalai and co-authors identify, in a 2026 study, a channel protein called connexin 50 that helps harmful alpha-synuclein clumps spread between brain cells. Clumping and spread of this protein mark several degenerative brain diseases, yet the routes of spread were unclear.

The protein was found touching synuclein clumps in human diseased brain tissue, and channel activity ran high in mouse diseased tissue unless the channel was blocked. Cells with the channel took up brain-derived clumps in a strain-dependent way. Lowering the channel in mixed nerve and support cell cultures cut uptake and clumping. It may be an early drug target.
pmc-13293756:
Nathan Andreani Netzel and colleagues design, in a 2026 paper, an onboard computer for small experimental rockets built by university teams. The computer must log sensor data, spot flight phases, and fire recovery charges reliably on a tight budget.

The board pairs a common microcontroller with motion and pressure sensors, memory storage, two firing channels, and a sturdy power system, run by strict real-time software. A hardware-in-the-loop rig feeds fake sensor signals from flight simulations to test the full chain without launching. Tests caught high-energy, low-energy, and peak-height phases reliably under realistic conditions. Design files and data are shared for reuse.
pmc-13293856:
Oscar Morton and co-authors measure how much forest loss mining sets off beyond the pit itself across sub-Saharan Africa, in a 2026 analysis. Demand for African minerals is climbing fast, and mines clear land directly for pits, waste ponds, and heaps. Using continent-wide land-use data and a statistical method that compares mined and unmined areas over time, the team assessed more than sixteen thousand mines between 2001 and 2020.

Direct clearing totaled 187,000 hectares of dense forest. The wider effect dwarfed it: for each hectare cleared at the mine, about thirty-four more hectares vanished nearby within five years through farms, settlements, and roads that follow mining. Elevated clearing persisted up to twenty kilometers away a decade later. Cobalt and copper mines drove the largest extra losses, a warning for clean-energy supply chains.
pmc-13294056:
Xiadiye Tuerhong and coauthors subtype colon adenocarcinoma by programmed cell death patterns in a 2026 multi-omics study. Ten clustering methods sorted tumors, and 113 machine learning approaches competed to build a risk signature from death-related genes. Single-cell and spatial data then located the lead gene, with bench tests to confirm its role.

Five subtypes emerged with distinct outlooks. An 18-gene signature predicted risk and survival across training and outside cohorts, and tied to immune surroundings, mutation load, and immunotherapy response. The core gene TERT sat mainly in malignant epithelial cells. Silencing TERT slowed growth, movement, invasion, and colony formation in lab cells.
pmc-13294156:
Yelda Fırat applies explainable machine learning to blood dendritic cells in non-infectious uveitis for a 2026 study. Eye inflammation from immune causes lacks clear molecular sorting. Transcript data for CD1c-positive dendritic cells came from two public cohorts totaling 78 people, merged with a leakage-free pipeline that selected 20 genes from 8,815 candidates using training data only.

A regularized logistic model won, with cross-checked area of 0.863 and test area of 0.855, plus recall of 90.9% in the reported metrics. Leaving one dataset out still averaged 0.82, backing portability. Explanation scores crowned CD180 and TLR7 as top markers, and pathway work pointed to chemokine and Toll-like signaling.
pmc-13294256:
Zhen Peng and co-authors model how cooperating molecular chains could have survived on the early Earth, in a 2026 origins-of-life study. Life's first genetic polymers faced a puzzle: complex jobs seem to need long chains, yet long chains are hard to build and copy. One answer is teamwork among shorter chains, each doing a simpler job. The team built a computer model that tracks such systems without enumerating every possible sequence, so chain length stays uncapped.

The model first reproduced known results: cooperation persists more easily when chains are short and efficient, and when they sit in compartments or spread slowly. The group then added a third partner, a catalyst that inhibits copying errors. Error control, they found, could plausibly emerge from a separate specialist molecule rather than one talented proofreading enzyme. The result widens the plausible routes from chemistry to inheritance.
pmc-13294356:
Yaxian Cheng and a large team, writing as a 2026 letter, boost protein output from natural messenger RNA without editing DNA. Permanent genome edits and RNA editors carry off-target risks, and direct control of translation stayed hard. Their trick guides CRISPR tools to place translation-friendly marks: the m6A reader YTHDF1, which helps ribosomes engage, is recruited to chosen transcripts.

Targeted reader engagement lifted protein production from the cell's own genes while leaving genome sequence and RNA letters untouched. Reversible, programmable tuning at the translation step could treat diseases of low protein output more gently than cutting DNA, a claim now needing disease-model tests.
pmc-13294456:
Petra Frýdlová and colleagues probe how leopard geckos sense an approaching predator, in a 2026 animal behavior study. These nocturnal lizards can pick up chemical traces, sights, and vibrations, yet which channel actually triggers defense was unclear. The team presented each cue alone and in combination, simulating a snake predator, and recorded both tongue flicking, a sampling behavior, and overt defensive displays.

Chemical information drove the show. Smell-track cues alone raised sampling and were the only trigger for defensive postures and mouth displays. Sight and vibration cues changed little on their own, but they amplified chemical sampling when paired with scent. Modeling suggested the senses mostly add together: secondary cues heighten alertness, while costly defense stays gated behind chemical confirmation. For a night hunter's prey, the nose rules.
pmc-13294756:
Jillian Cassidy and colleagues report a rare fluid problem after weight-loss stomach surgery, in a 2026 case report. A thirty-four-year-old woman had robotic sleeve gastrectomy, in which most of the stomach is removed. She came back with nausea, vomiting, and a swollen belly, and scans showed a large pool of fluid with no leak from the stomach itself.

Draining the fluid helped only briefly, since milky fluid built up again fast, a sign of chyle leaking from hurt lymph vessels. Drugs and a low-fat diet failed to stop the leak. Seventy-one days after the first operation, the team washed out six liters of milky fluid and placed drains near the spot that seemed to leak. The authors stress how rare lymph injury is after this surgery.
pmc-13294856:
Zhe Ling and Mingyang Ren ask whether anxiety during shingles predicts lasting nerve pain in a 2026 cohort study. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most common and distressing after-effect of herpes zoster. Whether feelings during the acute illness add warning value beyond age and pain itself was unclear.

Ninety-nine patients treated between January 2022 and January 2025 had anxiety measured at the start and were followed for pain lasting 90 days. About four in ten developed lasting pain, and those patients had started with clearly higher anxiety scores. Adding anxiety scores to age and pain measures sharpened prediction, supporting routine anxiety screening in acute shingles care.
pmc-13295056:
Agnes Candido Teixeira and co-authors load magnetic nanoparticles into a flexible hybrid material meant to cook diseased tissue gently, in a 2026 study. Magnetic hyperthermia heats iron oxide particles with an alternating field until nearby cells die, a minimally invasive cancer strategy. The particles here sit inside a siloxane and polyether matrix, and the team varied whether each particle's surface was water-loving or water-fearing to see how the coating steers the final material.

Structural checks confirmed the right iron oxide phases formed and the matrix stayed intact, though particles gathered into clusters with well-dispersed ones between. Water-fearing particles lost their coating inside the matrix, clumped more, and heated worse than their water-loving counterparts, which kept a stronger magnetic response. Surface chemistry, the authors conclude, must be chosen to survive embedding, or the therapy loses its punch before it starts.
pmc-13295156:
A 2026 correction by Said Al-Khalasi and co-authors fixes figure faults in their lamb feed study. One chart carried the wrong caption. It spoke of slaughter and carcass results, when the chart in fact showed digestibility values. The chart also sat in the wrong place in both the print and web forms of the article.

The notice gives the right caption for the chart. It renames the chart as Figure 1, so the order now reads straight through. All other figures were renumbered to match that order. The item is a correction only, and no results are changed by it.
pmc-13295456:
Zhenghang Li and colleagues add tomato pigment to sheep egg cells growing in the lab and watch them thrive, in a 2026 study. Lycopene, the red carotenoid in tomatoes, fights oxidative damage, and eggs matured in dishes suffer exactly that kind of harm from reactive oxygen. The team cultured sheep oocytes and then artificially activated embryos across four lycopene doses, checking maturation signs, embryo development, and cell health markers.

A middle dose did the most good. Eggs matured more completely, with tidier chromosome spindles and wider helper-cell expansion, and embryos cleaved and reached the blastocyst stage at higher rates. Reactive oxygen fell while the protective molecule glutathione rose, mitochondria worked harder, and blastocysts carried more cells. Genes for stress defense and cell death shifted in favorable directions. Too much lycopene backfired at the top dose, a reminder that supplements have sweet spots.
pmc-13295656:
Cundong Liu and colleagues search for shared targets of hormone-disrupting chemicals in four urogenital cancers in a 2026 study. Such chemicals leak from plastics, pesticides, and care products and may help cancers start. A combined computer framework linked 12 chemicals to bladder, kidney, prostate, and testicular tumours.

Each cancer showed its own short list of shared hub proteins, with a growth receptor appearing in three of the four. One predicted pairing, a common pollutant with a death-control protein, was taken to the bench for checking. Long exposure at realistic levels steadied that protein in several cancer cell lines, backing the predictions.
pmc-13295756:
Taiyo Ikeido and colleagues teach software to read surgical video with little hand labeling, in a 2026 study. Long operation films hold the steps and fine moves of surgery, but marking them by hand costs expert time. The team kept a pretrained surgical vision-language encoder frozen and added a light adapter that gathers frames into clips while staying true to the learned image-text space.

On a standard gallbladder surgery set, the adapter lifted step naming over the base model. A text-guided method with rich step prompts scored best among those tried. The setup also named fine action triplets, tool, act, and target, from a few examples, with no special classifier trained. The authors offer the route for surgical video work where labels are scarce.
pmc-13296156:
Omnia A. Basal, Entsar A. Saad and Rana R. El Sadda test, in 2026, whether an iron-rifampicin complex can shield mouse kidneys from doxorubicin, a cancer drug known to harm kidneys. Sixty male mice were split into six groups covering healthy, injured and treated conditions.

Doxorubicin cut body and kidney weight, drained antioxidant defences and raised waste markers in blood, while damaging kidney tissue under the microscope. The complex moved nearly all measures back toward normal, with the lower dose working best, mainly by easing oxidative stress. The authors propose it as a candidate kidney protector needing further validation.
pmc-13297156:
Eman Samy Shalaby and colleagues formulate an alcohol-free hand sanitizer built on nanostructured lipid carriers in a 2026 study. Alcohol rubs dry and damage skin with frequent use, a problem for sensitive users. Three cream formulas carrying chlorhexidine were tested for safety, microbe killing, and skin behaviour.

All three formulas proved safe in cell tests and killed microbes on laboratory plates. The leading formula released its cargo in two phases, sat well on skin, and flowed in a shear-thinning way. In fifteen volunteers it removed nearly all bacteria and fungi from hands. Virus reductions in laboratory tests were modest, though. The authors market the cream as an economical alcohol replacement.
pmc-13297656:
Vincenzo Caretti and colleagues build and test a questionnaire for the internal saboteur, the harsh inner voice that undercuts a person, in a 2026 study. The scale frames that voice through four strands: expecting rejection or judgement, devaluing the self, rumination, and inner destructiveness. Three hundred twenty-eight Italian adults, most of them women, completed the survey.

Statistical tests supported eight lower facets grouped under the four strands, and scores behaved the same for men and women. High saboteur scores went with insecure attachment, self-criticism, shame, and anger. They went against secure attachment, self-reassurance, and reading others' minds well. The team offers the scale for research and for clinical case work alike.
pmc-13298056:
Roberta Crispino and colleagues review animal evidence on whether statins change orthodontic tooth movement and relapse, in a 2026 systematic review. Searches of major databases up to late 2025 found seven in vivo studies meeting their rules. Simvastatin and atorvastatin dominated, though doses, routes, mechanics, and follow-up varied widely.

Some experiments showed slower active movement or less relapse with statins, yet results were not uniform. Tissue findings often pointed to fewer bone-resorbing cells or more mature alveolar bone, and molecular reports centred on bone signalling pathways. The authors warn that animal-only, uneven evidence cannot support clinical advice yet.
pmc-13298456:
Xuewu Zhang and An Jiang review light-activated drug therapy delivered inside the bile ducts for bile duct cancer, in a 2026 clinical survey. The treatment aims to keep ducts draining in patients whose tumours cannot be removed. Evidence reviewed covers drainage maintenance, bilirubin reduction, and delayed stent blockage.

Survival evidence conflicts, with early positive studies against a later negative randomised trial. Drainage quality, infection care, stent strategy, and access to systemic therapy all complicate comparisons. The authors frame the therapy as a context-dependent local palliative option, not a proven survival treatment, and they urge standardised reporting plus bile-specific endpoints in future trials.
pmc-13299256:
Some cells in spread prostate tumors are built to dodge hormone care, and they sit there from day one. Ryuta Watanabe and his team show that in a 2026 cell-by-cell study. They read gene use in 17,825 cells from the first biopsy of five men whose cancer had spread but who had not yet had hormone care.

Next to the bulk cells that lean on male hormones, each tumor held basal-like cells. Those cells barely heed male hormones and bear stem-like gene marks. Shape-shift gene sets that aid spread were strewn through many cell states, not penned in one group. No clear nerve-like cell group stood out. The team say these hormone-deaf cells may drive the grim path of the disease.
pmc-13300356:
T Huang and colleagues report a 2026 study hunting for the mapping measure that best predicts rhythm relapse after a first pulmonary vein isolation. Voltage recorded in the left atrium reflects diseased tissue, and candidate measures included average voltage, low voltage area, and atrial volume. High-density maps recorded during sinus rhythm in 278 patients were processed with an artificial intelligence algorithm to extract each measure consistently.

Recurrence reached about seventeen percent by twelve months and thirty percent by twenty-four months. In adjusted models, only persistent atrial fibrillation type and low voltage area at a set threshold predicted relapse at both time points. Separate area cut-offs separated outcomes for paroxysmal and persistent disease groups, with the persistent group showing the sharper split. The authors conclude that low voltage area deserves a central place in pre-procedure risk estimates.
pmc-13300756:
Carmelo Scribano and co-authors expose a shortcut bias in a popular pose estimation benchmark in a 2026 computer vision study. The Linemod dataset labels object poses using ArUco fiducial markers on the board, and those markers stay visible in the images. Saliency analysis showed trained networks devoting much of their attention to the markers instead of the objects, inflating their benchmark scores.

The team built a generative augmentation pipeline that erases the markers and swaps in realistic synthesized backgrounds. Models trained on the original data lost noticeable accuracy when judged in marker free scenes, confirming the bias. Retraining on the generative version improved robustness and generalization to unseen settings, although the problem did not vanish completely. The authors urge benchmark designers and industrial users to treat background cues as a first-class threat to reliability.
pmc-13301056:
Elena Durán González and co-authors test whether extra virgin olive oil inside a Mediterranean diet reshapes gut microbes in fibromyalgia, in a 2026 randomized trial. The double blind study enrolled 250 women, 206 with fibromyalgia and forty-four controls, who followed the diet for six months with either extra virgin or refined olive oil as the comparison fat. Stool microbes were profiled by gene sequencing at four time points.

At the start, patients showed lower microbial diversity than controls. The intervention did not lift overall diversity. Yet the extra virgin oil group gained specific organisms, including several butyrate producers prized for calming inflammation and feeding the gut lining, alongside other species linked to metabolic health. The authors read the selective gains as evidence that oil quality, not just the diet pattern, nudges the microbiome. They position diet as a complementary lever beside standard fibromyalgia care.
pmc-13301956:
A yeast that usually minds the skin killed a dialysis patient through his own heart valve, Kirun Gopal and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. The 43-year-old man arrived with fever and breathlessness, and doctors found endocarditis on his native aortic valve. Blood and valve tissue both grew Trichosporon mycotoxinivorans, a species rarely seen in this seat.

A large vegetation pushed the team to early valve replacement. After surgery he slid into fungal septic shock and died despite treatment. The authors stress that Trichosporon shrugs off echinocandin drugs, and invasive disease kills thirty to ninety percent of its victims. Surgery plus long antifungal courses remain the usual, uncertain recipe.
pmc-13302356:
Saverio Savio and co-authors study, in a 2026 laboratory paper, how light intensity changes what a small freshwater diatom produces and how those products affect a childhood brain tumour. The alga, Staurosirella pinnata, makes compounds with selective effects on cancer cells. Medulloblastoma cell lines served as the test target.

Cultures grown under standard light received five days of moderate or strong extra light after reaching a stable growth phase. Moderate light boosted growth strongly, while the strongest light suppressed growth and photosynthesis and shifted metabolism from sugars toward fats. Extracts from the strongest-light cultures killed medulloblastoma cells at levels matching standard-light extracts. Middle-intensity extracts showed no clear effect, underlining how growing conditions steer bioactivity.
pmc-13302756:
Pelvic screws tolerate error in some directions far better than others, Se Jun Park and colleagues quantify in a 2026 surgical study. They reviewed S2-alar-iliac fixations with before-and-after CT scans, comparing each screw's planned ideal angle against where it actually landed. Cortical breaches were matched against the size and direction of each deviation.

Lateral drift was the dangerous one: the safe corridor measured only 1.5 degrees before bone wall violations climbed. Medial error allowed 8.1 degrees, and downward error a generous 18.5 degrees, while upward deviation showed no clear link to breaches. Pelvic tilt and incidence also bent the ideal angles. The authors frame free-hand placement as managing a lopsided tolerance zone.
pmc-13302956:
Yilin Fan and Zhonglong Yin introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a special issue on membrane technology for cleaning water and fighting membrane fouling. Membranes desalinate and reclaim water efficiently, but clogging steadily cuts their flow and lifespan. Nine papers in the collection attack the problem from materials, design, and prediction angles.

One team grafted an antibacterial compound onto reverse-osmosis membranes, while another reviewed self-cleaning electrocatalytic designs built from carbon, metals, and framework materials. A redesigned feed spacer cut energy use sharply in tests. Further papers traced fouling in fermentation broths, forecast fouling timing with probability models, and tested sand and zeolite pre-treatment. The editors frame fouling control as the field's decisive challenge.
pmc-13303456:
Johanna Laine and Eila Kankaanpää offer a 2026 systematic review of how studies using routinely collected patient-reported outcome measures define who counts as eligible. Response rates depend on that denominator, yet reporting habits vary widely.

Searches across six databases yielded 92 articles covering 94 datasets. Eligibility meant all treated patients in about a quarter of studies, with the rest split between all recruited and other definitions. Nearly half of datasets calculated response rates in ways that clashed with their own definitions, and only a small share defined the rate clearly. Careful, stated denominators are needed before such data can guide care judgments.
pmc-13303556:
Aida Nurul Barokah and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on lasting brain effects of stress early in life. Separation from the mother is known to affect the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory and emotion.

Young BALB/c mice faced simple separation, separation plus stress for the mother, or normal care during the first two weeks of life. Gene activity for cell death and cell survival markers was later measured in the hippocampus, with added lab culture tests. A death-linked gene fell in the separation group, while a survival-linked gene rose in both stress groups. The pattern hints that brain cells adapt toward survival.
pmc-13304156:
Liang-Gen Wang and co-authors study what drives tiny drifting algae in Shantou Bay, a nutrient-rich estuary in the Taiwan Strait, in a 2026 modeling report. Seasonal monsoon shifts swing river flow and currents along the East Asian coast.

Field data from 2021 covered 359 algal species, whose counts swung widely by season. Path and curve models linked species turnover to currents and river input acting through water heat and salt. Summer peaks in the southwest strait traced to nutrient-rich land runoff plus upwelling effects. Heat and salt stood out as the master controls in this rich coastal zone.
pmc-13305656:
Ju-Hyun Yoon, Chae-Won Jeon, and Joo-Eun Kim compare, in a 2026 study, batch and continuous wet granulation for making amiodarone tablets. Drug makers are shifting toward continuous lines that run without pauses between steps, promising shorter lead times and steadier quality. Using design-of-experiments methods, the team tuned a twin-screw granulator against the traditional high-shear mixer process.

Granules and tablets from both routes matched on in-process controls, and every formulation hit its target dissolution profile. A similarity analysis confirmed the two products dissolved equivalently with strong statistical confidence. The continuous line cut manufacturing lead time by more than eighty percent. The authors conclude the switch is feasible without changing the formulation, offering a template for modernizing other tablet production.
pmc-13305756:
S Harshitha and colleagues report a 2026 audit of antibiotic use in a South Indian tertiary care hospital. Their work checks prescribing against the World Health Organization AWaRe system, which sorts antibiotics into Access, Watch, and Reserve groups. Records covered 257 inpatients seen during March 2026.

Watch drugs dominated, making up about seventy-three percent of prescriptions, while Access drugs accounted for only about eleven percent. Roughly sixty percent of prescriptions met the team's stewardship criteria, and cultures were sent in about two-thirds of cases. Patients who had cultures taken stayed on antibiotics longer. The authors argue that regular AWaRe audits could help hospitals target weak prescribing habits.
pmc-13306356:
Sergio Portillo explored learning-like behaviour in tiny fluid channels in a 2026 study of nanofluidic memristors. Cone-shaped pores change conductance with past voltage, much as synapses strengthen or weaken with use in the brain.

Series of rectangular voltage pulses varied in height, length and rate to drive strengthening and weakening effects plus short-term memory states. Networks of such pores carried out logic tasks and reservoir computing with pulse trains as inputs. As a playful proof, a supervised array learned to play tic-tac-toe, showing how ion-based hardware might handle simple learning jobs.
pmc-13306956:
Hajime Suzuki tuned a layered bismuth material to release oxygen in a water-splitting pair in a 2026 study. Mixing bromine and iodine in BiOBr1−xIx shifts light capture and energy levels smoothly, but stronger capture can weaken reaction drive.

A mix with iodine share at 0.1 balanced those forces and kept releasing oxygen steadily with iron ions carrying electrons in reported tests. Platinum coating by plasma spray stopped iodine loss and lifted activity further. Joined into a full Z-scheme pair, the system split water evenly for over 50 hours under visible light.
pmc-13307156:
Mashan Almutairi loaded the antifungal ketoconazole into sticky nanolipid carriers for skin use in a 2026 study. The drug fights many fungi but its fat-loving nature blocks good topical design, and oral use has drawn safety limits.

Carriers were tuned for size, charge, acidity, thickness, drug content and trapping, then set into a Carbopol gel to cling longer on skin. Release in dishes, passage through skin samples and live-animal checks judged the final gel. The aim is deeper skin delivery with stronger fungal kill at the site. The gel form may help the drug stay where skin fungi live and grow on the skin.
pmc-13307356:
Jing Huang and co-authors describe in 2026 a new masked group, called EBB, that is built to break apart and free an amine drug inside the body. Gold drives the key steps, which add a sulfur group, close a ring, and then split an amide bond under mild conditions.

To show a use case, the group paired the masked drug with a lectin guided artificial enzyme that seeks out cancer cells with excess sialic acid on their surface. The aim is selective drug release at the tumor site. Such bond breaking chemistry could widen the range of prodrugs that metal catalysts can switch on.
pmc-13307756:
Rayane Caroline Medeiros do Nascimento and colleagues compare blood markers in 2026 between Quarter Horses that compete in vaquejada, a fast Brazilian cattle sport, and resting non-athlete horses. Short, intense effort raises oxygen demand and can strain muscle and antioxidant systems. Samples covered clotting, oxidative stress, inflammation, and muscle damage markers.

Athlete horses showed clearer changes in coagulation and oxidative stress markers than the resting group. Inflammatory markers, by contrast, did not shift significantly between the groups. The pattern suggests conditioning for explosive effort leaves a measurable oxidative footprint even outside competition. The authors urge welfare monitoring for horses in the sport. Countering oxidative effects of brief maximal effort, they suggest, should become part of training and recovery planning.
pmc-13308656:
Faris Aldaghri reports in 2026 a lone forearm case of steatocystoma simplex, a rare benign growth from the oil gland unit that is seldom seen on the arm. A man aged 40 years came in with a firm, fixed lump that measured 3 by 2 centimetres and caused no pain.

Sound scans showed a neat cyst with bright debris inside and no rich blood flow through its wall. Cut out tissue showed a thin lining, a pink cuticle edge, and oil lobes in the wall, which sealed the call. Full removal with the sac intact left no return at long follow up. Tissue proof matters, since common cysts can look the same.
pmc-13309356:
Ashutosh Gupta and co-authors report in 2026 a case of LGI1 antibody autoimmune brain disease in a man in his late 60s, whose seizures were set off by body position sense cues. He first felt a month of right foot cramps and shock like pain that could climb to his hip, then spread into full body convulsions.

Early tests pointed to a nerve root disease, but LGI1 antibodies then turned up and reframed the whole case for the team. Vein immune globulin failed to stop the attacks, a course that breaks the usual script for this state. A B cell drug, rituximab, then brought clear gains in his course. Odd triggers should not rule out an immune cause.
pmc-13309456:
Pedro Ducatti de Oliveira e Silva led a 2026 study in Brazil on reading belly pressure from airway pressure during keyhole gallbladder surgery. High belly pressure can harm patients, but the standard bladder method is awkward during surgery. Breathing pressures are already watched minute by minute, so a link between the two would help.

Healthy surgical patients had belly pressure raised in steps while peak and plateau airway pressures were recorded at each level. Statistical models then tested how closely the two pressures moved together and how well airway values flagged high belly pressure. Care was taken to size the study for a clear result. The authors frame airway pressure as a handy stand-in when direct checks are hard.
pmc-13309556:
Ziyi Ren and co-authors review what spaceflight does to joint cartilage in a 2026 article. Cartilage cushions joints and has no direct blood supply, so it heals slowly even on Earth. Long missions add weightlessness and radiation, yet cartilage has drawn less study than bone or muscle.

Without load, cartilage cells slow their upkeep and the cushion matrix falls out of balance. Radiation, chemical stress, and immune activity add DNA harm and cell aging, speeding matrix breakdown. Exercise plans, diet, and drugs each help in part, but none covers all harms. The authors call for combined protection plans as crews head toward longer and deeper missions.
pmc-13310056:
Fang Liu and co-authors test two blood ratios as gauges of artery narrowing in older heart patients in a 2026 study. Coronary heart disease follows narrowed heart arteries, and swelling signals in blood may track how severe the narrowing runs. Two combined ratios, built from inflammation and cholesterol measures, were the focus.

Records for 786 older patients were split into training and check sets and grouped by a standard narrowing score. Both ratios ran higher in moderate to severe narrowing, tracked the narrowing score, and stood as independent risk factors in both sets of the analysis. The authors assess how well the ratios sort patients, including those with high blood pressure or diabetes, and propose them as cheap add-on gauges.
pmc-13310956:
Jonathan Aning led a 2026 survey of bladder cancer care paths in the United Kingdom health service. High risk bladder cancer that has not entered muscle needs swift, steady care, yet paths vary. The team asked health staff about team setup, diagnosis speed, drug care, surgery choices, and trial access to find upgrade points.

Seventy staff took part in online interviews from June to September 2025. Most patients reached diagnosis within six to eight weeks, though some faced longer delays. Drug maintenance length and finish rates varied widely. Bladder sparing choices stayed limited after drug failure. All backed shared quality checks and a national audit.
pmc-13311056:
Xiuwen Zhang and a large team profile a rare mixed lung cancer at gene and immune levels in a 2026 study. Pulmonary adenosquamous cancer holds both gland and squamous parts and acts aggressively, yet its origin and drivers were unclear. Clinical data and tissue gene tests were joined.

Care data covered 76 patients, and nine tumors were split into matched gland and squamous zones for gene reading. Shared trunk mutations and copy changes point to a single cell origin for both parts. Smokers held higher mutation loads and distinct mutation marks. Gland zones drew far more immune cells than squamous zones, which may shape drug response.
pmc-13311756:
Shirley H Bush and co-authors, in 2026, give a rapid review of clinical checklists that bundle non-drug steps for preventing and treating delirium on general hospital wards. Checklists help teams remember each step.

Five databases were searched from 1999 to early 2025, with grey sources checked in 2024. Eligible records described a checklist used by staff, family, or patients themselves to prompt multi-part delirium care for adults outside intensive care. Two reviewers screened records, and appraisal tools graded each study. The review sums up checklist contents and how their use was reported, to guide wards adopting them.
pmc-13311856:
Mohamed Adel Deniwar and co-authors present a 2026 case series on treating large aneurysms of the carotid artery outside the skull. Such aneurysms are rare, and standard options such as surgery or covered stents fit only some patients, while dedicated flow diverters can face off-label and payment barriers. The team instead layered multiple low-profile stents, called LVIS stents, across the aneurysm neck to rebuild the artery wall and raise metal coverage.

Five patients received the approach, three with double stent layers and two with triple or more. Over an average imaging follow-up of 24 months, two aneurysms closed completely and three closed partly, with no major clotting or bleeding complications recorded. Still, three patients needed extra or staged procedures, from balloon widening to added stents or coils. The authors judge the method feasible and fairly safe, but rarely sufficient alone for large, complex lesions.
pmc-13311956:
Michael J Tatterton and Alice Pickering comment in a 2026 article on a Spanish study of nurses' knowledge of children's palliative care in a children's hospital. Training and support from seasoned colleagues lifted skills.

Over 21.6 million children worldwide need palliative care, on the cited figure, and they now live longer with more complex needs. The discussed study by Pérez-Pérez and colleagues surveyed nurses in one hospital. The commentators draw the lesson that access to training and experienced backup improves awareness and proficiency. They call for research in specific settings with larger samples to pin down learning needs by ward type.
pmc-13312156:
Kai Zhao and co-authors introduce, in a 2026 study, a deep learning system that estimates the environmental footprint of products across many industries from written descriptions alone. Life cycle assessment normally demands slow, manual inventory work, and earlier machine learning tools each covered only one sector, leaving gaps where risks could hide.

Their model, LCA-TextNet, uses a Transformer design trained on more than 16,000 datasets to predict 25 impact indicators across 20 industrial sectors from text. It passed a strong accuracy bar in 70 percent of sectors, and adding domain grouping plus incremental learning cut the climate change error sharply during checks against a newer database version. The authors present text-driven assessment as a fast, broad route to environmental intelligence for green transitions.
pmc-13312356:
Lucrecia González-Tamayo and co-authors measure, in a 2026 retrospective study, how often syphilis appeared among repeat blood donors at a Colombian blood centre between 2012 and 2024. Syphilis can pass through transfusion, and Colombian surveillance concentrates on pregnant women, leaving the healthy donor population understudied. The team analyzed records for 64,166 repeat donors and modeled which characteristics tracked with new infection.

Overall incidence came to 5.1 cases per 1,000 donors. Risk ran higher in men, with a relative risk of 1.76 in the adjusted picture, and higher still among donors aged 60 to 65, unemployed donors, and replacement donors, whose relative risk reached 3.51 in the reported analysis. Donations collected at the centre itself also carried elevated incidence. Finding steady transmission inside a supposedly low-risk group, the authors argue local patterns like these should shape donor selection and targeted public health follow-up.
pmc-13312456:
Sovitj Pou and a large team revisit, in a 2026 study, a family of quinolone antimalarials aimed at the malaria parasite's cytochrome bc1 complex. The lead compound ELQ-300, which carries its key group at the 3-position of the ring, is deep in preclinical development. The authors asked whether moving that group to the 2-position could work just as well.

They synthesized the 2-position isomer, HLQ-102, with routes that avoid costly catalysts and open access to many related variants, then profiled the analogs for antimalarial activity and tracked the lead's pharmacokinetics. Cross-resistance testing indicated HLQ-102 hits the same Qi site of the bc1 complex as its predecessor. The authors infer the target protein holds two troughs able to house the bulky group at either ring position, widening design freedom for this drug class.
pmc-13313856:
Yulianna Puspitasari and a large team of co-authors review, in a 2026 article, the state of avian tuberculosis in birds. The chronic disease, caused by Mycobacterium avium subspecies avium, drains poultry through lost condition, falling egg output, and death. It strikes especially in young or weakened birds, and it can opportunistically infect immune-compromised people. The review ranges over cause, spread, disease development, signs, diagnosis, risk factors, economics, and control.

No single test settles a diagnosis. Clinical examination, tissue study, acid-fast staining, culture, molecular assays, and blood tests are typically combined. Because drug therapy works poorly, control leans on biosecurity, sanitation, isolating or culling infected birds, and vaccine efforts that remain difficult. The authors set their synthesis apart by joining epidemiology, zoonotic concerns, molecular diagnostics, and genomic surveillance. They press for integrated strategies that protect flocks, limit human risk, and cut economic losses at once.
pmc-13314456:
Dean Porter and colleagues test a micelle-packed immune booster in zebrafish in their 2026 study. Tiny fat bubbles can carry adjuvant drugs to the right spot and spare the rest of the body, a prized trait for vaccine design.

The micelles held 3M-052, a drug that fires the TLR7 and TLR8 sensors. Glowing tagged micelles were shot into see-through zebrafish larvae, and the team watched where they went and which immune cells came, using live microscopy in reporter fish. Whole-body gene tests added a broad view of the response. The micelles cleared slowly from the shot site and drew in neutrophils and macrophages, signs of local immune firing, and a type I interferon response followed. Larvae were also infected with a tagged Sindbis virus to track antiviral effect. The fish model gives a fast read on adjuvant behavior.
pmc-13315656:
Mindy A Patterson and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, what studies say about the fat content of milk produced after preterm birth. Fat drives the energy intake of preterm infants and supplies fatty acids the developing brain requires, yet values scatter widely. Searching three databases to July 2023, reviewers screened 884 articles and retained 69 studies covering 1,871 preterm infants born between 23 and 37 weeks of gestation.

Mean fat came to 3.76 grams per 100 milliliters of milk. It climbed across lactation stages, from 3.04 in colostrum early to 3.74 in transitional milk and 3.85 in mature milk later. Measurement method shifted the numbers, with the creamatocrit technique reading highest. Among fatty acids, oleic acid led at 35.7 percent of total fat and palmitic acid followed at 22.05 percent, while the essential linoleic acid averaged 13.7 percent. The authors offer the pooled figures as reference values, flagging the methodological variability behind them.
pmc-13315856:
Oliver Plechinger and colleagues describe in 2026 what shapes recovery for people after chronic critical illness during early rehab care. Better intensive care means more survivors, often after long ventilation, left with lasting physical limits, and therapy is central to regaining function.

As a further look at the CINAMOPS cohort, the study detailed therapy goals, actions, and mobility milestones for patients ventilated at least five days. A custom total milestone score captured uneven recovery paths. Regression checks weighed age, sex, nerve and muscle injury, sepsis, and breathing support factors against gains in daily function, guiding rehab planning.
pmc-13316056:
Mingling Yi and colleagues tested in 2026 a measurement-based care plan for cancer pain in patients getting morphine through an implanted spinal pump. Fifteen patients with strong pain, scoring at least seven on a ten-point scale, were treated at two pain centers in a retrospective study.

The plan loops through monitor, assess, and adjust steps. Pain and its effects were scored with several scales, doses were retitrated by set rules every fifteen minutes at pump start, aiming below a score of four, and systematic follow-up tracked progress. Early dosing began with vein-based control before the spinal system was implanted.
pmc-13316156:
Fang Liu and colleagues tested in 2026 how the acidic vaginal environment changes drug strength against rare yeasts that cause vaginal candidiasis. Forty-two isolates from vaginal samples were identified by molecular methods, led by Saccharomyces cerevisiae with eighteen isolates and Clavispora lusitaniae with nine.

Thirteen antifungal drugs were checked under standard methods at low pH versus neutral pH. Terconazole lost the most ground, needing up to three doubling steps higher doses across all isolates, while amphotericin B, nystatin, and micafungin also weakened for many isolates. Acid-aware testing may predict treatment success better than neutral lab conditions alone.
pmc-13316656:
Jiayi Shen, Jianhua Mao, and Qing Ye review, in a 2026 article, engineered CAR-T cell therapy for autoimmune disease through three lenses they call depth, breadth, and length. Born in blood cancer care, the therapy aims here to wipe out rogue immune cells and let a calmer system regrow.

Depth asks how fully harmful immune pockets are cleared, including inside organs; breadth covers which diseases and targets fit; length weighs how long cells persist and stay safe. Early reports describe drug-free remission after one infusion in lupus, muscle inflammation, and scleroderma, with use spreading to nerve immune disorders. The frame helps doctors judge results beyond a simple worked-or-not and plan safer, more precise trials.
pmc-13317856:
Jana Cahova and co-authors analyse, in 2026, a decade of fungal toxin testing in cattle feed in the Czech Republic, covering 2013 to 2023. Toxins from Fusarium and related fungi contaminate grain and forage. Even low levels can weaken immunity and vaccine responses in livestock.

State labs tested forage and concentrate feeds for dairy cows, calves and fattening cattle using checked methods. One toxin, deoxynivalenol, appeared at the highest levels, reflecting crop susceptibility to Fusarium under local conditions. Forage carried significantly more of three toxins than dairy concentrates. Most samples stayed below advised limits, and only a small share passed the guideline values for two toxins. Ongoing checks and prevention remain needed, the authors conclude.
pmc-13318556:
Nada O.F. Kassem leads a 2026 home-based trial comparing charcoal heating with electric heating for waterpipe tobacco, asking whether switching the heat source cuts the poisons smokers and bystanders take in. Fifty smokers and 25 non-smokers took part as controls.

Each smoker tried both heating methods, with carbon monoxide in room air and breath, heart rate, urine markers, and personal reactions recorded. Electric heating lowered carbon monoxide and heart rate rises and reduced benzene uptake, but nicotine and pyrene exposure stayed much the same as with charcoal. Smokers found the electric version harsher and less appealing, and tobacco in those sessions looked charred, so the authors urge device rules to prevent overheating and advise against indoor charcoal smoking.
pmc-13318856:
Tim Hulsen, Mark C. Scheper, and Steffen C. Pauws introduce a 2026 research collection on AI tools that write text, images, and data for healthcare. Such tools now draft record summaries, power patient chatbots, and back up clinical choices. The stakes for safety, privacy, and accuracy are high.

Fourteen papers make up the set, sorted into four parts. One part covers real-world use, decision support, and outcome checks. Another covers teaching, testing, and quality checks. A third covers notes, data capture, and made-up records. The last covers methods, prompting, and niche language uses. The editors give working examples alongside risks and pitfalls. Rules for safe rollout get special attention throughout.
pmc-13318956:
Caixia Xu and Hongliang Ma present a 2026 survey study of academic stress among social science doctoral students in China. The sample held 705 students. They modelled two routes from stress to self-rated achievement. One route runs through emotion regulation, the other through cognitive decline. Mind wandering was tested as a moderator of both.

Stress correlated positively with emotion regulation, which in turn linked to higher self-rated achievement. Stress also correlated with cognitive decline, which linked to lower achievement. That gives stress a double-edged character in the model. High mind wandering strengthened both pathways at once. It amplified the helpful regulation route and the harmful decline route. The authors suggest universities design stress programmes that fit each student's profile rather than one fixed approach.
pmc-13319956:
Todd Levin and co-authors model paths for long lasting energy storage in the United States grid in a 2026 study set in the year 2040. Wind and sun power swing with weather, so stores that hold power for a day or far longer could steady the grid and trim total costs. A least cost growth model tested how storage uptake shifts with plant mix and store prices.

A total of 369 growth paths were run with hour by hour detail for a full year. Cheap long stores cut plant building and system costs once day long and far longer stores fell below set price marks in the model runs. Uptake rose with wind and sun share and fell where peak and steady plants held more ground. Fine time detail proved key to valuing long stores.
pmc-13320356:
Tingting Meng and co-authors build a hybrid particle that jams cancer cell power houses in a 2026 study. Power house energy chains are a core joint of tumor growth, yet blocking one link alone gives weak kills. Their frame particle, built from zinc and a drug acid and cloaked in tumor skin fitted with an immune brake protein, hits two chain links at once.

Once inside tumor power houses, the particle breaks open under stress signals and frees both blockers, which stall the chain, flood the cell with harmful oxygen forms, and cut energy output. The wreck also flags tumor cells for immune attack, while the cloak lifts immune brakes on killer cells. The dual hit aims to turn cold tumors hot for immune care.
pmc-13320456:
Wen-Dong Wan and co-authors review a three way survival web in tumors in a 2026 article on metabolism, self eating, and cell death. Tumor cells live under steady stress from low food, low oxygen, and drug attack, and they lean on linked tricks to hold on. Cells rewire food burning for growth, eat their own parts to tide over lean spells, and dodge death signals that should kill them.

Each leg of the triangle feeds the others, and their joint play shapes how tumors grow and shrug off care. Key paths that run the web are mapped, along with death styles that care may still force. Turning the map into drugs will need sharp markers and drug pairs that cut more than one leg at once, the review argues.
pmc-13320556:
Bernhard Nagler and Thomas Staudinger reply in a 2026 letter to comments on their study of blood pressure drugs after lung support with a membrane oxygen machine. Their original work covered patients with severe breathing failure placed on venovenous ECMO. Commenters from Labanca and others had raised points about how blood flow recovery unfolds.

The authors welcome the added views and note agreement that fixing acid build-up in the blood is a key driver of steady blood flow. They explain that gains from carbon dioxide removal may appear within hours, but heavy sedation and fluids around tube placement can blur early signals. Their methods tried to allow for those effects within a backward looking design.
pmc-13323056:
Lea M Becker and co-authors use flipping aromatic rings to read protein motion in crystals and complexes, in a 2026 study of the protein GB1. Ring flips deep inside a protein are sensitive probes of its energy landscape, which neighbours in a crystal or a binding partner can reshape.

Mixing isotope labelling with quantitative NMR, the team found core rings flip nearly a thousand times less often in crystals than in solution. Simulations based on a new crystal structure of a GB1 variant reproduced those higher barriers and showed how the lattice holds back collective motion. The work warns that crystal structures can understate the movement proteins show in living settings.
pmc-13323556:
Zheqing Hu and co-authors explain stubborn mucus plugs in large airways, in a 2026 review covering cystic fibrosis, asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Swollen submucosal glands hold a huge mucus reservoir, and their output can overwhelm the surface of big airways.

Their flush-load model blames imbalance: serous fluid from glands, the flush, falls short of hydrating heavy mucins, the load, so osmotic pressure collapses the cilia and seals the airway. Each disease tips the balance its own way, through faulty ion channels, type 2 inflammation or growth-factor driven remodelling. Sticky MUC5B strands from glands weave with surface MUC5AC into a mesh. The authors urge upstream treatment of gland stem cells and ion balance.
pmc-13325156:
Servet Askin, Nevin Çankaya, and Halim Yılmaz tune microwave digestion settings for measuring heavy metals in apricot in a 2026 study. Apricots are widely eaten, and toxic metals in them need exact measurement to judge risk.

Kernel, shell, and flesh samples were digested under varied temperature, time, and power, then read by ICP-MS. The richest flesh values hit 25.49 micrograms per kg for cadmium and 14.21 for mercury under the best settings. Zinc and copper levels moved together strongly across conditions. A certified plankton reference checked accuracy, and intake models weighed the health risk. Settings clearly shaped how much metal the method could extract.
pmc-13325256:
Zubaer Hossen and co-authors review how artificial intelligence is reshaping farm biotechnology in a 2026 article. Growing populations and climate stress squeeze yields, and AI tools promise faster, sharper decisions from messy farm data.

The review searched PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and other databases for the field record. Applications span crop breeding and gene editing, genomic selection, pest and disease spotting, soil and nutrient care, and livestock work. The authors also chart fast growth in commercial patents beside academic output. Worries include who owns farm data and whether poor regions get left behind by the digital divide. Quantum computing is flagged as a coming frontier.
pmc-13327856:
Zebing Si and co-authors build an explainable fracture forecast for weak bones in a 2026 study from South China. They gathered 1,125 hospitalized patients with osteoporotic fractures who had bone density scans at one hospital between 2019 and 2025. From each record they drew 73 clinical, lab, and imaging features.

Six learning methods competed after a filter step cut weak features, and LightGBM won, reaching an AUC of 0.903 in training and 0.840 on the held-back test set in their checks. Explanation analysis named age, a hepatitis C antibody marker, and blood sodium as the top factors pushing risk upward. Such a tool could flag fragile patients early enough for preventive treatment.
pmc-13328256:
Xin Wang and co-authors review diet, gut microbes, and the gut-brain axis in mental disorders in a 2026 article. Gut microbes shape immunity, metabolism, and hormone balance, and diet is a chief lever on that community. Imbalance has been tied to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, depression, autism, and ADHD.

Routes from gut to brain include immune signaling, the vagus nerve, microbe-made chemicals, and control of the blood-brain barrier. Human proof still lags animal work, tangled by genes, diet variety, medicines, and lifestyle. The authors weigh precision nutrition, probiotics, and stool transplants with care, urging mechanism-first, personal strategies rather than blanket claims for microbe therapies.
pmc-13330556:
Marvin Taterra and team mapped how GABA-A receptor modulators used in clinics act through probe-dependent drug action. Their 2026 study combined molecular dynamics runs, deep learning-based enhanced sampling, dynamic pharmacophores, and the MDPath approach for mapping allosteric communication networks. Benzodiazepines, anesthetics, and Z-drugs all act on GABA-A receptors, yet their distinct allosteric mechanisms remain poorly known at the molecular level.

Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs use natural GABA through long-range allosteric coupling, binding in the transmembrane domain and steadying GABA receptor links at extracellular binding sites. Anesthetics, by contrast, form extra links for direct binding-driven channel activation independent of GABA, setting ago-PAMs apart from PAMs despite shared binding sites. Flumazenil disrupts interdomain allosteric communication, blocking extracellular-dependent modulators only while sparing anesthetics' direct effects. The team presents this as a guide for smart drug design in ligand-gated ion channels.
pmc-13330856:
Yujie Zuo and Sihui Long present the crystal structure of a quinoline-based fenamate analog. Their 2026 structure paper covers 2-[(3-chloro-2-methylphenyl)amino]quinoline-3-carboxylic acid, grown as single crystals by slow drying of an ethyl acetate. Fenamate-type diarylamine leads serve as key scaffolds for anti-inflammatory drug search, yet older ones suffer high shape-shifting and messy crystal packing, causing poor form stability and shaky pharmacological performance.

Swapping the benzene ring for a quinoline fused-ring moiety may add stiffness and packing stability. The compound was made in two steps by Buchwald-Hartwig cross-coupling then hydrolysis, cleaned by column chromatography, and grown as pale-yellow block-shaped crystals at room heat. In the crystal, pairs form acid-acid homodimers, with strong π-π stacking interactions seen. The report offers a characterized quinoline fenamate analog for anti-inflammatory lead work, where packing stability could mean more reliable pharmacological performance.
pmc-13331456:
Afnan Chaudhry and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a young man found unresponsive after taking at least 600 mg of propafenone along with other drugs. His heart tracing showed a sustained wide-complex fast rhythm, and his blood work showed severe acid build-up and kidney injury.

Propafenone blocks sodium channels, and the team treated that effect with an intravenous sodium bicarbonate drip aimed at mild alkalemia, plus close supportive care in intensive care. Within an hour the abnormal rhythm settled, the QRS complex narrowed, and sinus rhythm returned, with tracings still improving over the next day. The authors present QRS width as a live gauge of poisoning severity and argue for early bicarbonate treatment in this kind of overdose.
pmc-13332456:
Miguel Duran and co-authors map how the brain's central amygdala handles GLP-1 drugs in a 2026 mouse study. Medicines such as those used for diabetes and weight loss cut appetite through the brain, but which circuits they recruit directly has been unclear.

Using fiber photometry, the team watched the central amygdala light up quickly and durably after a dose of the GLP-1 agonist Exendin-4, an effect blocked by a GLP-1 blocker given beforehand. Silencing all central amygdala neurons with chemogenetics blunted the drug's appetite cut, and silencing two specific groups, the Prkcd and Glp1r neurons, also weakened it, while silencing somatostatin neurons did not. For a rich high-fat diet, blocking the Glp1r group clearly restored eating. The authors conclude this small limbic hub gates the full effect of GLP-1 drugs on food intake.
pmc-13332556:
Jerry R. Mendell and colleagues report 2026 five-year results for delandistrogene moxeparvovec in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. The therapy is a single intravenous dose of a virus-vector gene treatment tested in a phase 1/2a open-label trial. Four walking boys aged four to under eight at entry received the dose, and safety plus function were tracked for five years. Function measures included the North Star Ambulatory Assessment score, time to rise from the floor, and ten-metre walk or run time.

No new safety signals emerged over five years. Post hoc analyses compared treated boys with propensity-weighted external controls and with natural history predictions to place function in context. The tiny cohort limits firm claims, yet five-year follow-up is rare and valuable in this field. Families and clinicians gain a longer view of safety and function after a one-time gene therapy for Duchenne.
pmc-13334556:
Victor Udoewa wrote a 2026 essay on Black liberation futures and what he calls an ethics of hopelessness, the third part of a series on liberation system entanglements. Black liberation work spans community, health, education, work, food, and housing, all woven into wounded systems.

Udoewa argues that mainstream futures practice runs on an ethics of hope that excludes communities who have none, while oppressed communities have always practiced their own futurism. Reading futures work as spiritual practice through Black liberation theology, he describes Black Liberation Futures Design. There an impossible future means literally one that will never happen, and designing toward it anyway becomes the method. The essay challenges designers to drop hope as an entry requirement.
pmc-13335156:
Abdel Kader A Geraldo and colleagues present a 2026 curve-based machine-learning method for automated splitting of branch spines. Recent advances in brain wiring maps have been led by high-resolution rebuilds of large amounts of neural tissue using electron microscope imaging. This provides unmatched insights into brain structure and function. Branch spines, shifting bumps on neuronal dendrites, play key roles in synaptic change, influencing learning, memory, and various nerve disorders.

The paper introduces a novel automated framework that integrates shape math, machine learning, and three-dimensional image processing to analyze branch spines in complex environments. By making spine-shape patterns from high-resolution images with many thousands of spines, the method picks up fine shifts in spine shapes, giving a fine-grained view of their structure.
pmc-13335756:
Hua Lin and co-authors improved hard carbon anodes for sodium-ion batteries by combining nitrogen doping with presodiation in a 2026 materials study. Hard carbon is the leading anode candidate for these batteries, but it wastes sodium on first charge, dragging down efficiency.

Pyrolyzing a urea-hard carbon composite seeded many pyrrolic nitrogen sites into the material. Those sites grip sodium ions and capture electrolyte anions, helping a stable, inorganic-rich surface layer form during chemical presodiation. The treated anode reached an initial Coulombic efficiency of 98.54 percent and kept 90.6 percent of capacity after 1,000 cycles at a demanding rate in half-cell tests. In full cells, first-cycle efficiency jumped from 70.74 percent to 91.53 percent with the treatment. The design offers battery makers a lever against hard carbon's oldest flaw.
pmc-13336356:
Hong Lei and co-authors found that the RNA-binding protein RBM12 keeps glioma stem cells growing by feeding their amino acid supply in a 2026 cancer study. Fast-dividing cancer stem cells rewire amino acid metabolism, but the controllers were obscure.

RBM12 stabilizes the messenger RNA of SLC7A5, a transporter that imports large neutral amino acids. More transporter means more amino acids inside the cell, which switches on the mTORC1 growth pathway and drives proliferation, self-renewal, and tumor growth. RBM12 boosts stability by recruiting ALKBH5 to strip m6A marks from the transporter's message. A drug blocking SLC7A5, JPH203, effectively suppressed glioblastoma growth in their tests. The RBM12-SLC7A5 axis now stands as a candidate target against the stem cells that regrow tumors.
pmc-13336456:
Jie Yin and co-authors built a graph neural network that designs copper alloys together with their processing routes in a 2026 materials informatics study. Alloy performance depends on heat treatment and working history, but conventional models demand fixed inputs and cannot digest variable process chains.

Their heterogeneous graph treats elements and process steps as nodes joined by learnable edges, swallowing variable-length pathways without hand-crafted features or sparse-data blowups. Native elemental properties feed the model directly. Applied to design, the framework proposed a new copper alloy carrying chromium, zirconium, yttrium, lanthanum, magnesium, and zinc, with a tailored process. Experiments confirmed yield strength of 710 megapascals and tensile strength of 726 megapascals in the validated samples, alongside further properties. Unifying recipe and route in one model points AI design at how metals are actually made.
pmc-13336656:
Aravindan Kamatchi Sundaram and colleagues built a language model tool in 2026 to pull tidy facts from papers on complex metal mixes. Alloy research needs facts on how mixes perform and how green they are, yet that knowledge sits scattered through thousands of journal papers. Their tool reads both paper text and tables to build large fact banks.

From text it took mix makeup, processing steps, test methods, and key traits in 37,711 entries, while a second bank from tables held 148,069 entries. Clever prompts and search steps raised hit rates for alloy terms. The banks let scientists compare mixes fast and pick stronger, greener alloys for new designs.
pmc-13336856:
Mikhail V Polynski and Sergey M Kozlov chart volcano-shaped design maps for turning carbon dioxide into useful chemicals in a 2026 study. Making one- and two-carbon oxygen-bearing products from CO2 and hydrogen could cut emissions at scale, but the reaction web is tangled. Simple linear rules failed to predict step energies well across seven metal nanoparticles.

A neural network filled the energy gaps, and span modeling turned the webs into Sabatier volcano plots that name ideal binding traits. Good two-carbon output needs several traits at once that clash on single metals, the analysis found. Mixed, multi-metal catalysts look more realistic. The lean framework helps hunt catalysts when data and computing are limited.
pmc-13339756:
Siang Chen and colleagues show simple amino acids boosting mineral electrochemistry in a 2026 origin-of-life study. The iron-nickel sulfide mineral violarite may have catalyzed early metabolism before proteins existed. Diaminobutyric acid, a basic amino acid, was added to its surface.

The amino acid sped reduction of protons and carbon dioxide at the mineral in the reported tests. Look-alike compounds showed both amino groups are needed for the boost. Spectra suggest the molecule ferries protons to the surface. Early amino acids may thus have fed back to strengthen mineral catalysis long before enzymes evolved.
pmc-13339856:
Yi Kai Wong, Samuel Min Qian Heu, and Yu Hang Chua interview chiropractic teachers in Malaysia about work-life balance in a 2026 study. Ten full-time faculty with varied loads shared their experiences in recorded interviews. Themes were drawn out by careful reading of the transcripts.

Seven themes included blurred limits, overwork, and clashing roles as teacher, clinician, and researcher. Support from colleagues eased strain for some, while belonging ranged from strong ties to feeling shut out. Personal rules for limits helped unevenly against growing office demands. Findings show well-being here is shaped by the workplace as much as by the person, pointing leaders to workload and culture fixes.
pmc-13341156:
Language loss in bilingual people with primary progressive aphasia is charted in a 2026 retrospective study by Jessica de Leon's team. Chart review covered 69 bilingual patients, gathering reported symptoms, which language faltered first, and background details such as acquisition order and dominance.

Most presenting symptoms matched standard testing rules, though some were unique to bilingual speakers. The language first affected, and the one less preserved at evaluation, generally followed patterns tied to bilingual history. Because bilingual cases are rarely studied, these records help doctors judge whether one language is more at risk and how symptoms may differ from one-language cases.
pmc-13342956:
Wei Ng and co-authors compiled a 2026 dataset on how well growth factors used in cultured meat withstand heat. Stability data were scattered across papers and lab notebooks, so the team merged fresh thermal shift measurements with published values and computer predictions to speed media design.
