The shared table holds 513 melting temperature values across many growth factors and variants, plus deeper thermodynamic detail for 15 of them. Records note species origin, production host, method, and conditions in a standard format. A language-model curation workflow with manual checks gathered the literature values. The open set can feed machine learning, safety review, and culture media work for cultured meat and seafood.
pmc-13343156:
Sif G. Kaad and co-authors report a 2026 pilot gene therapy test for aniridia, a rare birth condition that steals vision through faults in the PAX6 gene. No cure exists, so the team tried adding a working PAX6 copy into the cornea of aniridic mice using a virus delivered into the corneal stroma.

Mice treated at three months were checked five months after injection. The delivered protein appeared in the stroma, corneal surface thickness improved, and four key signaling genes returned fully to normal reading levels when data were pooled. Sample sizes were small, so the authors treat gains as suggestive. Still, the result opens a path for treating the corneal damage that drives later vision loss.
pmc-13344256:
Kumaresh Pandian and co-authors tested in 2026 whether three plain blood tests can help grade a sudden pancreas attack. Early grading matters a lot. Mild cases often settle on their own. Severe cases need close watch and intensive care.

The team tracked 55 adults treated for sudden pancreas inflammation at one teaching hospital in India in 2020 and 2021. They measured C-reactive protein, lactate dehydrogenase, and calcium. They also scored each case on contrast scans. Drink caused most cases. Gallstones caused the rest. The first blood test tracked the scan score best. That cheap test could help staff sort patients sooner and use intensive care beds well.
pmc-13346056:
Wanqiu Zhu and co-authors characterize a plant bacterium found in human bile in 2026. The isolate came from a patient with bile duct stones, taken during a scope procedure. A routine bench system first called it part of the Enterobacter cloacae complex. Mass spectrometry named it Kosakonia radicincitans, a species known from plants and soil.

Full genome reading settled the identity, placing the strain inside the Kosakonia line with a single chromosome of about 5.5 million bases. The strain stayed sensitive to every drug tested and showed no alarming resistance or virulence gene load. Genome checks, the authors argue, should back up bench calls for such reclassified rarities.
pmc-13347156:
Ashkan Sadeghi and colleagues tested in 2026 whether resistance training, ursolic acid, or both can switch on muscle-building signals in aged diabetic rats. Muscle loss worsens in diabetes because ageing muscle resists anabolic signals, and ursolic acid, a natural plant compound, may restore that response.

Fifty 21-month-old rats were split into healthy controls, diabetic controls, and diabetic groups receiving training, ursolic acid, or both for eight weeks, with diabetes induced by a rich diet and low-dose streptozotocin. Training meant ladder climbing five days a week, and muscle proteins in the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway were measured by Western blot. The comparison tests whether exercise plus a natural compound beats either alone for ageing diabetic muscle.
pmc-13347656:
Mert Korkmaz, Adil Denizli, and Duygu Çimen build a light sensor moulded to a heart damage protein, in a study from 2026. Films stamped with the shape of cardiac myosin-binding protein C were laid on plasmon sensors, with unstamped films as controls. Surface checks plus timed binding runs covered doses from 0.05 to 300 ng per millilitre.

Detection reached 0.019 ng per millilitre with a counting limit of 0.064 ng per millilitre in the reported calibration, and each bind-wash cycle finished within ten minutes. Rival heart markers bound far less, with selectivity gains of 3.85 and 12.64 times for the two rivals tested. Fake plasma runs matched a standard lab assay, supporting bedside use.
pmc-13348056:
Joseph M. O'Brien and co-authors set out in 2026 the genome of phage vB_EcoM_SS01, a virus that kills Shigella sonnei. Shigella sonnei is a top cause of diarrhoeal illness. It is a World Health Organization priority pathogen for fluoroquinolone resistance. Lytic phages kill their hosts after copying. They are hopeful biocontrol agents against resistant bacteria.

Taken from London wastewater on a Shigella strain, the phage genome spans 88,160 base pairs. It holds 149 annotated genes with a GC share near 39 percent. Publishing the full sequence lets other labs test host range, stability, and safety. The note adds a charted candidate to the hunt for options when drugs fail against Shigella.
pmc-13348356:
Jennifer Chipps and colleagues survey distress and resilience in nursing students during the pandemic in the Western Cape, in a study from 2026. A total of 589 students at two universities answered distress, resilience, and virus fear scales during and after COVID waves. Juniors made up 75.2 percent of the group. Women made up 77.4 percent. The mean age was 22.5 years.

Overall distress and fear rated mild while resilience rated high in the reported scores, a sturdy showing under heavy strain. Senior students carried clearly higher distress than juniors yet lower virus fear. Resilience did not split by year, so the authors urge targeted support for seniors inside nurse training.
pmc-13349656:
Makiko Ikeda and Manabu Takaki told in 2026 of brexpiprazole treatment for a child with autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, hoarding symptoms, and separation anxiety, plus trauma-linked symptoms. Children with both autism and ADHD often carry several psychiatric ills at once. Severe emotional dysregulation muddies diagnosis and care.

The child gained little from talk therapy and standard drugs. Approved antipsychotics and ADHD drugs were capped by side effects despite multi-team backing, while outbursts and irritability stayed. Adding brexpiprazole brought some gains in hoarding acts and social drive. The case hints at a carefully watched add-on worth weighing when standard options fail for complex neurodevelopmental cases.
pmc-13349956:
Xuezhen Chen and colleagues studied a scan-derived inflammation marker in children with Kawasaki disease in a 2026 retrospective analysis. Kawasaki disease inflames blood vessels throughout the body and can damage the coronary arteries, causing widening, aneurysms, narrowing, or clots.

The marker, the fat attenuation index around coronary arteries, is read from CT angiography and reflects inflammation in nearby fat. Scans from 71 patients, 40 with artery lesions and 31 without, were compared with 30 matched controls. The team related index values to artery size scores and clinical data. A scan marker of vessel inflammation could help judge which children face the greatest heart artery risk.
pmc-13350256:
Lorenzo Sabatino and colleagues reviewed sinus disease caused by dental implants and grafting in a 2026 single-centre study of 45 patients treated between 2020 and 2025. Growing implant use is changing where this type of sinusitis comes from.

Cases tied to implants themselves dominated, making up 37 of 45 patients, with the rest stemming from procedures preparing the jaw for implants. The team classified each case, noted blockages, foreign material, and openings between mouth and sinus, and matched them to surgery through the nose, the mouth, or both at once. A classification-based playbook helps surgeons pick the least invasive route that fixes the cause.
pmc-13350656:
Yi Fu and Jian Li quantified in 2026 extra late deaths in long-term survivors of stomach cancer after stomach removal, using United States population data from 1992 to 2022. Long-term survival is increasingly common, yet patterns of death years after surgery, from second cancers versus other health conditions, remain incompletely mapped.

Among 8,637 long-term survivors, all-cause mortality ran 66 percent above expected levels, with non-cancer conditions becoming the predominant cause over time, alongside second malignancy risk. Subgroup analyses by demographics and tumour features showed which survivors carry the highest excess risk. The findings argue for survivorship care that looks beyond cancer recurrence to heart, lung, and other chronic disease prevention.
pmc-13351556:
Elettra Pomiato leads a 2026 cohort study on liver stiffness and outcomes in adults living with Fontan circulation and related liver disease. The group reviewed records from September 2014 to December 2023 at their centre. They asked whether stiffness measured by transient elastography could predict death or other adverse events.

Among 167 of 207 patients, with 613 scans and median follow-up of 56.0 months, stiffness stayed stable and did not predict adverse events. Forty events occurred, while albumin and the APRI score did predict illness. A value below 23.9 kPa helped separate advanced liver disease, so joint heart and liver follow-up is advised.
pmc-13351656:
Xiuwen Zheng and co-authors told in 2026 of a direct vein incision to salvage stuck port catheters. The patients were children with leukaemia. Hardened sheaths make removal hard. Traction may fail.

Totally implantable ports are vital for long-term vein access in child acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. Yet sheath hardening can trap the catheter. Looking back at five children with hard removals from 2022 to 2024, the team weighed a new path. All had 6 French ports in place for 25 to 44 months. Opening the jugular vein directly let surgeons dissect the scar sheath and pull the port. The technique gives a controlled salvage option when traction fails. It avoids vein harm or left fragments.
pmc-13352156:
Taha A. S. and co-authors study how nitrogen fertiliser and rice variety jointly shape stem borer damage and yield in 2026. Rice output depends on feeding, variety choice, and pest pressure together. Four rice genotypes were grown at four nitrogen levels across the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

Higher nitrogen raised grain yield but also raised borer attack, showing a clear trade-off. Attack was worst at 220 kg N/ha and least at 55 kg N/ha. The sensitive Super 302 variety held more chlorophyll, carbohydrates, and amines in its tissues. More resistant Giza 183 and GZ 10590 held more protective phenols and silica. Findings support pairing dose control with resistant varieties.
pmc-13352256:
Philip Newall and Mike W. Peacey offer a 2026 model of choices between sooner and later rewards. People often favour quick gains, a bias known since ancient Greek thought as akrasia. Standard hyperbolic models treat the bias as an irrational trade-off and suggest precommitment tricks, like Odysseus bound to the mast.

Their bounded model instead blames limited mental reach. People weigh future rewards sensibly but only up to a horizon they can simulate, after which detail fades. Limited attention for distant outcomes then produces preference reversals near the present. Three error types map onto addiction, procrastination, and picking smaller-sooner rewards. Stretching mental simulation further out cuts all three errors, matching early intervention findings.
pmc-13352756:
Diego A. Forero and Pentti Nieminen show in 2026 how AI-built tools can mine papers for statistical software reporting. Checking methods across many papers by hand is slow, and naming analysis software is a basic openness marker. A free Shiny app, built with generative AI help, pulled details automatically from random samples in PubMed Central.

Across 1,740 articles from 2021 and 2023, spanning nine study designs, commercial IBM SPSS still dominated reporting. Open-source tools were used less often despite repeated calls for wider adoption. A surprising share of papers named no software at all. The project also marks a first use of the Vibe Coding approach in statistical methods research.
pmc-13353056:
Weiwei Shang, Yilin He, and Bing Bai study what builds career calling in trainee teachers in 2026. A strong sense of calling drives lasting commitment to teaching, a pillar of quality education goals. A questionnaire survey covered 1,029 Chinese pre-service teachers, and structural models traced links among felt social support, expected career outcomes, professional identity, and calling.

Felt support linked positively to all three other factors. Expected outcomes and professional identity each carried part of the support-to-calling link on their own. Together in sequence, they carried it further, forming a chain from support to expectations to identity to calling. The authors urge multi-layer support systems during teacher training.
pmc-13354256:
Huijten and colleagues reported in 2026 on adapting a Canadian program to cut vaccination-related distress in the Dutch national immunization program. Such distress covers pain, needle fear, fainting, and anxiety around shots, and accounts for up to about 8 percent of child vaccination refusals, and far more in under-vaccinated groups. The Canadian CARD system, which stands for Comfort, Ask, Relax, and Distract, bundles teaching with practical calming steps.

A recent guideline sorts anti-distress steps into five groups covering process, procedure, body, drugs, and mind. Bundled programs like CARD work in Canada, but success there does not guarantee fit in the Netherlands. The team used a staged rollout framework to adapt CARD with Dutch user groups and prepare a local version for pilot testing. They share early lessons on cultural fit and engagement for others moving such programs across borders.
pmc-13354356:
Sarada Khadka and others told of a diagnostic dilemma in a 2026 case study: a high-grade breast cancer that looked like primary breast lymphoma. A thirty-five-year-old woman gave with a rapidly growing breast mass, and core biopsy showed sheets of atypical lymphoid-like cells. The resemblance to lymphoma threatened to send care down the wrong path.

Immunohistochemistry showed positive test for cytokeratin, progesterone target, CD10, CD117, and BCL2, with CD20, CD3, estrogen target, and HER2 clear and a very high proliferation index. Weighing all results jointly, the team diagnosed poorly differentiated deep breast cancer. The case teaches pathologists to test thoroughly before accepting a lymphoma finding in the breast.
pmc-13354956:
Steven Oud and co-authors built a computer model in 2026 to study how petal patterns form in flowering plants. Petal marks help draw pollinators and shield the flower, but the early steps that set the pattern were unclear. The team let gene networks evolve in the model until they split a petal into inner and outer zones, making a bullseye.

A third cell type often arose on its own at the border between the two zones, though the model never asked for it. The team then found such border cells in real flowers of Hibiscus trionum. The cells arose more when gene activity was noisy, which suggests they help buffer growth against small random shifts.
pmc-13355256:
Dongkai Xiao and co-authors compared two ways to stop bleeding in kidney-sparing surgery in a 2026 study of 66 patients. The surgery removes small kidney tumors through keyhole cuts without clamping the kidney's blood flow, which guards kidney function but makes bleeding control hard. One group had stitches, the other had heat sealing with an electric tool and no stitches.

The stitch-free group had shorter operations and kept slightly better kidney function after surgery, with no rise in complications. They did lose more blood during surgery, though. All tumor edges were clear and no tumors returned in the short term. The authors call the method promising but in need of larger, randomized trials.
pmc-13356756:
Fahri Erdi Malkoç and others derived gain thresholds for sleep and pain after reverse total shoulder arthroplasty, ran the exploratory study in 2026. Sleep disturbance is a common complaint after shoulder swap, but in clinic meaningful gain thresholds for sleep quality were unclear. Without thresholds, teams cannot judge whether a change matters to people.

Sixty-one people with complete pre-op and six-month scores for sleep quality, pain, and global rating of change were studied, with anchor-based thresholds derived for both results. The thresholds translate score changes into patient-perceived gain. Surgeons and teams gain interpretable benchmarks for judging recovery after reverse shoulder arthroplasty.
pmc-13358756:
Femke E. Lammes and co-authors review a safety tool for esophagus cancer surgery in a 2026 paper. Removing the esophagus with its nearby lymph nodes is a key cure path, but the nerve that moves the vocal cords runs right through the work zone. Damage to that nerve can leave a patient hoarse and prone to choking.

The authors discuss monitors that track the nerve's signal during surgery and warn the surgeon in real time. They weigh where the method helps most, in neck and chest dissections, and what proof supports it. Their review helps surgical teams decide how to guard the nerve while still clearing the cancer fully.
pmc-13359656:
Yiheng Wang and co-authors review how diabetes dulls the brain in a 2026 paper. In diabetic encephalopathy, thinking and memory fade as the disease advances. Two forces drive the decline: the brain stops answering insulin well, and its tissue stays inflamed. The review shows how each feeds the other in a loop that is hard to break.

Together they starve brain cells of energy, damage cell networks and synapses, and weaken the blood-brain barrier. Treatments that hit only one side of the loop may therefore disappoint. The authors argue for therapies that target insulin resistance and inflammation together to protect the diabetic brain.
pmc-13359756:
Abass Al-Momany and co-authors build a kidney disease screening model in a 2026 study. Chronic kidney disease often goes unnoticed until it is advanced. The team set out to catch it from blood and urine biomarkers using machine learning, while keeping the model's reasoning open to inspection rather than a black box.

They tested ten learning methods on two datasets, with careful handling of lopsided class counts. A boosted tree method called LightGBM performed best, sorting patients with very high accuracy at a chosen threshold. Tools that also explain each call, case by case, stand a better chance of being trusted in clinics.
pmc-13361356:
Montserrat Fernández-Guarino and co-authors review how mind drugs act on the skin in a 2026 paper. Compounds made for the brain also reach skin cells, which carry their own nerve-like signals and immune roles. Cannabis compounds such as THC, put on the skin, show strong calming of inflammation and itch, plus anti-aging effects. The review weighs these findings across several drug families.

The antidepressant fluoxetine tuned inflammatory signals in skin cells and helped wounds heal and regrow. Psychedelic drugs, acting on serotonin receptors, may slow cell aging and shift immune behavior. Some serotonin drugs even blocked skin cancer caused by ultraviolet light in studies. The authors map a fast-growing borderland between psychiatry and dermatology, where old drugs may gain new skin uses.
pmc-13363356:
Qinghui Wu and colleagues report a 2026 study on how the angle between two crystals affects fatigue life in a nickel superalloy used for jet engine blades. Even so-called single-crystal blades pick up stray grain boundaries during casting. The team cut two-crystal samples with boundary angles of 4, 8, and 12 degrees and cycled them under high-cycle fatigue loads until they failed.

Fatigue life dropped sharply as the angle rose from 4 to 8 degrees, then fell more slowly. Small angles let the two sides deform together and slowed cracking, while bigger angles piled up dislocations and sped cracks, with casting flaws adding harm. The team built a prediction model that folds in both angle and flaw size, and it beat simpler forecasts.
pmc-13363456:
Joanna Harasym and Edyta Nizio wrote a 2026 review on polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, a large family of pollutants born from incomplete burning of fuel, wood, and waste. These ring-shaped chemicals persist in air, water, and soil, build up in living tissue, and include known cancer drivers. The review traces the full chain, from how the molecules form to how they travel and finally harm the body.

The authors stress a gap in current rules: safety lists cover only 16 priority members, which may understate the cancer risk of real mixtures by several fold. Body enzymes can switch these chemicals into forms that bind DNA, and stress pathways add further harm. Mixture science is the open frontier they flag.
pmc-13363656:
Neetu Choudhary and colleagues present a 2026 study of how climate reaches child nutrition in India through water and food at home. Most prior work routes climate effects through farming alone. Using national survey data on more than 42,000 women and nearly 40,000 toddlers, the team modeled rainfall and heat against water-fetching time, mothers' diet variety, and child growth scores.

More rain meant shorter water trips and richer diets for women, while heat lengthened trips and thinned diets. Water time sat in the middle of the chain, carrying climate effects to both diet and child growth. Regional water supply changed the strength of these links. The authors urge climate plans to treat water access and nutrition as one joined problem.
pmc-13363856:
Jinpeng Chang, Chunguang Xu, and Yingjun Dai present a 2026 simulation study of leftover stress inside two-stage solid rocket propellant grains as they cure and cool. Such stress can crack grains in storage or flight, so makers need to know where it gathers. The team modeled the grain's rubbery binder with standard time-temperature tools and varied the grain's stiffness factor and length-to-width ratio.

High stress zones formed near the core mold and the shell, with a sharp jump where the two stages meet, since their materials differ. Curing itself built about a third of the final stress. Stiffer mixes raised stress overall, while longer, slimmer grains lowered it. The authors offer the maps for sizing grains and picking spots for safety checks.
pmc-13364656:
Tomas Konecny and co-workers sort in 2026 which spread colon tumors may answer immune drugs that fail most such cases. These tumors lack the DNA flaw that makes immune care work in kin tumors. The team read gene use in tumor bits from patients on a paired immune drug plan.

A map tool split tumors into four types, from immune rich to scar like and liver like. The immune rich and scar types fared best on care, with longer life. Drug care also pushed gene use toward immune rich states. The types could guide who gets these drugs next.
pmc-13367056:
Mary Broden and co-workers show in 2026 how a blood guard protein helps the gonorrhea germ dodge white cell eat. The germ draws a strong white cell rush yet lives on. The protein, a brake on a blood guard path, coats the germ and cuts white cell kill with no need of that path.

Tests with built cell hosts show the coat blocks germ grip on white cell locks that drive eat. Block strength shifts by lock type and lock arm length. Wide built forms of the coat block as well as the real one and stop eat by fresh white cells. A size shield tale fits the facts.
pmc-13367156:
Hengxiang Fan and others surveyed stem cell outside sacs for neuropsychiatric illnesses and translation, in 2026. Neuropsychiatric illnesses cause high rate, chronic disability, and socioeconomic burden, while stem cell care faces poor post-transplant living, limited joining, and tumour risk. Cell-free sacs offer a safer option.

Stem cell-derived sacs, mainly exosomes, can cross the blood-brain barrier with high biocompatibility and low immunogenicity. The review summarises vesicle origins, birth, preclinical evidence, and translational challenges. Doctors and teams gain a roadmap for cell-free regenerative ways to brain illnesses. The review also notes risks that still block clinic use.
pmc-13371556:
Emine Sezgunsay and colleagues test ChatGPT-supported teaching for nursing students learning endotracheal suctioning in a 2026 pilot trial. Thirty-two undergraduate nursing students were assigned at random to ChatGPT-integrated teaching or traditional teaching. Knowledge was tested before, right after, and six weeks after the session, with interviews exploring student views.

Immediate scores did not differ between groups, but the ChatGPT group retained more knowledge at six weeks. Students said interactive ChatGPT work encouraged active participation and reinforced learning. The pilot suggests that AI support may help less with first learning than with keeping knowledge over time, though larger trials are needed before schools adopt it widely.
pmc-13372656:
Artem Pavlovskyi and co-authors mapped a brain and gut signal switch in a 2026 study. The switch, when on, can cut hunger and raise body heat burn. That mix is prized in weight care, since most drugs now work by hunger cuts alone. The catch is that close kin switches cause side harms.

The team froze the switch with its key bound in place and read the shapes with a strong scope. Small tests then proved which touch points made the switch picky. The map shows how to build new drugs that hit just this switch. Such drugs could one day add heat burn to weight care, with fewer side harms.
pmc-13375156:
Hiroshi Sugawara reports a case of lymphocytic esophagitis that masqueraded as two other diseases, in a 2026 case report. A 59-year-old man endured five years of worsening trouble swallowing. Early scopes showed a narrowed food pipe with white deposits and fungal elements, and later scopes added furrows and rings that mimicked a related eosinophil disease.

Biopsies instead showed a dense buildup of lymphocytes without eosinophils, and staining showed mainly CD3 T cells, settling the call. Acid blockers, fungus drugs, and inhaled fluticasone all failed to bring lasting relief. The case shows why ongoing swallow trouble with mixed scope findings deserves biopsy-driven diagnosis.
pmc-13380956:
Manuel Cerdeiros and co-authors describe a 2026 case of compartment syndrome in a single finger caused by hydraulic oil forced in by a pressure machine. Pressure inside the finger's tight tissue space rose, cutting off its blood supply. Their patient arrived nine hours after injuring his right ring finger, with severe pain.

The fingertip looked pale and swollen. A small wound marked its palm side, and standard checks of blood flow and feeling were abnormal. X-rays showed no fracture. Surgeons cut the finger open at once to release the pressure, and left the wound open. By the third day the finger was clearly recovering. Speed of diagnosis decides the outcome.
pmc-13383456:
Şeyma Zehra Altunkürek's team compared cultural awareness and sensitivity among nursing students in Türkiye and Somalia, in a 2026 study. Care across cultures demands both traits, and the team surveyed 214 Somali and 199 Turkish students with two validated scales, one for each trait. The goal was to see how the two student groups differ and what background factors track with the scores.

Turkish students scored significantly higher on the awareness scale at 167.84 versus 151.00, and on the sensitivity scale at 87.78 versus 77.12, leading on every subscale of both measures. Regression work probed background drivers of the gap. The findings point to curricular differences worth borrowing across the two systems, and they give schools a baseline for future training.
pmc-13384156:
Yuri A. Gerasimov and colleagues review robotic focused radiation for early breast cancer in a 2026 structured literature review. The CyberKnife system aims radiation at part of the breast with steep dose fall-off and frequent image guidance. The team gathered clinical and dose studies published between 2011 and 2025.

Most groups used 30 gray in five daily sessions, a schedule that kept local return rates low at mid-term checks. Side effects were mostly mild, and cosmetic results rated good or excellent in the reports covered. The review weighs patient selection and motion tracking to place the method among current partial-breast options.
pmc-13385756:
Seyed Saeed Mottaghi and Sebastian Maerkl show that the PURE cell-free system can rebuild itself from its own products, in a 2026 synthetic biology study. A universal biochemical constructor that copies itself remains a distant goal, and PURE is a promising starting point. Its 36 non-ribosome proteins are the main parts that must be remade.

First each of the 36 proteins was made alone in PURE. Then pooled subsets of PURE-made proteins were purified and combined into a fully working PURE system. Finally all 36 were made together in one PURE reaction, then purified and rebuilt into a working system. Self-regeneration of the protein parts marks a key step toward a self-copying biochemistry.
pmc-13385856:
Sandvik and colleagues develop a standard way to photograph the cornea's nerve plexus, the subbasal nerve layer whose thinning signals nerve disease, in 2026 ophthalmic imaging research. Confocal microscopy can image these nerves in eyes, but without a landmark, repeat scans land in different spots and cannot be compared across visits or clinics. Their method anchors imaging to the inferior whorl, the spiral where the nerves converge, defining a 1.5 square millimeter region around it for consistent capture by operators.

No differences appeared between two operators or between repeated sessions by the same operator. A circle around the whorl landmark was captured in 85 percent of the image mosaics produced. Repeatability of the landmark's coordinates reached 0.996 and 0.997 on the scale for the two axes. For 61 percent of mosaics, the region was accurately positioned and fully imaged. Sandvik says the anchor improves comparability for multicenter studies, while full reliability needs further refinement.
pmc-13386456:
Osamu Inamoto and colleagues report a gentler operation for early duodenal cancer in two women in their eighties in a 2026 case report. Tumors near the stomach outlet were too risky for scope removal, yet full pancreas-head surgery seemed excessive at their ages. The chosen operation removed the duodenal segment plus the stomach's lower part, with selected node clearance.

Both patients achieved clean margins and left hospital within 14 days without major problems. They stayed free of recurrence at 58 and 35 months of follow-up, with nutrition and quality of life preserved. The authors present the method as a sound middle path for frail older patients.
pmc-13386556:
Melanie A. Mason, James Geiselman, and Shawn Spooner report swift decline after a mild head injury in an older woman in a 2026 case report. A 71-year-old woman fell from a ladder, and her mild brain injury went undiagnosed at first. A concussion specialist made the call 17 months later, after symptoms had persisted.

Brain testing then led to a diagnosis of probable Lewy body dementia, and decline ran fast from there. She died 33 months after the fall, the authors record. The case presses for better provider training, team-based follow-up, and fairer rural access to specialist care after head injury.
pmc-13388356:
Sven-Oliver Herter's team tested laboratory-made internal standards for measuring ergot alkaloids, toxic fungal compounds that can contaminate rye, wheat, and barley. Because labelled standards for these twelve regulated toxins were missing, routine testing relied on a slower standard-addition method, and the team had previously synthesised matching standards for all twelve.

In a comparison between two laboratories, the new standards better precision and trueness and agreed well with the standard-addition results. The team also built a rye-flour reference material under international guidelines, giving food-safety labs a firmer yardstick for checking cereal products against European limits.
pmc-13388756:
Rutchanee Rodpai's team surveyed worm infections in three rural villages of Champasak Province in southern Laos, where foodborne flukes and soil-transmitted worms overlap. They tested 242 adults with both stool examination and rapid antibody tests for the liver fluke Opisthorchis viverrini and the threadworm Strongyloides stercoralis.

Sixty-nine percent carried at least one worm species, with the liver fluke most common at about two thirds by joint testing. Multiple infections were frequent, and nearly one in ten people carried three or more species. The liver fluke raises bile-duct cancer risk and the threadworm can turn fatal, so the authors argue for joint testing in control programs.
pmc-13389156:
Jingru Chen and colleagues survey, in 2026, how often pneumonia follows surgery for osteoporotic fractures in older patients across China. Lung infection after this surgery is a severe and common problem, yet national figures on its rate and causes have been lacking.

The study drew patients from 594 hospitals between September and November 2023 using layered random sampling and a purpose-built questionnaire. The team compared patients who did and did not develop pneumonia and matched them one-to-one on baseline traits to isolate independent risks. Geriatric and orthopaedic readers gain a rare nationwide picture of who is most at risk, which can guide prevention steps before and after surgery for a fast-growing patient group.
pmc-13389356:
Facchiano and colleagues built a planning framework in 2026 that adds nanoscale detail to ion beam cancer treatment. Ion beams damage cells in clusters along their paths, and a quantity called cluster dose sums that clustering for a treated volume. Standard planning tools work only with total dose, so the team added cluster dose to an open-source planner using a fast pencil-beam method, which treats the beam as many thin beamlets.

They tested plans for a water block and a prostate patient using proton, helium, and carbon beams. Rechecks with a detailed simulation matched the fast method closely, with agreement rates above 97 percent in the block and above 98 percent in the patient. Plans tuned for cluster dose gave even coverage for every ion type, and heavier ions needed less total dose for the same cluster dose, as theory predicts. The work makes cluster-based planning practical.
pmc-13391356:
Sara Campinoti and co-authors review, in 2026, single-cell evidence that the liver's support cells are far more varied than their structural reputation suggests. Hepatic fibroblasts and stellate cells regulate liver development, daily balance, and disease, not merely scaffolding.

Drawing on single-cell and single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the review maps distinct subpopulations across fetal and adult liver, each with its own matrix-building programme and markers. The picture covers healthy tissue, development, and scarring disease. Liver researchers gain a cell-by-cell atlas of who remodels the liver matrix and when, guiding efforts to target only the subpopulations that drive fibrosis.
pmc-13392156:
Emilio Franco-Macias leads a 2026 prospective validation of an automated blood test for a phosphorylated tau marker of Alzheimer's disease in a real memory clinic population. Blood p-tau217 promises to ease diagnosis, but tests must prove themselves in mixed clinic patients, not only in research cohorts.

The study ran the Elecsys automated immunoassay in a heterogeneous memory clinic group, where patients carry varied diagnoses and other illnesses. Memory specialists gain real-world accuracy evidence for a platform already present in many hospital laboratories, a practical step toward blood-based triage for who needs confirmatory scans or spinal fluid tests.
pmc-13393156:

pmc-13393256:

The paper offers surgeons a possible bedside tool for spotting patients at higher risk after the operation.
pmc-13394556:

pmc-13394756:

pmc-13394856:

pmc-13395956:

pmc-13396356:

pmc-13396656:

pmc-13396856:

pmc-13397456:

pmc-13397656:

pmc-13397756:

pmc-13397956:

pmc-13398156:

pmc-13398356:

pmc-13398656:

pmc-13398856:

The team's ladder of responses runs from raising the head and controlled breathing through mannitol and steroids to simply waiting for flow to ebb. Imaging, surgical detail and outcomes feed an algorithm meant to calm a complication that unnerves implant surgeons.
pmc-13398956:

pmc-13399356:

pmc-13400756:

pmc-13401056:
Claire Wilson and Aditi Kanhere investigate, in 2026, an overlooked corner of gene regulation in cancer: CpG islands at the tail ends of genes. Their behavior at the three-prime end, which helps control message stability, is far less studied.

The study characterizes these tail-end islands as highly conserved across species, frequently methylated, unlike their start-of-gene cousins, and linked to cancer-related gene regulation. pmc-13401156:

pmc-13401556:

pmc-13401656:

pmc-13402356:

pmc-13402456:

pmc-13402656:

pmc-13402756:

pmc-13404156:

pmc-13404356:

pmc-13404456:

pmc-13404856:

pmc-13406456:

pmc-13407456:

pmc-13407856:

pmc-13407956:

pmc-13408056:

pmc-13408156:

pmc-13408356:

pmc-13409056:

pmc-13410456:

pmc-13410756:

pmc-13414556:

pmc-13415556:

pmc-13415656:

Blood loss measures and transfusion rates did not differ between platforms. Complications and urinary function gains through six months were likewise comparable. The authors conclude HoLEP is safe and effective on all three platforms, so access should not wait on owning the newest laser.
pmc-13416656:
John T. Strony and colleagues compare patch materials used to reinforce arthroscopic rotator cuff repairs, in a 2026 cohort study. One hundred twelve patients with full thickness tears had surgery between 2021 and 2024: forty with no patch, forty with a bioinductive collagen implant, and thirty-two with acellular dermal allograft. Healing was judged on MRI at least six months later.

Collagen implant repairs healed most often, at seventy-eight percent, versus about fifty-five percent for both other groups. In small to medium tears the collagen rate reached ninety-five percent. Adjusted modeling tied the collagen patch to better healing independently. Shoulder function scores never differed among groups.
pmc-13417156:
Zijin Fang and colleagues review protoplast work in medicinal plants in a 2026 article. A protoplast is a plant cell stripped of its wall, able in principle to regrow a whole plant. These cells help test gene function, yet making them well from medicinal species has long been difficult.

The review gathers what shapes success: plant material choice, pretreatment, enzyme mixes, digestion settings, and cleaning steps. Uses covered include gene editing, transformation, single cell sequencing, and cell fusion. Guidance aims to support breeding of medicinal plants, study of their active compounds, and design of better production strains for natural medicines.
pmc-13417656:
Wuan Shuen Yap, Wing Loong Cheong, and Li Ling Yeap review how Asia Pacific hospitals manage pharmacy stock, in a 2026 systematic review. Medicine shortages persist across the region, and practice varies even between hospitals in one country. Searches covered major databases plus grey sources from 39 countries, yielding 72 publications from 20 countries.

Three problem themes emerged: system constraints, weak infrastructure, and staff skill gaps. Suggested fixes include leaner spending, stronger central distribution, and contracts with several suppliers. Better storage space and tracking systems also matter. Training investment is urged so staff can follow good stock methods and keep medicines available for patients.
pmc-13418256:
Matt Walker and co-workers showed in 2026 how a quiet virus inside a gut germ remodels its host's propeller to boost fitness. Temperate phages can hide in bacterial genomes, and this one carries RNA-guided factors, called TldR, that switch which flagellin protein builds the flagellum.

The switch changed flagellar shape, improved swimming, helped the germ dodge mammalian immune detection, and improved gut colonization in mice, with cryo-electron microscopy revealing the new flagellar builds. The paper traces a CRISPR-like control system turned to a phage's advantage, with lessons for how gut microbes persist.
pmc-13420056:
Maria P Mogavero and colleagues trace how treatment for restless legs syndrome changed between 2015 and 2026, as one side effect reshaped practice. The condition brings an urge to move the legs that wrecks sleep onset and depth, draining daytime energy and mood. Clear diagnostic criteria turned a once-dismissed complaint into a defined nerve disorder over past decades.

The turning point in the story is augmentation, the worsening of symptoms under long use of the very drugs meant to calm them. Growing recognition of that trap pushed guidelines toward other drug classes and slower escalation. The review closes with mechanism-based drugs, better markers, and tailored care as the next frontiers. Clinicians get a decade of shifting practice in one account.
pmc-13420356:
Slade and colleagues present a 2026 review tracing how abortion methods have changed across history. Women have ended pregnancies in every era, despite religious and legal bans that persist in many countries. The authors walk through methods used in the first and second trimesters, from early eras to modern care, and note where access still fails.

Over time, methods grew safer, more effective, and more widely available, and deaths and injuries from abortion fell sharply as a result. Drug-based and surgical methods used today carry low risk when trained providers give them. Yet legal limits, supply problems, and social barriers still push many women toward unsafe options. The authors argue that work must continue worldwide so that every woman can reach safe care, which they frame as a basic health service rather than a privilege.
pmc-13421456:
Schayan Yousefian leads a large team reporting, in a 2026 study, why some patients respond to CAR-T cell therapy even when manufacturing limits force a low dose. CAR-T treatment reprogrammes a patient's own T cells against cancer, and higher doses are normally preferred, yet some low-dose patients enjoy durable responses.

Deep profiling of products from the HD-CAR-1 dose-escalation trial showed that responders' low-dose products were enriched for functional effector and effector memory-like cells, whose absolute count predicted response across doses and targets. Starting material mattered too: supportive myeloid cells in the collected blood fostered good products, while regulatory myeloid states bred dysfunctional ones. The authors propose cell counts as a biomarker for dose decisions.
pmc-13421756:
Di Feng, Shang-chia Chiou, Ying Zhou and Hongyi Li study, in a 2026 paper, how China's Grand Canal is changing from a working transport landscape into a cultural space. Their case is the Huai'an section, once central to grain shipping, where heritage value in visitors' eyes must somehow convert into satisfying tourist experiences.

Using canonical correlation analysis on survey data, they mapped how sets of perceived values line up with sets of experience demands. The relationship proved uneven rather than one-to-one. Narrative value and the spirit of place coupled most strongly with educational experiences, marking them as the levers of local identity. Cultural capital and social background also shaped how perception turned into demand, constraining heritage consumption for some visitors.
pmc-13422256:
Wang and colleagues uncover in 2026 how the protein Ana1, called Cep295 in mammals, lengthens centrioles, the barrel-shaped structures that organize cell division and seed the tails of sperm. They worked in fruit fly sperm development, where centrioles grow giant.

The study shows Ana1 drives lengthwise extension by gripping two partners at once: the protein Cep135 and the microtubules, the hollow tubes that form the centriole wall. That dual hold gives the growing barrel both a scaffold connection and a track to extend along. Losing either interaction disrupts the elongation program the team describes in fly spermatogenesis. Because centriole defects underlie human diseases of cilia and fertility, the authors present the mechanism as a new piece of the assembly puzzle. It explains how a single protein coordinates the building of exceptionally long centrioles.
pmc-13422856:
Seo-Yun Choi, Ju Hyun Kim, Soondool Chung and Yuri Jang investigate, in a 2026 study, the route from bladder leakage to low mood in older Korean Americans living in subsidised senior housing. Urinary incontinence and depressive symptoms often travel together, and the authors suspected sleep sits on the path between them.

Their sample of 306 residents averaged about seventy-nine years of age. Leakage and depressive symptoms were significantly linked, and formal mediation analysis showed the path through poor sleep carried roughly a quarter of the total association. The authors argue that mental-health help for older adults with incontinence should treat sleep as a target in its own right, not a side note.
pmc-13424556:
Haiwang Yong, an editorial board member, introduces a journal collection on ultrafast chemistry, the study of reactions as they happen on picosecond, femtosecond, and even attosecond timescales. At those speeds the motions of atoms and electrons that make and break bonds can be watched directly with timed flashes of light, rather than inferred from starting materials and products.

The essay traces the field from early efforts to catch fleeting intermediates to flash photolysis, the pump-and-probe method whose inventors shared the 1967 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Modern versions initiate a reaction with one pulse and interrogate it with a delayed second pulse. Yong outlines the collection's themes and the standing ambition: not just to film reactions, but to steer them.
pmc-13424656:
Ken Nagata and nine colleagues identify a thin membrane wrapping the superior mesenteric vessels and propose it as a reliable landmark for robot-assisted lymph node clearance in right-sided colon cancer. Complete removal of the central nodes demands dissecting along these great vessels, and a consistent anatomical signpost could standardise a difficult step.

Cadaver tissue and surgical specimens both showed a collagen-and-elastic sheet separating the vessels from surrounding fatty lymph tissue. Reviewing videos of seventy-eight robotic operations, two blinded surgeons found the membrane clearly visible in 88% of cases, regardless of patient weight or surgeon experience. No central vessel was injured. Blood loss and node counts matched whether the membrane showed clearly or poorly.
pmc-13424956:
Tao Shi and Tao Zhao comment on a study that pushes plant evolution's polyploid paradox toward resolution. Polyploids, plants carrying doubled genomes, are everywhere today, yet few ancient doubling events left descendants, a puzzle debated for a century. The study under discussion, from the Van de Peer laboratory and covering 470 flowering plant genomes, dated 132 independent ancient doublings, the largest such catalogue.

Doublings, it found, cluster around major environmental upheavals from the Cretaceous to the Neogene. Polyploids seem handicapped in calm times yet favoured in severe crises, so their establishment mixes a steady background rate with bursts during disruption. The commentators add that today's climate change and habitat loss may again favour new polyploids.
pmc-13425556:
Youngjoo Kang and colleagues set out a Cochrane review protocol to judge teaching programs that aim to stop dating violence among teens and young adults. Dating violence covers physical, sexual, and controlling abuse by current or former partners, in person or online.

The review will compare education and skills programs against inactive controls, such as waiting lists, usual care, or nothing. It will weigh both benefits and harms of the programs for young people in or entering relationships. Risk factors the protocol notes include past abuse, drinking and drug misuse, poverty, and norms that excuse violence. The protocol fixes its questions and methods in advance, so the later review can be checked against this plan.
pmc-13425856:
Linjin Li, Lutong Pan, and Dan Zhang studied health literacy and confidence in older adults living with several chronic conditions in a 2026 management-model analysis. Multimorbidity rises with population aging, and good outcomes depend partly on patients' own capacity to act. Their multistage stratified sampling examined how self-efficacy, meaning confidence in managing health, relates to health status, and whether health literacy carries part of that link.

Mediation findings give program designers a pathway to target: building understanding may translate confidence into better health. Services for older adults can use the model to refine support beyond medication schedules alone.
pmc-13426356:
Xiangran Chen and colleagues link a functional variant in CYP4V2 to asthma susceptibility in a 2026 multi-omics study. CYP4V2 participates in lipid metabolism, yet its role in asthma was unclear, so the team combined gene expression, genetic, and methylation data from blood cells in the Singapore and Malaysia cross-sectional cohort. Expression analyses tied the gene to asthma risk and to arachidonic acid pathway genes, while trait locus mapping found regulatory variants.

Methylation checks and promoter reporter assays confirmed that the candidate variant alters regulation through DNA methylation. The arachidonic acid connection gives asthma genetics a lipid pathway angle worth functional follow-up. Blood cells are easy to reach, so a gene mark found there can be run at scale in large groups with no need for lung tissue at all.
pmc-13427556:
Lirong Peng and colleagues present, in 2026, lab methods that let scientists study the most dangerous viruses without losing genetic detail. Work on Risk Group 4 viruses must happen inside maximum containment labs, called BSL-4. Steps that kill the virus so samples can leave the lab often damage the genetic material inside. The team set out to keep that material intact while staying fully safe.

They tested ways to inactivate, grind, and extract RNA from many sample types, then checked the quality of bulk and single-cell sequencing. Trial runs included cells exposed to Lassa virus. They also tuned methods to read viral genomes at great depth. Labs studying deadly viruses gain a tested playbook for rich genetic data without cutting safety corners.
pmc-13427756:
Erin E. Robertson and colleagues validate, in a 2026 study, a tablet-based hearing test that patients can take outside the clinic. Standard hearing tests need a sound-treated room and a trained tester, which burdens trial participants who must repeat them often. The Shoebox PureTest runs on an iPad and guides users through tone testing at home or at remote sites. Volunteers covered a wide range of hearing ability.

Across the main speech frequencies, results matched the clinic gold standard closely enough to count as statistically equivalent. More than 80 percent of users rated the app and its ease of use as good. Overall satisfaction was rated excellent by 92 percent of participants. Trial designers could cut travel and site costs, though the authors flag practical setup points for future use.
pmc-13427856:
Fiori and colleagues reported in 2026 long-term results for TESAR, a fully keyhole technique that repairs separated belly muscles and midline hernias from outside the abdominal cavity. One hundred twenty patients were treated between 2018 and 2025 and followed for a median of about two and a half years. The method places mesh in a pocket in front of the muscle layer, reached entirely by camera surgery.

No complications occurred during surgery, and problems afterward stayed low, at under seven percent. Adding a quilting stitch removed the troublesome fluid cases entirely. No hernia returned during follow-up, and quality of life scores rose from poor to near perfect by one year.
pmc-13428256:
Antoine Journé and co-authors hunt, in a 2026 French study, for gene clues to a dangerous tumor type in a rare inherited syndrome. Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 causes tumors in several hormone glands, and tumors of the thymus, a gland behind the breastbone, carry a poor outlook. The team used a national cohort of more than 1,600 patients gathered since the 1990s. All 52 men who developed thymic tumors were matched with 104 similar patients who did not.

One mutation type stood out: nonsense mutations, which cut the affected protein short, came with nearly four times the odds of a thymic tumor compared with another mutation type. Age at tumor appearance barely differed between groups, near 44 years either way. The authors suggest closer thymus watch for men carrying nonsense mutations. Genetic counseling for affected families gains a concrete risk marker.
pmc-13429056:
Malin Andtfolk and Linda Estman examine, in a 2026 paper, what social robots can and cannot mean for caring in health services. Social assistive robots chat, remind, and keep company, and they are entering wards and care homes as staff shortages bite. The authors judge them through Katie Eriksson's theory of caritative caring, which treats caring as a moral, relational act grounded in human dignity. That lens sets a high bar for any machine.

Robots, they argue, can imitate caring behavior yet cannot hold moral responsibility or true compassion, so they cannot care in the full sense. Still, robots may support safety, independence, and routine tasks when designed with care values in view. Their proper place is beside human caregivers, protecting the human relationship at care's core rather than replacing it. Ethicists and designers share the boundary drawn here.
pmc-13429556:
Zhengwei Tan and colleagues review cyclosporine, a drug that damps T-cell activation by blocking the calcineurin signalling path, across blood disorders. Its uses span severe and milder aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic neoplasms, graft-versus-host disease, and autoimmune low blood counts.

Treatment is steered by markers such as STAT3 status, T-cell clonality, and telomere shortening, with blood levels checked at trough and two hours after dosing to balance benefit and harm. The review also covers pairings with newer targeted agents. Haematologists get a current map for tailoring an old immune drug to each marrow failure pattern.
pmc-13431956:
Minji Park and Younhee Jeong prioritise teaching needs for early walking after abdominal surgery, from both nurses' and patients' viewpoints. Early walking anchors enhanced recovery, yet teaching gaps in nurse practice and patient participation stayed underexplored.

At a 2700-bed tertiary hospital in Seoul, one hundred surgical-ward nurses and 111 postoperative patients completed validated surveys from May to August 2022. Each rated the importance and performance of fifteen early-walking activities on five-point scales. Educational priorities were then ranked with the Borich needs model and a focus-plotting model, giving ward leaders a shared agenda for closing the biggest teaching gaps first.
pmc-13433956:
Dimosthenis Chrysikos and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how the lymph web shapes bowel cancer, from drain paths in the gut wall to the gene sparks that grow fresh lymph pipes. Spread to near nodes has long set outlook and add-on drug picks. Fresh reads cast the web as a live player, not a plain sieve for stray cells.

The review weighs how dense fresh pipes run in tumors and what that count means in clinic. Stage rules stir debate, above all how vessel breach should steer add-on drugs in early cases. Knife craft earns a long look: a through-rectum full cut and side basin node hunts, each weighed for cancer worth. Drain maps per patient can tune risk calls and cut picks, the authors close.
pmc-13434156:
Kexin Che and colleagues build a scoring model for judging where underground heating of tar-rich coal could work. Heating coal in place is a path to cleaner coal use, but sites must be picked with care first.

Their test site is a named seam in the Dananhu mining area of Xinjiang. Scores cover five broad areas, coal quality, seam layout, seal strength, water geology, and environment, with fifteen finer measures. A model that blends fuzzy maths, combined weights, and grey-TOPSIS then ranks sites, giving coal planners a clear way to pick ground for pilot heating.
pmc-13434456:
Happiness Ngobeni, Lufuno Makhado, and Thendo Gertie Makhado listen to family carers of people with epilepsy in rural South Africa in 2026. Talks with 60 carers in two provinces look past the usual talk of burden. The team frames daily care as work that stays unseen and unpaid.

Carers keep constant watch for seizures and stay ready to act at any hour. They guard against harm, give up travel, free time, and paid work, and face stigma with thin clinic support. In effect, homes supply care that clinics would otherwise owe. Health plans should fund and train carers as core staff.
pmc-13435056:
Zhen Jiang and coauthors review boron nitrogen units as building blocks for electron hungry plastics in 2026. Such n type materials run flexible screens, body sensors, and organic circuits. Balancing energy levels, charge flow, and ease of making has slowed their design.

Boron nitrogen bonds cut energy levels and raise electron hunger while keeping chains flat. The review sorts design rules, making routes, and structure to trait links across small molecules and polymers. Five device families show where the units shine. Open gaps in stability and scale up close the survey. Chemists get a single map of a fast growing field.
pmc-13435356:
Fan and colleagues set out in 2026 to find blood signals that warn which cancer patients will develop immune-related adverse events. These events are the harmful immune side effects of checkpoint inhibitor drugs. They focused on patients treated at Changxing People's Hospital in China.

The team profiled pretreatment serum from 55 patients with a method that measures hundreds of small molecules at once, then followed patients for 12 months. Thirty-four developed side effects and 21 did not. Seventy molecules differed between the groups, including ursodeoxycholic acid and uric acid, and five of them predicted later side effects with fair to good accuracy. Pathways for beta-alanine handling, sugar phosphate use, and coenzyme A production were also closely tied to the side effects.
pmc-13436656:
Travis Hase, Cindy Ndiaye, and Margaret Putman run an eight hour palliative care course for emergency residents in 2026. Lectures, a talking skills lab with actors, and a high fidelity simulation fill the day. Forty one residents from all three years took paired surveys around the course.

Self rated knowledge, comfort, and skill use rose sharply on every item. Effect sizes ran large across the domains scored. Residents rated the training as important for their work. Skills labs and simulation drew strong marks among the formats. Emergency wards serve many dying patients, so the gains carry daily weight.
pmc-13436956:
Kelsey Hern and a large team tested whether friendly bacteria placed in the airway could block a lung germ in mice. Their 2026 work targeted Burkholderia thailandensis, a soil germ that can cause serious lung infection. The team reasoned that microbes living in the airway meet incoming germs first, so a well-chosen mix might crowd a newcomer out.

Lab tests of how the friendly strains and the germ compete guided which mixes the researchers tried in the animals. Mixes whose food and living needs overlapped most with the germ's needs protected the mice best. That overlap, called niche overlap, predicted success in the body better than other traits. The study offers a design rule for building protective bacterial mixes: pick members that want the same resources as the germ they must exclude. The authors frame the work as a base for later efforts against chest infections.
pmc-13437456:
Antonino Mulè and colleagues evaluated ePhyLi, a set of digital tools from a European project teaching physical literacy, the knowledge and habits behind a lifetime of active living. The package holds an e-book, an app, and a learning platform. Their 2026 study invited eighty-six student-teachers to use the tools in three ways: woven into weekly lectures, left for solo study, or mixed.

Knowledge rose most when the e-book joined lectures with the platform and the app. Users rated the experience moderately well and found the game-like features engaging. Trainee primary school teachers also rated the app's usability, satisfaction, and playfulness clearly lower than sport science students did. The authors conclude that digital tools with game elements can lift teacher training. They call for usability polish and more evidence on which classroom model works best for which students.
pmc-13437656: A 2026 correction notice from the Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle fixes one sentence in the acknowledgements of a study. That study tested anamorelin during combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy in lung cancer patients with severe weight loss. The notice is a correction only. The published text credited data management and monitoring to a funding contract with Chugai Pharmaceutical. The correct company is Ono Pharmaceutical. Nothing in the study's design, data, or findings changes, and the publisher apologizes for the error.
pmc-13438756:
Laia Marín-Gual and colleagues compared how the genome folds in male germ cells across three vertebrate branches that last shared an ancestor some 350 million years ago: placental mammals, marsupials, and reptiles. Germ cells must remodel DNA packaging through meiosis to make sperm; the folding rules were known from few species. Their 2026 study sorted the cells, mapped chromosome contacts, and read gene activity in single cells.

Each lineage folded its germline genome in its own style. Chromosome shape and genome size set the limits on how far DNA loops reach and how often chromosomes touch. The team also watched sex chromosome silencing during meiosis, a quality-control step. In the tammar wallaby, patches of the X chromosome escaped that silencing, hinting the marsupial checkpoint runs looser. The authors offer the maps as a high-resolution record of how genome architecture and gene control evolved together.
pmc-13441256:
Khurana and colleagues report a 2026 case of midgut volvulus, a twisting of the small intestine, in a 78-year-old man, a diagnosis far more typical of infants. He came to the emergency department after two weeks of intermittent bloating and belly pain after meals, with a fast heart rate and mild abdominal swelling on examination.

A CT angiogram, a scan of the blood vessels, showed the volvulus. Emergency surgery found his bowel twisted clockwise around the mesentery, the tissue that anchors the gut. The team untwisted and assessed the bowel during an open operation. The authors use the case to stress that adult volvulus hides behind vague, on-and-off symptoms, and that delayed recognition risks blocked and dying bowel, so imaging should come early.
pmc-13441756:
Zhiwei He and colleagues examine two blood-fat ratios against stroke subtypes sorted by a Chinese classification system, reporting in 2026. The ratios, NHHR and the atherogenic index of plasma, bundle cholesterol measures into single risk gauges. Their ties to large artery atherosclerosis strokes versus penetrating artery disease strokes were unclear. Patients treated at Wuhan University's Renmin Hospital between 2018 and 2022 supplied the records, with demographics, history, and laboratory values compared across groups.

Both ratios differed significantly between the stroke subtype group and the non-stroke group, alongside age, sex, inflammation, diabetes, and blood pressure measures. Adjusted regression models probed each ratio's independent tie to subtype, while accuracy curves graded their diagnostic value. Mediation analysis asked whether the ratios carry part of the effect that hypertension and diabetes exert on subtype. The authors frame the pair as candidate markers for sorting stroke mechanism at the bedside.
pmc-13442656:
Leyong Ke and colleagues compare gut microbes in older adults with constipation or Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Many people with Parkinson disease also face constipation, so shared microbe marks may link the two states. The team drew stool records for 860 older adults from a public gut database, split into 378 with Parkinson disease, 189 with constipation, and 293 healthy peers.

Both ill groups held more Bacteroides and Akkermansia than the healthy group. Each ill group also held less Prevotella, Faecalibacterium, and Agathobacterium than healthy peers. Most microbe shifts lined up in the same direction across the two ill groups. The authors read the match as a hint that gut shifts may help drive both states. They stop short of cause claims, since the records came from pooled past work.
pmc-13442956:
Calle, Ferreiro-González, and Palma combined ion mobility spectrometry with machine learning to catch and quantify a common juice fraud: stretching orange, pineapple, or apple juice with cheaper white grape juice. European law regulates juice quality, but adulteration persists as economic fraud and an allergy risk for consumers.

Their workflow analyzes vapor above the juice by gas chromatography coupled to ion mobility spectrometry, then lets regression algorithms estimate the adulteration percentage from the chemical fingerprint. Support vector regression performed best, with a root mean square error of 1.831 percentage points and an R-squared of 0.987 on their test data. A Boruta feature selection step sharpened all the models tried, including partial least squares and random forest variants. The team also released an interactive web application so laboratories can process samples through the pipeline without building the analysis themselves.
pmc-13443356:
Megan Vahsen and colleagues grow an invader grass, cheatgrass, in common gardens to test climate fit in a 2026 study. The annual grass plagues dry western lands, and its spread under warming stays hard to call. Gardens at four sites over two years grew 96 gene lines, with 22,492 plants in all.

Surface shade cloth and plant density varied the soil microclimate for each line. Models that let gene lines answer climate in their own ways beat plain models. Home-climate fit proved real, since lines thrived near their source weather. Crowding dulled that home edge, and survival answered shade in density-tied ways. Heat gains in fitness showed in the broad model. The authors warn that invader forecasts must carry gene and crowd context.
pmc-13445656:
Lior Baruch and coauthors investigate a 2026 study of parental loss in midlife, an event often dismissed as expected yet socially underrecognized. The team studied 423 adults aged 35 to 65 across dual-loss, single-loss, and non-bereaved groups on distress, joy, health, grief strength, loss integration, and social support.

Groups did not differ on distress, joy, health, or grief strength overall. Models showed social recognition boosted grief settling, which in turn foretold lower grief strength, while emotional support eased general distress without touching grief-specific results. The authors call for community policies and care that validate midlife loss rather than treating it as routine.
pmc-13446256:
Eslam Abdelwahab Dawood and colleagues evaluate a 2026 registry study of AI-assisted versus expert implant planning in the esthetic upper front jaw, where small errors mar facial harmony. The team compared a hybrid AI framework against human experts across 35 single-tooth cases with paired cone-beam CT and intraoral scans.

AI planning met clinical thresholds in most cases, with mean deviations near 1 millimeter coronally, 1.24 millimeters apically, and 4.3 degrees angularly, while cutting median planning time by 41.4 percent and achieving perfect consistency. Bone measures and guide fit matched expert work. AI planning offers expert-comparable accuracy with greater speed and consistency, the authors conclude.
pmc-13447056:
Shuang Liang and colleagues grade the long-term care insurance policy texts of five pilot cities in Guangxi, China, in a 2026 study. Nine core documents from Hezhou, Nanning, Liuzhou, Beihai, and Guigang were mined and scored with a policy index model, with two coders working apart and then settling gaps. Tool use and stakeholder shares were mapped as well.

The average index landed in the good band, with Hezhou and Beihai rated excellent. Environment-shaping tools dominated, while supply and demand tools lagged, and building sites plus training staff drew few items. Payment rules ate up most demand-side text. Officials drove the system, with donors and care receivers near silent, and all five cities shared weak marks for timeliness and for reward and restraint design.
pmc-13447256:
Marcella Pecora Milazzotto and fellow editors open a 2026 collection on metabolism in the earliest days of the mammalian embryo. From fertilisation to the hollow ball stage called the blastocyst, the embryo must sense nutrients, make energy and build new material in step with gene programmes. Metabolism, the editors stress, drives that programme rather than merely fuelling it.

One study covered here finds a sugar-sensing protein that rebuilds fat droplets in mouse embryos, with a stall point just before the blastocyst stage when the protein is blocked. Work on cattle embryos maps a nutrient signal that concentrates in outer cells destined to form support tissues. Further papers extend the theme across species and pathways. Together they tie early metabolism to implantation, fetal health and success in assisted reproduction.
pmc-13447456:
Mohammed Raiss and coauthors report a 2026 look-back study of keyhole Heller myotomy for achalasia over 22 years in a resource-limited setting, where scope myotomy remains rare. The team went over 55 straight patients treated from 2000 to 2022, judging success by swallow trouble clearing and Eckardt score gain plus outside pressure and pH tests.

Swallow trouble cleared in 92.8 percent after about two years of follow-up, with mean Eckardt scores rising a lot, and two switches came after tear. Anti-reflux wraps cut reflux rates, whether Dor or Toupet type. Surgery with an anti-reflux wrap remains the gold standard locally, giving durable control and reflux stopping.
pmc-13447856:
Joudi Altaleb and coauthors report a 2026 early mouse study testing whether growth contact to traffic-derived fine bits harms young adult bone. Starting at six weeks, BALB/c mice got daily nose Sydney roadside bits for 12 weeks against saline controls, with metals, micro-CT structure, and bending strength tests taken.

No group gaps showed in metal buildup, bone shape, or physical strength, with normal age-related growth in both groups. The null result shifts focus from early-life weak spot to life-long total burden and aging shields. The study also sets up a path for future long-run bone research.
pmc-13448856:
William Hinton and colleagues use in 2026 British primary care records to ask whether pairing two diabetes drug classes protects the kidneys better than either one alone. Both drug types, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists, had already shown kidney benefits separately in trials. The CombiKid study matched people on the combination with similar people on a single drug, using records from 2013 to 2021.

Against SGLT2 inhibitor treatment alone, in 14,774 matched patients, adding the second drug made no difference to the decline in kidney filtration over one and two years. Against GLP-1 treatment alone, in 14,154 matched patients, the combination preserved filtration better, by about 2.2 units at one year and 2.1 at two years. The authors read this as a real-world case for combining when a GLP-1 drug is the starting point.
pmc-13449656:
Xueyu Zhu and colleagues present in 2026 a case of grid radiation therapy used to shrink a large liver bile-duct cancer enough for surgery. Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is often found late, and big tumors wrapping major vessels rule out the resection that offers the best survival. Grid therapy is a form of spatially fractionated radiation. Instead of an even dose, it lays down alternating peaks and valleys across the tumor. Its high-dose spots measure one to two centimeters, spaced a few centimeters apart.

The patient carried a stage IIIB tumor judged unresectable at diagnosis. After conversion treatment built around this grid approach, delivered through a multileaf collimator, the tumor came under significant control and the patient met the criteria for surgical resection. The authors use the case to argue that multidisciplinary conversion strategies, pairing patterned radiation with other modalities, can move some large-volume liver cancers from hopeless to operable.
pmc-13449956:
Nuno M. Campos and co-authors use rotational spectroscopy to pin down how molecules dock together in supramolecular synthons, the recurring binding motifs used to design molecular architectures. Weak carbon-based bonds offer programmable assembly routes, but proving the exact geometry is hard. Their 2026 study examines complexes of tetracyanocyclopropane, a small ring carrying four cyano groups, with tetrahydrofuran.

In a supersonic jet, the complexes formed through a tetrel bond between a ring carbon and the oxygen of tetrahydrofuran. Ordinary rotational constants could not distinguish candidate geometries. The nitrogen atoms in the cyano groups, however, reported their local electric environments through quadrupole splittings in the spectrum, giving an orientational fingerprint. Using symmetry among the four nitrogen sites and a tailored fitting method, the team extracted precise parameters that uniquely defined the docking of two derivatives. They propose nitrogen field gradients as structural sensors for noncovalent chemistry.
pmc-13450456:
Jiatong Li and colleagues built a clear machine-learning tool in 2026 to spot muscle loss in older adults whose overall reserves are falling. Muscle loss, called sarcopenia, is easy to miss in this group, yet it shapes falls, frailty, and care needs. The team used survey data from China on aging and retirement.

Among 6,134 adults aged fifty and up with falling reserves, 663 met muscle-loss rules from the 2025 Asian group. Seven models were tried, with a two-step pick that cut twelve traits to eight key ones. Models were scored on how well they sorted cases, how true their odds were, and how much they would help in a clinic. Clinics gain a plain tool that flags muscle loss early, with reasons a doctor can check.
pmc-13450556:
Jiaming Wang and co-authors present a 2026 case of a child's leg rash that looked like one skin disease yet proved to be a rare line form of lupus. The boy, aged eight and from China, had flat bumps in a line up his right lower leg for five years. Doctors first read the pattern as lichen striatus, a mild line rash of childhood.

Creams brought no gain, and a trip to high, sunny Tibet a year earlier had let the line spread toward the groin. Close skin views and the slow course pointed instead to lupus that follows early skin growth lines. The case shows how lupus in children can wear a plain mask and why a rash that defies first treatment needs a fresh look.
pmc-13451856:
Raza Ali Naqvi and co-authors find in 2026 that a calming immune cell type gathers in sore gums and softens gum disease. The cells, called MDSCs, are young immune cells that damp other immune cells, and their role in gum disease was murky. Gum tissue from patients held more of both MDSC kinds, next to rises in T cells and B cells.

In dishes, the cells curbed the growth of the patient's own T cells. In mice with tied-thread gum disease, giving the cells cut T cell inflow and swelling signals while lifting calming ones. Wiping the cells out made swelling and bone loss worse. The authors cast the cells as guards of gum and bone, with care potential.
pmc-13451956:
Pupo and colleagues study how a family history of chronic pain shapes patients' current condition in this 2026 Italian cross-sectional study. They recruited 174 adults at their first consultation with a specialist pain service in Parma, assessing pain with a standard inventory and mental disorders with a structured clinical interview. The question was whether pain running in the family predicts worse present-day status.

Seventy-two participants, about 41 percent, had a family history of chronic pain. In roughly two-thirds of those cases, the pain sat in the same body location. That matched where their relative's pain had been years earlier. Family history predicted higher current unemployment and was significantly tied to stronger current pain intensity. These patients also more often used psychotropic drugs for reasons other than pain relief.
pmc-13452056:
Zhang and colleagues present a neural network for predicting which proteins a drug targets in this 2026 paper. A drug's effects flow through its targets, but finding them experimentally is slow. Perturbation transcriptomics offers a shortcut: dose cells with a compound and read how gene activity changes. Their model, BioHSNet, groups genes by biological function into hyperedges, structures linking many genes at once, so it can learn higher-order response patterns.

The model also folds in the compound's chemical structure, bridging what a molecule looks like with how cells respond to it. BioHSNet beat other transcriptome-based methods on the Broad Institute's L1000 datasets. Those datasets are a standard resource of such experiments. The advantage was clearest in cold-start tests, where the drug or target was new to the model. A case study showed it ranking plausible targets for screening.
pmc-13452156:
Istiaque Zaeem and co-authors isolate in 2026 a virus that hunts a drug-proof wound germ and pack it in a gel for slow release. The germ, Klebsiella aerogenes, shrugs off many antibiotics and builds slime films that block wound healing. The team fished a killer phage for it from the wild and read its full gene set.

The phage carried no harm or drug-resistance genes and stood firm across body-like heat and acid ranges. It cut mature slime film mass by three fifths. Set in an alginate gel, it leaked out steadily and stayed active for two weeks. The authors pitch gel phage care for chronic wounds that drugs can no longer clear.
pmc-13453456:
Sun and Pezaris present a 2026 protocol for scAutoTune, an R software pipeline that automatically tunes the settings used to cluster single-cell RNA sequencing data. Choosing how many variable genes, components, and what clustering sharpness to use is usually trial and error, and the best choices differ by dataset. The protocol sweeps settings in a grid and scores each by how cleanly clusters separate.

Steps cover installing the tool, preparing data in the Seurat framework, sweeping the settings with optional batch correction, and viewing smoothed result landscapes to pick the optimum. Two reference datasets anchor the method. One is a 399-cell blood dataset with known labels, where tuned settings recovered the true immune populations well. The other is a 334-cell brain neuron subset with batch effects. The authors detail the full workflow for reuse.
pmc-13453656:
Takamitsu Iwata reviews the double life of hippocampal ripples, fast brain waves that can signal either epilepsy trouble or healthy memory work.
