In brain recordings, ripple band activity marks tissue prone to seizures and helps surgeons plan operations. Yet the same region makes sharp wave ripples that fix memories during sleep. His 2026 review weighs how to tell the two apart.

New tools include shared scoring rules, pattern analysis across time and space, and machine learning detectors. The meaning of a ripple seems to hinge on the brain's state, what the person is doing, and how close the ripple sits to the seizure focus. Iwata frames ripples as a sign of whole network state, not just a local event. Reading them well could let treatment curb seizures while sparing memory, he argues.
pmc-13453756:
Faris Alanazi and five co-authors survey ankle sprains and recovery habits among amateur padel players in Saudi Arabia. Padel, a racket sport played in walled courts, asks for jumps and sharp turns that stress ankles. Their 2026 study covers 187 amateur players, with a function score for the foot and ankle.

Sprains had hit 14.97 percent of the players, most often on landing and on the right side. Three quarters of the injured reported lasting limits, and 42.86 percent had sprained the same ankle again. Playing for over a year and playing twice a week or more each raised injury odds about three fold. Habits such as balance and strength work did not cut injury risk, yet players who did them scored clearly higher on function after injury.
pmc-13454356:
Huijuan Zhou and five colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, a receptor called LILRB4 as a driver of ovarian cancer growth and immune escape. Ovarian cancer is the deadliest cancer of the female reproductive system. The receptor was known from blood cancers, yet its role in solid tumors was unclear.

Among its family, LILRB4 showed the highest levels in ovarian tumors, and high levels tracked with shorter survival. Turning the receptor down in lab cells slowed growth, spread, and invasion, while raising it did the opposite. Tumors rich in the receptor drew in macrophages and pushed them toward a type that suppresses immunity. The team traced this effect to a signal chain involving the chemical CCL5 and the NF-kB pathway. Lowering the receptor also made cancer cells respond better to treatment in a mouse tumor model.
pmc-13455156:
Webb and colleagues spoke with 20 people with diverse nerve and brain conditions. They asked whether doctors ever asked about bladder, bowel, and sexual problems. These symptoms affect many patients from diagnosis onward, yet often stay unspoken. Participants ranged from 30 to 83 years old, and 13 of the 20 came from global majority backgrounds.

Analysis gave four themes, starting with dismissive clinical encounters and systemic pressures that squeezed these topics out of appointments. A second theme covered poor communication and expectation-setting, leaving patients to become rulers of their own care through self-advocacy and peer support networks. Grief ran through the third theme, as interviewees described mourning lost parts of themselves and struggling to describe altered sensations to professionals. The fourth, sex matters, captured gender differences and the persistently low priority of sexual health. The authors conclude diagnostic reasoning and management both neglect these functions.
pmc-13455256:
Katie Biggs and others probed life-quality impacts in the MissionEB trial in 2026, a qualitative sub-study of cord-cell infusions for recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa in children. RDEB is a rare gene skin state that makes skin fragile, blistered, and scarred. Umbilical cord stromal cells had shown cure promise in the phase 3 trial.

Semi-structured chats probed care impact at near three and twelve months past randomisation. Purposive sampling took ten parents and six children, with thirteen folk chatted twice, once in each study phase. Chats were typed word-for-word and coded alone, with broad takes agreed before unblinding. RDEB hit daily life hard through pain and care load in the told themes. Trial teams gain patient and parent views on cell care for a harsh skin disease.
pmc-13455356:
Brady Page, Elizabeth Moreton, David A. Wohl, and William A. Fischer review, in a 2026 study, bacterial infections that ride along with four deadly viral fevers: Ebola, Marburg, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, and Lassa fever. Fear of such coinfection makes blanket antibiotics standard in outbreaks, yet the true scale was murky. The team gathered thirty publications across the four diseases.

Bloodstream infection reports clustered in Crimean-Congo cases, with 46 patients, against 16 each for Ebola and Marburg and only two for Lassa. Bacteria surfaced a median of eleven days into illness, often with sepsis signs. The commonest preventive antibiotic, ceftriaxone, was predicted to cover only a minority of the germs found. Coinfection did not raise Ebola or Marburg deaths in the data, though it did in Crimean-Congo cases. The authors call for prospective studies with standard testing before antibiotic habits can be set wisely.
pmc-13455456:
Kittichai Tharawadeepimuk and co-authors asked whether combining two mental skills, controlled breathing and positive self-talk, could change both brain activity and coping in elite athletes. Their 2026 randomized trial enrolled 26 national-level competitors, 11 swimmers and 15 gymnasts, and gave half of them 16 training sessions spread over four weeks. The researchers recorded resting brain waves with EEG, a scalp test that measures electrical activity, before and after the program.

The trained athletes showed clear brain changes, including stronger theta waves in the front of the brain and weaker beta waves, patterns linked with calmer attention. They also scored higher on five parts of a standard coping questionnaire, covering adversity, concentration, confidence, goal setting, and performing under pressure. The authors caution that brain waves are indirect signs of mental states, not direct proof of them.
pmc-13457056:
Alice M. Burton leads an eleven-author field study, from 2026, of how gut parasites stir immune markers in the dung of Kenyan hoofed animals. Wildlife and livestock graze side by side in Laikipia, sharing worms and protozoa. The team sampled six wild and four domestic species, ten animals each, pairing DNA parasite censuses with egg counts and four stool immune measures.

No single parasite moved the same marker in every host. One worm genus lowered two antibody markers in cattle relatives yet left antelope readings untouched. Another raised markers in giraffes and antelope but not camels. A protozoan dragged antibodies down in cattle, horses, and camels by differing amounts. The authors say parasite effects are written in the host's own dialect, shaped by evolution and gut layout. Blanket rules for reading wildlife health from dung will not work, they warn.
pmc-13457556:
Shanyong Yi and colleagues map how the veterinary sedative xylazine might injure the testes in a 2026 computational study. Xylazine now appears as a cheap adulterant in illicit drug supplies, often with fentanyl, and its tissue harms are poorly understood. The team mined six drug and disease databases for xylazine targets tied to testicular injury, then narrowed the network with interaction tools and tested binding by molecular docking.

The search yielded 126 candidate targets and 18 core targets, including SRC and HSP90AA1, enriched in nerve signalling, cell death, calcium signalling and cancer pathways. Docking showed strong binding to those core targets, suggesting xylazine may disturb cell growth, death and inflammation in testicular tissue. The work is purely computational, so lab and animal tests must confirm whether these predicted pathways cause real injury.
pmc-13457856:
Iara De Schoenmacker and colleagues test whether body, mind and social factors together sort chronic pain severity in a 2026 study. Chronic pain resists simple diagnosis, and sensory tests alone often fail to separate mild from severe cases across diagnoses. The team studied 101 people with chronic pain and 63 pain-free controls. They were sorted into no pain, mild-to-moderate pain and severe pain with three models: sensory testing alone, sensory plus biopsychosocial data, and biopsychosocial data without sensory testing.

Sensory testing alone reached only 0.51 accuracy, while the full biopsychosocial model reached 0.71 and the model without sensory testing reached 0.60. Quality of life, loss of sensation, low mood, catastrophising, anxiety, fatigue and general health drove the best model. Clinicians gain evidence that mood, function and social context belong in pain assessment, not as extras but as core severity signals.
pmc-13458156:
Angharad N. de Cates and colleagues test whether stimulating the serotonin 5-HT4 receptor wakes memory circuits in people with depression. Cognitive problems linger in depressed patients and standard drugs barely touch them, while animal work and a related drug, prucalopride, hinted this receptor helps hippocampal learning. The RESTAND study, reported in 2026, randomly assigned 52 unmedicated, right-handed patients to six to nine days of the agonist PF-04995274 or placebo, then scanned their brains during a memory task.

The drug group showed stronger hippocampal responses to novel over known images, most on the left, and greater activation in the left inferior parietal lobule. Behavior told a quieter story: unlike prucalopride results, verbal learning and spatial working memory barely budged. The authors read the scans as proof the receptor can tune memory circuitry in depression, a foothold for treatments aimed at thinking. They warn that brain signals alone are not yet better recall.
pmc-13458256:
Rohit Nalavade, Aashiq H. Mirza, and Samie R. Jaffrey deliver a reality check to the field mapping chemical decorations on messenger RNA. Genome-wide maps claimed thousands of m1A marks, other teams disputed them, and an enzyme-based map revived the claim. Their 2026 paper describes SCARPET, a protocol cutting RNA at one chosen site, radioactively labeling the end, trimming it, and reading the letter by thin-layer chromatography.

Aimed at the new sites, SCARPET found no m1A at all. The positions instead held inosine, the product of A-to-I editing, a chemical impostor mimicking the mapping signal. A second contested mark, m7G, passed the same test at high occupancy, proving the method can say yes as well as no. The authors conclude genuine m1A inside messenger RNA is rare, and they offer SCARPET as a validation gate before any modification site enters textbooks.
pmc-13458356:
Jahinna Duplaix and colleagues count a decade of chatter about traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine on X, the platform formerly called Twitter. Their 2026 retrospective infodemiology study tracks 39 predefined terms in English, Spanish, and French posts from 2015 to 2024 using Brandwatch counts, spanning the pandemic years.

The 39 terms amassed nearly 192 million mentions, but three wellness labels swallowed the conversation: yoga at about 79.6 million, meditation at 55.6 million, and mindfulness at 18.9 million together made 80.3 percent of the total. English dominated at 88.6 percent of mentions. Between 2019 and 2020 meditation posted the largest absolute jump, rising 53.4 percent, while ayurveda posted the largest relative jump at 186.4 percent. Pre-pandemic trend mining found most significant English trends heading downward, with intermittent fasting the standout riser, while reiki and reflexology fell in all three languages. No lasting overall surge survived the raw descriptive picture.
pmc-13459156:
Minase Shenkute and colleagues measure preterm newborn deaths and their predictors in western Ethiopia in a 2026 cohort study. Preterm mortality remains high where neonatal care is thin, yet local rates and drivers at Wallaga University hospital were lacking. The team reviewed 264 preterm admissions to intensive care from July 2022 to June 2024, with 259 included in analysis over 2,737 newborn-days.

Forty-two newborns died, an incidence of 16.2 percent or 15.3 deaths per 1,000 newborn-days, with median survival of 28 days. Lack of antenatal care, home delivery and newborn hypothermia raised death risk sharply, while antenatal steroids cut risk by 56 percent. Strengthening antenatal visits, facility delivery, thermal care and steroid use emerges as a concrete, low-cost survival package for preterm infants in similar settings.
pmc-13459356:
Scott J Robson and co-authors audited who actually reaches a regional navigation service that connects Ontario children and youth to mental health and addiction care. The service, 1Call1Click.ca, is meant to simplify access, but equitable reach cannot be assumed. Their 2026 analysis covered all 9,694 clients aged up to twenty one who completed intake between June 2021 and December 2023. It compared their demographics with regional census figures and tested whether social traits predicted severity of need at intake.

Some groups used the service at higher than population rates: girls, non-binary and transgender youth, families at the lowest and highest incomes, and youth identifying with multiple or other racial backgrounds. Cisgender boys and middle income households were underrepresented, as were Filipino, Japanese, Chinese, South Asian, and Indigenous youth relative to their population shares. Differences in need severity across social groups were small. The authors flag the underrepresented groups for outreach.
pmc-13459456:
Xuebing Wang, Xunli Yin, Linlin Teng, and Dong Tao searched in 2026 for genes linked to PANoptosis that could help diagnose acute myocardial infarction, a heart attack. PANoptosis blends features of three cell-death pathways and drives inflammation. The team mined public gene-expression datasets to compare heart attack patients with controls. Network building and random forest modeling then narrowed hundreds of altered genes down to candidates. Findings were checked in patient blood samples.

Two genes, IL1B and NLRP3, emerged as hubs, and diagnostic models built on them performed well in both training and validation sets. Both genes tracked closely with immune cells that shift during a heart attack, and two shared regulators were identified. Five candidate drugs tied to the genes were also predicted, offering starting points for treatment research.
pmc-13461456:
Yao Tang, Boyin Yang, and Xingmei Luo hunted in 2026 for blood biomarkers of the thinking problems that follow a hypertensive brain hemorrhage. Cognitive impairment drives much of the long-term disability after such bleeds, yet its molecular roots are murky. Sequencing the gene activity in patient samples produced 247 altered genes linked to impairment. Network analysis and expression checks then nominated two candidates. Both ran higher in impaired patients and were confirmed by a second laboratory method.

The two genes, CXCL8 and FCGR3B, sit in pathways that include oxidative phosphorylation, the cell's main energy process. Regulatory mapping predicted dozens of small RNAs and several transcription factors controlling each gene, with two small RNAs shared between them. Hundreds of existing drugs were computationally matched against the pair, seeding future treatment studies.
pmc-13461556:
Andrea Luque-Bolivar and co-authors present a 2026 combined analysis of gene activity in human astrocytes, the star-shaped support cells of the brain. Astrocytes help control swelling and immune defense in the brain and spinal cord. The team pooled studies where astrocytes were exposed to signals linked to infection or inflammation. Their goal was to find a gene pattern that shows up again and again across triggers.

The search gathered 11 gene studies with 153 samples, of which 91 had been stimulated and the rest served as controls. Triggers ranged from immune signal proteins to a fatty acid and two germs. Pooling the results gave 130 genes that changed, nearly all switched on more strongly. Five genes sat at the center of the network the team built. The authors argue that astrocytes shift into a shared reactive state, one that can protect the brain yet may also feed long-term harmful swelling.
pmc-13461956:
Mawar Karsa and co-authors report that blocking two cell survival proteins at once makes standard steroid therapy far deadlier to infant leukemia cells in laboratory models. The disease, KMT2A rearranged acute lymphoblastic leukemia, strikes babies and resists treatment. It depends on the survival protein MCL1, which the rearranged gene switches on directly and which blunts both steroids and the BCL-2 blocker venetoclax. In their 2026 letter, the team combined an MCL1 inhibitor with venetoclax or the steroid dexamethasone in resistant and responsive cell lines.

The MCL1 blocker S63845 paired with either drug killed more effectively than single agents across the viability assays. Adding BCL-2 blockade deepened the effect further, with combination treatment measurably raising the cell death machinery's activation markers, including cleaved caspases. Since high MCL1 marks steroid resistance in infant samples, co inhibition attacks resistance at its root. The dual blockade is a preclinical rationale for trials.
pmc-13462456:
Wang and colleagues reported a 2026 case report and literature review on juvenile arthritis arising in a child with DiGeorge syndrome. DiGeorge is an inborn immune disorder caused by a missing piece of chromosome 22, and it can bring autoimmune disease. The patient was a twenty-two-month-old girl with frequent chest infections and delayed speech.

She had already had a heart defect repaired in infancy, when surgeons noticed her thymus gland was missing. Wang found inflamed joints in both knees and one hand that had lasted five months, plus positive immune blood markers. Standard anti-inflammatory drugs and methotrexate failed over four months of treatment. A biologic drug, etanercept, then brought remission within six months. Across fifty-one published cases, most children were girls diagnosed before age six with several joints involved.
pmc-13462756:
Mutian Zheng and colleagues build, in a 2026 records study, a chart-style tool for spotting a rare brain complication in children early. The condition, acute necrotizing encephalopathy, strikes after infections such as flu or COVID-19 and brings a poor outlook. The team studied children who arrived with seizures or disturbed consciousness after those infections at a children's hospital in Soochow between late 2021 and early 2024.

Four signs independently marked children who developed the complication: altered consciousness, plus three blood measures, two liver and tissue enzymes and a kidney waste marker. A scoring chart built from the four sorted cases with high accuracy in the building group and a held-back check group. Calibration and decision analyses supported its accuracy for flagging risk. The authors offer the chart as a way to catch high-risk children sooner and start care, while noting it needs testing at other hospitals before wide use.
pmc-13462856:
Ziwei Zhang and colleagues test, in a 2026 three-center study, whether an ultrasound-based prediction model still works when it travels to new hospitals. The model estimates hidden heavy spread to central neck nodes in papillary thyroid cancer that looks node-free before surgery. Data covered 957 patients, and the model joined clinical-ultrasound traits with a fixed radiomics score from the tumor image.

Heavy spread was present in about forty-two percent of patients, though one center ran far lower. Endpoint-positive patients had larger tumors, higher image scores, and richer blood flow. The study then tracked how accuracy and calibration drifted in a later cohort at the home center and at two outside centers, and what fixed risk cut-offs would do there. A light recalibration step was tested after the fact. The authors frame transport, calibration, and local updating as the real tests of clinical readiness.
pmc-13462956:
Maho Hayase and colleagues fused several microscope images in 2026 to link hydrogen spread with crystal direction in a vanadium-iron alloy. Hydrogen moving through metals can embrittle them, a worry as hydrogen energy grows, yet the role of grain direction was hard to pin down. The team combined light, electron, and diffraction images of one alloy sample into a single data set.

Two unsupervised methods then pulled patterns from the fused images that single images had missed. Grains aligned to the [111] and [101] directions spread hydrogen more freely than those aligned to [001]. Drift away from a pure direction also shifted spread, so the fused-image approach gives a clearer map of which crystal layouts invite hydrogen damage in vanadium parts.
pmc-13463256:
Yuan and colleagues build a smart nanoparticle for treating atherosclerosis, the fatty plaque buildup inside arteries, in 2026 nanomedicine research. Plaques grow when immune cells gorge on lipids, become foam cells, and then fail to be cleared because a signal called CD47 tells clearer cells not to eat them. The team's liposome carrier loads the cholesterol drug atorvastatin together with a peptide that blocks CD47, releasing its cargo where reactive oxygen species, a plaque hallmark, concentrate.

In mice fed a high-fat diet for 8 weeks to grow plaques, the full treatment cut aortic plaque area from 28.8 percent to 11.1 percent of the vessel surface. The plaque vulnerability index, a measure of rupture risk, fell from 1.14 to 0.55 versus untreated mice. Atorvastatin also lowered CD47 production inside the cell, so the two cargoes attacked the same signal by different routes. Yuan argues the dual blockade restores plaque cleanup.
pmc-13463556:
Dsouza and colleagues pooled randomized trials in 2026 on digital health tools for type 2 diabetes. The tools included phone apps, text reminders, and videos. The question was whether they improve blood sugar control in low- and middle-income countries. The review covered trials published from 2016 to 2025. Results were combined with a random-effects model, used when studies differ from each other.

Of 23 trials included, 15 showed clear gains. Across all studies, the tools lowered HbA1c by a bit more than half a percentage point versus usual care. HbA1c is the blood marker reflecting average sugar over roughly three months. Benefits appeared in short programs of about three months. They also appeared in longer ones running a year or more. Fasting blood sugar, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides improved too. The pattern supports remote coaching for medicines and daily habits.
pmc-13463756:
Mebrahtu Teweldemedhin Shfare and colleagues measured high-risk HPV infection in 2026 among women living with HIV in Mekelle, northern Ethiopia. High-risk HPV strains cause cervical and other cancers, and HIV-positive women face about double the infection risk. The team enrolled 390 women at five public clinics between December 2024 and July 2025 and tested cervical samples for 14 high-risk types.

Overall, 39.7% tested positive, with HPV-16 at 10.8%, HPV-18 at 3.6%, and other high-risk types together at 32.7%. Average age was about 43 years, and most women were of normal weight. The high share argues for tighter cervical screening and HPV follow-up in HIV care in the region, since early detection can stop cancers before they start.
pmc-13463956:
Zhang and co-authors surveyed 497 caregivers of stroke patients at a Beijing rehabilitation center in 2026. Their subject was post-stroke depression, the low mood that commonly follows stroke and slows recovery. A questionnaire scored knowledge, attitude, and day-to-day practice separately. Path analysis then showed how the three connect. Most caregivers were women, and the average age was about 43.

Caregivers scored well on willingness and habits. They reached about 83 percent of the attitude maximum and 90 percent of the practice maximum. Their knowledge reached only about 57 percent of its maximum. The weakest spots were recognizing symptoms and grasping that depression can bring self-harm risk. Knowing how to respond was weak too. Each extra unit of knowledge came with better attitudes and practices. The path model confirmed that knowledge feeds practice directly and through attitude. Structured teaching, the authors argue, would convert goodwill into competence.
pmc-13464256:
Vishal Gavali and colleagues report a 2026 case of a previously healthy 35-year-old man whose cardiac sarcoidosis drove repeated dangerous rhythms despite drugs. Sarcoidosis scars organs with small grain-like lumps, and heart involvement strikes 5 to 10% of patients. Imaging and tissue study confirmed the diagnosis after he arrived with a racing heart at 212 beats per minute.

A defibrillator was fitted for secondary prevention, yet rhythm storms continued, so surgeons cut sympathetic nerves on both sides through keyhole chest surgery. Ventricular rhythms stopped fully after the procedure. The case backs nerve-cutting as a salvage option when inflammation treatment and devices fail, within a team plan for refractory cardiac sarcoidosis.
pmc-13464856:
Diana Ioana Panaite leads a team that turns a public breast MRI archive into a clean test bed for foretelling treatment response. Early forecasts of full tumor kill during chemo could guide care sooner. The archive, though, was never packaged for paired before-and-during scans, so the team rebuilt it into 183 matched patients.

Hand-built image features and frozen deep-learning image codes were raced on the same patients. The best hand-built model used during-treatment scans alone and scored modestly. The best deep-code models, using change between scans or averaged codes, scored about the same. Full deep training on raw pairs overfit badly and was dropped. Both routes, the study shows, top out near the same modest ceiling today.
pmc-13465056:
Daniel Arriscado-Alsina and Raúl Jiménez-Boraita survey 949 schoolchildren in the Canary Islands on quality of life and its daily drivers. Questionnaires covered activity, sleep trouble, and well-being, while field tests measured fitness and body makeup. Grades and background factors joined the same dataset.

Children in the top well-being third moved more, slept better, and carried less belly fat than peers. They also jumped stronger, ran fitter, and reported better school results. In the joint model, sleep problems dragged well-being down most of all. Being in primary school, feeling able at schoolwork, daily movement, and leg strength each lifted scores. The authors back school plans that join sleep teaching with daily activity.
pmc-13465656:
Kordkatuli and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the world evidence on moral courage in health sciences students. Moral courage means acting on ethical values despite risk, the bridge between knowing right and doing right. The review followed standard guidelines across five databases for studies from 2000 to March 2025. Twenty-one studies with 4,719 students from varied cultures qualified.

A split ran by discipline. Nursing students generally showed moderate-to-high moral courage. Medical and dental students scored lower, often hemmed in by rigid hierarchies. The chief barriers were the hidden curriculum, fear of bad evaluations, and power gaps between trainees and seniors. Between 40 and 60 percent of trainees in various settings witness unethical conduct yet stay silent. Good role models, a sense of moral agency, and supportive peers helped students speak up. The authors urge treating courage as a trainable skill.
pmc-13465956:
Mei and co-authors compared two feeding tubes for stroke patients in 2026 under China's diagnosis-based payment system, which pays hospitals a fixed sum per case. A stomach tube through the nose is the standard route. A tube threaded deeper into the small intestine is the alternative. The study reviewed 322 patients at a central China hospital from 2021 to 2024. A matched subset of 66 pairs anchored the fairest comparison.

The deeper tube fed patients better. Hemoglobin and albumin rose more than with the stomach tube. Malnutrition and inflammation burden both ran lower. The deeper route cost more, though. Total hospital and nutrition bills were significantly higher, and the payment overrun rate reached about 77 percent against about 63 percent for the standard tube. Length of stay matched between groups. The authors recommend reserving the deeper tube for high-risk patients who gain most from it.
pmc-13466356:
Shlomit Tamir and colleagues audited what the label 'atypical hemangioma' actually meant in liver scan reports at two hospitals. Hemangiomas are benign blood-filled liver growths, usually named with confidence, but odd-looking ones get this fuzzy label.

The audit covered 327 lesions so labelled between 2013 and 2023, judged against follow-up, tissue tests, and stability. Most, 305 of them (93.3 percent), proved benign, but 22 (6.7 percent) were cancers hiding under the soft label. Half the cancers drew no recommendation for further checks, and nearly half never mentioned cancer as a possibility. Meanwhile 42 percent of benign lesions were diagnosable at once, yet many still got needless extra workup, Tamir reports.
pmc-13466456:
Yılmaz, Özer, and Topal test in this 2026 study how many children with severe hay fever but no asthma diagnosis actually have hidden airway narrowing during exercise. The children, aged 6 to 18, were starting allergen immunotherapy injections for moderate-to-severe persistent allergic rhinitis, and each completed a standardized exercise challenge with breathing measurements.

Among 62 children, 21 tested positive for exercise-induced bronchoconstriction, a prevalence of 33.9 percent in this supposedly non-asthmatic group, with the airflow drop most often appearing fifteen minutes after exercise. A family history of asthma was far more common among positive children, at 23.8 percent versus 2.4 percent among those who tested negative, and worse nasal symptom scores also flagged risk. Blood allergy markers, by contrast, did not separate the groups. The authors recommend exercise testing for similar children before immunotherapy proceeds.
pmc-13466556:
Yishu Wang and colleagues feed mice a jelly-like sugar polymer by mouth and test whether it shields the brain in a Parkinson-like condition, in a 2026 study. The compound, sodium hyaluronate, was given before the toxin that triggers the disease model, at three dose levels. The highest dose eased both movement problems and gut trouble in the animals.

That dose also rebalanced gut microbes, raised helpful short-chain fatty acids, and tightened both the gut wall and the blood-brain barrier. Less bacterial toxin leaked into blood and brain, quieting an inflammatory relay inside the substantia nigra. The chain links gut care to nerve protection along the gut-brain axis.
pmc-13466956:
Mandour and colleagues reviewed outcomes in 2026 for tirzepatide, a dual-action diabetes and weight drug, in people with partial lipodystrophy. In this rare condition, missing or faulty fat tissue forces lipids into other organs and drives severe insulin resistance. Treatment options are few, with only one specific licensed drug. Their single-center record review covered all forty patients treated with the drug from 2022 to 2025, most of them women with the commonest inherited subtype.

Over a median follow-up of about nine and a half months, body weight fell by roughly eight kilograms on median values. The long-term blood sugar marker dropped by a wide margin. Blood triglycerides, a fat measure that runs dangerously high in this condition, fell by about a third, and daily insulin needs dropped to about a third of their starting level. The authors call for prospective trials and earlier use studies.
pmc-13467356:
Ali Emre Bardak and eight colleagues published this 2026 study asking whether patients should keep taking nonselective beta-blockers after a TIPS procedure for liver cirrhosis. TIPS places a shunt inside the liver to relieve high pressure in the portal vein, the problem these drugs also target. Guidance usually favours stopping the drugs once the shunt works. The team mimicked a clinical trial using the large TriNetX health records network in the United States.

They studied 5,111 patients who had taken the drugs before TIPS and lived past day 90, then matched 2,180 pairs who continued or stopped. One-year survival was nearly identical, at 89.3 percent for those who stopped and 89.6 percent for those who continued treatment. Transplant-free survival was also similar. Continuing patients did face a higher hazard of hepatic encephalopathy, confusion caused by liver failure, with a hazard ratio of 1.29 in the analysis. Bleeding and intensive care admissions did not differ.
pmc-13467456:
Rao and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the heart failure drug vericiguat for elderly patients whose hearts pump weakly. Older patients with this condition form a fast-growing, mixed group marked by many illnesses, frailty, and long drug lists, all of which bend treatment response. Vericiguat stimulates a pathway that relaxes blood vessels and fights harmful remodelling of the heart, a pathway that fails as the disease advances.

Rao summarises the drug's rationale, body handling, and trial record, led by the large VICTORIA trial. The evidence backs use in selected patients whose condition recently worsened despite standard therapy. Trials in the preserved-pumping form of heart failure showed no clear benefit, and proof in frail elders with geriatric syndromes stays thin. The review maps how to place the drug in real care for complex older patients, with doses and cautions spelled out.
pmc-13467556:
Zuo and colleagues built in 2026 a neural network ensemble to forecast how asphalt road surfaces wear down over time. Road condition guides when crews should resurface, and older forecast models struggle with the curved, uneven way pavements decay under traffic and weather. The team aimed for sharper forecasts from a handful of road and climate measures.

Their model feeds seven inputs, among them road age, daily traffic, temperature range, rainfall, humidity, layer thickness, and surface strength, into networks tuned by a fast training method. Several tuned networks vote together as an ensemble, which steadies the output. Tested against a standard single network, the ensemble predicted the road condition index with lower error. The authors offer it as a planning aid for highway upkeep.
pmc-13467656:
Muhammad Maaz and colleagues review in 2026 the cancer-related evidence for extra virgin olive oil and its phenolic compounds, the bitter plant chemicals that give good olive oil its bite. The review searched four databases for work from 2015 to 2025 on whole oil, enriched oils, extracts, and four isolated compounds, including hydroxytyrosol and oleocanthal. Evidence was organized by cancer type, from breast and colorectal to brain and blood cancers.

Most of the molecular evidence comes from cell and animal studies rather than human trials. In those models, olive phenolics showed anticancer activity through several routes, including antioxidant action and interference with tumor growth signals. The authors also flag a practical problem: these compounds are poorly absorbed and quickly changed in the body, so lab doses may not match what eating the oil delivers. That gap shapes their cautious outlook for therapy.
pmc-13467756:
Wang and colleagues ask whether the time of day a person exercises changes fat loss, and whether a circadian gene variant matters, in 2026 exercise research. Thirty-one overweight or obese university students trained for 8 weeks with moderate-intensity continuous exercise, either in the morning between 7:00 and 10:00 or in the afternoon between 16:00 and 19:00. Groups were split by the PER3 gene variant rs228697, linked to morningness and eveningness tendencies.

Across the whole sample, weight, body mass index, waist size, body fat percentage, and total fat mass all fell over the 8 weeks of training. Descriptive comparisons favored the afternoon group carrying the common CC genotype, which showed larger reductions on several measures than the morning group. The subgroup of afternoon trainees carrying the G variant was very small, so its results count as exploratory only. Wang frames timing as a plausible lever on fat loss, not a settled prescription.
pmc-13468056:
Irene Ventura and Tiziana Lombardi test in 2026 how seed size and home population shape germination in a Mediterranean saltmarsh plant, Salicornia perennans. Saltmarsh plants face wildly variable salinity, and this species naturally makes two seed types, large and small. Seeds from three Tuscan coastal populations were sorted by type and germinated at four salt concentrations, from none up to 20 grams per liter.

Seed type proved the main driver of success. Large seeds reached higher final germination and a better germination index than small seeds in every population and salt level. Rising salt lowered germination totals but did not change how fast seeds germinated on average. The bet-hedging lesson is plain: producing two seed sizes spreads risk across the unpredictable salt conditions a saltmarsh delivers each spring.
pmc-13468356:
Prajwal Panthi and Brady R. Cox compare in 2026 three ways of converting fiber-optic strain records into the ground velocities that seismologists and engineers actually use. Distributed acoustic sensing turns buried cables into thousands of strain sensors, but its output units do not match conventional instruments. The test used a rare high-energy data set from Birds Landing, California, where a transmission tower collapse and sledgehammer blows were recorded by a 1.4 kilometer fiber array alongside 71 nodal stations.

Using 63 paired fiber and station locations, the authors scored each conversion method, including frequency-wavenumber rescaling, a curvelet-based method, and slant-stack summation, on amplitude and phase fidelity. Near-field, high-energy records are exactly where conversion errors would hurt most in earthquake engineering. The head-to-head scoring tells practitioners which method to trust when fiber sensing stands in for traditional seismometers.
pmc-13468556:
Stefania Toselli, Emanuela Gualdi-Russo, and Luciana Zaccagni compare in 2026 how African women who moved to Italy see their own bodies, against an Italian comparison group. Body image is shaped by weight, local ideals, and habits, and moving countries can shift those ideals over time. The study enrolled 131 women, 60 of them immigrants and 71 Italians. A silhouette scale captured the body each woman saw and the body she wanted.

The immigrant women weighed more on average, with higher body mass index. The two groups also spread differently across weight classes. Unhappiness with the body was scored as the gap between the body women saw and the body they wanted. The team also measured appearance anxiety, self-esteem, life satisfaction, exercise, and how closely diets matched the Mediterranean pattern. The study speaks to health care for migrant women, where weight advice that ignores local body ideals often fails before it starts.
pmc-13469556:
Amir Yazdanparast, Hala Tamim, Alison K Macpherson, and Jennifer L Kuk examine how the class of obesity relates to causes of death among American adults. They used national survey data gathered from 1999 to 2018, with deaths tracked through the end of 2019. Risks were compared across body mass index groups, split by age and by sex.

Adults under 65 with the highest obesity class faced clearly higher death rates than those in the lowest class. The gap covered heart causes, diabetes, and deaths outside heart disease and cancer. Among older adults the pattern was weaker, showing up mainly in men for heart and diabetes deaths. The two lower obesity classes differed little from each other. The authors suggest younger adults with severe obesity may gain most from intensive treatment.
pmc-13469656:
Jun Qi and colleagues present a pilot study, published in 2026. It looks beyond the usual suspects in platelet transfusion failure. In some patients, platelet counts fail to rise after transfusion. Antibodies against HLA tissue markers take most of the blame. The team asked whether antibodies against other targets also matter.

The team set 32 such patients against 20 healthy donors. They tested for sixty non-HLA antibodies. A gene deletion called GSTT1 was also tested. Non-HLA antibody patterns linked to transfusion failure. This did not depend on HLA sensitisation. Many past transfusions were linked to certain antibodies. Only patients missing both GSTT1 copies made antibodies against it. This suggests new markers for transfusion risk checks.
pmc-13470056:
Ashura Kassim Kiliza and colleagues measured severe undernutrition in 2026 among HIV-positive children under five on antiretroviral therapy in Ilala, Tanzania. Undernutrition and HIV compound each other in poor settings, yet local drivers for treated children were unclear. Records for 334 clinic children from 2020 to 2024 were scored against WHO growth standards, with models probing immune and viral thresholds.

Severe undernutrition reached 8.1% for underweight, 17.7% for stunting, and 3.0% for wasting. Adherence, CD4 count, age, food insecurity, meal frequency, and guardian occupation shaped outcomes, with three daily meals lifting weight scores and good adherence lifting height scores. Immune and viral thresholds explained up to 30.5% of wasting variation, offering triggers to intensify nutrition help.
pmc-13470256:
Tong and colleagues test whether a resting pulse forecasts cardiovascular trouble in dialysis patients. Their 2026 prospective cohort study follows 309 adults on maintenance hemodialysis, split into thirds by baseline resting heart rate. Evidence in this population had been inconsistent, and the team built and internally validated a multivariable prediction model with the event rate as its target.

Major cardiovascular events climbed steeply across the heart-rate thirds, from about one in five patients in the lowest group to over half in the highest. The top third carried nearly five times the adjusted odds of the bottom third. Diabetes and higher anxiety-depression scores also independently raised risk. A nomogram built from the model showed useful calibration and clinical benefit in decision analysis. The authors position resting heart rate, a measurement already taken at every session, as an independent and practical risk marker.
pmc-13470756:
Scala and colleagues published a 2026 study on greener ways to build peptides in the lab. Peptides are short protein chains used in many modern medicines. Their assembly usually swims in a harsh solvent called DMF. The team tested a friendlier solvent mix with a newer coupling reagent.

The mix paired ethyl acetate with a splash of DMSO as the medium. Couplings there matched the purity reached in the standard harsh solvent. The green setup also caused less unwanted flipping of molecule handedness. A helper additive proved useful only for the bulkiest building blocks tested. High-fidelity peptide making without DMF looks viable, the authors conclude. Several model peptides were built to test the system fairly.
pmc-13471356:
Vinodh Bhagyalakshmi Nanjayya leads a large critical care team setting out in 2026 to measure how often the pulse vanishes after extracorporeal resuscitation and what that loss means. In this rescue therapy, a machine takes over heart and lung work for patients whose hearts will not restart. Some patients afterward show a flat arterial trace, no pulse pressure at all, despite efforts to support the heart.

Earlier work on low, but not absent, pulse pressure linked it to poor survival and brain injury, yet complete loss had never been counted. The retrospective cohort study therefore aims first at incidence and then at outcomes for the affected patients. The authors frame the flat trace as a possible warning state that teams currently lack guidance on. Their results are intended to inform how such patients are monitored and weaned.
pmc-13471656:
Rudas and co-authors tested a hopeful idea: fixing the heart might reverse frailty itself, rather than frailty only blocking surgery. Their 2026 prospective cohort, the CURE-Frailty study, tracked 76 elective cardiac surgery patients with the Clinical Frailty Scale before surgery and at discharge, six months, and twelve months.

One year out, the median frailty score had dropped from 4 to 3 on the scale, a highly significant shift. Frailty improved in 35.5% of participants, worsened in only 5.2%, and held stable in 38.2% across the year. Regression singled out one helper: cardiac rehabilitation was the only factor significantly tied to improvement, leading the authors to push for routine rehab referral after discharge.
pmc-13473056:
Wang and co-authors fingered a receptor on tumor-associated macrophages, the immune cells that shield triple-negative breast cancer, as a drug target. Their 2026 study combined single-cell data, tissue arrays from 29 surgical patients, and mouse tumor models to trace how the UDP-sensing receptor P2RY6 steers macrophages into tumor-helping mode.

Activated P2RY6 pushed macrophages toward the M2-like state through a calcium signaling chain. It made them secrete S100A9, a protein that switches on NF-κB growth signaling in the cancer cells themselves. Tumors dense in P2RY6-positive macrophages carried a poor prognosis for patients. Blocking the receptor, genetically or with drugs, or neutralizing S100A9 slowed tumor growth in mice and restored sensitivity to chemotherapy, the team reports.
pmc-13473156:
Jing and colleagues compared in 2026 the treatment options for advanced lung cancer that grows again after targeted EGFR drugs stop working. At that point plain chemotherapy helps little, and many add-on regimens compete with differing gains and harms. The team pooled randomized trials and ranked eight strategies by both benefit and safety.

Eleven trials with 3,606 patients fed the analysis. Several add-ons slowed cancer growth more than chemotherapy alone, and two also lengthened life: a drug-conjugate called sacituzumab tirumotecan and chemotherapy paired with ivonescimab. Antibody-based pairs worked well too but raised the rate of severe side effects. When benefit and harm were weighed together, the same three strategies kept finishing on top.
pmc-13473356:
Gupta and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of the long-term effects of total-body irradiation and stem cell transplantation, treatments that reset the blood and immune system. Survivors face lasting immune and bone problems, but how the treatments interact with later inflammation is unclear. The team triggered arthritis in transplanted mice either two or ten weeks after transplant and tracked joints, immune cells, and bones.

Transplantation did not change how severe the induced arthritis became, an important negative result for fears that the procedure primes worse joint disease.  Separating timing, early against late challenge, shows whether risks fade or grow as the new immune system matures.
pmc-13473856:
Seabrook and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how Canadian public health bodies respond to extreme heat in three provinces. The scoping review covered British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec from 2005 to 2026. Sources were mapped against Canada's Essential Public Health Functions and checked for any evaluation of heat responses.

The team found twenty-six peer-reviewed articles and 429 grey literature sources. Only nine sources evaluated a heat response at all. Authorities in all three provinces played similar roles, focused on downstream response: heat alert systems and public prevention messages. Public health actors mostly advised intersectoral responses, though some co-led them. Upstream strategies, such as changing the conditions that make heat deadly, were scarce. The authors flag evaluation and upstream action as the two big gaps in Canadian heat planning.
pmc-13473956:
Marlieke Lisanne van Erp and nine colleagues published this 2026 study profiling proteins in blood immune cells of autistic children, hunting for protein signatures of autism spectrum disorder. Brain tissue is inaccessible in children, so the team used blood immune cells as a proxy. In a Thai cohort of 191 children with autism and 106 controls without autism, they measured the cells' proteins by mass spectrometry and related them to diagnosis and to symptom profiles.

Thirty-nine proteins differed between the autistic and control groups, and some varied within the autism group, echoing its diversity. Several differing proteins are encoded by genes tied to autism, and some matched proteins in blood and brain studies. The differences clustered in the cell skeleton and in chromatin, the DNA packaging machinery, around an actin-centred network. Protein patterns also tracked behavioural, social, sensory and cognitive measures. The authors propose blood proteomics for biology-based subgrouping.
pmc-13474756:
Muñoz Olivar and co-authors ran a two-round modified Delphi study in Colombia to choose measures for judging how well palliative care is woven into primary health care. They also tested whether an expert's profile bends the consensus. Their 2026 study seated 27 experts in round one and retained 23, an 85% retention rate, rating each candidate indicator for how relevant, feasible, and valid it was.

Consensus required at least 70% of experts rating an indicator 7 or higher out of 10 with tight agreement. Eighteen indicators survived the process. Self-organizing maps showed the two camps prioritizing differently, evidence that who sits on a Delphi panel shapes what it blesses. The authors argue profile-transparent selection makes the agreed indicators more trustworthy.
pmc-13474856:
Teng Liu and co-authors combine microbe growing with gene sequencing in 2026 to profile microbes inside womb cancer. Tumor, nearby normal tissue, and vaginal swabs came from thirty-two patients. Growing work isolated seventy-nine microbe species, with three genera shared across all sites. Sequencing mapped wider diversity beyond what growing could catch.

Some grown strains entered human cells at high rates and stirred strong inflammatory responses. Vaginal sites were rich in a protective genus, while womb tissue held more risky types. Certain genera tracked with more aggressive disease traits. Living microbe data add function to the usual sequence-only picture.
pmc-13474956:
Gloria Campos and co-authors check a gaming headset in 2026 as a low-cost tool for measuring arm movement. Thirty-nine healthy adults did five arm tasks while a lab-grade camera system and the Meta Quest 3 headset tracked them at once. Many movement measures were drawn from both recordings. The team also tested how smoothing the signals changed the values.

Errors between the two systems stayed small for most measures and tasks. Agreement and repeat strength rated high across the board. Smoothing choices did shift some values, so settings need care and reporting. A portable headset could bring motion labs into clinics that lack costly rigs.
pmc-13476356: Kruis and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their case report in Infection on a rare worm infection of the spine. The note is a correction, and it does not change the case or its results. It changes the rights terms for the work. The report first came out under a closed licence in 2025. It is now free for all to read and share, with credit to the team.
pmc-13478056:
Ma and co-authors review low-level light therapy for postherpetic neuralgia in 2026, the burning nerve pain that can linger after shingles heals. Shingles strikes 20 to 30 percent of people in a lifetime, and drug treatment for the lingering pain often gives incomplete relief. Cases of shingles in adults over 65 rose from 2.83 million in 1992 to a high of 6.52 million in 2021, the authors note, widening the pool at risk of lasting pain. In animal pain models, the light raised pain thresholds, cooled inflammatory signals, and shifted immune cells toward a healing profile in the tissue. Clinical reports in patients showed real pain reduction, and treating early may even cut how often the lasting pain develops after shingles.
pmc-13478456:
Du and colleagues built an image-based grading system in 2026 for cigar wrapper leaves, the outer leaves that decide a cigar's look and much of its value. On held-out test images the model reached 94.39 percent accuracy in assigning the correct grade to each leaf photographed. Its macro F1 score, balancing accuracy across grades, was 0.950, and its agreement-weighted kappa score reached 0.964 against human grades. pmc-13479556:
Feng Li and colleagues present a 2026 brain imaging study hunting for neural markers of resilience to major depression. Resilience research asks why some people at family risk never become ill. A measure of how centrally each brain region connects showed a telling pattern in the medial frontal gyrus: patients scored lowest, controls sat in the middle, and unaffected siblings scored highest. Connections between that region and a sensory area followed the same staircase. Neither measure tracked current symptom severity inside any group. The authors propose this frontal pattern as a candidate resilience signature, present most strongly in relatives who stayed well despite shared risk.
pmc-13479656:
Utsav Rajvanshi and coauthors published a 2026 case report on image-guided treatment of cesarean scar pregnancies, where an embryo implants in the scar of a past cesarean birth. It can cause womb rupture, massive bleeding, and loss of fertility, and it grows more common as cesarean rates climb. Standard care often means surgery that ends childbearing.

Fetal heartbeats stopped quickly in both, hormone levels fell, and no problems arose during the work. Ultrasound through the vagina guided both finding and treatment planning. The authors present image-guided methods as womb-sparing options worth wider use in well-chosen patients.
pmc-13480056:
Liu and co-authors used genetic statistics in 2026 to hunt drug targets for thoracic aortic aneurysm, a silent swelling of the chest aorta that can burst and kill. Their Mendelian randomization analysis, which uses inherited gene activity as a natural experiment, screened druggable genes against aneurysm risk. It flagged 31 candidate genes, and drug database matching plus molecular docking pointed to piceatannol, a grape and peanut compound, acting on a gene called STK33.

Human aneurysm tissue showed STK33 markedly reduced, and the same drop appeared in cell and mouse models of the disease used by the team. Piceatannol treatment cut aneurysm incidence, deaths, and aortic widening in two different mouse models of the condition. It also restored the contractile proteins that keep vessel muscle cells working, and silencing STK33 erased most of the benefit, confirming the compound acts through that target.
pmc-13480156:
Resha Reya Ganthan and co-authors describe a 2026 case of cardiac arrest with no clear cause, striking soon after a clean bill of health. A 50-year-old man passed a pre-surgery heart check for planned surgery, then collapsed about an hour later outside hospital. Bystanders gave chest compressions and a shock, and he survived.

Scans of the heart arteries, a detailed heart MRI, an electrical study, and gene tests all came back without answers. Doctors fitted a two-chamber defibrillator to guard against a repeat event. Later device checks caught a run of fast rhythm that the device stopped with pacing pulses. The case exposes limits in current risk checks for hidden rhythm disease and supports device cover for survivors of unexplained arrest.
pmc-13480256:
Chang Liu and co-authors describe a 2026 study of a long RNA strand that worsens severe lung infection in children. The team compared 160 children with severe community-acquired pneumonia against 160 healthy children. Blood levels of the RNA, named IL6-AS1, ran high in sick children and tracked with inflammation markers, while high levels also marked worse survival odds.

The RNA strand may serve as both a warning marker and a drug target, though human treatment tests remain distant.
pmc-13481556:
Qihong Huang and co-authors report a 2026 test of a rib plate that dissolves after the bone heals. Severe rib breaks often need plates, yet standard metal stays forever or demands a second removal surgery. Magnesium alloy melts away in the body but too fast for the ever-moving chest. The team coated the alloy with a calcium-phosphate skin and tested it in dishes and in animals with rib breaks.

Coated plates degraded far more slowly than bare ones in both settings. Animal ribs held better alignment and healed with cleaner shape under the coated plate. Six months of follow-up showed no clear harmful reactions. A slower melt may keep the plate strong through healing, then spare patients a removal operation. Human use still needs safety proof, yet the coating solves the core timing flaw.
pmc-13483156:
Yuqing Gao and co-authors present a 2026 study of how fake weightlessness harms egg cells and whether melatonin can shield them. Long spaceflight may strain female fertility, and eggs sit paused for years in a stage open to DNA harm. Mouse eggs turned in a rotating system that mimics weightlessness showed double-strand DNA breaks with alarm signals on. They also showed scattered energy factories and early cell death, yet no rise in general oxidative stress.

Melatonin in the dish eased DNA damage by favouring one repair route and tidied the energy factories, mostly without its classic receptors. During later ripening it fixed spindle faults, calmed an overfired stress response, and lifted the share of eggs that finished ripening and formed early embryos. Dose and timing mattered. The hormone may guard eggs on long missions, pending animal breeding proof.
pmc-13483756:
Alireza Nasirzadeh tests a soft wearable support for the knee during downhill walking, when thigh muscles brake hard with each step. Published in 2026, the study has fourteen healthy men walk on a treadmill tilted to a steep decline, with and without a passive trunk-to-thigh exosuit. A personalized body model estimates knee contact forces and balance margins from motion data.

Total load through the knee joint across stance fell by about 7 percent in the axial direction with assistance. Wearers also naturally took shorter, quicker, and wider steps, so part of the relief came from changed gait rather than device force alone. Sideways balance margin grew by 7.4 percent while front-back margin held steady. Knee power generation dipped in mid-stance. The cautious wide gait suggests users trade some natural rhythm for stability.
pmc-13486056:
Patryk Wiśniewski checks soil germs near the roots of a forest invader plant in northern Poland. The plant, small-flowered touch-me-not, spreads through much of Europe's woods. For this 2026 study, soil came from eight invaded plots and eight clean plots in mixed pine woods. Long-read gene scans named the germs, and job guesses were drawn from those names.

Invaded soil held more germ types in all, yet the balance of types stayed much the same. Rare new types thus joined the list while top types thinned out. No group grew richer in invaded soil, a sharp break from tales told for other invaders. Guessed work fell across 37 tasks, from nitrogen use to breakdown of tough plant stuff. Guesses are not proof, so the work sets up tests, not verdicts.
pmc-13486656:
Liu and co-authors built a video forensics system that not only flags deepfake clips but also names which forgery algorithm made them.
