Their 2026 design fuses a convolutional network, which reads local facial texture, with a transformer, which tracks long-range patterns across frames. Together they hunt the faint defects each generator leaves behind in space and time.

On the standard FaceForensics++ benchmark the system scored in the high ninety percent range for detection accuracy in the comparisons tabulated. It also attributed clips to the correct one of four forgery algorithms at a satisfactory rate, a task most detectors skip entirely. Performance held up better than rivals when videos were compressed, a common laundering step. Liu presents combined detection and attribution as the practical direction for deepfake defense.
pmc-13488356:
Min Ki Jeon and colleagues trial cheap wastewater sampling in a small nursing home in a 2026 year-long study. Twenty-four residents lived at the site, where outbreaks spread fast and routine testing is scarce. Tampons placed in the wastewater flow soaked up virus material passively. Weekly samples were tested for the COVID-19 virus and other respiratory viruses with a precise DNA counting method. Genome sequencing followed when amounts allowed.

A four-week run of COVID-19 detections built up before symptoms appeared, and clinical testing in week four confirmed infection in fifteen residents and staff. Virus genomes from wastewater matched the clinical strain. Flu viruses appeared in wastewater without confirmed cases, and a related virus showed once. The authors urge preset response thresholds.
pmc-13490456:
Zheng Su and others compare human and mouse genes by RNA action across a huge collection of levels data. In 2026, the study applies a Transformer model called GeneRAIN to about 777,000 bulk RNA reading samples, roughly 410,000 human and 366,000 mouse, to build RNA-based representations of genes. DNA similarity alone often misleads mouse model choice.

The analysis flags 2,407 genes with high DNA similarity but distinct RNA actions, which more often carry different disease associations. It also flags 3,070 genes divergent at both levels, marking high risk of cross-species mismatch. It also identifies long non-coding RNA counterparts by RNA conservation. Team choosing mouse models get a resource for judging which human genes a mouse gene truly mirrors.
pmc-13490556:
Ben Hadj Said and team compared semen samples from 48 men before and after COVID-19 vaccination, using each man as his own control to settle fertility worries. Vaccine hesitancy among men of reproductive age leaned heavily on feared sperm effects. Their 2026 study at a Tunisian reproductive biology department collected samples within three months either side of vaccination, excluding anyone treated between samples for conditions that sway sperm.

Sperm viability, both motility measures, and shape were statistically unchanged after vaccination across the group studied. Semen acidity decreased slightly and one concentration-related measure rose, shifts the authors report without alarm. The men averaged about forty years old and received a mix of messenger RNA, viral vector, and inactivated vaccines. Ben Hadj Said concludes the results should reassure men that vaccination leaves core semen quality intact.
pmc-13492856:
Shah and colleagues present a 2026 comparative study of adolescent gamers in northern India, examining reaction speed, reasoning, and body measures together. Two hundred males aged thirteen to twenty-one were split into gamers, at least five hours weekly, and non-gamers. The study's novelty is a confounding triad it measures alongside gaming: sleep, diet, and the type of screen used.

Reaction time, intelligence, spatial reasoning, and body fat were all measured with standard tools. By measuring the triad, the team aims to separate gaming's own effects from the lifestyle that travels with it: late nights, snacking, and small phone screens. Many gamer studies skip those controls and blame games for what sleep loss does. The design sets a stricter standard for judging gaming's real footprint.
pmc-13493356:
Zhenfeng Liu leads a fifteen-author team pooling in 2026 two randomized split-face trials of a peptide serum meant to help skin recover after cosmetic energy treatments. Each volunteer used the serum on one side of the face and a plain moisturizer on the other, so every person served as their own control. One trial followed fractional carbon dioxide laser treatment in twenty-six Asian subjects, and the other followed radiofrequency microneedling in twenty-five.

Blinded graders tracked redness, swelling, crusting, roughness, and water escaping through the skin over fourteen days. The serum side matched or beat the moisturizer side nearly everywhere, with a few advantages strong enough to survive strict statistical correction, including water loss on day three after laser work. By day fourteen most subjects in both trials judged the serum side better recovered, and side effects were few and mild.
pmc-13493656:
Linh H. Tran and others present a man with chronic gout whose urate deposits appear in exceptionally rare places. In 2026, the image report concerns a forty-seven-year-old with blood sugar illness, high blood pressure, and long-standing gout who stopped allopurinol and arrived with fever and acute left knee pain. Examination found firm nodules on finger joints, elbows, palms, and soles.

A serum uric acid level of 11.1 milligrams per decilitre supported presumed tophi, and colchicine eased the acute flare. He was advised to resume allopurinol, titrated to keep urate below six, so deposits shrink and flares fall. Palmar and plantar tophi can mimic warts, calluses, illness, or tumours, so exact recognition avoids unnecessary procedures.
pmc-13493956:
Negin Melek writes a deliberately educational study in 2026 asking how far careful classical machine learning can go in reading heart rhythm disorders from electrocardiograms. Rather than chasing ever deeper neural networks, the work walks through each pipeline stage, signal cleaning, feature building, feature pruning, and scoring, using the standard MIT-BIH arrhythmia database. Two feature styles compete: hand-crafted shape and timing measures, and a compact wavelet fingerprint.

Feature selection showed accuracy saturating at roughly fifteen features, meaning a small subset carries nearly all the diagnostic signal. A support vector machine on that subset reached about ninety-eight and a half percent accuracy, stable across configurations. The wavelet version balanced all scoring metrics most evenly. The study doubles as a teaching template for interpretable cardiac decision support.
pmc-13495156:
Nina Billows and a large team present, in a 2026 article, the first full chromosome-scale genome for Dermacentor reticulatus, a European tick that spreads germs to people and animals. The ornate cow tick thrives in meadows and pastures, feeds on livestock, deer, dogs, and at times people, and its range is growing. Yet its DNA had never been read end to end.

Long-read sequencing yielded an assembly in which near two thirds of the DNA is repeated sequence. Standard gene checks scored the assembly as highly complete, on par with kin species, and annotation predicted about twenty-one and a half thousand genes. Gene families tied to detoxifying chemicals, defense against microbes, and cholesterol handling stood out as enriched. The team also read the small mitochondrial genome in full. They offer the resource as a base for work on tick biology, evolution, and how ticks and germs interact.
pmc-13495956:
Wehmeier and colleagues present a 2026 measurement method that reads key electrical traits of semiconductors at the nanoscale using infrared to terahertz light. Chip features are now only a few nanometers wide, yet the scattering rate of charge carriers, a trait that shapes device behavior, has been hard to measure at that scale.

Their synchrotron-based nanospectroscopy measures both carrier concentration and scattering rate with percent-level accuracy, at a resolution near ten nanometers. Tests on silicon with different doping levels matched established far-field methods in bulk checks. Near-field readings ran about 30 percent lower than far-field values, a gap the team links to surface depletion, where carriers thin out near the surface. The method opens all-optical study of such surface effects.
pmc-13499856:
Valentina Bugelli and others systematically review machine minds for personal identification in forensic science. In 2026, the first part of the review searches PubMed and Scopus under PRISMA guidance, including eighty-nine studies from 2012 to 2026 on sex estimation, human identification, ancestry, and kinship. Most work uses imaging, mainly CT and radiographs, with deep learning most common.

Sex estimation dominated, at sixty-three percent of studies, and found rightness was mostly high, with a median of 91.4 percent among single-value reports, slightly favoring deep learning over traditional machine learning. Heterogeneity, population-specific data, and limited external testing still limit courtroom readiness. The authors call for same-form testing, multi-population data sets, and transparent reporting.
pmc-13500156:
Rega and colleagues reported extended twelve-month results in 2026 from the NIHP2019 trial, the first randomized test of hypothermic oxygenated perfusion, a cold, oxygen-fed machine preservation method, for donor hearts. Static cold storage, the standard, lets oxygen starvation injure the organ. Across fifteen centers in eight European countries, about two hundred transplant recipients received hearts preserved by machine or by cold storage; early results already favored the machine at thirty days.

At twelve months the combined outcome of death, graft problems, rejection, and severe early graft failure struck about a third of machine-preserved patients against nearly half of cold-storage patients. Severe early graft dysfunction showed the widest gap, at about one in twenty against one in five, and deaths also ran lower with the machine, though less decisively. Adjusted analysis agreed. The authors conclude the early gains persisted to one year without new safety worries.
pmc-13500556:
Zhongkun Liu and co-authors identify in 2026 a fat-making enzyme as a metabolic checkpoint that pancreatic tumours use to disarm killer T cells. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is notoriously resistant to immunotherapy, and its surroundings are rich in lipids that blunt immune attack. Blocking the enzyme DGAT1 in tumour cells rewired their fat handling. The cells pulled more fatty acids inside, draining the free fatty acids outside that were crippling CD8 T cells, the immune cells that kill cancer.

With less of one fatty acid available, stress inside T cells eased, a key longevity factor stayed active, and the cells developed toward stem-like memory forms rather than burning out. Resistance to exhaustion improved, and tumours in living models became sensitive to PD-1 checkpoint blockade therapy, which releases brakes on T cells. Lipid competition between tumour and immune cells emerges as a druggable barrier.
pmc-13500856:
Xiaoyuan Chen leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 cell study of sepsis-related lung injury and an RNA modification called m5C. The team modelled injury by treating human lung A549 cells with lipopolysaccharide, a bacterial toxin component. They measured inflammatory cytokines, cell death by flow cytometry, and mitophagy, the disposal of damaged mitochondria, through markers such as Parkin and LC3-II. A methyltransferase named NOP2, which adds the m5C mark to RNA, rose sharply after toxin treatment.

Silencing NOP2 eased inflammation and cell death while boosting mitophagy. The mechanism ran through PINK1, a protein that flags damaged mitochondria. Less NOP2 meant less m5C marking on PINK1 messenger RNA, especially at one site numbered 197, which stabilized the message and raised PINK1 levels. Silencing PINK1 as well reversed the protection, confirming the chain. The authors name the NOP2, m5C, and PINK1 sequence a candidate drug target.
pmc-13502956:
Giorgia Comai leads an eighteen-author team reporting a 2026 study of whether two scarred kidneys transplanted together can match healthier grafts. Organ shortage pushes centres toward marginal kidneys, yet biopsy scores showing chronic damage, measured on the Karpinski scale, often send organs to discard. The Italian centre reviewed 262 recipients transplanted between 2014 and 2021, all biopsied before implantation. Of these, 142 received a single lower-score kidney, 35 a dual pair under the threshold, and 85 a dual pair at or above a score of 9.

The high-score dual recipients, whose donors were older and riskier on paper, showed kidney function and urine protein at twelve and thirty-six months comparable to the other groups. Delayed function, rejection, and complications were similar, though clotting injury in the graft's small vessels occurred more often in dual recipients. Survival analyses found no gaps in graft failure or death. The authors endorse dual allocation for scarred kidneys.
pmc-13503656:
Tong Jiang and three colleagues present a 2026 method to find the stress level at which rock starts to crack from the inside. They use sound bursts given off by rock as it is squeezed, a method called acoustic emission. A math index called the Hurst exponent tracks how the burst pattern shifts as damage grows.

The team squeezed granite, sandstone, and basalt at five speeds and tracked the index over time. The index fell, then rose, then peaked as the rock neared failure. Values based on burst energy matched a standard strain method best. The approach worked well for hard rock loaded at slow speeds, which may aid warning systems in deep tunnels and mines.
pmc-13503756:
Majed Alwateer presents a lean deep learning model that grades kidney cancer from tissue images, in this 2026 paper. Grading guides care, yet it rests on subtle traits that tire human reviewers. Large models with heavy attention blocks are slow and hard to run in clinics.

The design adds one small attention block to a standard image network, which reweights color channels at low cost. It trained on tissue patches from a kidney data set with five grade classes. The model reached accuracy near 97 percent, with near-perfect scores at the two ends of the scale. Checks with dropped-out runs showed its confidence matched its hit rate well. The author notes that tests at more hospitals are still needed.
pmc-13503856:
Zhishan Xie and Liangyu Zhang propose a privacy-guarded way to score loan risk for rural borrowers, in a 2026 paper. Farm households often lack the records city scoring tools expect, and their data sits split across banks, village lenders, and state platforms. Pooling that data raw would break privacy rules.

Their plan trains a shared model across five kinds of data holders without moving raw records to one place. An attention module weighs each borrower's trait groups by context. Noise added for privacy is sized to each partner's data volume, shielding small partners most. Scores came close to a fully pooled model and beat other shared setups. The noise plan cut privacy cost by nearly half at the same accuracy.
pmc-13504056:
Qibin Xiao and three colleagues report the first known human eye infection by Shinella bacteria, in a 2026 case report. The germ lives in water and soil and had never been tied to human disease. The patient was a 49-year-old woman who farms and handles pond water.

She arrived with a week of sight loss, pain, and irritation in her right eye, after steroid treatment elsewhere had failed to help. Surgeons cleared the infected gel inside the eye, and gene sequencing of the gel named Shinella as the main germ. Targeted antibiotics went into the eye and the vein. Two weeks of treatment settled the swelling fully, and her sight came back almost whole. The case shows the worth of gene tests for odd eye infections.
pmc-13505156:
Xiao-Yu Liao and co-authors ran a double-blind trial of gentle alternating-current brain stimulation for arm recovery after stroke. Sixty-one patients in the first six months after a first stroke received either real stimulation over the movement area or a sham version, each followed by standard rehabilitation. Ten sessions ran across two weeks, with dense scalp recordings tracking brain activity.

Fifty-six patients finished the study, split evenly between groups. The stimulated group improved more on total arm scores right after treatment and again one month later. Gains were clearest for shoulder and upper-arm movement, while hand and finger recovery did not differ between groups. Brain recordings showed a shift away from slow-wave dominance, and patients whose slow-wave networks settled most tended to gain the most upper-arm function. Effects were larger in patients without a measurable muscle response to test stimulation.
pmc-13506156:
Shruti Mahto and colleagues audited how maintenance contracts relate to working medical equipment in a large tertiary hospital. Broken scanners, monitors, or ventilators can delay care and endanger patients, so hospitals choose among annual contracts, comprehensive contracts, warranties, and in-house repair. The audit sorted inventory records from selected departments by contract cover and functional state.

Equipment without active cover clustered among the non-functional items, and the risk concentrated in expensive, clinically critical devices. Comprehensive contracts gave the widest protection because they bundle preventive servicing, repairs, and spare parts into one agreement. Annual contracts and in-house teams covered less ground. The authors recommend risk-based planning: reserve comprehensive cover for the equipment a hospital can least afford to lose, and manage lower-risk items through leaner arrangements, with department-level gaps made visible for planners.
pmc-13506356:
Gogna and colleagues prepared and evaluated a cocrystal hydrate pairing caffeine with 4-hydroxybenzoic acid, in a 2026 study aimed at taming caffeine's uneven behavior in the body. Caffeine's solubility swings widely with acidity and its stability is moderate, limiting absorption predictability. Growing the two compounds together with water in a one-to-one-to-one ratio yields a new crystal form held together by hydrogen bonds.

Gogna confirmed the crystal's structure by X-ray methods, finding a distinct melting point well below either parent compound and little mass loss before melting, indicating purity and thermal stability. Surface analysis showed a larger share of hydrogen-oxygen contacts than in pure caffeine, explaining the lattice's cohesion. Dissolution tests found the cocrystal reshaped release timing rather than total solubility. Release started slowly in stomach-like acid then completed, while in intestinal-like conditions it released fully within an hour, slightly faster than pure caffeine.
pmc-13507256:
Nathan Drenkow and others launch a broad, type-blind method for spotting data set bias in medical machine minds. In 2026, the paper presents G-AUDIT, which measures shortcut learning risks by checking links among task labels, sensor readings, and patient, setting, and capture traits. Non-typical training data can amplify latent bias and hide it during testing.

Demos across image, text, and tabular medical data sets and multiple machine learning tasks well found shortcuts often missed by by-eye review, such as doctor markings raising false hits for skin lesions. The tool gives builders an ordered audit for bias before use, helping prevent harmful result gaps across patient groups.
pmc-13507356:
Fengyi Sun and Zhe Wang identify, in 2026 work, the membrane protein TMEM132A as a driver of cervical cancer growth acting through a scaffold partner called HOMER3. Cervical cancer still kills some 340,000 women yearly, and advanced disease resists current therapy. Database mining plus lab validation showed TMEM132A overproduced in tumors and cell lines, matching aggressive features.

Extra TMEM132A sped cell growth, migration, invasion, and entry into the DNA-copying phase, while silencing it reversed those gains. The protein raises HOMER3 levels, which switch on the FAK, PI3K, and AKT growth relay. Silencing HOMER3 erased the cancer-promoting effects. TMEM132A enters the list of candidate markers and drug targets for this cancer.
pmc-13508356:
Stefano De Polo and four co-authors report a bleeding disorder that appeared because of a rectal tumor, in a 2026 case report and literature review. The disorder, acquired von Willebrand syndrome, weakens a key clotting protein and is often missed. Their patient was a 62-year-old man with no past bleeding history. Chemo-radiation shrank his rectal cancer before planned surgery. A routine pre-surgery check found one clotting test running long, which led to deeper factor testing and the diagnosis.

Doctors gave replacement clotting factor cover, and the surgery went ahead without bleeding problems. After the cancer treatment finished, the bleeding disorder cleared on its own. The authors state this is the first reported link between this syndrome and rectal adenocarcinoma specifically. The lesson is practical: odd clotting results before surgery deserve a hunt, since finding this syndrome can prevent dangerous bleeding.
pmc-13508456:
Zhen-Zhen Kou and five co-authors gauge medical students' views on weaving social and ethical questions into anatomy teaching on the female reproductive system, in 2026 work. The hook was China's first uterus transplant, a local case rich in ethical puzzles. The survey covered 163 students across three class years at one Chinese medical university. Over 95 percent rated the issue-based teaching positively. An AI sentiment tool then scored the emotional tone of student writing on set ethical questions.

Views on embarrassment in transplants between close relatives did not split by class year. Neither did views on adoption as an alternative to childbirth by transplant. Feelings about ovarian transplantation sat neutral to slightly negative in every cohort. The authors take the steady pattern as a case for keeping such teaching in early curricula. They also show sentiment software can turn open student writing into measurable signals for course designers.
pmc-13509456:
Jianhua Mu and ten co-authors examine how blood-clotting genes interact with the immune setting of osteosarcoma, a bone cancer seen mostly in teenagers, in 2026 work. The group combined large-scale gene readings with single-cell data and patient outcome records. They scored each tumor for clotting-related gene activity and traced which cell types carried that signal.

Tumors with high clotting scores tended to be more advanced, and the score helped predict patient outcomes. Two cell types stood out in high-score tumors: a set of support cells tied to inflammation and a group of immune cells marked by a fat-handling protein. Signals passing between them through a protein pair called C3 and C3AR1 may push the immune cells toward a state that helps tumors grow. The authors name that pathway as a candidate target for future treatment.
pmc-13510556:
João Nuno Ribeiro and seven co-authors test a treadmill protocol built to mimic the stop-start running of futsal, the indoor soccer game played in short shifts, in 2026 work. Ten male players at national level ran four bouts with speeds rising and falling to match typical substitution patterns. The team tracked oxygen use, heart rate, blood lactate, felt effort, sense of recovery, and jump power across the bouts.

Heart rate climbed across bouts to levels typical of real matches, while oxygen use held steady. Felt effort rose and recovery sense fell step by step. Blood lactate stayed flat, and jump measures showed no clear drop, pointing to no systematic muscle fatigue across the protocol. The authors say the test loads the heart and the mind much like a match while staying repeatable in a lab, though its best uses still need study.
pmc-13510856:
Stan Heath and nine co-authors review a brain receptor called NMDA as a drug target across mental and nerve diseases, in 2026 work. The receptor passes signals between nerve cells and also works in tissues beyond the brain. When its activity goes wrong, links appear to Alzheimer disease, schizophrenia, epilepsy, and chronic pain, among other conditions.

Several drugs that act on this receptor already hold approval, including ketamine and memantine, and many more candidates sit in clinic or lab testing. Most approved drugs block the receptor, yet their weak aim between receptor spots inside and outside signal junctions brings side effects. The review weighs the chemistry and drug behavior of these compounds and looks ahead to finer targeting. The authors see strong promise if future drugs can separate helpful blockade from harmful spillover.
pmc-13510956:
Ioana Bujdei-Tebeică, Anca Mihaela Pantea-Stoian, Doina Andrada Mihai, Simona Diana Ștefan, and Cristian Serafinceanu study the quality of weight loss in adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, in 2026 work. Good loss should cut fat while sparing muscle and grip strength, a pattern the team calls myoprotective fat loss. The analysis covered 166 adults who stayed on the same metformin-based regimen for twelve months in a real-world clinic group.

About a third of patients cut fat mass by at least five percent, while most kept their lean mass and grip strength within tight limits. The full protective pattern appeared in about one fifth of patients and differed sharply by drug pairing. It showed most often with two newer drug classes added to metformin, and less often with older pairings. The authors argue diabetes care should grade weight change by what tissue is lost, not by kilos alone.
pmc-13511956:
Junhao Zhang, Yuwei Ma, Boyang Chen, and Li Yu explore genes tied to a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis in atrial fibrillation, the common irregular heartbeat, in 2026 work. The team merged public gene datasets for the condition with a curated list of pyroptosis genes, then checked which overlapping genes change activity in diseased tissue. Network building traced links between those genes, small RNA regulators, transcription factors, and drugs.

Pathway checks tied the gene set to a bacterial-sensing route, fat metabolism, and infection responses, all pointing at inflammation in the disease. A second dataset confirmed seven candidate genes as steady markers. One marker, a calcium-binding alarm protein, heads the confirmed list in the full text. Estimated immune cell mixes in diseased tissue were also mapped against the genes. The authors frame the work as exploratory groundwork for inflammation-based diagnosis or treatment ideas.
pmc-13512656:
Bovornpot Choompunuch, Emanyah Sani, Jutatip Sillabutra, and Jatuporn Ounprasertsuk study burnout among registered nurses in public hospitals in one Thai province through a two-phase mixed design, in 2026 work. Survey numbers came first, then interviews explained them. Work stress, quality of work life, and burnout were measured together, with nurses also describing daily pressures in their own words.

Stress and work-life quality together explained about a third of the differences in burnout scores. Balance between work and home, fair pay, chances to grow skills, workplace safety, fairness in the organization, and social belonging each tied to lower burnout. The authors urge hospital leaders to fix conditions rather than coach nurses to endure them: staffing support, balanced schedules, and a fair climate top the list. Occupational health nursing, they add, should target the ward-level causes of exhaustion.
pmc-13514456:
Pisi Suksakol and five co-authors describe, in a 2026 study, a two-strain bacterial treatment for fruit rot in longan orchards. The rot, driven by the fungus Lasiodiplodia pseudotheobromae, damages a valuable Thai export crop and is usually fought with chemical sprays. One selected Bacillus strain attacked the fungus strongly, while a second excelled at freeing phosphorus from soil and supporting plant growth.

In orchard trials, pairing the two strains with organic matter plus half the usual doses of fertiliser and fungicide cut disease sharply and lifted yield compared with untreated trees. Treated plots also ended with richer soil organic matter and far more available phosphorus for roots. Suksakol's team argues that helpful bacteria can carry part of the load now borne by chemicals, giving growers healthier fruit and soil at once. The work stays at field-trial scale, so wider testing across seasons would strengthen the case.
pmc-13515256:
Marwa A Gouda leads an eighteen-author team measuring exposure to the parasite Toxoplasma gondii across Egypt in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The parasite spreads through undercooked meat and contact with cats, and silent infection in blood donors raises transfusion concerns. The team tested blood from 2,000 symptom-free donors and 500 cattle and buffaloes across six governorates, pairing antibody tests with questionnaires on habits and exposures.

About forty-two percent of donors carried antibodies showing past infection, with sharp regional contrasts: two-thirds positive in Alexandria against sixteen percent in Cairo. Eating undercooked meat, contact with cats, and farm work stood out as the main risk factors. Livestock showed lower past-exposure rates but signs of active circulation of the parasite. Gouda's team argues for a One Health response joining public education, food safety, and targeted screening of high-risk people and animals, since human and animal exposure clearly overlap.
pmc-13518856:
Tzu-Shun Lin and Atul K Jain modeled world rice output to learn what kept harvests rising despite climate stress. Published in 2026, the study used a process model that tracks crop growth, water, carbon, and nitrogen across regions and farming methods. It compared the decade from 2006 to 2015 with the 1960s, when output stood at roughly half the recent level.

Farmed area growth drove most of the gain, with irrigated land adding the largest share and fertilizer and manure adding about a quarter. Transplanted rice outyielded directly sown rice by a quarter, and the first crop of the year gave the best yields. Rising carbon dioxide in the air lifted output by about three tenths, while a warming climate cut it by about seven hundredths. The findings argue that farm practice, not luck, sustained supply, and that future plans must weigh both management gains and climate losses.
pmc-13518956:
Zili Feng leads a nine-author team in 2026 showing a switchable electronic nematic state in the layered antiferromagnet CoTa3S6. Nematic order means electrons pick a preferred direction, breaking the crystal's turning symmetry without help from magnetism. Their material showed uneven conduction and light-splitting starting at a temperature of its own.

Squashing the crystal slightly with strain, or applying an in-plane magnetic field, rotated the preferred direction, and the field-set state persisted after the field was removed, a memory effect. A modest out-of-plane field brought back the threefold symmetry. Feng and colleagues suspect the nematicity springs from electron instabilities near van Hove singularities and see a tunable platform for antiferromagnetic devices.
pmc-13519856:
Hossam Algallie and four colleagues report a 2026 case of severe pancreatitis in pregnancy driven by sky-high blood triglycerides and worsened by preeclampsia. The patient, a 30-year-old woman at 33 weeks with type 2 diabetes and chronic hypertension, arrived with severe abdominal pain, headache, high blood pressure, and protein in her urine. Triglycerides exceeded 50 millimoles per liter.

Five expert teams managed her care jointly. Care mixed bowel rest, fluids, insulin-dextrose infusion, and plasma exchange, which filters the blood. Two exchange sessions cut triglycerides sharply and eased her state. Rising pain and worrying fetal traces then prompted an urgent cesarean that delivered a healthy preterm baby. Mother and child both left hospital stable.
pmc-13520156:
Jia-Ho Shiu leads a seven-author survey in 2026 of bacteria living in hyperacid volcanic soils of Taiwan's Tatun Volcanic Group, where fumarole soils reach pH 2 or lower. Such scorching, sulfur-rich niches are barely explored near vents. The team sampled 39 soils and 8 hot spring waters across four fumaroles in both dry and wet seasons.

One bacterial phylum, Pseudomonadota, overwhelmingly dominated, trailed by Bacillota and Actinomycetota. Wet-season communities looked more uniform, while dry-season soils varied more from place to place. Soil type mattered too, with Andisols hosting steadier communities than Inceptisols. Nitrate, ammonium, organic matter, and altitude each correlated with composition, and Delftia plus Pseudomonas emerged as key network members.
pmc-13520356:
Reza Ghalehtaki and colleagues pool in 2026 results on adding immune checkpoint drugs to chemoradiation before surgery for locally advanced rectal cancer where the tumour repairs DNA normally. Such tumours usually respond less to immune drugs, so added benefit was uncertain.

Eighteen studies with 1,619 patients entered the pool. Complete disappearance of tumour at surgery occurred in about four in ten patients, and trial comparisons favoured the combined approach over chemoradiation alone. Severe treatment side effects were more common with added immune drugs, while surgical and immune side effects stayed uncommon. The balance of gain and harm is laid out for tumour boards.
pmc-13520456:
Manal Hassan Baqeas and colleagues assess in 2026 how ready nursing students in northern Saudi Arabia feel for palliative care, covering knowledge, attitudes toward caring for dying patients, and spiritual care. Gaps in preparation have been reported widely, shaped locally by culture and uneven teaching.

Questionnaires reached 232 third- and fourth-year students. Knowledge averaged moderate, scoring about 13.78 out of 20, with stronger marks for psychiatric and breathlessness topics. Hands-on experience with dying patients tracked with higher knowledge. Attitudes were generally positive, while spiritual care readiness sat at a moderate level and varied little by training or experience.
pmc-13520656:
Kamal and colleagues presented in 2026 a first-year biology lesson built around pedigree charts, the family trees used to track inherited traits. Standard teaching leans on simple Mendelian rules and sorts people into affected or unaffected boxes. The authors warn that this shortcut can teach a false idea, that genes alone fix a person's traits, when in fact the environment and many genes shape outcomes.

Kamal's lesson centres on a character named Tori and an open question about colour vision, used to pull students into closer reading of a pedigree. Students must weigh messy evidence, gradual variation, and cases that resist neat labels. The aim is to build pedigree analysis skill while honouring how complex trait variation really is. The lesson targets a gap the authors see in teaching resources that hide this complexity instead of making light of it for discussion.
pmc-13520756:
Nadra Elfezzani and colleagues compare in 2026 blood pressure control in United States adults with high blood pressure. The split is by use of GLP-1 drugs. Data came from a national health survey for 2017 to early 2020. These drugs now spread for diabetes and weight care.

The study held 4,016 adults with high blood pressure. Only 45 people reported GLP-1 use. Weighted counts put users under one percent of this group at that time. Control meant average pressure below set cut-offs. Small user counts limit strong claims. Readers should keep that caveat in mind through all result tables.
pmc-13521956:
Aling Tang and colleagues identify in 2026 a newly described cell death route called disulfidptosis as a contributor to heart muscle loss during heart attack. Oxygen and glucose starvation drains a protective reducing molecule, letting faulty sulphur bonds pile up inside heart cells.

Two faults combine to drive collapse. A damaged thioredoxin defence system deepens sulphur stress, while calcium overload activates cutting enzymes that loosen the cell skeleton, removing barriers against bad bonding. Blocking the defence enzyme worsened death in models, whereas blocking the cutting enzymes or calcium entry preserved structure. The paired mechanism suggests combination drug strategies for limiting infarct damage.
pmc-13522356:
Audra-Lynne D Schlachter and colleagues infected ferrets through the nose with Rift Valley fever virus to trace how it invades the brain. Published in 2026, the study used fifteen ferrets, a species whose disease mirrors severe human cases with bleeding fever, eye inflammation, and brain inflammation. How the virus reaches the central nervous system has stayed poorly understood despite its known nerve tropism.

By day three, mild nose and lung inflammation appeared before brain spread. From day six, animals showed neurological signs with brain and spinal cord inflammation spreading from front to back, eye inflammation from day seven, and death in all infected animals by day eight. Evidence points to entry through the nose and smell nerves, with bloodstream spread as a possible second route. The work offers a model for studying human disease and, in time, for testing countermeasures.
pmc-13522456:
Maaia Margo Jentus and colleagues examine chromosome loss in parathyroid tumors that lack changes in a key gene, CDC73, in a 2026 study. Such tumors include benign adenomas, atypical tumors, and rare cancers of the small glands that control blood calcium. Genome-wide testing was applied to fourteen adenomas, three atypical tumors, and one additional cancer to map missing chromosome material.

Most adenomas, many of them of a particular cell type, had stable genomes with few changes. Patients whose adenomas did show changes had higher blood calcium before surgery. Large chromosome losses, leaving the genome close to half its usual content, appeared in two atypical tumors and in the cancer case. The pattern widens the range of genomic change known in these tumors.
pmc-13522556:
S Praveena leads a team presenting a neural network that explains itself for diagnosing Huntington disease in a 2026 computer study. Huntington disease is an inherited condition that damages nerve cells and slowly affects movement, thinking, and mood. Many deep learning tools give accurate answers without showing their reasoning, which limits clinical trust. The proposed model selects informative clinical features, classifies them with a transformer design, and then explains each call.

Explanation used a method that shows how much each feature pushed the result up or down. On a public Huntington dataset sourced from Kaggle, the model reached a score near ninety-seven percent, above the comparison techniques reported. The authors argue that pairing high scores with clear reasons makes such tools more usable for diagnosing nerve-cell diseases.
pmc-13523156:
Tom Velez leads a team building models to predict death in very ill children with suspected infection in a 2026 modeling study. Data from more than three thousand intensive care encounters, including one hundred seven deaths, covered the first twenty-four hours. Machine learning models were built in stages, adding vital sign extremes, variability and trends, treatment intensity, and laboratory patterns, and were tested against expert severity scores.

Simple vital sign extremes already discriminated well. Adding variability, slope, and the timing of breathing support and blood pressure drugs improved performance substantially, with laboratory trends adding more. Established severity scores, including two pediatric systems, added nothing beyond the data-derived features. The authors conclude that dense hourly data alone can reveal deterioration patterns strongly tied to early mortality.
pmc-13523356:
Kim and colleagues build a bedside score for a grim question: which surgical patients risk dying within thirty days? Existing scores are complicated, invasive, or built for narrow groups. Their 2026 HeLP-BAG score uses only ten routine measurements from the day before surgery. These include age, blood pressure, heart rate, haemoglobin, lactate, blood acidity, kidney and nutrition markers, plus intensive care admission. Cut points were chosen by an algorithm and polished by clinician consensus. Development used three large cohorts matched to reduce demographic bias.

In a combined validation group of nearly a hundred thousand patients, of whom roughly one in seventy died, the score discriminated almost as well as the anaesthetist's traditional physical status grade. It beat several published scores and machine learning models on the reported curve measure.
pmc-13524556:
Juran and colleagues profiled in 2026 the bile acids in blood from patients with two chronic liver diseases that block bile flow, primary sclerosing cholangitis and primary biliary cholangitis. The diseases overlap in symptoms but differ in biology, and bile acids sit at their core. The team measured bile acid mixes in about 260 to 270 patients per group plus matched controls, and linked the patterns to disease stage and liver failure events.

Juran found both diseases raised total bile acids, but their mixes differed clearly. One disease showed more joined, conjugated bile acids with a shifted ratio between two joining chemicals, while the other kept joining levels but favoured one chemical. Gut surgery and bowel inflammation reshaped the mix further in the first disease. Bile acid measures predicted liver failure about as well as standard lab scores, adding context rather than sharper forecasts.
pmc-13525556:
Chen and colleagues take stock of AI reading brain MRI scans across the epilepsy care pathway, asking how accurate the models really are. Their 2026 review covered four jobs: diagnosing epilepsy, deciding which side a temporal lobe focus sits on, localising the cortical malformation that causes seizures, and predicting surgical outcomes. From over three thousand papers, 159 studies with nearly twenty-seven thousand participants passed into review, and 127 into the pooled analysis.

Pooled accuracy looked strong across the board: models separated epilepsy patients from healthy controls with accuracy in the high eighties. They lateralised temporal lobe epilepsy a touch better, and predicted postsurgical outcome respectably in the results. Finding the lesion itself was the hardest task, with pooled accuracy in the low eighties and wide uncertainty. The authors warn that accuracy figures from small, single-centre datasets often shrink in real clinics, and they call for outside testing before deployment.
pmc-13526056:
Michael Gernert and colleagues run a 2026 prospective proof-of-concept study using a receptor-targeted PET tracer to image inflammatory activity in early systemic sclerosis with lung involvement. Scleroderma can scar the lungs, and standard imaging struggles to separate active inflammation from fixed fibrosis. The tracer binds CXCR4, a receptor found on white blood cells.

Uptake was highest in chest lymph nodes, fibrotic lung areas, and the heart's left ventricle, and all three sites exceeded control values significantly. Patients whose lung disease later progressed showed higher heart uptake and a numerical rise in lung uptake. The authors claim early evidence that the scan visualizes active processes.
pmc-13527956:
Rebeca Oliveira da Silva and six colleagues examine sex differences in Parkinson's disease hospitalizations across Brazil from 2010 to 2024, using the national hospital information system. Their analysis covers 17,108 admissions, with rates calculated per million residents for men and women, both raw and adjusted for age.

Men were hospitalized more often throughout the fifteen years, averaging about 6.7 admissions per million people against about 4.5 for women. The gap was statistically strong, with men's rate roughly one and a half times women's, and it held up under checks for year-to-year patterns in the data. The authors urge care strategies that account for sex, aiming to prevent avoidable admissions and improve everyday disease management.
pmc-13528156:
Xiangjun Kong and six colleagues test a nutrition score as a death warning in very ill patients with atrial fibrillation in a 2026 study. The score mixes albumin and lymphocyte counts from routine blood tests. The main group held 3,007 patients from a big United States intensive care database. A second database group of 2,741 patients checked the result.

Each ten-point rise in the score cut thirty-day death risk by about a third. The same held at ninety days and one year. Hospital death odds also fell with higher scores. The check group agreed on hospital deaths. Survival curves separated cleanly by score quarters. The link bent rather than running straight. The authors call the score a cheap extra signal for triage. It uses labs already drawn, which suits busy intensive care units.
pmc-13530056:

Radiation given before surgery remains uncommon and lacks firm guidance, while radiation after surgery is standard. The team tracked who received the earlier approach and how survival differed between the two paths.

After matching, the after-surgery group lived longer overall. For early-stage disease, triple-negative tumors, and breast-conserving surgery, both timings performed alike, while earlier radiation linked to fewer second cancers.
pmc-13530256:
Maryam Yazdi and co-authors ask in 2026 whether recent life stress raises breast cancer risk in women in Isfahan, Iran. The case-control study enrolled 600 women with a fresh diagnosis and 600 women from the general population, all aged 18 to 75, between 2021 and 2023.

Women reporting high stress in the prior year showed roughly triple the odds of breast cancer compared with the low-stress group, even after full adjustment. The link ran stronger before menopause than after it. Recall and selection biases limit certainty, so the authors urge forward-looking studies to test the direction of the link.
pmc-13530656:
Collinson and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 147, a study asking whether outcome scores can predict how fast elite college athletes return to sport. The scores were collected before or three months after hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement, a painful pinching inside the hip. Timing matters for eligibility windows and team planning.

No three-month score predicted timing, a null the authors report plainly.
pmc-13531056:
Miyu Umeda and co-authors report in 2026 a tearing of the aorta shortly after childbirth in a woman whose aorta had never widened. The 36-year-old mother developed sudden back pain eight days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Scans showed a type B dissection, a tear in the descending aorta.

pmc-13531556:
Victoria Silverwood and colleagues offered primary care guidance for spotting and supporting bipolar disorder earlier. Published in 2026, the clinical article explains bipolar as a lifelong severe illness of mood and energy swings, with lows of depression and highs of hypomania, mania, or psychosis. pmc-13532856:

pmc-13534256:

Symptom and severity scores improved clearly across the group as a whole. Quality-of-life scores rose, and most patients stuck to the diet well. pmc-13536556:
Ali Al-Mashat and colleagues survey in 2026 Australian general surgeons on nasogastric tube use for adhesional small bowel obstruction. pmc-13536656:
Cengiz Gül and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective study of premature infants treated for severe eye disease linked to early birth. The work follows babies who received an injection of bevacizumab, a medicine that blocks abnormal blood vessel growth in the retina. The authors ask how often the disease returns after treatment and which infants need further care.

Return was more common in the smallest and youngest infants, in babies given oxygen for longer, and in eyes with disease near the center or in an aggressive form. pmc-13536756:

pmc-13536856:

Outlook leaned upbeat overall, though confidence sometimes lagged. Teaching programs, watched practice stints, and mentoring lifted both knowledge and outlook bit by bit. Later study year, past dementia contact, sex, and city living also helped. The authors urge set dementia content with hands-on learning.
pmc-13538556:

Blocking the pathway or the messenger in living animals relieved brain inflammation, neuron injury, and memory loss. The authors nominate the whole chain as a drug target.
pmc-13538756:

pmc-13540856:

pmc-13540956:

Adherence slipped over the year as a whole. Stronger current positive symptoms lowered the odds of adherence. Past non-adherence also predicted later behaviour. Insight and negative symptoms showed no steady link. Functioning showed none either.
pmc-13542256:

pmc-13543356:

pmc-13543456:

pmc-13543556:

pmc-13544056:

pmc-13544756:
Nguyen and Ngo reported a 2026 case report of a fifty-two-year-old woman with a myxoma, a benign heart tumour, growing inside her left ventricle on the papillary muscle. Ultrasound of the heart showed a mobile mass about ten by eighteen millimetres attached to the front papillary muscle. Nguyen removed it through a fully endoscopic three dimensional approach passing through the mitral valve, lifting the valve leaflet for exposure. She went home on day six, tissue tests confirmed myxoma, and no recurrence appeared at twelve months.
pmc-13546556:

The authors weigh MNAT1 as a marker of outlook and treatment response, while noting the challenges of turning the biology into safe medicines.
pmc-13547256:

pmc-13547356:

pmc-13548556:

pmc-13550656:

The authors aim the synthesis at medicinal chemists designing the next generation.
pmc-13551756:

pmc-13551956:

pmc-13554056:

pmc-13554356:

pmc-13554456:

pmc-13554856:

pmc-13555856:

pmc-13556056:

pmc-13556256:

pmc-13557856:

pmc-13560156:

pmc-13560256:

pmc-13561956:

pmc-13562256:

pmc-13562456:

pmc-13562556:

Scan-change features proved steady across settings. The authors want larger forward-looking studies before the tool guides real triage.
pmc-13562656:
Zhihao Qi and four colleagues pool trial evidence on whether mixing aerobic and resistance exercise improves blood sugar control in young people with excess weight. Children and teenagers with obesity often show early insulin resistance, a step toward diabetes. Their 2026 review searched four databases to March 2026 and kept eighteen randomised trials with 682 participants aged eighteen or younger. Bias was rated with a standard tool, and evidence strength was graded separately for each outcome.

Against control conditions, the combined training lowered fasting blood sugar and fasting insulin. An index of insulin resistance also fell, though that reading rests on weaker ground. Effects shifted with sex, session length, age, and continent in deeper analyses. Certainty was rated low for the sugar and insulin findings and very low for the resistance index. The authors back combined exercise as a drug-free aid while warning that the pooled numbers deserve cautious reading.
pmc-13563856:
Anusha Jaganathan and four colleagues compare blood serotonin in adults with migraine against healthy peers, and probe its ties to sugar and blood measures. Serotonin sits at the heart of migraine biology, yet its links with metabolism and haemoglobin were murky. Their 2026 study enrolled 74 migraine patients diagnosed by international criteria and 82 controls at a teaching hospital. Fasting glucose, the sugar marker, haemoglobin, thyroid signal, blood pressure, and serotonin were recorded, then related with age-adjusted statistics.

The gap startled: serotonin averaged 10.72 nanograms per millilitre in migraine against 88.43 in controls, and it survived age adjustment. The migraine group ran older, with higher pressure, pulse, glucose, and sugar markers, and lower haemoglobin. Serotonin fell as sugar and pressure rose, and climbed with haemoglobin. Average glucose, haemoglobin, and age each predicted serotonin independently. The authors label the cross-sectional findings exploratory and ask for follow-up studies tracking patients over time.
pmc-13563956:
Hajime Hirano and colleagues present, in a 2026 case report, a young adult with advanced kidney disease and severe intellectual disability who could not take part in treatment decisions. Kidney disease came from birth defects of the kidney and urinary tract, and every form of kidney replacement therapy was considered as failure approached.

After repeated talks among clinicians and family, the team chose conservative kidney management, meaning care focused on comfort and symptoms without dialysis. Home medical visits and nursing supported the family, and the patient lived thirty-five more months before dying peacefully at home. The case gives clinicians an ethical worked example for decisions made on behalf of patients who cannot decide themselves.
pmc-13566456:
Kyra F. Mendes de Leon and colleagues asked how many people with HIV would trade daily pills for long-acting treatment. Long-acting regimens, such as injections every two months, promise more freedom and convenience, but clinics need to know whether patients actually want them. Their systematic review and meta-analysis searched PubMed and Embase to October 2024 and pooled 22 studies, nearly all from Europe or North America.

About 70 percent of participants said they would switch to some long-acting option, and 60 percent would accept two-monthly injections, the most studied form. No study feature explained why willingness varied so much between studies, suggesting preferences depend heavily on local context. Evidence on alternatives such as implants, tablets, and infusions remains thin, the authors note.
pmc-13568156:
Marta Dias Vaz leads a 2026 guideline protocol from European anesthesia societies on fasting before surgery in adults. Real fasting often runs far longer than rules require, leaving patients thirsty and anxious, so the panel plans evidence-based advice on two questions.

First, should clear fluids be allowed up to two hours, or even closer, before planned anesthesia instead of the usual two-to-four-hour window? Second, should stomach ultrasound be used routinely to check contents before surgery? Planned reviews will weigh benefits, harms, patient values, cost, and fairness using a standard grading method. Anesthetists get a transparent roadmap for rules still in development.
pmc-13572356:
Haofeng Wang and co-authors test, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether three simple ratios from routine blood counts can warn of spread to the armpit lymph nodes in early breast cancer. The counts are taken before surgery. Node status is a key staging fact. Records covered 293 patients with small tumors treated between 2019 and 2024, with node status proven by pathology afterward.

Nodes were involved in about forty-one percent. Patients with spread showed higher platelet and inflammation index values and a lower monocyte ratio, and all three stayed independently linked after adjustments. Accuracy was only modest, so the authors frame the ratios as supportive clues for risk grouping rather than stand-alone tests. Their appeal is cost: every surgical patient already has the blood counts.
pmc-13572556:
Md Sohel Rana, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 study that splits the link between lifestyle and breast cancer into direct and screening paths. Women who follow screening may differ in habits, and screening itself finds cancers earlier. The team asked how much of the lifestyle effect runs through screening adherence.

The cohort followed 10,579 women from ages 50 to 55 in 2001 through 2019, when 571 developed breast cancer. A four-way split method separated direct effects from those passed through screening. Higher body mass, alcohol use, and hormone therapy each raised overall risk. Direct effects stayed for body mass and alcohol after the split. Small indirect paths ran through screening for alcohol and hormone therapy. Oral contraceptive use showed a negative direct effect.
pmc-13573356:
Alondra Sánchez-Salinas, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 web tool that helps specialists sort the many-sided health profiles tied to frailty in older adults. Frailty spans body, mind, and social life, and the mixed data are hard to hold in one view. The team built the tool for older adults living in Hidalgo, a state in México.

The platform stores survey answers, body measures, and test scores in one place and runs stats and clustering on them. Data from 210 people split into two clusters with distinct body and mind profiles. The groups differed in muscle strength, calf size, body mass index, gratitude, and how people rated their own function. Specialists who tried the tool rated it acceptable for exploratory work. The authors stress it supports research, not diagnosis.
pmc-13573456:
Xiang Dong, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study of DNA methylation in the tung tree, a plant with separate male and female trees. Sex differences in such plants rest on genes and on epigenetic marks, chemical tags that tune gene use without changing the code. Methylation is the chief such tag, yet its role in tree sex differences was murky.

The team read both the methylation map and gene activity across four tissue types, in male and female flowers among them. Joining the two maps shows where a tag sits near a gene whose activity splits by sex. Those overlaps form networks that may steer the dimorphism, the split in form between the sexes. Tung trees bear oil-rich seeds, so sex control has farm value as well. The authors offer the joined data as a base for breeding and for basic sex biology.
pmc-13574856:
Stijn Bunk, with a large team, reports a 2026 check of whether AI measures on lung screening scans stay steady on a quick rescan. Screening scans reveal far more than nodules, from artery width to bone loss, but hand-measuring all of it buries radiologists. Trust in auto-measures hinges on the same scan giving the same numbers twice.

The team ran one commercial chest tool on scan pairs from 1,436 people in a Dutch screening trial, taken at most 120 days apart. Gaps between paired reads were tiny for artery width, spine height, and the share of spongy lung. Heart calcium volume varied more, as small clumps shift the count. Agreement scores ran good to excellent across all measures, and sorting into severity bands held up well. The authors back the tool for routine screening add-ons.
pmc-13576256:
Sixu Chen leads a 2026 study of a targeted nanoparticle system built to kill prostate cancer cells through three death routes at once. Advanced prostate cancer often resists the usual apoptosis route. Their nanozyme carries its own hydrogen peroxide supply, freeing it from the tumour's limited stock.

A guide peptide steers the particles to prostate tumours. Inside cells, one component releases peroxide and calcium, while an iron oxide part turns peroxide into highly toxic radicals that drive ferroptosis, an iron-based death. Calcium flooding pushes apoptosis, and a third ingredient opens a channel that adds more calcium and triggers pyroptosis, an inflammatory death. Cell and animal tests showed strong tumour killing with negligible side effects. The authors propose the combined design for treatment-resistant disease.
pmc-13576656:
Gabriel Matías Lorenz leads a 2026 study showing that a popular way of splitting neural information into shared and unique parts is badly skewed by small samples. The method, partial information decomposition, separates what single neurons say, what pairs repeat, and what only emerges from pairs together. Brain datasets are often small, which strains the maths.

The team showed that estimates of synergy, the emergent part, carry a much larger upward bias than redundancy, and the gap grows as the underlying probability model gets more complex. They built correction procedures for both common estimator types and gave rules of thumb for how many samples a clean estimate needs. On real brain recordings across species and methods, the corrections removed the inflated synergy. The authors say fair comparison of synergy and redundancy is now possible.
pmc-13578556:
Judith Gronwald and colleagues set a standard way to measure fat that hugs the heart on MRI scans, in a 2026 study. That fat layer tracks with heart and metabolic risk, yet the trusted measure comes from CT scans, which use radiation. MRI avoids radiation and reads heart function at the same visit, so the team checked how well an MRI method holds up.

Data came from 127 patients with a narrowed heart valve who had both scan types, plus eleven adults scanned twice for repeat checks. MRI gave higher fat values than CT, with a fair match between them overall. Repeat reads by the same and by different readers agreed very closely for both methods. The authors back MRI for tracking over time, while warning that its numbers cannot swap one for one with CT.
pmc-13579456:
Kevin Yijun Fan and colleagues report a three drug salvage plan for lung cancer that outgrew its first targeted drug, in a 2026 single center account from Toronto. The cancers carried a fault in a growth gene, and a drug aimed at that fault worked until a second fault, in the BRAF gene, opened an escape route. Five patients were treated with two added drugs that block the escape path at two points, alongside the first drug.

One patient shrank her tumor and held the gain for close to three years, with brain spread controlled as well. The other four saw their disease push on within months. Two patients paused or stopped treatment over gut side effects, and no fever appeared, a known risk with this drug class. The authors call for larger studies in hand picked patients.
pmc-13579756:
Yuan-Sheng Liu and colleagues report a rare colon cancer mix found in a 27 year old man, in a 2026 case report. The tumor blended two uncommon forms: a mucus heavy type and a signet ring type, named for cells whose trapped mucus shoves the core to one edge. Such blends are seldom caught early, since they often surface at an advanced stage.

The man came in with twenty days of repeated vomiting, an upper gut complaint that masked the lower gut cause. Scans showed a thickened wall in the sigmoid colon. The scope exam found a stiff, narrowed stretch eight centimeters long, coated in hard to wash white mucus. A biopsy named the mucus heavy type, surgery removed the left colon, and lab checks confirmed the blend. Four months into chemo he lived, ate, and worked as before.
pmc-13580156:
Alan Juárez-Barragán and colleagues measure the heat physics of a leukemia drug target and its two classic blockers, in a study of the Abl kinase. This enzyme, when stuck on, drives chronic myeloid leukemia. Three builds of the protein were compared: the working core alone, the core with its two regulator modules, and the same set after a phosphate tag was added, mimicking the active state.

Heat scans showed the core unfolds as one unit, with regulators adding slight stability. The phosphate tag split the core into two unfolding steps, as if a bridge between its lobes had snapped. The two drugs pulled that split in opposite ways and bound with distinct heat signatures. One drug lost much of its grip on the tagged form at a steep energy cost, while the other barely noticed, matching its stronger real world punch.
pmc-13582056:
Hüseyin Orta and colleagues track a platelet size marker in weak heart patients starting a modern drug class, in a 2026 real world study. Eighty patients with reduced pumping power were already on standard therapy when the drug was added. Blood values were read at the start and again six months later, with diuretic use counted so it could not fake the result.

Average platelet volume, a rough gauge of platelet buzz and clot risk, fell clearly over the six months. Platelet counts rose in the same window. Red cell measures drifted up without reaching firm ground, and other chemistry stayed flat. The size drop did not track the count rise person by person. The authors float platelet calming as one more route of the drug's heart benefit, pending randomized proof.
pmc-13585456:
Brown, Simonds, and Mosse report in 2026 a quality improvement project on pathologist reviews of peripheral blood smears. These are the manual microscope checks that laboratory rules trigger after abnormal automated blood counts. Many reviews change nothing, yet they consume scarce pathologist time.

Reviewing 1,782 laboratory-initiated reviews at their institution, the team found that 89 percent added no new information, and only six percent produced findings that appeared clinically important. Two triggers, abnormal platelet counts and low white cell counts, generated a disproportionate share of the useless reviews. Dropping those two triggers from the local criteria raised the share of reviews yielding new information from seven percent to sixteen percent. It also cut the number of reviews performed each month by seventeen percent in the follow-up period, from a smaller monthly total.
pmc-13585956:
Meredith A Gunder, Brian D Badgwell, and Kaitlyn J Kelly lay out a structured debate on skipping surgery for cancers at the join of stomach and food pipe. Drug treatment before surgery has grown so strong that some tumors vanish entirely by the time of the operation, which raises a hard question: who still needs a risky operation at all? Their 2026 article gives two expert camps their say.

The case for skipping rests on response rates: tumors with a certain repair defect cleared fully in about six of ten patients after immune therapy alone. The other camp notes that judging a full clear-out from scans and samples is unreliable, and that long-term proof is missing. The authors land on a split answer: skipping is worth weighing for that repair-defect group, while surgery stays standard for the rest.
pmc-13586356:
Anlin Luo and colleagues developed imaging markers that track lumbar disc ageing and degeneration risk in China. Disc degeneration drives much low back pain, yet diagnosis leans on images and clinician judgement, with no predictive or personalised tools. Their 2026 study used a multicentre lumbar MRI dataset to map degeneration across the lifespan in the Chinese population.

Three accelerated degeneration phases emerged, and L1–L3 segments degenerated in step with true age, giving a baseline for physiological ageing. A contrastive-learning network estimated age from slices with a mean error of 2.59 years, confirmed across centres. Two markers, Age Delta and Age Selta, were piloted in longitudinal cases. The authors present the approach as a feasible route to data-driven spinal ageing assessment.
pmc-13587056:
Mazumder and colleagues present in 2026 AcousticSceneBD, a real-world sound dataset recorded in Bangladesh for teaching machines to recognize acoustic scenes, the overall sound character of a place. Existing benchmark collections mostly capture Western environments.

The dataset holds 5,535 ten-second recordings across seven scene classes: bus, metro, park, metro station, restaurant, shopping mall, and university. Everything was captured with ordinary smartphone microphones and standardized to mono recordings, totaling over fifteen hours of audio. The team built the collection through an eight-stage collection and processing pipeline for consistency. Four baseline models were tested to prove the data usable. A pretrained audio network performed best, reaching accuracy in the low eighty percent range, while a classic random forest on extracted sound features landed near fifty-nine percent.
pmc-13589356:
Han and colleagues build a full-length transcript map of the nerve hub behind hay fever symptoms. Their 2026 paper profiles the trigeminal ganglion, the sensory relay driving nasal itching and sneezing in allergic rhinitis, in a mouse model. Short-read sequencing fragments transcripts, so the team paired it with long-read sequencing that captures whole RNA molecules, accepting weaker counting in exchange.

They catalogued 25,988 high-confidence isoforms in full-length form. These came from over 13,000 known genes plus 237 new ones. Nearly three in ten isoforms were previously unrecorded, and alternative first exons were the commonest splicing event, especially among the novel forms. Allergic inflammation shifted gene expression, splicing, and promoter use. Adding single-cell data showed splicing patterns were strongly cell-type specific even when overall gene expression was not, suggesting splicing diversifies nerve-cell function in allergy.
pmc-13589956:
Hong Toan Lai heads a large team reporting, in 2026, a designed plant like compound that attacks how cancer cells power themselves. Healthy cell power stations, the mitochondria, import many proteins through a two part gate formed by AIF and CHCHD4. Cancer cells lean on that gate to tune their energy use. The new compound, M30-E05, slips into a pocket on AIF and blocks the gate from forming.

With the gate broken, cancer cells lost key imported proteins, their power networks split apart, and their fuel use faltered. The compound killed bone cancer cells from adults and children, including cells grown from patient tumors. Fed to mice for two weeks, it shrank grafted tumors with no clear harm, Lai and the team report.
pmc-13591356:
Minhyuk Choi and nine colleagues report a giant Hall effect in a magnet built on a kagome lattice, a grid of corner sharing triangles. In such materials, electrons veer sideways in ways tied to the bend of their quantum paths. The compound studied, YMn6Sn6, orders its magnetism against itself. Strong magnetic fields tilt those spins, and the tilt reshapes key electron bands near the Fermi level.

That reshaping sent the sideways conductivity to a level among the highest yet seen in magnets, far past what static theory predicts. Part of the surge came from electrons being scattered unevenly in this very clean crystal. Choi and the team say field tuned spin tilt offers a knob for dialing topological responses in future spin devices.
pmc-13591656:
Xing Peng leads a large team reporting, in 2026, a sieve layer that could make water based zinc batteries last far longer. Zinc batteries are cheap and safe, yet stray water and sulfate ions corrode the zinc plate and grow spiky deposits that kill the cell. Their coating uses titanium oxide sheets one layer thick, pocked with atom sized holes. The holes pass zinc ions fast while blocking larger water clusters and sulfate.

Coated zinc cycled for more than 5,000 hours at a standard rate with little spiking or side damage, the team reports. A pouch cell of amp hour scale kept over 85 percent of its capacity after 300 cycles. Peng and colleagues offer confined ion sieving as a design rule for water based batteries.
pmc-13593656:
A. Abedinzade Zare and co-authors asked whether two silver treatments used to arrest tooth decay interfere with how well a filling material sticks to softened dentine in baby teeth. Their 2026 laboratory study used extracted primary molars, artificially softened to mimic active decay, then treated with ammonia-free silver fluoride, standard silver diamine fluoride, or plain water before bonding.

The ammonia-free product weakened the bond sharply, reaching less than half the strength of the water-treated control in microshear testing. Standard silver diamine fluoride matched the control on average, though its results varied much more from specimen to specimen. Most failures happened at the glue line itself. The practical message is that the ammonia-free formulation may cut how well resin-modified glass ionomer fillings hold when placed right after treatment, so combined decay-arrest and filling protocols may need adjusting.
pmc-13599356:
Jose A. Viteri and colleagues examine why strength fades with age, focusing on a part of the brain that earlier work had largely skipped. Weakness in old age predicts disability and early death, yet muscle shrinkage alone cannot explain it, since strength falls faster than muscle mass. Working with aged mice, the team studied the motor cortex, the brain region that commands movement, and the nerve and muscle links below it.

Aged mice proved weaker and less coordinated, and their nerves excited muscle less well. Even so, signals leaving the motor cortex were stronger than in young mice, and single brain cells fired more readily. Across 250 paired comparisons, stronger cortical firing tracked with worse muscle and behavior results. One firing measure alone accounted for 75 percent of the age effect on muscle function. The authors argue the motor cortex itself may help drive age-related weakness.
pmc-13612956:
Tetsuhito Kigata and colleagues report a 2026 anatomy study of the small arteries that feed the adrenal glands in the house musk shrew, a tiny mammal used in research. They examined 15 shrews to trace where these arteries branch from. In most animals the supply came from a single parent vessel, either the caudal phrenic artery, the abdominal aorta, or the renal artery, and one left gland drew from two sources.

The most common pattern was one middle and one lower adrenal artery on each side, with none at the top. Compared with other mammals, the shrew's pattern is simpler. Such maps matter because artery layouts differ between species and even between individuals, and knowing a lab animal's normal layout helps researchers read experiments and compare glands across species.
pmc-13616256:
Jie Zhu and colleagues engineer a gene circuit that senses the toxic protein clumps of Huntington's disease and switches on the cell's waste-clearing system only when they appear. The clumps of mutant huntingtin protein drive the disease, yet treatments cannot tell the toxic form from the healthy one. Their circuit joins a bacterial sensor to an antibody fragment that recognises the clumped shape, wired to a master switch for autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup.

The circuit's DNA is packed into fat bubbles decorated to cross into the brain. In R6/2 mice, a standard Huntington's model, treatment cut the toxic protein load, calmed brain inflammation, and rescued failing nerve connections. A therapy that sleeps until the poison shows itself could treat the disease while leaving healthy protein alone, a precision long missing in this field.
pmc-13618956:
Smart Z. Mabweazara and seven colleagues systematically review whether physical activity helps people living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa, where longer lives on antiretroviral therapy come with rising cardiometabolic disease. Searching five databases, they gathered randomized and quasi-experimental trials in adults involving aerobic exercise, resistance training, or both, delivered over six weeks to twelve months. They graded study quality with two standard checklists.

Seventeen studies covering one thousand one hundred thirty participants, just over half women, all on antiretroviral therapy, met the criteria; most were sound. Nearly all reported gains: lower blood pressure, better lipids, reduced body fat and waist size, plus improvements in depression, anxiety, self-efficacy, or quality of life. Two studies also showed higher step counts and weekly activity levels. Small samples and short follow-up limit certainty. The authors urge work on exercise dose and scalable programs for such settings.
pmc-13619356:
Fei Wu and nine colleagues resequenced the whole genomes of nineteen snakes of the species Rhabdophis nuchalis, drawn from four regions of China. Their goal was to measure genetic diversity and look for signs of local adaptation in a snake that has been little studied at the genome level. The work catalogued tens of millions of small DNA differences across the samples.

Snakes from Sichuan and Yunnan grouped together genetically, while those from Hubei and Shaanxi formed a second cluster. Yunnan snakes carried the highest diversity, and Shaanxi snakes showed a pattern pointing to a larger effective population size. Genes that differed most between groups tied to reproduction and to calcium-dependent cell adhesion, a way cells stick together. The authors say these patterns can guide conservation of the species' genetic variety.
pmc-13619456:
Laurence E Court and eight colleagues tested whether routine physics review can catch user errors in fully automated radiotherapy planning. A prototype system generated complete prostate treatment plans for twenty patients, and five of those plans deliberately contained wrong prescriptions or nonstandard safety margins. Five medical physicists then reviewed the plans as they would in normal clinic work, without extra guides.

Reviewers caught wrong prescriptions in most cases and never flagged a correct prescription by mistake. Margin errors were another story: two reviewers never checked margins at all, and those who did find the errors also flagged many correct plans. Adding margin details to structure names or extra reference shapes did not fix the problem. The authors conclude that automated planning needs built-in alerts and automated checks, because the human review step alone cannot carry this safety load.
pmc-13619856:
Tobias Wilferth and four colleagues designed an MRI sequence that captures two kinds of sodium images in one run, in a 2026 study. Sodium MRI reveals how tissue handles this ion, and two contrast styles give complementary views: one weighted toward total sodium, one that suppresses fluid signal. Running both normally costs extra scan time and forces later image alignment.

Their trick splits a standard flip pulse into two halves and slips an extra readout between them, weaving both contrasts into a single sequence at a very strong seven-tesla magnet. Tests in simulations, phantoms, and the calf muscles of six healthy volunteers matched the quality of the separate standard scans closely. Small trade-offs appeared in fluid suppression under uneven fields. The authors say the combined run removes the alignment step entirely.
pmc-13620056:
Qian Mou and three colleagues report a heart defect found by chance in a healthy-feeling thirty-two-year-old man. A checkup scan showed an aneurysm, a bulge in a weakened spot, in the wall between his ventricles, plus a stretched left ventricle and weaker pumping. Most such bulges follow heart attacks or injury, yet nothing in his history or lab tests explained this one.

Further scans pinned down the bulge and revealed a second surprise, a thin-walled cyst along the edge of the sac around the heart. Vessel imaging was normal, and blood markers for heart damage and inflammation stayed in range, so the team judged both findings congenital. He received heart failure medicines rather than surgery. A year later he had no symptoms, and his pumping measure had climbed into a healthier range. The authors offer that course as a cautious hint for similar cases.
pmc-13620256:
Jinzhen Huang and five colleagues improved a plastic binder used inside high-temperature fuel cells with a simple acid soak. The binder, a commercial polybenzimidazole, normally clumps into tight chains that cover the platinum catalyst and block reactions. Treating it with formic acid adds positive charges along the chains, so they push apart, spread evenly, and leave catalyst sites open.

The treated binder soaked up far more phosphoric acid and carried protons much better than the untreated version. Proton transport resistance inside the catalyst layer fell by nearly two thirds, and the active catalyst surface almost doubled.
