A test cell reached strong peak power while using an ultralow amount of platinum. The authors present chain loosening by protonation as a cheap design lever for fuel cells that must run hot with very little precious metal.
pmc-13621656:
Yanyan Wang, Youtao Chen, Hailin Wu, and Hong Ye report treating a rare congenital neck defect in children with a heat-based endoscopic technique, in 2026. A pyriform sinus fistula is a leftover channel from fetal development that invites repeated abscesses and thyroid infections, and open surgery has long been the standard fix. Their team at a Fujian children's hospital instead sealed the channel's opening with argon plasma coagulation, guided by a scope.

Thirty children treated between 2021 and 2025 all completed it successfully. None developed a new fistula, swallowing trouble, or infection around the tract afterward. Follow-up stretched from two weeks to three years, and not one case recurred. The authors credit the method's small wounds, low bleeding, and clear view of the opening. They present argon plasma sealing as a safe, effective option for infants and children deserving wider adoption, while the retrospective design leaves room for comparative trials.
pmc-13624056:
Nora Gavrea, Derek Harland, and Martin Speight study vibration patterns inside vortices of the gauged CP1 sigma model, a field theory whose lump-like solutions mimic cosmic strings and competing superconducting states. A vortex can hold still energy in internal oscillations called shape modes, and whether such modes exist depends on details of the model.

The authors build a geometric framework around the operator that governs small disturbances, leaning on an energy-splitting property of the model so the results can travel to similar theories. They prove that at least one shape mode exists for any vortex solution of this kind. For the round, symmetric vortex they compute modes and frequencies numerically. The frequencies land close to the edge where vibrations escape into the surroundings, suggesting these bound wobbles are loosely held. The paper argues that such weak binding may be a general trait of this model family.
pmc-13625856:
Todisco and colleagues studied in 2026 how a signalling pathway called BMP controls two proteins, Sox2 and CD44, in the mouse stomach. Both proteins are linked to metaplasia, a pre-cancer change where stomach lining cells take on a new type. The team blocked BMP signals in stomach stem cells marked by the receptor Lgr5. They also deleted the genes for Sox2 and CD44 in those cells, then read gene activity cell by cell.

Todisco found Sox2 normally appears in the lower stomach but not the upper region, yet it switched on in stem cells when BMP signalling was blocked. Blocking BMP also turned on metaplasia signature genes across many lining cell types. Deleting either Cd44 or Sox2 in the stem cells weakened the metaplasia pattern. The results show BMP normally restrains both proteins, and losing that restraint helps push the stomach lining toward a pre-cancer state.
pmc-13626256:
Jing Xie and co-authors harvest new chemistry from a fungus that lives on soft coral. The fungus, Cladosporium colombiae strain CSGL 10M10, yielded three new alkaloids, named colombiains A through C, plus eight known relatives. The team pinned down their shapes with spectroscopy, circular light tests, and X-ray crystal snapshots, the standard toolkit for natural product sleuths.

Two of the known compounds guarded heart muscle cells in a dish model of oxygen starvation and return, a stand-in for heart attack injury, at modest doses. A computer network analysis of one guardian suggested the beta-carboline family protects through many targets and paths at once rather than a single switch. Ocean fungi, the work argues, still hide drug leads worth the dive, even in a well-picked genus.
pmc-13628056:
Jonathan Lefkowitz and five colleagues chart how traumatic brain injury reshapes the proteostasis network, the cell system that keeps proteins folded and removes damaged ones, across different brain cell types. They reanalysed existing gene-expression data from mouse and human brains, including single-cell measurements, to see which parts of the network switch on or off after injury.

Each cell type carried its own proteostasis signature, and injury triggered broad changes in protein production, disposal, and nuclear quality control across nearly all of them. Some responses were specific to single cell types, and a portion matched between mouse and human despite different injuries. The authors present the map as a guide to mechanisms that future treatments might adjust.
pmc-13628656:
Yeela Talmor-Barkan and thirty-two colleagues compared two balloon-expandable replacement heart valves in real-world practice, using a multinational registry of 1,903 patients who received transcatheter aortic valve replacement. Published in 2026, the analysis set the established Sapien platform against the newer MyVal valve, with statistical matching to balance the groups.

Two-year death rates did not differ, and in-hospital complications and overall valve performance were comparable. Differences did appear at the margins: MyVal patients needed permanent pacemakers considerably more often and showed more leakage around the valve, while Sapien patients more often kept mildly elevated pressure gradients. The authors say both valves perform well overall, and that the contrasts should inform device choice and longer follow-up.
pmc-13629456:
J Harl and colleagues report the first case of kidney infection by Trichodina parasites in the Japanese rice fish, medaka, a 2026 veterinary and parasitology paper. The find came during work on a disease outbreak in a hobbyist's medaka collection, where parasites turned up inside kidney tubules. The team followed up with microscopy of fresh samples, tissue pathology, and DNA analysis, designing new primers for the 18S ribosomal gene across the whole order Mobilida.

Alongside the kidney parasites, one of eight fish carried gill parasites and a microsporidian infection, and all eight carried Mycobacterium bacteria. The kidney parasite's DNA sat close to three Trichodina species sampled from fish and mussels in China, differing by 2.2 to 2.5 percent. Aquarists and fish health workers get a first record plus genetic data for a fish-dwelling Trichodina, a baseline for recognizing kidney trichodinosis in medaka and for sorting out this still-shifting parasite family.
pmc-13634056:
Neil Cockburn, Joht Singh Chandan, and William Parry-Smith wrote this commentary on a twenty-year study of miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy admissions in England. The original study tracked admissions for both conditions over two decades. The commentators argue the two conditions answer to different forces. They warn against reading admission counts as a direct measure of how often these events truly happen.

Miscarriage admissions dropped sharply in a single pandemic year, stayed low for two more years, then recovered close to the pre-pandemic level by 2024. Conceptions rose over the same stretch. That pattern, the authors say, fits restored care-seeking and admission habits better than a change in real risk. Ectopic pregnancy admissions ignored the pandemic entirely and climbed to a twenty-year high. Separate primary care data confirm a long rise in England. The contrast marks the ectopic climb as a genuine concern.
pmc-13634556:
How hepatitis B and hepatitis C drive liver cancer through different routes is mapped by Baek and colleagues, using single-cell gene sequencing. Liver cancer known as hepatocellular carcinoma ranks among the world's deadliest cancers. Chronic infection with either virus accounts for most cases, yet the two viruses differ sharply in genome and replication style. The team built a single-cell atlas from fifty-one tissue samples, covering patients with each virus type and healthy liver controls.

Nearly two hundred thousand high-quality cells fell into forty-eight clusters across ten major cell types. Cell-type shares shifted between the healthy, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C groups. One signalling pathway in bile-duct cells ran in opposite directions, suppressed with hepatitis B and activated with hepatitis C. Baek and colleagues present these virus-specific signatures as clues for future research.
pmc-13639056:
Sigve Nakken and a large international group of colleagues set out a 2026 vision for decision support software in precision cancer medicine. Tumor boards already use such tools to interpret genetic findings, yet current systems focus narrowly on genomics and tie data, rules, and knowledge together in rigid ways.

The authors argue that the next generation should form an open ecosystem that combines many data types, learns from patient outcomes, and explains its reasoning clearly. They call for rigorous clinical testing before hospitals rely on artificial intelligence output. Their goal is software that helps specialists choose personal treatments with more confidence.
pmc-13639456:
Takashin Nakayama led a 2026 claims study comparing sleep trouble risk between two blood pressure drugs that block the mineralocorticoid receptor: older spironolactone and newer esaxerenone. The older drug's steroidal structure lets it bind sex hormone receptors as well, and sex hormones help regulate sleep, raising a sleep risk. The newer drug, a non-steroidal blocker with high selectivity, might avoid that off-target effect. The team studied new users with hypertension from a Japanese claims database, weighting groups fairly.

Among 5,091 people without prior sleep trouble, 1,910 started the older drug and 3,181 started the newer drug. Over a median follow-up of 512 days, 356 sleep trouble events occurred. Weighted analysis put sleep trouble risk about 66 percent higher with the older drug, with similar elevations in men and women. Prescribers get evidence favoring the newer drug on sleep grounds, tempered by the limits of data, where sleep trouble recording may miss milder cases.
pmc-13640356:
Yihan Liu led a 2026 study of how exercise-induced irisin may help clear the Parkinson's protein alpha-synuclein and ease thinking problems. Thinking problems are among the most disabling features of Parkinson's disease, and buildup of the protein plus synaptic failure drive them, yet disease-modifying options remain scarce. Irisin, a muscle messenger released during exercise, shows neuroprotective promise, but its receptor and clearance role were poorly defined. The team studied 21 Parkinson's patients alongside lab models.

Aerobic exercise raised circulating irisin, lowered blood levels of the protein, and improved cognition in the patient group. In cells, irisin acted through the integrin alpha-V/beta-5 receptor to boost immune cells taking up the protein, while stabilizing HMGB1 to support breakdown of the engulfed protein through the cell's recycling system. That coupling of uptake to disposal is the study's key insight.
pmc-13641456:
Francisco Lopes led a 2026 rodent study of how protective diets reshape gut microbes before kidney injury, seeking a shared mechanism behind diet-induced kidney protection. Acute kidney injury carries heavy illness and death, yet effective treatments are scarce, while fasting-mimicking diets, sulfur amino acid restriction, and calorie restriction each protect mouse kidneys from ischemic damage. How those diets work, and whether gut microbes mediate the benefit, was unclear. The team tested the three diets in parallel before ischemia-reperfusion injury.

Mice were assigned at eight weeks to one of the three regimens for fourteen days. The fasting-mimicking diet cycled low-energy days with normal feeding, and the other diets restricted sulfur amino acids or total calories. By comparing diets that protect through different routes, the authors aimed to find convergent microbial and metabolic signatures that generalize beyond any single diet.
pmc-13641956:
Jong Geol Jang and fifteen colleagues present a 2026 study of electronic cigarette and heated tobacco use among Korean adults across a decade. National survey data from 2013 to 2023 let the team track yearly prevalence and who uses these products.

Use rose overall to about seven percent in 2023, concentrated among men and people in their twenties and thirties, while ordinary cigarette smoking fell steadily. Ever having smoked was by far the strongest link, joined by younger age, higher body mass index, and being unmarried. The authors call for targeted public health action as tobacco habits shift toward newer products.
pmc-13642156:
Nathalie Lander Gower and nine colleagues present a 2026 physics study on a hidden limit to light output in quantum cascade lasers. These layered devices make light when electrons crowd into upper energy states, and adding more carriers was assumed to keep raising the gain.

Combining a doping series in terahertz lasers with detailed simulations, the team showed that crowding broadens each transition until neighboring states blur together. Gain peaked when the interaction-driven linewidth roughly equaled the spacing between levels, then fell. They propose that ratio as a universal design gauge for quantum light sources, marking where more carriers stop helping.
pmc-13643456:
María Alejandra Gutiérrez-Torres and Theresa S Betancourt wrote a 2026 piece on how war harms the minds of Ukrainian children far from the fight. UNICEF said in 2024 that over 473 million children lived amid armed conflict.

The piece draws on a school study from Ternopil, a city in west Ukraine far from the front. About forty percent of 4,753 children aged seven to seventeen showed strong signs of post-traumatic stress. Plans that focus only on front-line zones miss most of these children. The authors urge far wider mental health care for all children touched by war.
pmc-13645756:
Jing Du, Delin Yu, and Changsheng Hu survey hearing-impaired college students in China, mainly in Fujian and Sichuan, using network analysis to map how felt discrimination, shyness, and alexithymia connect. Alexithymia means trouble naming and describing one's own feelings. The study ran in March 2026 and used four questionnaires. Instead of treating each trait alone, the team charted links between single items across the scales.

Most links between the discrimination items and the other scales were weak, which suggests loose coupling overall. Two items stood out as bridges: feeling shut out of games linked the discrimination and shyness networks, while a dishonesty-related item bridged toward alexithymia. The authors name these bridge points as the best targets for counseling work. Their map offers colleges a focused starting point for supporting students who face both social exclusion and emotional strain.
pmc-13647456:
Nala Al-Khatib and six colleagues report a nine-year-old girl whose multiple brain abscesses were the first sign of a rare inherited vessel disorder. She arrived with five days of congestion, cough, and worsening headache during a COVID-19 infection, plus low oxygen and brief confusion. Brain imaging showed several ring-shaped lesions, and chest scans revealed abnormal lung vessels that let blood bypass the lung filter. A brain biopsy culture grew Streptococcus intermedius.

Gene sequencing then found a fresh SMAD4 variant, confirming an overlap syndrome that combines bowel polyps with the vessel disorder called HHT. The lung shunts explain how mouth bacteria reached her brain. The authors urge doctors to consider lung vessel malformations when a child's brain abscess has no clear source. They also argue for genetic testing in such cases even when the classic syndrome checklist is not met, since early recognition prevents brain complications.
pmc-13648756:
Rachel E. Strength and colleagues track drug-proof genes in the guts of babies who start life in a newborn intensive care unit. Sick babies often catch germs from their own gut, so proof genes there can shape drug choice. The team read stool DNA from 179 babies, from birth to age three.

One thousand stool samples came from two studies. Babies were split four ways: care unit or well-baby ward, and drugs in the first two months or none. Eleven key proof genes split the groups over time. Levels ran high early in care unit babies, with or without early drugs. The work maps how proof genes take hold in the first years of life.
pmc-13649456:
Rong Xiong and Yaoping Liu studied how craft learning keeps Miao embroidery alive in Guizhou, China. This stitched art passes from hand to hand through watching, talking, and joint work, not through formal classes. The team surveyed 280 Miao embroiderers and tested a model of how these forces connect.

Talk within the group, learning by watching, and hands-on practice each fed a shared learning culture. That culture, in turn, raised how much people joined in cultural life. Joining in proved the strongest driver of pride in identity, event turnout, and practice itself. Two chain effects were confirmed: learning shapes culture, and culture shapes belonging. Keeping the craft alive means keeping its learning culture strong, the authors argue.
pmc-13649756:
Nur Adilah Faizal and five colleagues asked what draws older adults into active ageing programmes, and what keeps them away. They spoke with 28 adults aged 50 and up, drawn from keen members, dropouts, and people who never joined a local programme. Two behaviour frames guided how the talks were read.

Drive sat at the centre of every story. People joined to gain knowledge, guard their health, and learn digital skills, while pain, low confidence, and fear of online scams held others back. Faulty memory and weak English also blocked some. Family cheers helped, and family doubts hurt. Time and travel shaped the choice too. The authors map fixes across skill, chance, and drive.
pmc-13649956:
Marios G. Krokidis and eight colleagues asked how the strongest gene risk for late-life Alzheimer's disease reshapes the fats in tiny parcels that brain cells shed. Those parcels, called extracellular vesicles, mirror the fat make-up of their parent cells and can be tracked in living people. The team grew human neurons from stem cells of healthy donors and patients.

The risk gene, APOE4, shifted parcel fats in cells from both healthy and sick donors. In patients who carried two copies, a clear fat signature stood out: less of one sugar-fat and more of a membrane fat tied to cell stress. Other shifts touched fats that guard membrane health. The authors see a risk profile that turns faulty only in disease.
pmc-13650356:
Peter Mandl and twenty-two colleagues, publishing in 2026, argue that artificial intelligence can turn medical imaging in rheumatology into precise, measurable biomarkers. Scans and ultrasound already guide diagnosis and monitoring of joint diseases, yet readings vary between observers, numbers are rarely extracted, and promising methods reach clinics slowly.

Writing for the AutoPiX consortium, the authors describe pipelines that segment images automatically, pull out quantitative features, and merge imaging with other patient data. Such numbers could sort patients into better-matched groups and give clinical trials endpoints that regulators accept. Voices from clinicians, patients, regulators, and industry are weighed in the paper. The group calls for shared imaging protocols, large pooled datasets, cross-disciplinary teamwork, and early talks with regulators so that AI-based measures can earn trust and enter routine care.
pmc-13650956:
Mario Sánchez-Migallón and six colleagues design iridium-based anticancer compounds meant to outflank the limits of platinum drugs such as cisplatin, whose usefulness is eroded by resistance and harsh side effects. Their five new complexes use a half-sandwich iridium center gripping a fused-ring ligand, with two structural tweaks.

Alkylating one nitrogen on the ligand and swapping the ring substituent between methoxy and cyano groups changed the molecules' fat solubility, stability, and killing power. The tweaks even pushed one design into a two-metal form. The complexes killed several cancer cell lines at low micromolar doses, comparable in scale to cisplatin. They killed through a different route, disrupting mitochondria, disturbing the cell's redox balance, and raising damaging reactive oxygen levels. They also bound moderately to a blood transport protein at a docking site. The authors offer the family as resistance-evading candidates for further development.
pmc-2478656:
Thomas and Harden explain methods for thematic synthesis of qualitative research inside systematic reviews. Health care improves when patients' experiences and views join trial numbers in the evidence base. Methods for merging such interview and observation studies were still being built when they wrote.

The authors set out how thematic analysis, a way of coding text for shared themes, can be used step by step in a review. Their approach lets reviewers draw fresh insight across studies while staying true to each source. Health teams use it to design services people actually accept.
pmc-3702256:
Luo and Brouwer present Pathview, an R and Bioconductor package for pathway-based data integration and visualisation. Pathview maps user data onto relevant pathway diagrams and renders the result. Users need only supply data and name the target pathway.

The package automatically downloads the pathway graph, parses it, and paints data values onto it. Seeing gene or metabolite changes on a familiar pathway picture makes patterns obvious at a glance. Pathview became a routine way to turn tables of measurements into interpretable biology.  Pathway pictures from the package appear in many theses and journal figures.
pmc-4491356:
Pham, Rajić, Greig, and their colleagues reviewed scoping reviews themselves in 2014. The scoping review had become a popular way to map research evidence in a field. It was still fairly new, with no universal definition or fixed procedure agreed on.

Their review of reviews aimed to give an overview of how the approach is used in practice. Wide variation in how teams run and report scoping reviews makes results hard to compare. Clearer guidance would help the method mature without losing its breadth. The paper supports teams who use scoping reviews to chart what is known before deeper synthesis.
pmc-4692656:
Andersson and Sotiropoulos described in 2016 a method to clean up diffusion MRI scans. Diffusion imaging tracks water movement to map brain wiring, but scans are distorted by eddy currents from the scanner and by subject movement. These off-resonance effects can ruin fine detail if left uncorrected.

Their approach estimates and corrects both distortions after the scan, in one integrated model. A susceptibility field map, if available, is folded into the same calculations. Cleaner images mean tract maps and measures of white matter are more trustworthy. Brain studies of development, aging, and disease depend on that accuracy.
pmc-5388856:
The GBD 2015 Risk Factors Collaborators published a comparative risk assessment in 2016. The Global Burden of Disease Study 2015 gives an up-to-date synthesis of evidence on risk factor exposure and the disease burden it causes. The analysis covered dozens of behavioral, environmental, occupational, and metabolic risks.

By providing national and subnational assessments spanning twenty-five years, the study can inform policy where it is made. It shows which risks drive the most illness in each place, from smoking and air pollution to high blood pressure. Rankings differ sharply between countries, so global averages mislead. Governments use these assessments to set prevention priorities and track whether they work.
pmc-5776756:
The GTEx Consortium published this study of genetic effects on gene activity across human tissues in 2017. Knowing the genome is not enough, since the same gene can be used differently in each tissue. The project collected samples from many organs of donors after death.

The team measured how common DNA variants change gene activity in each tissue. Many effects are shared across tissues, while others appear in only one. These maps help explain why variants found in disease studies matter and which tissue they act in. The resource is now a standard reference for linking genes to illness.
pmc-6291456:
The GBD 2016 Traumatic Brain Injury and Spinal Cord Injury Collaborators published this analysis in 2018. Brain and spinal injuries are rising health priorities worldwide. Most are preventable, yet the care they need is complex and costly.

The team measured new cases, people living with injury, and years lived with disability across most countries. Falls cause the largest share of brain injuries, while road crashes lead for spinal injuries in many regions. Totals grew as populations aged. The figures make a case for fall prevention, safer roads, and better trauma systems in poorer countries.
pmc-6435756:
Vincent Traag, Ludo Waltman, and Nees Jan van Eck exposed a flaw in a popular network algorithm in 2019. The Louvain method finds communities in large networks and is used almost everywhere. The authors show it can return communities that are badly connected inside.

Their Leiden method fixes that defect and guarantees well-connected communities. It is also faster in practice on large networks. Tests on real and synthetic networks show cleaner, more stable groupings. Because Louvain results fill thousands of papers, the correction matters far beyond computer science, reaching biology, sociology, and citation studies.
pmc-7039956:
Hao Xu, Li Zhong, Jia Deng, and coauthors studied ACE2 in the mouth early in the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020. ACE2 is the main door the new coronavirus uses to enter human cells. The team asked whether the mouth lining could be an entry route.

Using public RNA data, they found ACE2 strongly present on tongue and other oral lining cells. That presence hints the mouth may be an early infection site and a source of virus in saliva. The finding supported attention to oral spread and protection in dentistry. It was among the first clues that saliva testing could work.
prantl-1856-die-keime-der-alchemie-1856:
German scholars in 1856 could read this essay on the seeds of alchemy among the ancients in the first quarterly number of the Deutsche Vierteljahrs Schrift. Published by the house of Cotta in Stuttgart and Augsburg. The issue's contents place it among pieces on law, nationalism, fish breeding, and world trade. The essay itself, in the old Fraktur type, begins from a stated fact: alchemy first arose on the soil of Alexandria in the last centuries of antiquity.

From there it argues that Aristotle's way of speculating mattered most among earlier influences. Yet the true core was the thorough syncretism of the Alexandrian age, Aristotelian teaching fused with Platonic and Stoic views before and after him. The piece treats alchemy as intellectual history, not as fraud or as secret wisdom: a product of a place and a mixture of schools.
salaman-absal-fitzgerald-1856:
Edward FitzGerald rendered Jami's Salaman and Absal in 1856, the Sufi allegory that stands beside his Rubaiyat in his small shelf of Persian work. A prince loves a maiden, and the love that begins in the senses must be schooled into love of God. FitzGerald shaped the tale in stately English verse, drawn from the 1909 centenary gathering of his work.

The poem's surface is a romance; its depth is a map of the soul's ascent. Readers who know FitzGerald only for Omar's quatrains meet his graver side here. The Internet Archive copy preserves this rendering of Jami's classic, the soul's journey told as a lover's tale.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Volume ten of The German Classics is a patrons' edition of 1914. It holds Prince Otto von Bismarck, Count Helmuth von Moltke, and Ferdinand Lassalle. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The Bismarck part gives Kuno Francke on Bismarck as a national type. It gives his love letters and his letters with William I. It gives parts of Thoughts and Recollections. His speeches close the part. No full work can be read in this opening portion. So the texts cannot be stated here.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
Vol. 1, No. 56 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated December 2, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item comes from India. Soldiers on the frontier have done another brave deed. This time the heroes belonged to the Northamptonshire regiment. A party climbed a peak named Saran Sar, to learn whether the enemy lay encamped near it.

At the top they found a camp lately and hastily left. The signs told them the foe was near at hand on the same mountain. Their commander, fearing an ambush, ordered a retreat. The Afridis fired from behind every bush and rock. Then they rushed from cover into a hand-to-hand fight. General Westmacott hastened the retreat. One little party, in charge of a convoy of wounded men, became separated. The tribesmen surrounded them.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
Paris, the opening part of To Paris and Prison in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows Arthur Machen's translation of the 1894 London edition, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter One leaves Bologna in joy: Henriette speaks the short, magic sentence, 'Come to Parma.' Casanova falls at her feet, kissing her knees with gratitude. He swears never to beg even a kiss of her hand until he has shown himself worthy.

The captain traveling with them judges it wiser to proceed to Parma alone, so the lovers cause less talk. He takes a post-chaise from Reggio while the pair pass a delightful night there. Henriette will resume women's dress in Parma, after traveling in disguise. The chapter promises meetings with Casanova's relatives, whom he does not reveal himself to. Readers ride with two lovers whose happiness depends on secrecy, disguise, and one tactful captain.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 392 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, October 3, 1829, illustrates the Duke's Theatre in Dorset Gardens. The theatre rose in 1671, in what the article calls the brazen age of the drama, when Puritan prosecutions had just ceased. Surviving players after the wars gathered under Sir William Davenant at the Red Bull. A bookseller named Rhodes meanwhile fitted up Drury Lane's Cockpit with an entirely new company in 1659.

Rhodes's apprentices Betterton and Kynaston were that company's stars. The companies later united as the Duke's Company. Killigrew collected the old actors as the King's Company and opened the first Drury Lane theatre in 1663. Davenant obtained his patent in 1662 and opened in Little Lincoln's Inn Fields with his own Siege of Rhodes. In 1671 the company moved to Wren's new Dorset Gardens house. Readers get the Restoration stage rebuilt from patents, companies, and apprentices turned stars.
the-old-man-in-the-corner-pg10556: Baroness Orczy dedicated The Old Man in the Corner to her uncle and aunt, Count and Countess Wass of Czege, in October 1908, recalling happy days in Transylvania. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the stories themselves do not appear. A second record of the same book lists fewer chapters and carries a 1901 date; the two records differ and should not be merged silently. This list adds The Dublin Mystery, Forgery, and The Regent's Park Murder.
the-vigilance-committee-of-1856:
James O'Meara, a pioneer California journalist, writes about San Francisco's Vigilance Committee of 1856 from outside both camps. Earlier accounts, he says, came from members or favourers, so they are partial, imperfect, and full of omissions. O'Meara belonged neither to the committee nor to the opposing Law and Order body headed by General Sherman.

He opposed mob law in every form, yet supported law and order without joining its organisation. Friends stood on each side, and unworthy men held rank in both. Some, he charges, joined the committee to escape its own rope and bullets. Chapter one then names the forty-one men of the executive committee, with William T. Coleman as president.
tob-0156:
James Darmesteter, the great French orientalist, translated the Zend-Avesta, the scriptures of Zoroastrianism, into French. His Le Zend-Avesta presents the hymns, laws, and rituals of ancient Persia with a scholar's full notes. Zarathustra's religion reaches European readers here in one of its classic scholarly dressings.

Darmesteter treated the texts as a historian, dating layers and tracing ideas with care. French readers gained what Legge and Muller gave the English: a whole canon, weighed and explained. Verified from a pre-1930 edition, the work still serves students of Persian religion. It stands among the monuments of nineteenth-century Oriental scholarship.
tob-4056:
Volume three of the four-volume Secret Doctrine, edited after Blavatsky's death from her papers, continues her system into esoteric history and occult science. The same mixture of Eastern scripture, classical myth, and nineteenth-century research drives the argument. Initiates, secret doctrines, and hidden lineages of teachers stand closer to the surface here than in the cosmological first volume.

Fragmentary in places and formidable throughout, the volume reads partly as commentary and partly as workshop notes toward a system never finally settled. Readers working through the whole Secret Doctrine in order will find material here that later Theosophists treated as essential, and scholars treat as evidence of how the movement's teachings kept evolving.
tob-4156:
A. P. Sinnett's Esoteric Buddhism, first issued in 1883, carried Theosophy's teaching to thousands of ordinary readers. Sinnett, an Anglo-Indian editor, presented what he said the mahatmas taught: root races rising and falling, chains of worlds, and long cycles of rebirth for every soul.

The scheme claims to be Buddhism's inner meaning, hidden behind the outer doctrine. Scholars of Buddhism objected, then and since, yet the book's reach is beyond dispute. The New American Edition adds Sinnett's later introduction. More than any other single work, Esoteric Buddhism made Theosophy a household word in two hemispheres.
tocqueville-old-regime-bonner-1856:
Alexis de Tocqueville's The Old Regime and the Revolution appears in Henry Reeve's translation of 1856. Tocqueville, author of Democracy in America, turns to France's own revolution. His great claim is paradoxical: the Revolution completed the centralization it claimed to destroy. Kings had already leveled privilege and gathered power at Paris.

He shows how old taxes, intendants, and habits of tutelage survived 1789. The French, he argues, loved equality more than liberty. The book is his sequel and, some say, his masterpiece. It changed the study of the Revolution permanently. Reeve's version was the standard English text for years. Its insights still guide debate.
turgenev-rudin-1856:
Ivan Turgenev published Rudin in 1856, his first novel, the portrait of the superfluous man. The brilliant, ineffectual Rudin loves and loses in a tale of fine talk and failed action. Turgenev drew Rudin in part from Bakunin, the fiery exile he had known in Berlin.

Rudin descends on a provincial salon and dazzles it with talk of philosophy, progress, and the meaning of life. Natalya, the landowner's daughter, loves him and offers elopement, and at the pond he falters and bids her submit to fate. Lezhnev, the plain neighbor, states the verdict: Rudin's words are splendid and his will a hollow reed in the wind of life. Years later Rudin dies on a Paris barricade, brave at last in a cause not his own country's quarrel of 1848. The novel fixed the type of the talking hero for Russian fiction.
un-ga-res-a-69-56:
Money spent on arms is money not spent on schools, farms, and health. That trade-off drives Resolution A/69/56, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Charter itself dreams of peace kept with the least drain of human and trade wealth on arms. The text recalls the 1987 world meeting on the link between disarmament and growth, and a chain of votes since 1994.

Each cut in arms, the Assembly argues, frees real wealth for the work of growth. States are urged to weigh that gain when they set their arms plans. The vote keeps alive an old claim of the poor world: that disarmament is not just a safety aim, but a growth aim too.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly resolution 69/56 (2014) restates the link between disarmament and development. The Assembly recalls the Charter's aim of maintaining peace with the least diversion of human and economic resources to armaments. It voices concern at rising global military spending. That spending could otherwise meet development needs. It urges the international community to devote part of the savings from disarmament agreements to economic and social development. It asks the Secretary-General to keep implementing the 1987 action programme on the subject. It seeks member states' reports on their own transfers.
un-sc-res-1156:
On 16 March 1998, the Council adopted Resolution 1156 on Sierra Leone. The country's elected president had come home on 10 March 1998. His return followed months in exile after a military coup. Sanctions set in October 1997 had cut off oil and fuel supplies to pressure the junta.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council ends the ban on selling petroleum and fuel products to Sierra Leone at once. The other bans from 1997 stay in place for now. They will be reviewed as events unfold and after talks with the restored government. The Council also welcomes plans by the Secretary-General to propose a future United Nations role in the country.
un-sc-res-1356:
Aid workers in Somalia, a country with no working state for a decade, needed protective gear that the arms embargo banned. The embargo had been imposed by Resolution 733 in 1992. The Council restated that all states had to obey it in full. Resolution 1356, adopted unanimously on 19 June 2001, cuts two narrow gaps in that ban.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decided that the ban would not cover protective clothing. Flak jackets and military helmets were named in particular. United Nations staff, journalists, and aid workers could bring such gear in for their personal use, for a limited time. A second gap covered non-lethal military equipment meant only for humanitarian or protective use. That gear could go in only when the sanctions committee had approved it in advance. The rest of the embargo stood untouched.
un-sc-res-1456: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 1456, entered in this catalog under the year 2003. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1556:
The Security Council adopted Resolution 1556 on Darfur on 30 July 2004. Attacks on villages by Janjaweed militias had driven more than a million people from their homes. Some 200,000 refugees had fled into Chad. China and Pakistan abstained on the vote.

The text demands that Sudan's government disarm the Janjaweed and bring its leaders to justice. The Secretary-General must report on progress within thirty days and each month after. The Council bans the sale of arms to armed groups working in Darfur. It also backs African Union monitors and presses all sides to reach a political deal fast.
un-sc-res-156: Resolution 156 deals with a report from the Americas. The Council adopted it on 9 September 1960. The vote was nine to none. Poland and the Soviet Union abstained. The report came from the head of the Organization of American States. It passed on the Final Act of a meeting. Foreign ministers of the American republics had held that meeting. The Council takes note of the report. It notes one part in particular. The ministers had agreed on measures regarding the Dominican Republic.
un-sc-res-1656: Resolution 1656 dates to 2006 in the Council's output, preserved here from the official record via English Wikisource. Many of these texts are brief, built to answer one question at one meeting. The entry keeps the whole answer, preamble and decisions together, exactly as it entered the record of the world's security body.
un-sc-res-1756: Security Council Resolution 1756 is held in this collection as a Wikisource copy of the UN's official record. The act is one of hundreds in the Council's numbered series, each addressing the peace and security business of its moment. Its text follows the settled pattern, findings first and operative decisions after, and is preserved in full.
un-sc-res-1856:
Resolution 1856 gave the Council's ruling on the Democratic Republic of the Congo, adopted on 22 December 2008. Rebel attacks in North Kivu had driven huge crowds from their homes. The LRA struck in Orientale, and fighting flared again in Ituri. Regional summits in Nairobi had just named facilitators to help end the crisis.

The Council extends the mission, called MONUC, until 31 December 2009, with up to 19,815 troops. Its duties are ranked in strict order. Guarding civilians comes first, then disarming Congolese and foreign armed groups. The mission may inspect mines, trade routes, and markets to cut support drawn from stolen resources. Army training and border watching follow in the list.
un-sc-res-256:
Israeli air attacks on Jordan were condemned again by the Security Council on 16 August 1968. Two massive air attacks on Jordanian territory had been large in scale and planned with care. They broke resolution 248 (1968), which had condemned an earlier Israeli action and warned that grave breaches of the cease-fire could not be tolerated.

The Council reaffirmed resolution 248 (1968) and its warning of further, more effective steps. It deplored the loss of life and the heavy damage to property. It held that planned and repeated military attacks endanger the keeping of the peace. The new attacks were condemned as a flagrant breach of the United Nations Charter and of resolution 248. Israel was warned that any repeat would make the Council duly weigh its failure to comply. The text is one link in a chain of warnings over the Jordan front raids.
un-sc-res-456:
UNDOF's mandate on the Golan Heights ran to another renewal in late 1979. On 30 November 1979 the Security Council extended the force until 31 May 1980. The Secretary-General had reported on the mission. The decision keeps the standard three-part shape. The parties must apply resolution 338 without delay. A report on the term is due at its close.

China again took no part in the vote. The observers kept their posts in the separation zone. They had watched the line between Israel and Syria since 1974. The Council treated the renewal as steady maintenance of a working truce. Six months at a time, the mission rolled forward.
un-sc-res-56:
On 19 August 1948, the Council acted on Jerusalem by adopting Resolution 56. The city's truce kept breaking down. Reports from the UN mediator told of attacks by armed bands. The Council had set the truce terms a month earlier and now spelled out who bears blame.

The Council points both sides back to those terms. Each party answers for regular and irregular forces under its control. Each must use every means to stop truce breaches by people under its sway. Anyone who breaks the truce must face a speedy trial. Reprisal is no excuse for breaking the truce. No side may gain ground or favor by violating it.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Resolution 1156, adopted by the Security Council on 16 March 1998, responds to the restoration of democracy in Sierra Leone. It welcomes the return of the country's democratically elected president on 10 March 1998, after the military junta was driven from power. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminates with immediate effect the ban on selling petroleum and petroleum products to Sierra Leone imposed by Resolution 1132 (1997). The other 1132 prohibitions, including the arms embargo, are to be reviewed in light of developments and talks with Sierra Leone's government.

Nine years into the Somalia arms ban, the Council carved out two narrow gaps. On 19 June 2001, it adopted Resolution 1356 without dissent. It acted under Chapter VII. The ban, set by Resolution 733 in 1992, blocked all arms shipments to Somalia. Aid work in the country still went on, though.

The text first restates every state's duty to enforce the ban. It then frees two kinds of goods from the ban. Safety gear for personal use is one kind. Flak jackets and helmets for UN staff, press, and aid workers count here. Non-lethal gear for aid or guard use is the second kind. A sanctions panel must clear such gear in advance.

Foreign ministers meeting on 20 January 2003 issue a declaration on fighting terrorism, and the short resolution simply adopts the statement attached to it. The statement reflects the Council's shared position sixteen months after the September 2001 attacks.

Terrorism is called one of the gravest threats to peace and security, and all such acts are condemned without exception. The declaration warns of the growing danger that terrorists could gain nuclear, chemical, or biological materials, and of their use of modern technology and global finance. It demands stronger action to cut terrorist funding and to block links with organized crime, drug trafficking, and illegal arms sales.

Darfur's humanitarian catastrophe drives Resolution 1556, adopted on 30 July 2004. Janjaweed militia attacks, including rape and forced displacement, had put hundreds of thousands of lives at risk. Over a million people needed aid, and up to 200,000 refugees had fled into Chad. Sudan had promised to disarm the Janjaweed and open access to relief.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Sudan disarm the Janjaweed and bring their leaders to justice, with a progress report in 30 days and monthly after that. It warns of further measures if Sudan fails. It bans the sale or supply of arms and related gear to all non-governmental groups in North, South, and West Darfur. It backs the African Union's monitors and protection force and urges states to fund and equip them. It also extends the political mission for Sudan by 90 days, to 10 December 2004.

Regional action on the Dominican Republic is placed on the United Nations record on 9 September 1960. The Organization of American States had sent the Council the record of a meeting of American foreign ministers. At that meeting, the republics had agreed to apply measures against the Dominican Republic. The Council's short text simply takes note of that report and the agreement it described.

Georgia's observer mission, UNOMIG, is extended until 31 March 2006 in this text of 31 January 2006. The two-month renewal came just before a scheduled meeting of the Group of Friends on Georgia in Geneva on 2 and 3 February 2006. It kept the mission watching the Abkhazia ceasefire lines in place while the next stage of the peace process was prepared.

Congo's mission, MONUC, is extended until 31 December 2007 on 15 May 2007, with a defined mandate. Elections had completed the transition, but violence in Bas-Congo and Kinshasa in early 2007 showed how fragile security remained. Congo's government, it is stressed, bears the main duty for safety in its territory.

The mission's tasks centre on protecting civilians, supporting the new institutions, and helping reform the army and police. MONUC may use all necessary means, within its capacity and deployment areas, to carry out its mandate. The government is urged to extend state authority, disarm militias, and uphold the rule of law and human rights, as the mission begins planning for an eventual drawdown.

MONUC is extended at surge strength with the Kivus as its overriding priority in Resolution 1856, adopted on 22 December 2008. CNDP offensives had displaced masses of people in North Kivu. The LRA was attacking in Orientale. The temporary reinforcement authorized by Resolution 1843 (2008) was meant to let the mission reconfigure for civilian protection.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends MONUC until 31 December 2009 with up to 19,815 military personnel, 760 observers, 391 police, and 1,050 formed police personnel. Protection of civilians under imminent threat is its first mandate task, concentrated in the east. MONUC must deter attacks on the Goma and Nairobi processes and coordinate operations with Congolese brigades against local and foreign armed groups. It must cut their support from illicit resource trade and monitor the arms embargo with no-notice inspections, seizing violating weapons. Training the Congolese army and supporting democratic institutions complete the mandate.

Iraq's oil-revenue fund is given its final wind-down date in Resolution 1956, adopted on 15 December 2010. The Development Fund for Iraq and its monitoring board, created by Resolution 1483 (2003), had channelled Iraq's petroleum export proceeds under international oversight. Iraq's government said it would request no further extensions and had a transition plan; its prime minister's letter is annexed.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council terminates the Development Fund arrangements on 30 June 2011 and declares this the final extension. After that date, oil and gas export proceeds no longer go into the Fund. The Fund's proceeds transfer to the government's successor accounts. The monitoring board ends. The requirement that 5 percent of petroleum export proceeds go to the United Nations Compensation Fund established under Resolution 687 (1991) continues unchanged. The Secretary-General is to report every six months on the fund from 1 January 2012.

Resolution 256, adopted unanimously on 16 August 1968, condemns a fresh round of Israeli air attacks on Jordan. Both governments had written and spoken to the Council. Two massive air strikes on Jordanian territory had followed an earlier attack the Council condemned that March in resolution 248.

The Council reaffirmed that earlier text, with its warning that grave ceasefire violations cannot be tolerated. It deplored the loss of life and heavy property damage. It judged that planned, repeated attacks put peace itself at risk. And it condemned the new attacks as flagrant violations of the Charter, warning that a repetition would make the Council take Israel's defiance into account in earnest.

Resolution 356, adopted unanimously on 12 August 1974, recommends the Republic of Guinea-Bissau for United Nations membership. Its application, document S/11393, had been examined by the Council. The West African country had declared independence from Portugal in 1973 after an armed liberation struggle, and many states already recognized it before Lisbon did.

Recommending admission, the Council set up the General Assembly's vote to seat Guinea-Bissau. The step carried symbolic force: a movement that had fought Portuguese colonialism now took a place among member states. Portugal itself accepted Guinea-Bissau's independence weeks later, closing a war that had helped bring down the government in Lisbon that spring.

Fourteen members backed the Golan renewal in Resolution 456. China took no part in the vote. The decision came on 30 November 1979. The Secretary-General's report on the observer force, document S/13637, lay before the members. UNDOF's mandate between Israel and Syria was running out again.

The force won six more months, until 31 May 1980. The Council paired renewal with its familiar demand. Both parties had to carry out Resolution 338 of 1973 at once. The Secretary-General owed a closing report. It would cover events and steps toward that 1973 settlement. By 1979 these renewals were a settled rhythm. They kept a thin blue line in place while diplomacy stalled.

Jerusalem was a battlefield in August 1948, during the first Arab-Israeli war. A UN truce was in force on paper, but violations kept coming. The UN Mediator sent reports describing the disorder. Resolution 56, adopted on 19 August 1948, laid down strict rules for both sides.

Each party was made answerable for regular and irregular forces alike. Neither side could excuse a breach as payback. No one could use a truce violation to win military or political ground. Parties had to stop violations within their control. Offenders had to face speedy trials and punishment. The rules built on Resolution 54, the truce order passed that July.
